units.tr: CAELIUS SECUNDUS CURIO to the illustrious and magnificent lord Stanislaus Tencinus, Count Palatine of Kraków and Lublin, of Belz and Vededouia, Prefect, and to his noble son John: greetings and best wishes.

units.la: IDI statim, quum haec nostras Oratorias Explicationes ederem, TENCINI Comes Illustris, quid morosi quidam dicturi forent: quamquam parum tuta apud eos nostra existimatio futura esset. Nam quia aliquot alii uiri de literis praeclare meriti, suas in hunc Dialogum cogitationes euulgarunt, nos dicent non satis considerate fecisse, qui post tales uiros, aliquid in Oratorias partitiones edere uoluerimus: hoc est, Iliada post non dicā Homerū, sed Homeros conscripserimus. Quos etsi contenere, candidorum iudicio contentus, poteram: noluí tamen committere, ut eos sine responsione dimitterem. Quod cum fecce fecero, ad te Tencini sapientissime uenia: & cur hęc in tuo nomine apparere uoluerim, breuiter exponā. Aç primum illud dicam, me iis qui ante me lumē huic aureolo Dialogo pro sua quisq; portione & facultate afferre uoluerunt, & uiā ad eum intelligendū patefecerunt, gratiam habere: existimareq;, ab omnib. eloquentiæ studiosis habendā esse. Neq; enim is sum, qui ullius quāuis infimi laborē in re literaria contemnā: aliene uidelicet laudis minime inuidus, sed cādidus æstimator, nisi si quis sui tantū amans, aliorū molestus conteptor, quasi Suffenus alter extiterit. Huic enim, si quis fuerit, respondere, quod ille in senatu Romano dixit: Neminem alterius, qui fuę confidēret, uirtuti inuidere. Lacessere quenquam non cōsueui: lacessitus tero, quoad decet. Tum si quis est, qui di-ctū in se indemetius existimat esse, sic existimet: sciat respōnsum, nō dictū esse, ut ueteris pœtę uerbis utar.
units.tr: I thought at once, Count Tencinus, when I was publishing these Oratorical Explanations, about what some peevish men would say, though our reputation among them is hardly likely to be safe. For since several other men who have deserved well of letters have made their own thoughts on this Dialogue public, they will say that I have not acted with sufficient consideration in wishing to publish something on the Oratorical Partitions after such men: that is, as if, after not Homer but a crowd of Homers, I had written an Iliad. Although I could have despised them, content with the judgment of fair-minded readers, I did not wish to let them go without a reply. Since I have done this, I now turn to you, most wise Tencinus, asking your pardon, and I will briefly explain why I wished these pages to appear under your name. And first I will say this: I am grateful to all those who, before me, wished to bring light to this golden Dialogue, each according to his share and ability, and who opened the way to understanding it; and I believe all students of eloquence ought to hold them in such regard. For I am not one who scorns anyone's labour in literary matters; I am certainly not envious of another's praise, but a fair judge of it, unless someone is a lover of himself alone and a troublesome despiser of others, who has risen up as another Suffenus. To such a man, if there is one, I would answer what he said in the Roman senate: that no one who trusts in his own virtue envies another's. I am not accustomed to provoke anyone; when provoked, I answer as is fitting. So if there is anyone who thinks that he has been insulted beyond measure, let him think this: let him know that it is a reply, not an insult, to borrow the words of an old poet.

units.la: Sunt, certè sunt, quemadmodū & ratio docet, & ueteres testātur, gentes aliæ aliis perspicaciores, propter cœli primùm, deinde humorū temperationē: nullius tamē nationis cuncti homines tam stupidi inueniuntur, quín, si excolantur multū, in quauis re cōsequi possint. Attici, aliíq; Græci fere, propter cœli bonitatem, semper excelleti ingenio habiti sunt: unde & ab eis omnes fermè disciplinæ, quas modò colimus, emanarūt. contra Bœotij, in crassiore cœlo nati, lo cum dederūt prouerbio, Bœoticum ingeniū: & ut Horat. ait, Bœotū in crasso iurares aere natū: cū tamē ea gens Pindarū & Plutarchū, alterum poetā, eximiū philosophū alterū, & Epaminondā belli ducē præstantissimū dederit. Atq; idem de reliquis gentibus intelligendū est, eo acutiores, atq; ad omnes disciplinas aptiores esse, quo puriore, tēperatioreq; cœlo utantur: stupidiores fere, quo crassiore: nō ob animi uim quidē il-lam, Iam, uel maiorem uel minore, quæ ea dem est semper, quod ad ipsius natura attinet, sed propter corporis temperationem diuersam, quā animus sequitur: ut Galenus ea de re edito opere perspicue ostēdit. Hac naturarū, morū, gentiū uarietate teneat Orator oportet, sine quibus nō satis callide & perite (ut Cicero ait) poterit dicere. Hæc igitur ratio, quæ testem tota antiquitate habet, tantū apud me ualet, ut nullā gentē, nullā natio ne, nullū homine contemnendū putem: cū præsertim sciā, Deū huius diuersitatis autorē, & naturarū tēpera torem esse. Nec idcirco hæc scripsimus, quod aliorū conatus, operasq; irritas esse putemus: sed ut, quoniā in eadē arena uersamur, Spartam & ipsi nostrā pro nostra uīrili exornemus. Quod si nemini post alios scribere in aliquē autorē cōmentarios licet, cur post Aphrodiseū & Auerroem, Simpliciū, Themistiū, Philoponi, Suessani, Fabri, Schegkiū, Vicomercati, aliorūqș cōmentarij in Aristotelē legūt? Et ut ad Ciceronē ueniamus, cur in hasce Oratorias partitiones (ut alia eius omittā opera) post Georgiū Vallā, & Strebæū, Latomus, Sturmius, Hegēdorphinus, Melanthon, Camerarius, Vitus Amerpachius, suas cogitationes sensaqș protulerūt? Certe eadē causę ferē (quas honestas fuisse nō dubito) quæ illos, nos etiā ad scribendū excitarūt. Explicādę nobis fuerūt Oratoriæ partitiones: dum cura & cogitatione in hoc munus incumbimus, alia ex aliis, ut fit, in mentē uenerūt, neqș enim erant à nobis aliorū commentarij tantū recitandi, sed nostr nobis genius sequendus: ex eis, quātum quoqș modo uidebatur, sumendum: alia probanda, alia reijcienda, alia corrigenda, explicanda, confirmāda, differēda, atqș in certū ordinē digerēda: afferenda etiam noua fortassis aliqua: & ex ijsdem fontibus, e quib. ipse hauserat Cicero, hauriēda: atqș
units.tr: There are, certainly there are, as reason teaches and the ancients testify, nations more keen than others, first because of the climate and then because of the temperament of the humours. Yet no nation's people are found so dull that they cannot achieve something in any field if they are cultivated well enough. The Athenians and the other Greeks, on account of the mildness of their climate, were always regarded as excellent in talent, and nearly all the disciplines we now cultivate came forth from them. On the other hand, the Boeotians, born under a thicker sky, gave their name to a proverb, "Boeotian wit," and, as Horace says, you would swear they were born in the thick air of Boeotia. Yet that same people produced Pindar and Plutarch, the one a poet and the other an outstanding philosopher, and Epaminondas, the most distinguished general of war. The same must be understood of the other nations: the purer and more temperate the sky they live under, the sharper they are and the better suited to all the disciplines; the thicker the sky, the duller they generally are. This is not because of the power of the mind itself, which, greater or smaller, is always the same as far as its nature is concerned, but because of the different temperament of the body, which the mind follows. Galen shows this clearly in a work he published on the subject. The orator must grasp this variety of natures, customs and peoples, without which, as Cicero says, he will not be able to speak cleverly and skilfully. This reasoning, which has all of antiquity as its witness, carries such weight with me that I think no nation, no people, no individual should be despised. I know especially that God is the author of this diversity and the moderator of natures. Nor did I write these things because I think the efforts and labours of others are in vain. Rather, since we work on the same field, I want us also to adorn our own Sparta to the best of our ability. If no one may write commentaries on any author after others, why do we read the commentaries on Aristotle by Alexander of Aphrodisias and Averroes, Simplicius, Themistius, Philoponus, Suessanus, Faber, Schegk, Vicomercato, and others? And to come to Cicero: why, after Giorgio Valla, Strebaeus, Latomus, Sturm, Hegendorf, Melanchthon, Camerarius and Vitus Amerbach, did they put forth their own thoughts and views on these Oratorical Partitions (to pass over his other works)? Surely nearly the same causes, which I do not doubt were honourable, that moved them also moved us to write. The Oratorical Partitions had to be explained by us. While we applied our care and thought to this task, one thing and another came to mind, as happens. We were not merely to recite the commentaries of others, but to follow our own genius. From those commentaries we were to take what seemed useful in any way; some things we were to approve, some reject, some correct, explain, confirm or defer, and arrange them in a certain order; perhaps also to bring forward some new points, and to draw from the same sources from which Cicero himself had drawn.

units.la: œ 4 atq; ad cosdē fontes reuocanda. Cicero quoq; ipse, ex Cicerone (quæ optima interpretandi ratio est) explicandus. Hæc aut similia, fortasse illos, nos quidem ad scribendum impulerunt: quæ si minus præstitimus, præstare certe conati sumus: ac speramus æquos homines, & candidos, peritosq; ingeniorum æstimatores, nostros conatus in bonam partem accepturos. De adolescentibus autem, quibus hæc elaborauimus, ita præclarè sentio, ut existimē illos etiam nobis gratiam non parvam habituros. Iam superest, ut cur hæc edamus, & tuū illustre nomen præferre uelimus, indicemus; ne quid sine ratione suscepti à nobis esse uideatur. Cum ego iamprídem Polonam gentem, non ineptis aut leuibus de causis diligere & colere cœpissem, factū est, ut etiam quorundam interiore notitia, aut literis, aut consuetudine domestica contracta, uterer. Quare tanta facta est beneuolentiæ, obseruantiéq; accessio, ut hãc mihi aliquo publico monumento testandam esse putarem. Hinc factum est, ut primarios quosdã istius amplissimi Regni uiros literis nostris, atq; adeo Regē ipsum appellauerimus, eisq; lucubrationes quasdam nostras commendauerimus. Quod autem hactenus idē erga te non tentauerim, haud equidē factū est, quo nobis minus notus esses, aut quo te reliquis proceribus minoris facerē: sed quòd nulla mihi dum idonea occasio oblata uideretur. Neq; enim decebat me, hominem externum, ac tuis fortassis auribus inaudi tum, in tuũ conspectū temere irrumpere. Nam quod ad tui tuorumq; maiorum notitiā attinet, satis mihi cum fama illustri, tum uestrorum annalium lectione, Tenciniorū familia antiquissima, abipso Andrea Cracouiensi Palatino, uiro belli & pacis artibus magno, & Polonici senatus tum facile princípe, nota est. Huius uirtute atq; in patriam charitate imitati posteri, Nauoius, Stanislaus, Nicolaus, & Ioannes, res magnas, cum sibi gloriosas, tu Reip. salutares gefserunt. Inter quos Ioannis fides, eloquetiaq; maxime enituit. Nam qui in eligendo rege, studijs partiu omnia essent perturbata, & plerique deteriora consilia sequerentur: unus Ioannes Tencinius, oratione sua omnium mentes voluntatesq; conuertit, atq; ad saniora maturioraq; consilia reuocauit. Iniecta enim deliberandi ac decernendi mora, eo res adducta est tandem, ut Heduigis regni Vngari ci heres, puella lectissima, in regnum Polonicum accersita, Iagelloni magno Lituanorum Duci nuberet: quo sancto felicique conubio factum est, ut & Lituania antea falsorum deorum superstitioni assueta, Christianis initiaretur sacris: & tria potentissima regna coniungerentur: & Iagellonis, quae etiamnum feliciter regnat, heroica progenies, Sarmatarum imperium obtineret: qua nulla potuit omni regia laude augustior aut clarior inueniri. tantum unius hominis Tencinij prudens ualuit oratio. Omitto quę tum illi ipsi, tum alij maio res tui pro patria & religione contra externos hostes, ac Turcas praesertim, gesserunt, & sustinuerunt: ne non praefationem, aut epistolā, sed historiam uelle scribere uideamur. De te quoq;, qui Tencinios omnes tuos pietate ac dignitate superas, cū sit mihi nota modestia, grauitasq; tua, nūc reticebo. Quę cum ita sint, non ignoratione tui, ut dixi, tuæq; claritatis, nihil ad te, sed occasione, tempusq; obseruans, in hunc distuli diem, mei erga te animi significatio nem: quæ mihi non incōmoda oblata est. Nam cum proxima hyeme filium tuū charissimū Ioannē in Gallia mitteres, ut & ibi animi cultū aliquē caperet: & mores naturasq; hominū uarias pnosceret (quod ad prudentiam comparandā, & augendam, dam, non parũ habet ponderis) contigit ut hac iter faceret. Habebat autem à te comites datos, uiros nobiles, prudētes, & doctos. inter quos eminet Martinus Suiecitius, uir cor datus & grauis: quē tu & filij moribus, & totí eius familiæ præfecisti. Cũ aũt eos in hac urbe esse, mihi renuncíatũ esset, generosum filiũ tuũ (ut decuit) salutatũ ueni: à quo tāta humanitate acceptus fui, ut in eo familiæ uestræ antiquā magnificentiā recognoscerē. Hic ego, dũ uariè fermocinamur, cuí uiro, quàm moderato, quàm perspicaci, quanto vsu rerum perito, filiũ tuum commiseris, facilè perspexi. Aderat etiam inter cæteros Andreas Siemitius, iuuenis pererudītus, à quo filius tuus literis & moribus instituitur. Quid de filio ipso tuo dicam? quanta indole, quanta spe, quàm generoso animo mihi uisus est? qua attentione auscultabat nos colloquētes? qua modestia & oris suauitate rogatus re-spon-
units.tr: and to lead them back to those same sources. Cicero himself, too, must be explained from Cicero, which is the best method of interpretation. These or similar considerations perhaps moved those men to write, and they moved us. If we have not accomplished much, we have at least tried our best to accomplish it, and we hope that fair and candid men, and skilled judges of talent, will receive our efforts in a good light. As for the young men for whom we have laboured these pages, I think so highly of them that I believe they too will be very grateful to us. It remains to say why I want to publish these things and to put your illustrious name at the front, so that nothing may appear to have been undertaken without reason. I had long ago begun to love and cherish the Polish nation, not for trivial or foolish reasons, and it came about that, through a closer acquaintance with some of its people, whether through letters or through domestic intimacy, I came to enjoy their company. Thus my goodwill and esteem grew so much that I thought I should bear witness to it in some public monument. Hence it happened that I addressed some of the chief men of that most distinguished kingdom in my writings, and even the King himself, and I commended certain of my labours to them. As for why I had not made the same attempt with you until now, that was not because you were less known to me or because I valued you less than the other nobles. It was because no suitable occasion seemed to have offered itself. For it was not fitting that I, a foreigner, and perhaps unheard by your ears, should rush carelessly into your presence. As for your own knowledge and that of your ancestors, the Tencini family, most ancient, is well known to me both from its illustrious fame and from reading your annals, and from Andrew himself, Palatine of Kraków, a man great in the arts of war and peace, and then easily the leader of the Polish senate. Following his virtue and his love of country, his descendants, Nawoj, Stanislaus, Nicholas and John, performed great deeds, glorious for themselves and salutary for the commonwealth. Among them the faith and eloquence of John shone most brightly. When, in choosing a king, all things were thrown into confusion by factions, and most men were following worse counsels, John Tencinus alone turned the minds and wills of all by his speech and recalled them to sounder and more mature counsels. For once deliberation and decision were delayed, the affair was at last brought to this point: Hedwig, the heiress of the kingdom of Hungary, a most choice maiden, was summoned to the Polish kingdom and married Jagiełło, the great Duke of the Lithuanians. By this holy and happy marriage it came about that Lithuania, hitherto accustomed to the superstition of false gods, was initiated into Christian rites; that three very powerful kingdoms were joined; and that the heroic line of Jagiełło, which still reigns happily, obtained the empire of the Sarmatians, than which no more august or illustrious royal glory could be found. So much did the prudent speech of one man, Tencinus, prevail. I pass over what he himself and others of your house did and endured for their country and religion against foreign enemies, and especially the Turks, lest I seem to be writing not a preface or a letter but a history. About you too, who surpass all the Tencini in piety and dignity, I will now say nothing, since I know your modesty and gravity. Since these things are so, I have not neglected you, as I said, nor thought you unworthy of notice, but I have watched for an occasion and time, and have put off until this day the declaration of my goodwill towards you, which has now offered itself to me opportunely. For last winter, when you sent your dearest son John to France, so that he might also acquire some cultivation of mind there and learn the varied characters and natures of men, which has considerable weight for acquiring and increasing prudence, it happened that he passed through this city. He had been given companions by you: noble, prudent and learned men, among whom Martin Suiecicius stands out, a man of heart and gravity, whom you placed in charge of your son's conduct and of his whole household. When I was informed that they were in this city, I went to greet your noble son, as was fitting. I was received by him with such kindness that I recognised in him the ancient magnificence of your family. Here, while we talked on various topics, I easily perceived to what a moderate, perceptive and experienced man you had entrusted your son. Among the others was also present Andrew Siemiński, a very learned young man, by whom your son is taught in letters and manners. What shall I say of your son himself? What fine character, what hope, what a noble spirit he showed me! With what attention he listened to us as we talked! With what modesty and sweetness of countenance he answered when questioned! It was truly wonderful to me that a youth of that age should speak so elegantly and aptly.

units.la: s spondebat: mihi certè permirū fuit, ea ætate adolescentulum tam scitè atq; appositè loquentè audire. Sed duæ fūt, ut ego arbitror, eius rei causæ ortus ipse, & educatio. Nam ut Horat. ait, Fortes creātur fortibus, & bonis.
units.tr: I was truly astonished to hear a youth of that age speaking so skilfully and so aptly. But there are two causes of this, as I think: his birth and his upbringing. For as Horace says, Brave men are born of brave and good men.

units.la: Vtrūq; diuina prouidentia filio tuo contigit, ut & te parentem omni genere laudis cumulatum haberet, & pueritiæ suæ rectores atq; moderatores tales nancisceretur, quales eius egregia ac generosa indoles poscit: ut quod bonum est in natura, liberali educatione, doctrinaq; augeretur, & cōfirmaretur. In Galliā igitur, uti à te iussi erant, profecti sunt: quò etiā paulo post meus filius Horatius medicinæ, quā in Italia didicerat, usu confirmādæ causa profectus est: quiq; ab eodē filio tuo honesta conditione inuitatus, apud eum Lutetiæ agit. Ita factū est, ut hac inter nos quasi necessitudine, sermonib. & literis ultro citroq; missis contra‐ cta, uiam mihi ad te scribendi patefactam uideam. Cogitanti igitur mihi de aliquo literario munere ad te mittedo, ecce commodu nostrae hae Oratorie explicationes occurrerunt, quas filio tuo utiles esse putaui: si modo per te, ac tuis auspiciis, illas acciperet. Aequum enim est, ut ea qui bus utendu est filio, a parentis prudentia comprobentur: ut maiorem apud eum autoritate inueniant. Faciam igitur, quod utriusq; naturae charitatisq; necessitas postulat, ut ambos appellem: neq; eos mea oratione disiungam, quos tantis uinculis Deus Naturaq; coniunxit: praesertim cum hic pater & filius de doctrina dicendi inter se colloquatur. Eloquetiae praecepta sunt, quae principum uirorum & nobilium est propria: cuius quanta uis sit exprimere, quantaq; iis qui sint eam consequuti, dignitatem afferat, neq; pro‐ positum nobis est hocloco, neq; necessariûm:id enim aliis in locis fecimus. Hoc uerò sine ulla dubitatione cõfirmauerím,Eloquentiâ unam quandâ de summmis uirtutibus esse, quæ scientiam cõplexa rerum,sensa mentis & cõsilia sic uerbis explicat, ut eos qui audiát, quocũq; íncubuerit,possit impellere: quę quo maior est uis, hoc est magis probitate íungenda, summaq; prudētía: quarum uirtutũ expertibus,si dicêdí copiam tradiderímus,(ut uere Cicero dixit) nõ eos quídé oratores effecerímus, sed furetíb. quędâ arma dederímus. Hanc íneq; cogitādí pronũciandíq; ratione,uimq; dicēdi, ueteres sapietiam nominabãt. Hinc illi Lycurgi, hinc Pittaci,hinc Solones, atque ab hac similitudine Corũcaní nostri,Fabricij,Catones,Scipiones, Lælij, alisq; in aliis gentíb.fuerũt. Verũ hoc. cõmunc nomen posteritas eripuit; sapienterq; sententiendí, & ornatè dicendi scientiâ,re coherentes,separa- uit, tit. Hinc dissidium illud extitit quæ fi linguę atqꝫ cordis, absurdū sane & inutile, & reprehendendū, ut alij nos sapere, alij dicere docerent. ab hoc dissidio abhorres Cicero noster, nõ modo ipse scientia rerū cum dicendi arte, quasi Mineruā cum Mercurio, copulauit: uerum etiā in omnib. oratoris libris censuit esse faciendū. Idcirco & in hoc ipso Dialogo, tam amplam materiē, quāta quæstionis nomine continetur, oratori subiecit: id quod hoscē cōmentarios legēs, facile, quo est ingenij acumine, intelliget filius tuus: cuius institutioni hęc ipsa tanqꝫ adminicula, incitamē taqꝫ submittimus, atqꝫ in tui Palatini nominis tutelā emittimus. Oramus autem, ne muneris paruitate, sed præstā tē mea in te, filiiqꝫ tuū uoluntate spectes: existimesqꝫ te hic homine habere, qui Tenciniorū nomē illustre, summa fide, obseruatia, charitate colat. Vale. Basileæ, Cal. Sept. Anno à Christo nato 1556.
units.tr: Your son received both of these gifts through divine providence: he had you as a father, heaped with every kind of praise, and he found tutors and guardians of his boyhood such as his outstanding and noble nature required, so that what was good in his nature would be increased and strengthened by liberal education and learning. Accordingly, they set off for France, as you had ordered. My son Horatius also set off there a little later, to strengthen by practice the medicine he had learned in Italy; he was invited by your son on an honourable arrangement and practises medicine with him at Paris. So it has come about that, through this kind of bond between us, formed by conversations and letters sent back and forth, I see a way opened for me to write to you. As I was thinking about sending you some literary gift, these Oratorical Explanations of ours came to mind, which I thought would be useful to your son, provided he received them through you and under your auspices. For it is right that the things a son is to use should be approved by his parent's prudence, so that they may carry greater authority with him. I shall therefore do what the necessity of both nature and affection requires: I address you both, and I shall not separate in my address those whom God and Nature have joined by such strong bonds, especially since this father and son are conversing with each other about the art of speaking. The precepts of eloquence belong to leading and noble men. How great a power it is, and how much dignity it brings to those who have attained it, is neither our purpose here nor necessary to explain, for we have done so in other places. This much, however, I would affirm without any doubt: eloquence is one of the highest virtues, which, embracing knowledge of things, expresses the feelings and counsels of the mind in words so that it can move those who hear it wherever it has been directed. The greater its power, the more it must be joined with integrity and the highest prudence. If we were to hand over the abundance of speech to those who lack these virtues, then (as Cicero rightly said) we would not make them orators, but would be giving weapons to madmen. The ancients called this combination of the method of thinking and speaking, and the power of speech, wisdom. Hence came those men of Lycurgus, of Pittacus, of Solon, and by this same likeness our own Coruncanius, Fabricius, the Catos, the Scipios, Laelius, and others among other peoples. But later posterity took this common name away, and separated what belongs together, the knowledge of wise thinking and that of ornate speaking. From this arose that split between tongue and heart, absurd, useless and to be condemned, so that some taught us to be wise and others taught us to speak. Our Cicero, abhorring this division, not only joined knowledge of things with the art of speaking, as if joining Minerva with Mercury, but also judged that this must be done in all the books on the orator. Hence in this very Dialogue too he set before the orator a material as broad as the subject of the question contains. Your son, reading these commentaries, will easily understand this with the keenness of his intellect. To his education we send these aids, as it were as supports and incentives, and we put them out under the protection of your name as Palatine. I beg you, however, not to look at the smallness of the gift, but at my goodwill towards you and your son, and to think that you have here a man who cherishes the illustrious name of the Tenczynskis with the greatest loyalty, respect and affection. Farewell. Basel, 1 September, in the year of Christ's birth 1556.

units.la: CAELII S. C. IN M. T. CICERONIS PARTI- TIONES ORATORIAS EXPLICATIONUM LIBER PRIMUS.
units.tr: CAELII S. C. IN M. T. CICERONIS PARTITIONES ORATORIAS EXPLICATIONUM LIBER PRIMUS.

units.la: INSCRIPTIONIS EXPLICA- TIO: id est, cur Partitiones appellatae, & de Methodo pauca.
units.tr: Explanation of the Title: that is, why they were called Partitions, and a few words on the Method.

units.la: Artitiones appellauit Cicero, hunc de arte Rhetorica absolutissimum dialogum, propterea quòd artem ea methodo tradere proposuit, quæ διαίρεσις siue διαίρεσις appellatur: in qua sumpta artis definitione, à summis generibus ad ultimas usq; partes & formas progreditur: ex quibus demum tota ars constituitur. quæ ratio docendi cõmodissima est, & ad recordandum aptissima: idcirco à Platone ipso, itemq; Cicerone & Galeno usitata. Est autem Methodus, autore Galeno, uniuersalis quedam uia & ratio, omnium singularium eiusdem generis, qua omnia recte inueniuntur, & inuenta approbantur: quæ uero perperam habent, redarguuntur. Nam qui methodo utitur, uerba in primis, quibus utendum est, si obscura sint, explicat, atq; distinguit: res definit, definitas diuidit: à summis b mis usq; generibus, ad infimas formas, ubi opus est resoluit, componitq; : rei proportiones & causas inquirit: argumenta rationes que, ex natura, causis & effectibus rerum, ex iis denique quae aut sensibus aut rationi perspicua sunt, colligit: neque unquam quiescit, donec id, de quo quaeritur, ad sua principia fontesq; reuocauerit. Differt autem methodus ab arte, ut scientia ab actione, siue ut scire & docere. Est enim ars, eorum quae natura fiunt, notatio quaedam, & obseruatio: siue praeceptorum ad unum aliquem utilem & laudabilem finem coaccruatio. Methodus autem, artis est dispositio, atque tractatio: siue communis quaedam recte docendi ratio. Neque est hic requirenda illa subtilis distinctio partium & formarum, quae a nostro Cicerone in Topicis, atque item ab aliis traditur: propterea quod illic subtiliter distinguuntur, ut quot modis argumenta, & ex quot locis eruenda sint, intelligatur. extra autem illam rationem locorum, partes, tum pro formis, tum etiam pro ipsis partibus & membris usurpantur: & multis in locis Ciceronis inueniet, qui uolet. Ergo quoniam partiendi & diuidendi uia artem dicendi tradere instituit, in qua non solum formae, sed etiam partes cadunt: a communi, co que commodissimo nomine, Partitiones appellauit.
units.tr: Cicero called this most complete dialogue on the art of rhetoric Partitiones (Divisions), because he proposed to teach the art by that method which is called diairesis or diaeresis [διαίρεσις]: in which, after the definition of the art has been taken, he proceeds from the highest genera down to the last parts and forms, and from these at length the whole art is constituted. This way of teaching is most convenient and most apt for remembering; for this reason it was used by Plato himself, and likewise by Cicero and Galen. Now, method, according to Galen, is a certain universal way and reasoning, by which all the singulars of the same kind are rightly discovered, and, once discovered, are approved; and those things which are wrongly held are refuted. For he who uses method first explains and distinguishes the words he must use, if they are obscure; he defines things, and divides the defined; from the highest genera down to the lowest forms he resolves and composes, where need requires; he inquires into the proportions and causes of a thing; he gathers arguments and reasons from the nature, causes and effects of things, and finally from those things which are evident to the senses or to reason; and he never rests until he has traced back the matter under inquiry to its principles and sources. Now method differs from art as science differs from action, or as knowing differs from teaching. For art is a certain notation and observation of those things which are done by nature, or a gathering together of precepts toward one useful and praiseworthy end. Method, however, is the arrangement and handling of an art, or a common and right way of teaching. Nor is that subtle distinction of parts and forms required here, which is handed down by our Cicero in the Topics, and likewise by others; because there they are distinguished subtly, so that it may be understood in how many ways arguments are to be drawn out, and from how many places. Apart from that account of places, however, "parts" are used both for forms and for the parts and members themselves; and whoever wishes will find this in many places in Cicero. Therefore, since by the way of dividing and partitioning he has undertaken to teach the art of speaking, in which not only forms but also parts fall, he called it, from the common and most convenient name, Partitions.

units.la: Personae huiusce dialogi sunt, Pater & Filius. Filio partes interrogandi dantur, patri respondendi. & quoniam in Dialogis decorum maximè spectatur, idcirco filio attribuitur reuerentia: patri verò authoritas docendi. nam decorum illud potissimum in personis uersatur, in quibus aetas, sexus, genus, patria, uita, institutum, natura, mores, consideranturEt quoniam dialogi, omne dicendi genus admittunt, summum & medium & infimum: in hoc Partitionum dialogo, subtile tenuéq; illud dicendi genus elucet, cuiusmodi esse debet in hac ratione docendi: in qua omnia tenuiter & subtiliter, tum exquiruntur, tum etiam distribuuntur. Atq; haec de scribendi genere.
units.tr: The persons of this dialogue are a Father and a Son. The Son is given the role of questioning, the Father that of answering. And since in dialogues propriety is chiefly observed, therefore reverence is assigned to the son, but authority of teaching to the father. For that propriety lies chiefly in the persons, in whom age, sex, birth, country, way of life, calling, nature and manners are considered. And since dialogues admit every kind of speaking, the high, the middle and the low, in this dialogue of the Partitions that subtle and plain kind of speaking shines forth, such as ought to be in this method of teaching, in which everything is inquired into and also distributed finely and subtly. And so much concerning the style of writing.

units.la: Nunc pauca de totius operis summa distributione dicenda sunt. Totum harum Partitionum opus tres habet primas partes: principium, oratoriarum partitionum explicationem, & totius operis conclusionem. Principium duobus capitibus continetur, petitione & concessione. Expositio praeceptorum tribus: officio oratoris, oratione, quaestione: quas partes secuti, tres fecimus Explicationum libros: quarum rursum multae & variae sunt partes. Superest Conclusio, cuius capita & membra suo indicabimus loco.
units.tr: Now a few words must be said about the overall distribution of the whole work. The whole of these Partitions has three main parts: the beginning, the explanation of the rhetorical partitions, and the conclusion of the whole work. The beginning is contained in two chapters, the request and the concession. The exposition of the precepts in three: the duty of the orator, the speech, and the question; following these parts, we have made three books of Explanations, of which again there are many and varied parts. There remains the Conclusion, whose chapters and members we will indicate in their proper place.

units.la: PARTITIONVM Exordium.
units.tr: The Exordium of the Partitions.

units.la: Ciccro. Filius.
units.tr: Cicero the son.

units.la: Tudeo mí pater Latinè ex te audire ea, quæ mí-hi tu de ratione dicendi Græcè tradidisti: si modo tibi est ociû, & si uis.
units.tr: I would like, my father, to hear from you in Latin what you have taught me in Greek about the method of speaking, if you have leisure and are willing.

units.la: C. PAT. An est, mí Cicero, quod ego malím, quàm te quàm doctíssimum esse? Ocium autem primũ, & summum est, quoniã aliquando Roma exeundi potestas data est: deinde, ista tua studia uel maximis occupationibus meis anteferrem libenter. C. FIL. Vis'ne igitur, ut tu me Græcè soles ordine interrogare, sic ego te uicissim eisdem de reb. Latíne interrogem? C. P. Sanè, si placet. Sic enim & ego te meminisse intelligã, quæ accepisti: & tu ordine audies, quæ requiris.
units.tr: C. PAT. Mt Cicero, what could I want more than for you to become as learned as possible? Leisure is first and foremost something I value, since the chance to leave Rome has at last been granted to me. Besides, I would gladly put those studies of yours ahead of even my heaviest duties. C. FIL. Would you then allow me, just as you usually question me in Greek in order, to question you in turn about the same matters in Latin? C. P. Certainly, if you like. In this way I will know that you remember what you have learned, and you will hear in order the things you ask about.

units.la: C. F. Studeo mi pater. ) Quatuor sunt, ut Crassus apud Ciceronē lib.1. de Orat. docet, quæ ad
units.tr: C. F. I am eager to learn, father. There are four things, as Crassus teaches in Cicero, book 1 of De Oratore, that are required for attaining eloquence.

units.la: ) Quatuor sunt, ut Crassus apud Ciceronē lib.1. de Orat. docet, quæ ad eloquentiam assequendam requiruntur: Natura, siue ingenium primum: deinde studium, siue ardor animi: tertium, ars: quartū, exercitatio. quorum duo priora in nobis esse debent, ingenium ut delicet, & discendi cupiditas: reliqua duo extrinsecus assumuntur, nimirum doctrina & exercitatio. Sed quoniam voluntas & studiū, etiam in mediocrib. naturis & ingenijs multum possunt: idcirco Cicero filius, studium & desiderium discendi profitetur, artem uero à patre audire vult: exercitationem post adhibiturus, ubi artis praecepta ordine comprehenderit. Haec quidem quatuor, ut dixi, Crassus. Antonius autem lib. 2. de Oratore tria tantum facit, ut etiā Fabius Orat. instit. lib. 3. cap. 5. Et sic ad inueniendum, inquit Antonius, in dicendo tria sunt: acumen, deinde ratio (quam licet, si uolumus, appellemus artem) tertium diligentia, non possum equidem non ingenio primas concedere: sed tamē ipsum ingenium, diligentia etiā extarditate incitat. Et paulo post: Inter ingenium quidem & diligentiam perpaululum loci reliquū est arti. Ars demonstrat tantum, ubi quaeras, atq; ubi sit illud quod studeas inuenire. reliqua, quae sunt in cura, attentione animi, cogitatione, uigilantia, assiduitate, labore, comprehendar uno uerbo, quo saepe iam usi sumus, diligentia: qua una uirtute, omnes uirtutes reliquae continentur. Sed hic studium dium & uoluntate, ut etiam exercitationem, diligentiæ nomine cõplexus est. Cornificius autem ab ijs omnib. diuersa tradit lib. 1. Rhetorices: Omnia, inquit, tribus modis assequi poterimus, arte, imitatione, et exercitatione. Mox singula definitionib. explicat: Ars est, inquit, quæ dat certã uiā rationemq; dicēdi. Imitatio est, qua impellimur diligēti ratione, ut aliquorū similes in dicēdo esse ualeamus. Exercitatio est, assiduus vsus, cõfuetudoq; dicēdi. Hic neq; natura fiue ingenij habet, qua quis aptus ad aliquid fit: neq; studij ardore ue animi, quo incitetur quis ad præclarum opus & laborē: neq; illi imitationis meminerūt. Sed intelligendū est, naturam & studiū ab eloquentiæ studioso adferenda. nam donari ab arte, magistro ue, nō pofsunt: sunt enim illa naturæ dona diuinitus insita. Reliqua doceri & tradi possunt. Itaq; illa superiora requirit in oratore Cicero, non datut admoneat, sine illis oratorem fieri nō posse. Cornificius aut, quæ sui muneris sunt, proponit: & tria quæ tum in discētis, tum docentis sunt facultate, enumerat, omissis ijs quæ in deliberatione non cadūt: nec si nō adsunt, dari à quoquā mortali possunt. Quod autē addit Imitationem, quam alij seorsim non posuerunt, eam Quintilianus arti subiicit: alij exercitationi, siue diligentiæ. Atq; ita unusquisq; suum institutum secutus est, non sine ratione
units.tr: There are four things, as Crassus teaches in Cicero, book 1 of De Oratore, that are required for attaining eloquence: first, nature or natural talent; second, zeal, or ardour of mind; third, art; fourth, practice. Of these, the first two ought to be in us: that is, natural talent and a desire to learn. The other two are acquired from outside, namely learning and practice. But since will and zeal count for a great deal even in people of ordinary nature and talent, the son Cicero professes his zeal and desire to learn, while he wants to hear the art from his father, intending to add practice afterwards, once he has grasped the precepts of the art in order. Crassus gives these four, as I said. Antonius, in book 2 of De Oratore, makes only three, as does Fabius in Orat. instit. book 3, chapter 5. "So for invention in speaking," says Antonius, "there are three things: keenness; then method, which we may, if we wish, call art; third, diligence. I cannot of course deny that talent comes first, but talent itself is spurred on by diligence and by industry." And shortly after: "Between talent and diligence there is only a very small place left for art. Art only shows where you should look and where that thing lies which you are eager to find. The rest, which concern care, attention of mind, thought, watchfulness, constancy, and toil, are all comprised in one word, which we have often used already: diligence. In this one virtue all the other virtues are contained." But here he has included zeal and will, and also practice, under the name of diligence. Cornificius, however, in book 1 of his Rhetoric, hands down something quite different from all of these: "We shall be able," he says, "to attain everything in three ways: by art, by imitation, and by exercise." Then he explains each by a definition: "Art," he says, "is what gives a sure path and method of speaking. Imitation is that by which we are moved, through careful method, to be able to be like some people in speaking. Exercise is constant use and habit of speaking." Here he has neither natural talent, that is, the aptitude by which someone is suited to something, nor the ardour of mind by which someone is roused to a noble work and toil, nor does he mention that imitation. But it should be understood that nature and zeal must be brought by the student of eloquence himself, for they cannot be given by art or by a teacher; those natural gifts are implanted by God. The rest can be taught and handed on. So Cicero requires those earlier qualities in the orator, not as giving them, but to warn that without them no orator can be made. Cornificius sets out what belongs to his own office, and lists the three things that depend on the ability of both learner and teacher, leaving out those things which do not fall within deliberation and which, if they are absent, cannot be given by any mortal. As for his addition of imitation, which others did not list separately, Quintilian places it under art, others under practice or diligence. And so each has followed his own plan, not without reason

units.la: nc ne tamen. Vt aut ad Ciceronē filiū reuertamur, is uehementer patris animum sibi conciliat, dum suum discēdi studium & ardorem patri exponit.
units.tr: Nevertheless, to return to Cicero the son: he greatly wins over his father's heart while he sets out to his father his own eagerness and ardour for learning.

units.la: Quæ mihi de ratione dicēdi Græcè tradidisti.) Idcirco Græcè, quoniam pauci liberales artes, Latino sermone cōscripserant, antequam Cicero eis lumen Romani sermonis afferret. quare necessitas cogebat, è fontibus Græcorum haurire, quæ in Latinis non inueniebantur. Atq; hæc ipsa fuit etiam causa, cur Cicero præcepta dicendi, Ciceroni filio Græcè prius tradidisset: sed filius illius non contentus, eadē Latinè uoluit à patre discere, quem scit utrunq; præclare posse. Quod quidē facit paterno exemplo, qui in proœmio librorū de Officiis dicit, ad suam utilitatē se Græca cum Latinis semper coniunxisse: atq; idem filio censet esse faciendum, ut par sit in utriusq; orationis facultate.
units.tr: What you have taught me about the method of speaking in Greek. That is why it is in Greek: because few had written the liberal arts in the Latin language before Cicero brought light to them in the Roman tongue. Hence necessity compelled men to draw from the Greek springs what was not found in Latin. This was also the very reason why Cicero had first taught the precepts of speaking in Greek to his son Cicero. But the son, not content with this, wished to learn the same things in Latin from his father, whom he knows to be able to do both splendidly. He does this following his father's example, for in the preface to the books On Duties he says that he had always joined Greek with Latin for his own advantage; and he judges that the same should be done for his son, so that he may be equal in the skill of both languages of speech.

units.la: Si modò tibi est ocium, & si uis.) Duo sunt quæ ad omnem rē gerendam requiruntur, uoluntas & facultas, quem admodū ipsi quoq; Rhetores tradunt. hæc duo si adsint, nihil uetat, quo minus res conficiatur. Hec igitur duo si in patre adsint, non dubitat filius, quin dicendi rationem Latino sermone ab eo sit accepturus. Idcirco dicit: Si modò tibi est ocium, & si uis. quibus urbis, ingenuum pudorem, & modestiam, morumq; suauitatem præse fert hic adolescens.
units.tr: If you have leisure and are willing. There are two things required for accomplishing any task, will and ability, as the rhetoricians themselves also teach. If these two are present, nothing prevents the matter from being carried out. So if both are present in the father, the son does not doubt that he will receive the method of speaking from him in the Latin language. Therefore he says: "If you have leisure and are willing." In these words this young man displays also his gentlemanly modesty, his decency, and the sweetness of his character.

units.la: C. P. An est mi Cicero. ) Hic patris erga filiū studium & benevolentia ostēditur. quid enim magis cupiat pater, quàm filium suum eruditissimum & sapientissimum esse? Filius sapiens (inquit Solomo) gloria sui patris est. Cum igitur duo sint cū adiectione patri à filio proposita, ocium & voluntas: de voluntate prius respondet pater, deinde de ocio & facultate, cum ait:
units.tr: C. P. Yes, my Cicero. Here the father's zeal and goodwill towards his son is shown. For what does a father desire more than that his son should be most learned and most wise? "A wise son," says Solomon, "is the glory of his father." Since, therefore, the son has put two things to his father with an addition, leisure and will, the father first answers about the will, and then about the leisure and ability, when he says:

units.la: Ocium autem primum,& summum est.) Ocium significat temporis vacuitatem à consuetis laboribus & occupationibus: ex quo sequitur, aliud agendi facultas. Ocium, inquit, primum adest, idq; summum. nam particula illa Primum, ordinem significat, & respondet particulæ sequenti, Deinde. Duo enim proponit, quorum primū est, ocium adesse: alterum, etiamsi ocium non adesset, se tamen omnibus occupationibus filij studia antepositurum. Neq; est quod quisquam obiiciat illud, Primum non de duobus, sed de pluribus dici. Terētius enim in Heauton. Id primum dicam, inquit, deinde quòd veni eloquar. idem vsurpat Cicero in Ver. 2. & pro Rabirio perduellionis reo, & alibi sæpe.
units.tr: "But leisure first, and above all, is at hand." Leisure signifies the emptiness of time from customary labours and occupations; from this follows the ability to do something else. "Leisure," he says, "is first present, and that in the highest degree." For that particle "first" denotes order and corresponds to the following particle "then." For he sets out two things, of which the first is that leisure is present; the other, that even if leisure were not present, he would nevertheless put his son's studies before all his occupations. Nor is there reason for anyone to object that "first" is said not of two but of several. For Terence in the Heauton says: "I will say this first," he says, "then that I have come to speak." Cicero also uses it in the second Verrine, and in the Pro Rabirio, the defendant on a charge of treason, and often elsewhere.

units.la: Quoniam aliquando Romæ exeundi potestas data est. ) Ratione reddit, cur ocium summū esse dixit: nimirū, quia Cæsare dominante, illius vox nō audiebatur Reipub. opportuna. Itaq; secesserat ille in Tusculanum, ibiq; commentabatur. Videntur enim hæ Partitiones eo tempore conscriptæ, quo C. Cæsar deuicto Pompeio Romæ imperabat,cr omnia solus gubernabat. nam Topica post Cæsaris necem, Antonij gladios fugiens,conscripsit, ut in ipsis Topicis diximus.
units.tr: "Since at some time the opportunity of leaving Rome has been given." He gives the reason why he said leisure was of the highest importance: namely, because while Caesar was master, his voice was not heard, being unsuited to the state. And so he had withdrawn to his Tusculan villa, and there he was composing. For these Partitions seem to have been written at the time when Gaius Caesar, after defeating Pompey, ruled at Rome and governed everything alone. For after Caesar's death, fleeing the swords of Antony, he wrote the Topics, as we said in the Topics themselves.

units.la: C. F. Vis ne igitur,ut tu me Græcè soles ordine interrogare. ) Vult filius patrem interrogare, quod quidém nemo præter decorum fieri existimare debet. Sunt enim quæ adolescentulos ex senioribus percontari deceat, si modò ea eiusmodi sint,quæ senes docere non dedeceat. Quanquam nihil est, quod ab illis sciscitari non liceat, quibus nos charos esse sentimus.Quod si quis dicat, difficiliores esse partes recte interrogandi, quàm respondendi,idcirco minus adolescenti con ucnire:huic occurrit ipse filius, Vt tu me Græcè soles ordine interrogare.quibus uerbis significat, sibi à patre ordinem cr uiam interrogandi propositam : quam si sequatur, aberrare non possit.
units.tr: C. F. Do you wish, then, to question me in order, as you are wont to do in Greek? The son wishes to question his father, which indeed no one ought to think done beyond what is fitting. For there are things which it is proper for young men to ask of their elders, provided they are of such a kind that it would not be unbecoming for the old to teach them. Nor is there anything which may not be asked of those whom we feel to be dear to us. But if anyone says that the proper conduct of questioning is more difficult than that of answering, and that for this reason it is less suitable for a young man, the son himself meets this objection with, "as you are wont to question me in order in Greek." By these words he signifies that his father has set before him an order and method of questioning; if he follows it, he cannot go astray.

units.la: C. P. Sane,si placet. ) Hoc est,si magis tibi placet interrogare,quàm respondere, equidem annuo.
units.tr: C. P. Certainly, if you please. That is: if it pleases you more to ask than to answer, I indeed assent.

units.la: Sic enim cr ego te meminisse intelligam.) Duplicem fructũ ex huiusmodi interrogatione percipi ostendit: alterum, ad confirmandam memoriam eorum quæ ante didicerat:alterum uero, quòd, quæ non didicit, ordine sit accepturus. quæ duo sunt ab adolescétib. maximè notãda. Nam & confirmare memoriã debent, subinde repetendo quæ didicerunt: & quæ ignorant, ordine discere. Ordo enim & luce reb. affert, & memoriæ iuuat.
units.tr: For thus I shall understand that you remember. He shows that a double benefit is gained from questioning of this kind: one, to confirm the memory of what he had learned before; the other, that he will receive in order what he has not learned. These two things are especially to be noted by young men. For they ought both to confirm their memory, by repeating again and again what they have learned, and to learn in order what they do not know. For order both brings light to things and helps the memory.

units.la: SVMMA ET PRIMA RHE- toricæ partitio.
units.tr: The first and chief division of rhetoric.

units.la: c. F. Quot in partes distribueda est omnis doctrina dicendi? c. P. In treis. c. F. Cedò quas? c. P. Primùm in ipsam uim oratoris, deinde in orationem, tum in quæstionem.
units.tr: Son: Into how many parts should all teaching about speaking be divided? Father: Into three. Son: Name them, please. Father: First, into the power of the orator himself; then into the speech; and then into the question.

units.la: C. F. Quot in partes distribuenda est omnis doctrina dicédi? ) Proponit filius patri, artis Rhetoricæ definitionē, et simul eius partes primas requirit. Nã omnis quæ à ratione suscipitur de aliqua re institutio, debet à definitione proficisci, ut ipse Cicero de Off. li. i. testatur. Deinde hoc ipsum etiã requirit partiédi ratio, ut primùm id quod distribuendum sit definiatur: deinde ex ipsa definitione, partes totius rei primæ eliciantur.
units.tr: "Into how many parts should all teaching about speaking be divided?" The son puts to his father the definition of the art of rhetoric and at the same time asks for its first parts. For every systematic instruction in any subject, drawn from reason, ought to start from a definition, as Cicero himself attests in On Duties, book 1. Then the method of division itself requires that what is to be divided be defined first, and that the primary parts of the whole be derived from that definition.

units.la: Omnis doctrina dicédi. ) Quæri potest, an his verbis ars ipsa dicendi, quæ Rhetorica Græcè dicitur, intelligeda sit. uidetur aut nõ esse. Rhetoricæ enim partes sunt, ut omnes fatétur, quinq; illæ tantum: Inuentio, dispositio, elocutio, pronunciatio, me-
units.tr: "All teaching about speaking." One may ask whether by these words the art of speaking itself is meant, which is called rhetoric in Greek. It seems not. For the parts of rhetoric, as everyone agrees, are only those five: invention, arrangement, style, delivery and memory.

units.la: memoria. neq; enim oratio & quæstio partes artis esse possūt, cū oratio opus sit oratoris: & quæstio tanquā subiecta materia, quam tractet, & in qua uersetur. nisi etiā marmor, & statuam ipsam Herculis, fingendi artis partes esse uelimus: quod quidē fieri nō potest, cū ars sit ratio, et uis, qua aliquid efficimus. illa uerò subiecta quidē arti sunt, ad eamq; pertinēt, eius aūt partes dici nō possunt. Sed dicendū est, materiē & opus duob.modis cōsiderari. uno modo, quatenus res sunt oratori subiectæ: & ita partes artis nō sunt: altero, quatenus præceptis subijciūtur, arteq; tractātur. Ita oratio ipsa nō est pars Rhetoricæ, sed orationis præceptā. Idē de quæstiōe intelligēdū est. Quod aūt illæ quinq; Rhetoricæ partes magno cōsensu à Cicerone ne & ab alijs esse dicantur, id ita intelligendum est: quinq; esse proprias & naturales, quibus non modò ars ipsa constituitur, uerùm etiam orator efficitur, etiam si opus nullum eius extet. Reliquas duas, assumi extrinsecus: atq; eatenus partes esse, quatenus sub actionem oratoris cadunt, easq; artis praeceptis tractat & uersat. Id quod dico, illa uniuersali addita nota usus est innuere Cicero, Omnis doctrina: quasi diceret, Non ars sola Rhetorica, sed quicquid toto ambitu eloquentiae cōplectitur: quae nō modò praeceptis qbusdā cōtinetur, sed quae multis & magnis reb.cōstat. ut de Inventione tione idem loquitur: Omnis inquam doctrina dicendi, tum quæ proprie & angustè, tum quæ latè & improprie dicitur. Est igitur hæc Rhetoricæ brevis quædam definitio: ita plena tamen, ut omnia quæ quoquo modo ad eloquentiam pertineāt, complectatur. Nam Doctrinæ verbum loco generis est positum: dicendi verò, eius proprietatem continet, qua à reliquis doctrinis seiungitur, & in suo proprio genere reponitur. Nam cum tres sint artes in sermone, tanquam in communi quadam regione versantes, Grammatica, Dialectica, Rhetorica: hæc ita ab illis distinguitur duabus, ut cum Grammatica emendati & puri sermonis rationem habeat, Dialectica disputandi, hæc dicendi sibi assumpserit partes. De Grammatica perspicuum est, de Dialectica ac Rhetorica confirmat Cicero in Oratore: Aliud, inquit, videtur oratio esse, aliud disputatio: nec idem loqui esse, quod dicere: attamen utrunque in differendo est. Disputandi ratio & loquendi Dialecticorum sit: Oratorum autem, dicendi & ornandi. ubi verbum Ornandi expositionis gratia additum est, quod probant illa eiusdem post in eodem libro verba: Nec aliud quicquam est dicere, nisi omnes, aut certè plerasq; aliqua specie illuminare sententias. Interdū additur qualitas, ut cum bene dicendi artem esse dicunt: quod non tam necessitate faciunt, quàm declarandi causa. Nisi uelimus id, Bene, aliquid amplius significare, quàm ornatè, quod in dicèdi uerbo inclusum est: ut benedicere sit, non solum ornatè, sed etiam scienter & perite dicere. Vt autè ad huius loci definitionem redeamus, Rhetoricam dicemus esse doctrinâ dicèdi: quæ definitio idem valet, quod illa Cornificij lib. 1. qui Rhetoricam definiens ait: Ars est præceptio, quæ dat certam viam, rationemq; dicendi. Aristotelis autem ad Theodect. lib. 1. plenior esse videtur, sed tamen idem explicat. Rhetorica, inquit, est uis quædam perspicièdi, quid in quaq; re sit ad persuadendum accommodatum. Iam uidendum est, ad quâ Philosophiæ partem referenda sit Rhetorica. Non repetam autem ab ouo, quod dicitur, diuisionem artium, sed cui parti tum Aristoteles tum Cicero subiecerint, indicabo. Ac primum certū, eam ab his duobus, politiæ, hoc est, ciuilis scientiæ partem & quasi propaginē iudicari. Et Aristoteles quidem Rhet. lib. 1. idcirco eam à ciuili scientia manare dicit, quod de uita hominum ac moribus dicendum sit, & ab ea argumenta sint ducenda: quatenus autem oratione sit fides, atq; ex ijs argumenta ducuntur, quæ in quaq; re sint ad persuadendum accommodata, cum Dialectica similitudinem habere. Tria enim facit artificiosa fidei faciendæ genera, unum, quod in uita & moribus positum positiu est: secundū, in permouendo: tertiū, in oratione ipsa, cū probatur aliquid, aut probari videtur. Ex quo cōcludit, Rhetoricā parte esse Ciuilis scientiæ, paritim Dialecticæ similem esse. Cicero uero initio artis de Inuentione, Aristotelem interpretans: Ciuilis, inquit, quædā ratio est, quæ multis & magnis ex rebus constat: eius quædam magna & ampla pars est artificiosa eloquētia, quā Rhetoricam uocant. Nam neq; cū ijs sentimus, qui ciuilem scientiam eloquentiā nō putant indigere: & ab ijs, qui eam putant omnem Rhetoris ui & artificio contineri, magnopere differentimus. Quare hanc oratoriā facultatē in eo genere ponemus, ut eam ciuilis sciētiæ partem esse dicamus. In his Ciceronis uerbis tria obseruanda sunt. Primum, eum ciuilē rationem appellare, doctrinā de uita et moribus, quæ communi nomine ἠθικὴ καὶ πολιτικὴ à Græcis dicitur. Secundum est, quōd magnam ciuilis rationis partē Rhetoricā esse dicit, quā Aristoteles minorem esse uult, cū eam modò tāquam pullum & sobolem ad arboris stirpem adnatā dicit: modò particulam eiusdem uocat, in principio Rhetorices ad Theodectēn. Esse eius partem, ita demōstrauit Victorinus: Ciuilis, inquit, ratio duplex est: una, quæ res certas solenni cursu, & sine ullo tumultu agit: altera, quæ in lite ac disceptatione uersatur. illam priorē Ciuilem scientiā nomine mine generis, hanc eloquentiam artificiosam appellauit. Magnâ autem & amplam, propter magnitudine uarictatemq; causarum, quod etiam de Oratore docet Cicero. Aristoteles uero, paruâ eius parte dixit, quoniâ in Rhetorica ex ciuili doctrina pauca quaedâ quasi deriuatur, quæ copiosiorâ in philosophorum fontib. & libris inueniri possunt.
units.tr: Memory. Nor can the speech and the question be parts of the art, since the speech is the work of the orator, and the question is like the subject matter that he handles and in which he works. Unless we also want the marble and the statue of Hercules itself to be parts of the art of sculpture; which cannot be, since an art is a reasoned skill and power by which we produce something. Those things are indeed subject to the art and belong to it, but they cannot be called its parts. But it must be said that matter and work may be considered in two ways: in one way, insofar as things are subjected to the orator, and so they are not parts of the art; in the other, insofar as they are subjected to precepts and handled by the art. Thus the speech itself is not a part of rhetoric, but the precepts about speech are. The same is to be understood of the question. As to the fact that Cicero, with broad agreement, and others too, say that those five parts belong to rhetoric, this must be understood thus: they are five proper and natural parts, by which not only the art itself is constituted but the orator is made, even if no work of his survives. The remaining two are taken from outside, and are parts only insofar as they fall under the orator's action and are treated and handled by the precepts of the art. Cicero, by adding that universal mark, "all teaching," seems to indicate this: as if he said, "Rhetoric is not the art alone, but whatever is embraced in the whole range of eloquence; which is contained not only in certain precepts but consists of many and great things." As he says of invention: "All teaching, I say, about speaking, both that which is properly and narrowly so called, and that which is called broadly and improperly." This, then, is a brief definition of rhetoric, yet so full that it embraces all that pertains in any way to eloquence. For the word "teaching" is placed in the position of genus; the word "speaking" contains its particular quality, by which it is separated from the other disciplines and placed in its own proper kind. For since there are three arts concerned with discourse, as if working in a common region, grammar, dialectic and rhetoric, rhetoric is distinguished from the other two in this way: grammar has to do with the rule of correct and pure speech, dialectic with the art of disputing, and rhetoric has taken to itself the task of speaking. About grammar there is no doubt; about dialectic and rhetoric Cicero confirms it in the Orator: "Speech," he says, "seems one thing, disputation another; nor is to talk the same as to speak; yet both are used in arguing. The method of disputing and of talking belongs to the dialecticians, but that of speaking and adorning belongs to the orators." Here the word "adorning" is added by way of explanation, as the following words in the same book prove: "Nor is there anything else to speaking than to illuminate all, or at least most, of the thoughts with some kind of brilliance." Sometimes a qualifier is added, as when they call it the art of speaking well; they do this not so much from necessity as for clarity. Unless we want the word "well" to signify something more than "elegantly," which is already contained in the word for speaking, so that to speak well means not only to speak elegantly but also to speak wisely and skilfully. But to return to the definition of this passage: we shall say that rhetoric is the teaching of speaking; this definition means the same as that of Cornificius, book 1, who, defining rhetoric, says: "It is an art, a precept which gives a certain way and method of speaking." The definition of Aristotle in the Theodectea, book 1, seems fuller, but explains the same thing: "Rhetoric," he says, "is a certain power of seeing, in each matter, what is suited to persuading." Now we must consider to which part of philosophy rhetoric should be referred. I shall not, however, go back to the beginning and repeat the division of the arts that is commonly given, but I shall indicate under which part both Aristotle and Cicero placed it. First, it is certain that they judged it a part, or as it were an offshoot, of politics, that is, of civil science. And Aristotle, in the Rhetoric, book 1, says that it flows from civil science for this reason: that it must speak of the life and customs of men, and arguments must be drawn from these; and insofar as belief is produced by speech, and arguments are drawn from those things which are suited to persuading in each matter, it has a likeness to dialectic. For he makes three kinds of artful means of producing belief: one, which lies in life and customs; second, in stirring the emotions; third, in the speech itself, when something is proved or seems to be proved. From this he concludes that rhetoric is a part of civil science, and in a way is similar to dialectic. Cicero, at the beginning of his art of Invention, interpreting Aristotle, says: "Civil science is a certain reasoning, which consists of many and great matters; a certain great and wide part of it is artful eloquence, which they call rhetoric. For we do not agree with those who think civil science has no need of eloquence, and we differ greatly from those who think all of it is contained in the power and craft of the rhetorician. Therefore we shall place this oratorical faculty in that kind of thing, so that we may say it is a part of civil science." In these words of Cicero three things are to be observed. First, that he calls civil reasoning the teaching about life and customs, which the Greeks call by the common name ethics and politics [ἠθικὴ καὶ πολιτικὴ]. Second, that he says rhetoric is a large part of civil reasoning, while Aristotle wants it to be smaller, since he calls it now a shoot and offspring growing from the stem of a tree, now a particle of it, in the beginning of the Rhetoric to Theodectes. That it is a part of this, Victorinus demonstrated thus: "Civil reasoning," he says, "is twofold: one kind, which conducts settled affairs in the customary course and without any disturbance; the other, which is engaged in dispute and controversy. The former he called civil science by the name of the genus; the latter he called artful eloquence." And it is called large and wide because of the greatness and variety of causes, as Cicero also teaches in On the Orator. But Aristotle said it is a small part of it, since in the Rhetoric some few things are, as it were, derived from civil doctrine, which can be found more abundantly in the sources and books of the philosophers.

units.la: Et illud cogitandum est, Aristotelem ut philosophum magnam eius rei scientiam ab oratoribus detraxisse, quam Cicero summus orator eisdem attribuit: ut etiam in Oratorijs eius libris uidere licet. Tertium est, quod nec ciuilem scientiam sine eloquentia cōstare posse putat, neq; eloquentiam sine ciuili scientia: neq; tamē Rhetoris ui & artificio uult omnē scientiā cōtineri, quod quidā partim imperitia, partim ostentatione ac uento, partim aliis rebus impulsi (ut Aristoteles ait) putauerunt. Est autem alia quoq; causa, cur pars ciuilis rationis Rhetorica dicatur: nimirū, quòd siue ars est Rhetorica, siue prudentia quaedâ, eam ciuilis scientiæ partem esse necesse est: cum & illæ doctrinæ moralis, siue ciuiles sint partes, ut Aristot. lib. 6. ad Nicomachū docet, cū uirtutes quæ in ratione sitæ sunt enumerat.
units.tr: And this must be considered too: Aristotle, as a philosopher, took from the orators a great share of that science, which Cicero, the greatest orator, assigned to them; as can be seen also in his Oratorical books. Third, he thinks that civil science cannot stand without eloquence, nor eloquence without civil science; yet he does not want all science to be contained in the power and craft of the rhetorician, as some, driven partly by inexperience, partly by display and windy vanity, partly by other causes (as Aristotle says), have thought. There is also another reason why a part of civil reasoning is called rhetoric: namely, that whether rhetoric is an art or a kind of prudence, it must be a part of civil science, since those moral or civil teachings are parts too, as Aristotle teaches in the Nicomachean Ethics, book 6, when he lists the virtues which lie in reason.

units.la: Esse autem Dialecticæ similē Rhetoricā, et Aristoteles scripserat: et Cicero cōfirmauit, cū in Oratore dixit, eā ex altera parte respōdere Dialecticæ. Similitudinis quoq; Aristoteles ratione ponit initio Rhetoricæ. Rhetorices,tum quòd ambæ in eiusmodi reb.sint, quæ à cunctis hominibus quodammodo cognosci possunt: tum quòd non sint in aliquo definito ac certo genere scientiæ. ut numeri (exempli gratia) in Arithmetica, magnitudines in Geometria,in Musica soni;& id genus alia, tantum cernuntur. Artem porrò esse Rhetoricam,neque Aristoteles, neq; Hermogenes,neq; Cicero,neq; Quintilianus dubitarunt: ut ex illorum de ea libris, cuiusis perspicuum esse potest. Nam si certâ habet praeceptorum comprehensionem,si usum in omni vita magnum & honestum,certè ab artium ucrarum genere Rhetorica,non magis quàm vel Civilis ratio, vel Dialectica,quarum est sive pars,sive partus, sive imago,excludi potest. Sed sive est ars, sive artis quaedam similitudo,non est quidem ea propter maximas & plurimas utilitates negligenda.
units.tr: Aristotle had written that rhetoric is similar to dialectic, and Cicero confirmed it when he said in the Orator that rhetoric answers to dialectic from the other side. Aristotle also gives a reason for the similarity at the beginning of the Rhetoric: both deal with matters that all men can in some way know, and neither is confined to a definite and certain field of knowledge, as numbers are in arithmetic, magnitudes in geometry, and sounds in music, and as other such subjects are only perceived. Moreover, neither Aristotle, nor Hermogenes, nor Cicero, nor Quintilian doubted that rhetoric is an art, as anyone can see from their books on it. For if it has a definite body of precepts, and a great and honourable use in all of life, then rhetoric cannot be excluded from the class of true arts any more than civil science or dialectic can, of which it is either a part, or an offshoot, or an image. But whether it is an art or some likeness of an art, it is certainly not to be neglected, on account of its very great and numerous uses.

units.la: C. P. In trcis.) In hac divisione artis Rhetoricae,observat Cicero,quod ipse seruàdum esse de Oratore praecipit,cum dicit:Partes in dividendo definitas esse debere, non solum numero, sed etiam paucitate.illud innuens, illum non satis peritè partiri,qui aliquo numero partes alicuius rei comprehendit,nisi adsit etiam paucitas,quae in partitione seruatur: si genera ipsa prima rerum ponuntur, neq; permiste cum partibus implicantur, ut ipse de Inuent,lib.1,docet.Cum igitur neq; plures, neque pauciores esse possint partes Rhetoricæ, quàm tres, ut ostendam, rectè & appositè respondet pater.
units.tr: C. P. "In tribus." In this division of the art of rhetoric, Cicero observes what he himself prescribes in the De Oratore when he says: the parts in a division should be defined not only by their number but also by their fewness. He means by this that a person does not divide the parts of a thing well if he enumerates them in some number without also keeping them few, as is done in a proper partition; that is, when the first kinds of things are set out and are not mixed up and entangled with the parts, as he himself teaches in the first book of the De Inventione. Since rhetoric can have neither more nor fewer than three parts, as I will show, the father answers rightly and appropriately.

units.la: C. F. Cedò quas? ) Cedò flagitantis est verbum, à Comicis poetis sæpe usurpatum: & idem est quod Dic quæso, dic obsecro.
units.tr: C. F. "Cedo quas?" "Cedo" is a word of urging, often used by the comic poets, and it means the same as "Tell me, please, I beg you."

units.la: C. P. Primum in ipsam uim oratoris, deinde in orationem, tum in quæstionem. ) Vera est illa Platonis in Epinomide uox, Omnem doctrinam ingenuarum & humanarum artium, uno quodam societatis vinculo contineri. Vbi enim perspecta uis est rationis eius quà causæ rerum atq; exitus cognoscuntur, mirus quidam omnium quasi consensus doctrinarum, concentusq; reperitur. Hoc & in hac tripartita Rhetoricæ divisione videre licet. Tria enim sunt principia rerum naturalium, si Aristoteli credimus: materia, forma, & priuatio. Hæc pariter ad hanc artem suo modo quodam transferuntur: nisi quòd pro priuatione efficiens ponitur causa, ipsa nimirum uis oratoris. in quo fortassis Platonem sequi maluit, qui Deum, non priuationem, inter principia posuit: atque ab eo, una cum materia & forma, omnia effici voluit. nam priuatio ipsa, haud proprie principium est, sed fortuito. Sunt autem hæc tria in Rhetoricis, uis oratoris, oratio, & quæstio. Et quæstio quidem, materiæ loco est: oratio & forma; & opus est quoddam,siue potius effectio: Vis oratoris horum efficiens,est caussa,quam Cicero in Oratore tanquam in subiecto, vel quasi artificium & ideam in artifice,collocauit. Hæc etiam in communibus artibus licet animaduertere. Quid enim in statua fingenda ultra hæc tria magnopere desiderabis? Si enim Phidias (exempli gratia) & ebur vel aurum,& forma Iouis adsit,nihil vetat quo minus Iupiter Olympius fiat. Peritè igitur Cicero, tria statuit Rhetoricæ quasi principia,et caussas: Vim oratoris, orationem, & quæstionem. quod perinde est ac si diceret,ad persuadendum,qui finis est oratori propositus,opus esse artifice, materia et forma. nam artis cuiusq; cōstitutio,à finis cognitione recte proficiscitur. Sed hic videndum est, quomodo Quintiliani partitio cū Ciceronis partitione cōsentit. Is enim lib.1. Instit.orat.cap. 14. Rhetoricen diuidit in artem,artificē,& opus. Sed hic arti materiem cum inuentione et dispositione subiicit: operi vero,orationem cum elocutione,& memoriā & pronunciatione. Artificem porrò lib.12.instruit,& suis ornat virtutibus. Ex quo perspicuum est, eū diuersam à Ciceroue,& minus probatā uiam secutū esse. Quod autem idem lib. 3.cap.5.scribit,Facultatem orandi cōsummari (sic enim loquitur) natura, arte, exercitatione: non partes Rhetoricæ, sed adiumenta, & tanquam ininstrumenta dicendi, ut supra ostendimus, intellexit. Illud autem obseruandum est, uim oratoris esse,quod alibi officium appellauit. Quamobrem hic locus admonet,ut de oratoris officio,materia,& fine aliquid dicamus. Primùm,quam hic appellat uim,ea est,quæ abAriftotele in Rhetor. Δυνάμεις appellatur. Est enim Rhetorica Δυνά-μεις,hoc est uis & facultas,nō ἐπιστήμη,id est,scientia : nisi scientiam comuniter & latè intelligamus,quemadmodum Galenus posse capi dicit,initio libri de Arte medica. Est autem officium oratoris , de quauis re proposita dicere appositè ad perfuafionem: finis autè,persuadere dictione. Inter officium autem & finem hoc interest,quòd in officio quid fieri,in fine qui officio conuenit, consideratur.ut medici officium dicimus esse,curare appositè ad sanandum: finem, curatione sanare. Item oratoris, quid officiu, quid finem esse dicamus,intelligemus: cum id quod facere debet, officiu esse dicemus: illud cuius causa facere debet,fine appellabimus.Hæc Cicero lib.1.de Inuen. ex Ariftot.lib.1.ad Theodect. Iam de materia idem fentiendu est,quod et Ariftoteles,& Cicero, duo huius artis lumina senserunt. Etenim (inquit Cicero in proœmio lib.2.de Orat.) cæteræ ferè artes seipsæ per se tuentur singulæ: bene dicere autem,quod est scienter,& peritè,& ornatè dicere,
units.tr: C. P. "First in the power of the orator itself, then in the speech, then in the question." That saying of Plato in the Epinomis is true: all teaching of the liberal and humane arts is held together by a single bond of kinship. For when the power of reason is clearly seen, by which the causes and outcomes of things are known, a remarkable agreement and harmony of all teachings is found. This can also be seen in this threefold division of rhetoric. For there are three principles of natural things, if we believe Aristotle: matter, form, and privation. These are likewise transferred in their own way to this art, except that in place of privation an efficient cause is put, namely the power of the orator itself. Here perhaps he preferred to follow Plato, who placed God, not privation, among the principles, and wanted everything to be made by him, together with matter and form. For privation is not properly a principle, but an accidental one. Now in rhetoric these three are: the power of the orator, the speech, and the question. The question takes the place of matter; the speech takes the place of form, and it is a kind of work, or rather an effect; the power of the orator is its efficient cause, which Cicero placed in the Orator as in a subject, or as the craft and idea in the craftsman. This can also be noticed in the common arts. For what would you greatly need in carving a statue beyond these three? If Phidias (for example) and ivory or gold, and the form of Jove, are present, nothing prevents the Olympian Jupiter from being made. Cicero therefore wisely set down three principles and causes of rhetoric, as it were: the power of the orator, the speech, and the question. This is just as if he said that, for persuading, which is the end set before the orator, there must be a craftsman, matter, and form. For the constitution of any art rightly proceeds from knowledge of its end. But here we must see how Quintilian's division agrees with Cicero's. For in the first book of the Institutes of Oratory, chapter 14, he divides rhetoric into the art, the artist, and the work. But here he assigns to the art the matter, together with invention and arrangement; to the work, the speech, together with style, memory, and delivery. Further, in book 12 he instructs the artist and adorns him with his virtues. From this it is clear that he followed a path different from Cicero's and less approved. As for what he writes in the same work, book 3, chapter 5, that the faculty of speaking is perfected (for so he puts it) by nature, art, and practice, he understood these not as parts of rhetoric but as aids and, as it were, instruments of speaking, as we have shown above. But it must be noted that the power of the orator is what Cicero elsewhere called the duty. So this passage prompts us to say something about the orator's duty, matter, and end. First, what he here calls power is what Aristotle in the Rhetoric calls δύναμις [dynamis]. For rhetoric is a δύναμις [dynamis], that is, a power and faculty, not an ἐπιστήμη [epistēmē], that is, a science, unless we understand science in a common and broad sense, as Galen says it can be taken at the beginning of his book On the Art of Medicine. The duty of the orator is to speak appropriately to persuade on any subject proposed; the end, however, is to persuade by speech. Between duty and end this difference exists: in duty we consider what must be done, in end what fits the duty. Thus we say the duty of a physician is to treat appropriately for healing, and the end is to heal by treatment. So we shall understand what we should call the duty of the orator and what the end: what he ought to do we shall call the duty; that for the sake of which he ought to do it we shall call the end. Cicero says this in the first book of the De Inventione, from Aristotle's first book to Theodectes. Now concerning matter, the same must be felt as Aristotle and Cicero, the two lights of this art, felt. For (says Cicero in the preface to the second book of the De Oratore) the other arts for the most part each defend themselves by their own means; but to speak well, that is to speak knowledgeably, skilfully, and ornately, does not have any defined region, enclosed by fixed boundaries. Whatever can fall into human debate ought to be spoken about well by the one who professes he can do so; otherwise the name of eloquence must be given up. Therefore the definition of the duty was stated as: to speak appropriately on any subject for the purpose of persuading; and this is indeed common to this art and dialectic, Aristotle, first book of the Rhetoric. Therefore every question is set before the orator as his matter by our Cicero, in which he is to labour, exercise his power of speaking and his office, so that from it he may produce a noble work, namely the speech, which Sophocles called the queen of things; by which he may reach (if nothing hinders) what is the end, that is, to persuade.

units.la: non dam,siue potius effectio: Vis oratoris horum efficiens,est caussa,quam Cicero in Oratore tanquam in subiecto, uel quasi artificium & ideam in artifice,collocauit. Hæc etiam in communibus artibus liset animaduertere. Quid enim in statua fingenda ultra hæc tria magnopere desideverabis? Si enim Phidias (exempli gratia) & ebur uel aurum,& forma Iouis adsit,nihil uetat quo minus Iupiter Olympius fiat. Perite igitur Cicero, tria statuit Rhetoricæ quasi principia,et caussas: Vim oratoris, orationem, & quæstionem. quod perinde est ac si diceret,ad persuadendum,qui finis est oratori propositus,opus esse artifice, materia et forma. nam artis cuiusq; cōstitutio,à finis cognitione recte proficiscitur. Sed hic uidendum est, quomodo Quintiliani partitio cū Ciceronis partitione cōsentit. Is enim lib.1. Instit.orat.cap. 14. Rhetoricen diuidit in artem,artificē,& opus. Sed hic arti materiem cum inuentione et dispositione subiecit: operi uero,orationem cum elocutione,& memoriā & pronunciatione. Artificem porrò lib.12.instruit,& suis ornat uirtutibus.
