Inter officium autem & finem hoc interest, quòd in officio quid fieri, in fine quî officio conueniat, consideratur. ut medici officium dicimus esse, curare appositè ad sanandum: finem, curatione sanare. Item oratoris, quid officiū, quid finem esse dicamus, intelligemus: cum id quod facere debet, officiū esse dicemus: illud cuius caussa facere debet, fine appellabimus. Hæc Cicero lib.1. de Inuen. ex Aristot. lib.1. ad Theodect. Iam de materia idem sentiendũ est, quod et Aristoteles, & Cicero, duo huius artis lumina senserunt. Etenim (inquit Cicero in proœmio lib.2. de Orat.) cæteræ ferè artes seipsæ per se tuentur singulæ: bene dicere autem, quod est scienter, & perité, & ornatè dicere, non habet definitam aliquam regionem, cuius ter‐minis septa teneatur. Omnia quæcunque in homi‐ num disceptationem cadere possunt, bene sunt ei dicenda, qui hoc se posse profitetur: aut eloquen‐ tiæ nomen relinquendū est. Idcirco in definitione Officij positum est, De quauis re dicere appositè ad persuadendum: quod quidem huic arti cū Dia‐ lectica commune est. Aristot. lib. 1. Rhet. Quæstio igitur omnis à nostro Cicerone materia oratori proponitur, in qua elaboret, & uim suam dicēdi, munusq; exerceat: ut ex ea præclarum opus, ora‐ tionem nimirum, quam Sophocles reginam rerū appellauit, conficiat: qua sincm (si nihil impediat) assequi possit, quod est persuadere.

units.la: C. F. In quo est ipsa uis? C. P. In rebus, & uerbis. Sed & res & uerba inuenienda sunt, & collocanda. Pro‐ prie autem in reb. inuenire, in uerbis e‐loqui dicitur. Collocare autem, etsi est commune, tamen ad inueniendum refertur. Vox, motus, uultus atq; o‐ mnis actio eloquendi comes est, ea‐ rumq; omnium custos est memoria.
units.tr: C. F. In what does the power itself lie? C. P. In things and words. But things and words must both be discovered and arranged. Strictly speaking, we say that things are discovered and words are expressed. Arranging, though it belongs to both, is referred to invention. Voice, movement, expression, and all delivery accompany speaking, and memory is the guardian of all of them.

units.la: C. F. In quo est ipsa uis? C. P. In rebus & uer‐bis. ) Vim ipsam oratoris rebus & uerbis conti‐ neri ait: hoc est, artificio & scientia, qua res uerba tractare, expolireq; nouit. Et recte quidè res anteposuit uerbis, qui naturalis est ordo. Res enim natura priores sunt, uerba inuetis rebus imposita. Itaq; res fi adsit, facilè sequuntur uerba, ut inquit Horat.
units.tr: C. F. In what does the power itself lie? C. P. In things and words. He says that the orator's power itself is contained in things and words, that is, in the art and skill by which he knows how to handle and polish things and words. He rightly puts things before words, since that is the natural order. Things are prior by nature, and words are applied to things once they have been found. So if the matter is at hand, the words readily follow, as Horace says:

units.la: Rem tibi Socraticæ poterunt ostendere chartæ, Verbaq; prouisam rem non inuita sequentur.
units.tr: The Socratic writings will be able to show you the matter, and words will not reluctantly follow a subject that you have considered beforehand.

units.la: Et quoniam in figuris & ornamentis fententiarum schemata rebus respondent, naturalis ordo poscere uidetur, ut in tradenda arte, fententiarum lumina prius explicentur: deinde uerborū, quod Cicero in tertio de Oratore fecit, & Quintilianus, & Aquila Romanus, qui etiam cur id faciat rationem reddit: Natura, inquit, est prius sentire, quàm eloqui. Cornificius tamen contrarium est ordinem secutus libro 4. ad Herennium: quod etsi quidam minus probent, quòd artem traderet ex professo ut Rhetor: tamen cum Cicero idem fecerit in Bruto, & in Oratore ad eūdem, & in Partitionibus hisce, non uidetur esse reprehendedum: à facilioribus enim & simplicioribus incipere uoluerunt, quod etiam in docendo laudatur. Hinc Erasmus Roterodamus in opere de Duplici copia: Rerum, inquit, cognitio potior, uerborum prior. idcirco & ipse à copia uerborum exorsus est. Rerum nomine argumenta omnia, & rationes, quibus aliquid uel confirmatur, uel refellitur, intelligit, de quibus postea. Verba autem tum simplicia tum coniuncta intelliguntur, de quibus etiam suo loco dicet. In his igitur duobus omnes officij oratorij partes versantur, sed non uno modo. Quanquam enim & res & verba invenienda sunt, & collocanda, proprie tamen res inveniri dicuntur, & verba ad unam elocutionem referuntur. Collocare quoque, etsi amborum commune est, inventionis tamen proprie subijcitur. In quo iam habemus tres officij partes: Inventionem, elocutionem, & collocationem, sive dispositionem. Duae reliquae sunt, actio sive pronunciatio, & memoria. Ex his igitur apparet, perite scripsisse Cornificium, cum lib. 1. Rhetoricorum dixit: Oportet igitur in Oratore esse inventionem, dispositionem, elocutionem, memoriam, & pronunciationem. Duo enim complexus est, oratorem ipsum, & eius vim: hoc est, facultatem horum omnium quae enumerata sunt. Sed iam singula officia ex aliis Ciceronis locis sunt definienda. Inventio igitur (ut de Inventione idem definit) excogitatio est rerum verarum, aut verisimilium, quae causam probabilem reddunt. Dispositio sive collocatio, est rerum inventarum in ordinem distributio. Elocutio autem est, idoneorum verborum & sententiarum ad inventionem accommodatio: nimirum ut humilia submisse, mediocria temperate, magna graviter dicamus, ut Cicero ad Brutum ait. Actio sive pronunciatio est, ex rerum & verborum dignitate, vocis & corporis moderatio: sive (ut Cicero in Orat. ait) est corporis quædam eloquentia. Memoria postremò, horum omnium custos, est firma animi rerum ac verborum ad inventionem perceptio. Sed hic occurrit quæstio, Quomodo actionem orator in vocem, motum, & vultum distribuat: cum in Oratore, vocem tantum & motum ei subiecerit? Sed facilis est solutio. Nam motus nomine ibi vultum etiam complexus est. Complectitur enim motus duo genera: alterum obscurum, alterum clarum. obscurus motus in vultu est, clarus in reliquo corporis gestu: vox autem ad pronunciationem refertur. Atque hæc omnia actioni, tanquam generi summo, subiiciuntur: quæ elocutionis quasi comes est, & socia.
units.tr: And since in the figures and ornaments of sentences the schemata correspond to the things, the natural order seems to require that, in teaching the art, the ornaments of sentences be explained first and then the words. Cicero did this in the third book of On the Orator, and so did Quintilian and Aquila Romanus, who also gives the reason for doing so: "Nature," he says, "is to feel before one speaks." Cornificius, however, followed the opposite order in the fourth book of his work to Herennius. Although some disapprove of this because he taught the art openly, as a rhetorician, still, since Cicero did the same in the Brutus, in the Orator addressed to the same man, and in these Partitions, it does not seem to be blameworthy. They chose to begin with the easier and simpler things, which is also praised in teaching. Hence Erasmus of Rotterdam, in his work On the Double Copia: "Knowledge of things is more important, but knowledge of words comes first." That is why he himself began with the abundance of words. By "things" I understand all the arguments and reasons by which something is either confirmed or refuted, which I will discuss later. Words are understood both as single and as combined, and I will speak of these in their own place too. All the parts of the orator's office are concerned with these two, but not in one way. For although both things and words must be discovered and arranged, things are properly said to be discovered, and words are referred to a single department, elocution. Arranging, although it is common to both, is properly subordinated to invention. In this we now have three parts of the office: invention, elocution, and arrangement, or disposition. The remaining two are action, or delivery, and memory. From this it is clear that Cornificius wrote skilfully when, in the first book of his Rhetoric, he said: "Therefore the orator must have invention, disposition, elocution, memory, and delivery." For he has embraced two things: the orator himself and his power, that is, the faculty of all the things enumerated. But now each office must be defined from other passages of Cicero. Invention, then (as he defines it in the book On Invention), is the thinking out of true or probable things which make the case plausible. Disposition, or arrangement, is the distribution of the things found into order. Elocution is the adaptation of fitting words and sentences to the invention, namely, that we speak humble things plainly, middling things moderately, and great things weightily, as Cicero says to Brutus. Action, or delivery, is the regulation of voice and body according to the dignity of things and words; or (as Cicero says in the Orator) it is a certain eloquence of the body. Memory, finally, the guardian of all these, is the firm perception of the things and words for the invention. But here a question arises: how does the orator distribute action into voice, movement, and expression, when in the Orator he assigns to it only voice and movement? The solution is easy. For under the name of movement he there also included expression. Movement comprises two kinds: one obscure, the other clear. The obscure movement is in the face, the clear in the rest of the body's gesture. Voice, however, is referred to delivery. All these things are subordinated to action as the highest genus, which is, as it were, the companion and partner of elocution.

units.la: Sed quærat hic aliquis, Quomodo hæc officia oratoris cum illis conveniant, quæ in Oratore ad Brutum, ex Aristotelis Rhetoricorum tertio traduntur? Nam tria, inquit, videnda sunt Oratori: quid dicat, & quo quidque loco dicat, & quomodo. Item, cum officium oratoris esse ait, probare, delectare, flectere: in quibus primum sit necessitatis, secundum suavitatis, tertium victoriæ. Ad quod respondemus, illis etiam tribus hæc quinque contineri. Nam cum dicit, uidendum esse quid dicat, rerum inuentionem innuit: cum uero, quo quidque loco, collationem: & cum quomodo elocutionem, quae una actione quoq; secum trahit, quam idcirco eloquendi comitem hoc loco dicit orator. Nec a dicendi modo memoria excludi potest. nam si quis quarat, quomodo dicendum sit? respondendum est, Ornate & memoriter. Similiter dicendum de reliquis tribus. probare enim, est inuentionis: delectare, elocutionis: flectere autem, etsi est etiam collocationis, quatenus ad finem motumq; refertur, tamen magis inuentionis est, & elocutionis. Quinetiam quot sunt officia oratoris, ut in Oratore ait Cicero, tot sunt genera dicendi: subtile in probando, modicum in delectando, uehemens in flectendo: in quo uno uis omnis oratoris est. Sed de’ui oratoris hactenus, Iam de oratione breuiter uideamus: post latius omnia audiemus.
units.tr: But someone may ask here how these offices of the orator agree with those which, according to the third book of Aristotle's Rhetoric, are handed down in Cicero's Orator to Brutus. For, he says, three things must be seen by the orator: what he says, in what place he says each thing, and how. Likewise, when he says that the office of the orator is to prove, to delight, and to move, of which the first is of necessity, the second of charm, and the third of victory. To this we reply that these five are contained in those three. For when he says that one must consider what one says, he points to the discovery of things; when he says in what place each thing is said, he points to arrangement; and when he says how, he points to elocution, which also brings delivery with it, and which for this reason the orator here calls the companion of speaking. Nor can memory be excluded from the manner of speaking. For if someone asks how one should speak, the answer must be: ornately and from memory. The same should be said of the other three. For to prove belongs to invention, to delight to elocution; and to move, although it also belongs to arrangement insofar as it is referred to the end and the emotion, nevertheless belongs more to invention and elocution. Indeed, just as there are as many offices of the orator, as Cicero says in the Orator, so there are as many kinds of speaking: the subtle in proving, the moderate in delighting, the vehement in moving; and in this one thing lies the whole power of the orator. But so much for the orator; now let us briefly consider the speech, and afterwards we shall hear all things more fully.

units.la: Volumus autem statim initio Partitionum rem uniuersam Schemate ob oculos ponere, ut tota res sic melius percipiatur. Doctrina dicendi distribuitur in partes tres, in Vim oratoris, quæ habet Inventionem Rerum propriè, Verborum impropriè. Collocationem Rerum ad quas propriè refertur. Verborum impropriè. Elocutionem in verbis. Actionem eloquendi comitem, quæ est in Voce, Motu, Vultu. Memoriam, quæ custos est earum omnium. Orationè, cuius partes sunt quatuor: quarum aliæ utuntur ad Rem docendam, Narratio, Confirmatio. Impellendos animos, Principium, Peroratio. Quæstionem Infinitam, quæ Consultatio appellatur. Definitam, quæ Controversia & causa nominatur.
units.tr: We wish, moreover, to set out the whole subject at the very beginning of the Partitions in a diagram, so that the whole matter may be better grasped in this way. The doctrine of speaking is divided into three parts: into the power of the orator, which has invention, properly of things, improperly of words; arrangement of things, to which it is properly referred, and improperly of words; elocution, in words; action, the companion of speaking, which lies in voice, movement, and expression; and memory, which is the guardian of all these. The speech, whose parts are four: of which some are used to teach the matter, narration and confirmation; to move the minds, the exordium and peroration. The infinite question, which is called deliberation; the definite one, which is named controversy and case.

units.la: C. F. Quid? orationis quot sunt partes? C. P. Quatuor. earum duae valent ad rem docendam. narratio & confirmatio: ad impellendos animos duae, principium & peroratio.
units.tr: C. F. What then? How many parts does a speech have? C. P. Four. Two of them serve to teach the matter: narration and confirmation; two serve to move the minds: the exordium and peroration.

units.la: C. F. Quid? Orationis quot sunt partes?) Orationem oratoris pauci definiuerunt. Itaque primum illud sciendum est, quod & noster Cicero in Oratore tradit, quod quamquam omnis locutio oratio est: tamen unius oratoris locutionem, hoc proprio nomine, propter eius excellentiam significari. Oratio communiter Graece <bl>ἑρμηνία</bl> dicitur: hinc Aristoteles librum suum de oratione, sive mentis explicatione, <bl>περὶ</bl> <bl>ἑρμηνείας</bl> appellavit. Nam est oratio, ut idem philosophus ait, earum quae in animo sunt notionum interpres: scripta vero, orationis. Sed haec de qua hic loquimur, oratio, sic definiri potest: ut eam dicamus esse, cuiusque rei, quacunque dictione explicari possit, splendidam, copiosam, ornatam & aptam explicationem. Iam sequitur, ut de eius partibus videamus.
units.tr: C. F. What then? How many parts does a speech have? Few have defined the speech of the orator. So first we must know what our Cicero also teaches in the Orator: although every utterance is a speech, nevertheless the utterance of one orator is signified by this proper name, on account of its excellence. Speech is commonly called interpretation [ἑρμηνία] in Greek; hence Aristotle called his book on speech, or the explanation of the mind, On Interpretation [περὶ ἑρμηνείας]. For speech, as the same philosopher says, is the interpreter of the notions that are in the mind, while writings are the interpreters of speech. But this speech of which we are speaking here may be defined thus: that we say it is a splendid, copious, ornate, and fitting explanation of whatever thing can be explained by any diction. Now it follows that we should see what its parts are.

units.la: C. P. Quatuor.) Mediam viam tenuit Cicero. nam Aristoteles & duas facit, & quatuor: alii vero plures. Sunt (inquit Aristoteles libro 3. Rhetoricorum) partes orationis duae, necesse est enim
units.tr: C. P. Four. Cicero took a middle way. For Aristotle makes two parts and also four, and others make more. There are (says Aristotle in the third book of the Rhetoric) two parts of a speech, for it is necessary

units.la: [marginal note at right, illegible] enim rem primò, de qua agitur, exponere: deinde illam argumentis confirmare. horum autem alterum Propositio, alterum Fides appellatur. quemadmodum si quis diuideret aliquid in quæstionem & demonstrationem. Deinde paulo post: Necessariæ igitur sunt partes duæ, propositum & confirmatio. ac proprie quidem hæ duæ partes sunt: sed si plures fuerint, tunc erit proœmium, propositio, confirmatio, peroratio. Quoniam autem his aliqui, atque adeò ipse Cicero in Rhetoricis, addunt diuisionem siue partitionem, narrationem, & refutationem: sciendum est, diuisionem sub propositione contineri, & refutationem sub confirmatione, quæ communi nomine ab Aristotele πίστις, hoc est fides nominatur. Atque ita, ut plena fit partitio, sex partes numerabimus: Exordium, Narrationem, Partitionem, Confirmationem, Refutationem, & Perorationem. Est autem Exordium, principium orationis, per quod animus auditoris, aut iudicis constituitur uel apparatur ad audiendum. Narratio est, rerum gestarum, aut ut gestarum expositio. Partitio est, per quam aperimus, quid conueniat, & quid in controuersia sit, & per quam apponimus quibus de rebus simus dicturi. Confirmatio est, nostrorum argumentorum expositio, cum asseueratione. Confutatio siue reprehensio
units.tr: [marginal note at right, illegible] first to set out the matter under discussion, and then to confirm it by arguments. Of these, the one is called the proposition, the other the proof, just as if someone were to divide something into question and demonstration. Then a little later: Two parts are therefore necessary, the proposition and the confirmation. Strictly speaking these two are the parts; but if there are more, there will be the introduction, the proposition, the confirmation, and the peroration. Since some, and indeed Cicero himself in the Rhetoric, add division or partition, narration, and refutation, we must know that division is contained under the proposition, and refutation under the confirmation, which by Aristotle is called by the common name proof [πίστις]. And so, to make the partition complete, we shall count six parts: the exordium, the narration, the partition, the confirmation, the refutation, and the peroration. The exordium is the beginning of the speech, by which the mind of the hearer or judge is disposed or prepared to listen. The narration is the exposition of things done, or as done. The partition is that by which we make clear what agrees and what is in dispute, and by which we set out the matters about which we are going to speak. The confirmation is the exposition of our arguments, with assertion. The refutation or reprehension

units.la: c. f. Quid? orationis quot sunt partes? c. p. Quatuor. earum duae valent ad rem docendam. narratio & confirmatio: ad impellendos animos duae, principium & peroratio.
units.tr: C. F. What are the parts of an oration? C. P. Four. Of these, two serve to teach the matter, the narration and the confirmation; two serve to move the minds of the hearers, the exordium and the peroration.

units.la: C. F. Quid? Orationis quot sunt partes? ) Orationem oratoris pauci definiuerunt. Itaque primum illud sciendum est, quod & noster Cicero in Oratore tradit, quod quamquam omnis locutio oratio est: tamen unius oratoris locutionem, hoc proprio nomine, propter eius excellentiam significari. Oratio communiter Graece λόγος dicitur: hinc Aristoteles librum suum de oratione, sive mentis explicatione, περὶ ἑρμηνείας appellavit. Nam est oratio, ut idem philosophus ait, earum quae in animo sunt notionum interpres: scripta vero, orationis. Sed haec de qua hic loquimur, oratio, sic definiri potest: ut eam dicamus esse, cuiusque rei, quaecunque dictione explicari possit, splendidam, copiosam, ornatam & aptam explicationem. Iam sequitur, ut de eius partibus videamus.
units.tr: C. F. What are the parts of an oration? Few orators have defined an oration. So the first thing to know is what our Cicero also teaches in the Orator: although every utterance is a speech, the utterance of a single orator is signified by this name alone, on account of its excellence. In general, oratio is called λόγος [logos] in Greek; hence Aristotle named his book on oratio, or the explanation of the mind, περὶ ἑρμηνείας [peri hermeneias]. For, as the same philosopher says, speech is the interpreter of the notions that are in the mind, and writing is the interpreter of speech. But the oratio we are speaking of here can be defined thus: that it is a splendid, copious, ornate and fitting explanation, in whatever words can be given, of any matter whatever. Now it follows that we should look at its parts.

units.la: C. P. Quatuor.) Mediam viam tenuit Cicero. nam Aristoteles & duas facit, & quatuor: alij vero plures. Sunt (inquit Aristoteles libro 3. Rhetoricorum) partes orationis duae. necesse est
units.tr: C. P. Four. Cicero took the middle way. For Aristotle makes two parts, and also four, and others make more. There are (says Aristotle in book 3 of the Rhetoric) two parts of an oration. It is necessary

units.la: enim rem primò, de qua agitur, exponere: deinde illam argumentis confirmare. horum autem alterum Propositio, alterum Fides appellatur. quemadmodum si quis diuideret aliquid in quæstionem & demonstrationem. Deinde paulo post: Necessariæ igitur sunt partes duæ, propositum & confirmatio. ac proprie quidem hæ duæ partes sunt: sed si plures fuerint, tunc erit proœmium, propositio, confirmatio, peroratio. Quoniam autem his aliqui, atque adeò ipse Cicero in Rhetoricis, addunt diuisionem siue partitionem, narrationem, & refutationem: sciendum est, diuisionem sub propositione contineri, & refutationem sub confirmatione, quæ communi nomine ab Aristotele πίστις, hoc est fides nominatur. Atque ita, ut plena sit partitio, sex parteis numerabimus: Exordium, Narrationem, Partitionem, Confirmationem, Refutationem, & Perorationem. Est autem Exordium, principium orationis, per quod animus auditoris, aut iudicis constituitur vel apparatur ad audiendum. Narratio est, rerum gestarum, aut ut gestarum expositio. Partitio est, per quam aperimus, quid contineat, & quid in controversia sit, & per quam apponimus quibus de rebus simus dicturi. Confirmatio est, nostrorum argumentorum expositio, cum asseveratione. Confutatio siue reprehenfio est, contrariorum locorum dissolutio, quæ fiat aut diluendo, aut infirmando, aut elevando. Peroratio, siue Conclusio est, artificiosus terminus totius orationis. Singularum autem partium partes suis explicabimus locis. Illud porrò attendendum, quod orator dicit, earum partium quasdam ad rem docendam valere, alias ad animos impellendos. Quibus verbis significat, quosdam fines partibus orationis esse propositos, ut (exempli causa) principio & perorationi, motum: narrationi autem & confirmationi, doctrinam siue intelligentiam. Sed quoniam duos tantum fines recensset, cum alibi tres: admirari aliquis possit. Erit (inquit in Oratore) eloquens is, qui in foro causisq; ciuilibus ita dicit, ut probet, ut delectet, ut flectat: probare necessitatis est, delectare suauitatis, flectere victoriæ. Idem de optimo genere Oratorum: Optimus est enim orator, inquit, qui dicendo animos audientium & docet, & delectat, & permouet. Docere debitum est, delectare honorarium, permouere necessarium.
units.tr: first to set out the matter under discussion, and then to confirm it by arguments. Of these, the one is called the proposition, the other the proof; just as if someone were to divide something into a question and a demonstration. Then a little later: Two parts are necessary, then, the proposition and the confirmation. Strictly speaking these are the two parts; but if there are more, there will be the proem, the proposition, the confirmation, and the peroration. Since, however, some add to these, and Cicero himself in the Rhetoric, the division or partition, the narration, and the refutation, we should note that the division is contained under the proposition, and the refutation under the confirmation, which Aristotle calls by the common name πίστις [pistis], that is, proof. And so, to make the partition complete, we shall count six parts: the exordium, the narration, the partition, the confirmation, the refutation, and the peroration. The exordium is the beginning of the oration, by which the mind of the hearer or judge is disposed or prepared to listen. The narration is the exposition of things done, or as they were done. The partition is that by which we make clear what the matter comprises and what is in dispute, and by which we set out what we are going to speak about. The confirmation is the exposition of our arguments, with assertion. The confutation or reprehension is the dissolution of opposing arguments, which is done either by refuting, by weakening, or by lessening them. The peroration, or conclusion, is the skilful end of the whole oration. We shall explain the parts of each part in their own places. It must further be noted that the orator says some of these parts serve to teach the matter, others to move the minds. By these words he signifies that certain ends have been set for the parts of the oration: for example, motion for the exordium and the peroration, but instruction or understanding for the narration and the confirmation. But since he here lists only two ends, while elsewhere he gives three, one may well be surprised. (In the Orator he says) the eloquent man will be one who in the forum and in civil cases speaks so as to prove, to delight, and to sway: to prove is a necessity, to delight a charm, to sway a victory. The same, of the best kind of orator: For the best orator, he says, is one who in speaking both teaches, delights and moves the minds of his hearers. To teach is a duty, to delight an honour, to move a necessity.

units.la: De Oratore autem lib. 2. Ita ratio omnis dicendi, inquit, tribus ad persuadendum rebus est nixa, ut probemus vera esse ea quæ defendimus, ut conciliemus nobis eos qui audiunt, ut animos eorum ad quemcunq; causam pertulabit motu uocemus. Quæ sententia ad verbum sumpta est ex Aristot. Rhet.
units.tr: But in De Oratore book 2 he says: So all the method of speaking, he says, rests on three things for persuading: that we prove the things we defend to be true, that we win over those who hear us, and that we stir their minds to whatever cause he has brought forward. This opinion is taken word for word from Aristotle's Rhetoric.

units.la: lib.2. Sed ut hosce locos concilemus, illud ani-maduertendum est,illis duob. hæc tria contineri. Nam cum in Partitionibus dicit, Ad impellendos animos duæ:motum,quo animi impelluntur, signi ficauit.Impellere enim est,motum animis afferre. Atqui duplex est motus:unus moderatus, ad conciliandum,qui ἦθος dicitur Græcè:alter uehementior,qui πάθος appellatur. 'illo genere in exordijs,altero in amplificationibus & perorationibus utimur. Ac de his duobus generibus multa M. Fabius,Inst.orat.lib.6.cap.3.Sed diuinitùs & breuiter Cicero in Oratore: Duo sunt etiam, inquit,quæ bene tractata ab oratore, admirabilem eloquentiam faciunt. quorum alterum est, quod Græci ἡθικὸν uocant, ad naturam & mores, & ad omnem uitæ consuetudinem accommodatum: alterum, quod ijdem παθητικὸν nominant, quo perturbantur animi, & concitantur, in quo uno regnat oratio.Illud superius,come, iucundum, ad beneuolentiam conciliandam paratum:hoc uehementius,incensum,incitatum,quo caussæ eripiuntur, quòd cum rapidè fertur,sustineri nullo pacto potest.Hæc duo genera motuum ex uno codemq; sonte,nimirum ab animi ui, quæ appetitus dicitur, fluunt.Sed quoniam ea uis est duplex:una, in qua irarum existit ardor:altera,quæ uoluptate,cupiditateq; alitur, ut Aristoteles & Plato & Galenus nus docent: ex illa turbidi & concitati, ex hac leniores & suaviores animorum existunt motus. Bi partitam igitur motuum rationem in Partitionibus his est secutus, ut in diuidendo paucitatem illam, de qua de Inuentione libro primo praecipit, retineret: in aliis vero, in quibus hanc partiendi viam non tam subtiliter persequi voluit, distin ctius tripertito distribuit, genere relicto, partibus retentis, quod copiosius et maius fore existimabat.
units.tr: lib.2. But to reconcile these passages, we must notice that these three things are contained in those two. For when in the Partitions he says, two things for moving the minds, he signified the motion by which the minds are moved. For to impel is to bring motion to the minds. Yet the motion is twofold: one moderate, for winning over, which is called ἦθος [ethos] in Greek; the other more vehement, which is called πάθος [pathos]. We use the former kind in exordia, the latter in amplifications and perorations. M. Fabius, Institutes of Oratory book 6 chapter 3, has much on these two kinds. But Cicero in the Orator says it divinely and briefly: There are also two things, he says, which, well handled by the orator, make eloquence admirable. Of these, one is what the Greeks call ἡθικὸν [ethikon], suited to nature and manners and to every habit of life; the other, which the same call παθητικὸν [pathetikon], by which the minds are stirred and roused, and in which alone oratory reigns. The former, gentle and pleasing, is ready for winning goodwill; the latter, more vehement, inflamed and incited, by which causes are snatched away, since when it is carried along violently it cannot be restrained by any means. These two kinds of motion flow from one and the same source, namely the force of the mind, which is called appetite. But since this force is twofold: one in which the heat of anger exists, the other which is nourished by pleasure and desire, as Aristotle, Plato and Galen teach, from the former arise disturbed and agitated motions of the mind, from the latter gentler and sweeter ones. He has therefore followed this divided account of the motions in the Partitions, so that in dividing he retained that brevity which he teaches in book 1 of On Invention; but in other places, where he did not wish to pursue this way of dividing so finely, he distributed them more distinctly into three parts, leaving the genus and retaining the parts, which he thought would be fuller and more effective.

units.la: Possemus etiam dicere, cum ex tribus virtutibus oratoris, duas tantum posuisse, docere & impellere: propterea quod haec sint illa praecipua & necessaria. nam ut de Optimo genere oratorum ait, Docere debitum est, delectare honorarium, permouere necessarium. quod enim honorarium est, neque debitum, neque necessarium videri potest.
units.tr: We could also say that, of the three virtues of the orator, he set down only two, teaching and moving, because these are the chief and necessary ones. For as he says of the best kind of orators: To teach is a duty, to delight an honour, to move a necessity. For what is an honour, and not a duty, cannot be seen to be necessary.

units.la: Et debitum est, quod iure praestare debeas: necessarium, sine quo orator esse non possis: id est, neque munere tuo fungi, neque persuadere. Et docere ita debet orator, ut tamen sit ei cum multis aliis commune: permouere autem sic eius est proprium, ut in nullum alium transferri possit. Sed illud quoque aliquem mouere posset, quod in Oratore dixit, Probare necessitatis: de Optimo autem genere oratorum, Permouere necessarium. Sed hoc ita intelligendum est, ut necessarium dixerit in Oratore, pro eo quod debitum est, & cum dixit, Permouere necessarium, ei qui uelit uictoriam adipisci: hoc est, oratione persuadere. Nam tota spes uincendi, in illis uehementioribus permotionibus sita est, quibus animi in quam uelis partem flectuntur.
units.tr: And a duty is what you ought to perform by right; a necessity is that without which the orator cannot be an orator, that is, without which he can neither discharge his office nor persuade. And the orator ought to teach in such a way that this is still common to him with many others; but to move is so much his own that it can be transferred to no one else. Yet someone might also be troubled by what he said in the Orator, To prove is a necessity, and in the passage on the best kind of orators, To move is a necessity. But this must be understood so that he called it a necessity in the Orator in place of what is a duty; and when he said, To move is a necessity, he meant for one who wishes to obtain victory, that is, to persuade by speech. For the whole hope of winning lies in those more vehement motions, by which minds are turned towards whatever side you wish.

units.la: C. F. Quid? quæstio quas nam habet partes? C. P. Infinitam, quam cōsultationem appello: & definitā, quam caussam nomino.
units.tr: C. F. What? What parts does a question have? C. P. The unlimited, which I call the consultation; and the limited, which I name the cause.

units.la: C. F. Quid? Quæstio quas nā habet partes?) Indicatis duorum capitum partibus totius doctrinæ dicendi, iam ad tertiā se cōfert filius, hoc est, ad materiē subiectā oratori. nā id nomine Quæstionis intelligimus. Est enim quæstio, quā cōmuni nomine rhetores Græci στάσεις solent appellare, quicquid ad disceptandū proponitur, siue id de quo agitur & quaeritur, à quærendo & dubitādo appellata. Definit aūt quæstione Arist. de Interpret. in hūc modū: Quæstio, inquit, est respōsiōis petitio: ut uel propositio explicetur, uel pars altera repugnātiæ. Cicero aūt in Academicis: Quæstio, inquit, est appetitio cognitionis: quæstionis qς finis, inuētio. Possumus etiā breuissimē definire, ut dicamus: Quæstio Rhetorica, est quæstio probabilis. Vniuersam oratoris materiē in duas partes distribuit orator, in quæstionem scilicet infinitam, finitam, quæ θέσις dicitur Græcè: & definitam, quæ ὑπόθεσις, quæ partitione indicat, quod antea diximus, materiem oratoris nullo proprio aut definito genere contineri. quod etiam confirmat illa Aristotelis verba Rhet. 1. Rhetorica, inquit, de omni pene dixerim propositá quæstione apposite ad persuadendum dicere potest. De omni quæstione, inquit, nimirum tam definita quàm infinita: quandoquidem hæc est prima & summa quæstionum partitio. Sed illud etiam non est prætereundum, utrunq; genus non uno appellari modo. nam infinita illa, tum cófultatio tum propositum nominatur: definita verò, & cótrouerfia & cauffa. Quid, quod etiam nomine generis infinita uocatur? Quæstio enim dicitur à Cicerone, lib. 2. de Oratore. Prior illa infinita idcirco appellatur, quòd nullis quasi personarum & temporum feptis coclufa & circumscripta teneatur: altera uero definita, quòd habeat controuersiam in fe, in dicendo positam, cum certarum personarum & teporum interpositione, quemadmodum multis in locis autor noster describit. Hanc autem definitá, quæ causa dicitur, solam oratori subiectam materiem putauit Cicero adolescens adhuc, ut lib. 1. de Inuentione apparet: fortassis Aristotelem fecutus, quem tunc non fatis intellexit. Nam quemadmodum oftedimus, Aristoteles ipse omnem quæstionem fiionem
units.tr: C. F. What? What parts does a question have? Having indicated the parts of the two chapters of the whole doctrine of speaking, the son now turns to the third, that is, to the matter subject to the orator; for we understand this by the name of question. For a question, which the Greek rhetoricians commonly call στάσεις [stasis], is whatever is put forward for debate, named from seeking and doubting, whether the matter is one about which there is dispute and inquiry. Aristotle in On Interpretation defines a question in this way: A question, he says, is a request for an answer, either to explain a proposition, or the other part of a contradiction. Cicero in the Academics: A question, he says, is a seeking of knowledge; and the end of a question is discovery. We can also define it very briefly, saying: a rhetorical question is a probable question. The orator divides the whole matter of the orator into two parts, namely the unlimited question, which is called θέσις [thesis] in Greek, and the limited, which is ὑπόθεσις [hypothesis]; by this partition he indicates what we said before, that the matter of the orator is contained under no proper or definite kind. This Aristotle's words in Rhetoric book 1 also confirm: Rhetoric, he says, may speak apt to persuade on almost any question put forward, I would say. On any question, he says, certainly both limited and unlimited, since this is the first and highest division of questions. But it must also not be passed over that each kind is not called by one name only. For the unlimited is called both consultation and proposition; the limited is called both controversy and cause. What more, is the unlimited also called by the name of genus? For it is called a question by Cicero, in De Oratore book 2. The former is called unlimited because it is held as if unbounded and uncircumscribed by any fences of persons and times; the latter, limited, because it has in itself a controversy, placed in the speaking, with the interposition of certain persons and times, as our author describes in many places. Cicero, while still a young man, thought that this limited matter, which is called the cause, was the only matter subject to the orator, as appears from book 1 of On Invention, perhaps following Aristotle, whom he did not then sufficiently understand. For, as we have shown, Aristotle himself made every question the matter of rhetoric.

units.la: {*} Pages end mid-word in the printed text; the last line is partly cut off at the foot. stionem quasi materiē Rhetoricæ subiecit. Quòd si posteà Rhetoricæ genera numero tria idē Aristoteles statuit, & ex ijs caussarum totidem genera: id fecit, ut ostenderet id in quo sæpius uersaretur orator, non quid posset suscipere. Quare stat sententia, cum esse oratorem, qui quæcunque res inciderit, quæ sit dictione explicanda, prudenter & compositè, & ornatè, & memoriter dicat, cum quadam etiam actionis dignitate. Nam etiam si materia aliarum sit facultatum, ornatus tamē & tractatio semper erit oratoris, ut copiosè ostendit. Cicero de Orat. lib. 1. Hæsce quæstiones suo loco exemplis illustrabimus. nam suo quæque, & idoneo loco dicenda sunt.
units.tr: For Aristotle himself put every question as the subject matter of rhetoric. If he afterwards fixed three kinds of rhetoric, and from them the same number of kinds of cause, he did so to show what the orator most often deals with, not what he is able to take on. So the view stands that the orator is one who, whatever matter arises that must be explained in speech, speaks prudently, fittingly, ornately and memorably, and with a certain dignity of delivery as well. For even if the subject matter belongs to other skills, the ornament and treatment of it will always belong to the orator, as Cicero shows at length. Cicero, De Oratore, book 1. We will illustrate these questions with examples in their proper place, since each must be discussed in its own fitting place.

units.la: DE INVENTIONE.
units.tr: ON INVENTION.

units.la: C. F. Quoniam igitur primum est inuenire Oratoris, quid quæret?
units.tr: C. F. Since, then, the first task of the orator is to invent, what does he seek?

units.la: C. P. Vt inueniat, quemadmodum fidem faciat eis, quib. uolet persuadere, & quemadmodū motum eorum animis afferat.
units.tr: C. P. That he may invent how to make his hearers believe what he wishes to persuade them of, and how to stir their minds.

units.la: C. F. Quibus rebus fides fit? C. P. Argumētis, quæ ducuntur ex locis, aut in re ipsa infinitis, aut assumptis.
units.tr: C. F. By what means is belief produced? C. P. By arguments, which are drawn either from the places, infinite in the matter itself, or from things assumed from outside.

units.la: C. F. Quoniam igitur primum est inuenire oratoris. ) Iam redit ad inuētionem, quæ primas sibi partes,in officijs Oratoris deposcit: eius que munus & parteis quærit. Idcirco dixit, primum oratoris scilicet officium est, inuenire. Huic duas partes subijcit pater, fidem nimirum, & motum: id est, ut doceat fiue probet, & motum animis afferat.quod quidem fit, ut paulo ante diximus,tum conciliando,tum flectendo, fiue permouendo. Sed quærat aliquis, an non permouendis etiam animis fides fiat? Respondeo, verum esse. Sub fide enim, quam πίςιν appellauit Ariftoteles, tum probandi, tum mouedi ratio cõtinetur.Sed quoniam utrunq; separatim fieri poteft,aut alterū (nimirum motus) omitti, idcirco noster autor sub inuctione subijcere maluit tum fidem,tum etiam motum, & utrunq; ad perfuadendū (qui finis est cratoris& propofitū) refertur.Nam quoniam Rhetorica, ut diximus, est facultas & uis quædā perspiciendi, quid in quaq; re fit ad perfuadendū accommodatū:iure quærit, quid quærendum fit ad persuadendum. Quid autem fit motus & fides,postea dicet.
units.tr: C. F. "Since, then, the first task of the orator is to invent." Now he returns to invention, which claims first place among the duties of the orator, and he asks what its function and parts are. So he said that the first duty of the orator is, of course, to invent. The father assigns two parts to it, namely belief and emotion: that is, that he should teach or prove, and stir emotion in the minds of his hearers. This is done, as we said a little earlier, both by winning goodwill and by bending, that is, by moving. But someone may ask whether belief is not also produced by moving the emotions. I reply that this is true. For under belief, which Aristotle called faith [πίστις], both the method of proving and the method of moving are contained. But since each can be done separately, and one of them (namely emotion) can be omitted, our author preferred to place under invention both belief and emotion, and to refer both to persuasion, which is the aim and purpose of the orator. For since rhetoric, as we said, is the skill and power of seeing what is suited to persuasion in any matter, he rightly asks what must be sought in order to persuade. What emotion and belief are, he will say later.

units.la: C. F. Quibus rebus fides fit?) Primū cum dicit,fides fit,alludit ad fidei Etymologiam,quam Stoici (teste Cicerone de Offic.lib.1.)adhibebāt: nimirū fidem dicta esse,quod fiat quod dictū est. Deinde illud est obseruandum,facere fidem nihil aliud esse,quàm probare aliquid, & ratione confirmare. firmare. Item illud quod dixit, Quibus rebus: etsi res & uerba inuenienda sunt, tamē rerum inuentio & inquisitio prior esse debet, uerborum posterior. quoniam, ut ipse paulo ante dixit, proprie in rebus inuenire, in uerbis eloqui dicitur. Nam quoniam inuentio prior elocutione est, merito rerum cura praecedit. Rerum autem nomine quid intelligat, iam supra diximus, nimirum argumenta atq; sententias.
units.tr: C. F. "By what means is belief produced?" In saying first "belief is produced," he alludes to the etymology of fides (belief), which the Stoics used (as Cicero testifies in De Officiis, book 1): namely that fides is so called because what is said is done [fiat quod dictum est]. Next, it must be observed that making belief is nothing other than proving something and confirming it by reasoning. Likewise, in the words "By what means," although both things and words must be invented, the invention and inquiry of things ought to come first and that of words afterwards, since, as he himself said a little earlier, one is said to invent properly in things and to speak in words. For since invention comes before elocution, the care of things rightly precedes. By "things" he understands, as we said above, arguments and sentiments.

units.la: C. P. Argumentis, quae ducuntur ex locis.) Cum Rhetores hanc partē Dialecticæ, quæ inuenied orum argumentorum disciplinam continet, in suis praeceptis inserunt: non idcirco faciunt, quòd eius doctrinæ praecepta tradere, ad se pertinere putent: sed ut adolescentes admonent, debere eos Dialecticam discere, & ad Rhetoricā discendam afferre. Nam quoniā multi Rhetoricā, pauci uero Dialecticā tum discerent, prudentes uiri fonteis etiam, unde argumenta ducerētur, indicabant. Id ostenditur ex eo, quod neq; Hermagoras, neq; Hermogenes, ullam horum communium locorū in suis Rhetoricis mentionem fecerunt, sed locos tantū causarum & statuū tradiderūt. Quare factū est, ut necesse fuerit Ciceronem, quoties de hac arte scriberet, semper hosce communes locos satis enumerare, et digitos (quod dicitur) ad fonteis intedere. Quamobrē & nos quoq; breuissima indicatione contenti crimus: faciemus q;, quod Antonius lib. de Orat. 2. faciendi consulit, sedes uidelicet, & tanquam domicilia omnium argumentorum commonstrabimus: & ea breuiter illustrabimus, uerbisq; definiemus. Si quis autem copiosiorem explicationem requirat, uel Topica Ciceronis, cum Commentarijs quae ad ea scripsimus, legat: uel Perrionij secundum de Dialectica librum. Nam quos idem Antonius appellat riuulos, id est statuum locos proprios, eos diligenter postea, & accuratè nobis ipse Cicero explicabit. Primùm igitur locos Cicero in insitos & assumptos distribuit: quae distributio sumpta est ex primo Aristotelis lib. Rhetoricorum: Probationum autem, inquit ille, aliae quidem expertes artis, aliae uero artificiosae sunt. Expertes artis eas uoco, quae nostra opera non pariuntur, sed extrinsecus assumuntur: ut testimonia, & quaestiones, & eius generis cetera. Artificiosas autem eas, quas artis praesidio discimus: & cū inhaerent in ipsa re, reperiri industria nostra, atque inde erui possunt. Ita in superiore genere, de tractandis argumentis: in hoc etiam de inueniendis, cogitandum est. quae uerba Cicero in secundum de Oratore transtulit. Quod autem dicit, In re ipsa infitis: intelligit, in ipsa causa, siue quaestione. Sic enim saepe rem intelligit. C. F. Quos uocas locos? C. P. Eos, in quibus latent argumenta. C. F. Quid est argumentum? C. P. Probabile inuentum, ad faciendum fidem. C. F. Quomodo igitur duo genera ista diuidis? C. P. Quae sine arte putantur, ea remota appello, ut testimonia. C. F. Quid insita? C. P. Quae inhaerent in ipsa re.
units.tr: C. P. "By arguments, which are drawn from the places." Rhetoricians insert into their precepts this part of Dialectic, which contains the discipline of inventing arguments, not because they think it is their task to hand down the precepts of that teaching, but to warn young men that they ought to learn Dialectic and bring it to the study of rhetoric. For since many learned rhetoric but few learned dialectic at that time, wise men also pointed out the sources from which arguments might be drawn. This is shown by the fact that neither Hermagoras nor Hermogenes made any mention of these common places in their rhetorics, but only handed down the places of causes and issues. Hence it was necessary for Cicero, whenever he wrote on this art, always to list these common places sufficiently and, as the saying goes, to point his finger at the sources. Therefore we too will be content with a very brief indication, and we will do what Antonius recommends in De Oratore, book 2: we will show the seats, as it were the dwelling places, of all arguments, and briefly illustrate them and define them in words. If anyone wants a fuller explanation, let him read either Cicero's Topics with the commentaries we wrote on them, or the second book of Perrionius on Dialectic. For the streamlets which the same Antonius calls the proper places of the issues, Cicero himself will afterwards explain carefully and accurately. First, then, Cicero divides the places into inherent and assumed; this division was taken from the first book of Aristotle's Rhetoric: "Of proofs," he says, "some are outside art, others are artificial. I call those outside art which are not produced by our effort but are taken from outside, such as testimonies, and questions, and other things of that kind. Artificial proofs are those which we acquire by the help of art, and which, since they inhere in the matter itself, can be found by our diligence and drawn out from it." So in the earlier kind we must think about treating arguments, and in this one about inventing them. Cicero translated these words in the second book of De Oratore. When he says "inherent in the matter itself," he means in the cause itself, or the question; for he often uses "matter" in this sense. C. F. What do you call places? C. P. Those in which arguments lie hidden. C. F. What is an argument? C. P. A probable thing found, for producing belief. C. F. How then do you divide these two kinds? C. P. Those which are thought to be without art I call remote, such as testimonies. C. F. What are the inherent ones? C. P. Those which inhere in the matter itself.

units.la: C. F. Quos uocas locos?) Definitionem locorum quaerit filius: & respondet pater, Aristotelis uerbis. Eos enim, inquit libro primo: ego Dialecticos & Oratorios syllogismos uoco, qui ducuntur ex locis, in quibus latent argumenta: quos etiam ob id sedes argumentorum appellat, aequaliter omnibus communes. Quae definitio Aristotelis est diligenter obseruanda. Communes enim appellat, quoniam locorum alij sunt qui ad mores, alij ad naturam, alij ad ciuilem scientiam pertinet. Alij uero nullius proprie artis aut facultatis sunt: quoniam nullam habent certam subiectam materiam, sed adhibentur ad omne genus quaestionis communiter tractandum, cuiusmodi sunt ij quos Dialecticos appellamus.
units.tr: C. F. "What do you call places?" The son asks for a definition of places, and the father answers in Aristotle's words. For in the first book, he says: "I call dialectical and rhetorical syllogisms those which are drawn from places in which arguments lie hidden; which he also calls the seats of arguments for that reason, being common to all alike." This definition of Aristotle must be carefully observed. He calls them common because some places pertain to character, others to nature, others to civil knowledge. Others, however, belong properly to no art or skill, since they have no fixed subject matter of their own, but are used to treat every kind of question in common; such are those which we call dialectical.

units.la: C. F. Quid est argumentum?) Nunc argumenti mentione facta, poscit argumenti definitionem. Nam cum argumentū multis modis dicātur, definiēdum erat: ut quomodo in arte hac acciperetur, intelligi posset. Argumentum igitur di cit esse probabile inuentum, ad faciendam fidem: nimirum ab arguendo, id est, ostendendo, demonstrando, ꝙ probando diāu. ut illud Virgilij, Degeneres animos timor arguit. —
units.tr: C. F. "What is an argument?" Now that the mention of argument has been made, he asks for a definition of argument. For since "argument" is used in many ways, it had to be defined, so that it could be understood how the word is taken in this art. So he says that an argument is a probable thing found, for producing belief, namely from arguing, that is, showing, demonstrating, or proving. As in the line of Virgil: "Fear betrays degenerate spirits."

units.la: Est autē probabile, id quod sere fieri solet, aut quod in opinione positū est, aut quod habet in se ad hoc quandā similitudinē: siue id falsum est, si- ue uerū. de Inuent. lib. 1. Quæ definitio ex primo Rhetoricæ Aristotelis sumpta est: nec est admodum dissimilis ei, imò re ipsa idem continet, quod illa alia, quam initio Topicorū protulit idē Aristoteles: Probabilia, inquit, sunt, quæ probātur aut omnibus, aut plurimis, aut certè sapientibus. atque ea quæ huiusmodi probātur, aut sere fieri solent, aut uera sunt, aut quandam ueri similitudinem habent. In probabilibus cautio una adhibenda est, ut ea generibus hominum accōmodemus. ut si de hominum genere loquamur, ea probabilia afferāmus, quæ omnibus hominibus probentur, aut plu- rimis: sin uerò sermo fit ad priuata quædam genera hominum, cuiusmodi sunt, quæ ab ætate, patria, gente, sexu, conditione nominantur, ijs probabilib. utamur, quæ ei generi de quo agitur cōueniant. Et hoc est quod indicauit Aristot. Rhet. lib. 1. lib.1. Neque igitur,inquit, Rhetorica probabile quærit ciusmodi, quod unius alicuius opinioni cō ueniat,ut Socratis,aut Hippiæ:sed quod omnibus ad quos sermo habetur, qui ita animo sunt assecti,quemadmodū etiā Dialectica. Sed dicat aliquis, an nō etiam ex ueris interdū & necessarijs, non modò ex probabilib.& uerisimilibus,concludit tum Dialecticus, tum Orator? Fateor id fieri posse,& interdum quoq; euenire: uerū quoniā id raro fit,& fere probabiliter concludit,ideo de eo loquuntur,quod sæpius accidit, & in quo potissimum uersantur.Ex maiore enim parte, pleræque res nominantur,ut Cicero ait Tusculanarū quæ- stionū lib.5. Idcirco de Inuēt.lib.1. Omnis aut argumētatio, inquit Cicero,quæ ex his locis quos cō memoramus,sumitur,aut probabilis,aut necessaria debebit esse. Probabilis:ut,Si mater est,diliget filiū: Si auarus est, negligit iusiurandū: & huiusmodi. Necessaria uero:ut,Lac habet,igitur peperit: & quoniam cicatrix est,fuit uulnus.
units.tr: Now a probable thing is that which usually happens, or which rests on opinion, or which has some likeness to this; whether it is false or true. De Invent., book 1. This definition is taken from the first book of Aristotle's Rhetoric, and it is not very different from that other one which Aristotle himself gave at the beginning of the Topics: "Probable things," he says, "are those which are approved by all, or by most, or at least by the wise; and such things as are approved in this way either usually happen, or are true, or have a certain likeness to truth. In probable matters one caution must be observed: we should adapt them to kinds of men. So if we speak of the human race in general, we should bring forward probabilities that are approved by all men or most; but if the speech is directed to some particular kinds of men, such as those named from age, country, nation, sex, or condition, we should use probabilities that suit the kind with which we are dealing." This is what Aristotle indicated in the first book of the Rhetoric. Neither, he says, does rhetoric seek probability of the sort that agrees with the opinion of one particular man, such as Socrates or Hippias, but what is approved by all to whom the speech is addressed, who are disposed in mind in this way, just as dialectic does too. But someone may say: does not the dialectician, and the orator too, sometimes also conclude from things that are true and necessary, not only from probable and likely ones? I grant that this can happen and sometimes does happen; but since it happens rarely, and for the most part he concludes in a probable way, therefore they speak of what happens more often, and what they chiefly deal with. For most things are named from the greater part, as Cicero says in the fifth book of the Tusculan Disputations. Hence in De Inventione, book 1, Cicero says: "Every argument drawn from those places which we have mentioned must be either probable or necessary. Probable, as: If she is a mother, she loves her son; if he is greedy, he neglects his oath; and things of that kind. Necessary, as: She has milk, therefore she has given birth; and since there is a scar, there was a wound."

units.la: C. F. Quomodo igitur duo ista genera diuidis? ) De infitis & affumptis loquitur, ut postea in partitione locorum positum est,atq; utriusque quærit formas & partes.
units.tr: C. F. How, then, do you divide these two kinds? ) He speaks of inartificial and artificial proofs, as is set out later in the division of the topics, and he asks for the forms and parts of each.

units.la: C. P. Quæ sine arte putantur, ea remota appello, ut testimonia. ) Remota appellat, quod unre ipsa non sint,sed extrinsecus assumantur.
units.tr: C. P. Those things which are thought to lie outside art, I call remote, such as testimonies. ) He calls them remote because they are not in the thing itself but are brought in from outside.

units.la: d Nam quicquid assumitur foris, in re ipsa non fuit. Atq; ita in Topicis definit: Testimonium autem nunc dicimus, omne quod ab aliqua re externa sumitur, ad faciendam fidem. Sed non omnia pondus testimonij habent. ad faciendam enim fidem, in testimonio, uel in teste autoritas quaeritur. Sed autoritatem aut uirtus adfert, aut fortuna. Nam quos aliqua uirtute praeditos putamus, in eis autoritatem esse credimus. idem facimus in his, in quibus ingenium, opes, aetatem, artes, usum, potentiam esse uidemus.
units.tr: For whatever is brought in from outside was not in the matter itself. And so he defines it in the Topics: "Now we call testimony whatever is taken from some external thing to create belief. But not all testimonies carry weight. For in testimony, or in the witness, what is sought in creating belief is authority. Authority is conferred either by virtue or by fortune. For we believe that authority resides in those whom we think endowed with some virtue. We do the same with those in whom we see talent, wealth, age, skill, experience or power."

units.la: C. F. Quid insita?) Nunc non genera et partes, sed definitionem insitorum requirit. Et respondet pater, ea esse, quae inhaerent in ipsa re: idest, in caussa, siue in quaestione: uel quemadmodum in Topicis dixit, in eo ipso de quo agitur. Hoc autem intelligendum est, uel rem subiectam esse, uel quae attributa dicuntur, ut in hac quaestione, an Rhetorica sit utilis, argumentum elici potest aut ab ijs quae sunt in Rhetorica, ut ars, habitus, Rhetoricae definitio, Rhetoricae notatio, partes, causse, effecta, et id genus reliqua. Itemq; ab attributo, quod fuit utilis: in quo eadem quaeruntur fere, quae in Rhetorica quaeri posse dixi. Ergo semper id constitutum sit, argumenta quae eliciuntur ex ijs locis qui in re ipsa sunt, aut a subiecto, aut ab attributo, aut ab utroq; sumi posse.
units.tr: C. F. What are the inherent proofs? ) He now asks not for kinds and parts, but for the definition of inherent proofs. And the father answers that they are those which inhere in the thing itself, that is, in the cause or the question, or, as he put it in the Topics, in the very matter under discussion. This must be understood either as the subject itself or as what are called its attributes. So, in this question, whether rhetoric is useful, an argument can be drawn either from the things that belong to rhetoric, such as its art, its habit, its definition, its etymology, its parts, its causes, its effects, and the rest of that kind, or from the attribute, that it was useful. In this, almost the same things are asked as I said can be asked about rhetoric. So, to conclude: arguments drawn from those topics which lie in the thing itself may be taken either from the subject, or from the attribute, or from both.

units.la: Et testímoniorum quę sunt genera? Díuínum & humanū. Díuínum, ut oracula, ut auspicia, ut uaticínationes, & responsa sacerdotum, aruspicum, coniectorum. Humanum, quod spectatur ex autoritate, & ex uoluntate: & ex oratione aut libera, aut expressa. in quo insunt scripta, pacta, promissa, iurata, quæsita.
units.tr: And what are the kinds of testimonies? Divine and human. Divine, such as oracles, auspices, prophecies, and the responses of priests, haruspices and interpreters of dreams. Human, which is judged from authority and from will, and from speech, either free or express. In this category belong writings, agreements, promises, sworn statements and things sought under torture.

units.la: Et testimoniorum quæ sunt genera?) Hic primò obseruandum illud, Quæ sunt genera, pro, quot sunt genera? Et respondet pater, esse duo, diuinū & humanū. Sic enim fere ob omnib. qui de Rhetorica scripserunt, diuidi solent. Quaquam sunt qui putent, Aristotelem diuinorum testimoniorum nunquam mentionem fecisse: sed lōgè fallunturᵣ mea quidem sententia. Is enim Rhetoricorum lib.1. de testibus agens, cum eos diuisisset in eos qui præterita, & eos qui futura dicũt, Vates & Augures nominat: ijsq; qui de futuris testantur, subijcit, atque etiam testatur habere locum in consultationibus: producit que Themistoclis exemplum, qui cum nauali prælio confligendum esse probare uellet, Oraculum interpretatus est, quod iubebat, ut sese ligneo muro defenderet Athenienses. Ac Cicero diuinorum genera facit, oracula,auspicia,uaticinationes,itcm responsa sacerdotum,aruspicum,coniectorum.In his oracula primum ex eo ipso appellata sunt, ut in Topicis definit,quod incst in ijs dcorũ oratio: cuiusmodi sunt ( ut ucterum gentiũ superstitionẽ omittã ) quæ Deus ipse,aut Genij diuini,aut Christus,aut etiã eius discipuli sunt loquuti. Auspicia aūt,quæ scruabant augurcs,non in auib.tantũ aspiciendis, sed in fulminibus,tonitru,tempestatibus, eꝛ procellis.Vaticinationes,satidicorum eꝛ uatum prænũciationes sunt:ut Sibyllæ, Calchãs,apud Gręcos:in nostra ucrò religione, ut Dauidis, Esaiæ, aliorũq; ueridicorũ minimeq; mendaciũ.Responsa sacerdotum,sunt rerum diuinarum interpretationes.Sacerdotes enim,siue ut in nostra religione, theologi,eꝛ doctores, nodos religionis explicant,eꝛ de diuino iure respõdent.Aruspicũ erãt, qui quæ extis animaliũ atq; precordijs portendebantur,aperire norant.Exta enim à uiĉtimis exẽpta,decorũ putabantur indicare uoluntatẽ:si integra eꝛ sana,si corrupta,si deminuta,si qua ratione affecta. Cõiectores,qui somnia eꝛ uisa enoda= bant,ac naturalia à diuinis distinguebant,eꝛ quid quicq; denunciarent aperire poterãt: cuiusmodi fuere Iosephus ille in Aegypto, eꝛ Daniel Babylone. Humana sequũtur,quæ( ut inquit Cicero ) spectantur ex autoritate,eꝛ ex uolũtate:eꝛ ex oratione aut libera, aut expressa. Nam hæc genera sunt humanorum testimoniorum tria. Autoritas enim habet dignitatem, & præ se fert aliquid, quod imitandum esse uideatur. quæ aut faciat autoritatem, supra dictum est. Voluntas aut ualet in iis qui ius habent statuendi, ut principes atq; alij magistratus: quorum sunt edicta, plebiscita, senatusconsulta, leges. Deinde etiam parentes idem ius uoluntatis habent, & magistri, & qui testamentum facere possunt, qui aliquid mandare, qui priuilegiis donare.
units.tr: "And what are the kinds of testimonies?" Here we must first observe that "what are the kinds" means "how many kinds are there?" And the father answers that there are two, divine and human, for this is how nearly all writers on rhetoric usually divide them. Although there are some who think that Aristotle never mentioned divine testimonies, they are greatly mistaken, in my view. For in Book 1 of the Rhetoric, when he discusses witnesses, he divides them into those who speak of past things and those who speak of future things, and he names them seers and augurs. Of those who bear witness to future things he adds that they also have a place in deliberations, and he gives the example of Themistocles, who, wanting to persuade that a sea battle must be fought, interpreted the oracle which bade the Athenians defend themselves with a wooden wall. Cicero makes the kinds of divine testimony: oracles, auspices, prophecies, and likewise the responses of priests, haruspices and interpreters of dreams. Of these, oracles were first named from the very thing, as he defines in the Topics, because in them there is the speech of the gods. Such are those which God himself, or divine spirits, or Christ, or even his disciples, have spoken (I omit the superstition of the ancient nations). Auspices were those observed by augurs, not only in watching birds, but in lightning, thunder, storms and tempests. Prophecies are the forecasts of seers and prophets, such as those of the Sibyl and Calchas among the Greeks, and in our religion those of David, Isaiah, and other truthful men, never liars. Responses of priests are interpretations of divine matters. For priests, or in our religion theologians and teachers, explain the knots of religion and give answers on divine law. Haruspices were those who knew how to read what was portended by the entrails and the innards of animals. For the entrails taken from victims were thought to reveal the will of the gods, whether they were whole and sound, or diseased, or diminished, or affected in some other way. Interpreters of dreams were those who explained visions and dreams, distinguishing the natural from the divine, and were able to reveal what each foretold. Such were that Joseph in Egypt and Daniel at Babylon. Human testimonies follow, which (as Cicero says) are judged from authority, from will, and from speech, either free or express. For these are the three kinds of human testimony. For authority has dignity, and carries with it something that seems worth imitating; what makes authority has been said above. Will carries weight among those who have the right to decree, such as princes and other magistrates, whose edicts, plebiscites, decrees of the senate, and laws these are. Next, parents have the same right of will, and teachers, and those who can make a will, who can give a command, who can grant privileges.

units.la: Sequitur tertium, quod est Oratio: cuius duo sunt genera. Nam & libera est oratio, & expressa. Libera est, quam nulla ui coacti homines proferunt: cuiusmodi sunt poetarum, oratorum, philosophorum dicta & scriptæ sententiæ, ueluti cum Atheniefes Homeri testimonio de Salamine usi sunt, ut est apud Aristot. in Rhetoricis. Sic noster Paulus cum Athenis sermonem haberet, uatis Arati testimonium protulit, quo probaret, homines esse Dei cognatos, et cōsanguineos. Sic etiā referuntur proverbia et apophthegmata. Sequitur alterū membrū, de oratione expressa. Ea est, quā inuiti aut necessitate, aut conditione aliqua impulsi proferunt: ut illa q̄ in tormentis siue quæstionib. miseri confitetur, aut q̄ iureiurando astrictı dicimus, aut perturbatione aliqua incitati.
units.tr: Third follows what is speech. Of this there are two kinds, for speech is either free or express. It is free when men utter it without being compelled by any force; such are the sayings and written opinions of poets, orators and philosophers, as when the Athenians used the testimony of Homer about Salamis, as is found in Aristotle's Rhetoric. So also our Paul, when he was speaking at Athens, brought forward the testimony of the poet Aratus to prove that men are the offspring and kin of God. So too proverbs and apophthegms are cited. The second part follows, concerning express speech. This is speech which people utter unwillingly, driven by necessity or some condition, such as what a wretch confesses under torture or under questioning, or what we say when bound by an oath, or what is spoken when someone is stirred by some emotion.

units.la: Scripta uero, pacta & promissa, partim ad libera, partim ad expressa oratione referuntur: cuiusmodi sunt, chirographa, codicilli, stipulationes, tabulæ item accepti & expensi: quæ tamen potius liberæ orationis esse uidentur. Pactum uero est, quod inter aliquos couenit, quod iam ita iustum putatur, ut iuri præstare dicatur: de Inuent. lib. 2. Vel ut Iurisconsulti definiunt, pactum est duorum uel plurium in idem placitum & consensus. Differunt pacta à promissis: quod pacta minimum duorum sunt, promissum unius esse potest. Deinde omnia pacta promissa, at non contrà. Postremò pactu firmius est, promissum debilius. Scripta autem, omnium genera complectuntur. Nam hæc omnia scribi mandariq; literis possunt. locus communis horum omnium est, quod testimonia ad probandum, siue confirmandum ualeat, minimum uero ad refellendum seu negandum, nisi in diuinis. Neq; enim firmiter dixeris: Huius loci non meminit Aristoteles, ergo locus non est. Assumptos præterea locos, Aristoteles facit numero quinq;: Leges, Testimonia, Tabulas, Quæstiones, & Iusiurandum: quæ, ut uides, hac Ciceronis enumeratione continentur.
units.tr: Writings, agreements and promises are referred partly to free speech and partly to express speech. Such are bonds, codicils, stipulations, and also account books of receipts and expenses; yet these seem rather to belong to free speech. An agreement is what has been made between some people, and is thought to be so just that it is said to be binding in law (De Inventione, Book 2). Or, as the jurists define it, an agreement is the consent and common purpose of two or more persons to one thing. Agreements differ from promises in that an agreement requires at least two persons, while a promise can be made by one. Further, every agreement is a promise, but not the reverse. Finally, an agreement is firmer, a promise weaker. Writings, however, embrace all kinds, for all these things can be committed to writing. The common topic of all of them is that testimonies have force for proving or confirming, but very little for refuting or denying, except in divine matters. For you cannot firmly argue: "Aristotle does not mention this place, therefore the place does not exist." Aristotle also makes five assumed topics: laws, testimonies, tables, questionings, and oaths; and, as you see, these are contained in this enumeration of Cicero's.

units.la: C. F. Quæ sunt quæ dicis insita? C. P. Quæ infixa sunt rebus ipsis, tum ex toto, tum ex partibus, tum ex notatione, tum ex iis rebus quæ quodammodo
units.tr: C. F. What are those you call inherent? C. P. Those which are fixed in the things themselves, both from the whole, and from the parts, and from etymology, and from those things which are in some way

units.la: dammodo affectę sunt ad íd de quo quęritur. & ad íd totum de quo differítur,tum definítio adhíbetur,tum partium enumeratio, tum notatio uerbi.
units.tr: affected towards that about which the question is asked, and towards that whole which is discussed; and for these the definition is used, and the enumeration of parts, and the etymology of the word.

units.la: C. F. Quæ sunt quæ dicis insita?) Explicatis assumptorum locis, iam insitorum enumerationem poscit, quam breuiter pater prosequitur: atq; insitorum genus dicit ex toto appellari: ad quod quidem explicandum adhibeatur tum definitio,tum partium enumeratio, tum uerbi notatio. Ex quo satis liquct,totius nomine rem uniuersam intelligi,ad disceptandum propositam, quæ quæstio solet appellari. Quare ex hoc loco, quēadmodū etiam ex Topicis,perspicuū est, Ciceronem nostrum nullum aliud ex toto argumentum elici docuisse, quàm quod aut ex definitione, aut ex partibus,aut ex uerbo siue uocabulo eliceret. Sed illud animaducrtendum est,infitorū duo eum facere genera, quorū alij ex toto, alij ex ijs rebus quæ quodãmodo affectæ sunt ad id de quo quæritur,appellentur. Cur autem huiusmodi locos, ad aliquid affectos appellarit nouo modo Cicero, uariæ sunt eruditorū sententiæ. Nam alij affectā, quasi inchoata putant:quod non ut illa superiora totam rem consignent, sed consociatam cum ipsa re
units.tr: C. F. What are those you call inherent? ) Having explained the assumed topics, he now asks for an enumeration of the inherent ones, which the father briefly pursues; and he says the kind of inherent topics is named from the whole, to explain which the definition, the enumeration of parts, and the etymology of the word are used. From this it is clear that by the name of the whole is understood the entire matter put forward for dispute, which is usually called the question. Hence, from this topic, as also from the Topics, it is evident that our Cicero taught that no other argument is drawn from the whole except what is drawn from the definition, or from the parts, or from the word or term. But it must be noted that he makes two kinds of inherent topics, of which some are named from the whole, and others from those things which are in some way affected towards that about which the question is asked. Why Cicero has named such topics as "affected to something" in a new way is a matter of various opinions among the learned. For some think they are called affected as if they were inchoate, because they do not signify the whole thing as those earlier ones do, but a nature associated with the thing itself. Others want "affected" to mean the things which are relative (in Greek, the relatives), that is, things related or compared with something, because they declare themselves by mutual affection, like genus and species, and likewise in the same way...

units.la: C. F. [Commentary note in red at right margin, illegible] re naturam aliquam significent. Alij affecta, τὰ πρός τι uolunt esse: id est relata, uel quæ cum aliquo conferuntur, quòd mutua se affectione declarent, ut genus & species, itemque eodem modo reliqua. Alij affecta, cognata & propinqua intelligunt, quòd neque prorsus remota sint, ut testimonia: neque in re insita, ut definitio, partes, nomen, sed mediæ cuiusdam inter ea naturæ. Qui quidem omnes aliquid dicunt: sed quod dicunt, non satis probant aut declarant. Nos autem ad sua principia singula revocantes, affecta ad id de quo quæritur, ea intelligi hoc loco dicimus, quæ rei vel materiam tantum, vel formam separatim declarant. Cum enim res quæuis naturalis, atque ad eius similitudinem, artificiosa, ex materia forma'que constet: ea erit perfecta rei configuratio, & declaratio, quæ materiam simul formamq; complectitur: quæ alterum tantum, hoc est, vel materiam, vel formam, imperfecta. Ex ijs igitur principijs Cicero, quum unum genus locorum secisset, quo res tota, quasi dicas materia & forma ostenderetur, uidit aliud genus esse, quo non tota res declaratur, sed aliquid tamen ad eam ostendendam faceret: id igitur notauit, atq; à superiori genere seiunxit, proprioq; nomine donauit. Affecta enim ad reinde quæ quæritur, appellauit, quasi inchoatam & imperfectam rei notionē, cum superioribus illis collata,continentia. Nam rei definitio, & partium enumeratio, & nominis natura, cum toto ipso reciprocantur, & quasi materiam cum forma copleƈtuntur. In definitione enim (ut ex hac una quod uolo ostendā) genus pro materia, differetia uero siue proprietas pro forma sumitur. Reliqui uero loci, quos affeƈtos uocat, aut eiusdē generis nominū collatione, aut genus tantū rei, aut generis parte, aut similitudine tātū, aut differentia aliqua, aut rei cōtrarium quid, aut adiuƈtū, aut quod antecedit re, aut cōsequitur, aut eidē repugnet, aut quod sit rei caussa, aut effeƈtus: aut re aliqua maius, aut minus, aut par: quæ singula, uel materiem solam, uel formam, uel affeƈtionem quampiam ad ipsam rem declarant, rei que notionem gignunt imperfeƈtam. Ex quo aperte iam liquet, cur affeƈta sint huiusmodi appellata. Affeƈtio enim, non perfeƈtum habitum, sed inchoatum tantū, siue habitus principiū significat: ut in Qualitatis categoria Dialeƈtica docet. Quæ autē hic Ad rē affeƈta uocat, de Oratore lib. 2. quæ re illa de qua quæritur attingant, appellauit. Sed ut breuiter hosce locos omnes illustremus, definitionem primum, deinde reliquos percurremus.
units.tr: C. F. [red marginal note at right, illegible] ... signify some nature. Others want affecta to mean τὰ πρός τι [relatives]: that is, things that are related, or that are compared with one another, because they declare themselves through mutual affection, as genus and species do, and likewise the rest in the same way. Others understand affecta as kindred and neighbouring things, because they are neither wholly remote, like testimonies, nor inherent in the thing itself, like definition, parts, or name, but intermediate in nature between these. All of these say something, but they do not sufficiently prove or explain what they say. We, however, refer each matter back to its own principles and say that by affecta to the matter under inquiry we mean, in this place, those things which declare either only the matter or only the form of a thing, separately. For since any natural thing, and any artificial thing made after its likeness, consists of matter and form, the complete configuration and declaration of a thing is that which embraces matter and form together, whereas that which contains only one of them, that is, either matter or form, is incomplete. From these principles, then, Cicero, having made one kind of topic by which the whole thing is shown, as it were through its matter and form, saw that there was another kind, by which the whole thing is not declared but which nevertheless contributes something to showing it. This he noted, separated it from the former kind, and gave it a proper name. For he called them affecta to the matter under inquiry, as an incomplete and imperfect notion of the thing, related to those higher topics and contained in them. For the definition of a thing, the enumeration of its parts, and the nature of its name are reciprocal with the whole itself and together embrace, as it were, matter and form. In definition (to show what I mean from this one example), genus is taken for matter, and difference or property for form. The remaining topics, which he calls affecta, either by the comparison of names of the same kind, or by the genus of the thing alone, or by a part of the genus, or by similitude alone, or by some difference, or by something contrary to the thing, or by an adjunct, or by what precedes the thing, or follows it, or is repugnant to it, or by what is its cause or effect, or by something greater, less, or equal to it: each of these declares either only the matter, or only the form, or some affection of the thing itself, and produces an imperfect notion of it. From this it is now clearly evident why topics of this kind have been called affecta. For an affection signifies not a perfect habit but only an inchoate state, or the beginning of a habit, as dialectic teaches in the category of Quality. What he here calls affecta to the thing, in De Oratore book 2, he called those which touch upon the thing about which the question is. But to illustrate briefly all these topics, we shall go through the definition first, then the rest.

units.la: Tum definitio.) Definitio igitur est oratio, quæ id quod definitur, explicat quid sit. cuius duo sunt præcepta: alterum, ut nihil desit: alterum,ut nihil superfit.Constat aut definitio genere & differentia, aut proprietate quadam, aut communium frequentia. Definitionis communis locus est,Vt quae cadunt in definitionem,ea & in rem quae definitur cadant,& contrà.Nam definitio cum re definita reciprocatur. Exemplum: Si ueri falsiq; dijudicandi facultas tantopere expetitur,Dialectica expectenda est.
units.tr: Definition. A definition is a speech that explains what the thing defined is. It has two rules: first, that nothing be lacking; second, that nothing be superfluous. A definition consists either of genus and difference, or of some property, or of frequent common features. The common topic of definition: whatever falls under the definition also falls under the thing defined, and conversely, for a definition is reciprocal with the thing defined. Example: If the ability to distinguish true from false is so greatly sought, then dialectic must be pursued.

units.la: Tum partium enumeratio. ) Partium enumeratio est, cum partibus omnibus enumeratis totū concluditur,siue affirmando,siue negando:aut caeteris partibus remotis, una reliqua concluditur. Partes autem intelligimus tam earum rerum quae animo percipiuntur, quàm quae corporis sensib. ut leges, senatusconsulta, edicta magistratuum, iuris ciuilis partes dicuntur: & prora, pupis, carina,malus & antennae,nauis partes:ut nunc subtiliorem partium diuisionem omittamus. Quaquam etiam tum formae ipsae,tum differentiae,tum etiam accidentia, generis partes sint: quas etiam liceat enumeratione concludere. Proprie tamē generis in formas distributio,Diuisio dicitur:et Partitio,totius aut integri in sua membra.Locus communis est: Partibus omnib. sublatis, & totū tolli: & ijsdē attributis,similiter totum constitui. Exemplum fit : Ciccro & inueniendi & argmentandi peritus fuit; ergo Dialecticae scientiam habuit. Tum notatio uerbi.)
