Nota seu notatio uerbi est,cum ex ui & interpretatione uocabuli argumētum elicitur:sunt enim uerba rerū notæ.Locus communis est:Cui conuenit notatio seu interpretatio uerbi,eidem conuenit & nomen. quod argumentum in utranq; partem ualet, tum ad probandum, tum etiam ad refellendum. Exemplum: Si philosophia studium est sapientiæ, & sapientia nihil præstantius: ergo omnium artium præstantissima philosophia est.
units.tr: Enumeration of parts. Enumeration of parts is when, all the parts having been enumerated, the whole is concluded, either by affirming or by denying; or when, the other parts being removed, the one remaining is concluded. We understand as parts both those things that are grasped by the mind and those that are perceived by the bodily senses: laws, decrees of the senate, edicts of magistrates are called parts of civil law, and the prow, stern, keel, mast and yards are parts of a ship, though we may now omit a finer division of parts. Although forms, differences, and accidents are also parts of a genus, and it is permitted to conclude these by enumeration too, strictly speaking the distribution of a genus into its forms is called division, and the partition of a whole or integral thing into its members is called partition. The common topic is: with all the parts removed, the whole is removed; and with them attributed, the whole is likewise established. Example: Cicero was skilled both in invention and in argument; therefore he had a knowledge of dialectic. Notation of a word. Notation, or notatio, of a word is when an argument is drawn from the force and interpretation of a term, for words are the marks of things. The common topic is: whatever belongs to the notation or interpretation of a word also belongs to the name. This argument holds in either direction, both for proving and for refuting. Example: If philosophy is a pursuit of wisdom, and nothing is more excellent than wisdom, then philosophy is the most excellent of all the arts.

units.la: Ex ijs autem reb. quæ quodammodo affectę sunt,ad id de quo quæritur, alia coniugata appellantur,alia ex genere,alia ex forma,alia ex similitudine, alia ex differentia, alia ex contrario,alia ex coniunctis, alia ex antecedentibus, alia ex consequentibus, alia ex repugnantibus, alia ex caussis,alia ex affectibus, alia ex comparatione maiorum aut parium, aut minorum.
units.tr: From those things which are in some way affecta to the matter under inquiry, some are called conjugates, some are drawn from genus, some from form, some from similitude, some from difference, some from the contrary, some from conjuncts, some from antecedents, some from consequents, some from things repugnant, some from causes, some from effects, some from comparison with greater, equal, or lesser things.

units.la: Sequuntur affecta ad aliquid,quorum primus locus est,eorum quæ coniugata dicuntur,quæ sunt ex uerbis generis eiusdem. Eiusdem autem generis uerba sunt,quæ orta ab uno uarie commutantur:ut sapere,sapiens,sapientis,sapientior,sapientissimus, tissimus,sapientia,sapienter.Sed Aristoteles casus uerborum,& comparationes & aduerbia, casus proprie nominat, reliqua communi appellatione Coniugata.Locus cõmunis:Cuicunq; unü aliquod coniugatorum conuenit,aut nõ cõuenit, eidẽ etiã cætera necesse est cõuenire, aut non cõuenire: ut, Si uitiosum est dicere ornatè, pellatur omnis è ciuitate cloquentia. Quod si eloquentia laudatur, erit etiam orator laude dignus.
units.tr: Next follow the topics affecta ad aliquid, the first of which concerns the things called conjugates, which come from words of the same stem. Words of the same stem are those which, derived from one word, vary in form: as to be wise, wise, of the wise, wiser, wisest, wisdom, wisely. But Aristotle properly calls the cases of words, comparisons, and adverbs "cases," and the rest he groups under the common name of conjugates. The common topic: whatever one of the conjugates belongs to or does not belong to, the others must necessarily belong or not belong to it likewise. For example: If it is a fault to speak elegantly, let all eloquence be banished from the state. But if eloquence is praised, then the orator too will be worthy of praise.

units.la: Alia ex genere. ) Genus est, quod formas aliquas complectitur: uel notio est, quæ sui similcs cõmunione quadã, specie autem differentes duas aut plures complectitur partes:ut cupiditas. Genus ad probandam formam minimum ualet, plurimum ad refellendam. Item,totius generis affirmationem,consequitur affirmatio cuiuslibet formæ:& totius generis negationem, omnium pariter sormarũ negatio intelligitur.ut, Si nõ est magistratus,eũ tribunũ esse dicere nõ debes:Et si omnib.magistratib.parendũ est,ergo etiã tribuno.
units.tr: From genus. A genus is that which embraces certain forms, or a notion which, by a certain community, embraces two or more parts that are similar to one another but differ in species, as desire does. The genus is of very little use for proving a form, but of very great use for refuting one. Likewise, from the affirmation of the whole genus follows the affirmation of any form; and from the negation of the whole genus, the negation of all forms alike is understood. For example: If there is no magistrate, you ought not to call him a tribune; and if one must obey all magistrates, then one must obey the tribune too.

units.la: Alia ex forma. ) Forma est, quæ subest generi. Aut formæ sunt,quæ generibus iis ex quibus emanât,subiiciûtur: ut cupiditati amor, auaricia, & id genus reliqua. Forma siue species firmâ habet generis probationem, infirmam uero refutationem.Formis omnibus remotis,remouetur etiã genus:ut,Si neq; herbæ sunt, neq; frutices, neq; arbores, stirpes igitur non sunt. Forma quoad suum nomen retinet, nunquam à genere seiungitur: id est, semper de ea dicitur genus. ut, Si est herba, & stirps sit oportet: Si plebiscitum, lex igitur.
units.tr: From form. A form is what lies under a genus. Forms are those which are placed under the genera from which they spring, as love and avarice, and the rest of that kind, under desire. A form or species gives strong proof of its genus, but a weak refutation. With all the forms removed, the genus is removed too: for example, If there are neither herbs, nor shrubs, nor trees, then there are no stalks. A form keeps its own name and is never separated from its genus; that is, the genus is always predicated of it. For example: If it is an herb, it must be a stalk; if it is a plebiscite, then it is a law.

units.la: Alia ex similitudine. ) Similitudo est, rei positæ cum alia re collatio, qua res ipsa qualis sit ostenditur. Neque tamen necesse est, totam rem similem esse: sed ad eam similitudinem aliquam habere. Similitudinis formas tres facit Cicero in Topicis: Inductionem, collationem, et exemplum, siue fictum siue verum. Inductio est, ex pluribus collationibus confecta conclusio. ut, Si is optimus est gubernator, qui doctus: si ita auriga, si pædagogus: etiam Reip. rector is erit optimus, qui & doctissimus. Collatio est, cum una res uni, par pari comparatur. queadmodum illa: Vt corpora nostra sine mente, sic civitas sine lege, suis partibus, ut nervis ac sanguine & membris, uti non potest. Exemplum autem, est factî aut dicti, cu alicuius certi authoris nomine propositio: & est quædam inductio in pauculioribus tantum consistens, quam illa. ut, Si Sylla, si Marius, si item Iulius præsidium petiuit, quod tyrannidem affectaret: etiam Augustus, qui præsidium petit, ad principatum spectat. Locus communis est: Similis est ratio similium.
units.tr: From similitude. Similitude is the comparison of one thing set beside another, by which the thing itself is shown to be of a certain kind. It is not necessary, however, that the whole thing be like the other; it is enough that it have some likeness to it. Cicero, in the Topics, makes three forms of similitude: induction, collation, and example, whether invented or true. Induction is a conclusion made up of several collations. For example: If he is the best helmsman who is learned, and likewise the best charioteer and the best tutor, then the best ruler of the commonwealth will also be the one who is most learned. Collation is when one thing is compared with one thing, equal with equal, as in this: just as our bodies cannot make use of their parts, such as the sinews, blood, and limbs, without the mind, so a state cannot do so without law. An example, however, is a proposition of a deed or saying put forward under the name of some certain authority; it is a kind of induction, but one that consists of fewer instances than the former. For example: If Sulla, if Marius, and likewise Julius sought a guard because they aimed at tyranny, then Augustus too, who seeks a guard, aims at the principate. The common topic: the reasoning for like things is the same as for similar things.

units.la: Alia ex differentia. ) Differentia quæ hic dicitur, dissimilitudo in Topicis uocatur. Nam haec latius patet differentia, quam illa Dialecticorum. Est enim dissimilium rerum propria nota, ex qua aliquid dissimile demonstratur. Huius totidem sunt genera, quot similitudinis: ut, Certus dies no ut sacrificij, sic consilij expectari solet. Locus communis est: Dissimilium dissimilis est ratio. Et ille: Si rerum propositarum dissimilitudo est, idem esse non possunt.
units.tr: Another from difference. This difference, as it is called here, is named dissimilarity in the Topics, for it has a wider reach than the difference of the Dialecticians. It is the proper mark of dissimilar things, by which something dissimilar is shown. There are as many kinds of it as there are of similarity, for example: "A fixed day is usually looked for in a sacrifice, and in the same way in a council." The common topic is: the reasoning of dissimilar things is dissimilar. And that other one: if the things proposed are dissimilar, they cannot be the same.

units.la: Ex contrario. ) Contraria sunt, quae simul in eadem re esse non possunt. Sunt autem contrariorum genera quatuor: Aduersa, Priuantia, Relata, Negantia siue disparata. Aduersa sunt, quae in eodem genere plurimum differunt: ut, sapientia stultitia. In eodem autem genere dicuntur, quibus propositis occurrunt tanquam cregione quadam contraria: ut celeritati tarditas, quorum genus est motus. Priuatia sunt, quae priuationem rei quae edesse debeat, significant. Sunt autem duplicia. alia nomine simplici et sua ui priuantia sunt: alia nomine iuncto ex In praepositione. nomine simplici, ut auditus, surditas: nomine iuncto, ut dignitas, indignitas. Praepositio In priuat uerbum ea ui, quam haberet si In praepositum non fuisset. Haec autem duplicem habent considerationem: altera, ut priuantia: alteram, ut aduersa. sunt enim natura aduersa, coniunctione aut priuantia. Relata didicuntur, quae cum aliquo conferuntur, siue quae referuntur ad aliquid: ut simplum duplum, multa pauca, dominus seruus. Negantia siue disparata sunt, contraria dientibus, quae ab aliqua re per oppositionem negationis separantur: ut, Si hoc est, illud non est: Sapere, non sapere: de quibus Dialectici in pronunciatorum oppositione docet, ea quae appellant contradictoria, siue contradicentia. Locus communis: Contrarijs omnibus contraria conuenire: item, Contrariorum contraria sunt consequentia. Sed hoc intelligedum est de ijs contrarijs, quae medium non habent. nam quae medium habent, eorum alia est ratio: ex illis enim concludитur, ex his autem nihil certo concludi potest. Commune exemplum contrariorum hoc fit: Si consul Brutus, hostis Antonius: Si Antonius nefarie, praeclare Brutus.
units.tr: From the contrary. Contraries are those which cannot be together in the same thing. There are four kinds of contraries: opposed, privative, relative, and negating or disparate. Opposed contraries are those which differ most within the same genus, for example wisdom and folly. They are said to be in the same genus when, once one is proposed, the other comes to mind as if by a certain opposition, as slowness is to speed, their genus being motion. Privative contraries are those which signify the privation of something that ought to be present. They are of two kinds: some are privative by their simple name and their own force, as hearing and deafness; others by a compound name with the prefix in-, as dignity and indignity. The prefix in- privates the word with the force it would have had without the prefix. These have a double consideration: one as privatives, the other as opposites, for by nature they are opposed, but by combination they are privatives. Relative contraries are those which are compared with something, or which refer to something, as double and single, many and few, master and slave. Negating or disparate contraries are opposites which are separated from a thing by the opposition of negation, for example: if this is, that is not; to be wise, not to be wise. Of these the Dialecticians teach in their treatment of the opposition of propositions, calling them contradictories or contradicting things. The common topic is: contrary things belong to all contraries; likewise, the consequences of contraries are contrary. But this must be understood of those contraries which have no middle, for those which have a middle have a different reasoning. From the former something can be concluded, but from the latter nothing certain can be concluded. A common example of contraries is this: if Brutus was consul, Antony was an enemy; if Antony acted wickedly, Brutus acted nobly.

units.la: Alia ex coniunctis.
units.tr: From things conjoined.

units.la: ) Hec alia uocat in Topicis, Barbari contingentia, siue communiter accidentia. Hic autem locus tripertito consideratur. Nam in eo quaeritur, quid ante rem, quid cum re, quid post rem euenerit. Ante re, ut apparatus, colloquium, locus, conuiuium. cum re autem, ut pedit strepitus, fremitus hominum, corporum umbrae, et eiusmodi alia. post rem uero, rubor, pallor, titubatio, fuga, et si qua alia signa conscientiae: item illa; Restinctus ignis, gladius acutus, caeteraque quae suspi-
units.tr: The Topics call this "of the contingent" (the Barbarians' term), or of things commonly accompanying. This topic is considered in three parts, for in it one asks what happened before the thing, what with the thing, and what after the thing. Before the thing: preparations, a conversation, a place, a banquet. With the thing: the noise of footsteps, the murmur of people, the shadows of bodies, and other things of this kind. After the thing: blushing, paleness, stammering, flight, and whatever other signs of a guilty conscience there are; likewise such things as an extinguished fire, a drawn sword, and the rest which can arouse suspi-

units.la: suspicionem facti possunt mouere, in quibus conie&ture status dominatur. Locus communis: Ex adiunctis & signis factum declarari.
units.tr: suspicion of the deed, in which conjecture holds sway over the state of the case. The common topic is: a deed is shown by accompanying circumstances and signs.

units.la: Alia ex antecedentibus, alia ex confequentib. alia ex repugnantibus. ) Qui loci pro uno ftre fo lent haberi, quamuis tractatio eorum fit triplex, ut Cicero in Topicis ostendit: qui locus etiam ab adiunctis longe diuersus est. Nam adiuncta non semper cueniunt, cofequentia autem semper. Antecedentia ea uoco, quae necessario antecedunt: & confequetia, quae re necessario cofequuntur. Repugnantia autem eiusmodi sunt, ut cohaerere nunquam possint. Antecedetia, de Orat. li. 2. etiā praecurrētia: & cofequentia, ibidē cofentanea appellātur. Quae autem antecedant, quae ue cofequantur aut repugnent, discenda ex subtiliore doctrina sunt.
units.tr: From antecedents, from consequents, from repugnants. These topics are commonly held to be one, although their treatment is threefold, as Cicero shows in the Topics. This topic is also quite different from that of accompaniments, for accompaniments do not always occur, but consequents always do. I call antecedents those things which necessarily precede, and consequents those which necessarily follow. Repugnants are such that they can never cohere. In De Oratore book 2 antecedents are also called "preceding" things, and consequents are called "consentaneous." Which things precede, which follow, and which conflict must be learned from a more subtle doctrine.

units.la: Alia ex causis. ) Caussa id esse dicitur, quod efficit id cuius est caussa: ut uencnū mortem, & ignis ustionē. Locus cōmunis: Si causae sunt in bonis, etiam eff. ?us in bonis erunt: Sin causae in malis sint, etiam effectus. Qui loci reciprocantur. Exemplum: Si auariciam tollere uultis, mater eius tollenda est luxuries. Reliqua ad hunc locū pertinentia, infra docebit Cicero.
units.tr: From causes. A cause is that which brings about the thing of which it is the cause, as poison brings about death and fire brings about burning. The common topic is: if the causes are in good things, the effects will also be in good things; but if the causes are in bad things, so too will the effects be. These topics are reciprocal. Example: if you wish to remove avarice, its mother, luxury, must be removed. Cicero will teach the rest that pertains to this topic below.

units.la: Alia ex effectibus.) Sunt aut effectus, qui efficiuntur ex causis. Locus cōmunis: Effectus caufsarum natura sequūtur: & ut caussa effectu indicat, sic quod effectu est, quae fuerit caussa demonstrat. Quemadmodum (inquit Christus) non potest arbor bona malos fructus ferre, nec mala bonos. Exemplu erit huiusmodi: Si erarij copijs et ad belli adiumenta et ad ornameta pacis utimur, uectigalib. seruiamus.ite, Perijt in legatione Sulpitius, ergo Respub. ei causa mortis fuit.
units.tr: From effects. Effects are those which are produced from causes. The common topic is: effects follow the nature of their causes, and just as the cause indicates the effect, so what the effect is shows what the cause was. As Christ says: "A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit." An example will be of this kind: if we use the treasury's resources both for the supplies of war and for the adornments of peace, let us be slaves to the tributes. Sulpicius perished on an embassy; therefore the Republic was the cause of his death.

units.la: Alia ex comparatione.) Comparatio est, pariu aut imparium collatio. ea triplex est: aut pariu inter se, aut maioris cum minore, aut minoris cum maiore. Ex maiore quidem locus, solu firmus est in refutatione: qui ex minore, solum in confirmatione: qui autem ex pari, in utranq; partem ualet. Ex maiore quidem exemplum fit: Si Caesarem non tulimus, quomodo feremus Antonium? Locus communis: Quod in re maiore ualet, ualeat in minore. Ex minore: Si ars bene dicendi tanta cura discitur, quanto maiore ratio uiuendi comparanda est? Locus communis: Quod in minore ualet, ualeat in maiore. Ex pari autem: Si discere praeclarum est, an non etiam docere? Locus communis: Quod in re pari ualet, ualeat et in ea quae ei par est. Quod si non ualet in uno, nec in altero.
units.tr: From comparison. Comparison is the collation of equals or unequals. It is threefold: either of equals with equals, or of the greater with the lesser, or of the lesser with the greater. The topic from the greater is firm only in refutation; the topic from the lesser only in confirmation; the topic from equals holds good on either side. An example from the greater: if we did not put up with Caesar, how shall we bear Antony? The common topic: what holds in the greater matter holds in the lesser. From the lesser: if the art of speaking well is learned with such care, with how much greater care should the rule of living be acquired? The common topic: what holds in the lesser holds in the greater. From equals: if it is excellent to learn, is it not also excellent to teach? The common topic: what holds in an equal matter holds also in that which is equal to it. But if it does not hold in the one, neither does it in the other.

units.la: Vt definitio, ut contrarium, ut ea quae sunt ipsi, contrario ue eius, aut similia, aut dissimilia, aut consentanea,aut dissentanea, aut ea quę sunt quasi cõiuncta,aut ea quae sunt quasi pugnantia inter se,aut earum rerum rerum,de quibus agitur,caussæ: aut caussarum euentus, id est, quæ sunt effecta de causis,ut distributiones,ut genera partium, generum ue partes, ut primordia rerum, & quasi præcurrētia, in quibus inest aliquid argumenti, ut rerum contentiones, quid maius, quid par, quid minus fit, in quibus aut naturæ rerum aut facultates comparantur.
units.tr: Such as definition; such as the contrary; such as those things which are the same as it, or its contrary, or similar, or dissimilar, or consonant, or dissonant; or those which are, as it were, conjoined, or those which are, as it were, in conflict with one another; or the causes of the things under discussion; or the outcomes of causes, that is, what are effects of causes; such as distributions; such as the kinds of parts, or the parts of kinds; such as the beginnings of things and what, as it were, runs ahead, in which there is some element of argument; such as the contests of things: what is greater, what is equal, what is less, in which either the natures of things or their capacities are compared.

units.la: Vt definitio,&c.) Mirantur plerique omnes docti,quid sibi uelit hæc noua locorum repetitio. et sane difficile est,quid in ea spectarit,quid ue secutus sit Cicero,certò affirmare ac peruidere. Equidem,suo cuiq; iudicio relicto,duo afferā, quae mihi diligenter cuncta uersanti uerisimiliora uisa sunt. Dicam igitur de priore meam coniecturam,deinde de posteriore. Mihi uidetur hoc loco Ciceroni id accidisse,quod & nobis accidere plerunque uidemus. Duplicem locorum enumerationem sibi proposuit, nō quòd utrāq; forte probaret,sed ut illis descriptis,post diligentius utra esset retinenda iudicaret. Sed interea multa acciderunt, quæ cum ab huiusmodi animaduersione auerterunt. Incidit enim in turbulenta tempora tunc Caij Cæsaris, post Antonij & Augusti: ex quo factum esse uidetur, ut utraq; descriptio in eius ἀντεγραφῳ remaneret. hinc posteri putarunt, eü id iudicio fecisse: quare nihil mutare ausi sunt. Neq; enim debemus arbitrari, ueteres autores homines non fuisse, multáq; humanitus in eorum scripta non irrepsisse. Multorum certè præstantissimorum uirorum libri docere id possunt, in quibus nonnulla superuacanea, nonnulla etiam diminuta inueniuntur. Ex eo enim etiam mea hæc conieētu ra probari potest, quod omnes illi loci ad superiores possunt reuocari. Nam primum definitio continet etiam notationem, cum altera sit rei, altera nominis. Contrarium uerò, simile & dissimile, sunt superioribus tribus paria: nam dissimili nomine, etiam differentia intelligitur. Sequuntur consentanea, in quibus antecedentia & consequentia, quemadmodum etiam Perionius ostendit, continentur: in quibus consentaneis, non male etiam adiuncta includuntur. Dissentanea uerò, sunt repugnantia. Coniuncta in secundo de Orat. appellat, quæ alibi coiugata. Quasi pugnantia cū dissentaneis, natura coniunguntur: ut hoc sit tantum discrimen, quod dissentanea semper, hæc uerò non semper repugnant. Quamobrem dixit, c s Quasi pugnantia. His subiungit causas: deinde cuentus, qui nihil aliud sunt quam effecta de causis, ut ipsemet interpretatur. Deinde distributiones: quo nomine enumerationem intelligo, sive partium, sive formarum: post, genera partium, generum ue partes, quibus tum ex genere, tum ex forma argumentum intelligitur. Adduntur primordia rerum, & quasi precurrentia: quae uel leuiores sunt causae, quemadmodum ipse in Topicis ait: uel eo nomine adiuncta, quae rem antecedunt, intelligenda sunt. Atque ea hoc differre possunt ab antecedentibus: quod precurrentia ueri similia sunt, antecedentia necessaria. Postremo loco sunt rerum contentiones: quo nomine comparationem intelligi, nullus ignorat, uel ex eo quod sequitur: Quid maius, quid par, quid minus, quam coniecturam si accipimus, bene habet. Aut priorem tantum descriptionem sequemur, usque ad ea uerba, Aut minorum: quae cum illis coniugemus, quae secundae descriptioni adduntur, In quibus aut natura rerum, aut facultas comparantur. aut posteriorem, omissa priore, quae ab aliquo uidetur ex Topicis huc translata, & adscripta, ut in docendo inter se utrumque enumerationem locorum conferret, ut fieri interdum etiam a doctis solet. Quod si cui haec coniectura non placet, & uelit utrāq; descriptione quasi de mente Ciceronis retinere: tunc dicemus mente Ciceronis fuisse, indicatis locis, ex quib. firma & dialectica argumenta sumantur, alia locorum descriptione magis oratoria subijcere voluisse: ex quib. non tam firma, sed fere fallacia argumenta depromerentur. idq; Aristotelis more, q in Topicis ac Rhetoricis duplice ordine locorum statuere voluit: ut cum aliquid ponitur pro definitione, pro contrario, pro genere, atq; item in reliquis: cum tamen neq; vera definitio sit, neq; verum contrarium, neq; verum genus, quae etiam si ab acutis cognoscatur, interdum tamen refelli vix possunt. Quin & Cornificius ad Herenn. lib. 2. & Cicero ipse de Invent. lib. 1. vitiosas & leves argumentationes satis diligenter indicarunt: quod & hoc loco facere breviter voluisse videtur, praepositis singulis fere locis particula, Ut, sive Quasi: ut intelligeremus, non esse veram definitionem, aut verum genus, sed his similia potius. Nam satis constat, oratores legibus illis dialecticorum & philosophorum in argumentando sese astringi noluisse: & apparentia potius, quae quae in communi more versarentur, sectatos fuisse. Quamobrem haud praeter rationem fecisse dicetur, in huiusmodi locis ad Oratorum consuetudinem accommodandis. Et ut in definitione primum ostendamus, communis definitio est: Seditiosus est is, qui malus atque inutilis est civis.
units.tr: "Such as definition, etc." Most learned men wonder what this new repetition of topics is meant to do, and indeed it is hard to say with certainty what Cicero had in view or what he followed. For my part, leaving each man his own judgment, I will offer two conjectures which seemed to me the more probable after careful consideration of the whole matter. I will speak first of the former conjecture and then of the latter. It seems to me that what happened to Cicero in this passage is what we too commonly see happen to ourselves. He proposed to himself a double enumeration of topics, not because he perhaps approved of both, but so that, having set both down, he could later judge more carefully which should be kept. But in the meantime many things intervened which turned him away from such a review. For he fell into troubled times, first under Gaius Caesar, then under Antony and Augustus, and from this it seems to have happened that both descriptions remained in his [ἀντεγραφῷ, copy]. Hence later readers thought he had made this choice by judgment, and so they dared to change nothing. For we must not suppose that the ancient authors were not human, or that many human errors did not creep into their writings. The books of many most distinguished men can teach this, in which some superfluous and some also defective passages are found. From this my conjecture can also be confirmed, because all those topics can be traced back to the earlier ones. For first, the definition contains also the notation, since the one concerns the thing and the other the name. The contrary, however, and the similar and dissimilar are pairs matching the three earlier ones, for under the word dissimilar the difference is also understood. Next come the consonant things, in which antecedents and consequents are contained, as Perionius also shows; and among these consonant things, adjuncts are not badly included. The dissonant things are indeed the repugnant ones. The conjoined things are what he elsewhere calls "coupled," which in the second book of De Oratore he calls "conjoined." Things as it were in conflict are joined by nature with the dissonant ones, so that the only difference is that dissonant things always conflict, while these do not always do so. Therefore he said "as it were in conflict." To these he adds causes, then outcomes, which are nothing other than effects of causes, as he himself explains. Then distributions, by which name I understand enumeration, whether of parts or of forms; then kinds of parts or parts of kinds, from which an argument is drawn both from the genus and from the form. The beginnings of things and what runs ahead are added; these may be either lighter causes, as he himself says in the Topics, or adjuncts that go before the thing, under that name. And these can differ from antecedents in that things that run ahead are probable, while antecedents are necessary. Last come the contests of things, by which name no one fails to understand comparison, if only from what follows: "what is greater, what is equal, what is less." If we take this as a conjecture, the matter is in good order. Either we shall follow only the first description, up to the words "or the less," and join to these what is added to the second description, "in which either the natures of things or their capacities are compared;" or we shall follow the second description alone, omitting the first, which seems to have been carried over and added here from the Topics by someone, as learned men sometimes do when teaching, comparing the two enumerations of topics with each other. But if anyone does not like this conjecture and wishes to keep both descriptions as if they reflected Cicero's mind, then we shall say that Cicero intended, having indicated the topics from which firm and dialectical arguments are drawn, to set out by another description of topics those more suited to oratory, from which arguments that are not so firm, but nearly fallacious, are drawn. This would be in the manner of Aristotle, who in the Topics and the Rhetoric wished to set out topics in a double order, so that something is put forward as a definition, as a contrary, as a genus, and likewise in the rest, though it is neither a true definition, nor a true contrary, nor a true genus; such things, even if they are recognized by sharp minds, can nevertheless hardly be refuted. Indeed Cornificius in his Ad Herennium book 2, and Cicero himself in De Inventione book 1, have indicated with sufficient care the faulty and weak arguments; and this seems to be what he wished to do briefly here, by placing before almost each topic the particle "as" or "as if," so that we might understand that it is not a true definition or a true genus, but things rather similar to these. For it is well established that orators did not wish to bind themselves in argument by those rules of the dialecticians and philosophers, and rather pursued what was plausible and current in common usage. Therefore it will not be said to be unreasonable that he adapted these topics to the custom of orators. And to show first in the case of definition how this works, the common definition is: a seditious man is one who is a bad and useless citizen.

units.la: nam nā hoc nō magis seditiosi, quàm ambitiosi, quàm calumniatoris, quàm alicuius improbi hominis uim describit. Falsa: sapientia est pecuniæ acquirendæ intelligentia: Diminuta & leuis: Stultitia est immensæ gloriæ cupiditas. Sunt & illæ definitiones oratoriæ plane: Pax est secura libertas: Historia est magistra uitæ, lux veritatis, uita memoriæ: Mors est ultima linea rerum: Senectus est occasus uitæ: atq; huiusmodi sexcenta, non ueræ definitiones sunt, sed potius descriptiones, haud quidem à natura rerum sumptæ, sed à rebus fortuitis, & euentis.
units.tr: For this describes the force not so much of a seditious man as of an ambitious man, a slanderer, or some other wicked person. False: wisdom is the understanding of how to acquire money. Diminished and feeble: foolishness is an immoderate desire for glory. The oratorical definitions are plainly of this kind too: peace is secure liberty; history is the teacher of life, the light of truth, the life of memory; death is the final boundary of things; old age is the setting of life. Countless others of this sort are not true definitions but rather descriptions, drawn not from the nature of things but from chance circumstances and events.

units.la: Vt contrarium. ) Veluti si quis celeritati debilitatem contrariam ponat, aut album fusco colori: non contrarium reuera, sed contrario simile pofucerit. Nam celeritati tarditas contraria est, & debilitati firmitas, & albo colori niger. In quo uidendum erit, quæ nam contraria medium habeant, quæ ue non habeant.
units.tr: Opposite. For example, if someone were to set weakness against speed, or brown against white, he would not be giving a true opposite but something similar to an opposite. For slowness is opposed to speed, firmness to weakness, and black to white. Here we must see which opposites admit a middle and which do not.

units.la: Vt ea quæ sunt ipsi, contrarioue eius aut similia. ) Vt hunc locum intelligamus, ponamus duo contraria, uitam & mortem: item hæc duo, uer & hyemem. uer cum uita, cum morte hyemem coniungamus: ita uer simile erit uitæ, hyems morti, quæ uitæ ipsi contraria est. Ita uidemus ipsi contrario, quod est uita, hyemem & contrariam & similem esse. Aut disimilia. ) Eadem accipe contraria quæ modò posuimus,et hyemem cum uita,mortè cum uere componè:quæ, ut uides, dissimilia sunt contrario ipsi;tum etiam contrarij contrario.
units.tr: Things that are themselves, or similar to their opposite, or like it. To understand this place, let us posit two opposites, life and death, and likewise two others, spring and winter. If we pair spring with life and winter with death, spring will be similar to life and winter to death, which is the opposite of life itself. So we see that winter is both opposite and similar to life, the very opposite. Or dissimilar. Take the same opposites as before, but pair winter with life and death with spring: as you see, these are dissimilar to the opposite itself, and also opposite to the opposite.

units.la: Aut consentanea.) Sunt hic qui malint legere, Vt consentanea, atque item in reliquis: quod ego non improbo. Sed illud aio parum referre ad locos intelligendos, siue Aut siue Vt legas: quando quidem scimus,non de illis ueris locis, sed de uulgaribus agi,qui potius locorum similitudinem habent, sintq; magis apparentes loci quàm ueri. Quanquam uideo,si quis Aut, in his duobus legat,& sequentia per Vt, non quidem quatuor ordines locorum,sed duos tantum statuerit:& coniuncta erunt ea,quæ consentanea appellauit:& illa quæ quasi pugnantia uocat,erunt ipsa dissentanea. Sed tamen distinguamus ea nos, & quatuor esse locos putemus:ita ut consentanea & dissentanea infirmiora sint: quasi coniuncta uero, & quasi pugnantia,firmiora. Consentancorum sit hoc exemplum, sumptum ex signis: ut si quis dicat de aliquo, Quoniâ pallet,ægrotauit. nam eius,præter morbum corporis, multæ sunt aliæ causse: ut amor, metus, studium, inedia. Dissentanceorum uero illud: Aliquem bene ualere, & male coloratum esse.
units.tr: Or consistent. Some prefer to read "as consistent" and so on for the rest, and I do not object. But I say it matters little for understanding these places whether you read Aut or Vt, since we know we are dealing not with those true places but with common ones, which have rather the likeness of places and are more apparent than true. Yet I see that if someone reads Aut in these two and Vt in the following, he will posit not four classes of places but only two: the consistent and the conjoined will be one group, and what he calls opposing will be the inconsistent ones themselves. Still, let us distinguish them and hold that there are four places, so that the consistent and inconsistent are weaker, while the conjoined and opposed are stronger. An example of consistent places, drawn from signs: if someone says of a man, "Because he is pale, he has been ill." For there are many other causes of paleness besides bodily sickness, such as love, fear, zeal, and hunger. An example of inconsistent places: "He is in good health, yet has a bad complexion."

units.la: Quasi coniuncta, ) Ei bono fuit,ergo occidit. Strepitus hominum, corporum umbræ fuerunt: ergo maleficiũ commissum est. Hæc enim adiuncta sunt cum re ipsa.
units.tr: Conjoined. "He was a benefit to him, therefore he killed him." "There were noises of men and shadows of bodies, therefore a crime was committed." For these are circumstances joined to the thing itself.

units.la: Quasi pugnantia. ) ut, Studuisse aliquem, & indoctum esse.
units.tr: Opposed. For example, "He studied, and yet is unlearned."

units.la: Caussæ. ) Nisi Argo navis esset, Medea non mœreret. Literæ sunt uitandæ: nam aut desidiam, aut arrogantiam afferunt.
units.tr: Causes. "If the ship Argo had not existed, Medea would not be grieving." "Letters are to be avoided, for they bring either idleness or arrogance."

units.la: Caussarum euentus. ) Vt si quis dicat, idcirco aliquem literatum aut philosophum esse, quòd sit arrogans. Huc etiam pertinet, cum ex euentu factum, siue consilium, aut bonum, aut malum iudicatur. Quemadmodum illa dicit apud Ouidium puer Ila barbara:
units.tr: Outcomes of causes. For example, if someone says that a man is literate or a philosopher because he is arrogant. To this also belongs the case where an act or intention is judged good or bad from its outcome. Thus the barbarian boy Ila says in Ovid:

units.la: — Careat successibus opto
units.tr: — I wish that he may lack success,

units.la: Quisquis ab euentu facta notanda putat.
units.tr: whoever thinks that deeds are to be judged by their outcome.

units.la: Ad euentum item pertinere Cicero dicit, cum queri solet, quid ex quaque re euenire soleat: ut ex arrogantia odium, ex insolentia arrogantia, quem locum tractat de Inuent. lib. 1. & in oratione pro Sext. Roscio Amerino.
units.tr: Cicero also says that this place belongs to outcome, when one customarily asks what usually follows from each thing: from arrogance comes hatred, from insolence comes arrogance. He treats this place in the first book of De inventione and in the speech for Sextus Roscius of Ameria.

units.la: Vt distributiones. ) Id est, enumerationes, in quibus aliquid aut redundat, aut deest: quarum fallaciam ostendit Cornif. ad Herennium lib. 2. ut si quis dicat: Duæ res sunt iudices, quæ omnes ad maleficium impellunt, Luxuries & auaricia. Sunt enim alia permulta: ut amor, ut ambitio, ut metus. tus. Item: Tria sunt quæ omnes homines solicitant, metus, cupiditas, ægritudo. satis enim fuerat, dixisse metum & cupiditatem: quoniam ægritudo, cum utraque re coniuncta est.
units.tr: Distributions. These are enumerations in which something is either superfluous or lacking. Cornificius shows their fallacy in the second book of the Ad Herennium, as when someone says: "There are two things, judges, which drive all men to wrongdoing, luxury and avarice." For there are very many others, such as love, ambition, and fear. Likewise: "There are three things that trouble all men: fear, desire, and sorrow." For it would have been enough to say fear and desire, since sorrow is joined to both.

units.la: Vt genera partium.) Vt si quis dicat, uitam immortalitatis esse genus, & acrem uentum, cum eius potius affectio sit: de quibus Arist.Top.lib.4. Quoniam in genere & forma multis peccatur modis: idcirco diligentius tradit.
units.tr: Kinds or parts. For example, if someone says that life is a kind of immortality, or that the wind is a kind of air, when it is rather an affection of air. Aristotle discusses such matters in the fourth book of the Topics. Since many errors are made in genus and form in many ways, Cicero treats this more carefully.

units.la: Generum vel partes.) Vt si posita modo exempla inuertatur, et dicatur immortalitas uitæ pars, & aeris uentus.
units.tr: Of genera or parts. For example, if the examples just given were reversed, and one said that immortality is a part of life, and air a part of wind.

units.la: Vt primordia rerum.) Sunt leues causæ, de quib. in Top. Cicero: ut si quis ex colloquio amorem, ex amore flagitium colligeret, quibus oratores ad mouendam suspicionem sæpe utuntur. idcirco addit, In quibus inest aliquid argumenti, id est signi. Sic enim etiam certiora signa infrà appellabit, quæ Græci τεκμήρια nocant.
units.tr: Beginnings of things. These are slight causes, which Cicero discusses in the Topics: as if someone were to infer love from a conversation, and from love a crime. Orators often use such inferences to stir suspicion. Therefore he adds, "in which there is some element of argument," that is, of sign. For he will later call the more certain signs by the name the Greeks give them, τεκμήρια [tekmēria].

units.la: Vt rerum contentiones.) Id est, comparationes uehementiores: cuiusmodi potius ad ornandum & amplificandum, quàm ad probandum assumunt oratores, quanquam utrunque faciant: Cornif.lib.4. ad Herennium.
units.tr: Comparisons of things. These are more vehement comparisons. Orators use such comparisons more to adorn and amplify than to prove, though they do both. See Cornificius, Ad Herennium, book 4.

units.la: In quibus aut naturæ rerum, aut facultates coparantur.) Naturæ rerum, id est, res ipsæ: ut aurum auro, homo homini, equus equo comparatur: aut facultates, id est, rerum attributa, sive efficiendi vires, ut ex quantitate, ut ex qualitate, & caeteris eiusdem generis. Haec duo capita, Naturae & facultates, continent illa quatuor, quae in Top. comparationi subijcit Cicero: numerum videlicet, speciem, vim, & affectionem: ita ut numerus & vis ad facultates referantur, species ad naturam, affectio ad utrunque. de quibus copiose in Commentariolis nostris ad Topica Ciceronis.
units.tr: In which either the natures of things or their faculties are compared. The natures of things means the things themselves: as gold is compared with gold, man with man, horse with horse. Faculties means the attributes of things, or their powers of producing an effect, as in quantity, quality, and the other things of the same kind. These two heads, nature and faculties, contain the four that Cicero in the Topics adds under comparison: namely number, kind, force, and affection. Number and force refer to faculties, kind to nature, and affection to both. I have discussed these matters at length in my Commentariola on Cicero's Topics.

units.la: C. F. Omnibus ne igitur ex his locis argumenta sumemus? C. P. Imo vero scrutabimur, & quaeremus ex omnibus: sed adhibebimus iudicium, ut levia semper reiciamus, nonnunquam etiam communia praetermittamus, & non necessaria.
units.tr: C. F. Shall we then draw arguments from all these places? C. P. Indeed we shall search, and seek from all of them; but we shall apply judgement, so that we always reject trivial things, and sometimes also pass over common and unnecessary ones.

units.la: C. F. Omnibus ne igitur ex ijs locis argumenta sumenus? ) Videbat adolescens Cicero, magna sibi locorum propositam sylvam. dubitavit igitur, an omnia ex omnibus sumenda essent. Quamobrem rogat patrem, ut suo iudicio hanc sibi copiam & varietatem distinguat.
units.tr: C. F. Shall we then draw arguments from all these places? The young Cicero saw a great forest of places set before him. He therefore wondered whether everything should be taken from everything. So he asks his father to sort out this abundance and variety for him by his own judgement.

units.la: C. P. Imo vero scrutabimur. ) Quoniam idem est officium in hac re dialectici & oratoris, id faciendum esse monet Cicero Oratorem suum, quod Dialecticum Socrates, ut in perpetuo quasi venatu menatu'uersetur. Nam illud primum intelligendum est, nec ullam esse disputationem, ullam'ue quæstionem, in quam non aliquis locus incurrat: neq; fere omnes locos incidere in omnem quæstionem: & quibusdam quæstionibus alios, quibusdam alios aptiores esse. Percurret igitur omnes orator ille, utetur aptis generatim: nec inueniet solum quid dicat, sed etiam expendet. Nihil enim feracius ingenijs, ut Cicero in Oratore ait: ijs præsertim, quæ disciplinis exculta sunt. sed ut segetes fœcundæ & uberes non solum fruges, uerum herbas etiam effundunt inimicifimas frugibus: sic interdum ex illis locis aut leuia quedam, aut caussis aliena, aut non utilia gignuntur, quorum ab oratoris iudicio delectus magnus adhibebitur. Quamobrem excitanda est diligentia, & iudicium acuendum, ut qui loci in quäq; quæstionem apti sint & utiles, intelligatur. Hæc duo hoc loco requirit Cicero: diligëtiam, cum dicit, Scrutabimur & quæremus: alterum cum dicit, Adhibebimus iudicium. Diligentia excitatur quarendo, audiendo, legendo, disputando, scribendo. his enim copia locorum comparatur, ad quam copiâ deinde iudicium adhibendum est. Est autem iudicium, eorum quæ inuenta sunt, ordine certo collocandorum scientia. nam nisi ex copia, delectus haberi non potest. Ex hac igitur tanta copia, no-
units.tr: C. P. Indeed we shall search. Since the office of the dialectician and of the orator is the same in this matter, Cicero bids his orator do what Socrates did as dialectician: to be always, as it were, in a continual hunt. For we must first understand that there is no disputation or question into which some place does not fall; yet hardly all places fall into every question, and some places suit some questions better, others other questions. That orator will therefore run through all the places, and use those that suit each kind of question. He will not only discover what to say but also weigh it. For nothing is more fruitful than talent, as Cicero says in the Orator, especially talent cultivated by learning. But just as fertile and rich cornfields produce not only crops but also weeds most hostile to crops, so sometimes those places yield trivial things, things foreign to the cause, or useless ones. From these the orator will make a careful selection by his judgement. Therefore diligence must be aroused and judgement sharpened, so that it may be understood which places are apt and useful for each question. Cicero requires two things here: diligence, when he says "we shall search and seek," and judgement, when he says "we shall apply judgement." Diligence is aroused by seeking, hearing, reading, disputing, and writing, for by these the abundance of places is gained, and to this abundance judgement must then be applied. Judgement is the knowledge of arranging in a fixed order the things that have been found. For unless there is abundance, no selection can be made. From this great abundance, therefore,

units.la: {a} Annotations in red ink in the right margin are not transcribed. strum iudiciu instruit Cicero, ut leuia semper reſijciamus: nonnunquam etiam communia praetermit‑ tamus, & non necessaria. ex quib. uerbis colligi‑mus, tria esse genera argumentorum, quae deprom‑muntur ex locis. Nam alia leuia sunt, & quae hos‑tem ferire non possint: alia communia, alia uero ne‑ cessaria. Leuia dicuntur, quae pondus non habent, quaeque artificis ingenium minime prae se ferunt: nec haerent, cum in aduersarium contorquentur. Communia uero appellantur, aut quibus etiam aduersarius uti potest: aut quae tametsi probabilia appellentur, tamen confirmanda sunt antequam ex eis aliquid concludatur. cuius genera facit Cicero de Inuent. li. 1. Signum, credibile, iudicatum, comparabile: quorum explicatio illinc petenda est. Necessaria deniq; & firma, utiliaq; ea sunt, quae quod volumus, sine dubitatione concludunt, ut ab antecedentibus & consequentibus. ueris, ut ex genere & forma, ex causis & effectis, atq; etiam ex definitione. Itaq; necessariis semper utendum erit, communibinterdum pro causae utilitate: leuibus uero uix, & non nisi coactus dabit locum in sua oratione prudens orator, nisi fortasse ridiculi causa, aut si in turbam coniiciantur: ut Imperator bonus, seruis, aut imbelli iuuentute, ad bellum non nisi necessitate coactus utitur. Quod si leuib. utendum sit, ea erit collocatio quae copiarum esse solet, ut grauissima quaeq; queq; initio collocëtur, atq; etiā in subsidio: reliqua uero in medio cōijciātur, ut quasi aliorū robore ualeāt. Quin etiā illud in necessarijs & firmis faciendū esse, Cicero lib. de Orat. 2. præcipit, ut si ea ualde multa sunt, ea quæ ex ijs aut leuissima sunt, aut alijs grauioribus cōsimilia, secernātur, atq; ex oratione remoueantur, neque tam numerentur, quàm expendantur.
units.tr: Cicero also teaches us to judgement that we should always reject light arguments, and sometimes even set aside common and unnecessary ones. From these words we gather that there are three kinds of arguments, drawn from the topics. Some are light and cannot wound the enemy; some are common; and some are necessary. Light arguments are those that carry no weight and show little of the speaker's skill, and they do not stick when they are hurled at the opponent. Common arguments are those which the opponent can also use, or which, although called probable, must be confirmed before anything is concluded from them. Cicero lists their kinds in De Inventione, book 1: sign, credible, judged, comparable; their explanation should be sought there. Finally, necessary and firm arguments, which are also useful, are those which conclude without doubt what we want: from antecedents and consequents, from truths such as genus and form, from causes and effects, and even from definition. Therefore necessary arguments should always be used, and common ones sometimes, as the advantage of the case requires; light arguments scarcely at all, and a prudent orator will give them room in his speech only when compelled, perhaps for the sake of a joke, or if they are thrown in among a crowd, as a good general uses slaves or an unwarlike youth in war only under compulsion of necessity. But if light arguments must be used, the arrangement should be that which is customary for troops: the heaviest of each kind are placed at the beginning and likewise in reserve, and each is placed at the front, while the rest are put in the middle, so that they may be strong by the support of the others. Indeed Cicero, in De Oratore book 2, also teaches that among necessary and firm arguments, if there are very many, those which are the lightest or are very similar to other weightier ones should be separated out and removed from the speech, and they should be weighed rather than counted.

units.la: C. F. Quoniā de fide respōdisti, uo- lo audire de motu. C. P. Loco tu qui de quæris: sed planius quod uis ex- plicabitur, cum ad orationis ipsius quæstionumq; rationem uenero.
units.tr: C. F. Since you have answered about faith, I want to hear about emotion. C. P. You ask in the right place; but what you want will be explained more plainly when I come to the arrangement of the speech itself and the method of its questions.

units.la: C. F. Quoniā de fide respōdisti, uolo audire de motu.) Duæ partes inuētionis propositæ fuerūt, fides et motus. Sed quoniā quib. ex locis fides fiat, dictū est, ita ordine de motu quærit filius, ut inuētionis utrāq; partē intelligat. Verùm non omnia quouis in loco dicēda sunt, & explicāda: idcirco pater interrogādi ordinē, quē sequitur filius, probat: sed tamē alibi planius & cōmodius explicari posse indicat, nimirū cum ad orationis partes, & quæstionū siue causarū genera uētū fucrit. Nā cū duæ partes orationis ad impellēdos animos ualeant, principiū & peroratio: itemq; cū generibus causarum fines quidam propositi sint, qui motibus animorum continentur: perspicuum est, in illis explicandis, & de motu quoq; esse docendum. Valet hoc praeceptum Ciceronis, ut intelligamus eos in ratione docendi peccare, qui ubi aliquid rei fit mentio, omnia quae de ea tradi possint, docere uolunt. Est enim, ubi definitio tantum adhibenda sit, ubi etiam diuisio: est etiam, ubi nihil sit dicendum. Huic contrarium uitium est, cum locus maxime requirit explicationem, nihil dicere, & tanquam scopulum praeterubi.
units.tr: C. F. Since you have answered about faith, I want to hear about emotion.) Two parts of invention were proposed, faith and emotion. But since it has been said from which topics faith is produced, the son asks about emotion in such an order that he understands both parts of invention. Yet not everything must be said and explained in every place; therefore the father approves the order of questioning which the son follows, but indicates that it can be explained more plainly and conveniently elsewhere, namely when he comes to the parts of the speech and the kinds of questions or causes. For since two parts of the speech, the exordium and the peroration, serve to move the minds of the hearers, and since certain ends of the purpose are bound up with the emotions of the mind in each kind of cause, it is clear that in explaining these one must also teach about emotion. This precept of Cicero applies, so that we understand that those err in the method of teaching who, whenever something is mentioned, want to teach everything that can be handed down about it. For there is a place where only a definition should be given, and a place where a division is needed too, and a place where nothing need be said. The opposite fault is when the matter especially requires explanation, and one says nothing, sailing past it as if it were a rock.

units.la: C. F. Quid sequitur igitur? C. P. Cum inueneris, collocare: cuius in infinita quaestione ordo est idem fere, quem exposui locorum. Indefinita autem adhibenda sunt illa etiam, quae ad motus animorum pertinet. C. F. Quomodo igitur ista explicas? C.P. Habeo communia praecepta fidem faciendi, & commouendi.
units.tr: C. F. What follows, then? C. P. When you have found the arguments, arrange them; in the infinite question the order is almost the same as the one I have set out for topics. But in the definite question those arguments must also be used which pertain to the emotions of the mind. C. F. How then do you explain those? C. P. I have common precepts for producing belief and for stirring the emotions.

units.la: C. F. Quid sequitur igitur?) Deiectus adolescens de proposito interrogandi ordine, non satis meminit quo fit redeundum, quae uel pars officij oratorij sequatur. Sed pater illum ad id quod est quaerendum reuocat, nimirum ad collocationem. ea enim est in officio oratoris pars secunda: quae etsi ad uerba quoque pertineat, tamen, ut suprà dictum est, rerum est propria: id est, argumentorum, & partium orationis. Verum hic de argumentorum tantum ordine praecipit. Facit autem ordinem duplicem: alterum naturalem, alterum consilij & prudentiae. Prior ille ordo in infinita quaestione tractanda fere seruatur: is est, cum aliqua quaestio uel probanda, uel refellenda sumitur. Primum ea argumenta adhibentur, quae in infinitis locis latent: atq; a definitione exorsi, ad alios eo ordine quo expositi sunt, progredimur: deinde si opus sit, ad assumpta delabimur. nam quae in re ipsa sunt, siue naturalia, adventicijs & extra rei naturam positis, priora esse intelliguntur. Alter autem ordo qui pendet ex oratoris prudentia, & causae utilitate, ad definitam quaestionem refertur: in qua non solum docetur auditor, sed etiam variè concitatur. Quare in hac quaestione, dispositio ipsa argumentorum ad motus animorum est inflectenda. id quomodo & faciendum, & intelligendum sit, sequentibus praeceptis explicabit.
units.tr: C. F. What follows, then?) The young man, diverted from the plan of questioning, does not quite remember where he must return, or what part of the orator's office follows. But the father recalls him to what is to be asked, namely arrangement; for this is the second part of the orator's office, which, although it also pertains to words, is nevertheless, as has been said above, proper to things, that is, to arguments and the parts of the speech. Here, however, he teaches only about the order of arguments. He makes a twofold order: one natural, the other of judgement and prudence. The former order is generally kept in treating an infinite question, that is, when some question is taken up either to be proved or to be refuted. First those arguments are used which lie hidden in infinite places; beginning from definition, we proceed to the others in the order in which they were set out; then, if need be, we descend to the assumed ones, for those things which are in the matter itself, whether natural or external and placed outside the nature of the thing, are understood to be prior. The other order, which depends on the prudence of the orator and the advantage of the case, refers to the definite question; in it the hearer is not only taught but also variously stirred. Therefore in this question the very arrangement of the arguments must be bent to the emotions of the mind. How this is to be done and understood, he will explain in the following precepts.

units.la: C. F. Quomodo igitur ita explicas? C. P. Haec communia praecepta sunt idem faciendi, & commouendi.) Non fidem faciendi ut in infinita quaestione, sed ut in definita, siue causa: in qua non fides sola, ut dixi, sed motus quoq; quaeritur. Communia autem praecepta dicit, quoniam sunt etiam propria, quae ad causarum status & proprias actionum quæstiones,imò etiam ad singulos homines,& singula crimina pertinent. Præterea etiam communia,quod ex communi & in medio posita doctrina physica, in qua de animo disseritur, repetenda sunt.
units.tr: C. F. How then do you explain it? C. P. These are common precepts for the same purpose, of doing and of moving. Not for producing belief, as in an unlimited question, but as in a defined question, or case, in which not belief alone, as I said, but emotion too is sought. They are called common because they are also proper, pertaining to the states of causes and to the particular questions of actions, indeed even to individual persons and individual crimes. Besides, they are common because they must be drawn from common teaching, and from the physical doctrine placed in the middle, in which the soul is discussed.

units.la: DE COLLOCATIONE, seu Dispositione.
units.tr: ON ARRANGEMENT, or Disposition.

units.la: Quoniam fides est firma opinio, motus autem, animi incitatio, aut ad voluptatem, aut ad molestiam, aut ad metum, aut ad cupiditatem: tot enim sunt motus genera, partes plures generum singulorum, omnem collocationem ad finem accommodo quæstionis. Nam est in proposito finis, fides: in caussa, & fides & motus. Quare cum de caussa dixero, in qua est propositum, de utroque dixero.
units.tr: Since belief is a firm opinion, and emotion is an stirring of the mind, either towards pleasure, or towards distress, or towards fear, or towards desire (for there are as many kinds of emotion, with several species under each kind), I shape the whole arrangement to the aim of the question. For in a proposition the aim is belief; in a cause it is both belief and emotion. So when I have spoken of the cause, in which the proposition lies, I shall have spoken of both.

units.la: Quoniam fides est firma opinio.) Hanc definitionem fidei sumpsit ex quarto Topicorum Aristotelis: Fides, inquit, est in opinione: siquidem firmitas opinionis est, ex quo efficitur, opinionem credere. Item code libro post multa ostendit, fidē scientiam dici posse: Si scientia est, inquit, & is qui scientia præditus est, quia sciat, credit: prose-
units.tr: Since belief is a firm opinion.) He took this definition of belief from the fourth book of Aristotle's Topics: "Belief," he says, "lies in opinion, since firmness of opinion is what makes us believe an opinion." Likewise, in the same book, after many arguments, he shows that belief can be called knowledge: "If there is knowledge, and the one who has knowledge knows, he believes; therefore..." (...) belief must necessarily be knowledge.

units.la: fides scientia fides sit necesse est. Quo in loco uidere licet, scientiam pro opinione esse positam. Sed uidendum est, quomodo fides dicatur opinio, an ut pars, an ut nomen idem significans? nam certum est, hic fidem non ut iusticiæ parteni, sed pro persuasione capi, quæ fit argumentis, ut ante uisum est. non est autē dubium, quin fidem voluerit Cicero definire, et genere aliquo et proprietate definitionem constituere. Erit itaque opinio, genus: firma uero, proprietas, qua hæc opinio tum ab errore, tum ab opinione imbecilla seceRnitur, ut Fides sit uehemens de aliqua re opinio. Nam omnis animi cognitio aut ex probabilibus, aut ex necessarijs gignitur. Quæ ex probabilibus fit, opinio: quæ ex necessarijs, scientia proprie nominatur. Opinioni subijcitur coniectura, ars, fides: et si ex falsis, error. Sed cur firma dicitur, cum ea tantum firma dicatur, quæ ex certis necessarijsq; cognitio efficitur? Quia cum reliqua ex probabili tantum ratione oriantur, fides tum à probabili ratione, tum ab autoritate prouenit. Fides igitur cum alijs opinionis partibus, quæ infirmiores sunt, collata, firma est opinio: cum certis, uenis, et necessarijs, infirma et imbecilla est autem opinio, notitia eorum quæ sensibus deprehensa sunt, et memoria conseruata: uel ratione probabili industa cognitio.
units.tr: belief knowledge belief must be. Here we may see that knowledge is put for opinion. But we must consider how belief is called opinion: as a part, or as a word with the same meaning? For it is certain that here Cicero takes belief not as a part of justice, but for persuasion, which is produced by arguments, as was said above. And there is no doubt that Cicero meant to define belief, and to frame the definition by a genus and a property. Opinion, then, will be the genus; firm will be the property, by which this opinion is distinguished both from error and from weak opinion, so that belief is a strong opinion about some matter. For all knowledge of the mind arises either from probable things or from necessary things. Knowledge that arises from probable things is opinion; that from necessary things is properly called science. Under opinion fall conjecture, art, and belief; and if they rest on false things, error. But why is it called firm, when only that is called firm which comes from certain and necessary knowledge? Because the other opinions arise from probable reasoning alone, whereas belief comes both from probable reasoning and from authority. So belief, compared with the other parts of opinion, which are weaker, is a firm opinion; compared with certain, evident and necessary things, it is weak and feeble. Opinion, moreover, is knowledge of things grasped by the senses and kept in memory, or knowledge gained by probable reasoning.

units.la: Motus autem animi incitatio. ) Brèuissimus est motus definitio. Pleniores si quis requirat, legat nostri Ciceronis Tusculanas quaest. lib. 4. De animorum perturbationibus loquitur: quae quidem nō essent necessariae, si legib. omnia in caussis ageretur, quemadmodū Athenis in Areopago fieri solitū legimus: ubi prohibebāt, Oratorē quicquā extra causam dicere. Extra aut caussā intelligebant esse animorū istas permotiones: fidem uero proprià esse caussarū. neq; enim conuenit iudicē distorquere ad indignationem, uel inuidiam, uel misericordiam. id enim est, ac si quis eam qua usurus est regulam, obliquam ac tortuosam efficeret. Cur igitur (dicat aliquis) in motu tantum posucre ueteres oratores? Dicam. Si boni uiri fuerunt, idcirco motus, & illas amplificationum faces, ad impellendum iudicem, in eam partem à qua ueritas staret, & ius, adhibuerunt. Sin improbi, ut in quā nollent partem quo iure quaq; iniuria flecterent, & uictoriam siue iustam siue iniustam auferret. Omnis igitur ratio permouendorum animorum (ut mihi quidem uidetur) ad auditorum naturā & mores accommodanda est. Si enim talis sit, ut sua sponte æquitatem sequatur, satis erit docere, rem aut esse, aut non esse, aut factam aut non factam suisse. Sed si auditor talis erit, qui nisi malo coactus ueritatem sequi nolit, omni permotionū genere impellēdus erit, ut quod uerum et æquum est, huiusmodi machinatione amplecti cogatur. Hac igitur de caussa, sine reprehensione, uti animorum permotionibus licet. Nunc quae genera ponat Cicero, uideamus. Ponit autem quatuor: uoluptatem, molestiam, metum, & cupiditatem. quarum definitiones, & genera ijs subiecta, ex Tusculanarum libro 4. sumenda sunt. Sunt autem harum quatuor duae, quae in praesenti opinione cernuntur, uoluptas scilicet, & molestia: duae autē in rei futurae opinione, metus & cupiditas.
units.tr: Emotion, however, is a stirring of the mind.) This is a very brief definition of emotion. If anyone wants a fuller one, let him read our Cicero's Tusculan Disputations, book 4, which deals with the disturbances of the mind. These would not be necessary if everything in causes were done by laws, as we read was customary at Athens in the Areopagus, where the orator was forbidden to say anything outside the case. They understood those stirrings of the mind to lie outside the case, and belief to be the proper concern of causes. For it is not fitting to bend the judge towards indignation, or envy, or pity; that would be like making the rule one is going to use crooked and twisted. Why then, someone may ask, did the ancient orators place emotion alone among these? I shall say. If they were good men, they used emotions and those torches of amplification to drive the judge towards the side where truth and justice stand. If they were wicked, they used them to turn him, by right or by wrong, towards the side they did not want, and to win the victory, just or unjust. So every method of stirring the minds of hearers (as it seems to me) must be adapted to the nature and character of the audience. For if the audience is such that it follows fairness of its own accord, it will be enough to show that a thing is or is not, or was or was not done. But if the hearer is such that he will not follow the truth unless compelled by ill, he must be driven by every kind of emotional pressure, so that he is forced to embrace what is true and just by such contrivance. For this reason, then, it is permissible to use the emotions without blame. Now let us see what kinds Cicero lays down. He lays down four: pleasure, distress, fear and desire. Their definitions, and the species subordinate to them, must be taken from the fourth book of the Tusculans. Of these four, two are seen in present opinion, namely pleasure and distress; two in opinion about a future thing, fear and desire.

units.la: Voluptatem interdum etiam laetitiam uocant, & molestiam aegritudinem, & metum timorem, & cupiditatem libidinem.Illud autem magis operaepreciūm est intelligere, cur quatuor genera faciat Cicero, cum Aristoteles duo tantum fecerit Rhet. lib.2. aegritudinem nimirum & uoluptatem. Sed illud intelligendum est: Philosophum sub uoluptate cupiditatem, sub aegritudine metum etiam, ut mea opinio fert, comprehendisse. Qui praeterea in singulis tria docet esse consideranda: qui (exēpli caussa) ira afficiantur: deinde, quibus irasci soleant: tertium, quas ob res homines irascantur. nam si unum aut alterum tantum habeamus, & non omnia teneamus, nullo modo fieri poterit, ut animos audientium ad iram impellamus: quod de reliquis etiam perturbationibus sentiendum est,
units.tr: Pleasure they sometimes call joy, distress they call grief, fear they call dread, and desire they call lust. It is more worth our while to understand why Cicero makes four kinds, when Aristotle made only two in the second book of the Rhetoric: grief and pleasure. But we must understand this: the Philosopher included desire under pleasure, and fear under grief, as in my opinion they are also comprehended. He teaches, moreover, that in each one three things must be considered: first, who are affected (for example, by anger); then, by whom they are usually angered; third, for what causes men are angered. For if we have only one or two of these and do not hold all of them, it will in no way be possible to drive the minds of the hearers to anger; and the same must be felt about the other disturbances.

units.la: Idcirco idem philosophus hæc tria diligenter ibidem explicat: qui locus est ab eo, qui uelit hac facultate præditus esse, pernoscendus. Quanquam etiam Cicero de Oratore lib. 2. eundem non inelegante explicauit. Oriuntur autem animorum motus ex ea animi parte, siue facultate, quæ rationis expers dicitur, quæ est ὁρμή Græce, nos appetitum appellamus: in qua parte irarum existit ardor, ut Cicero de Diuinatione loquitur. Nam in participe rationis parte, quæ λόγικη dicitur Græce, ponunt tranquillitatem, id est placidam quietam, que constantiam: in illa altera, motus turbidos, tum iræ, tum cupiditatis, contrarios inimicosq; rationi, quæ λόγος appellatur.
units.tr: For this reason the same philosopher explains these three things carefully in the same place; this is a passage that anyone who wishes to be endowed with this faculty must learn thoroughly. Although Cicero too, in the second book of On the Orator, explained the same matter not inelegantly. Now the motions of the mind arise from that part of the mind, or faculty, which is called without reason, which the Greeks call [ὁρμή], and which we call appetite; in this part exists the heat of anger, as Cicero speaks in On Divination. For in the part that partakes of reason, which the Greeks call [λόγικη], they place tranquillity, that is, a calm and quiet constancy; in that other part they place turbulent motions, both of anger and of desire, which are opposed and hostile to reason, which is called [λόγος].

units.la: Omnem collocationem ad finem accômodo quæstionis. ) Quomodo ad finem quæstionis collocatio accômodetur, suprà dicere cœpimus, nec absoluimus tamen: quemadmodum nec Cicero, nec superiore, nec hoc loco absoluit: sed absoluet in sequentibus, unà cum ipsis generibus causarum. Nunc autem, qui fines duobus quæstionum generibus propositi sint, breuiter indicat. in proposito enim, fidem tantum spectari dicit: in causa uero, et fidem et motum. In quo primum illud uidendum est, cur ad propositum non pertineat motus? Ad quod primum dicimus, id fieri, quia cum personis, et reliquis maximis attributis propositum careat, in quibus caussæ motus existunt, perspicuum est, cur ad propositum motus non pertineat . Quod si quis dicat, in rebus etiam ipsis, non modò in personis,inesse motum: id nec nos negamus, sed ea ratione, si res ipsæ in personis ponantur,& in eis considerentur: alioqui res ipsæ per se,& simpliciter, omnis motus expertes omnino sunt.
units.tr: I shape the whole arrangement to the aim of the question.) How the arrangement is to be adapted to the aim of the question I have begun to say above, and yet I have not finished; nor does Cicero finish it either above or here: he will finish it in what follows, together with the very kinds of causes. Now, however, he briefly indicates what aims are set for the two kinds of questions. For in a proposition, he says, only belief is looked at; in a cause, both belief and emotion. Here the first thing to consider is why emotion does not belong to the proposition. To this first point we answer that it happens because the proposition lacks persons and the other greatest attributes, in which the causes of emotion exist; so it is plain why emotion does not belong to the proposition. But if someone says that emotion is present not only in persons but also in the things themselves, we do not deny it; but this holds if the things themselves are placed in persons and considered in them; otherwise the things in themselves, taken simply, are altogether free of all emotion.

units.la: Quare cum de caussa dixero,in qua est propositum,de utroq; dixero. ) Hic uides aperte,Cicero-nem in caussis ipsis,in quib. sunt personæ, propositum non nudè nobis considerandum proponere, ut oratorio more propositum ipsum cum suis attributis ad aliquem revocet motum . Sed quæritur,quomodo in caussa propositum esse dicatur? Multi multa afferunt:sed mihi uidetur Cicero ipse seipsum explicare.Dixit enim proximè, in caussa & fidem & motum inesse. Atqui fides ad propositum pertinet proprie:quæ cum sit etiā in caussa,ergo etiam propositum in caussa erit. Quanquam illud etiam possumus dicere, ita esse propositum in caussa,ut genus est in specie,quod Fabio placuit:uel ut pars in toto.
units.tr: Therefore when I have spoken of the cause, in which the proposition lies, I shall have spoken of both.) Here you see plainly that Cicero, in the causes themselves, in which there are persons, does not propose that we consider the proposition bare, but as in the orators' manner, he refers the proposition itself, with its attributes, to some emotion. But it is asked how the proposition is said to lie in the cause? Many have offered many answers; but it seems to me that Cicero explains himself. For he said just before that both belief and emotion are present in the cause. But belief properly belongs to the proposition; since it is also present in the cause, the proposition too will be in the cause. Though we can also say that the proposition is in the cause as the genus is in the species, which pleased Fabius, or as the part is in the whole.

units.la: C. F. Quid habes igitur de caussa dicere? C. P. Auditorū eam genere distingui, Nam aut auscultator est modò, qui audit, aut disceptator: idest, rei sententiæque moderator, ita ut delectetur, aut statuat aliquid. Statuit autē aut de præteritis, ut iudex: aut de futuris, ut senatus. Sic tria sunt genera, iudicij, deliberationis, exornationis: quæ, quia in laudationes maximè conferatur, proprium habet iam ex eo nomen. C. F. Quas res sibi proponet in istis tribus generibus orator? C. P. Delectationem in exornatione, in iudicio autē sæuitiam, aut clementiam iudicis: in suasione autem, aut spem, aut reformidationem deliberantis.
units.tr: Son: What, then, have you to say about the case? Father: The hearers are distinguished by kind. For the listener is either merely an auditor, who simply hears, or a judge of the matter, that is, one who moderates the speech and its sense, so that he is delighted, or he decides something. He decides either about past events, as a judge does, or about future ones, as the senate does. So there are three kinds: judicial, deliberative and epideictic, and the last, because it is applied mostly to praises, already has its name from that. Son: What matters will the orator set before himself in these three kinds? Father: In epideictic oratory, delight; in judicial oratory, the severity or the clemency of the judge; in deliberative oratory, either the hope or the fear of the one deliberating.

units.la: Quid habes igitur de causa dicere?) Cum igitur in causa propositu contineatur, & ad causam omnia referantur: quot sint genera causarum primùm, deinde qui fines, & quomodo ad eos fines collocatio omnis accommodanda sit, dicendum est. Et hoc est quod quærit à patre filius. Sed ut Ciceronem melius intelligamus, Aristoteles cum Cicerone coniungendus est. Nam & ex eius fontibus hæc omnis causarum doctrina, ut pleraq; alia in his Partitionibus, emanarunt. Primùm igitur sciendum est, tot esse genera causarum, quot auditorum genera reperiuntur. necesse enim est, ut is qui audit, vel auscultator tantum fit, vel etiam disceptator. Disceptator vero bipertito intelligitur: aut qui in senatu, vel in concione dicentem audit, aut in foro. in senatu, ut senator: in concione populus, in foro autem iudex. At vero auscultator de oratoris facultate iudicat in laudatione, aut vituperatione. ex quib. tria genera causarum effecta sunt: Iudiciale, Deliberativum, et Demonstrativum, quod qui a in exornandis laudandisque maxime claris viris confertur, proprium iam habet ex eo nomen, et exornationis genus, a meliore scilicet parte, appellatur. His autem generibus magno veterum consensu tria tempora proponuntur: Demonstrativo praesens, Deliberativo futurum, Iudiciali vero praeteritum. Et quoniam causa ex tribus constat, ex eo qui dicit, ex materia de qua dicitur, et ex eo apud quem verba fiunt: in his trib. alij atq; alij fines sunt considerandi. Nam si eum qui dicit spectemus, is in singulis causarum generib. et auditorum aliud atque aliud spectat. In rebus autem ipsis, id est, in generibus causarum, separatim haec sunt consideranda: in demonstrativo honestum et turpe, in deliberatione utile et inutile, in iudicio aequum et iniquum. Sin vero auditores ipsos respicias, in exorexornatione delectatione, in deliberatione spem aut reformidationem, in iudiciis saeuitiam aut clementiam sibi proponet orator. Ergo iam constat, materiem oratoris in iudiciali genere esse æquitatem aut iniuriam, in laudationibus honestatem, in consultationibus utilitatem. Sunt igitur in demonstrationibus quinque consideranda: laus et vituperatio, honestum et turpe, et quintum delectatio. In deliberationibus sex: suasio et dissuasio, utile inutile, spes et metus. In iudiciis totidem: accusatio, defensio, ius, iniuria, saeuitia, clementia. Sed tamen non ita haec quae diximus omnia intelligenda sunt, quasi mutare quicquam non liceat: commutantur enim et miscentur fines ipsi ita, ut in deliberationib. etiam de honesto agatur, et in iudiciis de utili, et in exornationibus de æquitate. Itemq; de temporibus idem dicendum est. nam et qui suadent, praeterita reuocant in memoriam: et qui laudant, de futuris coniectura faciunt: et praeterita reminiscentes commemorant. Sed de iis, suis locis plura.
units.tr: "What, then, have you to say about the case?" Since the proposition is contained in the case, and everything is referred to the case, we must first say how many kinds of cases there are, then what the ends are, and how all arrangement is to be adapted to those ends. This is what the son asks of the father. But to understand Cicero better, Aristotle must be joined with Cicero, for this whole doctrine of cases, like many other things in these Partitiones, flowed from his sources. First, then, we must know that there are as many kinds of cases as there are kinds of hearers. For the one who hears must either be merely a listener or else also a judge. A judge, moreover, is understood in two ways: either one who hears the speaker in the senate or in an assembly, or one who hears him in the forum. In the senate he is a senator; in an assembly, the people; in the forum, a judge. The mere listener, on the other hand, judges the orator's skill in praise or blame. From these three kinds of case arise: the judicial, the deliberative and the demonstrative, and the last, which is applied mostly to adorning and praising outstanding men, already has its name from this, and is called the kind of ornamentation, from its better part, of course. To these kinds the ancients by broad agreement assign three tenses: the demonstrative the present, the deliberative the future, the judicial the past. And since a case consists of three things, the speaker, the matter of which he speaks, and the one before whom the words are delivered, different ends must be considered in each of these three. For if we look at the speaker, he looks to one thing or another in each kind of case and kind of hearer. But in the matters themselves, that is, in the kinds of cases, these are to be considered separately: in the demonstrative, the honourable and the base; in the deliberative, the useful and the useless; in the judicial, the fair and the unfair. But if you look at the hearers themselves, the orator will set before himself, in ornamentation, delight; in deliberation, hope or fear; in trials, severity or clemency. So it is now clear that the matter of the orator in the judicial kind is fairness or injustice, in praises honour, in deliberations usefulness. There are therefore five things to be considered in demonstrations: praise and blame, the honourable and the base, and fifth, delight. In deliberations six: persuasion and dissuasion, the useful and the useless, hope and fear. In trials as many: accusation, defence, right, wrong, severity, clemency. But these things we have said are not to be understood so strictly as if nothing could be altered: the ends themselves are changed and mixed, so that in deliberations too the honourable is discussed, in trials the useful, and in ornaments fairness.
