The same must be said about times. For those who persuade also recall the past to memory, and those who praise also make conjectures about the future, and recalling the past they commemorate it. But more about these in their proper places.

units.la: C. F. Cur igitur exponis hoc loco genera controuersiarum? C. P. Vt rationem collocandi ad finem cuiusque accommodem. C. F. Quonam tandem modo? C. P. Quia quiquibus in orationibus delectatio finis est, uariij sunt ordines collocandi.
units.tr: Son: Why, then, do you set out the kinds of controversies at this point? Father: So that I may adapt the arrangement to the end of each. Son: In what way, pray? Father: Because in those speeches where delight is the end, there are various orders of arrangement to be followed.

units.la: C. F. Cur igitur exponis hoc loco genera controuersiarum? ) Caussarum genera quae essent, & unde orirentur, docuit proxime pater: itemq; in singulis, qui fines propositi essent. Quare cum non intelligeret filius, quorsum haec controuersiarum distinctio facta esset, cum haec pertineant ad quaestionum explicationem, quae postea tradetur: doceri cupit, cur pater anteuerterit, & hoc loco potius quam illo expofuerit.
units.tr: "Why, then, do you set out the kinds of controversies at this point?" The father has just taught what the kinds of cases are and where they arise, and likewise, in each, what the ends of the proposition are. So since the son did not understand why this division of controversies was made, when these things belong to the explanation of questions, which will be taught later, he wishes to be taught why the father anticipated it and set it out at this point rather than at that.

units.la: C. P. Vt rationem collocandi ad finem cuiusque accommodem.) Finis in omni re praestatissimus est, & propter finem aguntur omnia, ad eumq; referuntur. Itaq; respondet pater, se idcirco controuersiarum genera distinxisse, propter collocationem. Nam si collocatio & dispositio omnis ad finem accommodari debet, & fines ipsi in controuersijs inueniuntur, igitur controuersiae ipsae fuerunt indicandae: ut illis inuentis, ab ipsis ad fines ipsarum, tanquam manu duceretur oratoris collocatio.
units.tr: "So that I may adapt the arrangement to the end of each." Among all things the end is most excellent, and everything is done for the sake of the end and is referred to it. So the father answers that he distinguished the kinds of controversies for the sake of arrangement. For if all arrangement and disposition ought to be adapted to the end, and the ends themselves are found in controversies, then the controversies themselves had to be pointed out, so that once they were found, the orator's arrangement might be guided by them to their ends, as if by the hand.

units.la: C. F. Quo nam tandem modo? ) Vtile est, quod nunc scire cupit adolescens Cicero: nimirum methodu ipsam, & rationem in singulis generib. ad finem omnia collocandi, quam hic Cicero pater paucis & perspicuis praeceptis tradit, quo facilius memoria retineri possint.
units.tr: "In what way, pray?" This is useful, and the young Cicero now wishes to know it: namely the method itself and the reasoning, in each kind, of arranging everything towards the end, which Cicero the father here teaches in a few clear precepts, so that they may more easily be retained in memory.

units.la: C. P. Quia quibus in orationibus delectatio finis est, varij sunt ordines collocandi.) Varij, nimirum quatuor, in exornatione scilicet: de ea enim loquitur, cui delectatio finis est.
units.tr: "Because in those speeches where delight is the end, there are various orders of arrangement." "Various," namely four, in ornamentation, of course; for he is speaking of that kind in which delight is the end.

units.la: Nam aut temporum seruantur gradus, aut generum distributiones, aut a minoribus ad maiora ascendimus, aut a maioribus ad minora dilabimur, aut haec inaequabili varietate distinguimus, cum parua magnis, simplicia coniunctis, obscura dilucidis, laeta tristibus, incredibilia probabilibus intexîmus, quae in exornationem cadunt omnia.
units.tr: For either the steps of time are kept, or the distributions by kinds are followed, or we ascend from smaller things to greater, or we slide down from greater to smaller, or we vary these with an uneven variety, mixing small things with great, simple with compound, obscure with clear, joyful with sad, incredible with probable; all of which fall under ornamentation.

units.la: Nam aut temporum seruantur gradus.) Etsi multis modis in collocando temporis ordinem sequi licet: tamen illud est praestantissimum, cum in laudando vel vituperando, aetatum ordinem sequimur: & ut quidq; primum, aut secundum, aut postremum gestum, dictum ue est, recensemus. a pueritia siue infantia in hac ratione exordimur: deinde adolescentiae facta commemoramus: postmodum, qualis quisq; uir fuerit: & postremo, cuiusmodi modi extiterit eius senectus.Et si ulterius progredi uolumus,quid in morte, & post mortem acciderit,narrabimus. Possumus etiam ita distribuere tempora,in ea quae sine nobis extiterunt:cuiusmodi sunt patria,genus,parentes.tum quae nobiscum, quae pars totam hominis uitam complectitur.postremo quae post nos facta sunt,nostra tamen causa:ut funus, luctus,laudatio,pompa,sepultura.
units.tr: "For either the steps of time are kept." Although in arranging one may follow the order of time in many ways, that one is the most excellent, when in praising or blaming we follow the order of ages, and recount what was done, said or suffered first, second or last. We begin with this method from boyhood or infancy; then we recount the deeds of youth; afterwards what kind of man each was; and finally what sort of old age he had. And if we wish to go further, we shall narrate what happened at death and after death. We can also distribute times in another way: into those things which existed without us, such as country, family and parents; then those which were with us, which take up the whole span of a person's life; and finally those which were done after us, yet for our sake: such as the funeral, mourning, eulogy, procession and burial.

units.la: Aut genera distributiones.) Nimirum cum multa & varia facta in propria uirtutum genera digeruntur:ut quid prudenter,quid iuste,quid fortiter,quid temperanter,clementer ue aliquis secerit, aut etiam contra:sic enim Cicero infra interpretatur.
units.tr: "Or distributions by kinds." Namely, when many and various deeds are arranged under their own kinds of virtue: such as what someone did prudently, justly, bravely, temperately, or mercifully, or on the contrary. For so Cicero explains below.

units.la: Aut a minoribus ad maiora.) Hoc tertium est praeceptum collocandi, a comparatione sumptu. idq; duobus modis: aut a minoribus ad maiora scandendum est, quod fit in amplificando: aut a maioribus ad minora descendimus, quod fit extenuando. Aliquando etiam facta alicuius ita distribuimus,ut alia sint maiora, alia minora: quod facit Cicero in secunda Philippica, ubi leviora praeponit, & ad graviora sensim ascendit.
units.tr: "Or from smaller to greater." This is the third precept of arrangement, taken from comparison. And this in two ways: we must either ascend from smaller to greater, which is done in amplifying, or descend from greater to smaller, which is done in diminishing. Sometimes too we distribute a person's deeds so that some are greater and some smaller; as Cicero does in the Second Philippic, where he puts the lighter things first and gradually climbs to the weightier.

units.la: Aut haec inaequabili varietate distinguimus. ) Hic est quartus & ultimus collocandi modus, qui sumitur a varia rerum contentione. Varia inquam est rerum aut dissimilium, aut contrariarum. nam quoniam in hoc genere delectatio quaeritur, & nihil magis ad delectationem facit quam varietas, ut etiam ad satietatem similitudo, perspicuum est, hac varietate potissimum oratores delectationem & suavitatem aucupari. Huius quarti praecepti quinque sunt loci, sive contentionum genera: quorum primum est, cum parva magnis comparantur: secundum, cum simplicia coniunctis: tertium, cum obscura dilucidis: quartum, cum laeta tristibus: quintum, cum incredibilia credibilibus & probabilibus miscemus & condimus. quae singula sic intelligenda sunt. Primum haec omnia ad facta & hominum gesta referenda sunt, in quibus quaedam sunt parva, velut quae homines aut à fortuna, aut ab hominibus adiuti fecerunt. contrà, ea magna dicuntur, quae quis per se sine fortunae aut aliorum adminiculo gesserit: in quibus duobus uersatus est Cicero, laudando Caesare, pro Marcello.
units.tr: "Or we vary these with uneven variety." This is the fourth and last mode of arrangement, which is taken from the varied contrast of things. I say varied, of things either dissimilar or contrary. For since in this kind delight is sought, and nothing contributes more to delight than variety, as similarity does to satiety, it is plain that orators especially angle for delight and pleasantness by this variety. There are five places of this fourth precept, or kinds of contrast: the first is when small things are compared with great; the second, simple with compound; the third, obscure with clear; the fourth, joyful with sad; the fifth, when incredible things are mixed and seasoned with credible and probable ones. Each of these must be understood thus. First, all these are to be referred to deeds and the acts of men, in which some things are small, as those which men did aided either by fortune or by other men; on the contrary, those are called great which someone performed by himself, without the support of fortune or of others. In these two things Cicero was engaged when, praising Caesar, he spoke For Marcellus.

units.la: Simplicia coniunctis. ) Hunc locum nec Strebaeus, nec Daniel Barbarus, nec Latomus intellexerunt, neq; alius quisquam eorum qui Partitiones hasce adhuc scriptis explicarunt: unum Sturmium excipio, qui Aristotelicum esse uidit. Aristoteles enim lib. 3. Rhet. de narratione demonstratiui generis praecipiens, unum genus facit simplex & perpetuum, cum res scilicet ante ordine narrantur, postea seorsim confirmantur, aut amplificantur: neque enim haec narratio interrupta est interiectis rationibus, quibus singula probentur. Sic enim ex diuersis esset coniuncta. Alterum genus simplici & continenti contrarium est, quod Cicero coniunctum, Aristoteles uarium, multiplex, et minime exile uocat. Fit autem hoc genus, cum statim singulis rebus expositis, singulas rationes & argumenta interponimus. Quis enim non uidet, huiusmodi orationem esse uariam, & quasi multiformem? quae partim ex narratione, partim ex confirmatione rerum expositarum constat. narratio enim ac probatio res dissimiles sunt. Vt igitur illa plana simplex que, sic haec coniuncta, uaria que est. Hoc igitur genus Cicero, secutus Aristotelem, probat, in quo simplicia, id est res gestae, & facta, coniunctis rationibus inteximus, quod quidem tum ad delectationem, tum ad memoriam ualet. nam quae simpliciter omnia narrantur prius, post confirmantur, difficulter memoriae mandari solent, ut idem Aristoteles ibidem ait. Sequuntur obscura & dilucida. Sunt enim quaedam paucis nota, ut quae domi & apud priuatos homines gesta sunt. item quae in aperta luce, & in oculis omnium: ut quae in bello, in administranda Republica siue causæ siue tempora sunt,quib.principiu adhibeatur,ut docet Arist.li.3. Hæc aut sunt:persona, uel deliberatis scilicet,uel eorū qui ante dixerūt, si calūnijs aut cōtumelijs egerūt: aut cū re maiore,minore esse ostendere uolumus, quàm alij putet. aut postremò ornatus et decori cuiusdā causa,ne nimis prærupte in causa ingredi uideamur.
units.tr: Simple things with joined ones. Neither Strebaeus, nor Daniel Barbarus, nor Latomus understood this passage, nor has anyone else who has so far explained these Partitiones in writing. I make an exception of Sturm alone, who saw that it is Aristotelian. For Aristotle, in book 3 of the Rhetoric, when he gives instruction on narration in the demonstrative genre, makes one kind simple and continuous: the facts are first narrated in order and afterwards confirmed or amplified separately. Such a narration is not interrupted by reasons inserted between the parts to prove each point, for otherwise it would be made up of disjointed pieces. The second kind is the opposite of the simple and continuous, and Cicero calls it joined, while Aristotle calls it varied, manifold and by no means slender. This kind arises when, immediately after each thing is set out, we interpose the reasons and arguments for it. For who does not see that such a speech is varied and, as it were, many-formed? It consists partly of narration and partly of the confirmation of the things set out, since narration and proof are unlike things. So just as the first kind is plain and simple, this kind is joined and varied. Cicero, following Aristotle, approves this kind, in which we weave the simple things, that is the deeds and facts, together with the reasons joined to them. This is useful both for delight and for memory, for when everything is narrated simply first and confirmed afterwards, it is usually hard to commit to memory, as Aristotle says in the same place. There follow the obscure and the clear. Some things are known to few, such as what is done at home and among private persons. Likewise, some things are in open light and before everyone's eyes, such as what is done in war or in the government of the state, whether causes or times, to which a beginning is applied, as Aristotle teaches in book 3. These are the person, either of those deliberating or of those who spoke earlier, if they acted through slanders or insults; or when we wish to show that a matter is greater or less than others think; or finally for the sake of ornament and decorum, lest we seem to enter the case too abruptly.

units.la: Nec multum sané sæpe narrandū est.) Narrationem quoq; ut principium, Aristotelē secutus, non necessariam in genere deliberatiuo esse censet.cuius rei rationem affert, quod narratio præteritarum rerum aut præsentium fit, suasio uerò futurarum.Et recte quidem, si rei naturam spectemus.nemo enim narrat, nisi fortassis uaticinatione quadam, res futuras. Sed tamen non sine caussa dixit Cicero, Nec multum sæpe. interdum enim narrandum omnino est, aut reprehendendi, aut laudandi,aut confirmandi,aut memoriæ causa:ut tradit Aristot.lib.3. Hīs autem caussis excep-tis,ad fidem & admotum adhibenda est omnis oratio. Quibus verbis confirmatio sententiæ, & peroratio intelliguntur: in fide quidem confirmatio,in motu autem peroratio. Huc conserenda sunt, quæ antea de duplici ordine partium orationis diximus: altero nimirum naturali,altero libero, cuiusmodi suasionis hæc collocatio à Cicerone proposita est. C. F. Quid? in iudiciis quæ est collocatio? C. P. Non eadem accusatoris & rei: quòd accusator rerum ordinem prosequitur, & singula argumenta quasi hasta in manu collocata vehementer proponit, concludit acriter, confirmat tabulis, decretis, testimoniis, accuratus-que in singulis commoratur: perorationisq; præceptis, quæ ad incitandos animos valent, & in reliqua oratione paululũ digredìens de cursu dicendi, utitur, & vehementius in perorando. est enim propositum, ut iratum efficiat iudicem.
units.tr: Nor should much be narrated, nor often. Following Aristotle again, he judges that narration, like the exordium, is not necessary in the deliberative genre. He gives as the reason that narration concerns past or present things, while persuasion concerns future ones. And rightly so, if we consider the nature of the thing, for no one narrates future things except perhaps by some kind of prophecy. Yet Cicero did not speak without cause in saying "not much and not often", for sometimes narration must be given at all, for the sake of blaming, praising, confirming or memory, as Aristotle teaches in book 3. Apart from these causes, all speech is to be directed to proof and to emotion. By these words are understood the confirmation of the thought and the peroration: confirmation for proof, peroration for emotion. To this should be compared what we said before about the twofold order of the parts of a speech, the one natural and the other free, of which kind the arrangement of persuasion is set out by Cicero. C.F. What about the arrangement in trials? C.P. It is not the same for the accuser and the defendant. The accuser follows the order of the facts and vigorously sets forth each argument, as if placing a spear in hand; he concludes sharply, confirms with documents, decrees and testimonies, and lingers carefully over each point. He uses the precepts of peroration, which serve to stir the minds, and in the rest of the speech, digressing a little from the course of his speaking, he uses them more vehemently in the peroration. For his aim is to make the judge angry.

units.la: C. F. Quid? in iudiciis quæ est collocatio?) Iam qui fit ordo in genere iudiciali, quod tertium est causarum genus, requirit filius. Et respondet pater, non eundem esse accusatoris & rei. Cur autem non sit idem ordo, queri posset. Et respon-dendum est, quia fines sunt diversi: accusator enim seueritatem, clementiā reus sibi proponit. Quod cum ita sit, ut etiā quæ in fines ipsos referuntur, diuersa sint necesse est. Est autem ordo rerum tā in accusatione quàm in defensione duplex, & partiū ora-tionis, tionis, & argumentorum. Principia autem, accufator ad attentionem, & seueritatem iudicum accommodat. Est enim propositum (inquit noftcr) ut iratum efficiat iudicem. Quare principio nullo utitur ad conciliandum iudicem. Et hoc est, cur Cicero nihil de principij collocatione accusatori praecipit, sed reo tantu. Deinde ex eo quod praecipit de peroratione, quid in exordiendo faciendu fit, intelligi debet. Differt autem principiu a peroratione: quod cum motus animorum utraque in parte requirantur, in principijs tantum impelli iudicem leuiter oporteat, ut iam inclinato reliqua incumbat oratio: in perorationibus vero omnes permotionum faces iaciedae, ut Cicero de Oratore fecundo docet. In narratione vero accusator rerum gestarum ordine prosequitur, sed ita tamen, ut ea interpuncta suspicionibus fit, & membratim digesta: quod etiam faciendum in argumentis est. nam fe- gulatim efferenda sunt, nerum & motu incitata, & munita rationibus. Et hoc est quod dicit, singula argumenta quasi hasta in manu collocata uehementer proponit. Hastas enim argumenta uocat, quae fine hamctis & oratoris lacertis infirma sunt & leuiaaid est, fine cofirmatione & amplificatione. Quod autem dicit, Concludit acriter: de argumenti conclusione intelligit, quae conclusio, quam Graeci συμπέρασμα uocat, proposito positio atq; assumptione acrior esse debet. Quae enim sunt acria, sensum asperitate mouent: & acre telum dixit poeta, quod acutum est, atque altius infigitur. Translata sunt haec. nam cum proponitur argumentum, tum explicari atq; depromi telum dicitur: cum vero assumitur, & ad personam accommodatur, id est telum vibrare, & in aduersarium intendere. At vbi iam concluditur, tunc denique totis viribus in hostem contorquetur. Gratuitatem igitur reliqua poscunt, sed acrimoniam conclusio.
units.tr: C.F. What about the arrangement in trials? Here the son asks what order obtains in the judicial genus, which is the third kind of cause. The father answers that it is not the same for accuser and defendant. One could ask why the order should not be the same. The answer must be that the ends are different: the accuser sets severity before himself, the defendant clemency. Since this is so, it is necessary that even the things which refer to these ends should differ. The order of things, both in accusation and in defence, is twofold, as is that of the parts of speech and of the arguments. The accuser adapts the beginning to the attention and severity of the judges, for (says our author) the aim is to make the judge angry. Hence he uses no beginning to win over the judge. This is why Cicero prescribes nothing to the accuser about the placing of the exordium, but only to the defendant. Next, from what he prescribes about the peroration, we ought to understand what is to be done in the exordium. The exordium differs from the peroration in this: since motions of the mind are required in both parts, in the exordium the judge need only be lightly pushed, so that the rest of the speech may then bear down on him already inclined; but in the perorations all the torches of emotion are to be hurled, as Cicero teaches in the second book of De Oratore. In the narration the accuser follows the order of the things done, but in such a way that they are interspersed with suspicions and divided limb by limb, which should also be done with the arguments. For each must be brought forward separately, both stirred up with emotion and fortified with reasons. This is what he means by saying the accuser vehemently sets forth each argument as if placing a spear in hand. For he calls arguments spears, which without the iron point and the orator's arms are weak and light, that is, without confirmation and amplification. As for his words "concludes sharply", he means the conclusion of the argument, which the Greeks call [συμπέρασμα], and which ought to be sharper than the proposition, the positing and the assumption. For things that are sharp move the senses by their roughness, and the poet called a weapon "sharp" because it is pointed and sinks in deeper. These terms are transferred: when an argument is proposed, the weapon is said to be drawn out and brought forth; when it is assumed and applied to the person, that is to brandish the weapon and aim it at the adversary; and when at last it is concluded, then finally it is hurled at the enemy with all one's strength. So the rest demands gravity, but the conclusion sharpness.

units.la: Confirmat tabulis. ) De confirmatione accusatoris loquitur, quae assumptorum locis instruenda est: non quod insita non sint adhibenda, nam ex eis argumenta depromta sunt: sed quod assumpta insitis adiungenda sint. Quae enim hic nominat Cicero, tabulae, decreta, testimonia, in locis quae remota dicuntur, latent.
units.tr: Confirms with documents. He is speaking of the accuser's confirmation, which must be built from the places of the assumptions. This is not to say that the inherent places are not to be used, for arguments are drawn from them, but that the assumed matters must be joined to the inherent ones. For the things Cicero names here, documents, decrees and testimonies, lie hidden in the places called remote.

units.la: Accuratius q; in singulis commoratur.) Commoratio intemorationis quidem ornamenta numeratur: verum hic non quomodo fiat, sed qui sit eius usus, aptaq; collocatio, praecipitur. Idem intelligi debet de digressione, cuius hic mentionem facit. nam quo in loco eis utendum sit, ad collocandi partes, non eloquendi pertinet.
units.tr: And lingers more carefully over each point. Lingering is counted among the ornaments of amplification, but here it is not taught how it is done, only what its use is and where it is aptly placed. The same should be understood of the digression which he mentions here, for the place where they are to be used belongs to the arrangement of the parts, not to elocution.

units.la: Et vehementius in perorando.) His verbis significat, proprium locum augendi & digrediendi esse in perorratione: etsi in ipso quoq; orationis decursu,declinationes ad amplificandum dantur,confirmata re aliqua & reprehensa, ut infrà ipse dicet. Ratio autem est, quòd accusatori propositum est,ut iratum efficiat iudicem:id quod Ariftot.quoq; lib.3.Rhet.praecipit.
units.tr: And more vehemently in the peroration. By these words he signifies that the proper place for amplifying and digressing is the peroration, although declinations toward amplification are also allowed in the course of the speech itself, once some matter has been confirmed and blamed, as he himself will say below. The reason is that the accuser's aim is to make the judge angry, which Aristotle also prescribes in book 3 of the Rhetoric.

units.la: C. F. Quid faciendum est contrà reo? C. P. Omnia lògé secus. Sumèda principia ad benevolentiam conciliandam. Narrationes aut amputandæ, quæ lædunt: aut relinquendæ,si totæ sunt molestæ. Firmamenta ad fidem posita, aut per se diluenda,aut obscuranda, aut digressionibus obruenda: perorationes autem ad misericordiam conferendæ.
units.tr: C.F. What must be done against the defendant? C.P. Everything must be done in the opposite way. Beginnings must be taken to win goodwill. Narrations are to be cut away where they hurt, or left out entirely if they are wholly troublesome. Proofs set up to gain credibility are either to be refuted on their own, or obscured, or overwhelmed with digressions. Perorations, on the other hand, are to be directed toward pity.

units.la: C. F. Quid faciendum est contrà reo? ) Alius finis,ut ante dixi: alia quoque collocandi ratio. Vulnera infligit accusator,quæ reo obligãdafunt, & salubribus remedijs curanda: quæ Ariftoteles ἰατρεύματα vocat Rhet.3.Quare quos motus accusator in iudicum animis excitauit,& accendit: ij sunt à defensore aut sedandi, aut restinguēdi: & contrarij afferendi,benevolentia, studium,fauor,idq; in Exordijs.
units.tr: C.F. What must be done against the defendant? Another end, as I said before, and so another method of arrangement. The accuser inflicts wounds which the defendant must bind up, and cure with wholesome remedies, which Aristotle calls [ἰατρεύματα] in Rhetoric 3. So the emotions which the accuser has stirred up and kindled in the minds of the judges must be calmed or quenched by the defender, and contrary ones brought in: goodwill, zeal and favour, and this in the exordia.

units.la: Nam rationes aut amputanda.) Defensori minus narrandum est, ut inquit Ariftoteles libro 3. cum enim ei cum aduersario cotrouerfia fit, quod aliquid aut non fit factum, aut non nocuerit, aut non iniustum fuerit, aut non tantum quantum aduerfarius criminatus est: horum fi quae fatebitur, in illis non est immorandum: ideoq; narratione supersedendum est, nisi quod ad id quod fatebitur, quale fit demonstrandum, conducat. Nihil enim dicendum, quod laedat, immo quod non iuuet.
units.tr: For the defender, the reasons that are to be cut away should be told as little as possible, as Aristotle says in book 3. When the defender is in dispute with his opponent, the question may be whether something was not done, or did no harm, or was not unjust, or was not as great as the accuser alleges. If he admits any of these, there is no need to linger on them, and so the narration should be cut short, except insofar as it helps to show what kind of thing he admits. For nothing should be said that harms the case, and indeed nothing that does not help it.

units.la: Firmamenta ad fidem posita.) De collocatione refutationis agit. idcirco firmamenta vocat, aduersariorum argumenta: quae fi falsa fuerint, aut leuia, per fe facile diluentur: sin clara & illustria, praestantioribus obscuranda & insuscanda. Si vero magna & grauia, maioribus & grauioribus erit obruenda & opprimenda: quod digressionibus potissimum fieri solet. Et hoc est, quod de Oratore libro fecundo ait: Sed argumento resistendum est aut ijs, quae comprobandi eius caussa sumuntur, reprehendedis: aut demonftrando, id quod concludere illi uelint, non effici ex propositis, nec esse consequens: aut fi ita non refellas, afferendum est in contrariam partem, quod fit aut gravius, aut aeque graue. Ariftoteles vero libro tertio, refutandi tantum duo genera ponit: Quae obiecta sunt (inquit) ab aduersario,refutare debet,uel dissoluendo, uel contrà argumentando. Sed in eo quod dicit, Contra argumentando: duo alia Ciceronis intelligi possunt. Vide etiam 8.lib.Topicorum Aristotelis.
units.tr: "Firm arguments laid down as established": here he deals with the placing of refutation. He calls the opponent's arguments "firm" because, if they are false or weak, they can easily be dissolved in themselves; but if they are clear and striking, they must be obscured and undermined by stronger ones. If they are great and weighty, they must be overwhelmed and crushed by greater and weightier ones, which is usually done chiefly by digressions. This is what he says in the second book of De Oratore: the argument must be resisted either by criticising the premises taken to prove it, or by showing that what the opponent wants to conclude does not follow from the premises and is not a consequence of them; or, if you cannot refute it in this way, you must set up the contrary side, which is either weightier or equally weighty. Aristotle, however, in book 3, lays down only two kinds of refutation: "What is objected by the opponent," he says, "ought to be refuted either by dissolving it or by arguing against it." But in what he says, "by arguing against it," two other meanings of Cicero's may be understood. See also book 8 of Aristotle's Topics.

units.la: Perorationes autem ad misericordiam conserende.) Cum ad finem omnia referantur, ut sæpe diximus, & accusator iram scuitiamq; sbectet, & contrà omnia reo facienda sint:recte defensor ad clementiam & misericordiam omnia conferet in perorando, sicuti ad benevolentiam in exordiendo.Et hoc est quod dicit de Orat.lib.2. Illa autem quæ aut cõciliationis caussa leuiter, aut permotionis uchementer aguntur, contrarijs commotionibus inferenda sunt: ut odium benevolentia, & misericordia inuidia tollatur. Quærat fortasse aliquis,cur de confirmatione defensoris nihil dicat hoc loco? Cur id faciat, duæ sunt causse:altera,quòd confirmatio propria est accusatoris,ut patroni reprehensio: alteram verò adfert ipse Cicero de Orat.lib.2.Sed quia neque reprehendi,inquit,quæ contrà dicuntur possunt,nisi tua confirmes: neque hæc confirmari, nisi illa reprehendas:idcirco hæc & natura & utilitate & tractatione coniuncta sunt.
units.tr: "Perorations, however, to be directed to pity": since all things are referred to the end, as I have often said, and since the accuser seeks anger and hatred, while on the contrary everything must be done for the accused, the defender will rightly direct everything in the peroration to clemency and pity, just as he directs everything to goodwill in the exordium. This is what Cicero says in De Oratore book 2: "Those things which are done either lightly for the sake of conciliation or vehemently for the sake of stirring the emotions must be brought in with opposite emotions, so that hatred is removed by goodwill and envy by pity." Someone may perhaps ask why he says nothing here about the confirmation of the defender's case. There are two reasons. The first is that confirmation belongs properly to the accuser, just as refutation belongs to the advocate. The second is given by Cicero himself in De Oratore book 2: "But since what is said on the other side cannot be refuted unless you confirm your own case, and your own case cannot be confirmed unless you refute theirs, therefore these are joined together in nature, in usefulness and in treatment."

units.la: C. F. Semper'ne igitur ordinem collocandi, quem uolumus, tenere possumus? poslumus? C. P. Non sane. nam auditorum aures moderatur oratori prudenti, & prouido: & quod respuunt, immutandum est.
units.tr: C. F. Can we always keep to the order of arrangement that we wish? C. P. Certainly not. For the prudent and farsighted orator is guided by the ears of his hearers, and whatever they reject must be changed.

units.la: C. P. Semper ne igitur ordinem collocandi.) Sunt qui putent hic quæri, semper ne utendum sit ordine, qui in superioribus præscriptus à Cicerone est? quasi hic Cicero præcipiat de prudentiæ ordine, non de naturali. Sed falluntur mea quidem sententia. Quærit enim, cum duplex ordo propositus sit, naturalis & iudicij, sit ne in arbitrio Oratoris utro uclit uti? Ad quod respondet prudenter pater: Id in oratoris voluntate positum non esse, sed in auditorum auribus, ad quas omnis collocatio sit accommodanda: ut si agnouerit, eos sa cilius ordine eo qui ab institutione artis proficiscitur, in sententiam suam adduci, cum ordinem adhibeat: sin contrà, immutandum ordinem esse. qua de re præclarè in Orat. sic: Semper oratorum eloquentiæ moderatrix suit auditorum prudentia, inquit. omnes enim qui probari volunt, voluntatem eorum qui audiunt, intuentur, ad eamq; & ad eorum arbitrium & nutum totos se fingunt & accommodant. Atq; ut Aristoteles censet lib. 3. debet esse oratio, qualis esse Theodori uox uidebatur, ad aliorum histrionum uocem comparata. sinent omnia collocandi, quam hic Cicero pater paucis & perspicuis praeceptis tradit, quo facilius memoria retineri possint.
units.tr: C. P. Should we always keep to the order of arrangement? Some think that the question here is whether one must always use the order prescribed above by Cicero, as if Cicero were here teaching the order of prudence rather than the natural order. But in my view they are mistaken. For he asks, since two orders have been set out, the natural and the order of judgement, whether it is left to the orator's choice which he wishes to use. To this the father answers wisely: that this is not placed in the orator's will but in the ears of the hearers, to which every arrangement must be adapted; so that if he has recognised that they are more easily brought to his opinion by the order that proceeds from the rules of the art, he should adopt that order; but if the contrary, the order should be changed. On this matter he says excellently in Orator: "The prudence of the audience has always been the regulator of oratorical eloquence. For all who wish to be approved look to the will of those who listen, and they shape and adapt themselves entirely to it and to their judgement and nod." And, as Aristotle thinks in book 3, the speech ought to be such as Theodorus's voice seemed to be, fitted to the voice of other actors. Cicero the father here sets out in few and clear precepts the whole arrangement, so that they may be retained more easily in the memory.

units.la: C. P. Quia quibus in orationibus delectatio finis est, uarij sunt ordines collocandi. ) Varij, nimirum quatuor, in exornatione scilicet: de ea enim loquitur, cui delectatio finis est.
units.tr: C. P. Since in those speeches where delight is the end, there are various orders of arrangement. Various, namely four, in ornamentation, for it is of this that he speaks, the kind in which delight is the end.

units.la: Nam aut temporum feruantur gradus, aut generum distributiones, aut a minoribus ad maiora ascendimus, aut a maioribus ad minora dilabimur, aut haec inaequabili uarietate distinguimus, cum parua magnis, simplicia coniunctis, obscura dilucidis, laeta tristibus, incredibilia probabilibus intexímus, quae in exornatione cadunt omnia.
units.tr: For either the steps of time are kept, or the distributions by kinds are followed, or we ascend from smaller things to greater, or we descend from greater to smaller, or we vary these with an uneven variety, interweaving small things with great, simple with joined, obscure with clear, joyful with sad, incredible with probable; all of which fall under ornamentation.

units.la: Nam aut temporum feruantur gradus. ) Etsi multis modis in collocando temporis ordinem sequi licet: tamen illud est praestantissimum, cum in laudando vel vituperando aetatum ordinem sequimur: & ut quidque primum, aut secundum, aut postremum gestum, dictum ue est, recensemus. A puericia infantia in hac ratione exordimur: deinde adolescentia facta commemoramus: postmodum, qualis quisque uir fuerit: & postremo, cuiusque modi
units.tr: "For either the steps of time are kept." Although in arranging one may follow the order of time in many ways, that one is most excellent in which we follow the order of ages when praising or blaming, and we recount whatever was done, said or happened first, second, or last. In this method we begin from boyhood and infancy; then we relate the deeds of adolescence; afterwards what sort of man each was; and finally what kind of old age he had.

units.la: {?} Marginal notes are not legible on this scan. modi extiterit eius senectus. Et si ulterius progredi volumus, quid in morte, & post mortem acciderit, narrabimus. Possumus etiam ita distribuere tempora, in ea quae sine nobis extiterunt: cuiusmodi sunt patria, genus, parentes. Tum quae nobiscum, quae pars totam hominis vitam complectitur. Postremo quae post nos facta sunt, nostra tamen causa: ut funus, luctus, laudatio, pompa, sepultura.
units.tr: And if we wish to go further, we will tell what happened at death and after death. We may also distribute the times in this way: first those things which came about without us, such as country, family and parents; then those which were with us, which take in the whole of a man's life; and lastly those which were done after us, yet for our sake: such as the funeral, mourning, eulogy, procession and burial.

units.la: Aut genera distributiones.) Nimirum cum multa & varia facta in propria virtutum genera digeruntur: ut quid prudenter, quid iuste, quid fortiter, quid temperanter, clementer ue aliquis secerit, aut etiam contra: sic enim Cicero infra interpretatur.
units.tr: "Or distributions by kinds." That is, when many and various deeds are arranged under their own kinds of virtue: as what someone did prudently, what justly, what bravely, what temperately or mercifully, or on the contrary. For Cicero explains it in this way below.

units.la: Aut a minoribus ad maiora.) Hoc tertium est praeceptum collocandi, a comparatione sumptum. idque duobus modis: aut a minoribus ad maiora scandendum est, quod fit in amplificando: aut a maioribus ad minora descendimus, quod fit extenuando. Aliquando etiam facta alicuius ita distribuimus, ut alia sint maiora, alia minora: quod facit Cicero in secunda Philippica, ubi leviora praeponit, & ad graviora sensim ascendit.
units.tr: "Or we ascend from smaller things to greater." This is the third precept of arrangement, taken from comparison, and it has two forms: we either ascend from smaller things to greater, which is done in amplification, or we descend from greater to smaller, which is done in diminishment. Sometimes too we distribute a person's deeds so that some are greater and some smaller, as Cicero does in the second Philippic, where he puts the lighter things first and gradually rises to the weightier.

units.la: Aut haec inaequabili varietate distinguimus.) Hic est quartus & ultimus collocandi modus, qui sumitur a varia rerum contentione. Varia inquam est rerum aut dissimilium, aut contrariarum. nam quoniam in hoc genere delectatio quaeritur, & nihil magis ad delectationem facit quam varietas, ut etiam ad satietatem similitudo, perspicuum est, hac varietate potissimum oratores delectationem & suavitatem aucupari. Huius quarti praecepti quinque sunt loci, sive contentionum genera: quorum primum est, cum parva magnis comparantur: secundum, cum simplicia coniunctis: tertium, cum obscura dilucidis: quartum, cum laeta tristibus: quintum, cum incredibilia credibilib. & probabilibus miscemus & condimus. quae singula sic intelligenda sunt. Primum haec omnia ad facta & hominum gesta referenda sunt, in quibus quaedam sunt parva, velut quae homines aut a fortuna, aut ab hominibus adiuti fecerunt. contra, ea magna dicuntur, quae quis per se sine fortunae aut aliorum adminiculo gesserit: in quibus duobus versatus est Cicero, laudando Caesare, pro Marcello.
units.tr: "Or we vary these with an uneven variety." This is the fourth and last mode of arrangement, which is taken from the varied contrast of things. I say varied contrast of things either dissimilar or opposed. For since in this kind delight is sought, and nothing contributes more to delight than variety, just as similarity contributes to satiety, it is plain that orators especially catch at delight and pleasantness by this variety. There are five places, or kinds of contrast, of this fourth precept: the first is when small things are compared with great; the second, when simple things are joined with complex; the third, when obscure things are set against clear; the fourth, when joyful things are set against sad; the fifth, when incredible things are mixed and seasoned with credible and probable ones. Each of these must be understood thus. First, all these things are to be referred to deeds and the actions of men, among which some are small, such as those which men have done with help either from fortune or from other men. On the other hand, those are called great which someone has done of himself, without the aid of fortune or of others. In these two Cicero is engaged when he praises Caesar in the speech Pro Marcello.

units.la: Simplicia coniunctis. plex & perpetuum,cum res scilicet anté ordine narrantur,postea seorsim confirmantur, aut amplificantur: neque enim hæc narratio interrupta est interiectis rationibus, quibus singula probentur.sic enim ex diuersis esset coniuncta. Alterum genus simplici & continenti cōtrarium est, quod Cicero coniunctum, Aristoteles uarium, multiplex,et minimè exile uocat.Fit autem hoc genus, cum statim singulis rebus expositis, singulas rationes & argumenta interponimus. Quis enim non uidet, huiusmodi orationem esse uariam,& quasi multiformem? quæ partim ex narratione, partim ex confirmatione rerum expositarum constat. narratio enim ac probatio res dissimiles sunt. Vt igitur illa plana simplex que,sic hæc coniuncta,uaria que est. Hoc igitur genus Cicero,secutus Aristotelem, probat, in quo simplicia,idest res gestæ, & facta, coniunctis rationibus inteximus, quod quidem tum ad delectationem, tum ad memoriam ualet. nam quæ simpliciter omnia narrantur prius, post confirmantur,difficulter memoriæ mandari solent, ut idem Aristoteles ibidem ait. Sequuntur obscura & dilucida. Sunt enim quædam paucis nota, ut quæ domi & apud priuatos homines gesta sunt. item quæ in aperta luce, & in oculis omnium: ut quæ in bello,in administranda Republica aut provincia quisq; gesit: hæc dilucida, illa obscura appellantur. Simili quoq; ratione læta, tristiaq; dicuntur. nemo enim ignorat, & hominibus accidere, & ab ijsdem hominibus geri modo læta, modo tristia: quod quia perspicuum est, non immorabimur. Incredibilia quoq;, atq; ijs contraria probabilia, siue credibilia, à viris præstantibus geri obscurum nō est. Incredibile enim pene fuit, quod Cicero de Pompeio in orat. pro lege Manilia dicit, cum ait, eum plura bella gessisse quàm alij vel legerint, vel audierint. Idem ferè pro Cornelio Balbo confirmat. Item cum ait Pompeij voluntati non modo cives assensos fuisse, socios obtemperasse, hostes obediuisse, sed etiam ventos, tempestatesq; obsecundasse. Item illud quod antea dixerat: ita, tantum bellum, tam diuturnum, tam longè lateq; diffusum, quo bello omnes gentes ac nationes premebantur, Cn. Pompeius extrema hyeme apparauit, ineunte vere suscepit, media æstate confecit. Est hæc, inquit, incredibilis atque diuina virtus imperatoris. Probabilia quæ sint, nullus ignorat. Hæc autem varietatis vicissitudo mirificam habet delectationem. Idcirco inquit Aristot. lib. primo: Omnium rerum vicissitudo iucunda est.
units.tr: Simple joined with complex. Simple and continuous is the case when the facts are first narrated in order and afterwards each is confirmed or amplified separately; for this narration is not interrupted by reasons inserted between them to prove each point, since in that case it would be joined from disparate parts. The other kind is contrary to the simple and continuous one, which Cicero calls joined, Aristotle calls varied, manifold, and not at all plain. This kind arises when, as soon as each thing has been set out, we insert the reasons and arguments for each. For who does not see that such a speech is varied and, as it were, many-formed? It partly consists of narration and partly of confirmation of the things set out; for narration and proof are unlike things. So just as that first kind is plain and simple, this one is joined and varied. Cicero, following Aristotle, therefore approves this kind, in which we weave together simple matters, that is things done and deeds, with joined reasons, which is useful both for delight and for memory. For things which are all narrated first and afterwards confirmed are usually hard to commit to memory, as Aristotle says in the same place. There follow the obscure and the clear. For some things are known to few, such as what was done at home and among private persons; likewise what was done in the open light and before everyone's eyes, such as what someone did in war, in the government of the commonwealth or in a province: the latter are called clear, the former obscure. In a similar way things are called joyful and sad. For no one is ignorant that things happen to men, and are done by the same men, sometimes joyful, sometimes sad; since this is plain, we will not linger on it. That incredible things, and their opposites, probable or credible, are done by outstanding men is not obscure. For what Cicero says about Pompey in the speech For the Manilian Law was almost incredible, when he says that he waged more wars than others have either read or heard of. He confirms much the same for Cornelius Balbus. Likewise when he says that not only did the citizens assent to Pompey's will, and the allies obey, and the enemies submit, but even the winds and storms yielded to him. Likewise that which he had said before: that Gnaeus Pompey, in the very end of winter, prepared so great a war, so long-lasting and so widely spread, in which all peoples and nations were oppressed; he undertook it in early spring and finished it in midsummer. "This," he says, "is the incredible and divine courage of the commander." What is probable, no one fails to know. This alternation of variety has a wonderful delight. Therefore Aristotle says in book 1: "The alternation of all things is pleasant."

units.la: C. F. Quid in deliberatione, quid spectas? C. P. Principia, vel non longa, uel sæpe nulla. sunt enim ad audiendum, qui deliberant, suacaufsa parati: nec multum sanè sæpe narrandum est. est enim narratio præteritarum rerum, aut præsentium suasio, aut futurarum. Quare ad fidem & ad motum adhibenda est omnis oratio.
units.tr: C. F. What do you look for in deliberative speech? C. P. Introductions that are either not long or often none at all. For those who deliberate are ready to listen, each for his own sake, and there is seldom much need for narration. Narration concerns past events, persuasion concerns present or future ones. So all speech should be directed toward belief and emotion.

units.la: C. F. Quid? in deliberatione quid spectas? De collocatione deliberatiui generis quærit, in quem finem, & quo pacto referenda sit.
units.tr: C. F. What, then, do you look for in deliberative speech? Here he asks about the arrangement of the deliberative kind, to what end and in what manner it should be referred.

units.la: C. P. Principia uel non longa, uel sæpe nulla. Principiorum loci cum tres sint, scilicet benevolentia, attentio, & docilitas, ut infrà videbimus: hic de eo principio intelligit, in quo aperte beneuolentia comparatur. id enim fere remouet à deliberationibus: alioqui attentio ipsa & docilitas, quæ propositione & partitione parátur, sunt ita cum oratione coniuncta ut abesse uix unquam possint. Idcirco dicit noster Cicero in deliberationib. uel non longa, id est, breuia, ut pro lege Manilia & aliquot Philippicis: uel interdum nulla esse principia sive exordia, ut in prima Philippica. Et addit rationem: Quoniam qui deliberant, id est, qui consilium & sententiam aliorum audire uolunt, sua causa & utilitate parati sunt. Tres tamen fiue causæ fiue tëpora sunt,quib.principiu adhibeatur,ut docet Arift.li.3.Hæc aut sunt:persona, uel deliberatis scilicet,uel corü qui ante dixerut, fi calúnijs aut cõtumelijs egerút: aut cü re maio-re,minore esse oftedere uolumus, quàm alij putet. aut postremo ornatus et decori cuiufdã causæ,ne nimis præruptè in causa ingredi uideamur.
units.tr: C. P. Introductions are either not long or often none at all. Since there are three places of introduction, namely goodwill, attention and receptiveness, as we shall see below, here he means that introduction in which goodwill is openly won. For this is generally what deliberations lack. Otherwise attention and receptiveness, which are secured by the proposition and partition, are so bound up with the speech that they can scarcely ever be absent. So our Cicero says that in deliberations the introductions are either not long, that is, brief, as in the speech on the Manilian law and some of the Philippics, or sometimes there are no introductions or openings at all, as in the first Philippic. And he gives the reason: because those who deliberate, that is, who wish to hear the counsel and opinion of others, are ready for their own sake and advantage. There are, however, three causes or occasions on which an introduction is used, as Aristotle teaches in book 3. These are: the person, either of the deliberators themselves or of those who have spoken before, if they have acted with slanders or insults; or when we wish to show that the matter is of greater or lesser importance than others think; or lastly, for the sake of the grace and decorum of some cause, so that we do not seem to rush too abruptly into the matter.

units.la: Nec multum sanè sæpe narrandu est.) Narrationem quoq; ut principium, Ariftotele secutus, non necessariam in genere deliberatiuo esse censet.cuius rei rationem affert, quod narratio præteritarum rerum aut præsentium fit, fuafio uero futurarum.Et recte quidem, si rei naturam spectemus,nemo enim narrat, nisi fortasse uaticinatione quadam, res futuras. Sed tamen non sine caussa dixit Cicero, Nec multum sæpe.interdum enim narrandum omnino est, aut reprehendendi, aut laudandi,aut confirmandi,aut memoriæ cau-sa:ut tradit Ariftot.lib.3. His autem causis exceptis,ad fidem & admotum adhibenda est omnis oratio. Quibus uerbis confirmatio sententiæ, & peroratio intelliguntur: in fide quidem confirmatio,in motu autem peroratio. Huc conserenda sunt, quæ antea de duplici ordine partium orationis diximus: altero nimirum naturali,altero libero, cuiusmodi suasionis hæc collocatio à Cicerone proposita est.
units.tr: "Narration is seldom much needed." Following Aristotle, he judges that narration, like the introduction, is not necessary in the deliberative kind. He gives the reason that narration concerns past or present events, whereas persuasion concerns future ones. And indeed this is right if we consider the nature of the thing, for no one narrates future events except perhaps by some kind of prophecy. Yet Cicero did not say "seldom much" without reason. For sometimes narration is needed at all, either for blame, or praise, or confirmation, or for the sake of memory, as Aristotle relates in book 3. Apart from these causes, all speech should be directed toward belief and emotion. By these words both the confirmation of the opinion and the peroration are understood: confirmation for belief, peroration for emotion. To this should be compared what we said earlier about the double order of the parts of speech: the one natural, the other free, and of this kind is the arrangement of persuasion proposed by Cicero here.

units.la: C. F. Quid? in iudiciis quæ est collocatio? C. P. Non eadem accusatoris & rei: quòd accusator rerum ordinem prosequitur, & singula argumenta quasi hasta in manu collocata uehementer proponit, concludit acriter, confirmat tabulis, decretis, testimoniis, accuratus que in singulis commoratur: perorationisq; præceptis, quæ ad incitandos animos ualent, & in reliqua oratione paululũ digrediens de cursu dicendi, utitur, & uehementius in perorando. est enim propositum, ut iratum efficiat iudicem.
units.tr: C. F. What, then, is the arrangement in judicial cases? C. P. It is not the same for the accuser and for the defendant. For the accuser follows the order of the facts, and vigorously sets out each argument as if a spear were held in the hand, concludes sharply, confirms with documents, decrees and testimonies, and dwells carefully on each point. He makes use of the precepts of peroration, which serve to stir the feelings, and in the rest of the speech he departs somewhat from the course of his discourse, and is more vehement in the peroration. For the aim is to make the judge angry.

units.la: C. F. Quid? in iudiciis quae est collocatio?) Iam qui sit ordo in genere iudiciali, quod tertium est causarum genus, requirit filius. Et respondet pater, non eundem esse accusatoris & rei. Cur autem non sit idem ordo, quaeri posset. Et respondendum est, quia fines sunt diuersi: accusator enim seueritatem, clementiā reus sibi proponit. Quod cum ita sit, ut etiā quae in fines ipsos referuntur, diuersa sint necesse est. Est autem ordo rerum tā in accusatione quàm in defensione duplex, & partium oratio-nis, tionis,& argumentorum. Principia autem, accusator ad attentionem, & benevolentiam iudicum accommodat. Est enim propositum (inquit noster) ut iratum efficiat iudicem. Quare principio nullo utitur ad conciliandum iudicem. Et hoc est, cur Cicero nihil de principij collocatione accusatori praecipit, sed reo tantum. Deinde ex eo quod praecipit de peroratione, quid in exordiendo faciendum sit, intelligi debet. Differt autem principium a peroratione: quod cum motus animorum utraque in parte requirantur, in principijs tantum impelli iudicem leniter oporteat, ut iam inclinato reliqua incumbat oratio: in perorationibus vero omnes permotionum faces iaciedae, ut Cicero de Oratore secundo docet. In narratione vero accusator rerum gestarum ordine prosequitur, sed ita tamen, ut ea interpunctia suspicionibus fit, & membratim digesta: quod etiam faciendum in argumentis est. nam singulatim efferenda sunt, verum & motu incitata, & munita rationibus. Et hoc est quod dicit, singula argumenta quasi hasta in manu collocata uchementer proponit. Hastas enim argumenta vocat, quae finem hametis & oratoris lacertis infirma sunt & leviaxid est, sine confirmatione & amplificatione. Quod autem dicit, Concludit acriter: de argumenti conclusione intelligit, quae conclusio, quam Graeci συμπέρασμα vocat, propositio posito
units.tr: C. F. What, then, is the arrangement in judicial cases? Now the son asks what the order is in the judicial kind, which is the third kind of causes. And the father answers that it is not the same for the accuser and for the defendant. One could ask why the order is not the same. And the answer must be that the aims are different: for the accuser proposes to himself severity, the defendant clemency. Since this is so, the means that are referred to these very aims must also be different. The order of things, both in accusation and in defence, is twofold, and likewise that of the parts of the speech and of the arguments. The accuser adapts the introduction to securing the attention and goodwill of the judges. For the aim is (as our author says) to make the judge angry. Hence the accuser uses no introduction to win over the judge. This is why Cicero gives no precept about the placing of the introduction for the accuser, but only for the defendant. Further, what is to be done in the opening can be understood from what he prescribes about the peroration. The introduction differs from the peroration in this: since the stirring of the feelings is required in both parts, in the introduction the judge should be pushed only gently, so that the rest of the speech may lean upon him once he is already inclined; but in the perorations all the torches of emotion must be hurled, as Cicero teaches in the second book of De Oratore. In the narration the accuser follows the order of the events, but in such a way that it is interspersed with suspicions and divided into clauses; this must also be done with the arguments. For they must be presented one by one, both spirited with emotion and fortified with reasons. This is what he means by "sets out each argument as if a spear were held in the hand, vigorously." For he calls arguments spears, which are weak and slight in the hands of a bad soldier or orator, that is, without confirmation and amplification. As for his saying "concludes sharply," he means the conclusion of the argument, which the Greeks call conclusion [συμπέρασμα], and which, once the proposition and the assumption are laid down, ought to be more forceful.

units.la: Nota: the final line of the page is partly obscured. posito atq; assumptione acrior esse debet. Quæ enim sunt acria, sensum asperitate movent: & acre telum dixit poeta, quod acutum est, atque altius infigitur. Translata sunt hæc. nam cum proponitur argumentum, tum explicari atq; depromi telum dicitur: cum vero assumitur, & ad personam accommodatur, id est telum vibrare, & in adversarium intendere. At ubi iam concluditur, tunc denique totis viribus in hostem contorquetur. Gravitatem igitur reliqua poscunt, sed acrimoniam conclusio.
units.tr: Things that are sharp move the feelings by their harshness, and the poet called a weapon sharp when it is keen and sinks in more deeply. These terms are transferred. For when an argument is put forward, the weapon is said to be drawn out and brought forth; but when it is assumed and applied to the person, that is to brandish the weapon and aim it at the adversary. And when it is at last concluded, then finally it is hurled at the enemy with all one's strength. So the rest of the speech calls for weight, but the conclusion calls for sharpness.

units.la: Confirmat tabulis. ) De confirmatione accusatoris loquitur, quæ assumptorum locis instruenda est: non quod insita non sint adhibenda, nam ex eis argumenta depromta sunt: sed quod assumpta insitis adiungenda sint. Quæ enim hic nominat Cicero, tabulæ, decreta, testimonia, in locis quæ remota dicuntur, latent.
units.tr: "He confirms with documents." He speaks of the confirmation by the accuser, which must be built up from the places of the assumptions: not that the inherent places are not to be used, for the arguments are drawn from them, but that the assumed matters must be joined to the inherent ones. For the things Cicero names here, documents, decrees and testimonies, lie hidden in the places that are called remote.

units.la: Accuratius q; in singulis commoratur.) Commoratio interpretationis quidem ornamenta numeratur: verum hic non quomodo fiat, sed qui sit eius usus, aptaq; collocatio præcipitur. Idem intelligi debet de digressione, cuius hic mentionem facit. nam quo in loco eis utendum sit, ad collocandi partes, non cloquendi pertinet.
units.tr: "And dwells more carefully on each point." Dwelling on a point is counted among the ornaments of elaboration; but here he prescribes not how it is done, but what its use is and its suitable placing. The same should be understood of digression, which he mentions here. For the place where it is to be used belongs to the arrangement of the parts, not to the style of expression.

units.la: Et uehementius in perrorando. ) His verbis significat, proprium locum augendi & digrediendi esse in peroratione: etsi in ipso quoq; orationis decursu, declinationes ad amplificandum dantur, confirmata re aliqua & reprehensa, ut infrà ipse dicct. Ratio autem est, quòd accusatori propositum est, ut iratum efficiat iudicem: id quod Aristot. quoq; lib. 3. Rhet. praecipit.
units.tr: "And is more vehement in the peroration." By these words he signifies that the proper place for amplifying and digressing is the peroration, although in the course of the speech itself, too, there are opportunities for amplification, once some matter has been confirmed and refuted, as he himself says below. The reason is that the accuser's aim is to make the judge angry, which Aristotle also prescribes in book 3 of the Rhetoric.

units.la: C. F. Quid faciendum est contrà reo? C. P. Omnia lõgè secus. Sumèda principia ad benevolentiam conciliandam. Narrationes aut amputandae, quae laedunt: aut relinquendae, si totae sunt moleste. Firmamenta ad fidem posita, aut per se diluenda, aut obscuranda, aut digressionibus obruenda: perorationes autem ad misericordiam conferendae.
units.tr: C. F. What must be done by the defendant, on the contrary? C. P. Everything, by a long way, the reverse. Introductions must be taken up to win goodwill. Narrations must either be cut away where they do harm, or left out if they are wholly troublesome. Supports placed for belief must either be refuted outright, or obscured, or overwhelmed by digressions. Perorations, on the other hand, must be directed toward pity.

units.la: C. F. Quid faciendum est contrà reo?) Alius finis, ut ante dixi: alia quoque collocandi ratio. Vulnera infligit accusator, quae reo obligadafunt, & salubribus remedijs curanda: quae Aristoteles ἰατρεύματα vocat Rhet. 3. Quare quos motus accusator in iudicum animis excitauit, & accendit: ij sunt à defensore aut sedandi, aut restinguēdi: & contrarij afferendi, benevolentia, studium, fauor, idq; in Exordijs.
units.tr: C. F. What must be done by the defendant on the contrary? This is a different aim, as I said before, and so a different method of arrangement too. The accuser inflicts wounds which the defendant must bind up and cure with wholesome remedies; Aristotle calls these remedies [ἰατρεύματα] in Rhetoric 3. Therefore the emotions which the accuser has stirred and kindled in the judges' minds must be calmed or extinguished by the defendant, and opposite ones brought in: goodwill, zeal, favour, and this in the openings.

units.la: Narrationes aut amputandae.) Defensori minus nus narrandum est, ut inquit Aristoteles libro 3. cum enim ei cum aduersario cōtrouersia sit, quòd aliquid aut non sit factum, aut non nocuerit, aut non iniustum fecerit, aut non tantum quantum aduersarius criminatus est: horum si quæ fatebitur, in illis non est immorandum: idcoq; narratione supersedendum est, nisi quod ad id quod fatebitur, quale sit demonstrandum, conducat. Nihil enim dicendum, quod lædat, immò quod non iuuet.
units.tr: Narrations are to be cut back. The defender should narrate less, as Aristotle says in book 3. For when he is in dispute with his opponent over whether something was done, or did no harm, or was not unjust, or was not as great as the opponent alleges, he will not dwell on those points that he concedes. So he should drop the narration, unless it helps to show what sort of thing he concedes. For nothing should be said that harms him, or rather nothing that does not help him.

units.la: Firmamenta ad fidem posita.) De collocatione refutationis agit. idcirco firmamenta uocat, aduersariorum argumenta: quæ si falsa fierint, aut leuia, per se facilè diluentur: sin clara & illustria, præstantioribus obscuranda & insuscanda. Si uerò magna & grauia, maioribus & grauioribus erût obruenda & opprimenda: quod digressionibus potissimum fieri solet. Et hoc est, quod de Oratore libro secundo ait: Sed argumento resistendum est aut iis, quæ comprobandi eius caussa sumuntur, reprehendendis: aut demonstrando, id quod concludere illi uelint, non efficī ex propositis, nec esse consequens: aut si ita non refellas, afferendum est in contrariam partem, quod sit aut grauius, aut æquè graue. Aristoteles uerò libro tertio, refutandi tantum duo genera ponit: Quæ obiecta sunt (inquit) ab aduersario,refutare debet,uel dissoluendo, uel contrà argumentando. Sed in eo quod dicit, Contra argumentando: duo alia Ciceronis intelligi possunt. Vide etiam 8.lib.Topicorum Aristotelis.
units.tr: The props placed on trust: this concerns the arrangement of refutation. He calls the opponent's arguments "props" (firmamenta). If they are false or weak, they can easily be dissolved by themselves; but if they are clear and striking, they must be obscured and undermined by stronger arguments. If they are large and weighty, they must be overwhelmed and crushed by greater and weightier ones, which is usually done chiefly by digressions. This is what he says in the second book of On the Orator: "But an argument must be resisted either by censuring the things taken up to prove it, or by showing that what they wish to conclude does not follow from the premises and is not a consequence of them; or, if you cannot refute it in this way, you must put forward on the opposite side something that is either weightier or equally weighty." Aristotle, however, in book 3, lays down only two kinds of refutation: "What is objected by the opponent," he says, "must be refuted either by dissolving it or by arguing against it." But in what he says, "by arguing against it," two other things of Cicero's may be understood. See also book 8 of Aristotle's Topics.

units.la: Perorationes autem ad misericordiam conserendæ.) Cum ad finem omnia referantur, ut sæpe diximus, & accusator iram suspitiamq; spectet, & contrà omnia reo facienda sint:rectè defensor ad clementiam & misericordiam omnia conferet in perorando, sicuti ad beneuolentiam in exordiendo. Et hoc est quod dicit de Orat.lib.2. Illa autem quæ aut cōciliationis caussa leuiter, aut permotionis uchementer aguntur, contrarijs commotionibus inferenda sunt: ut odium beneuolentia, & misericordia inuidia tollatur. Quærat fortasse aliquis,cur de confirmatione defensoris nihil dicat hoc loco? Cur id faciat, duæ sunt caussæ:altera,quòd confirmatio propria est accusatoris,ut patroni reprehensio: alteram uero adfert ipse Cicero de Orat.lib.2.Sed quia neque reprehendi,inquit,quæ contrà dicūtur possunt,nisi tua confirmes: neque hæc confirmari, nisi illa reprehendas:idcirco hæc & natura & utilitate & tractatione coniuncta sunt.
units.tr: Perorations are to be directed to pity. Since all things are referred to the end, as we have often said, and the accuser aims at anger and suspicion, while on the contrary everything must be done to win the defendant favour, the defender will rightly direct everything in the peroration toward clemency and mercy, just as he directs everything toward goodwill in the exordium. This is what he says in On the Orator, book 2: "But those things which are done lightly for the sake of conciliation, or vehemently for the sake of arousing emotion, must be introduced with opposite emotions, so that hatred is removed by goodwill and envy by mercy." Someone may perhaps ask why he says nothing here about the defender's confirmation. There are two reasons for this. The first is that confirmation belongs properly to the accuser, as censure of the opposing advocate does. The second is given by Cicero himself in On the Orator, book 2: "But since those things that are said on the other side cannot be censured unless you confirm your own, and your own cannot be confirmed unless you censure theirs, therefore these are joined together in nature, in usefulness and in treatment."

units.la: C. F. Semper'ne igitur ordinem collocandi, quem uolumus, tenere possumus?
units.tr: Can we always keep to the order of arrangement that we want?

units.la: poslumus? C.P. Non sane. nam auditorum aures moderātur oratori prudenti, & prouido: & quod respuunt, immutandum est.
units.tr: C.P. Not at all. For the prudent and far-sighted orator is governed by the ears of his audience, and whatever they reject must be changed.

units.la: C. P. Semper ne igitur ordinem collocandi.) Sunt qui putent hic quæri, semper ne utendum sit ordine, qui in superioribus prǣscriptus à Cicerone est? quasi hic Cicero prǣcipiat de prudentiæ ordine, non de naturali. Sed falluntur mea quidem sententia. Quærit enim, cum duplex ordo propositus sit, naturalis & iudicij, sit ne in arbitrio Oratoris utro uelit uti? Ad quod respondet prudenter pater: Id in oratoris uoluntate positum non esse, sed in auditorum auribus, ad quas omnis collocatio sit accommodanda: ut si agnouerit, eos sa cilius ordine eo qui ab institutione artis proficiscitur, in sententiam suam adduci, cum ordinem adhibeat: sin contrà, immutandum ordinem esse. qua de re prǣclarè in Orat. sic: Semper oratorum eloquentiæ moderatrix suit auditorum prudentia, inquit. omnes enim qui probari uolunt, ut luntatem eorum qui audiunt, intuentur, ad eamq; & ad eorum arbitrium & nutum totos se fingunt & accommodant. Atq; ut Aristoteles censet lib. 3. debet esse oratio, qualis esse Theodori uox utdebatur, ad aliorum histrionum uocem compara-tā. tamnam eius ipsius qui dicebat illa esse uidebatur, uoces autem reliquorum alienæ. Et hoc illud est quod dicit Cicero de Orat.libro secundo: Summa deniq; huius generis hæc est, inquit, ut si in refellendo aduersario firmior esse oratio quàm in confirmandis nostris reb. poterit, omnia in illud conferam tela: sin nostra facilius probari, quàm illa redargui possunt, abducere animos à contraria defensione, & ad nostram conor traducere. Ad quæ quidem efficienda, ut idem libro primo ait, Acuto homine nobis opus est, et natura usu&q; callido: qui sagaciter perucstigetur quid sui ciues, ijq; homines quibus aliquid dicendo persuadere velit, cogitent, sentiant, opinentur, expectent. Teneat oportet uenas cuiusque generis, ætatis, ordinis: & eorum apud quos aliquid aget, aut erit acturus, mentes sensus q; degustet.
units.tr: C.P. Can we always keep to the order of arrangement? Some think that the question here is whether one must always use the order prescribed above by Cicero. As if Cicero were here instructing us about the order of prudence rather than the natural order. But in my opinion they are mistaken. For he is asking, since a twofold order has been proposed, the natural and the order of judgment, whether it is up to the orator's discretion which of the two he wishes to use. To this the father answers wisely: that this does not rest on the orator's will but on the ears of the audience, to which all arrangement must be adapted; so that if he recognises that they are more easily led to his opinion by the order that follows from the principles of the art, he should use that order; but if the contrary, the order must be changed. On this matter he says excellently in the Orator: "The prudence of the audience has always been the regulator of the eloquence of orators. For all who wish to be approved look to the will of those who listen, and they fashion and adapt themselves wholly to it and to their judgment and nod. And as Aristotle thinks in book 3, the speech ought to be like the voice of Theodorus, which seemed to be that of the speaker himself, while the voices of the others seemed foreign to him." And this is what Cicero means in On the Orator, book 2: "In sum, the principle of this kind is this: if in refuting the opponent our speech can be stronger than in confirming our own points, I will throw all my weapons at that; but if ours can be proved more easily than theirs can be refuted, I will strive to draw the minds away from the opposing defence and bring them over to ours." And to bring this about, as he says in book 1, "we need a man who is sharp, skilled by nature and practice, who will carefully investigate what his fellow citizens, and the men to whom he wishes to persuade by speaking, think, feel, suppose and expect. He must know the veins of each kind, age and rank, and taste the minds and feelings of those among whom he is or will be acting."

units.la: DE ELOCVTIONE.
units.tr: ON ELOCUTION.

units.la: C.F. Expone deinceps, quæ ipsius orationis uerborum que præceptasunt. C.P. Vnum igitur genus est eloquendi, sua sponte fusum: alterum, uersum atque mutatum. Prima uis est in simplicibus uerbis, in coniunctis secunda. Sim-pli-
units.tr: C.F. Next, explain the precepts concerning the words of the speech itself. C.P. There is therefore one kind of speaking, poured out of its own accord, and another, turned and altered. The main force lies in simple words, the second in combined ones. Simple words must be found; combined words must be arranged.

units.la: Note: the text on this page is a continuous column; no separate footnotes printed. plicia, inuenienda sunt: coniuncta, collocanda sunt.
units.tr: ...ple, must be found; combined ones must be arranged.

units.la: C. F. Expone deinceps quæ ipsius orationis verborum que præcepta sunt.) De elocutione quærit filius, quæ quoniam & verbis simplicibus constat, & coniunctis: orationem ad coniuncta, verba ad simplicia retulit. Idcirco recte hæc duo complexi sunt elocutionis definitione: Elocutio est idoneorum verborum & sententiarum ad inventionem accommodatio, ut initio libri primi etiam definiuimus. Cum autem quid, & quo loco dicat, orator inuenerit: illud est longè maximum, uidere quo'nam modo. Scitū est enim, quod Carneades dicere solebat (ut in Oratore Cicero scribit) Clitomachum eadem dicere, Carneadem autem eodem etiā modo dicere. Nam Clitomachus ille ieiunè & sine ulla varietate eadem dicebat: uerum Carneades nō solum eadem, sed etiam eodem modo, hoc est varie, ornatè & copiosè dicebat, atq; quocunque modo posceret causa. Quin eloquendi ratio, genusq; dicendi (ut Arist. lib.3. ait) quiddā necessariū habet in omni disciplina. Aliquantū enim interest ad rē explicandā, hoc an illo dicēdi genere qs utatur: nō tamē tātū, quantū in hac arte. Quæ Aristotelis verba interpretans Cicero in Oratore: Quod si in philosophia tantū interest (inquit) quemadmodum dicas, ubi res spe-
units.tr: C.F. Next, explain the precepts concerning the words of the speech itself. The son asks about elocution, which consists of both simple and combined words. So he has referred speech to combined words and words to simple ones. For this reason the two are rightly included in the definition of elocution: elocution is the fitting of suitable words and sentences to invention, as we also defined at the beginning of the first book. But once the orator has discovered what he is to say and where, the greatest thing by far is to see in what manner he should say it. It is a fine point, as Carneades used to say (as Cicero writes in the Orator), that Clitomachus said the same things as Carneades, but Carneades said them in a different manner. Clitomachus spoke those things dryly and without any variety; Carneades, however, spoke not only the same things but also in a different manner, that is, variously, ornately and copiously, and in whatever way the cause required. Indeed, the method of speaking and the style of discourse (as Aristotle says in book 3) has something necessary in every discipline. For it makes a considerable difference to the explanation of a subject whether one uses this or that style of speaking, though not as much as in this art. Interpreting these words of Aristotle, Cicero says in the Orator: "But if in philosophy it matters so much, he says, how you speak, where the subject is looked

units.la: {y} spectatur, nō uerba pendūtur: quid tandē in caussis existimandum est, quibus totis moderatur oratio? Est autē elocutio oratoris maximē propria, quem hoc uno excellere, id est oratione, cætera in eo latere, indicat nomen ipsum. nō enim inuentor, aut compositor, aut actor, hæc complexus est omnia: sed & Græcè ab eloquendo ῥήτωρ, & Latine eloques dictus est. Cæterarum enim rerum quæ sunt in oratore, partem aliquam sibi quisq; uendicat: dicendi autem, id est, eloquendi maxima uis soli huic concediter. Qua de re hæc & plura hic noster de Orat. lib. i. disputat, & in Qrat. ad Brutum docet. Hæc igitur caussa fuit, cur tam diligenter & accuratè de hac parte oratorij officij præceperit: adeò ut tertium de Oratore librum, in hac una explicanda consumpserit.
units.tr: at and the words are not weighed, what must be thought in lawsuits, which the whole speech governs?" Elocution is most especially proper to the orator. That he excels in this one thing, namely speech, while the rest lies hidden in him, the very name indicates. For the orator is not the inventor, arranger or performer who embraces all these things; he is called rhetor [ῥήτωρ] in Greek from speaking, and eloquens in Latin. Each man claims for himself some part of the other things that belong to the orator, but the greatest power of speaking, that is, of eloquence, is granted to this one alone. On this matter our author discusses these and more points here in the first book of On the Orator, and he teaches them in the Orator to Brutus. This was therefore the reason he taught so carefully and accurately about this part of the orator's office, so much so that he devoted the whole third book of On the Orator to the explanation of this one thing.

units.la: C. P. Vnū igitur genus est eloquendi, sua sponte susum. ) Hanc eloquendi siue orationis diuisionem, uidetur Cicero ex Aristotele mutuatus esse. Nam is per initia libri primi, ubi de occultando orationis artificio præcipit, sic inquit: Quare danda opera est, ut id clàm fiat, ne artificiū nostrum intelligatur, sed ut duce natura & sponte sermonem fundere uideamur: sic enim erit probabilis oratio. Cicero igitur, qui ferè singula uerba horū de Rhetorica Aristotelis librorum in numerato haberet, hoc loco admonitus, & ab ipsa quoq; ser-monis monis natura,hæc elocutionis siue sermonis, siue orationis duo genera fecit:unum, quod sua sponte fusum appellauit,uersum ac mutatum alterum. Sermo igitur sua sponte fusus is erat, quo tunc uulgo Romæ utebantur, qui ob id Romanus & Latinus dicebatur. Nunc autem eum esse dicimus, qui Grammaticorum præceptis traditur, purus, emendatus,planus ac dilucidus, cuiusmodi sermo in Plauto fere ac Terentio, Varrone & Catone de re rustica, in Commentarijs Cæsaris quoq;, & Ciceronis ad Atticum epistolis legitur. Est enim, ut Aristoteles Rhetoricorum lib.3.ait,initium & fundamentum elocutionis,emendatè loqui. Hanc meam sententiam probant illa uerba paulo post posita:Nam ut in simplicibus verbis quod non est Latinum,sic in coniunctis quod non est consequès, uituperandum est. Idem quoq; ex altero genere, uerso scilicet ac mutato,cognosci potest. Quòd si quis obijciat,in hoc sponte fuso & naturali modos & translationes tradi:huic opponam Aristotelem in tertio dicentem, Translatis in loquendo omnes uti. Versus autem est ille idem latinus & grammaticus sermo,oratoris ingenio uariè commutatus & expolitus.Verè enim Cicero de Orat. lib.3.Nihil est enim tam tenerũ, inquit, neq; tam flexibile, neq; quod tam facilè sequatur, quocũq; ducas,quàm oratio.ex hac uersus, ex eadè dispares numeri conficiuntur: ex hac, hæc etiam soluta uarijs modis, multorumq; generum oratio. non enim sunt alia sermonis, alia contentionis uerba: neque ex alio genere ad usum quotidianum, alio ad scenam pompam'que sumuntur. Sed ea nos cum iacentia sustulimus e medio, sicut mollissimam ceram, ad nostrum arbitrium formamus, & fingimus. itaque tum graues sumus, tum subtiles, tum medium quiddam tenemus. sic institutam nostram sententiam sequitur orationis genus, idq; ad omnem rationem, & aurium uoluptatem, & animorum motum mutatur & uertitur. Quibus in generibus illud tenendum est, ut neque semper fuso & naturali utamur: sed ueterum exemplo, hæc duo genera permisceamus. Quod quidem assequi poterimus, legendis ueterib. oratoribus & poetis: quorum sermone assuefacti qui erunt, ne cupientes quidem poterunt loqui nisi Latinè, & ut illi uerba collocarunt, collocare.
units.tr: C.P. There is therefore one kind of speaking, poured out of its own accord. This division of speech or of discourse seems to have been borrowed by Cicero from Aristotle. For Aristotle, in the opening of the first book, where he teaches how to conceal the art of oratory, says: "Therefore care must be taken that this is done secretly, so that our art is not recognised, but so that we seem to pour out our speech by the guidance of nature and of our own accord; for speech will thus be credible." Cicero, therefore, who had nearly every word of these books of Aristotle's Rhetoric committed to memory, was prompted by this passage, and also by the very nature of discourse, and made two kinds of elocution or discourse: one which he called poured out of its own accord, and the other turned and altered. The speech poured out of its own accord was that which was then commonly used at Rome, and for this reason was called Roman and Latin.
