Now we say it is that speech which is taught by the precepts of the grammarians: pure, correct, plain and clear, of the kind found in Plautus and Terence, in Varro and Cato's On Agriculture, in Caesar's Commentaries too, and in Cicero's letters to Atticus. For, as Aristotle says in book 3 of the Rhetoric, the beginning and foundation of elocution is to speak correctly. My view is confirmed by those words placed a little later: "For just as among simple words what is not Latin is to be blamed, so among combined words what is not consequent is to be blamed." The same can also be recognised from the other kind, the turned and altered. But if anyone objects that tropes and figures are taught in this poured-out and natural style, I shall oppose Aristotle, who says in the third book: "All use metaphors in speaking." The turned kind is that same Latin and grammatical speech, variously changed and polished by the orator's talent. For Cicero truly says in book 3 of On the Orator: "Nothing is so tender, he says, nor so flexible, nor which so easily follows wherever you lead, as speech. From this verse is made, from the same material are made various rhythms; from this, also, unbound speech in many ways and of many kinds. For there are not one set of words for ordinary talk and another for debate; nor are they taken from one kind for daily use and from another for the stage and display. But we have lifted these words, lying as they are, out of the common stock, and shape and mould them to our judgment like the softest wax. And so we are sometimes grave, sometimes subtle, and sometimes keep to a middle course. The kind of speech follows the principle we have laid down, and it is changed and turned to suit every method, and to please the ear and to move the minds." In these kinds we must keep to this rule: that we do not always use the poured-out and natural style, but, following the example of the ancients, mix these two kinds. This we shall be able to achieve by reading the ancient orators and poets; those who are accustomed to their speech will be unable, even if they wish, to speak anything but Latin, and will arrange words as they did.

units.la: Prima uis est in simplicib. uerbis, in coniunctis secunda.) Iam igitur dissoluendi uia genus dicedi in coniuncta uerba, & coniuncta in simplicia distribuit, tanquam in minores cuiuslibet partes. Sic in tertio de Oratore: Omnis igitur oratio, inquit, conficitur ex uerbis, quorum primum nobis ratio simpliciter uidenda est, deinde coniunctè. Simplicia intelligit singula uerba, siue illa sint omnino simplicia,ut Grammatici uocât:cuiusmodi hoc est, beatus.siue cõiuncta,ut perbeatus.Cõiuncta uerò ea appellat,ex quib.cõstat oratio: siue ea sit simplex Dialecticorũ more,ut, Omnia tẽpus habet: siue cõiuncta & copulata,ut, Si omnia tempus habet,igitur in adolescẽtia hæ artes cõparãdæ sunt. Nam quemadmodũ ex literis syllabæ, ex syllabis uerba,sic ex uerbis simul ad aliquid significandũ coniunctis, omnis conficitur & cõflatur oratio. Perinde igitur est,ac si dixisset:Verborũ uis & ratio duob.modis est cõsideranda, ut & in separatis uerbis quæ nam sint assumenda, & in coniunctis,quomodo sint collocanda,uideamus.
units.tr: The main force lies in simple words, the second in combined ones. Now, by way of dissolving, he divides the kind of speech into combined words, and combined words into simple ones, as into the smaller parts of any whole. So in the third book of On the Orator: "Every speech, he says, is made up of words, of which we must first consider the reason in the simple words, and then in the combined." By simple words he means single words, whether they are wholly simple, as the grammarians call them, such as beatus, or compound, such as perbeatus. By combined words he means those of which speech consists, whether it is a simple sentence in the manner of the dialecticians, as "all things have a time", or joined and linked, as "If all things have a time, therefore in youth these arts must be acquired." For just as syllables are made from letters and words from syllables, so from words joined together to signify something, the whole of speech is made and put together. It is therefore just as if he had said: "We must consider the force and reason of words in two ways, so that we may see both which words are to be chosen in their separate forms, and how they are to be arranged when joined."

units.la: Simplicia inuenienda sunt,coniuncta collocanda.) Initiò dixit, & res & uerba inuenienda esse,& collocanda. proprie tamen inuenire ad res, eloqui ad uerba retulit. Collocare uerò etsi commune est, tamen ad inueniendum potius referri. Iam igitur de inuentione uerborum, & collocatione præcipere incipit: distinguitq; à collocatione inuentione,ut inuentio in simplicib. & singulis uerbis,collocatio in cõiunctione & cõpositione spectetur. Quoniã igitur & uerba inuenieda sunt,& inuenire in uerbis est eloqui,& eloqui est cũ delectu loqui:inuenire certè erit uerba quaerere, inuestigare, deligere: quod quidem fieri non potest, nisi in copia. Verè enim Cæsar, ut in Brutho to Ciceronis,scripsit, uerborum delectum originem esse eloquentiæ.Quomodo autem sint collocanda,postea docebit.
units.tr: Simple words must be found, combined words must be arranged. He first said that both things and words must be found and arranged. Properly, however, he referred invention to things and speaking to words. Arranging, although it is a common term, is rather referred to invention. Now he begins to teach about the invention and arrangement of words, and he distinguishes arrangement from invention: invention is considered in simple and single words, arrangement in the joining and composition of them. Since therefore words must be found, and to find in words is to speak, and to speak is to speak with selection, then to find will certainly be to seek, investigate and choose words; and this cannot be done unless there is abundance. For Caesar, as Cicero reports in the Brutus, truly wrote that the choice of words is the origin of eloquence. How words are to be arranged he will teach afterwards.

units.la: Et simplicia uerba partim natiua sunt, partim reperta. Natiua, ea quæ significata sunt sensu: reperta, quæ ex his facta sunt, & nouata aut similitudine, aut imitatione, aut inflexione,aut adiunctione uerborum.
units.tr: Simple words are partly native and partly coined. Native are those which are signified by the senses; coined are those which are made from these, and renewed either by likeness, or by imitation, or by inflection, or by the addition of words.

units.la: Et simplicia uerba, partim natiua sunt, partim reperta. ) Diuisio hæc est simplicium uerborum, in natiua & reperta. Natiua de Orat. ea esse dicit, quæ propria sunt, & certa quasi uocabula rerum, pene una nata cum rebus ipsis. hic autem ea esse dicit, quæ significata sunt sensu: illud intelligens, hominum sensu naturali, qui naturam nominum explorarit, facta esse: & ita res ipsas cis uerbis significatas, ac si cum ipsis rebus nata essent. Reperta uero, quæ ex illis primis & natiuis facta sunt. hæc autem in Oratore aliena appellauit, quia non sunt natiua & propria: quibus nimirum alienis multa genera subiecit eodem loco.
units.tr: And simple words are partly native, partly coined. ) This division of simple words into native and coined is given here. In On the Orator he calls native those words that are proper and fixed, as it were the names of things, almost born together with the things themselves. Here he calls them those words that were given meaning by the senses, understanding that they were made by the natural sense of men who have examined the nature of names, so that the things themselves are signified by these words as if they had been born together with the things. Coined words are those made from those first and native words. In the Orator he called these foreign, because they are not native and proper, and he indeed placed many kinds of foreign words under that heading in the same place.

units.la: Reperta, quæ ex ijs facta sunt, & nouata.) Vides etiam hic eadem nouata dici: ut intelligas, reperta,nouata,facta, Ciceroni hoc loco idem esse. Non sunt igitur noua omnino,sed nouata: ut si uestis iam usitata, alia forma & ratione nouaretur, non compararetur noua. Nam & in Orat. factum à nouo distinguit. Nouari uero hic quatuor modis uerba dicere uidetur, si modò incorruptus est locus: aut similitudine, aut imitatione, aut inflexione, aut adiunctione uerborum. sic enim legitur: cum tamen ipsemet de Oratore tria tantum esse dicat, quæ orator afferat in uerbo simplici: aut inusitatum uerbum, aut nouum, aut translatū. Et paulo post, nouari dicit uerba duob. modis, uel coniungendis uerbis, uel sine coniuncstione: quod fit inflexione, seu derinatione quadã. Quare fortassis legendum sit, Aut similitudine, aut imitatione, ut inflexione, ut adiunctione uerborum, nimirum ut inflexio ad similitudinem, & adiunctio ad imitationem referatur: quod tamen mihi non probatur. Itaq; quanta maxima potero facilitate & breuitate, quid sentiam, indicabo. Aliam uiam tenuit hic Cicero, & quidem subtiliorem, utpote in Partitionibus, quam in alijs Oratorijs libris. Quare non est mirum, si tum paulo aliter, tum etiam distinctius & plurib. modis uerba nouari, hoc libro tradit. Sed ante quàm ad explicationem singulorum ueniamus, explicanda est illa quæstio, de qua plerofq; ambigere uideo: Liceat'ne & hodie nobis, quod olim lingua Romana in populo uigente licuisse legimus, uerba nouanouare, & fingere: aut nouis rebus noua imponere nomina? Qui uolunt sibi licere, Ciceronis auto ritate niti uidentur, qui in principio tertij libri de Finib. scribit: Stoicorum autem nō ignoras quàm fit subtile, uel spinosum potius differendi genus, idq; cum Græcis, tum magis nobis, quibus etiā uerba parienda sunt, imponendaq; nouis reb. nomina. Itemq; in Oratore: In omnib. fit artibus, inquit, ut cum id appellandū fit, quod propter rerū ignorantiam ipsarū nullū habuerit ante nomē, necessitas cogit aut nouū facere uerbū, aut à simili mutuari. Afferunt & illud Horatij ex Poetica:
units.tr: Coined words, which are made from them, and newly formed.) You see here that the same words are also called newly formed, so that you may understand that coined, newly formed and made are the same thing for Cicero in this place. They are therefore not new in the full sense, but newly formed: as when a garment already in use is renewed in a different shape and fashion, it is not called new. For in the Orator too he distinguishes the made from the new. Here he seems to say that words are renewed in four ways, if the text is sound: by likeness, by imitation, by inflection, or by the combining of words. For so it is read. Yet in the same work he himself says there are only three things an orator brings to a simple word: either an unusual word, or a new one, or a transferred one. And a little later he says that words are renewed in two ways, either by joining words together or without joining, which is done by inflection or some kind of derivation. Perhaps, then, it should be read: "either by likeness or by imitation, or by inflection or by the joining of words," so that inflection is referred to likeness and joining to imitation. This, however, does not seem right to me. So I will state, as briefly and clearly as I can, what I think. Cicero follows a different and subtler path here, as is proper in the Partitions, than in his other rhetorical books. It is therefore no wonder if he teaches here that words are renewed sometimes in a slightly different way, and more distinctly and in more ways. But before we come to the explanation of the individual items, we must explain a question about which I see many are in doubt: Are we also today allowed to renew words and coin them, or to give new names to new things, as we read that the Roman language once allowed among a flourishing people? Those who want to be permitted this seem to rely on the authority of Cicero, who at the beginning of the third book of the On Ends writes: "You are not unaware how subtle, or rather thorny, the Stoic manner of disputing is, and this is so both for the Greeks and still more for us, for whom words must be created and names imposed on new things." And likewise in the Orator: "In all the arts," he says, "it happens that when something must be named which, because of ignorance of the things themselves, had no name before, necessity compels us either to make a new word or to borrow one from something similar." They also cite that verse of Horace from the Poetics:

units.la: — Licuit, semperq; licebit Signatū præsente nota procudere uerbū. Ite illa: Multa renascentur, quæ iam cecidere, cadentq;, Quæ nunc sunt in honore uocabula, si uolet usus: Quē penes arbitriū est, & uis & norma loquendi.
units.tr: It has been allowed, and always will be, to coin a word stamped with the present mark. Also those lines: Many words that have now fallen will be born again, and those that now stand in honour will fall, if usage wills it, in whose power lies the judgement, the force and the rule of speech.

units.la: Hæc illi habet, in quib. & necessitas & auctoritas tantorum uirorū, & nouare & fingere noua uerba permittere uidetur. At longè aliter res habet, quàm illi opinentur. Permittut quidē illi suis, aut permiserunt potius, nō alienis. Fuit aut erat, qui Latinè à puero loquebatur: quorū linguæ usus erat proprius, ac natiuus. neq; enim id aut Græcis, aut Scythis permittebatur, ut Romanis uoces facerēt, nō suas: quemadmodum nec illi Romanis. Quis enim hodie ferret, aut Germanus Italiū, aut Italus Germanu,sua pro natiuis & ueris ingeretem?Iam nos quicunq; fimus fiue Itali, fiue Galli, fiue Germani, fi linguas nostras natiuas spectes, à Latinis illis ueterib. prorsum alienifumus,cisq; barbari. Quare uoce nulla q latina fit,eis parere ullo modo possumus. Quod fi cuiq; fit liberu,uel parua fata mutatione,fiue inflexione, quasi Latina ufupare,Latinisq; asciscere: uel nouis reb.no ua uocabula imponere,deinde in oratione Latina pro Latinis uti,iam quanta breui facta fuerit Latini sermonis cofufio,uidebis.quod quide fuperiorib.annis,cum omnia omnes sibi licere putarent, nimiu uidimus. Nam uix iam tot annos infudates, prauam consuetudine profligamus. Hoc etiã sentiebat Cicero suo tepore. idcirco illa in Bruto que rebatur,cu ait: Confluxerut enim & Athenas, & in hanc urbe,multi inquinatè loquentes,ex diuerfis locis:quo magis expurgadus est sermo, & adhibeda,quasi obrufa,ratio quæ mutari nõ potest, nec utendu prauissima consuetudinis regula. Licuit igitur,femperq; licebit,ut ait Horatius, Signatum praefente nota procudere uerbum: Sed in sua natiua cuiq; populo lingua, non in aliena. & liceret etiam hodie in Latina, fi populus & ciuitates latine,ut uideteres, loqueretur. Sed ne hoc quidè maiorib. nostris ufq; adeò liberum fuit. Monet enim Cicero oratore,in libro qui Orator tor inscribitur, ne audax sit in uerbis faciendis, & in transferendis sit uerecundus & parcus. Item Quintilianus lib. 1. cap. 5. Noua, inquit, non sine quodam periculo fingimus. Et lib. 8. cap. 3. Fingere, ut primo libro dixi, Græcis magis concessum est & paucis interpositis: Nostri autem in iungendo aut deriuando, paulum aliquid ausi, uix in hoc satis recipiuntur. hæc illi: nos autem omnia nobis licere putamus, quod secus est. Nec hæc mea solius hodie sententia est, sed omnium qui bene latine sciunt: quos nihil nominare opus est, cum sint suis egregijs monumentis clari. nam reliqui hac de re loquendi nullum ius habent. Video autem quid mihi obijci possit: nimirum si ita res habet, ut nefas sit aliquod uerbum vel maxima inopia fingere, ac gignere: sæpe etiam ei qui perbene latine sciat, esse tacendum: cum nō omnia quæ hodie nominantur, aut fiunt, in latinis autoribus expressa inueniantur. Ego vero minime tacendum esse puto. nam sunt huic incommodo remedia, cadq; tutissima ac certissima. Primum est, ut si quid nouū appellandum sit, quæras apud maiores illos an aliquid simile fuerit, cuius nomen nouæ rei accommodari, ut antiqua uestis huius temporis homini, possit. ut in bombarda (quod nomen à sono præclare finxit vulgus) quæ cum pene idem sit quod apud maiores fuit tormentum militare, tormenti nomine commodè appellabitur: & pro bõbardare, ucrberare, pulsare, percutere urbem recte dicemus. Idem faciendum erit in ijs, quae etsi alio nunc nomine appellentur, quàm apud maiores, res tamen eadem sunt: id quod unusquisque in sua lingua diligenter obseruare atque inuestigare debet. ut apud nostros Italos est rhedae celerrimae & leuissimae genus, quod dicitur, il cocchio: id ipsum Cisium ueteres appellarunt, ut est apud Ciceronem in oratione pro Sexto Roscio Amerino: & ipsa rheda quam modò nominaui, ea est qua Italae mulieres magnificè uehuntur, nostri appellant la carretta: quae & quadrigae dici possunt. Quod si neq; simile, neq; idem apud ueteres reperiri possit, tum faciendum erit, quod Cicero se in uertendis Graecis fecisse scribit: ut quod uno uerbo non posset, pluribus notaret. nam circumscriptione, quae periphrasis dicitur Graecè, utendum erit: Vt pro staffa, instrumentum quo pedes sustinet eques, uel pedum equitis adminiculum: pro campana, aes campanum, aut aeneum uas in alto suspensum, cuius pulsu & sono, aliquid publicè significatur: aut aliquid huiusmodi. Erit & illud non incommodum, ut Latina aliqua uoce destituti, Graecis utamur puris: quod etiam facitauit Cicero. ut cum, quod fieri non potest, quod quidam impossibile dicunt, ipse ἀδύνατον diccdicebat: pro condolentia, συμπαθείας: et ὑμ-παθῶς, pro condolenter: et ὑπερβολικῶς, pro ex-cessiue, atque code modo fexcenta. Postremo, si minus concessa uoce uti cogemur omnino, eo modo recte illam usurpabimus, si, ut Cicero, in duorioribus paulo translationibus, aut etiam uerbis quae non fatis latina ei uidebantur, ueniam praefabimur, hoc modo: Vt aiunt, ut ita dicam, ut nostri appellant, si licet ita dicere aut appellare, et huius generis multis modis: ut Fabius monet libro octauo, capite tertio: quibus et infolentium uitabimus, et doctorum atque elegantium reprehensionem. Recte enim Cæsar, uerbum inauditum atque insolens, tanquam scopulum fugiendum censuit. His cognitis, deinceps facilior erit sequentium explicatio.
units.tr: Those are his words, in which both the necessity and the authority of such great men seem to permit renewing and inventing new words. But the matter stands very differently from what they suppose. Those things are permitted to his own people, or rather were permitted, not to foreigners. There were, and there were those who from boyhood spoke Latin, and for them the use of the language was proper and native. For it was not permitted to Greeks or Scythians to make words for the Romans that were not their own, just as the Romans could not do so for them. For who would tolerate today, either a German being an Italian, or an Italian being a German, thrusting his own words in place of native and true ones? Indeed, we, whoever we are, whether Italians, Frenchmen or Germans, if you look at our native tongues, are wholly alien from those ancient Latins and barbarous compared with them. Therefore we can in no way produce any word that is Latin. If each person were free, with some slight change or inflection, to use as if Latin, and to adopt into Latin, or to impose new words for new things and then use them in Latin speech as if they were Latin, you would see how soon the Latin language would be thrown into confusion. In the past years, when everyone thought everything was permitted to everyone, we saw too much of this. For we have hardly now, after so many years of effort, got rid of that corrupt habit. Cicero too felt this in his own time, which is why in the Brutus he complains, when he says: "For many who speak corruptly have flowed together to Athens and into this city from different places, so that the speech must be all the more purged, and the reason, as if buried, must be brought back, which cannot be changed, nor must the most corrupt rule of custom be followed." It has been allowed, therefore, and always will be, as Horace says, to coin a word stamped with the present mark. But this is so in one's own native language for each people, not in a foreign one. And it would be allowed even today in Latin, if the people and the cities spoke Latin as they once did. But not even our ancestors enjoyed this freedom to such an extent. For Cicero, in the book entitled The Orator, warns the orator not to be bold in making words, and to be modest and sparing in transferring them. Likewise Quintilian, book 1, chapter 5: "We coin new words not without a certain danger." And book 8, chapter 3: "To coin words, as I said in the first book, has been granted more to the Greeks, and with few exceptions; but we Romans, if we venture something a little in compounding or deriving, are scarcely admitted even in this." So far he. But we think everything is permitted to us, which is the opposite. Nor is this only my opinion today, but that of all who know Latin well, whom there is no need to name, since they are famous for their outstanding monuments. For the rest have no right to speak on this matter. I see, however, what may be objected to me: namely, that if the matter stands thus, it would be wrong to invent or beget any word even in the greatest want, and that often even one who knows Latin very well must keep silent, since not everything that is named or done today is found expressed in the Latin authors. But I think that we must by no means keep silent. For there are remedies for this inconvenience, and they are very safe and sure. The first is that if something new has to be named, you should look among those older writers to see whether there was something similar whose name could be fitted to the new thing, as an ancient garment can be fitted to a man of this time. Thus for bombarda (a name the common people aptly coined from the sound), since it is nearly the same as what among the ancients was the tormentum militare, it will be suitably called by the name tormentum; and we will rightly say bombardare for to batter, to beat, to strike, to strike the city. The same must be done in those cases where, although they are now called by a different name from that of the ancients, the things are still the same; this everyone must carefully observe and investigate in his own language. Thus among us Italians there is a kind of very swift and light carriage, which is called il cocchio; the ancients called this very thing cisium, as it is in Cicero's speech for Sextus Roscius of Ameria. And the rheda I have just mentioned, the carriage in which Italian women are grandly conveyed, our people call la carretta; these too can be called quadrigae. But if nothing similar or identical can be found among the ancients, then we must do what Cicero writes that he did in translating from the Greek: when a thing could not be expressed in one word, he marked it with several. For we will have to use circumlocution, which is called periphrasis in Greek: for staffa, the instrument on which the rider supports his feet, or the support of the rider's feet; for campana, a bronze bell, or a bronze vessel hung high, by whose striking and sound something is signified publicly; or something of this kind. It will also not be inappropriate, when we are lacking a Latin word, to use pure Greek words, as Cicero too did. Thus, when he said something could not be done, which some call impossibile, he himself said adynaton [ἀδύνατον]; for sympathy he used sympatheias [συμπαθείας]; for "in sympathy" homopathōs [ὁμοπαθῶς]; for "excessively" hyperbolikōs [ὑπερβολικῶς], and many others of this kind. Finally, if we are altogether compelled to use a word not generally accepted, we will use it correctly in that way, if, as Cicero did, we put forward an apology for somewhat bolder transfers, or even for words that seemed to him not Latin enough, in this manner: "as they say, as I may put it, as our people call it, if it is allowed to speak or name it so," and in many such ways, as Fabius advises in book eight, chapter three. By this we will avoid both the unusual and the insolent, and the censure of the learned and the refined. For Caesar rightly judged that an unheard-of and strange word should be avoided like a reef. With these things understood, the explanation of what follows will be easier.

units.la: Aut similitudine.) Haec est prima faciendorum uerborum ratio, quae Analogia, ut quidam dicitur, et est etiam uerisimile. Latine proportio, coparatio, et similitudo dici potest, ut probat Fabius: qui lib. 5. cap. 11. eam similitudinis subiecit affirmat. Ea inuenta est, poftqua loquebantur homines, ut idem Fabius ait lib. 1. cap. 6. et notatum in sermone, quid quomodo caderet. Itaque non ratione nititur, sed exemplo: nec lex est loquendi, sed obseruatio: ut ipsam analogiam nullares alia fecerit, quam consuetudo. Varro, qui de ea re docte & copiose scripsit, tria dicit esse consideranda: formam, finem, & declinationem. Similitudine videtur Cicero beatitatem & beatitudinem, quae bonitati & habitudini similia sunt, fecisse. Item que Ennius, dici videns sermo sermonis, ipse homo hominis fecit, pro hominis, illo aersu:
units.tr: Or by similarity.) This is the first method of forming words. Some call it analogy, and it is probably the right term. In Latin it can be called proportion, comparison, and similitude, as Fabius shows. In book 5, chapter 11, he adds it under similitude and affirms it. It was discovered after men began to speak, as the same Fabius says in book 1, chapter 6, when people observed in speech how each word was inflected. So it rests not on reason but on example. It is not a rule of speaking but an observation, and custom alone has made analogy. Varro, who wrote about this learnedly and fully, says three things must be considered: form, end, and declension. By similarity, Cicero seems to have formed beatitas and beatitudo, which are like bonitas and habitudo. Likewise Ennius, seeing that sermo was formed from sermonis, himself made homo from hominis, in the line:

units.la: Vulturis in sylvis miserum mandebat hominem. Ø
units.tr: In the woods a vulture was devouring the wretched man.

units.la: Sed obsoletum est. Potest etiam similitudo ea intelligi, de qua paulo ante dixi, cum rei nove, sed alicui rei quae apud maiores fuerit simili, idem nomen aptamus: ut quoniam hodie arenae fluxu in utreis uasis horas metimur, quemadmodum veteres aqua faciebant, uas hoc nostrum horarium clepsydram possumus appellare. Sunt qui similitudine hoc loco ipsam translationem intelligunt, cum tropis & modificatis omnibus: quod quam sit cum sequenti Ciceronis partitione consentaneum, ipsi viderint. Certe si ita accipimus, non plena erit partitio, sed etiam inaniter redundans: quod alterum est partitionis vitium. non dico, translationem similitudinem non esse: sed illud nego, omnem similitudinem recte translationem appellari: quod quia perspicuum est, nihil amplius dicam.
units.tr: But this is obsolete. Similarity can also be understood in the sense I mentioned a little earlier: when for a new thing we apply the name of something similar that existed among our ancestors. For example, since today we measure hours by the flow of sand in glass vessels, as the ancients did with water, we can call this timepiece of ours a clepsydra. Some understand similarity here to mean translation itself, with all tropes and figures. How well that agrees with Cicero's following division, they themselves will see. Certainly if we take it this way, the division will not be complete but also uselessly redundant, which is the other fault of a division. I do not say that translation is not a similitude. I deny that every similitude is rightly called translation, and since this is clear, I will say no more.

units.la: Aut imitatione.) Sunt & qui imitatione non solum, sed aut exempli esse velint, ut cum Graeca latine ininterpretantur: aut uerborum nostræ linguæ, ut si,quemadmodum Cicero qualitates nominauit, nos quantitates faceremus. Sed melius est, ut imitatione nomen factum à sono & affectibus factum intelligamus, quæ Græce ὀνοματοποιΐα dicitur: ut Bambalio quidam pater, qui, ut ait Cicero Philippica tertia, propter hæsitantiam linguæ, stuporemq; cordis, cognomen ex contumelia traxit. Ex hac factus clamorq; uirûm, clangorq; tubarum. De hac Fabius lib.8. cap.6. ὀνοματοποιΐα quidem, id est fictio nominis, Græcis inter maximas habita uirtutes, nobis uix permittitur. Et sunt plurima ita posita, ab ijs qui sermonem primi fecerunt, aptantes affectib.uocem. nam mugitus,& sibilus,& murmur, inde uenerunt. Quod autem aiunt, hæc non ex natiuis nouari, sed per se gigni, parum momenti habet. Est enim mugitus natiuus in boue, ut tinnitus in ære: sed nouatũ ab eo, qui primus in oratione usurpauit. Quod uero etiam dicunt, imitationem nõ solum in talibus, uerum etiam in omnibus esse uerbis: quod Aristoteles nomina μιμήματα rerum esse ait: facile soluitur. Primò, Aristotelem μιμήματα rerum dixisse, pro rerum notis, ut alibi ipse explicat. Deinde, alia est imitatio illa communis omnium, alia est hæc iucunda, sonorum & uocum. Quod si ista illorû ratio ualeret, nulla esset ὀνοματοποιΐα illa Græcis
units.tr: Or by imitation.) Some want it to mean not only imitation but also example, as when Greek words are rendered into Latin, or words of our own tongue, as if, just as Cicero named qualitates, we made quantitates. But it is better to understand a name made by imitating sound and feeling, which in Greek is called onomatopoeia. Thus a certain father, Bambalio, who, as Cicero says in the Third Philippic, got a nickname from insult because of his stammering tongue and dull heart. From this is formed "clamor of men and clangor of trumpets." Fabius speaks of this in book 8, chapter 6. Onomatopoeia, that is the making of names, the Greeks counted among their greatest virtues, but it is hardly allowed to us. Many words are formed this way by those who first made speech, fitting the voice to the feeling; from this came mugitus, sibilus, and murmur. As for their claim that these words are not renewed from natural sounds but generated by themselves, this has little weight. The lowing is natural in the ox, as the ringing is in bronze, but the word was renewed from it by the one who first used it in speech. As for their further claim that imitation is found not only in such words but in all words, which Aristotle says names are imitations of things, this is easily answered. First, Aristotle spoke of imitations of things to mean the marks of things, as he explains elsewhere. Second, that common imitation found in all words is one thing, and this pleasing imitation of sounds and voices is another. If their argument held, there would be no such onomatopoeia that the Greeks praised so highly.

units.la: {y} (fluporemq;) The left-margin note carries no separate printed text beyond the marginal mark. Græcis tantopere laudata. Sed quoniam hæc imitatio non uno tantum modo intelligi potest, cum pleƈtatur sane etiam priorem illam sententiam: & utroq; modo imitatione uerba nouari intelligantur.
units.tr: (stuporemque;) Yet since this imitation cannot be understood in only one way, it certainly also touches that former opinion, and words are understood to be renewed by imitation in both ways.

units.la: Aut inflexione.) Cum sine exemplo & analogia, simplex uerbum modicè flectedo aut deriuando, siue ex Græca siue ex Latina lingua nouemus: quæ ratio uctcrib.magnâ uerborum peperit copiâ. hinc enim illa, Fimbriatus, fibulatus, consulatus, tribunatus, prætura, dictatura, paludatus, scutatus, decimare, aquari, lignari, philosophari, sullaturire: item illa Ciceronis lib. 3. de Orat. Indigenitalis, ubertas, incuruescere, & id genus innumerabilia: in quibus fœlices sunt Græci, qui & hæc παραγώγα uocarunt, ut est apud Quintilianum libro 8. cap. 6. De Græcis est illud Horatij in Poetica: Et nouâ, fictaq; nuper, habebunt uerba fidem, si Græco fonte cadant, parce detorta. —
units.tr: Or by inflection.) When, without precedent or analogy, we make a new word by slightly inflecting or deriving a simple word, whether from the Greek or the Latin language. This method has brought great abundance of words to the ancients. Hence come fimbriatus, fibulatus, consulatus, tribunatus, praetura, dictatura, paludatus, scutatus, decimare, aquari, lignari, philosophari, sullaturire. Also Cicero's indigenitas, ubertas, incurvescere in book 3 of De Oratore, and countless words of that kind. In this the Greeks are fortunate, for they called these words paragoga, as Quintilian has it in book 8, chapter 6. From the Greeks comes Horace's line in the Poetics: "New words, and lately made, will win credit if they fall from a Greek source, sparingly altered." —

units.la: Ex hoc genere sunt illa apud maiores nostros ex Græcis, sed ad Latinorum formam normamq; inflexa, aer, æther, politia, politicus, sal, mus, clepo, clepsydra: item artium multarum nomina, Grammatica, Dialectica, Rhetorica, Arithmetica, Geometria, Musica, Astrologia, siue Astronomia, Sphæra, & pene eodem modo alia infinita: quæ quæ ratio non modò linguam Latinam, uerumetiam alias, ut Italicam, Gallicam, Germanicam, uehementer locupletauit.
units.tr: Of this kind are those words our ancestors took from the Greeks but bent to the form and norm of Latin: aer, aether, politia, politicus, sal, mus, clepo, clepsydra. Also the names of many arts: grammatica, dialectica, rhetorica, arithmetica, geometria, musica, astrologia or astronomia, sphaera, and almost in the same way countless others. This method has greatly enriched not only the Latin language but also others, such as Italian, French, and German.

units.la: Aut adiunctione uerborum.) Cum uerba' ab eo qui dicit gignuntur,ac fiunt coniungendis uerbis:ut Cic.in.3.de Orat. loquitur. cuius hæc sunt exempla:Tum pauor sapientiam mihi omnem ex animo expectorat.Item, Versutiloquas malitias: & quo Terentius libenter usus est,exanimare. For taßis etiam uerborum productiones illæ huc referri possunt,quibus ad finem uerbi aliquid adiungitur, quod Parelcon morion uocant ueteres Grammatici:ut meditulium,poßliminium,finitimus,legitimus, ædititimus:quibus tulium, liminiu, timus,particulæ sunt ad uerba adiunctæ. de quib. in Topicis,in explicatione Notationis.
units.tr: Or by joining words.) When words are born and made by the speaker joining words together, as Cicero speaks of in book 3 of De Oratore. Examples of this are: "Then fear drains all wisdom from my mind," and "versutiloquas malitias," and exanimare, which Terence liked to use. Those lengthenings of words can also be referred here, in which something is added to the end of a word, which the ancient grammarians call parelcon morion [παρέλκον μόριον]: meditulium, postliminium, finitimus, legitimus, aedititimus, in which tulium, liminium, and timus are particles attached to the words. More on these in the Topics, in the explanation of notation.

units.la: Atqp etiá est hæc distinctio in uerbis:altera natura, tractatione altera. Natura, ut sint alia consonantiora, grauiora, leuiora, & quodammodo nitidiora,alia contrá.
units.tr: And there is also this distinction among words: one by nature, another by treatment. By nature, some words are more consonant, weightier, lighter, and in a way more polished, while others are the opposite.

units.la: Atq; etiam est hæc distinctio in verbis.) Tertia hæc est uerborum partitio, quòd a lia natura ualent, alia tractatione. Vbi naturam opposuit arti,cum uerba ipsa, qualia describit, ad dicendum sumuntur,non aliqua nouitate exornantur. Nam alia reperiuntur confonantiora, ut donat quàm dat, memorare quàm dicere, obruere quàm tegere, informare quàm instituere, inflämatus quàm incensus: Conspectus uester mihi multò iucundissimus, hic autem locus ad agendum amplissimus, ad dicendum ornatissimus est uisus: quae sonatiora sunt, quàm iucundus, amplus, ornatus. Item coniuncta uerba, ut consceleratus, pertimesco, quàm simplicia. His contraria sunt, quae exilia, obscura, & absona uocantur, quae aurium iudicio expenduntur.
units.tr: And there is also this distinction among words.) This is the third division of words: some have their force by nature, others by treatment. Here he set nature against art, since the words themselves, of the kind he describes, are taken for speaking and not adorned by any novelty. Some are found more consonant, as donat rather than dat, memorare rather than dicere, obruere rather than tegere, informare rather than instituere, inflammatus rather than incensus. "Your sight is most pleasing to me, but this place seems most ample for acting and most ornate for speaking": these are more sonorous than iucundus, amplus, ornatus. Likewise compound words, such as consceleratus and pertimesco, rather than simple ones. The opposites of these are called exilia, obscura, and absona, which are judged by the ear.

units.la: Grauiora.) Grauia, quae & grandia dicuntur, sunt, quae rem maximè explanant, ut ipse in Oratore ait: ut grandiora sunt, charitas quàm amor, uastum quàm desertum, saxum quàm lapis, implicatus quàm implicitus, parricida quàm fceleratus aut homicida, grandæuus quàm senex: tum ea, quae inter confonantiora posuimus, superlata & coniuncta uerba. Gravibus siue grandibus contraria sunt humilia, leuia, parua.
units.tr: Weightier.) Weighty words, which are also called grand, are those that explain a thing most fully, as he himself says in the Orator. Thus charitas is grander than amor, vastum than desertum, saxum than lapis, implicatus than implicitus, parricida than sceleratus or homicida, grandaevus than senex. Then there are the superlatives and compound words, which we placed among the more consonant. The opposites of weighty or grand words are humble, light, and small.

units.la: Leniora.) Vt lumen quàm lux, lugere quàm lachrimari, molestus quàm atrox aut infestus. Leniribus aspera & dura contraria sunt. Hæc quoq; auribus ponderantur.
units.tr: Milder.) Thus lumen rather than lux, lugere rather than lachrimari, molestus rather than atrox or infestus. Harsh and hard words are the opposites of milder ones. These too are weighed by the ears.

units.la: Et quodammodo nitidiora.) Hæc quae sint, ex ipsorum contrariis elucet. nam nitidis, siue splendidis & mundis, opponuntur sordida, obscæna, turpia,agrestia. Quod autem addit, Quodámodo,significauit hæc uocabula,quæ uerbis attribuuntur, esse translata è rebus corporatis. Nitida, & grauia,significandi potc.late expedenda sunt. Sed quid est, quod de Oratore lib.1. nitida uerba ab oratore remouere uidetur? cum ait: Nitidum quoddam genus est uerborum, & lætum, sed palęstræ magis & olei, quàm huius ciuilis turbæ ac fori. Non remouet omnino, sed quid sit uitiosum ostendit. Nullum uerbum nisi nitidum usurpare, & omnes uerborum lepores aucupari, palæstræ & exercitationis est, atq; sophistarum sontibus petitum,ut in Oratore scribit. Verum si hoc fiat modice & cum delectu, nec huiusmodi flosculis enerutur oratio,tuc nitida uerba in oratore laudantur. Et hic Cicero genera uerborum oratori proponit,ut cum delectu uti,& in loco possit.
units.tr: And in a way more polished.) What these are is clear from their opposites, for polished, bright, and clean words are opposed by sordid, obscene, foul, and rustic words. That he adds "in a way" signifies that these words, which are attributed to speech, are transferred from bodily things. Polished and weighty words should be explained broadly in their meaning. But why does Cicero in De Oratore book 1 seem to remove polished words from the orator, when he says: "There is a certain kind of words that is polished and cheerful, but it belongs more to the wrestling-ground and oil than to this civic crowd and forum"? He does not remove them altogether, but shows what is faulty. To use only polished words and to hunt out every charm of words belongs to the palaestra and exercise, and is drawn from the sophists' sources, as he writes in the Orator. But if this is done moderately and with selection, and the speech is not enervated by such flowers, then polished words are praised in the orator. Here Cicero sets before the orator kinds of words, so that he may use them with selection and in the right place.

units.la: Tractatione autem,cum aut propria sumuntur rerum uocabula, aut addita ad nomen, aut noua, aut prisca,aut ab oratore modificata, & in-flexa quodammodo: qualia sunt ea quæ transferuntur, aut immutatur, aut ea quibus tanquam abutimur, aut ea quæ obscuramus, quæ incresdibiliter tollimus, quæsq; mirabilius quàm sermonis cõsuetudo patitur, ornamus.
units.tr: But by treatment, when either the proper names of things are used, or words added to a noun, or new words, or archaic ones, or words modified and somewhat bent by the orator, such as those that are transferred or changed, those we use as it were improperly, those we obscure, and those we raise beyond belief and adorn more wonderfully than ordinary speech allows.

units.la: Tractatione autem.) Tractatio est uerborum quædam fabricatio & expolitio, cum uerbis in medio positis & iacentibus arte adiungit orator, atq; ædificat quodammodo. Tractatione autem quinq; modis expoliuntur uerba: cum aut propria sumuntur, id est deliguntur & ex multis tolluntur meliora, aut epitheta, aut noua, aut prisca, aut modificata. Propria quidem, aut alienæ, aut nostræ sunt linguæ: sed hic de nostris agimus, non alienis. Item propria, aut noua sunt & usitata, aut prisca, siue inusitata, siue uetusta. hæc autem sumuntur, id est iudicio aurium deliguntur. Ne autem propria hic intelligas, cuiusmodi à Grammaticis aut Dialecticis appellantur, quæ indiuidua etiam uocât: sed propria intelligimus, non translata aut modificata, omnium rerum uocabula, ut terram, aquam, aerem, ignem, cœlum, stellas, animalia, stirpes.
units.tr: But by treatment.) Treatment is a certain shaping and polishing of words, when the orator skilfully adds to words that lie in the middle and are unused, and builds them up in a way. Words are polished by treatment in five ways: when they are taken as proper, that is, chosen and the better ones picked out from many; or as epithets; or as new; or as archaic; or as modified. Proper words belong either to a foreign or to our own language, but here we are speaking of our own, not foreign ones. Likewise, proper words are either new and in use, or archaic, whether unusual or old. These are taken, that is, chosen by the judgement of the ear. Do not understand "proper" here in the sense the grammarians or dialecticians use, who also call them individual; rather we mean by proper the names of all things that are not transferred or modified, such as earth, water, air, fire, heaven, stars, animals, plants.

units.la: Aut addita ad nomen.) Quæ etiam infrà Adiuncta ad nomen uocat, Græcè dicuntur ἐπίθετα: ut indulgès pater, feucrus iudex, immortalis gloria, & id genus infinita: quæ si uel longius petita sint, uel intempestiuè adhibita, uel crebra, frigida faciunt & ineptam locutionem, ut Aristot. lib.3. Quibus tamen poeta si utatur, non ita uiciosum esse, atq; in oratione soluta, idem testatur Aristoteles.
units.tr: Or added to a noun.) Which he elsewhere below calls "attached to the noun." In Greek they are called epithets [ἐπίθετα]: such as "indulgent father," "cruel judge," "immortal glory," and countless others of that kind. If these are fetched from too far off, or used at an unsuitable moment, or heaped up, they make the speech cold and inept, as Aristotle says in book 3. Yet Aristotle also testifies that if a poet uses them, they are not so faulty, and that the same does not hold in prose.

units.la: Aut noua.) Hoc est, nuper inuenta, quibus interdum uti necessitas cogit. Quod uenia petita faciendum est, quo mollius, ut supra diximus, accipiantur. Haec autem a nouatis, atque ijs quae facit orator, differunt: quod noua ab oratore non fiunt ipso, sed cum paulo ante facta fuerint, ab eo assumuntur: ut fauor, & urbanus, tempore Ciceronis, quod uerbum paulo ante erat factum: sicut obsequium, quo usus est Terentius. Sed quae facit orator ipse, nouata & facta dicuntur, ut supra satis est oStensum.
units.tr: Or new.) That is, recently invented words, which necessity sometimes compels us to use. These must be used with pardon sought, so that they may be received the more gently, as we said above. They differ from neologisms, which the orator himself makes: a new word is not made by the orator himself, but once it has been made shortly before, he takes it up. Examples are "favor" and "urbanus" in Cicero's time, which had been coined a little earlier, and likewise "obsequium," which Terence used. But words that the orator himself makes are called neologisms and coinages, as has been sufficiently shown above.

units.la: Aut prisca. ) Id est, ut ante dixi, inusitata & uetusta, quae etiam sunt in proprijs, sed mediam quandam naturam habent: ut neque plane aliena sint, quia fuerunt olim propria: neque plane propria, quia uetusta & inusitata: idcirco illis raro utemur. Sunt tamen poetarum licentiae liberiora, quam oratorum: habent que in oratione, si parce usurpentur, dignitatem, ut Cicero in 3. & Aristot. in 3. testantur. qui etiam dicunt, grandiorem fieri poeticis verbis orationem. si tamen saepius eis quis utatur, eam obscurabunt: quod est contra proprioorum naturam, quae idcirco assumuntur, ut dilucidam faciant locutionem. Atque haec sunt illa quatuor, quae Ciceroni nostro extra modificationem & translationem numerantur. Aristoteles tamen ἐwiδετα subijcit translationi.
units.tr: Or archaic.) That is, as I said before, unusual and old words, which are also among the proper words but have a certain intermediate nature: they are not plainly foreign, since they were once proper, nor plainly proper, since they are old and unusual. Therefore we shall use them rarely. Yet the licences of poets are freer than those of orators, and such words give dignity to speech if used sparingly, as Cicero in book 3 and Aristotle in book 3 testify; they also say that speech is made grander by poetic words. Yet if someone uses them too often, he will obscure the speech, which runs contrary to the nature of proper words, which are taken up precisely to make speech clear. These are the four that are counted for our Cicero outside modification and transference. Aristotle, however, adds epithets [ἐπίθετα] to transference.

units.la: Aut ab oratore modificata, & inflexa quodam modo.) Tropos, quos Græci uocant, intelligit: qui à nostro Cicerone tum hic, tum de Oratore lib.3. modi dicuntur. hinc modificata & inflexa appellauit. Facit autem modorum duo genera, translationem scilicet, & immutationem. Sed Aristot. uno nomine translationis, tropos omnes intelligit, translationiq; subiungit: cuius sententiam Cic. in Oratore ad Brutum probat.
units.tr: Or modified and in a way bent by the orator.) He means the tropes, which the Greeks call tropes, and which our Cicero, both here and in De Oratore book 3, calls "modes." Hence he named them modified and bent. He makes two kinds of modes, namely transference and change. Aristotle, however, under the single name of transference, understands all the tropes and subjoins change to transference; Cicero, in the Orator to Brutus, approves this view.

units.la: Qualia sunt ea quæ transferuntur.) Translata uocat in Orat. quæ per similitudinem ab alia re, aut suauitatis, aut inopiæ caussa, transferuntur: Inopiæ caussa, ut, gemmare uites, luxuriem segetum, pedem in naui: Suauitatis caussa, ut splendor imperij, ignorantiæ tenebræ, flos ætatis. Oportet autem translationes accommodatas sumere. hoc autem fiet, si proportio cõseruabitur, ut inquit Aristot. lib.3. sin minus, indecorū apparebit. & ut inquit Cicero, uerecunda debet esse translatio, ut deducta esse in alienum locum, non irruisse uideatur. Sumuntur autem translationes à rebus honestis, uel sono, uel potestate, uel affectu, uel alio aliquo sensu, & maximè oculorum, qui est sensus acerrimus. Nam & odor urbanitatis, & mollitudo humanitatis, & murmur maris, & dulcedo orationis, nis,sunt ducta à ceteris sensibus. Cum vero auroram rosfcam siue purpuream dicimus, & cruentam orationem,ad oculorum sensus admouentur. Est etiam illud notandum, duci translationes tam ab iis rebus quae sub sensum cadunt, quàm quae animo tantum percipiuntur: itemq; à rebus inanimis & animatis,ratione praeditis & rationis expertibus. Sunt vero & allegoriae & aenigmata translationis quaedam genera.Allegoria Cornificius permutatione uocat, Fabius inuersionem. ea autem nihil aliud est,quàm ex pluribus continuatis,ciscq; translatis uerbis quaedam connexio:ut aliud dicatur,aliud intelligendum fit.ut,Oucm lupo commisisti:quo significatur, hominem innocentem,inimico aut crudeli commissum: & id genus innumerabilia.nam est amplissimus huiusmodi eam pus. Aenigmata vero,obscurae sunt allegoriae,quas scrupos vcteres appellabat.quae fugienda esse,praecipit Cicero:quia obscurant orationem,cuius propria virtus est perspicuitas. Aristoteles tamen ea non omnino reiicit,& affert etiam exemplum, Vidi hominem qui alteri homini es igne adglutinabat.quod fit, cum in vaporarijs cucurbitulae admouentur.& idcirco eis interdum usus est Cicero, ut in oratione pro Sext.Rof. Amer. Quis ibi non est vulneratus ferro Phrygio? Quum intelligeret, in foro multos è Romanis iudicibus iniuria contødemnatos. Aristoteles imagine, quam εἰκὼν vocat, etiam refert ad translationem, ita tamen, ut à pura translatione tantum adiunctione particule unius differat. ut si de homine dicas, Tanquam leo irruebat: imago est. cum autem, Leo irruebat, est translatio. Sed ea raro utendum esse praecipit, quoniam magis poetas decet.
units.tr: Such as are those that are transferred.) In the Orator, Cicero calls "transferred" those words that are carried over from one thing to another by likeness, either for the sake of pleasantness or from lack of a word. For lack of a word: "to bud the vines," "the luxuriance of the crops," "the foot of a ship." For pleasantness: "the splendour of rule," "the darkness of ignorance," "the flower of youth." Transferences ought to be fitting, and they will be if the proportion is kept, as Aristotle says in book 3; otherwise they will appear unseemly. And as Cicero says, a transference should be modest, as if it has been led into a foreign place and does not seem to have burst in. Transferences are taken from honourable things, whether from sound, power, feeling, or some other sense, and especially from sight, which is the keenest sense. For the scent of urbanity, the softness of humanity, the murmur of the sea, and the sweetness of speech are all drawn from the other senses. When we call the dawn rosy or purple, or speech bloody, they are addressed to the sense of sight. It must also be noted that transferences are drawn both from things that fall under the senses and from those perceived only by the mind; likewise from inanimate and animate things, both those endowed with reason and those without. There are also allegories and riddles, which are certain kinds of transference. Cornificius calls allegory "permutation," and Fabius calls it "inversion." It is nothing but a connection of several continued and transferred words, so that one thing is said and another is to be understood, as "you have committed the sheep to the wolf," which signifies an innocent man entrusted to an enemy or a cruel person; and countless others of that kind, for this kind of thing is very wide-ranging. Riddles, however, are obscure allegories, which the ancients called "scrupi." Cicero advises that they are to be avoided, because they obscure speech, whose proper virtue is clarity. Aristotle, however, does not reject them altogether, and gives the example: "I saw a man who glued one man to another with fire," which happens when cupping-glasses are applied in steam baths. And so Cicero sometimes used them, as in the speech for Sextus Roscius of Ameria: "Who there was not wounded by Phrygian steel?", since he understood that many of the Roman judges had been unjustly condemned in the forum. Aristotle also refers the image, which he calls eikon [εἰκών], to transference, though it differs from pure transference only by the addition of a single particle: if you say of a man, "he rushed like a lion," that is an image; but "the lion rushed" is a transference. Yet he advises that it be used rarely, since it suits poets more.

units.la: Aut immutantur. ) Mutata & immutata dicit in Oratore, in quibus pro verbo proprio subiicitur aliud, quod idem significet, sumptum ex re aliqua cosequeti. Hic, inquit Cicero, ὑπαλλαγὴν Rhetores, quia quasi submutantur verba pro verbis: μετωνυμίαν Grammatici vocant, quod nomina transferuntur, alio tamen modo quàm in translatione, de qua dictum est. Sunt autem huius multae species, quarum primam nomine generis appellant, nimirum ὑπαλλαγὴν, ut dixi, sive μετωνυμίαν: Cicero traductionem, atq; immutationem. ut, Gracia pro Gracis, Africa pro Afris, circuncisio pro circuncisis (ut Paulus Tarsensis loquitur) Roma pro Romanis. Alia est denominatio, quam puto recte παρωνυμίαν dici. frequens orationis est modus: ex quo genere haec sunt, Mars pro bello, Neptunus pro mari, Toga pro pace, Moses pro lege, Christus pro veritate. quo item in genere virtutes & vitia, pro ipsis in quibus illa sunt, appellantur: ut si quis dicat, Iustitiam terris excecssisse,id est,nullos homines esse iustos: salutē pro homine,aut pro re salutari. Huic finitima alia figura est,minus quidē illa ornata,sed tamē nō ignoranda,quū intelligi uolumus aut ex parte totum,ut pro ædificijs cū parietes aut tecta dicimus: aut ex toto partem, uelut quum unam turmam, equitatum: aut ex uno plures,ut Romanus homo: aut quum ex pluribus intelligimus unum,quomodo sæpe loquuntur autores, Nos scripsimus, nos diximus. Hic modus συνεκδοχὴ appellatur, intelleĉtio Latinè.Huc etiam referunt ἀιρωνίαν,quam dissimulationem & illusionem uocat Cicero: uelut quum improbum hominem bonum uirum appellamus. nam contrarium semper intelligitur. Latissimè autem patet ἀιρωνία, nec est difficilis cognitu. nam aut risu,aut rei natura,aut persona significatur. Solet etiam inferi aliquod uerbum, quod ironiam esse subindicet:cuiusmodi sunt, credo,scilicet, aut aliquid simile. Hanc sub permutatione Cornificius lib.4.comprehendit.
units.tr: Cicero calls "changed" and "exchanged" those words in the Orator in which another word is put for the proper word, signifying the same thing, taken from some related thing. Here, says Cicero, the rhetoricians call it hypallage [ὑπαλλαγή], since words are as it were exchanged for words; the grammarians call it metonymy [μετωνυμία], since names are transferred, yet in a different way from the transference discussed earlier. There are many species of this, the first of which they name after the genus, namely hypallage, as I said, or metonymy; Cicero calls it "traduction" and "immutation." For example, Greece for the Greeks, Africa for the Africans, circumcision for the circumcised (as Paul of Tarsus says), Rome for the Romans. Another is denomination, which I think is rightly called paronymy [παρωνυμία]. It is a frequent mode of speech; of this kind are: Mars for war, Neptune for the sea, toga for peace, Moses for the law, Christ for truth. In this kind also virtues and vices are named for the things in which they are, as when someone says "justice has departed from the earth," that is, there are no just men; or "salvation" for a man, or for a saving thing. Close to this is another figure, less ornate indeed but not to be ignored, when we wish something to be understood: from the part the whole, as when we say "walls" or "roofs" for buildings; from the whole a part, as when we say "cavalry" for a single squadron; from one, many, as "a Roman man"; or when from many we understand one, as authors often speak: "we wrote," "we said." This mode is called synecdoche [συνεκδοχή], in Latin "intellection." To this they also refer irony [εἰρωνία], which Cicero calls dissimulation and mockery, as when we call a wicked man "good man," for the contrary is always understood. Irony is very widely extended and is not hard to recognise: it is signified either by laughter, or by the nature of the thing, or by the person. Usually some word is also inserted which hints that it is irony, such as "I suppose," "of course," or something similar. Cornificius in book 4 comprehends this under permutation.

units.la: Aut ea quibus tanquam abutimur.) νατάχρησιν intelligit:quæ fit,quoties uerbo simili & propinquo pro certo & proprio abutimur, non tam eleganter quàm in transferendo: sed etiam si licentius, tamen interdum non imprudenter: ut, quum grādem orationem, minutum animum,uir gregis ipse caper, equum edificare, in arundi-ne ne equitare, ⁊ plcraq; generis eiusdem, dicimus. Aut ea quæ obscuramus.)Hoc de allegorijs & ænigmatibus intelligi potest, quod mihi non improbatur: sed de eis iam dictum est.Potest etiam Cicero loqui de Aristotelico ὑποκορισμῷ, cuius mentionem fecit lib.3. quæ nil aliud esset, quàm diminutio quædam, idq; duobus modis:altero, ut ipse Arist. interpretatur, quæ uel bonum uel malum minus videri facit in uno uerbo:ut pro aureo aurcolum,pro conuicio conuiciolum, pro homine homuncio, pro anu anicula. alio modo,ut opponatur ὑπερβολῇ, & quod illa in cœlum tollit, hæc in terram deprimit, hoc pacto: si quis ausugerit,cum discesssisse dicamus: item, cum qui graviter ulnerauit, tetigisse. Quanquam superlatio tam minuendi quàm augendi caussa fit,ut statim ostendam.
units.tr: Or those things which we use as if by abuse.) He means catachresis: this happens whenever we misuse a word that is similar and related in place of the certain and proper word. It is not as elegant as in transference, but even if it is rather bold, it is sometimes not unskilfully done, as when we say "a grand speech," "a small-minded man," "the goat itself is a herd-master," "to build a horse," "to ride a reed," and many others of this kind. Or those things which we obscure.) This can be understood of allegories and riddles, which I do not reject; but these have already been discussed. Cicero may also be speaking of the Aristotelian hypocorism, which he mentioned in book 3. This would be nothing other than a certain diminution, and this in two ways: in one way, as Aristotle himself explains, which makes something seem either good or bad less in a single word: as "aureolum" for "aureum," "conviciolum" for "convicium," "homuncio" for "homo," "anicula" for "anus." In the other way, it is set against hyperbole, and what the latter raises to heaven, this lowers to the earth, in this manner: if someone has fled, we say he has "departed"; likewise, when someone has wounded severely, we say he has "touched." Although superlation is used both for diminishing and for augmenting, as I shall show immediately.

units.la: Quæ incredibiliter tollimus.) Hæc, ut modò dixi,ὑπερβολὴ dicitur Græcis:nostris autè superlatio,atq; exuberantia & traiectio nominatur. Ea à Cornificio definitur, oratio superans veritate: uel, ut Cicero,modus est quo aliquid incredibiliter tollimus. Qui modus ornatissimus est, latissime que patet, non solum apud poetas, ucrùm etiam oratores. Hoc modo tum augendo aliquid, tum minuendo utimur. ut, Nam quem virtutis gloria cum summa laude ad cœlum extulit, euncundem inimicorum inuidia indignißimè opprefsum,deprimit ad supplicium: niuc cădidior,ocyor euro,sole clarior,testudine tardior, Frigidius glacie pectus amantis erat.
units.tr: Which we raise incredibly.) This, as I have just said, is called hyperbole by the Greeks; but ours call it superlatio, exuberantia, or traiectio. Cornificius defines it as speech exceeding the truth; or, as Cicero says, it is a mode by which we raise something incredibly. This mode is most ornate and extends very widely, not only among the poets but also among the orators. In this way we both augment and diminish something, as: "For the man whom the glory of virtue has raised to heaven with the highest praise, this same man, most unjustly crushed by the envy of enemies, he casts down to punishment"; "whiter than snow, swifter than the wind, clearer than the sun, slower than a tortoise"; "the breast of the lover was colder than ice."

units.la: Quaeq; mirabilius, quàm sermonis confuetudo patitur,ornamus. ) Si modum unü tantum intelligit (ut ego sentio )is erit αὐτονομασία,quam Cornificius pronominationem uocat: quae sicuti cognomine quodă extraneo demonstrat, id quod suo nomine appellari quidem,sed non tam ornatè commodè'ue potest. Ea sumitur tam ad laudem, quàm ad uituperationem:aut ab animo, aut à corpore,aut ab extrancis rebus. Item uel simpliciter tractatur,uel periphrasi, quae rursum uarios habet modos:de quibus,& de aliis tropis,diligenter & perite Valentinus Erythraeus scripsit. Pronominatio igitur est, quum crudelem hominem & tyrannum, Neronem aut Herodem nominamus. item illa,pater patriæ, eloquentiæ parens, philosophorum deus.itē in sacris, panis & linguæ angelorum,mons Dei, siue mons diuinus. item poetam pro Homero aut Vergilio,oratorem pro Demosthene aut Ciceronę,Dominum aut Scruatorē pro Christo. Hoc enim pacto aliquid mirabilius, quàm sermonis consuetudo patitur, ornamus. Sic alios voluit his uerbis significare modos, quibus à cōsuetudine sermonis recedētes, uerba ipsa sim plicia exornamus: tum imaginem, de qua suprà, tum ambigua verba, tum ea quæ lepore quodam condiunt orationem, verba intelligemus: de quibus de Oratore lib. 2. multa eleganter disputatur. Huc etiā illa prosopopœia adnocari potest, cum multis rebus, sensus quasi tribuitur. ut pro Plancio: Quorum honoribus agri, prope dicam, ipsi, montesq; fauerunt. item illa pro Archia, Saxa voce respondent.
units.tr: And we adorn things more wonderfully than the custom of speech allows.) If he means only one mode (as I think), it will be antonomasia, which Cornificius calls pronomination; this, as if by some foreign surname, shows what can indeed be named by its own name, but not so elegantly or fittingly. It is used both for praise and for blame, and from the mind, or the body, or external things. Likewise it is treated either simply or by periphrasis, which again has various modes; on these and on other tropes Valentinus Erythraeus has written diligently and skilfully. Pronomination, then, is when we name a cruel man and tyrant "Nero" or "Herod"; also such phrases as "father of his country," "parent of eloquence," "god of philosophers"; and in sacred usage, "bread and tongue of angels," "mountain of God," or "divine mountain"; also "the poet" for Homer or Virgil, "the orator" for Demosthenes or Cicero, "the Lord" or "the Saviour" for Christ. For in this way we adorn something more wonderfully than the custom of speech allows. Thus he wished to indicate by these words other modes, by which, departing from the usual practice of speech, we adorn even simple words: then the image, of which above; then ambiguous words; then those things which season the speech with a certain charm; we shall understand these as words, about which much is elegantly discussed in book 2 of De Oratore. Here also that prosopopoeia can be referred, when feeling is, as it were, attributed to many things: as in the Pro Plancio, "by whose honours the fields, I may almost say, and the mountains themselves, favoured them"; and likewise that in the Pro Archia, "the rocks answer with a voice."

units.la: C. F. Habeo de simplicibus verbis, nunc de coniunctis quæro.
units.tr: C. F. I have spoken of simple words; now I ask about joined words.

units.la: C. P. Numeri quidam sunt in coiunctione seruandi, cōsecutioq; verborum. Numeros, aures ipsæ metiuntur, ne aut non cōpleas verbis, quod proposueris, aut redundes. Consecutio autem, ne generibus, numeris, temporibus, personis, casibus perturbetur oratio. Nā ut in simplicibus verbis, quod non est Latinum, sic in coniunctis, quod non est consequēs, vituperandum est.
units.tr: C. P. There are certain rhythms to be observed in the joining of words, and the sequence of words. The ears themselves measure the rhythms, lest you either fail to complete with words what you have proposed, or overflow. The sequence, however, is that speech not be disturbed by genders, numbers, tenses, persons, and cases. For just as in simple words what is not Latin is to be blamed, so in joined words what does not follow is to be blamed.

units.la: C.F. Habeo de simplicibus verbis, nunc de coniunctione quæro.) In generibus eloquendi duo spectanda esse dixit: simplicia scilicet verba, & coniuncta. De simplicibus hactenus, nunc de coniunctis quærit, nimirum quæ sint in verborum coniunctione seruanda. Respondet pater: Duo esse, numeros quosdam, & consecutionem. Numerus dicitur, quicquid est, quod sub aurium mensuram aliquam cadit, etiamsi abest à versu (nam id quidem orationis est vitium) qui Græce ῥυθμὸς dicitur. nam μέτρον versum appellant. Aut si breuius definire volumus: Numerus est, breuium & longarum syllabarum collocatio, ex qua pedes constant, qui & ipsi numeri vocantur. Cur autem numeri siue pedes ex poetica oratione in solutã & oratoriam transferantur, ratione reddit Cicero, cum ait: Numeros aures ipsæ metiuntur, ne aut non compleas verbis quod propositueris, aut redundes. quibus verbis significat, neq; prorsus vincta esse pedibus orationem, neq; prorsus solutam, sed quibusdã numeris, ne fugiat, aut erret plusquam par est, sibi ipsam moderari: id quod fit potissimum c ōtinuationis initio & fine, quibus in locis duo aut tres sunt seruandi pedes, ex quib. magna auribus suauitas conciliatur. Initijs hos potissimum probat Cicero, Heroos scilicet, dactylū, anapæstū, et spondæum: item pæana priorem, q primus à poetis dicitur, et creticū, q et amphimacrus. In extremo aut comprehensionis, Heroos alternos, & cū alijs mixtos: deinde pæana posteriorem, q quartus in poeticis est: itemq; creticū, et dichoræum, siue ditrochæū, et dochimū, qui ex bachio et iambo constat: quorum pedum mensurae et interualla sunt ex poeticis discenda. Haec de numeris breuiter: qui plura uolet, uel tertium de Oratore extremum, uel Oratore ad Brutum legat.
units.tr: C. F. I have spoken of simple words; now I ask about the joining of words.) He said that two things are to be considered in the kinds of speaking: simple words and joined words. About simple words so far; now he asks about joined words, namely what is to be observed in the joining of words. The father answers: there are two things, certain rhythms and sequence. Rhythm is called whatever falls under some measure of the ears, even if it is absent from verse (for that is indeed a fault of speech), and which in Greek is called rhythmos; for they call verse metron. Or, if we wish to define it more briefly: rhythm is the arrangement of short and long syllables, from which feet are formed, which are themselves also called numbers. Why numbers or feet are transferred from poetic into prose and oratorical speech, Cicero gives the reason when he says: "The ears themselves measure the numbers, lest you either fail to complete with words what you have proposed, or overflow." By these words he signifies that speech is neither wholly bound by feet nor wholly loose, but moderates itself by certain numbers, lest it run away or wander more than is fitting; which happens especially at the beginning and end of a period, where two or three feet are to be observed, from which great sweetness is won for the ears. At the beginnings Cicero especially approves these: the heroic, that is the dactyl, anapaest, and spondee; likewise the first paean, which is said by the poets to be the first, and the cretic, which is also the amphimacer. At the end of a period, the alternating heroics, and mixed with others; then the second paean, which is the fourth among poetic feet; likewise the cretic, the dichoreus or ditrochaeus, and the dochmius, which consists of a bacchius and an iamb. The measures and intervals of these feet are to be learned from the poets. Of numbers, this is said briefly; whoever wishes more may read the third book of De Oratore, its last part, or the Orator to Brutus.

units.la: Consecutio autem.) Consecutio est uerborum conpositio, qua et Latini sermonis puritas conseruatur, et cocinnitas affingitur quaedam. Puritas constat conseruatis Grammaticae praeceptis, usuque loquendi, qui in bonis autoribus inuenitur: si modo sit ita etiam fundamentum bonorum uerborum, quae latina dicuntur. Nam quasi solum quoddam atque fundamentum est, uerborum usus et copia bonorum. Ergo ut Latine loquamur, non solum uidendum est, ut et uerba efferamus ea, quae nemo iure reprehendat: uerumetiam, ut ea sic et casibus et temporibus, et generi et personis, et numero conformemus, ne quid perturbatum ac discrepans, aut praepostere fit, sine ambiguo uerbo, no nimis longa continuatione uerborum, no discerptis sententiis, no perturbato ordine.
units.tr: Sequence, however.) Sequence is the arrangement of words, by which both the purity of the Latin language is preserved and a certain elegance is added. Purity consists in keeping the precepts of grammar and the usage of speaking found in good authors, if indeed this too is the foundation of good words, which are called Latin. For the usage and abundance of good words is, as it were, a kind of sole and foundation. Therefore, that we may speak Latin, we must see not only that we utter those words which no one could rightly reprehend, but also that we so conform them in cases, tenses, genders, persons, and number, that nothing is disturbed, discordant, or put in wrong order; without an ambiguous word, without an overly long continuation of words, without broken-up sentences, without a disordered arrangement.

units.la: Nam ut in simplicibus uerbis quod non est Latinum.) id est, usu bene loquentium comprobatum, uituperandum est. Sunt enim duo uitia maxime fugienda, solecismus, et barbarismus. Solecismus fit, cum uerbis prioribus consequens uerbum non accommodatur. Barbarismus uero, cum uerbum aliquod uitiosum, aut peregrinum in oratione Latina immisceamus: quae uitia Latinitas refugit, quae sermone purum rum conseruat, atque ab omni uicio remotum.
units.tr: For as in simple words what is not Latin.) that is, not approved by the usage of those who speak well, is to be blamed. For there are two faults above all to be avoided: solecism and barbarism. Solecism occurs when a following word is not fitted to the preceding words. Barbarism occurs when we mix into Latin speech some faulty or foreign word; Latinity shuns these faults, which keeps speech pure and free from every blemish.

units.la: DE GENERIBVS DI- cendi.
units.tr: On the Kinds of Speaking

units.la: Communia autem simplicium, coniunctorumq; sunt, haec quinque quasi lumina: dilucidum, breue, probabile, illustre, suaue.
units.tr: The qualities common to the simple and the combined styles are these five, as it were lights: clarity, brevity, plausibility, brilliance, and charm.

units.la: Communia autem simplicium coniunctorumq;, sunt, haec quinq; quasi lumina.) Lumina appellat, quas Hermogenes ἰδέας, id est formas: Aristoteles autem ἀρετάς, hoc est uirtutes elocutionis nominauit. Cicero etiam σχήματα, quasi dicas orationis gestus quosdā & conformationes, quas Graeci σχηματισμούς. Nec aliud sunt, quàm eloquendi siue dicendi certa genera. neq; enim aliud quicquam est dicere, nisi omnes, aut certe plerasq; aliqua specie illuminare sententias: Eas in hunc modum licet definire, ut sint orationis formae quaedam, quam sermonis consuetudo patitur, illustriores. Vel hoc modo: σχῆμα est, arte aliqua nouata dicendi forma. Horum sunt duo genera, uerborū & rerum, siue sententiarum. Sed inter conformationem uerborum & sententiarum hoc interest, quòd uerborum tollitur, si uerba mutaris: sententiarum permanet, quibuscunque uerbis uti velis. Vsus earum duplex est, tanquā armorum: nam & ad pu-
units.tr: "The qualities common to the simple and the combined styles are these five, as it were lights." He calls them lights, which Hermogenes called ideas [ἰδέας], that is, forms; Aristotle, however, named them virtues of expression [ἀρετάς]. Cicero also calls them figures [σχήματα], as if you were to say certain gestures and shapes of speech, which the Greeks call figurations [σχηματισμούς]. They are nothing other than certain fixed kinds of speaking or expressing. For to speak is nothing other than to illuminate all, or at least most, sentences with some appearance. They may be defined thus: they are certain forms of speech, more brilliant than ordinary usage allows. Or in this way: a figure [σχῆμα] is a form of speaking devised by some art. There are two kinds of these, of words and of things or sentences. But between the shaping of words and the shaping of sentences this difference lies: the figure of words is lost if you change the words, whereas that of sentences remains whatever words you use. Their use is twofold, like that of weapons: they have force both for fighting, and the handling itself lends charm.

units.la: { } ... pugnā uim habent, & ad uenustatē facit ipsa tra- ctatio. Earum nomina, & quasi descriptiones, habet lib. 3. de Orat. itemq; Orator ad Brutū. copiosiorem aut explicationem, præter Quintilianū, Cornificij quartus ad Herennium liber. Exemplorum uero copiam in omni genere, orationes Ciceronis suppeditabunt ei, qui eas diligenter & studiosè inuestigauerit. Sed dicat aliquis, cur cōmunia simplicium & coiunctorum esse dicūtur? Quia propria uidelicet sunt singulis generibus afsignata uerborum & sententiarū ornamenta: & quia unaquæq; dicēdi figura ex his quinq;, quæ enumerat hic noster, sua habet uerborum & coniunctionis genera. Verùm difficilior quæstio exoritur, quomodo uidelicet hæc quinq;, cum illis quatuor, itemq; cum tribus, quæ in 3. de Oratore proponit Cicero, conueniant. Nam sub initium libri: Qui nam igitur, inquit, dicendi modus me- lior, quàm ut Latinè, ut plane, ut ornatè, ut ad id quodcunq; agetur aptè congruenterq; dicamus? Deinde in fine eiusdem libri, & alibi, tres facit dicendi formas: unam plenam, alteram mediam, tertiam tenuem. Quod si etiam septem illa Hermogenis huc conferre uolumus, non erit incommodum. sunt autem hæc: magnum, pulchrum, moratū, ucrū, aptū, uelox, dilucidū. sed nos hæc in hūc cōciliamus modū, uti subiecta descriptio docebit.
units.tr: Their names, and something like descriptions of them, are given in book 3 of De Oratore and likewise in the Orator to Brutus. A fuller explanation, besides Quintilian, is in the fourth book of Cornificius to Herennius. Examples of every kind will be supplied by Cicero's orations to anyone who investigates them diligently and carefully. But someone may ask: why are these qualities said to be common to the simple and the combined? Because, of course, each kind has its own ornaments of words and sentences assigned to it, and because each figure of speaking has its own kinds of words and arrangement drawn from these five which our author lists here. A more difficult question arises, however: how exactly these five agree with those four, and likewise with the three which Cicero sets out in book 3 of De Oratore. For at the beginning of that book he says: "What mode of speaking, then, is better than that we speak Latinly, clearly, ornately, and fittingly and congruently to whatever is being treated?" Then at the end of the same book, and elsewhere, he makes three forms of speaking: one full, a second middle, a third slender. And if we also wish to bring in here those seven of Hermogenes, it will not be inconvenient. They are: grand, beautiful, characterful, true, apt, swift, and clear. We bring these together in the way the descriptive table below will show.

units.la: Dicendi
units.tr: Of the Kinds of Speaking

units.la: Dicendi genera omnia Ciceronis & Hermogenis ad tria genera accommodata: Plenum, Ornatum Illustre Magnum Medium, Aptum Probabile Suaue Pulchrum Moratum Verum Tenue, Latinum Planum Dilucidum Breue Velox dicitur.
units.tr: All the kinds of speaking of Cicero and Hermogenes are fitted to three kinds. Full: Ornate, Brilliant, Great. Middle: Apt, Plausible, Charming, Beautiful, Characterful, True. Slender: Latinate, Plain, Clear, Brief, Swift.

units.la: Neq; tamen, quòd ita genera distiximus, & inter se comparauimus, conciliauimusq;, existimandum est, nō posse miscéri, si res ista poscat. Quinetiam quædam ita communia omnium, & singulorum generum sunt, ut sine illis nulla possit esse laudabilis oratio: cuiusmodi sunt, latinum, planum, siue dilucidum, & probabile.
units.tr: Nor should it be thought, because we have distinguished the kinds in this way, compared them and reconciled them, that they cannot be mixed when the matter demands it. Indeed, some qualities are so common to all kinds, and to each single kind, that no speech can be praiseworthy without them: such are Latinity, plainness or clarity, and plausibility.

units.la: Dilucidum fit, usitatis uerbis, pro prijs, dispositis, aut circumscriptione conclusa, aut intermissione, aut concisi- one uerborum.
units.tr: Clarity is achieved by ordinary words used in their proper sense, by arrangement, by a closed circumlocution, by pausing, or by the breaking up of words.

units.la: Dilucidum fit.) Iam lumina illa dicendi proposita explicare aggreditur, incipitq; à dilucido genere: & merito. Nam prima uirtus elocutionis est, & orationis, ut sit plana & dilucida. Cuius rei signum est, quòd nisi oratio sit clara & aperta, finem suum non assequitur, ut Aristoteles lib. 3. ait: Idcirco rectè inquit Cicero lib. 3. neq; enim conamur docere eum dicere, qui loqui nesciat: nec sperare, qui Latinè non possit, hunc ornatè esse dicturum: neq; uero, qui non dicat quod intelligamus, hunc posse quod admiremur dicere. Sed claritas orationis ex propriis usitatisq; uerbis maximè constat. Nam quæ transferuntur, propriis obscuriora esse necesse est: & inusitata uerba non tam facilè, quam usitata & quotidiana, intelliguntur.
units.tr: "Clarity is achieved." Now he sets about explaining those ornaments of speech that have been proposed, and he begins with the clear style, and rightly so. For the first virtue of style and of speech is that it be plain and clear. A sign of this is that unless speech is clear and open, it does not attain its end, as Aristotle says in book 3. Hence Cicero rightly says in book 3: "For we do not undertake to teach someone to speak who does not know how to talk, nor do we expect that one who cannot speak Latin will speak with ornament; nor indeed can one who does not say what we understand say what we admire." But clarity of speech depends chiefly on proper and ordinary words. For words that are used figuratively must necessarily be less clear than proper ones, and unusual words are not understood as easily as common and everyday ones.

units.la: Dispositis, aut circumscriptione conclusa, aut intermissione, aut concisione uerborum.) De collocatione coniunctioneq; uerborum loquitur, aut potius innuit: de qua proximè præcipere cœperat. Idcirco dicit, Dispositis, scilicet uerbis. Nā disponere nihil aliud est, quàm in oratione uerba collocare. Huius duæ sunt uirtutes: collocationis enim primum est, componere & struere verba sic, ut nec ue asper eorum concursus, nec ue hiulcus sit, sed quodammodo coagmentatus & lenis, ex quo iuncta fiat oratio, & æquabiliter fluens: & hæc proprie iunctura nominatur. Altera uirtus est, ut circumscriptione conclusa sit, aut intermissione, aut conclusione uerborum: quæ uirtus tota in ratione periodorum continetur. Est enim elocutio duplex, ut Aristoteles quoque in tertio Rhet. tradit: uel tracta ac pendens, quæ copulatione fit una, cuiusmodi Herodotus in Historia utitur. Voco autem tractam ac pendentem elocutionem, quæ nullum extra finem habet, nisi res quæ exponitur, ad finem peruenerit: quæ sane est iniucunda, quoniam infinitè fertur. Altera autem ambitu comprehensa est, quæ periodis constat. Periodum voco orationem, quæ principium & finem ex se habet: & magnitudinem, quæ facile perlustrari possit.
