Huiusmodi autem oratio suavis est, & facile percipi potest: suavis, & quia ei contraria est quæ infinitè fertur, & quia facilius intelligitur. Facile autem percipitur, quia memoriæ facile mandari potest. Quod accidit, quia numeros habet in periodis, qui rem maximè aptâ faciunt ad recordandum. Periodi partes, si materiè species, sunt quæ κῶλα & κόμματα Græci: nos illa, incisa siue articulos: hæc, membra vocamus: ut periodum tum ambitum, tum circuitum, tum comprehensionem, tum complexionem ucrborum,tum cotinuationem, tum circunfcriptionem,aut etiam conuersionem dicimus. Omnis enim oratio in comprehensiones, in membra & incifa distribuitur.Ex quo sequitur,incifum, mebri partē esse:& membrū,cotinuationis.Incifum est,sensus nō expleto numero cōclufus.Membrū, sensus numeris cōclufus.Cōprehenfio est cōtinua tio uerborū,ita circūscripta atq; conclusa, ut numerofe cadat,perfeƈta sententia.Incifum solet sex aut octo syllabis terminari:membrū aut decē & octo,aut paulo plurib.aut pauciorib.Quæ membra pari fere syllabarum numero constant, comparia nominantur.Hoc non de cnumeratione nostra fiet:nam id quidem puerile est, nisi initio discendi fiat:sed affert usus & exercitatio facultatis,ut animi quodam sensu & aurium par membrū superiori referre possimus.hoc modo:In præ lio mortem pater oppetebat, domi filius nuptias comparabat. Interdum non sunt paria membra circuitus:sed aut breuiora extremaprimis,aut lōgiora. quod melius & iucundius esse censet Cicero de Orat.3. Constat autem ille ambitus & plena cōprehenfio ē quatuor fere partibus, quæ membra dicimus, quasi hexametrorū instar uersuum, ut & aures impleat,& ne breuior fit quàm satis est,neq; longior.Quanquā utrunq; nonnunquam,
units.tr: "By arrangement, by a closed circumlocution, by pausing, or by the cutting up of words." He speaks, or rather hints, about the placing and joining of words, which he had just begun to teach. Hence he says "by arrangement", namely of words. For to arrange is nothing other than to place words in speech. This has two virtues. The first virtue of placement is to compose and build words so that their collision is neither harsh nor gaping, but in some way fitted together and smooth, from which speech is made continuous and flows evenly; this is properly called juncture. The other virtue is that speech be closed by a circumlocution, or by pausing, or by the closing of words; and this whole virtue is contained in the structure of periods. For there are two kinds of style, as Aristotle also teaches in the third book of the Rhetoric: one loose and hanging, which proceeds by continual linking, such as Herodotus uses in his History. I call a loose and hanging style one which has no end beyond the point at which the matter being set out reaches its conclusion; this is indeed unpleasant, since it runs on without limit. The other is enclosed within a circuit, and consists of periods. I call a period a speech which has its beginning and end within itself, and a magnitude that can easily be taken in at a glance. Such speech is pleasant and can be easily grasped: pleasant, both because it is the opposite of that which runs on without limit, and because it is more easily understood. It is grasped easily because it can be readily committed to memory. This happens because periods have numbers (rhythm), which make the matter very fit for remembering. The parts of a period, if we consider the kinds of its matter, are what the Greeks call κῶλα [kōla] and κόμματα [kommata]; we call them incisa or articuli (cola and commata), and membra (members). So we call a period by the names ambitus, circuitus, comprehensio, complexio verborum, continuatio, circumscriptio, or even conversio. For all speech is divided into comprehensiones, membra and incisa. From this it follows that the incisum is part of the membrum, and the membrum part of the continuatio. An incisum is a meaning concluded without a complete number of syllables; a membrum is a meaning concluded with a rhythmic number; a comprehensio is a continuous linking of words, so circumscribed and closed that it falls with a rhythm and forms a complete sentence. An incisum usually ends in six or eight syllables; a membrum in eighteen, or a little more or fewer. Members that have nearly equal numbers of syllables are called paired (comparia). This is not to be done by counting, for that is indeed childish unless it is done at the start of learning; but practice and exercise bring the skill, so that by a certain sense of mind and ear we can match a member to the preceding one, as in this example: "In battle the father was meeting death, at home the son was preparing a wedding." Sometimes the members of a circuit are not equal, but the last are either shorter than the first, or longer. Cicero thinks this better and more pleasing, in De Oratore 3. That circuit and full comprehension consists of about four parts, which we call members, like the lines of hexameter verses, so that it fills the ears, and is neither shorter than is sufficient nor longer. Yet both of these sometimes,

units.la: uel potius sæpe accidit, ut aut citius insistendum fit, aut longius procedendum: ne breuitas defraudasse aures uideatur, ne ue longitudo obtudisse. cuiusmodi est illa: Si quid est in me ingenij, iudices, quod sentio quàm sit exiguum: aut si qua exercitatio dicendi, in qua me non inficior mediocriter esse uersatum: aut si huiusce rei ratio aliqua ab optimarum artium studijs & disciplina profesta, à qua ego nullum confiteor ætatis meæ tempus abhorruisse: earum rerum omnium uel in primis hic A. Licinius fructum à me repetere, prope suo iure debet. Hæc igitur, ut dixi, perfecta est & plena comprehensio. illa uerò quæ duobus membris constat, breuissima dicitur: quoniam ea nulla potest esse breuior, ut Cicero in Oratore testatur. ut, Incurristi amens in columnas, it in alienos infanus infanifti. item, Missos faciant patronos, prodeant ipsi. Hoc autem, membratim dicere appellat Cicero: & membrum, Cornificius ad Heren. lib. 4. Nam quod quidam aiunt, posse ex uno membro constare periodum, non plus uerum est, quàm si quis dicat, brachium aut caput auulsum à corpore, homine uel corpus hominis esse. quod si fiat ut in oratione aliqua membrum solitarium esseratur: iam non periodus, sed mutilatum membrum nominabitur. Inter illam perfectam, & hanc bimembrem, quam ἀντιθέτον uocant Græci, interest tertia, quæ τρίωλος dicitur. Ea tribus membris perficitur. cuiusmodi est illa: Nec Reip. consuluisti, nec amicis profuisti, nec inimicis restitisti. item illa, quæ Brutum dialogum exorsus est: Quum e Cilicia Rhodum uenissem, & eo mihi de Q. Hortensij morte esset allatū, opinione omnium maiore animo cæpi dolorem. Incisa vero, in ipsa periodo nullum certū numerū habet. Sunt enim modo plura, modo pauciora in singulis membris. Sed aliquando ut membratim, sic etiā incisim dicimus, ut initio secundæ in Catilinā: Abijt, excessit, evasit, erupit. item illa pro Cluētio: Vt eam nō pudor, nō pudicitia, nō pietas, nō macula familiæ, nō hominū fama, nō filij dolor, nō filiæ mœror, à cupiditate revocaret. item illa: Quæ sperem parentis, memoriā nominis, subsidium generis, hæredem familiæ, designatum Reip. ciuē sustulisset. Hoc genus à Cornificio articulus nominatur. Debent igitur ista in oratione variari, ut modo incisim, modo membratim dicamus: nunc illa pleniore periodo, quæ τετράκωλος dicitur, aliàs breuiore utendū erit: ut delectatio quæratur, uitetur satietas: ita tamen, ut breuiora illa, excipiatur lōgioribus: quæ si cōstitutū modū excesserint, & quātū uolui uno spiritu possit proferantur, iā nō periodi, sed περιοδικαὶ complexiones uocabūtur, quas ob id etiā Græci πνεύματα uocāt, cuiusmodi plures sunt in Cicerone.
units.tr: or rather often, it happens that one must either dwell more briefly, or proceed at greater length, lest brevity seem to have cheated the ears, or length to have dulled them. Such is that passage: "If there is any talent in me, judges, which I feel to be so small; or if any practice in speaking, in which I do not deny that I have been moderately engaged; or if any reasoning in this matter derived from the study and discipline of the best arts, from which I confess that no time of my life has shrunk: of all these things, A. Licinius here ought, almost by his own right, to claim the fruit from me above all." This, then, as I said, is a perfect and full comprehension. But that which consists of two members is called very short, since none can be shorter, as Cicero attests in the Orator. For example: "You ran in madness into the pillars; you went among others, mad, you went mad." Likewise: "Let them dismiss the advocates; let them come forward themselves." Cicero calls this way of speaking membratim, and Cornificius in Ad Herennium book 4 calls the members membrum. For what some say, that a period can consist of one member, is no more true than if someone said that an arm or head torn from the body is a man, or the body of a man. If it happens that in some speech a solitary member is produced, then it is no longer called a period but a mutilated member. Between the full period and this two-membered one, which the Greeks call ἀντιθέτον [antithetos], there lies a third, which is called τρίκωλος [trikōlos]. It is made up of three members, as in this example: "You have neither consulted the Republic, nor profited your friends, nor resisted your enemies." Also that which begins the dialogue Brutus: "When I had come from Cilicia to Rhodes, and the news of the death of Q. Hortensius had been brought to me, I began to grieve with greater courage than everyone's expectation." But the incisum, in the period itself, has no fixed number: for there are sometimes more, sometimes fewer, in the individual members. But sometimes we speak not only membratim but also incisim, as at the beginning of the second Catilinarian: "He went away, he departed, he escaped, he burst out." Likewise that in Pro Cluentio: "That neither shame, nor chastity, nor piety, nor the stain on the family, nor the reputation of men, nor the grief of a son, nor the mourning of a daughter, called him back from desire." Likewise: "Who had removed the hope of a parent, the memory of a name, the support of a family, the heir of a household, a citizen designated for the Republic." Cornificius calls this kind articulus. Therefore these things must be varied in speech, so that we sometimes speak incisim and sometimes membratim; now a fuller period, which is called τετράκωλος [tetrakōlos], must be used, at other times a shorter one, so that pleasure is sought and satiety avoided; yet in such a way that the shorter ones are followed by longer ones. If these exceed the fixed measure, and are uttered in as much as can be delivered in one breath, they will no longer be called periods but περιοδικαὶ complexiones [periodikai complexiones], periodic combinations; for this reason the Greeks also call them πνεύματα [pneumata], breaths, of which there are many in Cicero.

units.la: Obscurum autem aut longitudi‐ ne, aut contractione orationis, aut ambiguitate, aut inflexione atq; im‐ mutatione uerborum.
units.tr: Obscure speech arises either from length, or from compression of expression, or from ambiguity, or from the inflection and alteration of words.

units.la: Obscurum autem. ) Quòd Cicero de obscuro genere dicendi præcipiat, id non facit quòd obscu‐ ritatem in oratione probet (est enim prima uir‐ tus orationis, ut antè diximus, diluciditas) sed ut, quid contrarium diluciditati sit, doceat: ut non so‐ lum quid sequendum, uerùm etiam quid uitandũ sit, intelligamus. Hinc est, quòd in luminum enu‐ meratione obscurum hoc genus non posuit. Qua‐ tuor igitur sunt, quæ orationem obscuram faciunt: Si periodi sint nimis longæ: si nimis breues (quas mutilas uocat Arist. lib. 3. nam quæ longæ sunt, officiunt memoriæ: quæ mutilæ & contractæ, intel‐ligentiæ: sequitur igitur, ut ambæ sint obscuræ.) Reliqua duo sunt, ambiguitas, inflexioq; uerbo‐ rum. Ambiguitas, aut in uerbis ipsis, quæ Græci ὁμώνυμα, nos ambigua appellamus, ut ὁμωνυμίαν ambiguitatem: ut genus, species, canis, pater. aut compositione: ut, Vidi hominem leonem sustinê‐ tem. Hæc autem ambigua melius norunt, qui Dia‐ lectici uocantur. Inflexio uerborum, atq; immuta‐ tio, de qua suprà in tractatione uerborũ diximus. Sunt enim omnia modificata & inflexa, proprijs & et usitatis obscuriora. Itaq;, ut cõcludamus, Lõgitudo & contractio, circumscriptioni conclusæ: inflexio immutatioq; uerborũ, usitatis uerbis & proprijs: ambiguitas partim dispositioni, partim etiam proprietati uerborum opponitur. Ad obscurum etiam dicendi genus pertinet Synchysis seu hyperbaton, aliaq; nonnulla, de quibus Grammatici abunde præcipiunt.
units.tr: "Obscure speech." When Cicero prescribes an obscure kind of speaking, he does not do so because he approves of obscurity in speech (for clarity is, as I said before, the first virtue of speech), but so that we may learn what is contrary to clarity, and understand not only what is to be followed but also what is to be avoided. Hence in his enumeration of the ornaments of style he did not list this obscure kind. There are therefore four things that make speech obscure: periods that are too long, and periods that are too short (which Aristotle in book 3 calls "mutilated"). For long periods burden the memory, while mutilated and contracted ones burden the understanding; it follows that both are obscure. The remaining two are ambiguity and the inflection of words. Ambiguity lies either in the words themselves, which the Greeks call ὁμώνυμα (homonyms) and we call ambiguous words, as the Greeks call the ambiguity ὁμωνυμίαν; examples are "kind", "appearance", "dog" (or "star"), "father". Or it lies in the composition, as in "I saw a man holding a lion." Those who are called dialecticians know these ambiguities best. The inflection and alteration of words we discussed above in the treatment of words: for all such things are modified and inflected, and so are more obscure than proper and ordinary words. To conclude, then: length and compression are opposed to a closed and circumscribed form; inflection and alteration of words are opposed to ordinary and proper words; ambiguity is opposed partly to arrangement and partly to the propriety of words. To the obscure kind of speaking also belong synchysis or hyperbaton, and some other devices, about which the grammarians give ample instruction.

units.la: Breuitas autem conficitur simpli- cibus uerbis, semel unaquaq; re di- cenda: nulli rei, nisi ut dilucide dicas, seruiendo.
units.tr: Brevity is achieved with simple words, with each thing said once, and with nothing done except to speak clearly.

units.la: Breuitas autem, ) De secundo genere dicendi, quod breue nominauit, explicat. Hæc autem breuitas non est illa contractio, de qua in obscuro genere dictum est, quæ συντομία dicitur: sed ea quæ βραχύτητα, & βραχυλογίαν Graeci dicunt. illa enim uiciofa est, hæc laudabilis. Est enim eiusdem oratoris, & breuiter & splendide dicere. hanc breuitatem Cornificius lib. 4. uidetur definire. Breuitas, inquit, est oratio, ipsis tantummodo uerbis necessarijs expedita. Antonius uero apud Ciceronem de Orat. lib. 2. de Crassi breuitate loquens: Breuis, inquit, est L. Crassi oratio: si tamen est breuitas, quum tantum uerborum est, quantum necesse est. Hæc tribus efficitur: uerbis, tractatione, & perspicuitate. Verba esse debent simplicia, non coniunctione facta, neque idem significatia quae συνώνυμα uocant: ut, sceleratus, non confsceleratus: abijt, non abijt, excessit, euasit, erupit. Tractatio uero breuitas comparatur, uitandis repetitionibus, commorationibus, circuitionibus, et id genus illustribus figuris, quae breuitati contrariae sunt, et ad illustre illud genus conficiendum adhibentur. Reliqua ex dilucidi generis praeceptis sumenda sunt, atque ex ijs quae de breuitate narrationis traduntur.
units.tr: Brevity. He explains the second kind of style, which he called brief. This brevity is not that contraction discussed under the obscure kind, which is called συντομία, but the one the Greeks call βραχύτητα and βραχυλογίαν. The former is faulty, the latter praiseworthy; for it is the mark of the same orator to speak both briefly and splendidly. Cornificius, in book 4, seems to define this brevity: "Brevity," he says, "is speech made expeditious by the necessary words alone." Antonius, however, in Cicero's De Oratore book 2, speaking of Crassus's brevity, says: "The speech of L. Crassus is brief; yet there is brevity only when there are as many words as are necessary." This brevity is produced by three things: the words, the treatment, and clarity. The words should be simple, not compounded, and not synonyms (συνώνυμα): for example, "wicked" rather than "thoroughly wicked"; "he went away" rather than "he departed", "he withdrew", "he escaped", "he burst out". Brevity of treatment is achieved by avoiding repetitions, delays, circumlocutions, and the like illustrious figures, which are contrary to brevity and are used to produce the illustrious kind. The rest is to be taken from the precepts of the clear kind, and from what is handed down about brevity in narration.

units.la: Probabile autem genus est orationis, si non nimis est comptum, atque expolitu, si est autoritas & pondus in uerbis, si sententiae uel graues uel aptae opinionib. hominum, & moribus.
units.tr: The probable kind of speech is one that is not overly adorned or polished, that has authority and weight in its words, and whose sentiments are either weighty or suited to the opinions and customs of men.

units.la: Probabile autem genus. ) Quid sit probabile, alibi docuimus. Sed hic tria sunt consideranda: ornatus, uerba, sententiae. Ornatus debet esse simplex, parcus, et rarus. Simplex est enim ueritatis oratio: et quae nimis compta sunt, suspicione non carent: ut mulier nimis ornata, et fuco illita, parum proba putatur. Vitandus est igitur in hoc genere, nimius ille nitor et splendor, qualis est sophistarum, qui nihil sine aliquo insigni ornatu tu proferunt: quos Cicero in Oratore reprehendit. Sunt enim ineptis pictoribus similes, qui sine umbris, illustrium tantum colorum uarietate, tabulâ exornant: quæ ob id improbatur maximè, quod nimia luce & splendore oculos perstringat. Verba autem eligenda sunt, quæ pondus habent, & autoritatem. Pondus, non in sono, sed in uerbi significatione spectatur: ut si res ueras, uel uerisimiles significent. Autoritas aut in eo cernitur, si uerbum sit antiquum, ut patrare, prosapia, clepere: aut rei magnæ. Sunt uerò res magnæ aut natura, ut cœlestia, ut diuina, ut quæ in obscuritate naturæ uersantur: aut usu, ut charitate, amore, honestate, siue uirtute: aut si uerbum sit alicuius magni & excellentis autoris, ut Homeri, Platonis, Virgilij, Ciceronis. Sententiæ denique (quod tertium fuit in hoc genere spectandum) erunt graues, quæ ex rerum & uerborum gravitate constabunt: erunt aptæ opinionibus & moribus hominum. de quibus in probabilibus suprà dictum est, & infrà in verisimilibus dicetur. Hoc genus sententiarum graviū & probabilium non sectantur sophistæ, qui quanquam eosdem flores adhibeant, quos adhibet Orator in causis, tamen id & apertius faciunt, & crebrius, quàm il-li: sententias que magis concinnas exquirunt, quàm probabiles.
units.tr: Probable kind. We have explained elsewhere what is probable. Here, however, three things must be considered: ornament, words, and sentiments. Ornament should be simple, sparing, and rare. It should be simple, for the speech of truth is simple, and things that are overly adorned do not escape suspicion: a woman too much dressed up and smeared with paint is thought not very honest. So in this kind one must avoid that excessive polish and splendour, such as belongs to the sophists, who produce nothing without some striking ornament, and which Cicero criticises in the Orator. For they are like clumsy painters, who decorate a panel without shadows, using only a variety of bright colours; and this is disapproved above all because its excessive light and brilliance dazzles the eyes. The words to be chosen are those that have weight and authority. Weight is judged not by sound but by the meaning of the word, namely whether it signifies true or plausible things. Authority lies either in the word being old, such as "to accomplish", "lineage", "to steal" (patrare, prosapia, clepere), or in the thing being great. Great things are so either by nature, such as heavenly and divine things, and those that lie in the obscurity of nature; or by use, such as charity, love, honour, or virtue; or when the word belongs to some great and excellent author, such as Homer, Plato, Virgil, or Cicero. Finally, the sentiments (the third thing to be considered in this kind) will be weighty, arising from the weight of things and words; they will be suited to the opinions and customs of men, as was said above under probables and will be said below under verisimilar. The sophists do not pursue this kind of weighty and probable sentiment: although they use the same flowers the orator uses in causes, they do so more openly and more often than he does, and they seek sentiments that are more elegant than probable.

units.la: Illustris autem oratio est,si & uer-ba grauitate delecta ponuntur, ac translata, & superlata, & ad nomen adiuncta,& duplicata, & idem significatia,atq; ab ipsa actione atq; imitatione rerum non abhorrentia. Est enim hæc pars orationis, quæ rem constituat pene ante oculos.ıs enim maxime sensus attingitur: sed cæteri tamen, & maxime mens ipsa moueri potest. Sed quæ dicta sunt de oratione dilucida, cadunt in hanc illustrem omnia.est enim plus aliquanto illustre, quàm illud dilucidum. altero fit, ut intelligamus: altero uerò, ut uidere uideamur.
units.tr: Illustrious speech is that in which the words are chosen for their weight, and are transferred, superlative, and added to nouns, and doubled, and of the same meaning, and not out of keeping with the very action and imitation of things. For this is the part of speech that sets a thing almost before the eyes. It touches the senses most, but the other faculties, and especially the mind itself, can also be moved. All that has been said about clear speech falls under this illustrious kind, for it is somewhat more illustrious than the clear. In the one case it happens that we understand; in the other, that we seem to see.

units.la: Illustris autem oratio est.) Illustre genus di-cendi est,id quod alibi plenum & graue dicitur, contrarium breuitati:quamobrem quæ à breuitate remota sunt,cadunt in hoc genus omnia. quod sic paucis definiri potest: Illustris oratio est, quæ constat ex uerborum grauium & illustrium ma-gna & ornata constructione. In hoc genere tria præcepta dat Ciccro, quorum unum ad uerba lecta & modificata, alterum ad ornamenta, tertiũ ad compositionem pertinet. Electio uerborum grauium et sonantium est: modus in translatis, superlatis, siue incredibiliter sublatis: item in ἐπι-θέτοις, quæ ad nomen adiuncta hic uocat: et in coniunctis uerbis, quæ duplicata dicit: in idem significatibus, quæ συνώνυμα diximus appellari: et in ijs quæ imitatione fiunt, de quib. omnib. antea explicatum est. Secundum præceptum est, quod in quodam genere ornamentorum uersatur. id autè Græci ὑποτύπωσιν, et interdū ἐνάργειαν uocant: nos evidentiam, et illustrationem, et demonstrationem, et illustrem explanationem, et subiectionem ante oculos. Sic enim Cicero ipse li. 3. de Orat. Illustris explanatio, inquit, rerum quæ quasi geruntur, sub aspectu pene subiectio, quæ et in exponenda re plurimum valet: et ad illustrandum id quod exponitur, et ad amplificandum, ut ijs qui audierint, illud quod augebimus, quantum efficere oratio poterit, tantum esse videatur. Breuius autem definiuit Cornificius: Demonstratio est, inquit, cum ita res verbis exprimitur, ut geri negocium, et res ante oculos esse videatur. Exempla cum ex eodem libro Cornificij peti possunt, tum vel maximè ex ipsis Ciceronis orationibus. in hoc genus cõgruunt omnia illa ornamenta, quæ à breuitate remouimus: cuiusmodi sunt, circuitio, descriptio, expolitio, frequentatio, commoratio, confirmatio, & id genus alia, quibus augetur oratio. Tertium præceptum totum in compositione, siue constructione uerborum consumitur: in quo seruanda erunt ea præcepta, quæ in dilucido genere tradita sunt, ubi rationes periodorum complexi sumus. Nam dilucidum & illustre, in eo tantū differūt, quantū minor lux à maiore, matutinū tempus à meridiano distinguitur: alterū facit, ut et intelligamus, quod est animi & mētis: alterum ut uidere & sentire uideamur, quod est oculorum, quorum acerrimus sensus est.
units.tr: Illustrious speech. The illustrious kind of speaking is what elsewhere is called full and grave, and it is the opposite of brevity; so everything remote from brevity falls into this kind. It can be briefly defined thus: illustrious speech is that which consists of a grand and ornate construction of weighty and striking words. In this kind Cicero gives three precepts: one concerns chosen and modified words, another ornaments, a third composition. The choice of words is that they be weighty and sonorous; the measure lies in transferred words, superlatives, or words raised beyond belief; likewise in epithets (ἐπιθέτοις), which here he calls words added to a noun; in joined words, which he calls doubled; in words of the same meaning, which we said are called synonyms; and in those formed by imitation, all of which has been explained before. The second precept concerns a certain class of ornaments. The Greeks call this ὑποτύπωσιν and sometimes ἐνάργειαν; we call it evidence, illustration, demonstration, illustrious explanation, or placing before the eyes. Cicero himself says so in book 3 of De Oratore: "An illustrious explanation of things as though they were being done, almost a placing under the eyes, which is of great value both in setting forth the matter, in illustrating what is set forth, and in amplifying it, so that to those who have heard, what we enlarge may seem as great as speech can make it." Cornificius defined it more briefly: "Demonstration," he says, "is when a thing is so expressed in words that the business seems to be carried on and the thing seems to be before the eyes." Examples may be taken both from the same book of Cornificius and above all from Cicero's own speeches. All those ornaments that we removed from brevity belong to this kind: circumlocution, description, polishing, repetition, delay, confirmation, and other such things by which speech is enlarged. The third precept is wholly concerned with the composition, or construction, of words; in it the rules must be kept that were handed down for the clear kind, where we discussed the principles of periods. For the clear and the illustrious differ only as much as a lesser light differs from a greater, or morning from midday: the one makes us understand, which belongs to the mind and intellect; the other makes us seem to see and feel, which belongs to the eyes, whose sense is the keenest.

units.la: Suaue autem genus erit dicendi, primùm elegantia & iucunditate uerborum sonantium & lenium: deinde coniunctione, quæ neque asperos habeat concursus, neque disiunctos atque hiantes: & sit circumscripta non longo anfractu, sed ad spiritum uocis apto: habeatque similitudinem æqualitatemque uerborum, tum ex contrariis sumpta uerbis, crebra crebris, paria paribus respondeant: relata que ad idem uerbum, & geminata, atque duplicata, uel etiam sæpius iterata ponantur: constructioque uerborum tum coniunctionibus copuletur, tum dissolutionibus relaxetur.
units.tr: The smooth style of speaking will be, first, one of elegance and pleasantness in words that are sonorous and gentle; second, one of construction that avoids harsh collisions of sounds, as well as disjointed and gaping ones; and its periods should be bounded not by a long winding turn but by one suited to the breath of the voice. It should have a likeness and evenness of words: contrasting words are taken and set in frequent pairs, like with like, matching with matching; words that refer to the same term are placed repeated, doubled, or even iterated more often; and the construction of words is joined together by conjunctions at one time and loosened by asyndeton at another.

units.la: Suaue autē genus. ) Suaue dicitur, quod uoluptate aliqua sensus afficit, atq; titillat iucunditate. In hoc dicendi genere, quinq; seruanda præcipit: quorū primū est in uerbis, secundū in coniunctione uerborū, tertiū in periodis & mēbris, quartū in figuris, quintū in sententijs. Verba elegātia primum esse debent, quæ nitida ante uocauit. Deinde cōsonantia, de quib. ante dictum est: sed addenda sunt etiam illa lenia, in quibus iucunditas inest. Coniunctio sequitur, in qua, uti etiā supra diximus, asperi concursus uitandi sunt, qui fiunt asperis & crebris cōsonantibus literis: ut, Tum ferri rigor: & ferrę stridulus usus. item, ô Tite tute Tati tibi tanta tyranne tulisti: itē quæ uastā & hiantem oratione reddunt, quod accidet ob crebras uocaliū cōcursiones: ut in illo, Baccæ æneæ amœnissimæ impendebāt. itē principiū Ciceronis epistolę primæ ad Lentulū, Ego omni officio, ac potius pietate: ut quidā uolūt. sed eo loco uiciosum nō est, sed magna cum uenustate positū: est enim principiū epistolæ, in qua cōpositiōis negligētia laudatur. Suauia uero sunt uerba, in quib. a, & o, itēq; diphthōgi crebræ sunt, modò ne concurrant uastius.
units.tr: The smooth kind. Something is called smooth when it affects the senses with a certain pleasure and tickles them with delight. In this kind of speaking he prescribes five things to be observed: the first concerns words, the second the joining of words, the third periods and clauses, the fourth figures, and the fifth thoughts. The words should first be elegant, which he earlier called polished. Next, they should be consonant, as was said before; but those gentle words in which pleasantness lies must also be added. Then comes the joining, in which, as we also said above, harsh collisions must be avoided, those that arise from harsh and frequent consonants, as in Then the stiffness of iron, and the grating use of iron. Likewise, O Titus, you yourself, tyrant, have brought upon yourself such great things as Tatius did. Likewise those that make the speech gaping and wide, which happens because of frequent meetings of vowels, as in that line, Bronze berries, most lovely, hung there. Likewise the opening of Cicero's first letter to Lentulus, I, with all duty, or rather with piety, as some would have it. But in that place it is not a fault; it is placed with great charm, for it is the opening of a letter, in which carelessness of composition is praised. Words are smooth when they contain frequent a's and o's and also diphthongs, provided they do not run together too widely.

units.la: Aulai in medio libabant pocula Bacchi,
units.tr: In the middle of the hall they poured libations of Bacchus's wine,

units.la: sonantia sunt. illa uero lenia, Et secum sola sicca fpaciatur arena.
units.tr: these are sonorous. Those, however, are gentle: "And the dry sand walks alone by itself."

units.la: De periodo & membris diximus antea, eam que aures implet, & ad spiritum uocis apta fit, suauem esse: longam autem & mutilam, infuauem. Iam de figuris, quibus suauitas quaedam conciliatur, dicendum est. Fiunt huiusmodi figurae, genere uerborum quodam: in quibus ea sunt, quae similitudinem aut aequalitatem habet. ea proprio nomine similiter cadentia, & similiter definentia dicuntur. Prioris exemplum est: Hominem laudas, egentem uirtutis, abundantem felicitatis. Posterioris uero: Turpiter audes facere, nequiter studes dicere. Item, crebra crebris, & paria paribus relata, contraria, aut etiam similia & dissimilia. Crebra dicuntur, quum singula singulis referuntur: paria uero, quum aliquot uerbis caesa oratione propositis, totidem illis redduntur pari ratione. De hoc genere eum loqui arbitror de Orat. li. 3. in ornamentis uerborum recensendis, quum ait: Et quod de singulis rebus propositis ductum refertur ad singula. Nam quae ibidem paribus paria referri ait, existimo de his intelligi debere, quae comparia appellauit Cornificius li. 4. quum membra constent ex pari fere numero syllabarum. Horum autem exemplum est pulcherrimum in Miloniana. Incipit autem a crebris, & mox ad paria delabitur, rurfumq; tanquam in orbem ad crebra rereuertitur, & cœptum ornatū absoluit: Est enim, iudices, hæc non scripta, sed nata lex: quā non didicimus, accepimus, legimus: uerū ex natura ipsa arripuimus, hausimus, expressimus: ad quam non docti, sed facti: non instituti, sed imbuti sumus. Paria tantum, illa in Rosciana: Iis de rebus tantis tamq; atrocibus, neq; satis me commodè dicere, neq; satis grauiter conqueri, neq; satis libere uociferari posse intelligo. Nam commoditati ingenium, grauitati ætas, libertati tempora sunt impedimento. Illa uero in Catilina 2. crebra crebris primùm, deinde paribus paria, magna cum ui & copia contraria referūtur, hoc modo: Ex hac enim parte pudor pugnat, illinc petulantia, hinc pudicitia: illinc stuprū, hinc fides: illinc fraudatio, hinc pietas: illinc scelus, hinc constantia: illinc furor, hinc honestas: illinc turpitudo, hinc continentia: illinc libido, deniq; æquitas, temperātia, fortitudo, pietas, virtutes omnes certant cum iniquitate, cum luxuria, cum ignauia, cum temeritate, cum uitiis omnibus. In his exemplis tū contraria contrariis, tum etiam dissimilia & differentia referuntur: in quibus omnibus ea concinnitas cernitur, quæ numerosam facit orationē. Differt autem numerus, ab eo quod numerosum est. Numerus enim, pedes poeticos complectitur tantum: numerosum uero, non modò numerum habet, uerùm etiam genere ipso uerborum Et secum sola sicca spaciatur arena.
units.tr: We have said before that the period and clauses which fill the ears and suit the breath of the voice are smooth, while long and broken ones are unpleasant. Now we must speak of the figures by which a certain smoothness is produced. Figures of this kind arise from a certain arrangement of words, in which there is likeness or equality. Those which end alike and close alike are called, by their proper name, similarly falling and similarly ending. An example of the first is: You praise a man lacking in virtue, abounding in good fortune. Of the second: You dare to do shamefully, you strive to speak wickedly. Likewise, frequent words related to frequent ones, and equal words related to equal ones, contrasting, or even similar and dissimilar. Words are called frequent when single words are referred to single words; they are called equal when, with several words proposed in the sentence, as many are answered in the same measure. I think he means this kind in the third book of De Oratore, where, in listing the ornaments of words, he says: "and what, from single things proposed, is drawn and referred to single things." But what he says is referred to equal parts with equal parts in the same place, I think should be understood of those which Cornificius, in book 4, called comparable, when the clauses consist of nearly the same number of syllables. The most beautiful example of these is in the Pro Milone. It begins with frequent words, soon slides into equal ones, and then, as if returning in a circle, goes back again to frequent ones, and finishes the ornament it began: "For this, judges, is not a written law but a born one; we have not learned it, received it, or read it, but have seized it, drawn it, and impressed it from nature itself; we were not taught for it but made for it, not instructed but imbued." Only equal words occur in the Pro Roscio: "On such great and atrocious matters I understand that I cannot speak conveniently enough, nor complain seriously enough, nor cry out freely enough. For my talent is an obstacle to convenience, my age to seriousness, and the times to freedom." But in the second Catilinarian, frequent words are first set against frequent ones, then equal against equal, and contraries are brought together with great force and abundance, in this way: "For on this side fights modesty, on that side wantonness; here chastity, there lust; here good faith, there deceit; here piety, there wickedness; here constancy, there frenzy; here honour, there baseness; here self-restraint, there appetite; finally, here equity, temperance, fortitude, piety, all the virtues, contend with injustice, luxury, sloth, rashness, and all vices." In these examples contraries are set against contraries, and also dissimilar and differing things; in all of them that harmony is seen which makes the speech rhythmical. Yet "numerus" differs from "numerosum." For "numerus" embraces only poetic feet, whereas the rhythmical "numerosum" has not only number but also, by the very kind of words, a harmony like numbers, even though it is far from metre. And the dry sand walks alone by itself.

units.la: Relataq; ad idem verbum.) Hæc ea figura continentur, quæ ςἱvyμα Græcis dicitur. ea fit duobus modis: aut cū interpositione verbi, & superiores partes orationis comprehenduntur, & inferiores. hoc modo: Formæ dignitas aut morbo deflorescit, aut uctustate. & hæc appellatur Coniunctio à Ccrnificio. Aut cū verbo, quo res comprehenditur, nō interponimus, sed aut primū aut postremum collocamus, quæ Adiūctio nominatur. Prioris exemplū est: Deflorescit formæ dignitas aut morbo, aut uctustate. posterioris sic: Aut morbo, aut uctustate, formæ dignitas deflorescit.
units.tr: "Relataque ad idem verbum": this is the figure that the Greeks call [σχῆμα]. It is made in two ways. Either a word is inserted, and the earlier and later parts of the sentence are both included, as in: "The beauty of form fades either through sickness or through age." This is called Coniunction by Cornificius. Or we do not insert a word that comprises the matter, but place the repeated word first or last, which is called Adjunction. An example of the first kind: "The beauty of form fades, either through sickness or through age." Of the second kind: "Either through sickness or through age, the beauty of form fades."

units.la: Et geminata.) Geminata verba, & iterata, differunt inter se: quòd geminata absque interuallo ponuntur, iterata uerò interpositum aliquid habent. Geminata sunt: Vos uos obtestor Dij immortales. iterata: Fuit hoc quondam, fuit proprium populi Rom. longè à domo bellare: pro Leg. Manil. De duplicatis ante dictū est. Quanquam duplicata uidetur hic exponendi causa addidisse: geminata, id est duplicata. Tum coniunctionib. copulata, ca sunt, quæ polysyndeta Græci dicūt. Ασύνδετα, contraria iis quæ dissoluta et fine coniunctione dicimus. Horū duorū exēpla sint: Et amico proderas, & amicū lædebas, & tibi ipsi nō concōsulebas. alterius hoc: Gere more pareti, pare cognatis, obsequere amicis, obtempera legibus. Item pro Cluetio: Remoueantur autoritates censoriae, tollatur id ex causa, quod in causa non est: doce quam pecuniam Cluentius dederit, unde dederit, quemadmodum dederit.
units.tr: "Et geminata": doubled words and repeated words differ from one another. Doubled words are placed without any interval, whereas repeated words have something placed between them. Doubled words: "You, I beseech you, immortal gods." Repeated words: "This was once, it was the peculiar mark of the Roman people, to make war far from home" (Pro Lege Manilia). I have already spoken about duplicated words. Although here he seems to have added the phrase for the sake of explanation: "doubled, that is, duplicated." Then there are the words joined by conjunctions, which the Greeks call [πολυσύνδετα]. Their opposite is what we call [ἀσύνδετα], the dissolved or unconnected words, that is, without conjunction. Examples of these two: "You both helped your friend, and harmed your friend, and did not even look after yourself." An example of the other: "Behave according to custom, obey your parents, be obedient to your friends, submit to the laws." Likewise in the Pro Cluentio: "Let the censors' authority be set aside; let that be removed from the case which is not in the case; show what money Cluentius gave, from where he gave it, in what manner he gave it."

units.la: Fit etiā suauis oratio, cū aliquid aut inuisum, aut inauditū, aut nouū dicas. Delectat enim, quicquid est admirabile: maximeq; mouet ea, quae motum aliquē animi miscet, oratio, queq; significat oratoris ipsius amabiles mores, qui exprimūtur aut significando iudicio ipsius ex animo humano, ac liberali, aut inflexione sermonis: cū aut augēdi alterius, aut minuēdi sui causa, alia dici ab oratore, alia existimari uidetur: idq; comitate fieri magis, quàm natiuitate. Sed multa sunt suauitatis praecepta, quae orationem aut magis obscuram, aut minus probabilem faciunt. Itaq; etiam hoc loco nobis est ipsis, quid causa postulet, iudicandum.
units.tr: Speech also becomes pleasing when you say something hateful, unheard of, or new. For whatever is wonderful delights, and speech that mixes in some emotion of the mind moves most strongly, and speech that shows the amiable character of the orator himself, which is expressed either by the judgment he reveals, drawn from a human and generous spirit, or by the manner of his discourse, when the orator seems to say one thing and mean another, either to magnify someone else or to diminish himself. This comes about more through courtesy than through nature. But there are many precepts of pleasantness which make the speech either more obscure or less credible. Therefore, even here, we must judge for ourselves what the case requires.

units.la: Fit etiam suauis oratio.) Supersunt sententiæ, quarū sunt genera tria. Nā aut sunt admirabiles, aut quæ motum habent, aut ad conciliandum ua-lent. Mirabiles aut de inuisis sunt, aut inauditis, aut nouis. Inuisa sunt, quæ nemo oculis uidit: inaudita, quæ ad aures eorum qui audiunt, nunquam peruenerunt. Noua deniq;, neque uisa neq; audita unquam sunt: quorum exempla suppeditabit oratio pro lege Manilia. Motum habet, quæ iram, odiū, inuidiam, & id genus permotiones in animis auditorum excitant. nam in permotionibus quoq; inest iucunditas, quemadmodum Homerus de ira cecinit: Dulcior effuso quàm melle in pectore gliscit,
units.tr: "Fit etiam suavis oratio": there remain the sentences, of which there are three kinds. For they are either admirable, or they have an emotional force, or they are effective for winning goodwill. Admirable sentences concern either hateful things, or unheard-of things, or new things. Hateful things are those that no one has seen with their eyes; unheard-of things are those that have never reached the ears of those who listen; new things, finally, are those that have never been seen or heard. Examples of these will be supplied by the speech for the Lex Manilia. That which has emotional force stirs up anger, hatred, envy and that kind of agitation in the minds of the hearers. For there is also pleasure in agitations, as Homer sang of anger: "It grows sweeter than honey in the breast when poured out."

units.la: ut ostendit Ariftot. lib.1. Rhet. & quomodo quibus ʼuc de causis id fiat docet. Ad conciliandum uero faciunt, quæ amabiles oratoris mores significant: qui aut in humanitate eius, ac liberalitate elucent: aut in flexione sermonis. idq; duob. modis, uel augendi alterius, uel minuedi sui causa: quæ quidem duo εἰρωνεία urbanitate ue aliqua cōsequemur. Præcepta uero urbanitatis à Cicerone traditur li.1. de Orat. Sed cū aliter dicit, aliter intelligi uult orator: id facit nō uanitate aliqua, id est, mentiendi caussa, sed comitate quadā & modestia. Possunt esse et alia quæ iucunda efficiat oratione: uerum ea aut ad obscurũ dicendi genus, quod uitandũ est, pertinet: aut quia fidē orationi detrahunt, sunt omittenda, & sophistis relinquē-da. da. Iudicium igitur etiam in his deligendis, quae suauitatem habent, adhibendum est, & ad utilitatem causae omnia referenda. Illud praeterea sciendum, nullam esse orationem, quae uno aliquo horum generum tota constet: sed idcirco seorsim horum praecepta traduntur, ut ex his generibus & luminibus orationem temperemus. Sed praestat, ut hanc totam de generibus dicendi doctrinam, uerbis Ciceronis ex tertio de Oratore concludamus: Quoniam, inquit, de ornatu omni orationis, si non sunt omnes patefacti, at certe commostrati loci, nunc quid aptum sit, hoc est, quid maxime decet in oratione, uideamus. Quanquam id quidem perspicuum est, non omni causae, nec audito ri, neq; personae, neq; tempori congruere orationis unum genus. Nam & causae capitis, aliud quiddam uerborum sonum requirunt, alium rerum priuatarum atq; paruarum: & aliud dicendi genus deliberationes, aliud laudationes, aliud iudicia, aliud sermones, aliud consolatio, aliud obiurgatio, aliud disputatio, aliud historia desiderat. Refert etiam, qui audiant, senatus, an populus, an iudices: frequentes, an pauci, an singuli: & quales ipsi quoque oratores, qua sint aetate, honore, autoritate, debet uideri: tempus pacis, an belli, festinationis, an otij. Itaq; hoc loco nihil sane est quod praecipi posse uideatur, nisi ut figuram orationis plenioris,
units.tr: As Aristotle shows in book 1 of the Rhetoric, he also teaches for what reasons this happens. Sentences that serve to win goodwill are those that show the amiable character of the orator, which shines forth either in his humanity and generosity, or in the manner of his speech. This too takes two forms, either for the sake of magnifying another or diminishing oneself; these two we attain through [εἰρωνεία] or some kind of urbanity. The precepts of urbanity are indeed handed down by Cicero in book 1 of De Oratore. But when the orator says one thing and wants another to be understood, he does this not from some vanity, that is, for the sake of lying, but from a certain courtesy and modesty. There may be other things which make the speech pleasing; but these either pertain to the obscure kind of speaking, which must be avoided, or because they detract from the credibility of the speech, they must be omitted and left to the sophists. Therefore judgment must be applied also in choosing those things which have pleasantness, and everything must be referred to the advantage of the case. It should also be known that there is no speech which consists wholly of one of these kinds; rather, the precepts of each are handed down separately so that we may temper our speech with these kinds and ornaments. But it is better to conclude this whole doctrine of the kinds of speaking in Cicero's own words from the third book of De Oratore: "Since," he says, "concerning all the ornament of speech, if not all places have been opened up, at least they have been pointed out, let us now see what is fitting, that is, what is most becoming in speech. Yet it is clear that one kind of speech does not suit every case, nor every hearer, nor every person, nor every occasion. For cases involving capital charges require one sound of words, and those concerning private and trivial matters another; and one kind of speaking befits deliberations, another praises, another trials, another conversations, another consolation, another rebuke, another debate, another history. It matters also who the hearers are: the senate, or the people, or the judges; a crowd, or a few, or single persons; and what sort the orators themselves are, in age, office and authority, must be seen; a time of peace, or of war, of haste, or of leisure. Therefore nothing can really be prescribed here, except that we choose a fuller, a plainer, and a middling style of speech, suited to what we are doing."

units.la: l oris,& tenuioris, & item illius mediocris ad id quod agimus accommodata deligamus. Ornamentis ijsdem uti ferè licebit, aliàs cōtentius, aliàs submissius: omniq; in re posse quod deceat facere, artis & naturæ est: scire quid, quandoq; deceat, prudentiæ. Atq; ut in Oratore ait: Is enim est eloquēs, qui & humilia subtiliter, & magna graviter, & mediocria temperatè potest dicere.
units.tr: ...and a middling one, as suits what we are about. It will generally be permitted to use the same ornaments, at one time more intensely, at another more gently; and to be able to do what is fitting in every matter belongs to art and nature; to know what is fitting, and when, belongs to prudence. And as he says in the Orator: "For he is eloquent who can speak subtly of humble things, weightily of great things, and moderately of middling things."

units.la: C. F. Reliquum est igitur, ut dicas de conuersa oratione, atque mutata. C. P. Est itaque id genus totum situm in commutatione uerborum, quæ simplicibus in verbis ita tractatur, ut aut ex uerbo dilatetur, aut in uerbum contrahatur oratio. Ex uerbo, cū aut propriū, aut idē significās, aut factum uerbum in plura uerba deducitur. Ex oratione, cū aut definitio ad unum uerbum reuocatur, aut assumpta uerba remouentur, aut in circuitus diriguntur, aut in coniunctione fit unum uerbum ex duobus.
units.tr: C. F. "It remains, then, that you speak of converted and changed speech." C. P. This whole kind therefore consists in the change of words, which is handled in simple words in such a way that speech is either expanded from a word or contracted into a word. Speech is expanded from a word when either a proper word, or one with the same meaning, or a made word is drawn out into several words. Speech is contracted when either a definition is recalled to a single word, or added words are removed, or are directed into circumlocutions, or one word is made from two by combination.

units.la: Reliquum est igitur ut dicas de conuersa oratione atque mutata. ) Supră dictum est, unū esse eloquendi genus, sua sponte susum: alterum uersum, sum, atq; mutatum. Ac de priore satis dictum est. Sequitur nunc, ut de altero, in quo naturalis ille ordo orationis, conuersus, & uarijs modis est commutatus, aliquid dicatur. Et hoc genus, ut illud prius, simplicium est, & coniunctorum. In simplicibus autem duplex commutandi ratio est: altera dilatandi, contrahendi altera. Nam, quemadmodum antea dixi, in eo vis oratoris cernitur, side eadem re & copiose et breuiter possit dicere. Sed tamen uidendum est, ne ea dilatemus, quae sunt cōstringenda: aut ea constringamus, quae dilatanda sunt. decorum enim & loci, & temporis, & personarum, atque etiam rerum ipsarum seruandum erit.
units.tr: "It remains, then, that you speak of converted and changed speech." It has been said above that there is one kind of speaking, which runs of its own accord, and another that is turned and changed. About the former enough has been said. Now follows what is to be said about the other, in which that natural order of speech is turned and altered in various ways. And this kind, like the former, concerns both simple and combined words. In simple words there is a twofold method of change: one of expanding, the other of contracting. For, as I said before, in this lies the power of the orator, to be able to speak about the same thing both copiously and briefly. Yet we must take care that we do not expand what should be compressed, nor compress what should be expanded. For the fitness of place, time, persons, and even of the things themselves must be observed.

units.la: Ex uerbo. ) Hoc praeceptum est dilatandae orationis, cum ex nomine, aut aliqua breui sententia, fit oratio. Ex nomine inquam, siue illud proprium fit, id est, non translatum, ut Scipio, amor: siue idem significans, cuiusmodi sunt synonyma, & translata uerba, de quibus satis dictum est: siue immutata, de quib. etiam explicauimus, ut Ceres pro frugibus, aut pane: siue fit factum, uel coniunctione, quod duplicatum etiam appellauimus, ut compransor: uel sine coniunctione, ut urbanitas, quod quidem uerbum simplex est, non coniunctum. Ex huiusmodi igitur uerbis deducitur oratio: quod Cicero dixit, Verbum in plura uerba deducitur. At quot modis id fiat, non docet hic Cicero: sed ex praeceptis, cōtrahendae ad unum uerbum orationis intelligi potest. Idcirco nos ad sequentem præceptionem ueniemus, & in ea utrunq; demonstrabimus.
units.tr: "From a word." This is the precept of expanding speech, when speech is made from a noun, or from some brief sentence. From a noun, I say, whether it is a proper noun, that is, not transferred, such as Scipio or amor; or a word with the same meaning, of which kind are synonyms and transferred words, about which enough has been said; or an altered word, about which we have also explained, such as Ceres for grain, or bread; or a made word, either by combination, which we have also called duplicated, such as compransor; or without combination, such as urbanitas, which is indeed a simple, not a compound, word. Speech is therefore drawn out from such words, which is what Cicero said: "a word is drawn out into several words." But in what ways this is done Cicero does not teach here; yet it can be understood from the precepts for contracting speech into a single word. For this reason we will come to the following precept, and in it we will demonstrate both.

units.la: Ex oratione. ) Scilicet ad unum uerbum reuocatur sententia: atq; huius contractionis præcepta sunt quatuor.
units.tr: From the speech: namely, the sentence is recalled to one word, and there are four rules for this contraction.

units.la: Cum autem definitio ad unum uerbum reuocatur.) Definitio hic pro quauis descriptione poni-tur, ut pro Milone: Qui nullam uim cœlestem existimat, numen ue diuinum. Hæc descriptio ad unum uerbum reuocatur, si pro ea impium dicas: & contrà ex uerbo dilatabitur, si eam definitionem pro impio posueris.
units.tr: When a definition is recalled to one word: here "definition" is used for any description, as for Milo, "one who thinks there is no heavenly power or divine will." This description is recalled to one word if you call him impious instead. Conversely, it will be expanded from the word if you put the definition in place of "impious."

units.la: Aut assumpta uerba remouentur. ) Ponamus illud uerbum: Non facile, homo, patrem, occidit. singula hæc uerba dilatemus ex Rosciana, & primum illa, Non facile, sic: Multum ualet communio sanguinis: reclamat istiusmodi suspicionibus ipsa natura: monstrum atq; portentum certissimum est. hæc tria membra, pro illis, non facile, posita sunt. Sequitur Homo: Esse aliquem humana specie atq; figura. deinde, Crudelis: qui tātum immanitate bestias uicerit. iam Patrem ita describit: ut propter quos hanc suauissimam lucem aspexerit. tot enim uerbis patrem significauit. Superest uerbum unum, Occidit, quod, sic dilatauit Cicero: Eos indignißimè luce priuarit, cum etiam ferac inter se partus atq; educatio, & ipsa natura conciliet. Ab his omnibus, si assumpta uerba remoueantur, relinquetur tantum illa prima sententia. Sed quoniam non semper ita remouentur assumpta, ut unum tantum uerbum relinquatur: abijciamus nos ex hac Ciceronis dilatatione, quae uere assumpta sunt: hoc est, quae in re ipsa insita non erant: Multum ualet communio sanguinis: reclamat ipsa natura. esse aliquem humana specie atq; figura, qui propter quos hanc suauißimam lucem aspexerit, eos indignißimè luce priuarit.
units.tr: Or the added words are removed: let us take the sentence "Not easily, man, kills a father." Let us expand each of these words from the Roscian speech, and first "not easily," thus: "The fellowship of blood carries great weight; nature herself protests against such suspicions; it is a most certain monstrosity and portent." These three clauses are put in place of "not easily." Then comes "man": "being someone of human appearance and form." Then "cruel": "who has surpassed beasts in savagery." He describes "father" thus: "for whose sake he has beheld this most sweet light," for he signified "father" by so many words. One word remains, "kills," which Cicero expanded thus: "has deprived of light most unworthily those whom wild beasts, the bearing and rearing of offspring, and nature itself unite." If the added words are removed from all these, only that first sentence will remain. But since the added words are not always removed so that only one word is left, let us cast out from this Ciceronian expansion those words which were truly added, that is, which were not inherent in the matter itself: "The fellowship of blood carries great weight; nature herself protests," and "being someone of human appearance and form, who has deprived of light most unworthily those for whose sake he has beheld this most sweet light."

units.la: Aut in circuitus diriguntur.) Scilicet uerba siue assumpta, siue insita. In circuitus diriguntur, id est, quae copiosè seorsim, aut membratim, aut caesim dilatata sunt, & quasi dissoluta, circuitu uno, & comprehensione, uinciuntur. Id autè fit, aut conclusione oratoria, aut coniunctione, aut adiunctione, aut frequentatione: de quibus Cornificius lib. 4. ad Herennium: Conclusione enim, & frequentatione, quae sparsa erant, in unum locum atq; ambitum orationis coguntur: coniunctione uerò, & adiunctione, quae per se singula constabant, & proprijs uerbis nitebantur, ad unum commune reuocatur. Haec duobus exemplis ostendo, primùm cõclusionis, deinde adiunctionis.
units.tr: Or they are directed into circuits: namely, words, whether added or inherent. "Directed into circuits" means those words which have been expanded copiously, separately, or by members or cola, and which, as if dissolved, are bound together by one circuit and one comprehension. This happens either by oratorical conclusion, by conjunction, by addition, or by repetition. Cornificius speaks of these in book 4 of the Rhetoric to Herennius: "For by conclusion and repetition, things that were scattered are gathered into one place and into the compass of the speech; but by conjunction and addition, things that each stood on their own and relied on their own words are recalled to one common term." I show this by two examples, first of conclusion, then of addition.

units.la: Quod si Danais datum erat oraculû, non posse ca pi Troiam sine Philoctetæ sagittis: hæ autem nihil aliud fecerunt, nisi Alexandrum perculerunt: hunc extinguere, id nimirum capi fuit Troiam. Hoc exemplum Cornificij est: quod sequitur, Ciceronis, ex tertia in Verrem: Certet mea diligētia cum illorum omnium cupiditate: uestra integritas, cum illius pecunia: testium constantia, cū illius patronorum minis atq; potentia.
units.tr: "But if it was given to the Danaans by oracle that Troy could not be taken without the arrows of Philoctetes, and these arrows did nothing else but strike down Alexander, then to extinguish him was surely to take Troy." This example is Cornificius's. What follows is Cicero's, from the third Verrine: "Let my diligence contend with the greed of all those men; your integrity with his money; the steadfastness of the witnesses with the threats and power of his advocates."

units.la: Aut in coniunctione fit unum uerbum ex duobus.) Id fit multis modis, ut sequentia exempla indicabunt. In urbem, quæ uestra est, uenit: in uestrum urbem. hic relatiuum remotum est. In nauim conscendi, & naui gaui: naui conscensa nauigaui. In hoc exemplo remouimus coniunctionem, & uerbum in participium comutauimus. Item coniunctione ex duobus unum fit: simul pascere, compascere: ualde humanus, perhumanus. Diminutio quoq; eandē contrahēdi uim habet. parũ corpus, corpusculum: pusillus homo, homuncio. Item negantibus aduerbijs in præpositiones commutatis, aut in contraria uerba: Non sepultus, insepultus: non odit, amat.
units.tr: Or in conjunction one word is made from two. This happens in many ways, as the following examples will show. "He came into the city which is yours": "into your city." Here the relative clause is removed. "I embarked on the ship and sailed by ship": "having embarked on the ship, I sailed." In this example we removed the conjunction and changed the verb into a participle. Likewise by conjunction one word is made from two: "to feed together," "to pasture together"; "very humane," "perhumane." Diminution also has the same power of contraction: "a little body," "a small body"; "a puny man," "a little man." Also, when negating adverbs are changed into prepositions or into contrary words: "not buried," "unburied"; "does not love," "hates."

units.la: In cōiunctis aūt uerbis triplex adhiberi potest cōmutatio, nō uerborum, sed ordinis tantūmodo: ut cum semel dictū sit directe, sicut natura ipsa tulerit, inuertatur ordo, & idem quasi sursum uersus, retroq; dicatur, deinde idē intercise, atq; permiste. Eloquedi aut exercitatio maxime in hoc toto cōuertedi genere uersatur.
units.tr: In conjoined words a threefold change can be applied, not of the words but only of their order: when something has been said directly, as nature itself dictates, the order is inverted, and it is said as if upward and backward; then the same thing is said interlaced and mixed. The practice of speaking is especially engaged in this whole genus of inversion.

units.la: In coniunctis autem.) Dixit de commutatione uerborum simplicium. iam de cōmutatione coniunctorum, qui quidē triplex est: aut cōtrario omnino ei qui directus & naturalis dicitur, aut intercisus, aut permistus. Nā directus ille, et sua spō te fusus, quod quidā putāt, nō numeratur. est enim materia, in qua fit hæc mutatio, siue cōuersio. Nō debere aut cōnumerari, signū illud est, quod hic id genus quod cōuersum dicitur, tractatur: nō sua sponte fusum. male etiā quidā existimant, intercisum ac permistū ordine eundem esse: atq; ideo nō triplex, sed duplex, hoc loco legēdū esse: cū unde id probēt, habeat nihil. Nos igitur hæc præcepta, consensum & fidem codicum secuti, explicemus. Illud primum sciendum est, in hac triplici conuersione, uerba semper eadem manere, ordine tantum commutato. Primus ordo est, cum dicitur retro ac quasi sursum uersus, idem quod directe diceretur, aut dictū prius fuerit. ut in hoc exemplo: Omnis natura est diligens sui. Cōtrario ordine nec sic: Sui diligens est natura omnis. Altera ratio,cum intercise commutamus id quod tum fieri intelligo, cum circuitus inciditur,& in alium ordinem,partibus integris, conuertitur, fitq; plane alia orationis sicies, ut in illo: Est enim liberale officium,serere beneficium, ut metere possis fructum. Intercise hoc modo commutari potest: Est enim liberale officium, ut metere possis fructum,serere beneficium. aut sic: Serere beneficiū, ut metere possis fructum, liberale officium est. Ite si quis illud quod pro Milone dixit Cicero, intercife uelit conuertere: Hoc & ratio doctis, & necessitas barbaris,& mos gentibus, & feris natura ipsa præscripsit,ut omnem semper uim,quacunq; ope possent, à corpore, à capite, à uita sua propulsarent:sic facere poterit. Hoc & feris natura ipsa præscripsit,& ratio doctis, & mos gentibus,& necessitas barbaris,ut à capite, à uita,à corpore, omnem semper uim, quacunq; ope possent,propulsarent. Permiste autem, ubi retentis tantū verbis, nullo ordine seruato, aut verborū, aut incisorū,aut membrorū,qui prius fuerit,nos novii,atq; omnino nostrū quendā ordine efficimus, & in aliū orbem atq; in quadrū concinnè dirigimus. Exēpli gratia,dixit Cicero in quadā epistola:Tibi aūt id cōsilij do,quod mihimetipsi,ut uite mus oculos hominū, si linguas minus facilè possumus.hoc inquâ nostro arbitratu sic pmiscebimus: Id autem tibi do consilij, quod ipsimet mihi, ut si minus hominum linguas facile possumus, oculos uitemus.Hoc tertium genus idcirco permistum dicitur, tum quòd ex duobus superioribus generibus constat,tum etiam quòd in eo permiscere omnia manentibus uerbis liceat.
units.tr: He spoke about the change of simple words; now about the change of conjoined words, which is threefold: either entirely contrary to what is called direct and natural, or interlaced, or mixed. For that direct order, which flows of its own accord, which some think should not be counted, is the material in which this change or conversion takes place. That it should not be counted is shown by the fact that here we deal with the kind which is called converted, not with that which flows of its own accord. Some also wrongly hold that the interlaced and the mixed are the same in order, and that therefore the text here should be read not as threefold but as twofold; yet they have nothing from which to prove it. We, therefore, following the agreement and authority of the manuscripts, will explain these precepts. First, one must know that in this threefold conversion the words always remain the same, only their order changed. The first kind is when what is said backward and as if upward is the same as what would have been said directly, or was said before. As in this example: "Every nature is careful of itself." In the contrary order it is not so: "Careful of itself is every nature." The other method is when we change what is interlaced. I understand this happens when a circuit is cut and converted into another order, with its parts kept whole, so that it becomes a plainly different form of speech, as in: "For it is a liberal duty to sow a benefit, so that you may reap the fruit." Interlaced, it can be changed thus: "For it is a liberal duty, so that you may reap the fruit, to sow a benefit." Or so: "To sow a benefit, so that you may reap the fruit, is a liberal duty." Likewise, if anyone wishes to interlace what Cicero said for Milo: "Reason has prescribed this for the learned, necessity for barbarians, custom for the nations, and nature itself for wild beasts: that they should always repel every force, by whatever means they could, from the body, from the head, from their life." He could make it thus: "Nature itself has prescribed this for wild beasts, and reason for the learned, custom for the nations, and necessity for barbarians: that from the head, from life, from the body, they should repel every force by whatever means they could." The mixed kind is when, keeping only the words and observing no order, we make whichever of the words, clauses or members came first come last, and we arrange our own order, directing it neatly into another orb and quadrangle. For example, Cicero said in a certain letter: "But I give you this advice, which I give to myself: that we should avoid the eyes of men, if we can less easily avoid their tongues." We, on our own judgement, will mix this thus: "But I give you this advice, which I give to myself: that if we can less easily avoid the tongues of men, we should avoid their eyes." This third kind is called mixed both because it consists of the two earlier kinds and because in it everything may be mixed up while the words remain the same.

units.la: Eloquendi autem exercitatio maximè in hoc toto conuertendi genere uersatur. ) De exercitatione hic admonet,sine qua nemo unquam ulla in arte excelluit.Ea est asiduus usus, consuetudoq; dicendi,de qua lib.1. de Oratore Crassus diligenter præcipit.Illud modò in omnibus his generib. uidendum est,ne commutatione deterior fiat compositio,& eneruetur oratio.
units.tr: The practice of speaking is especially engaged in this whole genus of conversion. Here he gives a reminder about practice, without which no one has ever excelled in any art. This is constant use and habit of speaking, about which Crassus carefully instructs in book 1 of On the Orator. Only this must be watched for in all these kinds: that the composition is not made worse by the change, and the speech is not enfeebled.

units.la: DE ACTIONE.
units.tr: ON ACTION.

units.la: C. F. Actio igitur sequitur,ut opinor. C. P. Est ita, quæ quidem oratori & cum rerū, & cum uerborum momentis cõmutanda maximè est. Facit enim &dilucidam orationem, & illustrem, & probabilem, & suauem,non uerbis,sed uarietate uocū, motu corporis, uultu: quæ plurimū ualebunt,si cū orationis genere consentient,eiusq; uim ac uarietatē subsequentur. C. F. Actio igitur sequitur, ut opinor.) Actio, quarta pars est oratorij officij, quae quid sit, initio diximus, ubi etiam de eius partib. disputauimus, hoc autem loco Cicero, non tam eius partes, quàm usum & uim indicare uidetur. Duo ex eius uerbis praecepta colliguntur: quorum prius pertinet ad usum, alterum ad uim, & efficiendi facultatem. Ad usum pertinet, id quod dicit in principio & fine huius praeceptionis: actionem esse cum rerum & uerborum motus commutandi, id est ad orationis genus accommodandum. Ad uim autem, cum dicit, Ab actione dilucidam, & illustrem, & probabilem, & suaue orationem fieri: non quidem uerbis, nam de his in elocutione praecepta sunt tradita: sed uarietate uocum, motu corporis, et vultu. Ac vocis quidem bonitas optanda est: non est enim in nobis situm, ut eam bonam habeamus, sed tractatio atque usus in nobis. Vocis mutationes totidem sunt, quot animorum, qui maximè voce commouentur. Aliud enim vocis genus iracundia sibi sumit, acutum, incitatum, crebrò incidens: aliud miseratio, ac maeror, flexibile, plenum, interruptum, flebile: aliud metus, demissum & haesitans, & abiectum: aliud ira, contentum, vehemens, imminens, quadam incitatione grauitatis: aliud voluptas, effusum, lene, tenerum, hilaratum & remissum: aliud molestia sine commiseratione, graue quiddam, & uno pressu ac sono obductum. Sed haec ex poetarum & musicorum praeceptis manant. Omnes autem hos motus et uocũ uarietates,sequitur corporis motus & gestus:nõ ille scenicus,sed uniuersam rem & sen-tentiã significatione declarans: status erectus & celsus:rarus pedũ motus,nec lõgus:nulla mollicia ceruicũ,nulla argutiæ digitorũ:non ad numerum articulus cadẽs:truco magis toto se ipse moderãs, & uirili laterũ flexione,brachij proiectiõe, quasi quodã telo in cõtentionibus,cõtractione in remissis.Motus uero qui secundũ uocẽ plurimũ potest,magnã affert tũ dignitatẽ,tum uenustatẽ: in quo cũ effeceris,ne quid ineptũ aut uultuosum sit, tum oculorũ est quædã magna moderatio. Nã ut imago est animi uultus,sic indices oculi:quorũ & bilaritatis,& uicißim tristitiæ modũ res ipsæ,de quib.agetur,tẽperabunt.Hæc sunt in summia,quæ de actione præcipit Cicero,sine qua summus orator esse in numero nullo pŏt:mediocris ac instructus,sumos sæpe superare:ut iã nõ sine causa Demosthenes tribuerit,& primas,et secũdas,& tertias,actioni.
units.tr: C. F. Action, then, comes next, I think. C. P. It does. And action, which the orator must above all adapt to both the weight of the matter and the weight of the words, makes a speech clear, vivid, convincing and pleasing. It does this not through the words but through variation of the voice, movement of the body and expression of the face. These will carry great weight if they match the kind of speech and follow its force and variety. C. F. Action, then, comes next, I think. Action is the fourth part of the orator's office. What it is, we said at the beginning, where we also discussed its parts. Here, however, Cicero seems to indicate not so much its parts as its use and force. Two precepts are gathered from his words. The first concerns use, the second concerns force and the power of producing an effect. It concerns use in what he says at the beginning and end of this precept: that action consists in changing the movement of things and words, that is, in fitting it to the kind of speech. It concerns force when he says that action makes a speech clear, vivid, convincing and pleasing. This is done not by words, for precepts about these have been given under style, but by variety of voice, movement of the body and expression of the face. The goodness of the voice is to be desired. We do not have it by nature; it is a matter of training and practice on our part. The changes of voice are as many as the emotions that move the voice most. One kind of voice is taken on by anger: sharp, urgent, often breaking in. Another belongs to pity and grief: pliant, full, broken, tearful. Another to fear: lowered, hesitant and abject. Another to indignation: tense, vehement, threatening, with a certain driving seriousness. Another to pleasure: flowing, soft, tender, cheerful and relaxed. Another to vexation without pity: somewhat heavy, and held down with one pressure and one tone. These, however, come from the precepts of poets and musicians. Following all these movements and variations of the voice comes the movement and gesture of the body. It is not theatrical, but expresses the whole matter and sentiment by its meaning. The stance is upright and lofty; the steps are few and not long; the neck shows no softness and the fingers no affectation; the joints do not move in time to a beat; the whole man controls himself with a rather rough bearing, with a manly bending of the sides, a thrust of the arm, as if hurling a weapon in contests, and a drawing back in calmer moments. The movement that has most power alongside the voice brings great dignity and grace. When you have made sure that nothing is awkward or affected in it, there is then a great restraint of the eyes. For as the face is the image of the mind, so the eyes are its indicators. The very matters to be discussed will govern the measure of their cheerfulness and, in turn, of their sadness. These are, in short, the things Cicero prescribes about action. Without action no one can be counted among the highest orators. A moderate and well-trained speaker can often surpass the most gifted, and so it was not without reason that Demosthenes gave action first, second and third place.

units.la: DE MEMORIA.
units.tr: ON MEMORY.

units.la: C. F. Nunquid iam de oratore ipso restat? C. P. Nihil sane, præter memoriã, quæ est gemma literaturæ quodammodo,& in dissimili genere persimilis. Nam ut illa constat ex notis literarum, & ex eo in quo imprimuntur illæ notæ: sic confectio memoriæ tanquam cera locis utitur, & in his imagines, ut literas collocat.
units.tr: C. F. Is anything still left to say about the orator himself? C. P. Nothing, really, except memory. It is in a way the jewel of letters, and in a different kind it is very like them. For as writing consists of the marks of letters and of the surface on which those marks are impressed, so the construction of memory, like wax, uses places, and places the images in them as letters.

units.la: C. F. Nunquid nam de oratore ipso restat. ) De ipso oratore inquit, in quo est ipsa vis quinquepertita, ut ostendimus.
units.tr: C. F. Is anything still left to say about the orator himself? Here he means the orator himself, in whom lies the very power of the five parts, as we have shown.

units.la: C. P. Nihil sane præter memoriam. ) Extrema officij oratoris pars est memoria, quam thesaurum rerum omnium, de Oratore appellat: quæ nisi custos inventis cogitatisq; rebus & verbis adhibeatur, intelligimus omnia, etiamsi præclarissima fuerint, in oratore periturα. Hæc non tam oratoris propria, Ciceronis sententia, quàm communis est multarum artium: immo animalium, & in his præcipuè hominis: sed in aliis maior, in aliis minor, pro cerebri temperatione, autore Galeno: quæ sicca si fuerit, res difficilè comprehendit, diu tamen retinet, ut in senibus: si humecta, facilè, sed ægrè conferuat, ut in iuvenibus: si frigida, nihil planè, aut parum capit: si calida, & moderata, felix est in facilè percipiendo, & fideliter continendo, quæ duplex est memoriæ virtus. Quomodo autem definiretur, etiam initiò ostendimus. Sed de Inuent. lib. 2. prudentiæ partem memoriam facit: eamq; definit animi vim, per quam animus repetit petit illa quæ fuerunt. Sed hæc est naturalis memoriæ definitio. Hic autem Cicero de ea quæ arte & præceptis continetur, agit: qua naturalis illa excitatur, iuuatur & confirmatur: idcirco eam dicit esse germanam literaturæ quodammodo, & in dissimili genere persimilem: significans, scripturæ admodum similem esse. Id quod ipse etiam sequentibus verbis declarat. Vt enim in charta siue tabulis, literas notamus, quæ coniunctæ, nobis sensa reddant: sic in locis imagines collocamus, quæ in mentem reducant nobis, quæ volumus meminisse. Locos appellamus eos, qui breuiter, persecte, insigniter, aut natura, aut manu sunt absoluti, ut eos facilè naturali memoria comprehendere & amplecti queamus: ut ædes, intercolunia, angulos, fornices, & alia quæ his similia sunt. Imagines uero, sunt formæ quædam & notæ, & simulachra earum rerum, quarum meminisse volumus. Quod genus, equi, leones, aquilæ, naues: quorum memoriam si uolumus habere, imagines eorum certis in locis illustribus, non nimium distantibus collocare nos oportebit, & sæpe ea ab eis repetere, quæ eis credidimus: ut multo & magno usu, nullo negocio post, quicquid voluerimus meminisse, in promptu habeamus. Hæc de artificiosa memoria dicuntur, quæ pluribus tum à Cornificio, tum ab aliis qui de hac arte scripserunt, explicantur. Sed tatamē meo iudicio nihil melius ad memoriam, aut commodius est, quàm primùm eam quæ in cerebro sedem habet, quod facilè turbatur, non obruere nimio cibo, aut potu, aut somno: deinde ordine in dicēdo sequi, qui cura & diligentia sæpe repetitus, adiutusq; intelligentia, nobis eadē præstiterit, & multo uberiora, quàm ullum memoriæ artificium. Quod autē quidā pro germana, geminā legunt: illis assentire, si idoneis id testimonijs comprobaret. Verùm cū ea quæ afferunt, huic loquēdi formulæ dissimilia sint: satis apparet, germana, quasi diceres, soror literaturæ, esse legendū: quod quidē significat persimile & cognatā esse literaturæ memoriā, quēadmodum de duab. sororibus ait Terentius: Qui utrāuis norit, ambas noucrit. Qui autē pro germana gemmam legunt, suis inceptis, ne dicā Ciceronis uerbis, refelluntur.
units.tr: C. P. Nothing except memory. Memory is the last part of the orator's office, which Cicero in De Oratore calls the treasury of all things. We understand that unless it is applied as a guardian of inventions, thoughts, words and matters, everything in the orator, however splendid, will perish. This is not, in Cicero's view, peculiar to the orator, but common to many arts, indeed to animals and above all to man. In some it is greater, in others less, according to the temperament of the brain, as Galen says. If the brain is dry, it grasps things with difficulty but retains them long, as in old men. If it is moist, it takes things in easily but keeps them poorly, as in young men. If it is cold, it grasps almost nothing or very little. If it is warm and moderate, it is happy in taking things in easily and holding them faithfully, and these are the two virtues of memory. How memory is defined we showed at the beginning. In De Inventione book 2, Cicero makes memory a part of prudence and defines it as the power of the mind by which it recalls and seeks what has been. But this is the definition of natural memory. Here, however, Cicero is dealing with the memory that is contained in art and precepts, by which natural memory is stirred, aided and strengthened. Therefore he says it is in a way the sister of letters and in a different kind very like them, meaning that it is very similar to writing. He himself makes this clear in the words that follow. For as we mark letters on paper or tablets, which, joined together, convey meanings to us, so we place images in places, which bring back to our minds what we wish to remember. We call places those spots which are finished briefly, perfectly and distinctly, either by nature or by hand, so that we can easily take them in and hold them in natural memory: such as houses, the spaces between columns, corners, vaults and other things like these. Images are forms and marks, and likenesses of those things we wish to remember. Of this kind are horses, lions, eagles and ships. If we wish to have their memory, we shall have to place their images in certain conspicuous places, not too far apart, and often to recall from them what we have entrusted to them. Then, by long and great practice, we shall have at hand, without any trouble afterwards, whatever we wish to remember. These things are said about artificial memory, which is explained at length by Cornificius and others who wrote on this art. Yet in my judgement nothing is better or more useful for memory than first not to overload the seat of memory in the brain, which is easily disturbed, with too much food, drink or sleep.
