Then we should follow order in speaking, which, repeated often with care and diligence, and aided by understanding, will give us the same benefits and far richer ones than any artifice of memory. As for those who read germana [sister] instead of gemma, they would be right to agree with them if they confirmed it by suitable witnesses. But since the things they cite are unlike this way of speaking, it is clear that we ought to read germana, as if you were to say "sister of letters", which indeed means that memory is very like letters and akin to them, just as Terence says of two sisters: whoever knows the one knows both. Those who read gemma (jewel) are refuted in their undertakings, not to say by Cicero's own words.

units.la: EXPLICATIONVM Oratoriarum liber Secundus.
units.tr: EXPLICATIONS of Cicero's Oratorical Partitions, Book Two.

units.la: DE ORATIONE.
units.tr: ON ORATION.

units.la: C. F. Quoniam igitur uis oratoris omnis exposita est, quid habēs de orationis præceptis dicerēt C. P. Quatuor esse eius partes, quarū prima & postrema ad motum animi ualet: ĭs enim initiis est, & peroratiōnibus nibus concitandus. Secunda narratio,& tertia confirmatio,fidem facit orationi. Sed amplificatio quanquā habet proprium locum, sæpe etiam primum, postremum quidem fere semper: tamen reliquo in cursu orationis adhibēda est, maximeq; cum aliquid aut confirmatum est, aut reprehensum. Itaque ad fidem quoq; uel plurimùm ualet. Est enim amplificatio,uehemens quædā argumentatio: ut illa docendi caussa fit, hæc commouendi.
units.tr: C. F. Since, then, the whole power of the orator has been set out, what do you say about the precepts of oratory? C. P. There are four parts of it: the first and last serve to move the mind, for these must be used to rouse the hearers at the beginning and in the peroration. The second, the narration, and the third, the confirmation, make the speech credible. But amplification, although it has its own proper place, and often comes first, and almost always last, must still be employed in the rest of the course of the speech, and especially when something has been confirmed or refuted. Thus it also counts for very much in producing credibility. For amplification is a kind of vehement argumentation: the one is done for the sake of teaching, the other for the sake of stirring the emotions.

units.la: C. F. Quoniā igitur uis oratoris omnis expositā est.) Tres fuerūt propositæ Rhetoricæ partes: uis oratoris,deinde oratio,tū etiā quæstio. Iā uis omnis oratoris exposita est tū à Cicerone, tū etiā à nobis. Deinceps hoc fecūdo Partitionū libro,de orationis præceptis explicandū relinquitur. Rursum igitur quatuor orationis partes assumit,easq;singillatim explicat,nihil quod in eas cadat prætermittens.
units.tr: C. F. "Since, then, the whole power of the orator has been set out": three parts of rhetoric were proposed: the power of the orator, then the speech, and then also the question. Now the whole power of the orator has been set out, both by Cicero and by us. Next, in this second book of the Partitions, what concerns the precepts of speaking remains to be explained. Again, then, he takes up the four parts of the speech and explains each one separately, omitting nothing that falls under them.

units.la: C. P. Quatuor esse eius partes.) Hæc abūde libro superiore explicata sunt,quæ tamē Cicero repetit,ut cum cæteris coniungat,quæ dicta nō fuerunt:sicq; integra partium explicatio habeatur.
units.tr: C. P. "There are four parts of it": these things were explained fully in the previous book, yet Cicero repeats them, so that he may join to the rest what was not said, and so that a complete explanation of the parts may be had.

units.la: Sed amplificatio. ) Enumeratis orationis partibus, occurrebat amplificatio, siue digressio, de qua potuisset quis dubitare, quinam eius esset in oratione locus. Id igitur hic breuiter docet, nimirum proprium eam habere locum in peroratione: posse tamen saepe etiam ad alias partes assumi: praesertim ad exordium ipsum: nonnunquam etiam ad reliquas partes, & in toto orationis cursu adhibendam esse. Nam amplificatio non modo ad permouendum, verum etiam ad fidem quoque faciendam plurimum valet: quae, ut hic & infra definit, uehemens est quaedam argumentatio, quae motu animorum conciliet in dicendo fidem. Vis enim docendi in argumentatione est, commouendi uero in amplificatione. Sed cum argumentatio ipsa amplificatione instruitur, tunc ipsa amplificatio dicitur utrunque facere, & docere siue probare, & permouere siue flectere. Ex his quae dicta sunt, duo intelligimus: uidelicet uim amplificationis, & locum in partibus orationis. Reliqua quae de amplificatione inuenienda & tractanda, tradenda sunt, ea in peroratione uidebimus.
units.tr: "But amplification": having listed the parts of the speech, amplification, or digression, presented itself, about which someone might have doubted where in the speech it belongs. Here, then, he briefly teaches this: namely, that it has its proper place in the peroration, but may often be taken up also into the other parts, especially into the exordium itself, and sometimes into the remaining parts, and is to be used throughout the whole course of the speech. For amplification counts for much not only in stirring the emotions but also in producing credibility; and this, as he defines here and below, is a kind of vehement argumentation, which by moving the minds of the hearers wins credibility in speaking. For the power of teaching lies in argumentation, but the power of stirring in amplification. But when argumentation itself is furnished with amplification, then amplification itself is said to do both, to teach or prove, and to move or sway. From what has been said we understand two things: namely, the power of amplification, and its place among the parts of the speech. The remaining matters concerning the finding and handling of amplification are to be handed down, and we shall see them in the peroration.

units.la: DE EXORDIIS.
units.tr: ON THE EXORDIA.

units.la: C. F. Perge igitur ordine quatuor mihi istas partes explicare. C. P. Faciam, & à principiis primum ordiar. Quiæ
units.tr: C. F. Go on, then, and explain these four parts to me in order. C. P. I will, and I will begin with the beginnings.

units.la: Quæ quidem ducũtuur, aut ex personis, aut ex rebus ipsis. Sumuntur autem trium rerum gratia, ut amicè, ut intelligenter, ut attentè audiamur.
units.tr: These are drawn either from the persons or from the matters themselves. They are used for three purposes: so that we may be heard favourably, so that we may be heard intelligently, and so that we may be heard attentively.

units.la: C. F. Perge igitur ordine quatuor mihi istas partes explicare. ) Cognita patris uoluntate, cui nihil carius est, quàm filiũ esse quàm doctissimũ: liberè hortatur, ut pergat singulas explicare orationis partes.
units.tr: C. F. Go on, then, and explain these four parts to me in order. Here, knowing his father's wish, which is that his son be as learned as possible, he freely urges him to go on and explain each part of the speech.

units.la: C. P. Faciã, & à principijs primũm ordiar. ) Exordiorum duo sunt genera: principium, quod Græcè προοίμιον appellatur: & insinuatio, quæ ἐφοδος dicitur. Principium est, oratio perspicuè & protinus perficiens auditorem beneuolum, aut docilem, aut attentum. Insinuatio est, oratio quadam dissimulatione et circuitione obscurè subiens auditoris animum. In caussis honestis principio utimur: in turpibus uero, aut ualde humilibus, infinuationc: de quibus in reliquis Rhetoricis libris præcipitur copiosius. Hic autem Cicero de principio tantum præcepta tradit, illud haud dubiè innuens, honestas, non turpes caussas esse suscipiendas.
units.tr: C. P. I will, and I will begin with the beginnings. There are two kinds of exordium: the principium, which is called προοίμιον [prooimion] in Greek, and the insinuatio, which is called ἐφοδος [ephodos]. The principium is a speech that clearly and at once makes the hearer well disposed, or teachable, or attentive. The insinuatio is a speech that, by a certain dissimulation and indirection, creeps obscurely into the hearer's mind. We use the principium in honourable causes, and the insinuatio in shameful or very base ones. The rhetorical books elsewhere give fuller precepts on these. Here Cicero gives precepts only on the principium, and in doing so he clearly implies that honourable, not shameful, causes are to be taken up.

units.la: Quæ quidem ducuntur aut ex personis, aut ex rebus ipsis. ) Vnde principia ducãtur, aperire incipit. & cum dicit, ea aut ex personis, aut ex rebus ipsis esse ducenda, illud significat, non debere esse uulgaria, aut communia, aut longius petita: sed cohærentia, & ex ipsis uisceribus caussæ eruta: quemadmodum ipse in 2. de Orat. docet. Sed explicemus singula. Persona dicitur hominis qualitas, & conditio, quæcunque tādem illa sit: ut Rei, accusatoris, patroni, iudicis. de qua qui plura desiderat, eaq; erudita, legat caput 34. lib. 6. Elegantiarum Laurentij Vallæ. Res uero, caussa dicitur, quemadmodum libro 1. de Inuent. ostendit. Nam cum unde benevolētia comparetur docet: Ab nostra (inquit) ab aduersariorum, ab iudicum persona, & ab ipsa caussa. Deinde ubi, quomodo ab ipsa caussa comparetur, explicare uellet: Ab ipsis rebus (inquit) si nostram caussam laudando extollemus, aduersariorum caussam per contemptionem deprimemus. Quæ ex personis & rebus sumuntur, ad conciliandum pertinent. Conciliandi autem ratio tria continet: aut benevolentiā, ut amicè: aut docilitatem, ut intelligenter: aut diligentiam, ut attentè audiamur.
units.tr: These are drawn either from the persons or from the matters themselves. Here he begins to explain where the beginnings are to be drawn from. When he says that they should be drawn from the persons or from the matters themselves, he means that they should not be commonplace, or general, or far-fetched, but should cohere with the subject and be drawn out of the very heart of the cause, as he himself teaches in the second book of On the Orator. But let us explain each point. A person (persona) is the quality and condition of a man, whatever it may be: for example, of a defendant, an accuser, a advocate, a judge. Whoever wants more on this, and learned treatment of it, should read chapter 34 of book 6 of Laurentius Valla's Elegantiae. A matter (res) is called a cause, as he shows in the first book of On Invention. For when he teaches how goodwill is won, he says: "from our own person, from that of our opponents, from that of the judges, and from the cause itself." Then, wishing to explain how goodwill is won from the cause itself, he says: "From the matters themselves: if we exalt our own cause by praising it, we shall depress the opponents' cause by contempt." The things taken from persons and matters pertain to winning over the hearers. The method of winning them contains three aims: goodwill, so that we may be heard favourably; teachability, so that we may be heard intelligently; or attentiveness, so that we may be heard attentively.

units.la: Quorum primus locus est in personis, nostris, disceptatorum, aduersariorum, è quibus initia benevolentiæ conciliandæ comparantur: aut memeritis nostris, aut dignitate, aut aliquo genere uirtutis, & maxime liberalitatis, officij, iusticiæ, fidei, contrarisq; rebus in aduersarios conserendis, & cum iis, qui disceptant aliqua coniunctionis aut caussa, aut spe significanda: & si in nos aliquod odium, offensio ue collata sit, tollēda ea, minuenda ue, aut diluēdo, aut extenuando, aut compensando, aut deprecando.
units.tr: The first of these topics lies in the persons: our own, those of the parties in dispute, and those of our opponents. From these the beginnings of winning goodwill are derived: from our services, our dignity, or some kind of virtue, above all liberality, duty, justice, and good faith; by setting the opposite qualities against our adversaries; and by signalling some bond or hope of union with those who are in dispute. If any hatred or offence has been brought against us, it must be removed or lessened, either by refutation, by extenuation, by compensation, or by entreaty.

units.la: Quorum primus locus est in personis. ) Personæ autem tripertitæ sunt: Nostra, disceptatorum & aduersariorum. Quarum prima & postrema tam oratorem quàm reum comprehendit, cū his qui aut in nostris, aut in aduersarij partib. sunt. Disceptatorū verò nomine, auditorū genera intelligūtur, quorū est de caussa cognoscere. Quanquā, ut initiò dictū est, disceptator proprie ad iudicem & senatū pertinet, auscultator verò ad populum. Et quoniā reorū mentio facta est, Reos appello, quorū res est: hoc est, nō modò qui arguuntur, sed omnes quorū de re caussaq; disceptatur, ut Cicero de Orat. 1. definit. Quæ verò ducūtur à personis, omnia ad beneuolentiā referuntur. In qua tria sunt cōsiderāda: cōmendatio, criminatio, occupatio. Commendatio tribus rebus comparatur: aut meritorum nostrorum significatione, aut dignitatis, aut alicuius uirtutis. Merita sunt beneficia, quibus aliquos nobis obstrinximus. Dignitas est, alicuius honcsta, & cultu & honore & uerecundia digna autoritas: de Inuent. lib.2. Virtutes aut quæ præcipuè his requiruntur, sunt, liberalitas, officium, iusticia, fides, quæ uirtutes in uita aut in rebus gestis eluceant. Liberalitas, & fides, partes sunt iusticiæ. Officiū uero id esse dicitur, quod cur fiat, ratio reddi potest. Velut cū Cicero caussam reddit, cur quenq; defendat: ut pro Rabirio perduellionis reo, multas causas affert officij sui. Quid autem sint reliquæ uirtutes, ex philosophia petendum est, de quibus tamen infrà in quæstione dicetur. Differunt autem dignitas & uirtutes, quòd uirtutes semper sunt laudabiles, sed non semper autoritate munitæ: quemadmodum nec uirtutibus dignitas. sunt enim sæpenumero uirtutes in homine priuato, ut in Socrate: & dignitas in eo qui uirtute caret, ut in Clodio. Quam quam reuera ea dignitas dici non debet, quæ cum honestate coniuncta non est. Perfectum autem id est, in quo utrunq; inuenitur: ut in Catone, & Cicerone. Criminatio commendationi contraria est. ergo ei omnia contraria conueniunt, quæ erūt in aduersarios conijcienda, ex quibus odium, invidia, uidia, & contemptio gignantur. In odium rapicimus, si quid ab aduersarijs spurcè, superbè, perfidiosè, crudeliter, cõfidenter, maliciosè, flagitiosè factum proferemus: ut Cicero in Catilinam. In inuidiam trahemus, si uim, si potētiam, factionē, diuitias, incontinentiam, nobilitatem, clientelas, hospitia, sodalitates, affinitates aduersariorum proferemus, & ijs magis quàm ueritati eos confidere aperiemus. In contemptionem adducemus, si inertiam, ignauiam, desidiam, luxuriam aduersariorum proferemus. Ab auditorū aut persona beneuolentia colligetur, si cum eis aliqua coniunctionis aut caussa, aut spes significabitur: hoc est, si res eorū fortiter, sapienter, mansuetè, magnificè iudicatas dicemus: & si quæ de his existimatio, quæ iudicij expectatio sit, aperiemus. Tertia pars superest beneuolentiæ conciliandæ, quã occupatione appellauimus. eam νόσιμ Aristoteles lib. 3. uocat. hæc valet ad delendā ex animis malā existimationē. quod fit, aut tollendis offensionibus, aut minuēdis. Tollūtur negādo, & argumētis diluēdo: minuūtur extenuādo, quæ nimiū sunt ab aduersarijs adaucta: aut cōpensando, cū meliora aut maiora opponimus: aut deprecādo, si aliis adiumētis destituimur. horū exēpla in oratorib. obscura nō sunt: ut inuidiæ et beneuolētiæ, pro Quintio: meritorū, pro Deiotaro: officij, pro Sestio. Intelligenter autem ut audiamur, & attente, à rebus ipsis ordiendum est. Sed facillimè auditor discit, & quid agatur intelligit, si complectare à principio genus, naturāq; causas: si definias, si diuidas: si neq; prudentiam eius impedias confusione partium, nec memoriam multitudine. quæq; mox de narratione dilucida dicentur, eadem etiam huc poterunt rectè referri.
units.tr: The first of these topics lies in the persons. The persons are of three kinds: our own, those of the disputants, and those of our opponents. The first and last include both the orator and the defendant, together with those who are on our side or the opposing side. By the name of disputants are understood the kinds of hearers who have to decide the cause. Although, as was said at the beginning, the disputant properly belongs to the judge and the senate, and the listener to the people. And since mention has been made of defendants, I call them "those whose business it is," that is, not only those who are accused, but all those about whose matter and cause the dispute is, as Cicero defines it in the first book of On the Orator. Everything drawn from persons is referred to goodwill. Three things must be considered in it: commendation, accusation, and occupation. Commendation is achieved by three means: by pointing out our services, our dignity, or some virtue. Services are benefits by which we have bound certain people to us. Dignity is the authority of someone which is honourable and worthy of respect, reverence and honour (On Invention, book 2). The virtues that are chiefly required here are liberality, duty, justice, and good faith, which shine forth in a person's life or in what he has done. Liberality and good faith are parts of justice. Duty is that which can be given a reason for why it is done. Thus, when Cicero gives a reason why he defends this or that person, as in the speech for Rabirius, a defendant on a charge of treason, he offers many reasons for his own duty. What the remaining virtues are must be sought from philosophy, and these will be discussed below in the section on the question. Dignity and virtues differ in that virtues are always praiseworthy but not always supported by authority, just as dignity is not always accompanied by virtue. For virtues are often found in a private man, as in Socrates, and dignity in one who lacks virtue, as in Clodius. Yet, strictly speaking, that should not be called dignity which is not joined with honesty. That is perfect in which both are found, as in Cato and Cicero. Accusation is contrary to commendation, and so all the things that are contrary to it apply, which are to be thrown against the adversaries, and from which hatred, envy, ill-will and contempt arise. We stir up hatred if we bring forward whatever the adversaries have done shamefully, arrogantly, treacherously, cruelly, recklessly, maliciously, or scandalously, as Cicero does against Catiline. We bring them into envy if we bring forward the adversaries' power, influence, factions, riches, lack of self-control, nobility, clienteles, hospitalities, companionships and marriage alliances, and show that they rely on these rather than on the truth. We bring them into contempt if we bring forward the adversaries' inactivity, cowardice, idleness and luxury. Goodwill from the person of the hearers is gathered if some bond or cause of union or some hope with them is pointed out: that is, if we say that their affairs have been judged bravely, wisely, mildly and magnificently, and if we reveal what opinion there is of them and what expectation of their judgment. A third part remains for winning goodwill, which we have called occupation; Aristotle in book 3 calls it [νόσιμ]. This is useful for removing bad opinion from minds. It is done either by removing offences or by lessening them. They are removed by denying and refuting by arguments; they are lessened by extenuating whatever has been inflated too much by the adversaries, or by compensating when we set against them better or greater things, or by entreaty, if we are deprived of other aids. Examples of these in the orators are not obscure: of envy and goodwill, in the speech for Quinctius; of services, in the speech for Deiotarus; of duty, in the speech for Sestius. But in order that we may be heard intelligently and attentively, we must begin from the matters themselves. The hearer learns most easily, and understands what is being done, if you embrace from the start the genus, the nature and the causes; if you define; if you divide; and if you neither hinder his judgment by a confusion of parts nor burden his memory with a multitude. And what will soon be said about clear narration can also rightly be referred here.

units.la: Intelligenter autem ut audiamur, & attente.) Vt benevolentia à personis ducitur, sic docilitas & attetio à rebus ipsis, id est, ex causis est petenda.
units.tr: In order that we may be heard intelligently and attentively. Just as goodwill is drawn from the persons, so teachability and attention are to be sought from the matters themselves, that is, from the causes.

units.la: Sed facillime auditor discit.) Variae sunt in his de docilitate praeceptis explicandis sententiae: sed nos à Ciceronis verbis nihil aberrabimus, uiamq; faciliorem sequemur. Docilitatem quatuor rebus comparari ait. Propositione, cum dicit: Si complectare ab initio genus naturam que causas: definitione, & diuisione, & dilucide dicendo. Nā quod ait, Si neque prudentiam eius impedias confusione partium, nec memoriam multitudine, pertinet ad rectam diuidendi rationem, cuius duo dat praecepta: quorum alterum ad intelligētiam proprie, alterum ad memoriam pertinere ait. Qui æduo praecepta de Inuent.1. paucitatem & breuitatem appellat. Paucitas, genera cum partibus non confundit:Breuitas autem, nisi necessarium, nullum assumit uerbum. Addit etiam Cicero absolutionem, qua fit, ut nulla pars praetermittatur necessaria.sed propositione utitur in oratione pro Pompeio:Dicendum est enim,inquit,de Cn. Pompeij singulari eximiaq; uirtute.Definitione,pro C.Rabirio,ubi definit maiestatem. Diuisione,siue partitione,in eadem oratione pro lege Manilia, post propositionem: item statim initio pro Cluetio. Brevissima partitio duarum est partium, longissima quatuor, moderata trium. Ut autem dilucide dicamus,docet praecepta de dilucido & illustri dicendi genere,quae eadem sunt narrationis.
units.tr: But the hearer learns most easily. There are various opinions about explaining these precepts on teachability, but we shall not stray from Cicero's words, and we shall follow the easier path. He says teachability is won by four things: by a proposition, when he says: "If you embrace from the beginning the genus, the nature, and the causes"; by definition; by division; and by speaking clearly. For what he says, "If you neither hinder his judgment by a confusion of parts nor burden his memory with a multitude," pertains to the correct method of dividing, of which he gives two precepts: of which one pertains properly to understanding, the other, he says, to memory. These two precepts he calls, in On Invention book 1, fewness and brevity. Fewness does not confuse genera with parts; brevity admits no word unless it is necessary. Cicero also adds completeness, by which it happens that no necessary part is left out. He uses a proposition in the speech for Pompey: "For it must be said," he says, "about the singular and extraordinary virtue of Gnaeus Pompey." A definition, in the speech for Rabirius, where he defines majesty. A division, or partition, in the same speech for the Manilian law, after the proposition; likewise at the very beginning of the speech for Cluentius. The shortest partition has two parts, the longest four, the moderate three. As for speaking clearly, he teaches the precepts about the clear and illustrious kind of speaking, which are the same as those of narration.

units.la: Ut attente autem audiamur, trium rerum aliqua consequemur. Nam aut magna quaedam proponemus, aut necessaria, aut coniuncta cum ipsis, apud quos res agetur.
units.tr: So that we may be listened to attentively, we shall gain it through one of three things. For we shall either set forth certain great matters, or necessary ones, or matters connected with the very people before whom the case will be argued.

units.la: Ut attente aut audiamur. ) Tribus reb.parari dicit attentione:aut magnis,aut necessarijs,aut coniunctis cum ipsis apud quos agetur: id est: proprijs & priuatis eorum commodis commemorandis.Arist.3. lib.addit res mirabiles et iucundas.sed haec partim in magnis, partim in proprijs & priuatis continetur.
units.tr: Ut attente aut audiamur. He says that attention is obtained by three things: great matters, necessary matters, or matters connected with the very people before whom the case is pleaded; that is, by mentioning their own proper and private advantages. Aristotle, in book 3, adds remarkable and pleasing things, but these are partly contained in the great matters and partly in what is proper and private.

units.la: Nam & quæ ualde magna sunt, solent esse mirabilia: & unicuiq; propria utilitas suauis & iucunda est. utilis tamen fuerit etiam horum duorum seperata consideratio. Quod si non attentos, sed negligentes & solutos auditores habere voluerimus, quod interdum utile est, dicemus rem esse paruam, nihil ad eos pertinentem, molestam, & usitatam. Item attentos & dociles facere commune est omnium partium: neq; principij magis proprium, quàm reliquarum. Faciliora etiam in principijs, quod & attenti tum maximè sunt, cum omnia expectant: & dociles magis initijs esse possunt.quod & Aristoteles lib.3. & Cicero de Orat. lib.2. testantur. Illud uero etiam Aristotelis tenendum est,hæc omnia esse extra causam posita. Nam & qui malam causam habere volunt, proœmijs utuntur. Nam in quouis loco commorari potius, melius est eis, quàm in ipsa causa: & ad depravatum auditorem spectant, & ad eum qui libenter audit,quæ nihil ad rem faciunt. nam nisi talis sit, nihil opus erit proœmio, sed sufficit id quod causa postulat,summatim dicere: ut iudex caput illud,tanquam corpus causæ totius habeat. Illud etiam sciendum est,quæ præcepta sunt attentionis,eadem ad docilitatem pertinere.ucrè enim Cornificius:Docilis is,inquit,est, qui attente uult audire. Sit autem hoc postremum attentionis præceptum & clausula: Atte rogabimus ut attentè audiant. Quemadmodum Cicero pro Cluentio: Quaeso ut me attentè benigneq; audiatis item in cursu orationis reliquae: Sed attendite animos ad ea quae auditis, ut contra Rullum ait.
units.tr: For things that are very great are usually remarkable, and each person's own advantage is agreeable and pleasing. Still, it will be useful to consider these two separately. But if we wish our hearers to be inattentive, careless and relaxed, which is sometimes useful, we shall say that the matter is small, has nothing to do with them, is tiresome and commonplace. Likewise, making the hearers attentive and teachable is common to all parts of the speech, and belongs no more to the beginning than to the rest. It is also easier to do in the beginnings, since hearers are most attentive when they expect everything, and are more teachable at the start; Aristotle in book 3 and Cicero in De Oratore book 2 bear witness to this. But we must also keep to what Aristotle said, that all these things lie outside the cause itself. For those who wish to have a bad cause also use exordia: it is better for them to linger on something other than the cause itself, and they aim at a dull hearer and at one who gladly listens to things that have nothing to do with the matter. For if the hearer were not such, there would be no need for an exordium, and it would be enough to state briefly what the cause requires, so that the judge has that point as the head of the whole case, as it were its body. We must also know that the precepts for gaining attention pertain equally to making the hearer teachable. For Cornificius rightly says: "He is teachable who wishes to listen attentively." Let this final precept of attention also serve as the closing clause: "Finally, we shall ask that they listen attentively," as Cicero says in Pro Cluentio: "I beg that you listen to me attentively and kindly," and likewise in the course of the rest of the speech: "But attend closely to the things you hear," as he says against Rullus.

units.la: Sit autem hoc etiã in praeceptis, ut si quando tempus ipsum, aut res, aut locus, aut interuentus alicuius, aut interpellatio, aut ab aduersario dictum aliquod, & maxime in perorando, dederit occasionem nobis ali-quam, ut dicamus aliquid ad tempus apte, ne derelinquamus. & quae suo loco de amplificatione dicemus, multa ex his poterunt ad principiorum praecepta transferri.
units.tr: This also belongs among the precepts: if ever the occasion itself, or the matter, or the place, or some interruption of someone, or some interjection, or something said by the opponent, and especially in the peroration, offers us some opportunity to say something fittingly at the moment, we should not let it go. And many of the things we shall say in their place about amplification can be transferred from these to the precepts of the beginnings.

units.la: Sit autem hoc etiam in praeceptis. ) Praeceptum hoc generale est, docetque; non a personis et causis solum, verum etiam ex personarum & causarum adiunctis, principia duci solere. Personis enim applicantur non liberi modo, sed etiam propinquitates, amicitiae, regiones, civitates: & si quid aliud eius quem defendimus personam attingit, ad causam extra pertinet. tempus, unde principium pro Caelio: locus, unde pro Deiotaro: habitus, unde pro Milone: opinio, unde in Verrem: ac ne omnia enumerem, fama iudiciorum, expectatio vulgi, ut pro Sex. Rosc. nihil enim horum in causa est, ad causam tamen pertinet. Sic Quintilianus lib. 4. Idcirco autem sic interdum licet exordiri, ne oratio meditata esse videatur. Nam sic de improviso exordientes, fidem maiorem emerebimur. Quod autem Cicero adiungit, sumendam esse occasionem exordij ab eo potissimum, quod adversarius dixerit in perorando: Cur id fieri debeat, docet Aristoteles Rhetoricorum libro tertio: Quia accusator in peroratione calumniatur, defensor vicissim calumniis medetur in exordio.
units.tr: This also belongs among the precepts.) This is a general precept, and it teaches that beginnings are usually drawn not only from the persons and the causes but also from the circumstances of the persons and causes. For to persons are applied not only children but also kinships, friendships, regions and cities; and whatever else touches the person whom we defend pertains to the cause from outside. Time gives rise to the beginning in Pro Caelio; place, in Pro Deiotaro; condition, whence in Pro Milone; opinion, whence in In Verrem; and, not to list everything, the reputation of the courts and the expectation of the crowd, as in Pro Sexto Roscio. For none of these is part of the cause, yet they pertain to the cause. So Quintilian in book 4. Moreover, it is sometimes permitted to begin in this way so that the speech does not seem prepared in advance; for by beginning thus unexpectedly we shall gain greater trust. As for what Cicero adds, that the beginning should be taken above all from what the opponent has said in the peroration, Aristotle in book 3 of the Rhetoric explains why this should be done: because the accuser slanders in the peroration, and the defender in turn remedies the slanders in the exordium.

units.la: Et quae suo loco de amplificatione dicemus.) illic enim de rebus magnis, et utilibus, et necessariis tractatur, quae ad conciliandum auditorem maxime faciunt.
units.tr: And what we shall say in its place about amplification: for there great, useful and necessary matters are treated, which contribute most to winning over the listener.

units.la: DE NARRATIONE.
units.tr: DE NARRATIONE (On Narration)

units.la: C. F. Quid in narratione? quae tandem conseruanda sunt? C. P. Quoniam narratio est rerum explicatio, & quaedam quasi sedes ac fundamentum constituendae fidei, ea sunt in ea seruanda maxime, quae etiam in reliquis fere dicendi partibus, quae partim sunt necessaria, partim sunt
units.tr: C. F. What must be observed in narration? What, finally, is to be preserved in it? C. P. Since narration is the explanation of things, and a kind of seat and foundation on which belief is built, those qualities must be preserved in it above all which are nearly the same in the other parts of speaking, some of which are necessary, and some

units.la: Verum sic ut narrationi esse memoriter aliquem, non elaborata. assumpta ad ornandum. Nam ut dilucidè, probabiliterq; narremus, necessarium est, sed assumimus etiam suauitatem: ergo ad dilucidè narrandum eadem illa superiora explicandi & illustrandi præcepta repetemus, in quibus est breuitas: eaq; sæpissimè in narratione laudatur, de qua suprà dictum est.
units.tr: But so that narration should have some memorable quality, not laboured, but taken up for ornament. For to narrate clearly and credibly is necessary, but we also take on pleasantness. Therefore, to narrate clearly, we shall repeat those same precepts of explaining and illustrating given above, in which brevity lies, and this is praised most often in narration, as was said above.

units.la: C. F. Quid in narratione, quæ tandem conferuanda sunt.) In narratione quinq; uidenda sunt: quid sit narratio, quot eius genera, quæ ei tribuenda, tum quomodo ea comparanda sint, postremò quando sit narratione utendum. Hoc postremum suprà in collocatione indicatum est: restat igitur, ut reliqua quatuor uideamus.
units.tr: C. F. What must be preserved in narration? In narration five things are to be considered: what narration is, how many kinds of it there are, what must be assigned to it, then how it is to be prepared, and finally when narration is to be used. The last of these was indicated above in the discussion of arrangement, so it remains that we consider the other four.

units.la: C. P. Quoniam narratio est rerum explicatio, & quasi sedes.) Hæc est narrationis definitio, quæ fere eadem est quæ locorum, unde argumenta sumuntur. id autem ita circo, quia in ea tanquam in loco fœcundissimo latet argumentorum omnium semina, quæ in confirmatione singula sunt explicanda. Fundamentum uero, quòd tanquam fundamento domus reliquæ structura, sic oratiois et probationum narratio nititur & sustetatur. Omnis enim orationis reliquæ fons est narratio, ut ait Cic. de Orat. lib.2. Quæ partim sunt necessaria.) Indicat his verbis, duo esse narrationum genera, quorum alterum necessarium appellat, alterum assumptum.
units.tr: C. P. Since narration is the explanation of things, and as it were a seat. This is the definition of narration, which is nearly the same as that of the topics from which arguments are drawn. It is called so because, as in a most fertile place, the seeds of all the arguments lie hidden in it, each of which is to be explained in the confirmation. It is called a foundation because, as the rest of a house's structure rests on its foundation, so the narration supports and sustains the rest of the speech and the proofs. For, as Cicero says in De Oratore, book 2, narration is the source of all the rest of the oration. "Some of which are necessary": by these words he indicates that there are two kinds of narration, of which he calls one necessary and the other assumptum (taken up).

units.la: Sic etiam Fabius, duas esse in iudiciis narrationis species exîstimat: alteram ipsius causæ propriā, altera rerū ad causam pertinentiū expositione, quam assumptam Cicero vocauit. Dilucida, & probabilis narratio, necessaria est et propria: Suauitas verò assumpta, & tanquam extranea. Sunt igitur eius attributa tria: Dilucidum, Probabile, & Suaue. Additur etiam breuitas: sed eam in dilucido genere contineri dicit Cicero. Sed ut dilucida sit narratio, ex dilucido & illustri dicendi orationis genere ratio petenda est: de quibus suprà est explicatum. Quod aut ad breuitatem attinet narrationis, ridiculos censet Aristoteles eos, qui eam iubent breuem esse oportere: idemque facere eos dicit, ut si pistor interrogaret, durum an molle pinseret, quasi non esset inter ea mediocritas, nimirum ut bene pinseret: hoc est, neque durum, neque molle: sic narrationem neque longam neque breuem esse oportere innuens, sed talē, quæ causæ satisfaciat probè. quam sententiam indicant Antonius lib.2. de Orat. ubi de narratione præcipit. Quo in loco non solum de breuitate idem sentit, uerumetiā de perspicuitate. Apertam, inquit, narrationem tam esse oportet, quàm cateras: hoc magis in hac elaborandum est, quod & difficilius est, non esse obscurum in re narranda, quàm aut in principio, aut in argumento, aut in purgando, aut perorando: & maiore periculo hæc pars orationis obscura est, quàm cæteræ: vel quia, si quo alio in loco, est dictum quid obscurius, tantum id perit quod dictum est: narratio obscura totam obcæcat orationem. vel quod illa possis, semel, si obscurius dixeris, dicere alio loco planius, narrationis unus est in caussa locus. erit autem perspicua narratio, si verbis usitatis, si ordine temporum conseruato, si non interrupte narrabitur.
units.tr: So too Fabius thinks there are two kinds of narration in judicial cases: one proper to the cause itself, the other the exposition of matters pertaining to the cause, which Cicero called assumptum. A clear and credible narration is necessary and proper; but pleasantness is assumed, and as it were extraneous. Therefore its attributes are three: clear, credible, and pleasant. Brevity is also added, but Cicero says that it is contained in the clear kind. But for narration to be clear, the method is to be sought from the clear and illustrious kind of speaking, which has been explained above. As for the brevity of narration, Aristotle thinks ridiculous those who order that it must be brief. He says that they do the same as if a baker were to ask whether he should knead the dough hard or soft, as if there were no middle course, namely that he should knead it well, that is, neither hard nor soft. Thus he implies that narration should be neither long nor short, but of such a kind as adequately satisfies the cause. Antonius in book 2 of De Oratore indicates the same opinion, where he gives precepts on narration. In that place he thinks the same not only about brevity but also about perspicuity. "A narration," he says, "ought to be as open as the other parts. This must be laboured over in this part more than in others, because it is more difficult not to be obscure in relating a matter than in the exordium, the argument, the refutation, or the peroration; and this part of the speech is obscure with greater danger than the others: either because if something is said somewhat obscurely in another place, only that which was said is lost, whereas an obscure narration blinds the whole oration; or because in the other parts, if you have spoken somewhat obscurely, you can say it more plainly at another point, whereas the narration has only one place in the case. A narration will be perspicuous if it uses common words, if the order of times is kept, and if it is related without interruption."

units.la: Probabilis autem erit, si personis, si temporibus, si locis, ea quæ narrabuntur, consentient, si cuiuscunque facti & euenti caussa ponetur, si testata dici uidebitur, si cum hominum opinione, autoritate, si cū lege, cūmo re, cum religione coniuncta, si probitas narrantis significabitur, si antiquitas, si memoria, si orationis veritas, & vitæ fides.
units.tr: A narration will be credible if the things related agree with the persons, the times, and the places; if the cause of each deed and event is given; if it seems to be attested; if it is joined with the opinion and authority of men, with law, custom, and religion; if the probity of the narrator is shown; if there is antiquity, memory, the truth of the speech, and the trustworthiness of his life.

units.la: Probabilis autem erit.) Iam de secundo attributo, siue virtute narrationis præcipit, & quibus rebus ea comparanda sit, docet: ut probabilis, siue verisimilis, siue credibilis sit. Probabilis ea narratio
units.tr: A narration will be credible. Now he gives precepts on the second attribute, or virtue, of narration, and teaches by what means it is to be prepared, so that it may be credible, or plausible, or believable. A credible narration

units.la: Quæ partim sunt necessaria.) Indicat his verbis,duo esse narrationum genera, quorum alterum necessarium appellat, alterum assumptum.
units.tr: "Some of which are necessary": by these words he indicates that there are two kinds of narration, of which he calls one necessary and the other assumed.

units.la: Handwritten marginal annotation in Greek, right margin, not transcribed. narratio dicitur, quæ rationibus est munita. Assumitur aut rationes, ex rerū attributis, quas circū stantias uocāt, ex personis, temporibus, locis, caussit, factis, euentis: de quib. infrà in uerisimilib. explicabit Cicero. Itē ex testimonijs, & opinione: item ex autoritate, more, lege, religione: itē ex probata narratis, antiquitate, memoria, fide. De testimonijs suo loco infrà. Opinio est, nō ex causis, & certis principijs, sed signis collecta scientia. Autoritas, aut uirtute, aut fortuna parta existimatio. Lex est, iustorū iniustorūq; distinctio, & recta ratio in iubēdo, uetādo, et permittēdo sita. Mos, ius est, quod aut leuiter à natura tractum, aluit, & maius fecit usus, siue cōsuetudo. Religio est, superioris naturæ cultus. Probitas, quæ elucet ex uitæ genere integritas: ea cognoscitur ex ueritate, & fide: confirmat etiam antiquitas, & memoria. Antiquitatem intelligit, antiquitatis cognitionem, & multarum rerum usum, quæ prudētia cōtinentur: memoriā uero eam uim, per quā animus repetit ea quæ fuerunt. Huiusmodi enim hominibus facile credimus, quoniā graviores putamus, quàm ut metiri uclint, aut fallere. Sunt qui hæc duo membra coiungant: Si antiquitatis memoria, ut de Oratore, & in Bruto loquitur. Sed eadē propemodum sententia est, ueritas autem in oratione & conuentis cernitur: fides autem in tota uitæ constantia. quæ duo sub iusticia comprehenduntur, quemadmodum etiam religio. Et hæc sunt, quæ moratam faciunt narrationem, quæ sita sunt in probitate. Non est autem intelligendum, in narrando debere nos aut testes producere, aut legem morem ue proferre, quæ sunt confirmationis: sed ita narrare oportere, ut hæc pro nobis feramus: & quæ dicimus, cum his coniuncta esse uideantur.
units.tr: [Handwritten marginal annotation in Greek in the right margin, not transcribed.] is called a narration that is fortified by reasons. Reasons are taken from the attributes of things, which they call circumstances: from persons, times, places, causes, deeds, and events. Cicero will explain these more fully below, in the discussion of probabilities. Likewise from testimonies and opinion; likewise from authority, custom, law, and religion; likewise from the proven character of the narrator, antiquity, memory, and trustworthiness. Testimonies will be treated in their place below. Opinion is knowledge gathered not from causes and certain principles but from signs. Authority is esteem gained either by virtue or by fortune. Law is the distinction between the just and the unjust, and right reason lying in commanding, forbidding, and permitting. Custom is law which, drawn lightly from nature, has been nourished and made greater by use, or habit. Religion is the worship of a higher nature. Probity is integrity, which shines forth from the kind of life; it is known from truth and trustworthiness. Antiquity and memory also confirm it. By antiquity he means knowledge of antiquity and experience of many things, which are contained in prudence; by memory he means that power by which the mind recalls what has been. For we readily believe such men, since we think them too serious to wish to measure or deceive. There are those who join these two members: "the memory of antiquity," as he speaks of it in De Oratore and in the Brutus. But the sense is nearly the same; truth, however, is seen in the speech and in its agreement, and trustworthiness in the constancy of the whole life. These two are comprehended under justice, just as religion is too. These are the things that make the narration moral, and they lie in probity. But it is not to be understood that in narrating we ought to produce witnesses, or cite law or custom, for these belong to confirmation; rather we ought to narrate in such a way that we bring these things forward on our side, and that what we say seems to be joined with them.

units.la: Suauis autem narratio est, quæ habet admirationes, expectationes, exitus inopinatos, si interpositos motus animorū, colloquia personarum, dolores, iracūdias, metus, lætitias, cupiditates. sed iam ad reliqua pergamus.
units.tr: Narration is pleasing when it contains surprises, expectations, unexpected outcomes, emotions of the mind that are woven in, conversations between persons, griefs, angers, fears, joys and desires. But let us now go on to the remaining matters.

units.la: Suauis autem narratio est. ) Suauitatis præcepta, ut etiam probabilitatis, supra in generibus dicendi tradita sunt. Sed ea sucrunt orationis, hæc ucrò caussæ & negotij. Suauitatem narrationis Cicero hoc loco, in duobus ponit: in rebus uidelicet, & in tractatione. Res siue facta partim sunt læta, partim tristia. nam etiam res tristes ad suauitatem pertinent, & delectatione quandā: itā tamen, ut si ijs exponantur, ad quos non pertinet dolor.
units.tr: Narration is pleasing. The rules for pleasantness, like those for plausibility, were given above among the kinds of speaking. But those were rules of the style, whereas these concern the case and the subject matter. Here Cicero places the pleasantness of narration in two things: in the matters themselves and in their handling. The matters, or deeds, are partly joyful and partly sad. Sad matters also contribute to pleasantness, and with a certain delight, provided they are related to those to whom the grief does not pertain.

units.la: Suauis autem narratio est. ) Suauitatis præcepta, ut etiam probabilitatis, supra in generibus dicendi tradita sunt. dolor. ueluti si patri narres, filiuni, qui fanus cubitum iuerat, mane inuentum mortuum: hæc certè fabula eum non delectabit. uerùm si aut iudicibus, aut alijs id exposueris, ipsa rei nouitas, & casus inexpectatus, afferet cum admiratione suauitatem. Res præterea læta, siue tristes, aut magnæ sunt, aut raræ, aut paruæ, aut uulgares. sed parua & uulgata ridiculâ esse debent, & ad recordandum grata, alioqui nullam habebunt delectationem. Tractatio deinde sita est in colloquijs personarum, qui Διαλογισμοί à Græcis nominantur, à nostris etiam sermocinationes: atq; inter ornamenta numerantur, ut lib.4. ad Heren. uidere licet. Posita est etiam in consiliorum explicatione, ac tertio, in animorum permotione.
units.tr: Narration is pleasing. The rules for pleasantness, like those for plausibility, were given above among the kinds of speaking. grief. For example, if you tell a father that his son, who had gone to bed well, was found dead in the morning, that story will certainly not delight him. But if you set it out to judges or others, the very novelty of the event and the unexpected accident will bring pleasantness along with wonder. Moreover, joyful or sad matters are either great, rare, small or common. But small and common matters ought to be amusing and pleasant to recall, otherwise they will have no delight. Handling then lies in the conversations of persons, which the Greeks call dialogues [Διαλογισμοί] and we call sermocinations. These are counted among the ornaments, as can be seen in Book 4 of the Ad Herennium. Handling also lies in the explanation of plans and, third, in the stirring of the emotions.

units.la: DE CONFIRMATIONE.
units.tr: ON CONFIRMATION.

units.la: C. F. Nempe ea sequuntur, quæ ad faciendam fidem pertinent. C. P. Ita est, quæ quidem in confirmationem, & in reprehensionem diuiduntur. Nam in confirmādo, nostra probare uolumus, in reprehendendo redarguere contraria. Quoniam igitur omne, quod in controuersiam uenit, id aut sit, nec ne sit, aut quid sit, aut quale sit, quæritur; in primo coiectura ualet, in altero definitio, in tertio ratio.
units.tr: C.F. Surely those things follow which pertain to producing belief. C.P. So it is; these are divided into confirmation and refutation. For in confirming we wish to prove our own points, and in refuting we wish to overturn the contrary ones. Since whatever comes into controversy is asked either whether it is or is not, or what it is, or what sort it is: in the first, conjecture has its force; in the second, definition; in the third, reasoning.

units.la: C. F. Nempe ea sequuntur, quae ad faciendam fidem pertinent.) De fide facienda, quae pars tertia orationis posita est, docere incipit. Fidem autem supra firmam opinionem esse definiuit: ea autem fit argumentis, quae ex locis eruuntur. Sed mirari quis hoc loco posit, cur, cum initio quae ad fidem faciendam pertinerent, tradiderit, locosq; demonstrauerit, in quibus latent argumenta: nunc de fide rursus tractet? Respondendum est, non idem hic tradere, quod illic de fide facienda tradiderit. nam communes ibi omnium quaestionum locos indicauit: hic vero proprios. singulis statibus causarum assignat, quibus controuersiae muniantur: illic fontes magnarum quaestionum, hic riuulos ad paruas & angustas quaestiones inducit. sic enim hosce controuersiarum locos de Orat. 2. appellat Antonius.
units.tr: C.F. Surely those things follow which pertain to producing belief. The author begins to teach about producing belief, which is set as the third part of the speech. He defined belief as a firm opinion, and this is produced by arguments drawn from the topics. But someone may wonder here why, after having taught earlier what pertains to producing belief and shown the topics in which arguments lie hidden, he now treats belief again. It must be answered that he does not here teach the same thing he taught there. For there he indicated the common topics of all questions; here, the proper ones. He assigns them to the individual states of cases, by which controversies are fortified. There he leads to the sources of great questions; here he leads to the rivulets for small and narrow questions. For so Antonius in De Oratore 2 calls these topics of controversies.

units.la: C. P. Ita est, quae quidem in confirmationem & reprehensionem diuiduntur.) Fidem in duas partes diuidit, in confirmationem & reprehensionem, siue refutationem. Altera enim in confirmandis nostris, altera in confutandis contrarijs rationibus versatur.
units.tr: C.P. So it is; these are divided into confirmation and refutation. He divides belief into two parts, confirmation and refutation, or rebuttal. The one is concerned with confirming our own arguments, the other with overthrowing the contrary ones.

units.la: Quoniam igitur omne quod in controuersiam uenit.) Iam controuersiarum genera tria ponit,
units.tr: Since therefore whatever comes into controversy. Now he sets out three kinds of controversy.

units.la: n & & singulis generibus suos accommodat locos. nam, An fit, nec ne, coniectura quaeritur: Quid fit, definitione explicatur: Quale fit, ratione confirmatur. Primus status dicitur facti, secundus non minus, tertius iuris & aequitatis: idcirco rationis mentionem fecit. Primi generis exemplum est: Sustulerit ne veneno Oppianicum Cluentius? Alterius: Minuerit ne maiestate Rabirius? Tertij, in quo qualitas facti quaeritur, hoc est, iure ne an iniuria factum sit: ut, Recte ne Clodium Milo interfecerit? Horum statuum locos omnes sigillatim explicabit orator, idcirco iam initium facit a coniectura.
units.tr: He assigns to each kind its own topics. For whether a thing is or is not is sought by conjecture; what it is is explained by definition; what sort it is is confirmed by reasoning. The first is called the status of fact, the second the status of the name or definition, and the third the status of law and equity; therefore he has made mention of reasoning. An example of the first kind: Did Cluentius remove Oppianicus by poison? Of the second: Did Rabirius diminish the majesty (of the people)? Of the third, in which the quality of the deed is asked, that is, whether it was done rightly or wrongly: for example, Did Milo rightly kill Clodius? The orator will explain all the topics of these statuses one by one, and therefore he now makes a beginning with conjecture.

units.la: DE CONIECTVRAE locis.
units.tr: On the places of conjecture.

units.la: C. F. Teneo istam distributionem. Nunc coniecturae locos quaero. C. P. In verisimilibus, & in proprijs rerum notis posita est tota. Sed appellemus docendi gratia verisimile, quod plerunque ita fiat, ut adolescentiam procliviorem esse ad libidinem. Propriae autem notae argumentum, quod nunquam aliter fit, certūqs declarat, ut fumus ignem.
units.tr: C. F. I accept that division. Now I am looking for the places of conjecture. C. P. The whole matter rests on probabilities and on the proper signs of things. But, for the sake of teaching, let us call probable what usually happens in a certain way, as youth is more inclined to lust. The argument drawn from a proper sign, which never happens otherwise and clearly declares the fact, is like smoke for fire.

units.la: C. F. Teneo istam distributionem, nunc coniectura. &tura locos quaro. ) Coniectura, quae γεχνσμὸς Graecè dicitur, latißimè patet, ita ut uix alius locus pateat latius, aut plures habeat inuestigandi uias. Nec est locus ullus, qui magis oratoris ostendat ingenium.
units.tr: C. F. I accept that division. Now I seek the places of conjecture. Conjecture, which is called [στοχασμός] in Greek, extends more widely than almost any other place, and it offers more ways of inquiry. Nor is there any place that better shows the talent of the orator.

units.la: C. P. In uerisimilibus & in proprijs rerum notis posita est tota. ) Coniectūrae partes facit duas: uerisimilia, & proprias rerum notas. Verisimilia siue probabilia intelligit, quae Aristot. lib. 1. Rhet. εἰκότα uocat: & proprias rerum notas, quae ille τεκμήρια dicit, id quod ex sequentibus definitionibus patebit.
units.tr: C. P. The whole lies in probabilities and in the proper signs of things. Conjecture has two parts: probabilities, and the proper signs of things. By probabilities he means what Aristotle in the first book of the Rhetoric calls [εἰκότα]; and by proper signs, what he calls [τεκμήρια], as will become clear from the definitions that follow.

units.la: Sed appellemus uerisimile, quod plerunq; ita fiat.) Haec definitio ex codē Aristotelis loco sumpta est. Cui duo genera signorū subijcit. unū, quod ita se habet ad id cuius signū est, sicuti singulae res ad uniuersum genus: ut si quis affirmet signū esse, uiros sapientes esse etiā iustos, quia Socrates & sapiēs & iustus erat, quod quidē necessariū nō est, facileq; dissolui potest. Alterū genus signorum, quod ita se habet ad id cuius est signū, ut quod est in uniuerso genere, ad id quod in parte est: uelut si quis diceret, quempiam febri laborare, signum esse, quòd crebrò respiret. quod etiam facilè refelli potest, quoniam crebrò interdum respirant alias ob caussas, ut cursu, aut alio labore fatigati. Verum hæc duo signorum genera non ita subtisubtiliter distinguit Cicero, & quoniam utrunq; infirmum est, uno nomine comprehendit: ut, Adolescentiam procliuiorem esse ad libidinem, quàm proueētiorem ætatem. quod quidem necessarium non est in omnibus, cum contrà fieri sæpe reperiatur.
units.tr: But let us call probable what usually happens in a certain way. This definition is taken from the same passage of Aristotle. To it Cicero adds two kinds of sign. The first is related to that of which it is the sign as a single thing is to the whole genus: as if someone should claim that a sign that men are wise is that they are also just, because Socrates was both wise and just. This is not necessarily so and can easily be refuted. The second kind of sign is related to that of which it is the sign as what is found in the whole genus is to what is found in a part: as if someone said that a man suffering from fever is shown by the sign that he often breathes hard. This too can easily be refuted, since people sometimes breathe hard for other reasons, such as when they are worn out by running or some other labour. Cicero does not distinguish these two kinds of sign so subtly, and since both are weak, he comprehends them under one name: that youth is more inclined to lust than mature age. This is certainly not necessary in every case, since the opposite is often found to happen.

units.la: Propria autem notæ argumentum.) Definitio est necessariæ conclusionis, quæ τεκμήριον dicitur. τέκμαρ enim prisca Græcorum lingua, teste Aristotele, idem erat quod extremum atque ultimum, quod nullo modo solui posse existimarent. ut si quis dicat, aliquam mulierem peperisse, signū esse, quoniā lac habeat. est enim id propria eius rei notā & signum, quod refelli non potest: idcirco dixit Cicero, id esse, quod nunquam aliter fit, certumq; declarat, ut fumus ignem: nam si est fumus, est etiam ignis necessario. Verum quoniam necessarijs raro utuntur oratores, verisimilibus autem frequentius, idcirco de his plura dicit: sunt enim fere in opinione posita, & quæ aliter se habere possunt, quæ in causis controuersijs que versantur.
units.tr: But the argument from a proper sign. This is the definition of a necessary conclusion, which is called [τεκμήριον]. For [τέκμαρ], in the ancient Greek language, as Aristotle attests, meant the same as the extreme and final point, which they thought could in no way be dissolved. For example, if someone says that a certain woman has given birth, the sign is that she has milk; for this is a proper mark and sign of that thing, which cannot be refuted. Therefore Cicero said that it is what never happens otherwise and clearly declares, like smoke for fire: for if there is smoke, there is necessarily fire too. But since orators use necessary arguments rarely and probable ones more often, he therefore speaks more about the latter. For probabilities mostly rest on opinion, and they are the things that can be otherwise, which are at issue in disputed cases.

units.la: VERISIMILIVM INVEN- tio & partitio.
units.tr: The invention and division of probabilities.

units.la: Verisimilia reperiuntur ex partibus, & quasi membris narrationis. ea sunt in personis, in locis, in temporibus, in factis, in euentis, in rerum ip-sarum, negotiorumque naturis. In personis, naturae primum spectantur, ualetudinis, figurae, uirium, aetatis, marium, foeminarum. atque haec quidem in corpore.
units.tr: Probabilities are found from the parts, and as it were the limbs, of the narration. These are in persons, places, times, deeds, events, and in the natures of things and affairs. In persons, their natural qualities are considered first: health, figure, strength, age, male and female. And these concern the body.

units.la: Verisimilia reperiuntur ex partibus & quasi membris narrationis.) Sedem, fundamentum, & fontem uerisimilium docet esse narrationem: quod diligenter notandum est, ut supra quoq; in narratione dictum est. Nam in narratione duo sunt: personae, & res. ex personarum igitur attributis & rebus, uerisimilia omnia eliciuntur. Res autem sunt, locus, tempus, facta, euentus, & rerum ipsarum negotiorumque natura, quae adiecta personis sex constituunt uerisimilium genera.
units.tr: Probabilities are found from the parts and, as it were, the limbs of the narration. He teaches that narration is the seat, foundation and source of probabilities; this must be carefully noted, as was also said above in the discussion of narration. For in narration there are two things, persons and things. Therefore all probabilities are drawn from the attributes of persons and from things. Things are place, time, deeds, events, and the nature of things and affairs, which, added to persons, make up six kinds of probabilities.

units.la: In personis naturae primum spectantur.) Personae locus in natura & fortuna spectatur. In natura duo sunt consideranda, corporis attributa, & animi: corporis, ut ualetudo, figura, uires, aetas, mares, foeminae. Valetudo, ut si quis aegrotet, an prospera ualetudine utatur, in quo etiam genera morborum considerantur. Figura, ut sit ne deförmis an formosus, procerus an brevis. Virēs, robore ne polleat, an contrà sit imbecillis. Aetas, in-fans, fans, puer, adolescens, uiridi ætate, an decrepita, & senio affecta. Mares an fœmina, qui ad sexum referuntur. facilius enim ueneficium creditur in fœmina, quam in uiro: & contrà, cædes facta, aut furtum, in uiro, quam in fœmina.
units.tr: In persons, natural qualities are considered first. The person is viewed in respect of nature and fortune. In nature two things are to be considered, the attributes of body and of mind. Of the body: health, figure, strength, age, male and female. Health: whether someone is sick or enjoys good health, where the kinds of illness are also considered. Figure: whether he is ugly or handsome, tall or short. Strength: whether he is powerful in vigour or, on the contrary, weak. Age: infant, boy, youth, in the green age, or decrepit and worn out by old age. Male or female, which relate to sex: for poisoning is more readily believed of a woman than of a man, and conversely, homicide or theft is more readily believed of a man than of a woman.

units.la: Animi autē, aut quemadmodū affecti sunt, uirtutibus, uitiis, artibus, inertiis: aut quemadmodū commoti, cupiditate, metu, uoluptate, molestia. atqz hæc quidem in natura spe ƈtantur. In fortuna, genus, amicitiæ, liberi, propinqui, affines, opes, honores, potestates, diuitiæ, libertas, & ea quæ sunt iis contraria.
units.tr: But of the mind: either how they are disposed, by virtues, vices, skills and lack of skills; or how they are moved, by desire, fear, pleasure, or pain. These are considered in nature. In fortune: birth, friendships, children, relatives, connections by marriage, resources, honours, powers, riches, liberty, and the things contrary to these.

units.la: Animi autem. ) Recenset animorum attributa, quæ duplicia sunt: aut habitus, aut commotiones. De habitu intelligit, cum dicit, Quemadmodum affecti sunt: de commotionibus uero, cum ait, Quemadmodum commoti. Ad habitū referuntur, uirtutes & uitia, artes & inertiæ. Sed illa sunt uoluntatis, hæ aut intelligentiæ. Et obseruanda est uox inertiæ, quæ non aliquam significat ignauiam, aut pigritiam, sed artis priuationem, quod uocabulum à Cicerone factum & nouatum est. Artes autem cuiuscunq; generis intelligendæ sunt, siue scientiæ & cognitionis, quæ ἐπιστήμαι dicuntur GreGræce: siue actionis, quæ πραντικὰ: itē quæ opus aliquod post se relinquunt, & in faciendo uersantur: quas μηχανικὰς Græci uocant. Commotiones autē sunt quatuor, Cupiditas, metus, uoluptas, molestia: ex quib. cōiectura sumitur ad aliquod factum uel excusandū, uel damnandū. ut, Metuebat Milonē Clodius, ergo etiā oderat: ergo é uiuis sub latiū uoluit, & de eo interficiēdo cogitauit. Quæ hactenus recensuimus, in persona natura spectātur. Sequitur fortuna, in qua hæc spectari solent.
units.tr: But of the mind. He lists the attributes of the mind, which are twofold: either habits or emotions. He means habits when he says "how they are disposed," and emotions when he says "how they are moved." To habits belong virtues and vices, skills and lack of skills. But the former belong to the will, the latter to the understanding. The word inertia must be noted: it does not signify some idleness or laziness, but a privation of skill; this word was coined and newly introduced by Cicero. Skills, moreover, are to be understood of any kind, whether of knowledge and understanding, which the Greeks call [ἐπιστήμαι], or of action, which they call [πρακτικά]; likewise those that leave some work behind them and are concerned with making, which the Greeks call [μηχανικά]. There are four emotions: desire, fear, pleasure, and pain. From these a conjecture is drawn either to excuse or to condemn some deed. For example: Clodius feared Milo, therefore he also hated him; therefore he wished him out of the living and thought about killing him. These we have so far listed as they are considered in the person's nature. Next comes fortune, in which these are usually considered.

units.la: Genus: ut, obscuro an claro genere ortus, bonisne an prauis parentibus. Amicitiæ: ut, quibus amicis, multis ne an paucis, bonis an improbis. Liberi: qui si liberaliter educati fuerint, & bonis moribus præditi, in parentum laude ponendum est: in uituperatione autem, si secus. Propinqui: nam propinquorum & affinium honestas & turpitudo, nonnihil etiam in suos redundat. Opes: quo nomine omnes magnæ res, quibus aliquis abundat, significantur. Honores: alicui habiti quæ præmia sunt uirtutis. Potestas: in qua magistratus, & omnis generis imperia intelligūtur. Diuitiæ: quæ in sola pecunia & fructibus cernuntur. Libertas, quæ est potestas uiuendi ut uelis: ut, seruus ne aliquis sit, an liber, an forte libertinus. Nam in his omnibus attributis fortuitis, contraria semper intelligēda sunt. Et hæc de personarū
units.tr: Birth: for example, whether someone was born of obscure or illustrious family, and of good or bad parents. Friendships: with what friends, many or few, good or bad. Children: if they have been liberally educated and endowed with good morals, this is to be placed to the parents' credit; if otherwise, to their blame. Relatives: for the honour or disgrace of relatives and connections by marriage spills over somewhat onto their own kin. Resources: a term under which all the great things in which someone abounds are signified. Honours: those bestowed on someone as rewards of virtue. Power: under which magistracy and every kind of command are understood. Riches: which consist in money and revenues alone. Liberty: which is the power to live as one wishes; for example, whether someone is a slave, or free, or perhaps a freedman. For in all these fortuitous attributes, the contraries must always be understood. And these are the attributes of persons,

units.la: attributis, in quibus tria genera rerum bonarum, totidemq; malarum cernere licuit: animi, corporis, & fortunæ, siue externa. Hæc nos breuiter, in tanta rerum sylua, qui tamen singulorum copiosam explicationem cupit, legat diligenter Aristotelis Rhetoricorum lib. 1. ubi de felicitate loquitur in genere deliberatiuo: itemq; paulo post de virtute & uitio, in genere demonstratiuo.
units.tr: in which we have been able to discern three kinds of good things and as many of bad: those of the mind, of the body, and of fortune, or external things. We have touched on these briefly, in such a great forest of matter. Whoever, however, desires a full explanation of each should carefully read the first book of Aristotle's Rhetoric, where he speaks of happiness in the deliberative genus, and likewise a little later of virtue and vice in the demonstrative genus.

units.la: In locis autem & illa naturalia, maritimi, an remoti à mari, plani, an mo tuosi, leues, an asperi, salubres, an pestilentes, opaci, an aprici: & illa fortuita, culti, an inculti, celebres, an deserti, coædificati, an uasti, obscuri, an rerum gestarum uestigijs nobilitati, consecrati, an profani.
units.tr: In places, the natural ones are: maritime or remote from the sea, flat or hilly, smooth or rough, healthy or pestilential, shaded or sunny; and the accidental ones: cultivated or uncultivated, frequented or deserted, built up or waste, obscure or made famous by the traces of deeds done, consecrated or profane.

units.la: In locis autem & illa naturalia.) Secundus est uerisimilium locus, cuius hic Cicero pulcherrimā & expeditissimam partitionem tradit, nimirum eam quam etiam in personis: ut naturalia primum expediat, deinde fortuita. Est autem locus, quæuis extremitas corpus ambiens. in quib. locis illa sunt naturalia: Maritimi, qua uoce tam illa loca intelliguntur quæ in mari sunt, quàm quæ prope mare sita. quibus contrarij sunt, à mari remota, quæ mediterranea Geographi uocant. Plani, id est, qui in planicie aliqua sunt, aut etiam in uallibus: quibus opponuntur montuosi, malim tamen legere montosi, quæ in montibus seu collibus sunt. Leues intelliguntur, quæ salebris aut saxis impedita non sunt: nam si ita sint, appellantur aspera.
units.tr: In places, again, there are also natural ones. This is the second topic of probabilities, and Cicero gives a very neat and convenient division of it, the same one he gave for persons: natural features first, then accidental ones. A place is any extent that surrounds a body. Among places, the natural ones are these: maritime, a word that covers both places that lie in the sea and places that lie near it; the opposites are places remote from the sea, which the geographers call inland. Level, that is, places that lie on a plain or even in valleys; the opposites are mountainous, though I would prefer to read "montosi", meaning places in mountains or hills. Smooth are those not hindered by rough ground or rocks; if they are, they are called rough.

units.la: Salubres. ) Salubritas hæc ex cœli, aquarū, et uctorū natura potissimū constat. Sūt enim hæc tria salubritatis et pestilētiæ siue insalubritatis causæ. Opaci: quæ raro illustrat sol, opaca dicūtur, quasi operta: quib. cōtraria sunt aprica, quæ soli aperta et expositæ sunt. Hæc decē genera in naturalib. numerātur: quod si quæ aliæ uarietates locorū naturales sint, ad hæc genera referēdæ sunt. Sequitur fortuita, quæ nō natura, sed hominū industria aut ignauia, huiusmodi sunt: quorū totidē sunt genera, quot naturaliū. nā aut culti, aut inculti sunt, quod quidē ad agricultură pertinet: aut celebres, id est habitati: aut deserti, scilicet ab hominib. uacui, aut coædificati: cuiusmodi sunt oppida, urbes et uillæ. nā qui cōtrarij sunt, hoc est sine ædificijs et domibus, uasti dicuntur. Aut obscuri, id est nullis rebus gestis clari: aut contrā gestarum rerum uestigijs nobilitati, cuiusmodi Thessaliæ campi sunt, Pharsalia appellati, qui Cæsaris et Pompeij luctuosa pugna nobilitati sunt, et multa alia loca uarijs rebus et facinoribus illustria. Aut consecrati, si aliqua religione, aut templo, tumulis, aut sepulsepulchris. nam hoc locum faciunt religiosum, unde illud in Miloniana: Vos Albani tumuli, aut profani, id est non consecrati, neque ulla religione a communi usu separati. et haec de locis. Quomodo autem ex hac varietate aut laudes, aut vituperationes, aut argumenta in utranque partem sumantur, nulla est Oratoris oratio, quae id non aperte docere possit. unde illud in Miloniana: Videamus nunc id quod caput est, inquit. Locus ad insidias ille ipse, ubi congressi sunt, utri tandem fuerit aptior: et cetera ibidem. item pro Sex. Rosc. Amer. Romae Sex. Rosc. occiditur, cum in agro Amerino esset filius. ex quo Cicero necessario uult effici (est enim hoc argumentum necessarium) a filio patrem occidi non potuisse. Illud autem probabile: Literas credo (inquit) alicui siccario misit, qui Romae noverat neminem.
units.tr: Healthy. Healthiness depends mainly on the nature of the air, the waters and the soil. These three are the causes of health and of pestilence or unhealthiness. Shaded: places rarely lit by the sun are called shaded, as if covered over; their opposites are sunny, which lie open and exposed to the sun. These ten kinds are counted among natural features; if there are any other natural varieties of places, they must be referred to these kinds. Next come the accidental features, which arise not from nature but from human industry or idleness. These are of as many kinds as the natural ones. For places are either cultivated or uncultivated, which pertains to agriculture; either populous, that is inhabited, or deserted, that is empty of people; or built up, such as towns, cities and villages. Those that are the opposite, that is without buildings and houses, are called waste. Or obscure, that is not famous for any deeds done there; or on the contrary, made noble by traces of deeds done there, such as the plains of Thessaly called Pharsalia, which were made famous by the mournful battle of Caesar and Pompey, and many other places made illustrious by various events and crimes. Or consecrated, if they are sacred by some religion, a temple or tombs or graves, for these make a place religious; hence that line in the Pro Milone: "You Alban mounds". Or profane, that is not consecrated, and not set apart from common use by any religion. So much for places. How praises, blame, or arguments on either side may be drawn from this variety, no oration of the orator fails to show clearly; hence that passage in the Pro Milone: "Let us now look at what is the main point," he says: "that ambush place itself, where they met, which of them it was more suited to." And the rest there. Likewise in the Pro Sexto Roscio Amerino: Sextus Roscius is killed at Rome, when his son was in the Amerian country. From this Cicero necessarily wants it to follow (for this is a necessary argument) that the father could not have been killed by the son. But this is probable: "I believe," he says, "he sent a letter to some assassin who knew no one at Rome."

units.la: In temporibus autem, praesentia & praeterita, & futura cernuntur. In his ipsis, vetusta, recentia, instantia paulo post, aut aliquando futura. Insunt etiam in temporib. illa, quae temporis quasi natura notat, ut hyems, ver, aestas, autumnus: aut anni tempora, ut menses, ut dies, ut nox, hora, tempestas, quae sunt naturalia. Fortuita aut, sacrificia, festi dies, nuptiæ.
units.tr: In times, present, past and future are perceived. Within these, ancient, recent, those about to happen shortly after, or sometimes future. Also included among times are those things which denote the nature of the time, as winter, spring, summer, autumn; or the seasons of the year, such as months, days, night, hour, weather; these are natural. Accidental ones are sacrifices, feast days, weddings.

units.la: In temporibus autem.) Tempus dicitur mēsura motus, et pars quædā æternitatis: cuius est eadem diuisio, quæ superiorum. Nam et naturalia quædā sunt tempora, quædā autem fortuita, id est hominū instituto distincta et reperta. Naturalium alia sunt plane et simpliciter naturalia, alia autē temporis qualitatē etiam et affectione quandam notant. Prioris generis sunt præsentia, præterita, et futura: in præteritis, alia uctusta sunt, alia posterioris temporis, quæ recentia dicuntur, in futuris uero sunt instantia, quæ pene præsentia sunt: aut paulo post futura quæ medij sunt tēporis: aut aliquādo futura, quæ longius absunt. Quæ autem cum natura etiā qualitatem significat temporis, quæ idcirco Cicero dicit, quasi tēporis natura notarc: ea sunt primum, quæ tanquā quatuor elemē ta, tēpora distinguūt, ut hyems, ver, æstas, autumnus: quasi dicas, terra, aer, ignis, aqua. Aut anni tēpora, id est partes, et spacia: ut menses, dies, nox, hora, tēpestas: quæ in hac diminutione tēporis ut detur momentū, aut horæ partē significare. Neq; tamē nescio, tempestatē etiam tēpus quoduis simpliciter significare: ut cū dicimus, hac tempestate toto Mars regnat impius orbe. itē, usurpari etiā pro uehementi cœli marisq; cōmotione: ueluti cū Poeta dicit, Quid tēpestates cœli, et sidera dicāt
units.tr: In times. Time is called the measure of motion and a part of eternity; its division is the same as that of the earlier items. For some times are natural, and others accidental, that is, distinguished and devised by human institution. Of the natural ones, some are plainly and simply natural, while others also denote a quality or a certain condition of time. Of the first kind are present, past and future: among past times some are ancient and others of a later period, which are called recent; among future times there are those immediately impending, which are almost present; or those shortly to come, which are of a middle period; or sometimes future things that lie further off. Those which, together with nature, also signify a quality of time, and which Cicero therefore says denote the nature of time, are first those which, like the four elements, divide the times: winter, spring, summer, autumn, as if you were to say earth, air, fire, water. Or the seasons of the year, that is parts and spans: such as months, days, night, hour, weather; which, in this subdivision of time, are given to signify a moment or a part of an hour. Nor do I deny that weather also simply signifies any time whatever, as when we say: "In this weather Mars rules the whole impious world"; and that it is used also for a violent disturbance of sky and sea, as when the poet says: "What do the storms of the sky and the stars say?"

units.la: Fortuita autem.) Hæc sunt, quæ hominum usus certis & statais temporibus fieri voluit, & idcirco temporis quoque nomen inuenerunt: cum non ipsius temporis natura sint, sed ei accidant, separariq; sine eius interitu possint. Horū facit tria genera: Sacrificia, id est solenes sacrificiorum dies: Festi dies, quæ Sabata vocât Ebræi: Nuptiæ, id est nuptiarum dies. Si qua autem alia sunt, ad hæc genera quoque annumerari possunt. ut, bello Punico, id est, quo tempore bellum Punicum gestum est: item, Consule Cicerone, Priamo rege, id est, qua tempestate Cicero consul erat, & Priamus rex. Iam uno atq; altero exemplo temporis hæc momenta illustremus. De sacrificijs, ut illud Philippica 3. Certus autem dies, non ut sacrificij, sic consilij expectari solet. De festis diebus est illud pro Milone: Eo die Miloni iter erat solenne ad Flaminem prodendum. Item pro Cluent. Quod sacere ante, nisi ludis publicis, aut festis diebus, non solebat. Item pro Cluentio diluit crimen veneni, à nuptiarum die: Quod autem tempus (inquit) dandi veneni, illo die, in illa frequentia? Itemq; ab hominis ætate, Cic. in Rosciana: Corrumpi Sex. Roscius non potuit: est enim natus annos 40.
units.tr: Accidental times. These are the times which human custom has willed to be observed on fixed and appointed occasions, and therefore they have also found a name of time, since they are not the nature of time itself but happen to it, and can be separated from it without its perishing. Of these he makes three kinds: sacrifices, that is the solemn days of sacrifices; feast days, which the Hebrews call Sabbaths; weddings, that is the days of weddings. If there are any other such times, they too can be counted under these kinds: as, in the Punic war, that is, the time when the Punic war was waged; likewise, in the consulship of Cicero, in the reign of Priam, that is, at the time when Cicero was consul and Priam king. Now let us illustrate these markers of time with one or two examples. On sacrifices, as in the Third Philippic: "But a fixed day, as for a sacrifice, is not usually awaited for a decision." On feast days there is that in the Pro Milone: "On that day Milo had a solemn journey to make to Lanuvium." Likewise in the Pro Cluentio: "What he was not accustomed to do before, except on public games or feast days." Also in the Pro Cluentio he refutes the charge of poisoning from the day of a wedding: "But what time (he says) was there for giving poison, on that day, in that crowd?" And likewise from a person's age, Cicero in the Pro Roscio: "Sextus Roscius could not have been corrupted: for he was born forty years ago."

units.la: Iam facta & euentus, aut consilij sunt, aut imprudentiæ: quæ est aut in casu, aut in quadam animi permotione. Casu, cum aliter accidit, ac putatum sit: permotione, cum aut oblivio, aut error, aut metus, aut aliqua cupiditatis caussa permouit. Est etiā in imprudentia necessitas ponenda.
units.tr: Now deeds and events are either intentional or unintentional; the latter occurs either by chance or through some agitation of mind. By chance, when something happens otherwise than was thought; through agitation, when forgetfulness, error, fear, or some cause of desire has moved a person. There must also be placed among the unintentional the necessity.

units.la: Iam facta & euentus.) Hic est quartus verisimilium locus.
