Facta autem & euentus, sunt ex causis effecta. nam horum mentione facta, caussas exquirit. ut enim caussa effectum indicat, sic quod effectum est, quae fuerit caussa demonstrat: & ue re dicitur, Tale quidq; esse, qualis fuerit eius causfa. Quod si caussa in aliquo non est, cum ne euentum quidem praestare oportet. Factorum autem nomine, intelligere debemus non solum quae facta sunt, uerum etiam quae sunt omissa, in suspicionem uenire: Non uenit in Senatum Antonius Consul, cum tamen Senatum ipse indixisset: ergo aliquid aut metus, aut fraudis subest. Vix a factis euentus differunt: est tamen discrimen aliquod. nam facta antecedunt, sequuntur euentus. Est enim euentus, alicuius exitus negotij, in quo quaeri solet, quid ex quaq; re euenerit, eueniat, eueturū ue fit. ut ex arrogantia facto, odium, ex liberalitate & humanitate, benevolentia euenire solet. Namq; ut Terentius ait, Obsequium amicos, veritas odium parit. Sed, quemadmodum dixi, quoniam non tantum facta
units.tr: Deeds and events. This is the fourth topic of probabilities. Deeds and events are effects produced by causes; for when we mention these, we inquire into their causes. For just as a cause indicates its effect, so what has been effected shows what its cause was; and it is rightly said that anything is such as its cause was. But if there is no cause in some matter, one ought not even to vouch for the outcome. By the name of deeds we must understand not only what has been done but also what has been left undone, which comes under suspicion: Antony the consul did not come into the Senate, although he himself had called the Senate together; therefore there lies some fear or some fraud beneath it. Deeds and events hardly differ; yet there is some distinction. For deeds come before, events follow. For an event is the outcome of some business, in which one usually asks what has come of, comes of, or will come of some matter. Thus from a deed of arrogance hatred usually follows, and from liberality and kindness goodwill. For, as Terence says: "Compliance wins friends, truth begets hatred." But, as I said, since we consider not only deeds

units.la: ita sta ipsa considerantur, sed factorum caussæ, ex quib. ipsa facta ponderantur: uidendum erit, consilio ne an imprudentia quicquã factum sit, aut euenerit. Nã ex his duobus omnia quæ fiunt emanare solent. Consilium est, aliquid faciendi, aut nõ faciendi, excogitata ratio. Imprudentia uero ea fieri dicuntur, in quibus neq; consilium, neq; prouisio ulla fuit. Imprudentiæ partes Cic. tres facit: casum, animi permotionē, & necessitatē. Casum, cum aliter accidit, ac putatũ sit: ut cum Imperator putans se uictoriã consecuturũ, congreditur cum hostibus, uincitur, accusatur, in casum, siue fortuna caussam reiecit amissi exercitus. Permotio, ad quã referuntur, quæ aut obliuione, aut errore, aut metu, aut aliqua cupiditate committuntur. Necessitas uero duplex est, & absoluta, & cum adiunctione. Abso luta: ut, omne quod natũ est, occidere. cum adiunctione uero, quã cum exceptione siue conditione uocant: ut, In tempestate maris eijcere merces necesse est, nisi malint, retentis mercibus, in nau perire. Ad necessitudinē illud quoq; referendũ est, cũ quis ad diem dictã cõmeatum nõ aduexit, q, cum aquæ aut latrones impediuerint. In casu & in necessitate uoluntas non est, in permotione uero est.
units.tr: Thus the facts themselves are considered, and the causes of the facts, from which the facts themselves are weighed: we must see whether anything was done or came about by design or by imprudence. For all things that happen are wont to flow from these two. Design is a plan, a reasoned decision to do or not to do something. Those things are said to be done through imprudence in which there was neither design nor any foresight. Cicero makes three parts of imprudence: chance, disturbance of mind, and necessity. Chance is when something turns out otherwise than was thought: as when a general, believing he will win the victory, joins battle with the enemy, is defeated, and is called to account; he lays the blame on chance, or fortune, for the loss of his army. Disturbance is the category to which belong those things committed through forgetfulness, error, fear, or some desire. Necessity is twofold, absolute and conditional. Absolute: as that everything born must die. Conditional, which they call necessity with an exception or condition: as, in a storm at sea it is necessary to throw the cargo overboard, unless men prefer to keep the cargo and perish in the ship. To necessity this also must be referred: when someone has not brought the supplies to the appointed day, because waters or robbers have hindered him. In chance and in necessity there is no will; in disturbance, however, there is.

units.la: Rerum autem bonarum & malarum tria sunt genera. Nam aut in animis, aut in corporibus, aut extrà esse possunt.
units.tr: Things that are good and bad are of three kinds. For they can belong either to the soul, or to the body, or to what lies outside us.

units.la: sunt.Huius igitur materiæ ad argu‐ mentum subiectæ, perlustrandæ a‐nimo partes erunt omnes, & ad id quod agetur, ex singulis coniectu‐ ra capienda.
units.tr: The whole of this subject-matter, then, which is placed under the argument, will have all its parts to be surveyed by the mind, and from each one a conjecture must be drawn for the matter in hand.

units.la: Rerum autem bonarum & malarum tria sunt genera.) Hæc ad postremum locum uerisimilium referri debet:hoc est,ad rerum negotiorumq; nas turas.Et hic locus ad caussas pertinet, cum efficientes,tum maximè finRes. hi enim in reb. bonis & malis latêt,propter quæ uel cõsequenda uel uitanda,actiones omnes suscipiuntur quâ, spe cõmodorum,& incõmodorum metu,& uitatione Rhetores uocât.ut in Rosciana:Vidit Chrysogonus Sex. Roscii optima habere prædia:quæ ut consequeretur, Roscii iussit occidi, & inter proscriptos annumerari.Itê in Miloniana:Metuebat Clodius Milonem, idcirco ei insidias secit. Quod aût de triplici bonorum genere mentionê facit,est ea partitio Peripateticorũ, qui bona animi uirtutes & artes,de quibus antea dictum est,appellarût. Corporis aût,quæ supra in personis enumerata sunt:extra aût quæ possût esse,fortuita nominâtur,siue bona fortunæ,de quib.antea quoq; dictû est.Homines enim animũ exornare,corpus cõseruare, postremò & corpus et animâ voluptate afficere volût. Huius igitur materiæ ad argumentum subiectæ.) Admonet hoc epilogo, in superioribus locis ad coniecturam capiendam latere materiam, quam Græci ὕλλω, nos etiā Syluam dicimus. Huius materiæ partes loci illi sunt propositi, non ut ex omnibus ad omnia argumenta sumamus: sed ut ad causam de qua agetur, quæ conueniunt adhibeamus, omittamus reliqua. Iudicium igitur adhibendum erit in singulis partibus perlustrandis, & utilibus seligendis.
units.tr: "Things that are good and bad are of three kinds." This should be referred to the last place of probabilities, that is, to the natures of things and affairs. And this topic concerns causes, both efficient and especially final. For these lie hidden in good and bad things, for the sake of which all actions are undertaken, either to attain or to avoid them. The rhetoricians call this the hope of advantages, the fear of disadvantages, and avoidance. As in the Roscian speech: Chrysogonus saw that Sextus Roscius had excellent estates, and in order to obtain them he had Roscius put to death and enrolled among the proscribed. Likewise in the speech for Milo: Clodius feared Milo, and therefore he laid an ambush for him. But as to his mention of the threefold kind of good things, this is the division of the Peripatetics, who called the goods of the soul virtues and arts, which were spoken of earlier. The goods of the body, which were listed above among the personal qualities, and those which can lie outside us, are called fortuitous, or goods of fortune, which were also spoken of earlier. For men wish to adorn the soul, to preserve the body, and finally to afford both body and soul pleasure. "The whole of this subject-matter, then, which is placed under the argument": in this epilogue he warns that in the earlier topics there lies, for the sake of drawing a conjecture, a matter which the Greeks call hylē, and which we too call silva (the material). The parts of this matter are those topics which have been proposed, not so that we take from all of them for all arguments, but so that we apply to the cause under discussion those which fit, and omit the rest. Judgement, therefore, must be exercised in surveying each part, and in selecting the useful ones.

units.la: Est etiam genus argumentorum aliud, quod ex facti uestigiis sumitur: ut telum, cruor, clamor editus, titubatio, permutatio coloris, oratio inconstās, tremor, & eorum aliquid quod sensu percipi possit, etiā si præparatum aliquid, si communicatum cū aliquo, si postea uisum, auditum, indicatum.
units.tr: There is also another kind of argument, which is drawn from the traces of the deed: such as a weapon, blood, a cry raised, faltering, a change of colour, a disjointed speech, trembling, and anything of this kind which can be perceived by the senses; even if something was prepared beforehand, if it was shared with someone, if afterwards it was seen, heard, or reported.

units.la: Est etiam genus argumētorum aliud quod ex facti uestigijs.) Primùm sciendum est, loqui Cicerone de eo genere signorū, quæ σημεῖα ab Aristotele uocata sunt. Nam etsi superiora illa sunt etiā signa, tamē hæc singulari quadā ratione, proprie signa sunt appellata. idcirco à Cicerone de Inuēt. lib. 1, Sic definiuntur: Signum est (inquit) quod sub sensum aliquem cadit, & quidda significat, quod ex ipso profectum uidetur, quod aut ante fuerit, aut in ipso negocio, aut post fit consecutum: & tamen indiget testimonij, & gravioris confirmationis. Ex quibus verbis constat, hoc etiam genus signorum in tria tempora diuidi: Præteritum, instans, & consequens. Ad præteritum referuntur illa, Etiam si præparatum aliquid, si communicatum cum aliquo, si postea usum, auditum, indicatum. Ad instans vero, Num quid strepitus, aut clamor editus? Ad consequens, Telum, cruor, titubatio, permutatio coloris, oratio inconstans, tremor, & eorum aliquid quod sensu percipi possit: de quib. signis qui plura desideret, legat libro ad Heren. 2. ubi colectubefore partes explicantur. Quanquam & ipse Cicero, infra plura explicabit. Sed hic dubitari posset, an non & hæc, ad facta & e-uentus possint referri? Quod quidem non negamus, sed tamen perspicue quoq; ab eis distinguuntur. nam hæc (ut infra dicet Cicero) maxime suspicionem mouent, & quasi tacita sunt criminum testimonia: illa vero, rationes. hæc adferuntur ad oratorem tanquam artis expertia, illa ab oratore tanquam artificiosa inueniuntur. inveniuntur autem, cum ab eo finguntur pleraq;, in illis præsertim quæ probare nihil est opus. cuiusmodi multa in Cluentiana de veneno, in Miloniana de insidiis, dijs,in Catilinarijs de coiuratione: quæ quidè etsi ostendi nõ poterant,tamen quia uerisimilia sunt, quasi facta sint,ita licuit exponere. Magnã hæc signa uim habẽt,quib. nemo unquã,nec Demosthenes qdè,aut crebrius,aut rectius usus est Cicerone.
units.tr: "There is also another kind of argument, which is drawn from the traces of the deed." First it must be understood that Cicero is speaking of that kind of sign which Aristotle called sēmeia. For although those earlier things are also signs, these alone are called signs in a special and proper sense. Hence Cicero in De Inventione book 1 defines them thus: "A sign is," he says, "that which falls under some sense and signifies something, which is seen to proceed from the thing itself, and which either came before, or occurred in the matter itself, or followed after; and yet it needs testimony and a stronger confirmation." From these words it is clear that this kind of sign too is divided into three times: past, present, and future. To the past belong those things: "even if something was prepared beforehand, if it was shared with someone, if afterwards it was used, heard, reported." To the present belong: "Was there any noise, or a cry raised?" To the future: "A weapon, blood, faltering, change of colour, a disjointed speech, trembling, and anything of this kind which can be perceived by the senses." Whoever wants more about these signs should read the second book of the Ad Herennium, where the individual parts are explained. Cicero himself, however, will explain more below. But here one might doubt whether these too can be referred to deeds and events? This indeed we do not deny, yet they are also clearly distinguished from them. For these (as Cicero says below) chiefly stir suspicion and are, as it were, silent testimonies of crimes; whereas those are reasons. These are brought forward to the orator as things free of art, whereas those are discovered by the orator as things contrived by skill. They are discovered, moreover, when for the most part they are invented by him, especially in those things which there is no need to prove. Of this kind are many things in the Cluentius speech about poison, in the Milo speech about ambushes and gods, and in the Catilinarian speeches about the conspiracy; which indeed, although they could not be shown, nevertheless, because they are probable, were allowed to be set forth as if they had happened. These signs have great force, and no one, not even Demosthenes, has used them more often or more correctly than Cicero.

units.la: Verisimilia autem partim singula mouent suo pondere: partim etiã, si uidentur esse exigua per se, multum tamen, cũ sunt coacervata, proficiunt. Atq; in his verisimilibus insunt nõnunquam etiam certæ rerum, & propriæ notæ.
units.tr: Probabilities, moreover, partly move by their own weight taken singly; partly also, even if they seem slight in themselves, they achieve much when they are heaped together. And in these probabilities there sometimes also lie certain marks and proper signs of things.

units.la: Verisimilia autem partim singula.) Absoluta uerisimiliũ locorũ partitione, iam tractatione paucis indicat, in qua tria nobis consideranda proponit, genera, collocatione, & expolitione. Genera uerisimiliũ in tractatione duo facit, nõ quidè locis distincta, sed natura & pondere. Nã partim singula mouet suo pondere, ac certa firmaq; sunt, partim infirma. Firma sunt, ut manus cruore respersæ, cructus gladius: & in eo ipso loco, in quo cædes facta est, repertum esse uidetur, exempli caussa: Aiax in sylua, postquam resciuit quæ fecisset per insaniam, gladio incubit: Vlysses interuenit: occisum cõspicatur: è corpore cruentũ gladiũ educit. Teucer interuenit: cũ fratrem occisum, & inimicum fratris cũ gladio cruëto uidet, capitis arceffit.qua de re uide etiā pulcherrimũ exemplũ de Inuent.lib.2.paulo post libri exordiũ. Hæc firma quidē uidentur, & sunt certè, si rectè tractentur: sed tamen non necessaria omnino. Quare argumentis cõfirmanda sunt. Infirma uerò, ut illud, Inimicus erat:nõ tamē sequitur, occidisse:est enim admodũ incertũ. Sequitur collocatio,in qua magna uis est tractatiõis.Ea dupliciter cõsideratur, ex põdere nimirũ,& leuitate probabiliũ.Nã si firma erũt,singula separatim poni possunt:suo enim põdere mouët.ut in Rosciana:Pater filiũ exhæredare uoluit:ergo utile filio fuit,patrẽ non diutius uiuere.ex quo sequitur satis firma cõclusio,patrẽ à filio necatũ.Est tamẽ argumetis cõfirmanda,ut ante dixi:Quod si uerisimilia infirma erũt,& uidebũtur esse exigua per se,condensanda crunt, ut sic coaceruata proficiãt: & nõ solũ condẽsanda, uerum ctiã repetitionib. & cõmorationib.expolienda.quod tertium fuit in tractatiõe uidendum. ut in Rosciana: Quid si accedit eõdem,ut tenuis antea fueris? quid si,ut auarus? quid si, ut audax? quid si,ut illius qui occisus est,inimicißimus?num quærenda caussa,quæ te ad tantum facinus adduxerit?Hactenus bonus orator coaceruata multa proposuit, quæ deinceps confirmat, post confirmationem concludendo repetit,& exponit.
units.tr: "Probabilities, moreover, partly taken singly." Having completed the division of the probable topics, he now briefly indicates the treatment, in which he proposes three things for us to consider: the kinds, the arrangement, and the elaboration. In the treatment he makes two kinds of probabilities, not distinguished by topics but by nature and weight. For some move by their own weight taken singly, and are certain and firm; others are weak. The firm ones are such as hands spattered with blood, a bloodied sword; and that it seems to have been found in the very place where the slaughter was done, for example: Ajax in the wood, after he came to know what he had done in his madness, falls upon his sword; Ulysses comes in, sees him dead, and draws the bloody sword from the body. Teucer comes in, and when he sees his brother slain and his brother's enemy with a bloody sword, he is seized with rage. On this matter see also the very beautiful example in the second book of De Inventione, shortly after the opening of the book. These firm things seem indeed to be firm, and certainly are, if they are rightly handled; yet they are not altogether necessary. Therefore they must be confirmed by arguments. The weak ones are such as this: "He was an enemy; yet it does not follow that he killed him," for this is quite uncertain. Next comes the arrangement, in which there is great force in the treatment. This is considered in two ways, namely by the weight and the lightness of the probabilities. For if they are firm, they can be set out separately, for they move by their own weight. As in the Roscian speech: A father wanted to disinherit his son; therefore it was useful to the son that the father should not live any longer. From this follows a sufficiently firm conclusion, that the father was killed by the son. Yet it must be confirmed by arguments, as I said before. But if the probabilities are weak, and seem slight in themselves, they must be condensed so that, heaped together, they may be effective; and they must be not only condensed but also elaborated by repetitions and delays, which was the third thing to be considered in the treatment. As in the Roscian speech: "What if it also happens that you were poor before? What if, as a miser? What if, as a daring man? What if, as the most hostile enemy of the man who was killed?" Are we to seek a cause which led you to so great a crime? Thus far the good orator has set forth many heaped-up points, which he then confirms; after the confirmation, he repeats them in concluding, and sets them forth.

units.la: Maximam autem facit fidem ad similitudinem ueri, primùm exemplum, deinde introducta rei similitudo: fabula etiam nonnunquam, etsi sit incredibilis, tamen homines commouet.
units.tr: Moreover, a likeness to the truth is most of all produced by an example first, then by a likeness of the thing introduced; sometimes also a fable, even if it is incredible, nevertheless moves men.

units.la: Maximam autē facit fidem.) Hic aliud quoddam genus uerisimilium, siue potiue, ut ego censeo, ex quibus uerisimilia confirmantur: quæ quidem sunt tria, exemplum, similitudo, & fabula. De exemplo in eadem Rosciana, ubi exemplum adducit cuiusdam Clælij: Tarracinensis, qui cum cœnatus, cubitum in idem conclaue, cum duobus adolescentib. filijs isset, inuentus est manè iugulatus: qui tamè filij, cū manè dormiêtes essêt reperti, iudicio absoluti, & suspicione omni liberati sunt. nemo enim putabat, quenquam esse, qui cum omnia diuina atque humana iura scelere nefario polluisset, somnum statim capere potuisset: propterea quòd, qui tantum facinus commiserunt, nō modò sine cura quiescere, sed ne spirare quidem sine metu possunt. Item illud in eadem: Lucius Cassius ille, quem populus Romanus uerisimum & sapientissimum iudicem putabat, identidem in caussis quærere solebat, Cui bono fuisset. Ex quo exemplo concludit Cicero, à Capitone Roscio, nō à Sexto filio, Sex. Roscium patrem occisum: cum ille amplissimâ pecuniam possideret, hic in summa mendicitate esset. Similitudo, ut in eadê: Portentum atq; monstrum certissimum est, esse aliquem humana specie & figura, qui tantum immanitate bestiis uicerit, ut propter quos hâc suauissimam lucem aspexerit, eos indignissimè luce priuarit: cum etiâ feras inter se, partus, atq; educatio, & natura ipsa concilicet. Est enim similitudo, qua hominem cum bestiis confert. Fabula, fabulosum exemplum significat, quæ unde melius quàm ex eodem Cicerone sumemus? is enim, ut in reliquis, sic etiam in hac parte excellit. In eadem igitur Rosciana: Quid tandem, inquit, tibi uidetur (ut ad fabulas ueniamus) senex ille Cæcilianus, minoris facere Eutychum filium rusticum, quàm illum alterum Chærestratum? & reliqua ibidem. Sed hoc ex Comœdia sumptum est. afferamus & aliud ex eadem: Videtisne, inquit, quod nobis poetæ tradiderunt, patris ulciscendi causa supplicium de matre sumpsisse, cum præsertim deorum immortalium iußis atq; oraculis id secisse dicantur: tamen ut eos agitent Furiæ, neque cõ sistere usquam patiantur, quòd ne pij quidem sine scelere esse potuerunt? Ex qua fabula illud uult ingeniosus orator consequi, non esse verisimile, à Sex. Roscio patrem interfectum, qui tam pacato & tranquillo animo fit. Hactenus de uerisimilibus locis, eorumq; tractatione.
units.tr: "Moreover, a likeness to the truth is most of all produced." Here is another kind of probabilities, or rather, as I think, the kinds by which probabilities are confirmed: and these are three, example, likeness, and fable. Concerning the example, in the same Roscian speech, where he adduces the example of a certain Caelius of Tarracina: who, when he had dined and gone to bed in the same room with his two adolescent sons, was found in the morning with his throat cut; yet those sons, when they were found sleeping in the morning, were acquitted by judgement and freed from all suspicion. For no one thought that anyone who had polluted all divine and human laws with a nefarious crime could immediately fall asleep; because those who have committed so great a deed cannot rest without care, nor even breathe without fear. Likewise that other example in the same speech: that famous Lucius Cassius, whom the Roman people thought to be a truthful and most wise judge, used often in causes to ask, "To whose advantage was it?" From this example Cicero concludes that Sextus Roscius the father was killed not by Capito Roscius but by the son Sextus: since the one possessed very great wealth, while the other was in utmost destitution. A likeness, as in the same speech: It is a portent and a most certain monstrosity that someone with a human appearance and form should exceed beasts in savagery so greatly that he deprived of light, most unworthily, those through whom he had seen this most pleasant light; when even wild beasts, in their mating, birth, and rearing, agree among themselves by nature itself. For this is a likeness, by which he compares a man with beasts. A fable signifies a fabulous example; from what source could we take this better than from Cicero himself? For he, as in other things, so also in this part excels. In the same Roscian speech, then: "What, pray," he says, "does it seem to you (to come to fables) that that old man Caecilianus esteems his rustic son Eutychus less than that other, Chaerestratus?" and the rest in the same place. But this was taken from comedy. Let us bring forward also another from the same: "Do you see," he says, "what the poets have handed down to us, that to avenge his father he took punishment on his mother, although it is said that he did this by the commands and oracles of the immortal gods; yet the Furies harass him and do not allow him to rest anywhere, because not even the pious could be without wickedness?" From this fable the ingenious orator wishes this to follow, that it is not probable that the father was killed by Sextus Roscius, who was of so calm and tranquil a mind. Thus far concerning probable topics, and their treatment.

units.la: DE LOCIS DEFINI- tiui status.
units.tr: On the Places of the Definitive Status

units.la: C. F. Quid definitionis ⁊ quæ ratio est, & quæ uia? C. P. Non dubium est id quidem, quin definitio genere declaretur, & proprietate quadam, aut etiam communium frequentia, ex quibus proprium quid sit eluceat. Sed quoniam de proprijs oritur plerumque magna difsensio, definiendum est sæpe ex contrarijs, sæpe etiam ex dissimilibus, sæpe ex paribus. Quamobrem descriptiones quoque sunt in hoc genere sæpe aptæ, & enumeratio consequentium, in primisq; commouet explicatio uocabuli ac nominis.
units.tr: C. F. What is definition, what is its method, and what is its way? C. P. There is no doubt that definition is made by genus and by some property, or also by the frequent accumulation of common attributes, from which what is proper to the thing becomes clear. But since a great dispute usually arises over proper attributes, we must often define from contraries, often from dissimilar things, and often from equals. For this reason descriptions are often also suitable in this kind of case, and the enumeration of consequences, and above all the explanation of a word or name, which moves the hearer most.

units.la: C. F. Quid definitionis? quæ ratio est, & quæ uia? ) Explicata coniectura, definitionis statu, eiusq; locos, hoc est uiam & rationem definiendi requirit filius. Facit autem Cicero hic definitionum genera duo, quæ quidem à facultatum & artium uarietate sumuntur. Vnum genus est philosophorum proprium, alterum oratorum. Atq; hæc genera, ut dixi, ab eorum facultatib. ducūtur. Nam disputationes sunt philosophorum, actiones autem oratorum: illi ad docendum tantū suas definitiones dirigunt, hi etiam ad permouendū. Idcirco illæ proprio nomine definitiones appellantur, hæ uero descriptiones, & explicationes, siue expolitiones. Et philosophi quidem breuius, copiosius & liberius oratores definire consueuerunt. Alia est enim, cū inter doctos homines disputatur: alia, cū ad sensum auditorum popularis accōmodatur oratio. Etenim definitio primum, ut Antonius lib.2. ait, reprehenso uerbo uno, aut addito, aut dempto, sæpe exturquetur è manib. deinde genere ipso doctrinam redolet, exercitationemq; penè puerile: tum & in sensum, & in mente iudicis intrare nō potest: ante enim præterlabitur, quàm præcepta est. Definitionis aūt eius quæ philosophi maximè utuntur, duo genera cōstituere uidetur Cicero: unum quod genere constat, & proprietate quadam, siue differentia: alterum frequentia rerum communium, quæ uni rei attribui solent, quæ accidentia, ni fallor, uocant: ex quibus cogestis, proprium aliquod unum declaratur. hoc autem fit, cum proprietas rei una, singularisq; non inuenitur, de quibus generibus satis alibi dictum est. sed tamen uno aut altero exemplo hunc locum illustremus. Definitio est oratio, quæ re quid sit, proprie & breuiter explicat.hæc definitio genere & differentia, siue proprietate quadam confecta est: Laurus est arbor quinq; cubitorum longitudine, cortice palleti, ramis in altum protensis & rectis, foliis semper uiretibus, odoratis, baccis nigris, subamaris, odore grauibus: quæ arbor fulmine non tangitur. Hæc autem communium constat frequentia. Ea autem definitio, qua oratores in causis utuntur, quam etiam descriptionem appellari diximus, conficitur plerunq; enumeratione contrariorum, dissimiliū, parium, consequentium, explicatione uocabuli ac nominis, quam notationem in subtili arte solent appellare. Bellum est, cum pax nō est: quam tractat Cicero Philippica 8. Orator est, qui dialectico in dicēdo est copiosior. Ciuitas sine lege, est sine mente corpus. prima constat ex contrarijs, secunda ex dissimilibus, tertia ex paribus, aut etiam similibus: nisi quòd oratores plura solent (ut dixi) uocabula colligere, & liberius definire consequentium enumerationem. Si quis requirat, pulcherrimum exemplum habet lib. 3. de Orat. ubi Crassus eloquentiæ descriptionem profert, admirabili rerum consequentiū frequentatione: quanquam & orationes ipsæ Ciceronis, passim exempla suppeditant, cuiusmodi est illa definitio gloriæ Philip. 1. De notatione uero satis quoq; multa dicta sunt. De tumultu idem Cicero Philip. 8. Quid enim tumultus, nisi perturbatio tanta, ut maior timor oriatur? unde etiam nomen ductum est, tumultus.
units.tr: C. F. What is definition? What is its method and its way? The son asks this, since the status of definition, once the conjecture has been explained, requires its places, that is, the way and method of defining. Cicero here makes two kinds of definition, taken from the difference between the faculties and arts. One kind belongs to the philosophers, the other to the orators. These kinds, as I said, are derived from their respective faculties. For disputations belong to philosophers, but speeches belong to orators: the former direct their definitions only to teaching, the latter also to moving the audience. For this reason the former are called definitions by their proper name, while the latter are called descriptions, explanations, or elaborations. Philosophers are accustomed to define more briefly, and orators more fully and freely. The case is different when something is disputed among learned men and when a speech is adapted to the understanding of a popular audience. Indeed, as Antonius says in book 2, a definition, once a single word has been caught and either added or removed, is often wrested from one's hands; then, by its very kind, it smells of learning and is almost childish exercise; and further, it cannot enter into the feeling or the mind of the judge, for it slips past before it has been grasped. Cicero seems to set up two kinds of the definition that philosophers use most: one that consists of a genus and some property or difference, and another that consists of the frequent accumulation of common attributes, which are usually assigned to one thing and which, unless I am mistaken, they call accidents; when these are gathered together, some one proper feature is revealed. This happens when no single and unique property of the thing is found. These kinds have been discussed sufficiently elsewhere, but let us illustrate this place with one or two examples. A definition is a speech which explains properly and briefly what a thing is. This definition is made up of genus and difference, or some property: The laurel is a tree five cubits high, with bark the colour of pale ash, with branches stretching upward and straight, with leaves always green, fragrant, with black berries, somewhat bitter, of heavy smell, which tree is not struck by lightning. This, however, consists of a frequent accumulation of common attributes. The definition that orators use in their cases, which we have said is also called a description, is usually made by enumerating contraries, dissimilar things, equals, and consequences, and by explaining a word or name, which they are accustomed to call notation in the subtle art. War is when there is no peace: Cicero treats this in the Philippics, book 8. An orator is someone who is more fluent in speaking than a dialectician. A state without law is a body without mind. The first is made from contraries, the second from dissimilar things, the third from equals or even similar things; except that, as I said, orators usually gather more words, and define more freely by enumerating consequences. If anyone wants a most beautiful example, he has it in book 3 of On the Orator, where Crassus gives a description of eloquence by a remarkable accumulation of consequent things; though Cicero's own speeches supply examples everywhere, such as that definition of glory in the first Philippic. Indeed, enough has also been said about notation. Cicero, in the eighth Philippic, speaks of tumult likewise: For what is tumult, unless it is such great confusion that a greater fear arises? From this also the name tumult is derived.

units.la: DE QVALITATIS locis.
units.tr: On the places of quality.

units.la: C. F. Sunt exposita iam ferè ea, quæ de facto, quæq; de facti appellatione quæruntur. Nempe igitur ea restant, quæ, cum factum constet, & nomen, qualia sint, uocatur in dubium. C. P. Est ita, ut dicis. C. F. Quę sunt igitur in eo genere partes?
units.tr: C. F. The points concerning the fact, and concerning the naming of the fact, have now been nearly all set out. What remains is what is disputed once the fact and its name are established: what sort of thing it is. C. P. So it is, as you say. C. F. What, then, are the parts of that kind?

units.la: C. F. Sunt exposita iam ferè ea quæ de facto, quæq; de facti appellatione quæruntur.) Significat, duas constitutiones expositas esse, quarum altera de facto, quæ coniecturalis, altera de facti appellatione, quæ definitiva dicitur: ex quo concludit, restare tertiam, quæ iuris & qualitatis nominatur.
units.tr: C. F. The points concerning the fact, and concerning the naming of the fact, have now been nearly all set out.) He means that two constitutions have been explained: one concerning the fact, which is called conjectural, and one concerning the naming of the fact, which is called definitive. From this he concludes that a third remains, which is called juridical and concerning quality.

units.la: C. F. Quæ sunt igitur in eo genere partes?) Mirum uideri possit, cur hic appellet parteis, cum in coniectura locos appellauerit. Verum sciendum est, recte dici partes, quoniam eo nomine formas species'ue intelligit. Nam ut constabit, partes ipsæ generis nomine dicuntur: sunt enim qualitatis status.
units.tr: C. F. What, then, are the parts of that kind?) It may seem strange why he now calls them parts, when in conjecture he called them places. But it must be understood that they are rightly called parts, since by that name he means forms or species. For, as will be made clear, the parts themselves are named by the general term, since they are the statuses of quality.

units.la: o ş · C. P.
units.tr: C. P.

units.la: C. P. Aut iure factum depellitur, aut ulcisccndi doloris gratia, aut pietatis, aut pudicitiae, aut religiōis, aut patriae nomine, aut deniq; necessitate, infscitia, casu. Nam quae motu animi, & perturbatione facta sine ratione sunt; ea defensionem contra crímen, in legitimis iudiciis non habent, in liberis disceptationibus habere possunt.
units.tr: C. P. Either the act is defended by right, or on account of avenging a grief, or of piety, or of chastity, or of religion, or in the name of the fatherland, or finally by necessity, ignorance, or chance. For acts that are done without reason, from some movement and disturbance of the mind, do not have a defence against a charge in lawful courts, but they can have one in free debates.

units.la: C. P. Aut iure factum depellitur.) Sequentib. verbis innuit, duo illa usitata genera huius constitutionis, quae & qualitatis, & iuridicialis, & legitima vocatur: quarum altera absoluta est, altera afsumptiua. Absoluta dicitur, quae ipsa in se recti & non recti quaestionem continet. ea defensionem ha bet in ipso iure aut naturae, aut scripto: & in iure quidem naturae, religionem, pietatem, gratiam, vindicationem, obseruantiam, veritatem: verùm multo magis in iure ciuili. Ex quo patet, ius ciuile esse disputandum ei, qui hanc partem tractare uelit. Exempla ex Rhetoricis ad Herennium, siue de Inuentione petenda sunt. Altera vero pars assumptiua tunc dicitur, cum ipsum per se factū probari non potest: aliquo autem foris adiuncto argumento defenditur, cuius partes sunt quatuor, comcomparatio, relatio criminis, remotio criminis, concessio.harum partiũ definitiones & exempla habet Cicero lib. 2. de Inuent. idcirco qui uolet, inde petat licebit. Priorem partē significauit Cicero,cum dixit,aut iure factum depellitur:posteriorem uerò, sequentibus, Aut ulcisci endi doloris gratia,& reliquis. Doloris quidem gratia: ut cū Horatius sororem in victoria Romanorum lugentem interfecit.Pietatis:uelut cum Orestes matrē, à qua pater interfectus fuerat, sustulit.Pudicitiæ: ut ille qui Centurionem siue tribunum, in castris pudicitiæ suæ uim afferentem, interemit. Religionis: ut si quis uiolantem sacra perimat. Patriæ: ut cum Rabirius Saturninum Tribunum plebis interfecit, aut Scipio Tib. Gracchum Reipub. statum labefactantem. De necessitate, imprudentia,& casu,dictum est in coniectura. nam miscentur interdum statuum loci.
units.tr: C. P. Either the act is defended by right.) By the following words he hints at the two common kinds of this constitution, which is called both of quality and juridical and legal: one of these is absolute, the other assumptive. It is called absolute when it itself contains the question of what is right and not right. Such a case has its defence in the right itself, either of nature or of written law; and in the right of nature, in religion, piety, grace, vindication, observance and truth, but much more in civil right. From this it is clear that civil law must be discussed by anyone who wishes to handle this part. Examples may be sought from the Rhetorica ad Herennium or from Cicero's De inventione. The other part, the assumptive, is so called when the act itself cannot be proved by itself, but is defended by some argument added from outside. Its parts are four: comparison, transfer of the charge, removal of the charge, and concession. Cicero gives definitions and examples of these parts in the second book of De inventione, so whoever wishes may seek them there. Cicero indicated the first part when he said, "either the act is defended by right"; the second he indicated in the following words, "either on account of avenging a grief," and the rest. Examples of "on account of a grief": when Horatius killed his sister who was mourning the victory of the Romans. Of piety: as when Orestes took his mother, by whom his father had been killed. Of chastity: as that man who killed a centurion or tribune who was offering violence to his chastity in the camp. Of religion: as if someone should kill a man who violates sacred things. Of the fatherland: as when Rabirius killed Saturninus, the tribune of the plebs, or Scipio killed Tiberius Gracchus, who was undermining the state of the republic. Necessity, ignorance and chance were discussed under conjecture; for the places of the statuses are sometimes mixed.

units.la: Nam quæ motu animi.) Ad concessionis partem respicit orator, quæ Deprecatio dicitur, in qua non defensio facti, sed ignoscendi postulatio continetur. Nam tunc reus & peccasse se,& consulto fecisse confitetur: & tamen postulat, ut sibi ignoscatur. & tunc Cicero negat, defensionem, qui huiusmodi peccauit,in legitimis iudicijs habere:ideo quod concesso peccato, difficile est ab eo qui peccatorum uindex esse debet,& legib.astri {ëtus} est,ut ignoscat,impetrare. nam non merum, sed mixtum tantum habet imperium, ut iurifperiti loquuntur. In liberis autem disceptationibus,quae solutae legibus sunt,quaeq; ex aequo & bo no,non ex scripto iure aguntur, ut apud Senatu aut Imperatorem, defensionem habere no negat. Est enim in liberis ciuitatibus summa potestas senatus, & regis fiue principis in suo regno, & Imperatoris in castris merum imperium,& libera ignoscendi facultas.quo in genere sunt orationes pro Ligario, & pro Deiotaro rege.
units.tr: For acts that are done from some movement of the mind.) The orator looks to the part of concession, which is called deprecation, in which there is contained not a defence of the act but a plea for pardon. For then the accused confesses both that he has sinned and that he did it deliberately, and yet asks that he be forgiven. And at that point Cicero says that one who has sinned in this way does not have a defence in lawful courts, because once the sin is granted, it is difficult to obtain pardon from one who ought to be the avenger of sins and is bound by the laws to punish. For he has not full power but only a limited one, as lawyers put it. But in free debates, which are loosed from the laws and are conducted by what is fair and good, not by written law, as before the Senate or an emperor, he does not deny that a defence may be made. For in free states the supreme power lies with the Senate, and in a king or prince in his own kingdom, and in an emperor in the camp there is full power and the free faculty of pardoning. To this kind belong the speeches For Ligarius and For King Deiotarus.

units.la: Hoc in genere, in quo quale fit quaeritur,ex controuersia,iure, & re cténeactum fit,queri solet:quorum disputatio ex locorum descriptione fumenda est.
units.tr: In this kind, in which the quality of the act is asked about, it is customary to inquire from the controversy about right and about fact; the discussion of these must be taken from the description of the places.

units.la: Hoc in genere,in quo quale fit quaeritur.) Duo sequentibus uerbis indicat, quae nos iam supra in suo ordine posuimus: quorum alterum est, quid in hoc statu quaeratur. queritur enim aequi & iniqui natura,aut praemij aut poenae ratio. Alterum est,ex quibus locis instruatur haec conftitutio: & remittit nos ad iuris ( quemadmodum dixi ) & aequi locos, quorum esse certam defcriptionem in alijs Rhetoricis,admonuimus.Quanquam de qualitate etiam infra nonnihil dicetur.
units.tr: In this kind, in which the quality of the act is asked about.) By the following words he indicates two things, which we have already set out in their order above: the first is what is asked in this status. For what is asked is the nature of the fair and unfair, or the reason for reward or punishment. The second is from which places this constitution is equipped; and he refers us to the places of right (as I have said) and of equity, of which we have advised that a certain description is to be found in other rhetorics. Although something more about quality will also be said below.

units.la: DE REFVTATIONE.
units.tr: ON REFUTATION.

units.la: 'C. F. Agefis, quoniam in confirmationem & reprehẽsionem diuíseras orationis fidem, & dictum de altero est, expone nunc de reprehẽdendo. C. P. Aut totum est negandum, quod in argumentatione aduersarius sumpserit, si fictum aut salsum esse possis dicere: aut redarguenda ea, quæ pro uerisimílibus sumpta sunt. Primum, dubía sumpta esse pro certis: deinde, etiã in perspicuè falsis eadẽ posse dici: tum ex iis quæ sumpserint, non effici quæ uelint.
units.tr: C. F. Agesis, since you have divided the proof of a speech into confirmation and refutation, and we have spoken about the first, now explain how to refute. C. P. Either the whole of what the opponent has assumed in his argument must be denied, if you can say that it is invented or false; or those things which have been assumed as probable must be refuted. First, doubtful matters have been assumed as certain; second, even things which are clearly false can be said to be the same; third, the conclusions the opponent wants do not follow from what he has assumed.

units.la: C.F. Agefis ergo, quoniam in confirmationem.) Hortatur patrem, ut sibi uiam & rationẽ adiumenta aduersariorum refellendi, quæ fidei al tera pars est, tradat.
units.tr: C. F. Agesis, therefore, since in confirmation.) He asks his father to pass on to him the method and reasoning for refuting the opponent's supports, which is the other part of the proof.

units.la: C. P. Aut totum est negandum.) Tria hic proponit: primùm, genera ipsa eorum quæ ab aduersario ad confirmandum inuenta fuerant: deinde refellendi uiam docet: postremò, quæ sit refutationis trastatio, siue collocatio. Sunt igitur quæ aduersarius attulit, aut ficta, aut falsa, aut dubia, quæ quidem reprehendi possint, nam de ueris perspicuè certis nulla fit mentio: & eorum quæ patcant reprehensioni, ultra hæc tria genera nihil est. Differunt autem à falsis ficta quòd hæc ueri aliquam similitudinem habent, etiamsi uera non sunt: falsa uerò ea intelligimus, in quibus apertum est mendacium. Et dubia quidem trium sunt generum. aut enim uera esse non constat: hoc est, tam incerta est ratio quæ affertur, quàm ficti ipsum: ut, Patre occidit Sex. Roscius, nam erat patri inuisus: utrūq; æquè incertū. aut ad propositū nihil pertinent, ut in Rabiriana: Nisi forte de locis religiosis ac delubris tibi respondendum putas. Huc pertinent etiam maledicta litium, quæ calumniandi caussa commemorari solent: cuiusmodi multa sunt in Cluentiana, & Cœliana, quorum mentionem nomine maledictorum fecit Cicero. Tertium genus dubiorū est, cum ex eis non efficitur quod uoluit aducrfarius: ut, Non fi in uilla filium habuit pater, idcirco oderat, sed amabat magis. De generibus eorum quæ reprehendi possunt, hactenus: sequitur ratio diffoluedi. Quæ ficta & falsa erunt, ut uerbo proposita sunt, ita uerbo neganda fuerint: nisi etiam fingendi rationem & consilia aperire uelis, & falsa simili ratione eludere. Sin erunt incerta, amplior suppeditabitur redarguendi ratio. Et quoniam dubia tripertito constare diximus: totidem erunt re-
units.tr: C. P. Either the whole must be denied.) Here he sets out three things: first, the kinds of material that the opponent has found to support his case; second, he teaches the method of refuting them; last, the arrangement or ordering of the refutation. So, of what the opponent has brought forward, some is invented, some false, some doubtful; these, indeed, can be refuted, for there is no mention of things that are plainly true and certain; and beyond these three kinds there is nothing that is open to refutation. Invented things differ from false ones in that the former have some resemblance to the truth even though they are not true, whereas we understand false things to be those in which the lie is obvious. Doubtful matters are of three kinds. Either it is not established that they are true, that is, the reasoning offered is as uncertain as the invented thing itself; for example, "Sextus Roscius killed his father, for he was hated by him," which is equally uncertain on both sides. Or they have no bearing on the issue, as in the Rabirian case: "Unless perhaps you think you must answer about sacred places and shrines." To this belong also the abusive remarks of lawsuits, which are commonly brought up for the sake of slander; there are many of this kind in the Cluentian and Caelian speeches, whose mention as abuse Cicero made. The third kind of doubtful matter is when what the opponent wanted does not follow from them; for example, "Because the father had a son on his farm, it does not follow that he hated him; rather he loved him more." So much for the kinds of things that can be refuted; next comes the method of dissolving them. Things that are invented and false, just as they have been put forward in words, should be denied in words, unless you also want to reveal the method and intentions of the invention and to mock the falsehood by a similar method. But if they are uncertain, a broader means of refutation will be available. And since we have said that doubtful matters consist of three parts, there will be as many ways of refuting them.

units.la: reprehendendi modi. Primum, si utrunq; incertum fuerit, aut caussæ rogandæ erunt: aut si quæ videatur esse, aut si quas aduersarius attulit, refutandæ erunt, & inanes ostendendæ: id quod sæpe ipse orator facit, præsertim in Miloniana, & Rosciana. Si ad rem nihil faciunt, neq; pertinent ad quæstionem, quæ aduersarius attulit argumenta: aut erunt diluenda, aut tanquam incepta contemnenda & irridenda. Quod si ex cis non id sequetur quod putauit, idem quod proximè dixi faciendum est. Sin uero communia sunt, atque ἀντιστρέφοντος ἀνsαm præbent, ea in aduersarium retorquebimus, eadem complexione, ut illud in Rosciana: Erat ciusmodi tempus, inquit Erucius, quo impunè licebat occidere: ergo Sex. Rosc. patrem occidit. Imò, inquit Cicero, quia ita erat, magis licuit sectoribus bonorum & collorum, quàm simplici agricolæ. Sed hæc retorsio est etiam alijs verisimilium locis munienda.
units.tr: First, if both sides are uncertain, either the grounds must be questioned, or whatever seem to be grounds, or whatever the opponent has brought forward, must be refuted and shown to be empty; something the orator himself often does, especially in the Milo and Roscius speeches. If the opponent's arguments have nothing to do with the matter and do not bear on the question, they must either be dissolved or scorned and ridiculed as beginnings that have come to nothing. But if from them the conclusion he thought would follow does not follow, the same thing that I have just said must be done. But if the points are common and offer a reciprocal necessity [ἀντιστρέφοντος ἀνάγκην], we shall turn them back against the opponent with the same combination, as in the Roscius speech: "It was such a time," says Erucius, "when it was lawful to kill with impunity; therefore Sextus Roscius killed his father." On the contrary, says Cicero, because it was so, it was more lawful for the stewards of the estates and the contractors to do it than for a simple farmer. But this kind of counter-argument must also be fortified by other arguments from probability.

units.la: Accedere autem oportet ad singula, sic uniuersa frangentur. Commemoranda sunt etiam exempla, quibus simili in disputatione creditum non sit, conquerenda condiıtio communis periculi, si ingeniis hominum criminosorum fit expo. sita uita innocentium.
units.tr: One must also take up the individual points; in this way the whole will be broken down. Examples should also be recalled in which credence was not given in a similar dispute; and the common condition of danger should be lamented, if the lives of innocent people are exposed to the cleverness of criminal men.

units.la: Accedere autem oportet ad singula.) Hæc est tertia illa pars, qua tractatio & collocatio repre henfionis docetur. Supra in confirmatione dictum est, Quæ per fe non ualent uerisimilia, esse coaceruanda, & condensanda. Iam contrario modo est defensori faciendum: nimirum ut quæ coaccrua uit aduersarius, ut coniuncta nocerent magis, ea singula tractet ex interuallo, ut leuia esse uideantur. Adolescens corruptus, audax, luxuriosus: igitur à scelere non abhorrens. hæc singula seorsim fumenda, atq; eneruanda in refutatione.
units.tr: One must take up the individual points.) This is the third part, in which the handling and arrangement of refutation is taught. Above, in confirmation, it was said that probabilities which are not strong in themselves should be heaped up and condensed. Now the defender must proceed in the opposite way: namely, he should treat singly, and at a distance from one another, the points the opponent has piled up, so that, though together they would harm more, separately they may seem slight. A young man is corrupt, bold, and given to luxury; therefore he does not shrink from crime. These items must be taken separately and weakened in the refutation.

units.la: Commemoranda sunt etiam exempla.) Vt Cleliorum in Rofciana, de quo exemplo alibi diximus. ea enim rei iudicatæ uim & pondus obtinet, præbentq; in simili negocio iudicaturis exemplum. ad quod etiam ualent testimonia & autoritates.
units.tr: Examples should also be recalled.) As the Cloelii in the Roscius speech, about which example we have spoken elsewhere. For this has the force and weight of a decided case, and provides an example for judges who must decide a similar matter. To this also testimonies and authorities are relevant.

units.la: Conquerenda conditio communis periculi.) Conquestio hæc duo continet, indignationem, & terrorem. non enim solum cum indignatione communia pericula & conditionem temporum deploramus, uerum etiam aduersariis terrorem incutimus. ut Cicero pro Sex. Rofcio in peroratione: O rem miseram atq; acerbam. item in Catilinam: O conditionem miseram, non modo administrandæ,sed etiam conseruandæ Reipublicæ.item ubi pro Sex.Roscio minatur aduersarijs literam illam condemnationis, quam tantopere horrebant.Huiusmodi querelarum & comminationum plenæ sunt orationes.
units.tr: The common condition of danger should be lamented.) This complaint contains two things: indignation and terror. For we bewail common dangers and the condition of the times not only with indignation, but we also strike terror into our opponents, as Cicero does in the peroration of the Roscius speech: "O wretched and bitter state of affairs!" Likewise in the Catiline speeches: "O miserable condition, not only of administering but even of preserving the Republic!" Likewise where, in the Roscius speech, he threatens the opponents with that letter of condemnation which they dreaded so much. Speeches are full of complaints and threats of this kind.

units.la: DE ARGVMENTATIONE.
units.tr: ON ARGUMENTATION.

units.la: C. F. Quoniā unde inueniuntur quæ ad finē pertinent, habeo, quē admodum in dicendo singula tractentur expecto. C.P. Argumentationem quærere uideris, quæ est argumenti explicatio: quæ sumpta ex iis locis, qui sunt expositi, confi cienda &distinguenda dilucidè est. C. F. Plane istuc ipsum desidero.
units.tr: C. F. Since I have found where the things that bear on the end are located, I am eager to learn how each matter is to be handled in speaking. C. P. You seem to be looking for argumentation, which is the explanation of an argument. It is drawn from the topics already set out, and it must be clearly constructed and distinguished. C. F. That is exactly what I want.

units.la: C. P. Est ergo, ut supra dictum est, explicatio argumenti, argumentatio:sed ea conficitur, cum sumpseris aut nō dubia, aut probabilia, ex quí bus id efficias, quod aut dubium, aut minus probabile per se uidetur.
units.tr: C. P. So, as was said above, argumentation is the explanation of an argument. It is constructed when you take either indisputable or probable premises, by which you prove what seems in itself doubtful or less probable.

units.la: C. F. Quoniam unde inueniuntur.) Quoniā ad confirmandum & refellendum opus est argumentis: & argumenta, argumentatione explicantur:quoniam quæ unde argumenta depromerentur, locos ostendit, & confirmandi refellendiq; uiam & modum patefecit: consequens est, ut de argumentatione explicet & doceat. in qua illa quærenda occurrunt, quid sit argumentatio, ex quibus conficiatur, quæ argumentandi genera: tum denique, quæ sit argumentationis varietas, expolitio siue tractatio. Hæc omnia diuina breuitate in sequentibus noster docet Cicero.
units.tr: C. F. "Since from where things are discovered." Arguments are needed for confirming and refuting, and arguments are set out by argumentation. Since the topics have shown where arguments are to be drawn from, and have revealed the way and method of confirming and refuting, it follows that he should explain and teach argumentation. Here the following questions arise: what argumentation is, what it is constructed from, what kinds of argumentation there are, and finally what variety, arrangement or treatment argumentation admits. Our Cicero teaches all of these in the sequel, with divine brevity.

units.la: C. P. Argumentationem quærere uideris.) Quid sit argumentatio, hic atque altera responsione declarat. Argumentatio, inquit, est argumenti explicatio. Recte definiuit generatim argumentationē: nam nullum genus est, nullaq; forma argumentandi, quæ non sit argumenti explicatio. Græci Rhetores argumentationem, & argumentum, ἐπιχείρημα uocant: utrunq; uidelicet uno nomine. quod etiam interdum faciunt Latini, secus quàm docti quidam putět. Cicero lib. 1. de Inuentione: Nam & argumentatio, inquit, nomine uno res duas significat, ideo quòd & inuentum aliquam in rem probabile, aut necessarium, argumentatio uocatur, & eius inuenti artificiosa expositio.
units.tr: C. P. "You seem to be looking for argumentation." What argumentation is, he explains here and in the other reply. "Argumentation," he says, "is the explanation of an argument." He has defined argumentation in general terms correctly, for there is no kind or form of arguing that is not an explanation of an argument. The Greek rhetoricians call both argumentation and argument by the word ἐπιχείρημα [epicheirema], that is, they use the one word for both. The Latins sometimes do the same, contrary to what some learned men suppose. Cicero, in book 1 of De inventione: "For argumentatio," he says, "by one name signifies two things, because both a discovery made in support of something probable or necessary is called argumentatio, and also the skilled exposition of that discovery."

units.la: Sed ea conficitur.) Iam secundum ex ijs quæ proposuimus aggreditur, nimirū ea ex quib. argumentatio conficitur: quod quidē ad ipsius qualitatem pertinet.Duo aut sunt,ex quib.rhetorica conficitur argumentatio: quarum alia nō dubia uocat,hoc est certa siue necessaria, quæ tecmeria diximus ab Aristotele appellari:alia probabilia,de quib.iam satis suprà in ueri similib.dictum est.neque enim unquam aut fictis, aut falsis utendum esse, docet optimi magistri:sed si ab aliquo allata sint, quomodo refellantur & reprehendantur,ostendunt. Ergo illud in argumentādo expendendum est,quæ sit natura propositionum, siue argumentorum.Nam,ut inquit Aristoteles lib. 1. Rhetorices,propositiones necesse est propositionibus eiusdem naturæ confirmari:dubia igitur non dubijs,minus probabilia magis probabilibus confirmanda sunt.
units.tr: "But it is constructed." Now he takes up, second, the matters we have proposed, namely the materials from which argumentation is constructed; this pertains to its very quality. There are two kinds from which rhetorical argumentation is constructed. One kind he calls indisputable, that is, certain or necessary; Aristotle called these tekmeria [τεκμήρια]. The other kind is probable, about which enough has already been said above in the discussion of probabilities. The best teachers indeed never teach that one should use fictions or falsehoods; but if such things have been advanced by someone, they show how they may be refuted and rebuked. Therefore in arguing one must consider what the nature of the propositions or arguments is. For, as Aristotle says in book 1 of the Rhetoric, propositions must necessarily be confirmed by propositions of the same nature: doubtful things therefore must not be confirmed by indisputable ones, and less probable things must be confirmed by more probable ones.

units.la: Argumentandi autē duo sunt genera, quarū alterū ad fidem directo spectat, alterum se inflectit ad motum.Dirigitur,cū propositum aliquid quod probaret,sumpsitq; ea quibus uteretur:atq; his cōfirmatis,ad propositum se retulit, atq; conclusit.
units.tr: There are two kinds of argumentation: one of these is directed toward belief, the other turns toward emotion. It is directed when one takes up some point that he wishes to prove and takes the premises he will use; and when these are confirmed, he returns to the point proposed and draws his conclusion.

units.la: Argumentandi autē duo sunt genera.) Quoniam in caussa & fides & motus spectatur, idcirco duo argumentorum genera Rhetores inuenerunt:unum, quod ad fidē dirigitur: alterū, quod inflectitur ad motum: tanquam diceres, alterum ad rem dirigi, alterum ad personam. At res ipsa fiue quæstio fidem poscit, persona uero motum. nam in personis motus excitatur. Et hæc sunt illa duo oratoris officia, de quibus alibi diximus: reliquum autem est tertium, ut delectet. quod etsi in ipso motu etiam continetur, consideratur tamen seorsum, & utrunque sine argumentatione effici potest. Summam tamen meretur laudem is orator, qui duobus illis etiam tertium adiungit. Verum quoniam de argumentatione agitur, duo tanquam necessaria proponuntur: fides nimirum, & motus. Prius illud genus quod directum dicitur, id est, quod numerum, & naturalem propositionum ordinem seruat, quod omnino dialecticum est & philosophicum: in quo duæ sunt propositiones necessariæ, præter conclusionem: ratiocinatio uidelicet, quæ maior propositio dicitur: & assumptio, quæ minor appellatur. Hæc in hunc definiturmodum, de Inuent. lib. 1. Ratiocinatio est oratio, ex ipsa re probabile aliquid eliciens, quod expositum, & perspecognitum, sua se ui & ratione confirmet. Reliquæ partes quas Rhetores enumerant, ut etiam dialectici in prosyllogismo, approbationes sunt maioris & minoris. nam Rhetores solent plenam & perfectam argumentationem uocare, quæ quinque partibus constat: id quod etiam hoc loco Cicero innuit, in ea quæ dirigitur ad finem argumentatione. Dirigitur, cum proposuit aliquid quod probaret, inquit: quibus uerbis propositum, siue maiorem propositionem fignificauit. cum autem addit, Sumpsitq; ea quibus uteretur: assumptionem, siue minorem, in illis autè, Atq; his confirmatis, præmissis adiungenda confirmationem docet. Iam conclusionem extremis illis uerbis indicauit, Ad propositum se retulit, atq; conclusit. ita perfectæ argumentationis apud oratores sunt quinq; partes: Propositio, per quam breuiter locus is exponitur, ex quo omnis uis pendet ratiocinationis: Approbatio, per quam id quod breuiter expositum est, rationibus firmatū probabilius & apertius fit: Assumptio, per quam id quod ex propositione ad ostendendum pertinent, assumitur: Assumptionis approbatio, per quam id quod assumptum est, ratione confirmatur: & deniq; ipsa Complexio, siue conclusio, per quam id quod conficitur ex omni argumentatione, breuiter exponitur. Exempla præstò sunt nō modò in orationibus, sed etiam copiosa & varia in arte ipsa, ubi de argumentatione præcipitur, ad Heren. lib. 2. & de Inuent. lib. 1.
units.tr: "There are two kinds of argumentation." Since in a cause both belief and emotion are at stake, the rhetoricians devised two kinds of argument: one directed toward belief, the other turned toward emotion, as if one were to say that one is directed at the matter, the other at the person. For the matter itself, or the question, demands belief, while the person stirs emotion; for emotion is aroused in persons. These are the two duties of the orator, of which we have spoken elsewhere. The remaining one is the third, to delight; and although this too is contained in emotion itself, it is considered separately, and either of the two can be achieved without argumentation. Nevertheless, the orator who adds the third to those two deserves the highest praise. But since argumentation is the subject, two kinds are set forth as necessary: namely belief and emotion. The first kind, which is called direct, that is, which observes the number and natural order of the propositions, is wholly dialectical and philosophical. In it there are two necessary propositions besides the conclusion: namely the ratiocinatio, which is called the major proposition, and the assumptio, which is called the minor. Cicero defines these in this way, in De inventione book 1: "Ratiocinatio is a speech drawing out something probable from the matter itself, which, once set forth and clearly known, establishes itself by its own force and reason." The remaining parts that the rhetoricians enumerate, as the dialecticians also do in the prosyllogism, are approbations of the major and minor. For the rhetoricians are accustomed to call a full and perfect argumentation one that consists of five parts; and Cicero here hints at this in the argumentation that is directed to belief. "It is directed when he has set forth something that he wishes to prove," he says: by these words he meant the proposition, or major proposition. When he adds "and takes the premises he will use," he means the assumption, or minor. In the words "and when these are confirmed," he teaches the confirmation to be added to the premises. Finally, he indicated the conclusion in the last words: "he returns to the point proposed and draws his conclusion." So the perfect argumentation among the orators has five parts: the proposition, by which the topic is briefly set out, on which all the force of the reasoning depends; the approbation, by which what has been briefly set out is made more probable and clearer by reasons; the assumption, by which what pertains to the proof is taken from the proposition; the approbation of the assumption, by which what has been assumed is confirmed by reason; and lastly the complexio, or conclusion, by which what is produced from the whole argumentation is briefly set forth. Examples are at hand, not only in the orations but also, abundant and varied, in the art itself, where argumentation is taught: Rhetorica ad Herennium book 2, and De inventione book 1.

units.la: Illa autem altera argumentatio, quasi retro, & contra prius sumit, quæ uult, eaq; confirmat. deinde id quod proponendum fuit, permotis animis ita ut ad extremum.
units.tr: That other argumentation, however, takes up the premises backward and in the opposite order to the earlier one, which it wishes and confirms; then, once the minds are stirred, it sets forth at the end the point that had to be proposed.

units.la: Illa autem altera argumentatio. Iam eius argumentationis dispositionē tradit, quae se inflectit ad motum. Ea autem est, cum aut ordo partium, qui in directo argumentandi ordine praescriptus est, immutatur: aut cum ad motum, & quasi ab ipsa causa, in personam declinamus. In priore modo triplex est ratio. Nam aut inductionis, aut ornatus, aut occultationis causa ordine naturali inuertimus, quemadmodū docet Aristoteles Top. lib.8. ubi de exornanda & occultanda conclusione utilem doctrinam tradit. Altera vero, quae declinat ad motum, varias amplificationes continet: ex quibus aut odium, aut ira, aut inuidia excitatur. Cicero hunc ordinem & viam huius argumentationis ponit, ut primum locum occupet assumptio, deinde assumptionis confirmatio, post propositio maior, deinde alia confirmatio, ad permouendos animos accommodata: ad cuius finem, tanquam iaculum conijciatur conclusio. quo fit, ut qui audit, prorsus conclusionem ignoret, donec sibi inflictum senserit uulnus. Huius exemplum pulcherrimum est in Roscianā, ubi contra Tit. Capitonem dicit, ubi leguntur haec uerba: Videte iam porrò cætera iudices, ut intelligatis, fingi malescicium nullum posse, quo iste sesc non contaminarit. In rebus minoribus socium fallere turpissimum est: et cetera quae ibidem sequuntur. quanquam in eadem oratione alia eiusmodi diligens lector inueniet. Nos quoq; de hoc genere argumentationis, quaedam non poenitenda scripsimus in tertio Dialecticæ Perionij.
units.tr: "That other argumentation." Now he gives the arrangement of that argumentation which turns toward emotion. This happens either when the order of the parts, which is prescribed in the direct order of arguing, is changed, or when we pass from the cause itself to the person, as it were. In the first way there is a threefold reason. For we invert the natural order either for the sake of arrangement, or of ornament, or of concealment, as Aristotle teaches in Topics book 8, where he gives useful instruction on adorning and concealing a conclusion. The second way, which inclines toward emotion, contains various amplifications, by which hatred, anger or envy is aroused. Cicero sets out this order and method of this argumentation: first the assumption occupies the place, then the confirmation of the assumption, after that the major proposition, then another confirmation suited to moving the minds; at its end the conclusion is hurled as a javelin. The result is that the listener does not know the conclusion at all until he feels the wound inflicted on him. The most beautiful example of this is in the Pro Roscio, where he speaks against Titus Capito; there these words are read: "Now look further, judges, at the rest, so that you may understand that no crime could be devised by which that man would not have stained himself. In small matters to deceive a partner is most shameful," and the rest that follows there. Yet a diligent reader will find other such examples in the same speech. I too have written some things on this kind of argumentation, not to be regretted, in the third book of my Dialectic, on Perionius.

units.la: Est autem illa varietas in argumentando, & non iniucunda distinctio, ut cum interrogamus nosmetipsos, aut percunctamur, aut imperamus, aut optamus, quae sunt cum aliis compluribus sententiarum ornamenta.
units.tr: There is also another variety in arguing, and a not unpleasant distinction: when we question ourselves, or ask questions, or give commands, or express wishes, and these, together with many other figures of speech, are the ornaments of sentences.

units.la: Est autem illa varietas in argumentando.) Translatio sequitur argumentationis, quae tantum momenti habet, ut ea sola inter summos oratores & mediocres quid intersit cognoscatur. facit enim ea varietas, ut non similiter semper argumentatione utamur. Nam omnibus in rebus similitudo est satietatis mater: quae hac iucunda varietate & distinctione nitatur. Est etiam in ea alia utilitas, quae maxime in disputando & dicendo commendatur: quod ea celatur artificiu, & puncta argumentorum plerunque occultentur, ne quis ea numerare possit, quae quidem re distinguuntur, verbis aut ui-
units.tr: "There is also another variety in arguing." The discussion moves on to variety in argumentation, which has such importance that by it alone the difference between the greatest orators and the mediocre is recognised. For this variety means that we do not always use argumentation in the same way. For in all things similarity is the mother of satiety, and this is sustained by pleasing variety and distinction. There is also another advantage in it, which is especially commended in disputing and speaking: the art is hidden in this way, and the points of the arguments are for the most part concealed, so that no one can count those things which are indeed distinguished in substance, but in words or in force are...

units.la: uidetur esse cofusa. Tractatiōis duæ sunt partes: Elocutio siue expolitio, & propositionum dispositio. Expolitio in ornamentis sententiarum uersatur, & quidem in omnibus: quanquam Cicero hic quatuor tātum enumerat. quod idcirco facit, quia hæc quatuor tanquam generalia & cōmunia reliquorū omnium sunt. nam fere omnia aut interrogatione, aut percūctatione, aut iussione, aut optatione tractari possunt. hæc enim sunt illa quatuor, quæ hoc loco uerbis, non nominibus, à Cicerone proponuntur. Hæc igitur quatuor nūc satis erit nos exemplis illustrare: & primum interrogationem, siue rogationem, ut Cicero 3. de Orat. uocat. Interrogatio autem non omnis grauis est, neq; concinna: sed ea præsertim, quæ, cum enumerata sunt quæ obsunt caussæ aduersariorū, cōfirmat superiorem orationem: aut grauiter etiā ante urget aduersarium. Prioris exemplū, Cicero pro Cluetio: Quis tamē auderet dicere, nocentē condemnatū esse Opianicū? quis nūc audet negare? et id genus reliqua ibidem. item illa pro eodem: Vter igitur facilius suæ sententiæ rationem redderet? is'ne, qui se & sibi & rei iudicatæ constitisse dicit: an ille, qui se in principem maleficij lenem, in adiutores eius & conscios uchementißimū esse respondit? hac exornatione tota fere C. Rabirij oratio acrior & uchementior, adde de etiam iucundior, facta est. Alterius exemplum est in exordio statim primae orationis in Catilinam: Quo usque tandem abutere Catilina patientia nostra? quandiu nos etiā furor iste tuus eludet? quem ad finem sese effrenata iactabit audacia? Quo in loco plus quàm decem interrogationes sequuntur. Secundum ornamentum est Percunctatio: quae quid à rogatione differat, docet ipse 3.de Oratore, ubi ait: Et rogatio, atque huic finitima quasi percunctatio, expositioque sententiae suae. Quibus verbis intelligimus, rogationem simplicem esse, hoc est, sine sententiae suae expositione: percunctationem autem, semper adiunctam sententiae suae expositionem habere. Et idcirco in Oratore ad Brutum sic de utraque figura scribit: Ut interrogando urgeat, ut rursus quasi ad interrogata sibi ipse respondeat. Nihil autem refert, suo an adversarij nomine respondeat Orator. ut antequam iret in exilium: Num igitur potest fieri, à clientibus ut recipiar? cum à quibus debeat retineri, reijcere instituantur. Item in eadem: Vim uolunt afferre? Praesto sum: eijcere uolunt? exeo. indicta causa nolunt audire? causam non dico, aliud quippiam conantur? agat. Hanc, subiectionem uocat Cornificius lib. 4. Tertia autem figura ea est, cum quid imperamus, aut iubemus: quae idcirco iussio dici potest. cuius tamen mentionem à Cicerone factam alibi, non inuenies. Ego autē, ni fallor, puto illam ea contineri, quæ ab eodem lib. 3. de Oratore interpellatio nominatur. quāquam his uerbis in Oratore profert, ut interpellatorem coerceat: quod quidē sine iussu et imperio fieri non potest. Exempla duo proferam, quorum alterum directo iussionem continet: alterū cum iussione, interpellatoris coercionem. Iussionis illud est, in I. Catil. Quid est Catilina? num dubitas, id me imperante facere, quod iam tua sponte faciebas? exire ex urbe Consul hostem iubet. Item in eadem: Quamobrem, inquit, ut sæpe iam dixi, proficiscere: ac si mihi inimico (ut prædicas) tuo conflare uis inuidiā, rectà perge in exilium. et reliqua in eadem sententia. Item pro C. Rabirio, alterius exemplū habes: Quin continetis uocem, indicem stultitiæ uestræ, testem paucitatis. Hæc speciē habet obiurgationis. De optatione quoq; ne longum faciamus, cum alibi sæpe, tum in eadem Rabiriana: Utinam hanc facultatem mihi caussa cōcederet, ut possem hoc prædicare, C. Rabirij manu L. Saturninū hostem populi Romani interfectum. Exorditur etiam orationes eadem figura: sunt enim multæ optationis formæ. ut pro Sylla: Maxime uellem Iudices, et reliqua. Item Philip. 9. Vellem dij immortales fecissent, P. C. et quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: seem to be confused. Treatment has two parts: elocution, or embellishment, and the arrangement of the propositions. Embellishment lies in the ornaments of sentences, and in all of them, although Cicero here lists only four. He does this because these four are general and common to all the rest, for almost everything can be treated by means of a question, an inquiry, a command or a wish. These are the four that Cicero here names by verbs rather than by nouns. So for now it will be enough to illustrate these four with examples, and first the question, or interrogation, which Cicero in book 3 of On the Orator calls rogatio. Not every question is weighty or elegant, however; especially those which, once the advantages of the opponent's case have been enumerated, confirm the preceding speech, or else press the opponent sharply at the outset. An example of the first kind is Cicero in the Pro Cluentio: "Yet who would dare to say that Oppianicus was condemned as a guilty man?" "Who now dares to deny it?" and the rest of the same kind in that passage. Likewise in the same speech: "Which of the two would more easily give a reason for his opinion: he who says that he has been consistent both with himself and with the judgment given, or he who replied that he was very lenient toward the principal of the crime and very harsh toward its accomplices and accessories?" By this ornament nearly the whole speech of Gaius Rabirius became sharper and more vehement, and, add, more pleasing. An example of the second kind is at the very start of the first speech against Catiline: "How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience? How long will that madness of yours mock us? To what end will your unbridled audacity hurl itself about?" In this passage more than ten questions follow. The second ornament is the inquiry, or percunctatio, and what it differs from the question Cicero himself explains in book 3 of On the Orator, where he says: "The question, and the inquiry closely akin to it, and the setting out of one's own opinion." From these words we understand that the question is simple, that is, without any statement of one's own opinion, but the inquiry always has a statement of one's own opinion attached. And so in the Orator to Brutus he writes thus of each figure: "So that he may press by questioning, and then, as if answering his own questions, reply himself." It makes no difference, however, whether the orator answers in his own name or in that of his opponent. For example, before he went into exile: "Can it then happen that I am taken back by my clients, when those by whom I ought to be held back are set on rejecting me?" Likewise in the same speech: "Do they want to use force? I am here. Do they want to drive me out? I am leaving. Do they refuse to hear the case though it has not been argued? I do not speak of the case. Are they attempting something else? Let them do it." Cornificius in book 4 calls this figure subiectio. The third figure is when we command or order something, and it may therefore be called iussio. Yet you will not find any mention of it made by Cicero elsewhere. I, unless I am mistaken, think that it is contained in what the same Cicero in book 3 of On the Orator calls interpellatio, although in the Orator he introduces it in words that restrain an interrupter, which certainly cannot be done without a command and an order. I will offer two examples, one of which contains a direct command, and the other a command together with the restraining of an interrupter. The first is in the first speech against Catiline: "What is it, Catiline? Do you doubt that I am ordering you to do what you were already doing of your own accord? The consul orders the enemy to leave the city." Likewise in the same: "Therefore, as I have often said already, set out; and if you wish to stir up hatred against me, your enemy (as you proclaim), go straight into exile," and the rest in the same vein. Likewise in the Pro Rabirio you have an example of the other kind: "Why do you not hold back your voices, the proof of your folly, the witness of your small number?" This has the appearance of rebuke. Concerning the wish, too, that we may not make the matter long, we may cite it both elsewhere often and in the same Rabirian speech: "Would that the case had granted me this opportunity, that I might proclaim that Lucius Saturninus, enemy of the Roman people, was killed by the hand of Gaius Rabirius." Orations also begin with this same figure, for there are many forms of the wish, as in the Pro Sulla: "I should most wish, judges," and the rest. Likewise in the ninth Philippic: "I wish the immortal gods had done it, conscript fathers," and what follows.

units.la: Vitare
units.tr: Avoiding monotony

units.la: Vitare autem similitudinem poterimus, non semper à proposito ordientes, & si non omnia confirmando disputabimus: breuiterq; interdum, quæ erunt satis aperta, ponemus. quodq; ex his efficietur, si id apertum sit, non habebimus necesse semper concludere.
units.tr: We shall be able to avoid similarity if we do not always begin from the proposition, and if we do not confirm everything in our argument; we shall sometimes state briefly what will be sufficiently clear, and what follows from this, if it is evident, we shall not need always to conclude.

units.la: Vitare autè similitudinem poterimus. ) Iam de altera tractationis parte, quam diximus in dispositione propositionū & argumentationis ucr fari. ea autem duo habet: & ordinis immutationem, & propositionum omissionem, interdum quoq; approbationum. De ordine mutando suprà in inflexo argumentandi genere diximus. quod autem ad omissionem attinet, ea fit aut in enthymematc, aut simplici conclusione, aut dilemmate, quam complexionem Latinè diximus, & interdum etiam inductionem nominari. Nam hæc uarietas ex omissione alicuius, aut aliquarū propositionū nascitur. Qua de re præclare etiā, & cum hoc loco qui est in Partitionib. congruenter, præcipit tum Cornific. lib. 2. tum Cic. ipse de Inuent. lib. 1. Absolutissima (inquit Cornificius) est argumentatio ea, quæ ex quinq; partibus constat: sed ea non semper necesse est uti. tum enim com-
units.tr: We shall be able to avoid similarity. Now let us turn to the other part of treatment, which we said lies in the arrangement of the propositions and of the argument. This part has two aspects: a change of order and the omission of propositions, and sometimes also of the approvals.
