About changing the order we have already spoken above, in the discussion of the inflected kind of argument. As for omission, it occurs either in the enthymeme, or in the simple conclusion, or in the dilemma, which we have called in Latin the complexio, and which sometimes is also called induction. For this variety arises from the omission of one or several propositions. Concerning this matter, Cornificius in book 2 and Cicero himself in book 1 of On Invention prescribe excellently, and in agreement with the passage here in the Partitiones. Cornificius says: "The most complete argument is the one that consists of five parts, but it is not always necessary to use it. For then the conclusion" [he means the conclusion by complexio] ...

units.la: ) Iam de altera tractationis parte, quam diximus in dispositione propositionum et argumentationis uersari. complexione (conclusionem intelligit) superfedendum est, si res breuis est, ut facile memoria comprehendatur: tum exornatio prætermittenda est, si parum locuples ad amplificandum & exornandum res uidetur esse. sin & breuis erit argumentatio, & res tenuis & humilis, tum exornatione & complexione supersedendum est. Quibus uerbis non solum quid faciendum sit, sed etiam quam ob causam, docet. Sed earum, quas proposuimus, argumentationum exempla proferamus. Enthymematis illud sit: nam subtilior eius ratio in Dialecticis traditur. Clodius insidias fecit Miloni: ergo iure interfectus est. hic enim maior abest. Potest autem in Enthymemate aut maior aut minor abesse, interdum etiam conclusio. rectè e- nim Cicero: Quodq; ex iis efficitur, si id apertum fit, non habebimus necesse semper concludere. Simplex conclusio illa est, quæ ex necessaria consecutione conficitur tantum: Cum pater Roscij Romæ interfectus est, Roscius Ameriæ fuit. Complexionis autem ea ratio est, ut utrumuis cōcesseris, reprehendatur, ad hunc modum: Si improbus est, cur uteris? Si probus, cur accusas? Item pro Cœlio: Quo quidem in crimine primum illud requiram, dixerit ne Clodiæ, quam ad rem aurum tunc sumeret, an non dixerit. si nō dixit, cur dedit? Si dixit, eodem se conscientiæ scelere deuinxit. hæc à CorCornificio, diuisio nominatur. De inductione & enumeratione, uide libro de Inuentio ne primo.
units.tr: ...the complexio may be dispensed with if the matter is brief, so that it is easily held in memory; then the embellishment may be omitted if the matter seems too meagre to be amplified and adorned. But if the argument is also brief, and the matter slight and humble, then both the embellishment and the complexio may be dispensed with. In these words he teaches not only what should be done, but also the reason why. But let us set out examples of the arguments we have proposed. For the enthymeme let this be the example, since its finer theory is handed down in the Dialectic books: Clodius laid an ambush for Milo; therefore he was rightly killed. Here the major premise is absent. In an enthymeme either the major or the minor may be absent, and sometimes even the conclusion. Cicero rightly says: "And what follows from these things, if it is clear, we shall not need always to conclude." The simple conclusion is that which is drawn only from a necessary consequence: "When Roscius's father was killed at Rome, Roscius was at Ameria." The method of the complexio is this: whichever of the two you grant, you are rebuked, as follows: "If he is wicked, why do you use him? If he is good, why do you accuse him?" Likewise in the Pro Caelio: "In this charge I shall first ask whether she [Clodia] spoke of what purpose she was then taking the gold, or did not speak of it. If she did not speak, why did she give it? If she did speak, she bound herself by the same crime of conscience." Cornificius calls this figure divisio. Concerning induction and enumeration, see the first book of On Invention.

units.la: DE ASSVMPTORVM LO- CORUM tractatione.
units.tr: On the handling of the assumed topics

units.la: C.F. Quid illa quę sine arte appellantur, quæ iamdudum assumpta dixisti, hæc quo nam modo, quo nam loco artis indigent? C. P. Illa uerò indigent. & nec eo dicuntur sine arte, quòd ita sunt: sed quòd ea non parit oratoris ars, sed foris ad se delata, tamen arte tractat, & maximè in testibus.
units.tr: F. What about those things which are called inartificial, which you said a little while ago were assumed? In what way, and in what place, do these need art? P. They certainly need it. They are not called inartificial because of what they are, but because the orator's art does not produce them; they are brought to him from outside. Still, art handles them, and especially in the case of witnesses.

units.la: C. F. Quid illa quæ Sine arte appellantur.) Perfecta & explicata omni insitorum locorum ratione, quæstionem mouet filius, cur quæ Assumpta initio Partitionum appellata sunt, Sine arte (Græci dicunt ἀτεχνα) dicantur. Ex quo sequitur, quærendum esse, an aliquo pacto, & quónam loco artis indigeat. Nam si sine arte, ergo locum in arte non habent: quod si habent, cur sine arte appellantur?
units.tr: F. What about those which are called inartificial? Having fully explained the whole doctrine of the intrinsic topics, the son raises the question why those things which were called assumed at the beginning of the Partitions are called inartificial (the Greeks say atechna [ἀτεχνα]). From this it follows that we must ask whether they need art in some way, and in what place. For if they are without art, then they have no place within art; but if they do have a place, why are they called inartificial?

units.la: C. P. Illa uerò indigent.) Commodè atq; apposite soluit quæstionem pater: atq; ex eo occasione sumpta, de eorum tractatione subtiliter disserit. Nam de toto genere testium.) Etsi alia in testimoniorum loco quaerātur, ut rumores, leges, iusiurandum, tabulæ: tamē frequens in foro usus est testium, siue in ciuilibus causis, siue etiam capitalibus, ut Iurisconsulti aiunt. ff. lib.22. de Test.l.1.quo loco etiā, qui'nam testes audiendi sint, Modestinus ijs uerbis l.2.praeclarè docet: In testimoniis autem (inquit) fides, dignitas, mores, grauitas examinanda est: & ideo testes, qui aduersus fidem testationis uacillant, audiendi non sunt. In testibus igitur duo quaerenda proponit Cicero: sententias, & ipsam tractationis rationem. Sententiae autem, aut in genere uniuerso, aut in singulis testibus uersantur. Ad genus uniuersum, siue ad infinitam quaestionem, referuntur illa uerba, Nam de toto genere testium: ad ὑπόθεσιν uerò, & ad partem, illa, Et de singulis testibus. quorum alterum in re ipsa est, alterum in personis. Ad infinitum genus pertinet illa sententia, siue locus communis: Testimonia certa esse, rationes incertas: qui quidem locus in confirmando valet, siue, ut aiunt, pro testibus. Contra autem contra testes est ille locus: Argumenta rerum esse propria, testimonia uoluntatum. atq; ad hosce duos locos, siue sententias contrarias, omnes reliquae sunt referendae. sunt enim penè innumerabiles, nec arte tradi possunt, utpote quas Oratores è re nata, aut ex lo cis uerisimilium sunt. Quod etsi uerum est, tamen omnes aut pro testibus, aut contra testes assumuntur. Ad singulos vero testes, sive probados sive improbados, sententia ex natura et vita testium, et constantia testimoniorum capiuntur. ut a testibus, pro Archia: Ipse adest vir summa auctoritate et religione ac fide M. Lucullus, qui se non opinari, sed scire: non audiuisse, sed vidisse: non interfuisse, sed egisse dicit. adsunt Heraclien ses legati, nobilissimi homines. Contra testes autem, pro Flacco: At quos testes? Primum dicam, id quod est commune, Graecos. Item in Caeliana: Equidem vos abducam a testibus, neque huius iudicij veritatem, quae mutari nullo modo potest, in voluntate testium collocari sinam: quae facillime effingi, nullo negotio flecti ac detorqueri potest. Argumentis agemus, signis omni luce clarioribus crimina refellemus: res cum re, causa cum causa, ratio cum ratione pugnabit. Iam sequitur postremum illud caput, in quo tractandi ratio continetur: ea tota posita est in comparatione exemplorum, ac praesertim cum minora cum maioribus comparantur, non solum vera, sed etiam ficta. Sed quoniam verorum est facilis inventio, fictorum unum exemplum ex RoscLana proferemus: Aphricanus (inquit) si sua res ageretur, testimonium non diceret: si diceret, non crederetur.Ex quo significat,multo minus testi-bus qui proponebantur in illa caussa,esse credendum, utpote minoris longè, quàm Aphricanus, autoritatis. Orationes in quibus tum de toto genere testium,tum etiam de singulis testib.agitur, sunt illæ præcipuè: in Vatinium testem, pro M. Fonteio,pro M.Cælio,atq; in Verrinis omnibus.
units.tr: P. They certainly need it. The father resolves the question neatly and appropriately, and, taking occasion from it, discusses their handling in detail. For concerning the whole class of witnesses: although other matters are examined under the heading of testimony, such as rumours, laws, oaths and documents, the use of witnesses is nonetheless frequent in the courts, whether in civil cases or even capital ones, as the jurists say (Digest, book 22, title On Witnesses, law 1). In the same place, Modestinus, in law 2, teaches clearly what kind of witnesses should be heard: "In testimony," he says, "faithfulness, standing, character and seriousness must be examined; and therefore witnesses who waver in the reliability of their testimony are not to be heard." So in dealing with witnesses Cicero proposes two things to be examined: the opinions, and the method of handling itself. Opinions concern either the whole class or individual witnesses. The words "For concerning the whole class of witnesses" refer to the unlimited question, the general one; the words "and concerning individual witnesses" refer to the particular case and to persons: the former concerns the matter itself, the latter the persons. To the unlimited class belongs that opinion, or common place: "Testimonies are certain, reasons uncertain." This place is useful in confirming, or, as they say, for witnesses. Against witnesses, on the other hand, is that place: "Arguments belong to the facts, testimonies to the wills [of witnesses]." All the remaining places are to be referred to these two opposed places or opinions. For they are almost countless and cannot be taught by art, since orators draw them from the circumstances as they arise, or from the places of probability. Although this is true, all of them are assumed either for witnesses or against witnesses. As for individual witnesses, whether approved or disapproved, opinions are taken from the nature and life of the witnesses and from the consistency of their testimony. For example, from witnesses, in the speech for Archias: "Here in person is the man of the highest authority, religion and good faith, Marcus Lucullus, who says he does not suppose but knows, has not heard but seen, has not been present but acted. Here are the envoys of Heraclea, very noble men." Against witnesses, in the speech for Flaccus: "But what witnesses? First I shall speak of what is common to them: they are Greeks." Likewise in the Caelian speech: "Indeed I shall lead you away from the witnesses, and I shall not allow the truth of this trial, which can in no way be changed, to be placed in the will of witnesses, which can very easily be fashioned and bent and twisted without any trouble. We shall argue by arguments, we shall refute charges by signs clearer than any light: fact will fight against fact, cause against cause, reason against reason." Now follows that last head, in which the method of handling is contained. It rests entirely on the comparison of examples, especially when lesser things are compared with greater, and not only real but also invented ones. But since real examples are easy to find, we shall bring forward one invented example from the Roscius speech: "Africanus," he says, "if his own affair were being tried, would not give testimony; if he gave it, it would not be believed." By this he means that the witnesses who were put forward in that case are much less to be believed, since they are far inferior in authority to Africanus. The speeches in which both the whole class of witnesses and individual witnesses are discussed are chiefly these: against the witness Vatinius, for Marcus Fonteius, for Marcus Caelius, and in all the Verrines.

units.la: Sæpe etiam quæstionib. resistendum est: quòd & dolorem fugientes multi in tormentis ementiti persæpe sunt, moriq; maluerunt falsum fatendo, quàm inficiādo dolere. multi etiam suam vitam neglexerunt, ut eos qui his cariores, quàm ipsi sibi essent, liberarent. Alij autem aut natura corporis, aut consuetudine dolendi, aut metu supplicij, aut mortis, uim tormentorum pertulerunt.
units.tr: Often one must also resist interrogations under torture, because many people, fleeing pain, have often lied under torments, and have preferred to die by confessing falsely rather than to suffer by denying. Many too have neglected their own lives so that they might free those who were dearer to them than they were to themselves. Others, by the nature of their bodies, by the habit of enduring pain, or by fear of punishment or death, have borne the force of the torments.

units.la: Sæpe etiam quæstionib.resistendū est.) Quæstiones etiam testimonia quædā sunt,quæ videntur ea de caussa fidē facere, quia necessitas quædam eis inest. eadem vero ratio quæstionum est, quæ fuit testiū: nisi quod hic tormentis, viiq; admota veritas quaeritur, unde quæstiones sunt appellatæ. Testes autem non semper tormentis, sed iureiurando astricti,de aliqua re fatentur. Nam ut
units.tr: Often one must also resist interrogations. Interrogations are also a kind of testimony, which seem to inspire belief for this reason, that a certain necessity is present in them. The reasoning about interrogations is the same as that about witnesses, except that here the truth is sought by torments and by force applied, whence they are called interrogations. Witnesses, however, do not always testify about some matter under torture, but are bound by an oath. For as

units.la: de toto genere testiū,et de singulis testib.dicitur, sic etiā de toto genere quæstionū,deq; singulis et certis personis, quæ in quæstionem uocantur. In quibus omnibus duo quærenda sunt: et sententiæ, et ipsa tractatio. Atq; hæc in utrāq; partem: hoc est, à quæstionib.et contra quæstiones. Tametsi enim Cicero tantū cōtra quæstiones locos afferre uideatur, tamen in eis etiam contrarij intelligendi sunt, qui à quæstionibus, siue pro quæstionibus dicuntur. Nam si pro nobis faciant, eas augere poterimus, ac dicere, solas ex omni genere testimoniorū esse ueras. Quod si nobis cōtrariæ fuerint, et pro aduersario fecerint fidem, earum uim licebit eleuare, de genere toto quæstionū disputando.quib. enim acerbitates tormentorum adhibentur, ij non minus falsa quàm uera dicere solent.nam uel dolorem tolerantes, uerum occultant: uel facilè mentiuntur, ut citius à cruciatu liberentur. Id enim etiā iurisconsulti testātur, quēadmodū habetur Digestorum lib. 48.l.1.tit. de Quæstionibus.§.Quæstioni. Quæstioni (inquit Adrianus imperator) fidē nō semper,nec tamen nunquam habendam,constitutionib. declaratur. etenim res est fragilis et periculosa, et quæ ueritatē fallat.Nam pleriq; patientia, siue duritia tormentorū,ita tormenta conténunt,ut exprimi ab eis ueritas nullo modo possit. Alij tanta sunt impatientia, ut quiduis mētiri quàm pati tormēta malint: ꝇ ita fit, ut etiam uario modo fateantur, neq; tantum sc, uerùm etiam alios criminentur. Loci uerò, siue sententiæ, infinitæ in hoc genere sunt, omnia illa quæ hic in Cicerone leguntur: nisi quis malit esse sententiarum approbationes, ut illæ sint sententiæ, Quæstionibus esse credendum, cui subiiciātur rationes illæ: quod ꝇ dolore fugientes multi, in tormētis ementiti persæpe sunt: ꝇ reliqua id genus. Contra quæstiones pulcherrimus est locus in Orat. pro Sylla: qui locus, quòd prolixè tractatur, ad eū lectorem reijcio.
units.tr: are said of the whole class of witnesses and of individual witnesses, so also of the whole class of interrogations, and of individual and specific persons who are summoned to interrogation. In all these two things are to be examined: the opinions, and the handling itself. And this in both directions: that is, from interrogations and against interrogations. For although Cicero seems to bring forward places only against interrogations, nevertheless the opposite ones are also to be understood in them, which are said from interrogations or in favour of interrogations. For if they favour us, we can increase their force and say that they alone are true out of every kind of testimony. But if they are contrary to us and make belief for the adversary, it will be allowed to weaken their force by disputing about the whole class of interrogations. For those to whom the bitterness of torments is applied are accustomed to say false things no less than true ones: for either they conceal the truth while enduring the pain, or they lie easily so that they may be freed more quickly from the torture. The jurists also testify to this, as is found in the Digest, book 48, title On Interrogations, §Interrogation. "Belief is not always to be given to interrogation, yet not never either, as the constitutions declare" (says the emperor Hadrian). "For the thing is fragile and dangerous, and one that deceives the truth. For many, through patience or hardness toward torments, so endure them that truth cannot in any way be drawn from them. Others are so impatient that they prefer to lie about anything rather than endure the torments; and so it happens that they confess in various ways, and accuse not only themselves but others." The places, or opinions, of this kind are unlimited: all those which are read here in Cicero, unless someone prefers to take them as approvals of opinions, so that these are the opinions: "Belief is to be given to interrogation," with those reasons subjoined, namely that many people, fleeing pain, have often lied under torments; and the rest of that kind. Against interrogations, the most splendid place is in the speech for Sulla. Since this place is treated at length, I refer the reader to it.

units.la: Alij ementiti sunt in eos, quos oderāt. atq; hæc exemplis firmanda sunt. Neq; est obscurū, quin, quoniā in utraq; parte sunt exēpla, & item ad coniecturā faciendā loci, in contrarijs contraria sint sumenda.
units.tr: Others have lied against those whom they hated. These things must be confirmed by examples. Nor is it obscure that, since there are examples on both sides, and likewise places for making conjecture, contrary things must be taken from the contraries.

units.la: Alij ementiti sunt in eos quos oderant. ) Vt enim gratiæ causa homines mentiuntur, sic etiam odij. idcirco rectè Imperator Digest. lib. 4. leg. prima. §. Præterea. Præterea, inquit, inimicorum quæstioni fides haberi non debet, quia facilè mētiuntur. neq; tamen prætextu inimicitiarum detrahenda erit fides quæstioni: sed causa cognita, aut habenda fides, aut non habenda. Atq; hæc exemplis firmanda sunt.) Tractationem attingit, in qua proderit exempla proferre, quæ aliàs acciderunt, & ipsis iudicibus cognita sunt, ut recte admonet Aristoteles Rhet.1. Quē- admodum autem in testimonijs diximus, etiam lo ci in contrarias partes ad hunc locum ex conieEturis sumendi sunt. Vide Val. Max. de quæstionibus & testibus, lib.8.
units.tr: Others have lied against those whom they hated. For just as men lie for the sake of favour, so also they lie out of hatred. Therefore the emperor rightly says in the Digest, book 4, law 1, §Moreover: "Moreover, belief should not be given to the interrogation of enemies, because they lie easily. Yet belief in an interrogation is not to be taken away on the pretext of enmity; rather, once the case has been examined, belief is either to be given or not to be given." And these things are to be confirmed by examples. He touches on the handling itself, in which it will be useful to bring forward examples which have happened at other times and are known to the judges themselves, as Aristotle rightly advises in the first book of the Rhetoric. As we said about testimonies, places must also be taken from conjectures for the contrary side in this place. See Valerius Maximus, On Interrogations and Witnesses, book 8.

units.la: Atq; etiam incurrit alia quædam in testibus, & in quæstionibus ratio. Sæpe enim ea quæ dicta sunt, si aut ambiguè, aut inconstanter, aut in- credibiliter dicta sunt, aut etiam aliter ab alio dicta, subtiliter reprehenduntur.
units.tr: Another consideration also arises concerning witnesses and examinations. Often what has been said is subtly criticised if it was said ambiguously, inconsistently, or incredibly, or if it was said by one person differently from another.

units.la: Atq; etiam incurrit alia quædam in testib. & in quæstionibus ratio.) Præceptum quoddam in tractandis testibus & quæstionibus commune tradit: ut si quæ dicta sunt aut ambiguè, ut in contrarias partes intelligi possint: aut inconstanter, ut cum modò hoc, modò illud aiunt, aut affirmant: aut incredibiliter & supra fidē, & quæ fieri non possint, aut difficillimè possint: aut postremò, cū aliter ab alio dicta sunt, quàm ab ipso qui torquetur, ea subtiliter reprehendantur: id quod fit po- tissimū διαλογισμῷ, hoc est altercatione & disputatione tatione quadam,quam rem usu melius norút re-rum capitalium iudíces,quàm doćti uiri.Quanquam & de hac re iurísconsulti cautionem quoq; tradiderint,ut habetur Digest.lib.48.de quæstionibus.l.10.§.Plurimum. Plurimum(inquit Arca dius) quoq; in excutienda ueritate, etiam uoxipsa,& subtilis cognitionis diligentia, affert. Nã & ex sermone,& ex eo qua quis constantia,qua trepidatione quid diceret,uel cuius existimationis quisq; in ciuitate sua est, quædam ad illuminandâ ueritatem in lucē emergunt. Exèpla subtilis huius diligentiæ in teste exquirendo,habentur in oratione in Vatinium testem. Illud autè postremò sciendum est, Romæ seruos tantum,nõ dominos torqueri solitos.quëadmodũ non solũ orationes Ciceronis & historia antiqua docet, uerũm etiâ Iurifcõsulti eodem de Quæstionib. titulo.
units.tr: Another consideration also arises concerning witnesses and examinations. He gives a general precept for handling witnesses and examinations: if what has been said can be understood in opposite senses because it is ambiguous; or if it is inconsistent, as when they say or affirm now this and now that; or if it is incredible, beyond belief, impossible, or very hard to be possible; or finally, when one person has said something differently from another, and not from the one who is being examined, then it is subtly criticised. This is done chiefly by dialogismos [διαλογισμῷ], that is, by a kind of cross-examination and debate, a matter which judges in capital cases understand better from experience than learned men do. Yet the jurists also gave a caution on this point, as found in Digest 48, the title on examinations, law 10, §. Plurimum. "Very much," says Arcadius, "in investigating the truth also contributes the very voice itself and careful attention to subtle discernment. For from the speech, and from the manner in which someone speaks, with what steadiness or what trembling, and from the reputation each person has in his own city, certain things emerge into the light that clarify the truth." Examples of this subtle care in examining a witness are found in the speech against the witness Vatinius. Finally, it must be known that at Rome only slaves, and not masters, were usually put to torture, as not only the speeches of Cicero and ancient history teach, but also the jurists under the same title on examinations.

units.la: DE PERORATIONE, IN QVA primum de Amplificatione agit.
units.tr: On the Peroration, in which he first treats of Amplification

units.la: C. F. Extrema tibi pars restat o-rationis, quæ posita in perorando est, de qua sane uelim audire. C. P. Facilior est explicatio perorationis. Nam est díuisa in duas partes, amplificationem & enumerationem. Augendi autem & hïc est proprius locus in perorando, & in cursu ipso orationis declinationes ad amplificandum dantur, confirmata re aliqua, aut reprehensa.
units.tr: C. F. There remains for you the last part of the speech, the one placed in the peroration, about which I would very much like to hear. C. P. The explanation of the peroration is easier. For it is divided into two parts, amplification and enumeration. The proper place for amplifying is also in the peroration, and in the course of the speech digressions are allowed for amplifying, once some matter has been confirmed or refuted.

units.la: C. F. Extrema tibi pars restat orationis.) Præpaaatio est, ad perorationis explicationem, quæ quatuor fiue sex partiū orationis postrema est, etiam conclusio nominata, Græcè ἐπίλογος.
units.tr: There remains for you the last part of the speech. This is a preface to the explanation of the peroration, which is the last of the four or six parts of a speech. It is also called the conclusion, in Greek epilogos [ἐπίλογος].

units.la: C. P. Facilior est explicatio perorationis.) Caussa facilitatis est, quod in peroratione ea traduntur, quæ magna ex parte in officio oratoris & partibus orationis explicata sunt.
units.tr: The explanation of the peroration is easier. The reason for its ease is that the peroration deals with things that have for the most part already been explained in the office of the orator and in the parts of the speech.

units.la: Nam est diuisa in duas partes.)Idcirco in duas partes, quoniam duplex est finis propositus in perorādo: motus scilicet, atq; memoria. idcirco amplificatio ad motum, ad memoriā enumeratio spectat, illa ἀνάκρισις, hæc uero ἀνακεφαλαίωσις à Græcis magistris appellata. quomodo aūt motus quo utimur in exordio, differret à perorationis motu, & ut ille lenior, hic uerò uehementior esse deberet, supra in exordij explicatione diɛtū est.
units.tr: For it is divided into two parts. It is divided into two because the peroration has a twofold aim: namely, stirring the emotions and aiding the memory. Hence amplification serves the emotions, and enumeration serves the memory. The Greek masters call the former anakrisis [ἀνάκρισις] and the latter anakephalaiosis [ἀνακεφαλαίωσις]. How the emotion we use in the exordium differs from the emotion of the peroration, and how the former ought to be milder and the latter more vehement, was said above in the explanation of the exordium.

units.la: Augendi autem. )Et de loco amplificationis, & digressionum, quas declinationes hic appellat, alibi indicatum.
units.tr: Moreover, the proper place for amplifying. The place of amplification and of digressions, which he here calls declinations, has been indicated elsewhere.

units.la: Est igis amplificatio grauior quædam affirmatio, quæ motu animorū concōciliet in dicēdo fidē. ea & uerborū genere cōficit, & rerū uerba ponēda fūt, quę uim habeat illustrādi, nec ab usu sint abhorrentia, grauia, plena, sonātia, iūcta, facta, cognominata, non uulgata, superlata, in primiscq; translata, nec in singulis uerbbis, sed in cōtinētib. soluta, quę dicūtur sine cōiūctiōe ut plura uideant,
units.tr: Amplification, then, is a rather weighty affirmation which, by moving the minds of the hearers, wins belief in what is said. It is achieved also by the kind of words used. The words chosen should have the power to illustrate and should not be out of keeping with ordinary usage: they should be weighty, full, sonorous, joined, made, compounded, not vulgar, hyperbolic, and especially transferred. They should be loosened not only in single words but in continuous phrases, which are said to lack conjunctions so that they may appear more numerous.

units.la: Est igitur amplificatio.) Definitio est amplificationis, de qua etiam antea, quātū satis est. Illud igitur potius uidendū erit, quæ sint amplificationis partes, quæ materia, quæ itē tractatio. Amplificatio diuiditur in indignatione & cōquestione, siue cōmiseratione. Indignatio est oratio, per quā cōficitur, ut in aliquē hominē magnū odiū, aut in re grauis offensio cōcitetur. Cōquestio uerò est oratio, auditorū misericordiā captans: de quib. partib. extremo loco dicetur. nūc de materia, eiusq; partib. & locis explicandū. Materia sumitur ex ijs quæ magna uocātur. magna enim sint necesse est, quæ mouēt: parua impellere haud magnopere possunt. Magnitudo uerò in uerborum genere cernitur, & rerū. In uerbis ea magna dicimus, quæ uim habet illustrādi: cuiusmodi sunt primum nō inusitata, q̄ Cicero dicit, nec ab usu abhorrētia. inusitata enim, ut alibi diximus, obscuritatē habent. Item grauia: ut, parricida, uel siccarius, grauius est, quàm homicida: patriæ parens, quàm bonus ciuis. Item sonātia, quæ consonantiora dixit antea: ut orando, numerādo, sonantius est, quàm orare, numerare. Plena, quæ & grauitatem & sonum habent: ut horrendus, scelceratus. Iuncta, quæ suprà duplicata dixit, ut cōsceleratus, perterrefactus. Facta, ut infinitas, insanitas, perpetuitas, loquuntor, & colloquuntor: quib. moderatè utendū, ut Cicero facit. Cognominata, quæ & agnominata, in quib. aut simili sonus, aut syllabarum complexio paululum immuta ta: quæ & idem significantium sunt, & diuersæ potestatis: amans, amens, diuersa sunt, etsi sono & syllabis consimilia: mutum forum, elinguem curiam, tacitam & fractam ciuitatem uidebatis: crudelis & nefaria mulier, eiusdem sunt potestatis.
units.tr: Amplification, then. This is the definition of amplification, which was also given earlier, as far as is sufficient. It will be better now to consider what the parts of amplification are, what its matter is, and likewise how it is handled. Amplification is divided into indignation and complaint, or commiseration. Indignation is speech by which great hatred against some man is stirred up, or serious offence is aroused at some matter. Complaint is speech that seeks the pity of the hearers. These parts will be discussed in the last place. Now I must explain the matter and its parts and places. The matter is taken from those things that are called great. For those things which move must necessarily be great; small things can hardly push strongly. Greatness is seen both in the kind of words and in the matter. In words we call great those which have the power to illustrate. Such are, first, words not unusual, as Cicero says, and not out of keeping with common usage. For unusual words, as I said elsewhere, carry obscurity. Likewise weighty words: "parricide" or "assassin" is weightier than "murderer"; "parent of the fatherland" than "good citizen." Likewise sonorous words, which he called more consonant earlier: "orando, numerando" [in speaking, in counting] is more sonorous than "orare, numerare" [to speak, to count]. Full words, which have both weight and sound: "horrendous," "accursed." Joined words, which above he called doubled: "consceleratus," "perterrefactus" [very wicked, thoroughly terrified]. Made words, such as "infinitas," "insanitas," "perpetuitas," "loquuntor," and "colloquuntor" [infinity, insanity, perpetuity, they speak, they converse], which must be used with moderation, as Cicero does. Compounded words, which are also called agnominated, in which either a similar sound or a slight alteration of the syllables is found. These words may have the same meaning and yet different force, or different meanings with similar sound. "Amans" and "amens" [loving and mad] are different though similar in sound and syllables. You saw "a mute forum, a tongueless senate-house, a silent and broken city." "Cruel" and "wicked" as applied to a woman are of the same force.

units.la: Non uulgata. ) quæ in ore omnium sunt, etiā uulgarium, ea uulgata, siue peruulgata, siue uulgaria dicuntur. Rara uerò, & singulariā, & electa, siue delecta, quæ præstantium tantum sunt in usu uirorum, uulgatis contraria sunt. Ergo illa superiora grādi oratori, præsertim in amplificā do, sunt relinquēda: hæc uerò assumēda. Hic igi turualedicendū Tacitis, Suetonijs, Plinijs, Quin tilianis, Apuleijs, Senccis, Martialibus, ac multo magis quibusdam alijs longè obscurioribus in ratione dicendi: & cōtrà, Cafares, Salustij, Cicero nes, Vergilij, Liuijq;, atq; horũ similes usurpādi.
units.tr: Not vulgar. Words that are on everyone's lips, even those of common people, are called vulgar, or very common, or commonplace. Rare, singular, and select or chosen words, which are used only by outstanding men, are the opposite of the vulgar. Therefore the former should be left aside by the grand orator, especially in amplifying, and the latter should be taken up. Here we must bid farewell to Tacitus, Suetonius, Pliny, Quintilian, Apuleius, Seneca, Martial, and much more to certain others far more obscure in their manner of speaking. On the contrary, the Caesars, Sallust, Cicero, Virgil, Livy, and those like them should be used.

units.la: Superlata.) ut, Diuinum atq; incredibile genus orationis, uestra immortalia beneficia. Sunt qui superlata putent, cū mutis rebus sensus quasi tribuitur, ut pro Plancio: Quorum honoribus agri, propè dicam, ipsi, montesq; faucrūt. Item illa pro Archia: Saxa uoce respondent. Translata: ut flumen orationis, negotiorum undæ siue fluctus. Soluta.) sunt, quæ dicuntur sine coniunctione, ut plura uidcantur. De dissolutione loquitur, siue dissoluto, quod fit tum in simplicib. uerbis, tum in coniunctis: quæ Cicero hic & singula uerba, & continentia uocat. In simplicibus: A parentibus nobis uita, patrimonium, libertas, ciuitas tradita est: Cicero in Senatu. In coniūctis, siue continentibus, siue continuatis uerbis, ut in peroratione eiusdem orationis: Quare cum me uestra autoritas accersierit, Po. Ro. reuocarit, Resp.implorarit, Italia cuncta pene suis humeris reportarit, non committam ut, &c.
units.tr: Hyperbolic. For example: "a divine and incredible kind of speech, your immortal benefits." Some think words are hyperbolic when feeling is given to inanimate things, as in the speech for Plancius: "by whose honours the fields, I may almost say themselves, and the mountains have spoken." Likewise in the speech for Archias: "the rocks answer with a voice." Transferred words, such as "the flood of speech," "the waves or floods of affairs." Loosened: these are phrases said without conjunction so that they seem more. He speaks of dissolution, or a dissolved style, which occurs both in simple words and in joined ones. Cicero here calls these both single words and continuous words. In simple words: "Life, inheritance, liberty, and citizenship were handed down to us by our parents," Cicero in the Senate. In joined, or continuous, or connected words, as in the peroration of the same speech: "Wherefore, since your authority has summoned me, the Roman people has recalled me, the Republic has implored me, and nearly all Italy has carried me back on its own shoulders, I will not allow that, etc."

units.la: Augent etiam relata uerba, iterata, duplicata, & ea quæ ascendūt gradatim ab humilioribus uerbis ad superiora. omninoq; semper quasi naturalis, & non explanata oratio, sed grauibus referta uerbis, ad augendum accommodatior.
units.tr: Related words, repeated words, and doubled words also augment, and so do those that rise step by step from lower words to higher ones. In general, the speech should always appear as if natural and unlaboured, yet filled with weighty words, which are better suited to amplifying.

units.la: Augent etiam relata uerba, iterata, duplicata.) Reliqua uerborum ornamenta enumerat, quae quidem aliquid obscuritatis habent: quoniam alibi alijs atq; alijs nominibus utitur. nam quis diuinare posset, quae hic relata uocet? Supra enim in suaui genere dicendi relata ad idem uerbum appellauit, & de Oratore Relationem: si modo eaedem figurae sunt. An fortasis intelligit, quae de singulis propositis dicta, referuntur ad singula? an uero paria paribus, aut contraria contrarijs relata? aut utrunq;? Melius certe erit, utrunq; figurae genus intelligere. Nam exiguum discrimen est inter comparia illa, & de singulis ducta, ad singula relata. Alterum uero genus erit eorum quae ad unum uerbum referuntur: ut, Vicit pudorem libido, timorem audacia, rationem amentia, quae coniunctio & adiunctio nominatur. Superioris exemplum illud ex Manliana sumi potest: Cuius adolescentia ad scientiam rei militaris non alienis praeceptis, sed suis imperijs: non offensionib. belli, sed uictorijs: nō stipen diijs, sed triumphis est traducta. Quanquam in hoc exemplo omnia etiam ad unum uerbū referūtur.
units.tr: Related, repeated, and doubled words also augment. He lists the remaining ornaments of words, which indeed carry some obscurity, since elsewhere he uses different names for them. For who could guess what he means here by "related" words? Above, in the gentle kind of speaking, he called "related" those figures that refer to the same word, and in De Oratore he spoke of "relatio," if these are indeed the same figures. Or does he perhaps mean things said of single items and referred to single items? Or rather like to like, or contrary to contrary, or both? It will surely be better to understand both kinds of figure. For the difference between those comparisons and those drawn from single items and referred to single items is slight. The other kind will be those referred to one word, as in: "Lust overcame modesty, boldness overcame fear, madness overcame reason." This is called conjunction and adjunction. An example of the first kind can be taken from the speech for the Manilian law: "his youth was devoted to knowledge of military affairs not by the precepts of others but by his own commands, not by the hardships of war but by victories, not by pay but by triumphs." Though in this example, too, everything is also referred to one word.

units.la: Iterata.) ut, Ego sum ille consul, ego inquā, etc.
units.tr: Repeated: as in "I am that consul, I, I say," and so on.

units.la: Duplicata.) Sunt, quæ suprà geminata dixit, in generibus dicendi: ut, Me me adsum qui feci. Ac de his ornamentis uerborū cursim diximus, propterca quòd in elocutione sunt pene omnia diligentius perlustrata.
units.tr: Doubled: these are what he above called geminated, among the kinds of speech, as in "Me, me, here I am, the one who did it." I have touched on these ornaments of words only briefly, because nearly all of them in elocution have already been examined more carefully.

units.la: Et ea quæ ascendunt gradatim.)Puto hoc esse schema, quod incrementum Quintilianus uocat: ubi uerba aliquot ponuntur, quorū alterum altero grauius est: et ut in gradibus scalarū uidemus, altius & superius. cuiusmodi sunt illa: Miserum, acerbum, calamitosum, funestū: item, indignum, luctuosum, horribile: item, facinus, scelus, parricidium: item, amentia, furor, scelus: item, improbus, nefarius, pestilens: item, caudex, stipes, truncus: item hebes, stupidus, plumbeus: item, uerberare, affligere, iugulare: item, fordidare, conspurcare, cruentare, funestare: item, uincire, uerberare, necare, atq; eiusmodi sexcenta.
units.tr: And those that rise step by step. I think this is the figure that Quintilian calls incrementum [climax], in which several words are placed, one of which is weightier than another, rising higher and higher as we see on the steps of a staircase. Such are: "wretched, bitter, calamitous, deadly"; likewise "unworthy, mournful, dreadful"; likewise "deed, crime, parricide"; likewise "madness, frenzy, crime"; likewise "wicked, nefarious, pestilent"; likewise "blockhead, stump, trunk"; likewise "dull, stupid, leaden"; likewise "to beat, to afflict, to slaughter"; likewise "to defile, to foul, to stain with blood, to make deadly"; likewise "to bind, to beat, to kill," and six hundred others of the same kind.

units.la: Omnino quæ semper quasi naturalis.) Naturalis oratio est, quæ sua sponte fusa dicitur, nullis uerborum floribus distincta & compta. Huic contraria est, quæ explanata & expolita dicitur. At quasi naturalis, & non explanata, ut hic Cicero dicit, est, etiamsi artificium habeat: neglecta tamen, & sine exquisito ornatu uideuidetur. neq; enim omnia uerborum ornamenta admittit, sed ea tantum quae grauitatem habent. non igitur in amplificatione, tam ornatus, leporesq;, quam gravitas est verborum requirenda. Exemplo haec demonstrari non possunt, quoniam haec laus fusa est per totam perorationem: & perorationes Ciceronis, praesertim in causis forensibus, hanc nobis orationis faciem ostendunt.
units.tr: Altogether, what is always as if natural. Natural speech is that which is said to flow of its own accord, distinguished and adorned by no flowers of words. Opposite to it is what is called elaborate and polished. But speech "as if natural and not elaborated," as Cicero says here, even if it has artistry, is nevertheless neglected and seems to lack exquisite ornament. For it does not admit every ornament of words, but only those that have weight. Therefore in amplification one should seek not so much ornament and charm as weight of words. These things cannot be demonstrated by example, since this praise is spread through the whole peroration; and the perorations of Cicero, especially in forensic cases, show us this look of speech.

units.la: Haec igitur in verbis, quib. actio vocis, vultus & gestus, congruens & apta ad animos permouendos accommodata est. Sed & in verbis, & in actione causa erit tenenda, & pro re agenda. Nam haec quia videntur perabsurda, cum graviora sunt, quam causa, diligenter fere, quid quenq; deceat, iudicandum est. Rerum amplificatio sumitur eisdem locis omnibus, quibus illa quae dicta sunt ad fidem, maximeq; definitiones valent conglobatae, & consequentium frequentatio, & contrariarum, & dissimilium, & inter se pugnantium rerum conflictio, & causae, & ea quae sunt de causis orta, maximeq; similitulitudines, & exempla: fictæ etiam personæ, muta denique loquantur.
units.tr: These things, then, in words, to which the delivery of the voice, the face and the gestures are fitted, congruent and suited to moving the minds of the audience. But both in words and in delivery the cause must be kept in view, and the thing itself must be treated. For these things, because they seem utterly absurd when they are greater than the cause, must be judged carefully, roughly, as to what suits each person. The amplification of things is drawn from all the same topics from which those things said to establish belief are drawn, and especially the definitions, when they are massed together, and the frequent use of consequences, and of contraries and dissimilar things, and the clash of things that fight against each other, and causes, and those things which have arisen from causes, and above all comparisons and examples; and fictitious persons, and finally even dumb things may speak.

units.la: Hæc igitur in uerbis quibus actio uocis.) De seruando in amplificationibus decoro præcipit. Vt enim in uita, sic in oratione, nihil est difficilius, quàm quid deceat uidere: ut non sine caussa dictum sit à Crasso, Caput esse, decere quod agas. Est autem, quid deceat, Oratori uidendum, nō in sententijs & rebus solum, sed etiam in uerbis: & Cicero, quoniam præcepta tradidit uerborū quæ amplificationem decent, quoniā idipsum ad elocutionē pertinet, & actio quoq; cum elocutione coniuncta est, idcirco actionis siue pronunciationis meminit: monetq; eam pronunciatione actionemq; adhibeamus, quæ non modò rebus, sed etiam uerbis congruens sit. Quod quidem faciemus, si caussam ipsam tenuerimus. neq; enim tantis clamoribus de pecunia, quàm de parricidio agemus. Cauendūq; erit, ne ex musca elephantum (quod dicitur) aut contrà faciamus. ac nullum est tam graue uerbum, quod si inepte pronuncietur, uim non amittat suam, obscuriusq; esse uideatur.
units.tr: "These things, then, in words, to which the delivery of the voice..." He prescribes what is fitting in amplifications. For as in life, so in speech, nothing is more difficult than to see what is fitting; hence it is not without reason that Crassus said that the chief thing is to see what is fitting for what you are doing. Now the orator must see what is fitting not only in thoughts and things but also in words. And since Cicero has delivered precepts about the words that befit amplification, and since this matter pertains to style, and delivery too is joined with style, he therefore mentions delivery or pronunciation, and he warns that we should employ a pronunciation and delivery that agree not only with the things but also with the words. We shall do this if we keep hold of the cause itself: for we shall not argue about money with as great outcries as about parricide. And care must be taken lest we make an elephant out of a fly, as the saying goes, or the reverse. And there is no word so weighty that, if it is pronounced clumsily, it does not lose its force and seem more obscure.

units.la: Rerum amplificatio.) Diximus, amplificationem ex magnitudine oriri. Magnitudinē uerò in rebus & uerbis spectari. De magnitudine & amplificatione uerborum dictum est: iam de rebus est uidendum. Res autem ipsæ aut in locis, ex quibus fides fit, latent: aut in rerum generibus, ex quibus sententiæ argumenta ue ducuntur. Est enim rerum amplificatio, quæ rem aliquâ aut magnam, aut præclaram, aut atrocè argumentis augeat, atq; sententijs. Etsi autem loci omnes qui ad fidem faciendam suprà numerati sunt, argumenta ad amplificandum nobis suppeditare possunt: potissimum tamen, quæ hic à Cicerone nominatur. Ait enim: Maximeq; definitiones ualent conglobatæ. Definitiones conglobatas, descriptiones copiosas & uarias uocat, cuiusmodi sunt illæ pro Cluentio de Safsia: Cuius ea stultitia est (inquit) ut eam nemo homine: ea uis, ut nemo fœminam: ea crudelitas, ut nemo matrem appellare possit. Atq; hæc per negationem. Illa uero quæ sequuntur, per affirmationem: Atq; etiã nomina necessitudinum, non solum naturæ nomen & iura mutauit: Vxor generi, nouerca filij, filiæ pellex: eò iam denique adducta est, ut sibi præter formam, nihil ad similitudinem hominis reseruarit. Huc etiam pertinent illa de gloria, in prima Philippica: cuius exemplum in Contrarijs commemorabo.
units.tr: "The amplification of things." We have said that amplification arises from magnitude, and that magnitude is to be looked for in things and in words. Concerning the magnitude and amplification of words we have spoken; now we must see to things. Now the things themselves either lie hidden in the topics from which proof comes, or in the kinds of things from which arguments and sentiments are drawn. For the amplification of things is that which enlarges a thing, whether great, or notable, or atrocious, by arguments and by sentiments. Although all the topics which were enumerated above for producing belief can supply us with arguments for amplifying, yet the one named here by Cicero is especially powerful. For he says: "and above all definitions, when massed together, are powerful." Massed definitions, he calls copious and varied descriptions, such as those in the speech for Cluentius about Sassia: "Her folly is such" (he says) "that no one would call it human; her violence is such that no one could call her a woman; her cruelty is such that no one could call her a mother." And these are by negation. But those which follow are by affirmation: "And even the names of kinship she has changed, not only the name and rights of nature: a wife to her son-in-law, a stepmother to her son, a concubine to her daughter; and at last she has been brought to the point that, apart from her form, she has kept nothing in common with the likeness of a human being." To this also belong those passages about glory in the first Philippic, whose example I shall mention among the contraries.

units.la: Et consequentiũ frequentatio.) Quam hic appellat frequentationem, descriptionem appellauit libro de Oratore tertio: Vel grauissimum (inquit) augendi lumen descriptio, atque eodem nomine mine eam etiam appellat Cornificius. Nam frequentatio, quam idem Cornificius ponit, longe alia est ab hac Ciceronis frequentatione. Exempla quoniam prolixa sunt, praetermittimus: ea si quis uolet, aut ex Cicerone, aut ex Cornificio petat.
units.tr: "And the frequent use of consequences." What he here calls frequency, he called description in the third book of De Oratore: "The most weighty light of amplification (he says) is description"; and Cornificius also calls it by the same name. For the frequency which Cornificius sets forth is quite different from this frequency of Cicero's. Since the examples are lengthy, we pass them over; if anyone wishes them, let him seek them from Cicero or from Cornificius.

units.la: Et contrariarum & dissimilium & inter se pugnantium rerum conflictio.) Obseruanda est primum uarietas: definitiones dixit conglobatas, consequentium frequentationem, contrariorum uero conflictionem: cum tamen nihil intelligat aliud, quam earum rerum quas nominat, crebritatem & densitatem quandam. De contrarijs habes Philippica prima: Carum esse ciuibus, bene de Republica mereri, laudari, coli, diligi, gloriosum est: metui uero, & in odio esse, inuidiosum, detestabile, imbecillum, caducum. Dissimilium uero, praeclarum est exemplum in peroratione Quintianae defensionis, item in peroratione Philippicae secundae, vbi Antonium cum Caesare contendit. Eadem est ratio pugnantium, quae contrariorum & dissimilium.
units.tr: "And the clash of contraries and of dissimilar and mutually fighting things." First, the variety is to be observed: he called the definitions "massed," the frequent use of consequences, but the clash of contraries; yet he means nothing other than a certain abundance and density of those things which he names. You have an example of contraries in the first Philippic: "To be dear to the citizens, to deserve well of the Republic, to be praised, cherished, loved, is glorious; but to be feared and to be in hatred is hateful, detestable, feeble, fleeting." Of dissimilar things there is a notable example in the peroration of the Quinctian defence, and likewise in the peroration of the second Philippic, where he sets Antony against Caesar. The principle for mutually fighting things is the same as for contraries and dissimilar things.

units.la: Et causse, & ea quae sunt de causis orta.) Et haec quoq; facilia sunt. nam postea quam sumpta sunt ex locis suis, si tantum ad probandum adhibeantur, sola esse possunt, & singula: sin etiam ad amplificandum, tum causse, tum quae sunt effecta de causis, condensanda & frequentanda sunt: quemadmodum facit Cicero Philippica prima, ubi sic percontatur: Unde igitur subito ista tanta mutatio? & reliqua quae sequuntur ibidem, paulo ante perorationem.
units.tr: "And causes, and those things which have arisen from causes." These too are easy. For after they have been taken from their own topics, if they are used only to prove, they can be alone and single; but if they are also used to amplify, then both causes and what has been effected by causes must be condensed and multiplied, as Cicero does in the first Philippic, where he asks thus: "Whence, then, this sudden and so great change?" and the rest that follow in the same place, shortly before the peroration.

units.la: Maximeque similitudines.) Cuiusmodi est illa ad Quirites post reditum: Sed, tanquam bona valetudo iucundior est eis qui e graui morbo recreati sunt, quam qui nunquam aegro corpore fuerunt: sic ea omnia desiderata magis, quam assidue percepta, delectant.
units.tr: "And above all comparisons." Of this sort is that passage to the Romans after his return: "But, as good health is more pleasing to those who have been restored from a grave illness than to those who have never been sick in body, so all those things, longed for, delight more than when constantly enjoyed."

units.la: Et exempla.) Meminimus Cinnam nimis potentem, Syllam postea dominantem, modo Caesarem regnantem uideramus. Item paulo post, in eiusdem Philippicae secundae peroratione: Tarquinium Brutus bello est persecutus, qui tum rex fuit, cum esse Romae regē liceret: Sp. Cassius, Sp. Melius, M. Manlius, propter suspicionem regni appetendi sunt necati.
units.tr: "And examples." "We remember Cinna grown too powerful, Sulla afterwards dominant, and we have just seen Caesar reigning." Likewise a little later, in the peroration of the same second Philippic: "Brutus pursued Tarquin in war, who was then king when it was lawful for a king to be at Rome; Spurius Cassius, Spurius Maelius, Marcus Manlius were put to death on suspicion of seeking kingship."

units.la: Fictae etiam personae, muta denique loquantur.) De προσωποποιία loquitur, quā conformationem vocat Cornificius. Exempla habes in oratione pro Caelio, & in prima Catilinaria, ubi patria loquens inducitur.
units.tr: "And finally, fictitious persons, and dumb things may speak." He speaks of prosopopoeia, which Cornificius calls conformation. You have examples in the speech for Caelius and in the first Catilinarian, where the fatherland is introduced speaking.

units.la: Omninoque ea sunt adhibenda, si causa patitur, quae magna habentur. quorum est duplex genus: alia enim magna natura videntur, alia usu. Natura, ut coelestia, ut divina, ut ea quorum obscurae causae: ut in terris, mundoq; admirabilia quae sunt. ex quibus, similibusq;, si attendas, ad augendum permulta suppetent. Usu, quae videntur hominibus aut prodesse, aut obesse vehementius: quorum sunt genera ad amplificandum tria. nam aut caritate moventur homines; ut deorum, ut patriae, ut parentum: aut amore, ut fratrum, coniugum, ut liberorum, ut familiarium: aut honestate, ut virtutum, maximeq; earum quae ad communionem hominum & liberalitatem valent.
units.tr: And in general those things are to be used, if the cause allows, which are regarded as great. Of these there are two kinds: for some seem great by nature, others by use. By nature, such as heavenly things, divine things, and those whose causes are obscure, as the wonders that are on earth and in the world. From these and similar things, if you attend to them, very many materials for amplifying will be at hand. By use, those things which seem to men either to benefit or to harm more strongly; and of these there are three kinds for amplifying. For men are moved either by affection, as for the gods, for country, for parents; or by love, as for brothers, spouses, children, and household members; or by honour, as for virtues, and especially those which avail for the fellowship and generosity of men.

units.la: Omninoq; ea sunt adhibenda, si causa patitur, quae magna habentur.) Hoc est, quod ante diximus, ad amplificandum magna esse assumeda. Cicero hic addit, Si causa patitur, quia semper iudicium est adhibendum: & is eloquens est, qui & humilia subtiliter, & magna graviter, & mediocria temperate potest dicere, ut in Oratore ait Cicero. Quorum est duplex genus.) Rerum genere magnarum partitionem ponit: atque alia magna natura uideri ait, alia usu. Natura, inquit: id est, quorum etiamsi usus non accedat, tamen ea suapte ui nos mouent, et in admirationem rapiunt. usu uero magna dicuntur, quae magnam utilitatem aut detrimenta afferre possunt. At natura magna tribus generibus continentur. sunt enim aut caelestia, aut diuina, aut humana: quorum obscurae sunt et latentes causae. Caelestia, ut primum ipse mundus, eiusque omnis ordo, et ornatus: Diuina, ut Deus ipse immortalis, tum quae diuinitus in aere et terris et mari et animantibus ipsis eueniunt: ex quibus omnibus, hisque similibus, si quis diligenter attendat, permagna ad amplificandum suppetit copia. Earum autem rerum quae usu magna dicuntur, sunt item genera tria: caritas, amor, et honestas. Videtur Cicero inter caritatem et amorem ita distinguere, ut caritas sit erga superiores, amor autem erga inferiores. et caritas est amor cum observantia et reuerentia quadam, quae Graece dicitur ἀγάπη: amor uero φιλοστοργία, affectus quidam humanus, cum caritas diuinus potius sit. Ex hac distinctione in Oratione ad Quirites post reditu, dixit de fratre suo: Amore idem qui fuit frater. Charitatem porro eam esse puto. to, quæ proprie erga Deos religio, erga patriam & parentes pietas nominatur. Sequitur honestas, siue honestum. id autem est, quod suaui & natura nos alliciens, laudabile est: uel quod cum bonum sit, est etiam iucundum, quatenus bonum, ut Aristoteles definit Rhetor. libro primo. Quod si honestas est huiusmodi, necesse est uirtutem honestam esse: quoniam cum sit bona, est etiam laudabilis: ut iustitia, liberalitas, fortitudo. Sed uidendum est, cur Cicero dicat, ut uirtutum, maximeq; carum quæ ad communionem hominum & liberalitatem ualent. Videtur enim duo genera uirtutum facere, & rectè quidem. Nam idem quoque fecit de Oratore libro secundo. Virtus autem, inquit, quæ est per seipsa laudabilis, et sine qua nihil laudari potest, tamen habet plureis partes, quarum alia est ad laudationem aptior. Sunt enim aliæ uirtutes, quæ uidentur in moribus hominum, & quadam comitate ac beneficentia positæ: aliæ quæ in ingenij aliqua facultate, aut animi magnitudine ac robore. nam clementia, iustitia, benignitas, fides, fortitudo in periculis communibus, iucunda est auditu in laudationibus. Omnes enim hæ uirtutes non tam ipsis qui eas in se habent, quàm generi hominum fructuosæ putantur. Sapientia & magnitudo animi, quæ omnes Quorum est duplex genus.) Omnes enim hæ uirtutes non tam ipsis qui eas in se habent, quam generi hominum fructuosæ putantur. Sapientia & magnitudo animi, qua omnes
units.tr: Such things should be used, if the case allows, which are regarded as great. This is what we said before: great things are to be taken up for amplification. Cicero adds "if the case allows" because judgement must always be applied. He is an eloquent speaker who can treat humble things subtly, great things weightily, and middling things moderately, as Cicero says in the Orator. "There are two kinds of these." He sets out a division of great things: some, he says, are great by nature, others by use. "By nature," he says, meaning those things which, even without use, move us by their own force and carry us into admiration. Things are called great by use when they can bring great benefit or great harm. Things great by nature fall into three kinds: they are heavenly, divine, or human, and their causes are obscure and hidden. Heavenly things are the world itself with its whole order and adornment. Divine things are God himself, immortal, and the things that happen by divine agency in the air, on the earth, in the sea, and in living creatures. From all these, and similar things, if anyone attends carefully, there is a very great abundance for amplification. Of those things called great by use, there are likewise three kinds: charity, love, and honour. Cicero seems to distinguish charity from love in this way: charity is directed towards superiors, love towards inferiors. Charity is love joined with a certain observance and reverence, which in Greek is called agapē [ἀγάπη]; love, however, is philostorgia [φιλοστοργία], a human feeling, whereas charity is rather divine. From this distinction, in the speech to the Quirites after his return, he said of his brother: "by love, the same who had always been a brother." I think that is charity, which properly is called religion towards the gods and piety towards country and parents. Next comes honour, or the honourable. That is honourable which, drawing us by its own force and nature, is praiseworthy; or which, being good, is also pleasing insofar as it is good, as Aristotle defines it in the first book of the Rhetoric. If honour is of this kind, virtue must be honourable, since being good it is also praiseworthy, as justice, liberality, and fortitude are. But we must consider why Cicero says "of the virtues, and especially those which serve human fellowship and liberality." He seems to make two kinds of virtue, and rightly so. For he did the same in the second book of the De Oratore. "Virtue," he says, "which is praiseworthy in itself, and without which nothing can be praised, nevertheless has several parts, of which one is more suited to praise. For there are some virtues which appear in the conduct of men and consist in a certain courtesy and beneficence; others lie in some faculty of mind, or in greatness and strength of spirit. For clemency, justice, kindness, good faith, and fortitude in common dangers are pleasing to hear in panegyrics. For all these virtues are thought fruitful not so much to those who possess them as to the human race. Wisdom and greatness of spirit, by which all

units.la: res humanæ feruntur, tenues & pro nihilo putantur. Idem dicit de Offic. libro primo, vbi de beneficentia agit. Exempla in Orationibus creebra occurrunt: quare nos ad vsum rerum magnarum, tractationemq; transeamus.
units.tr: human affairs are carried on, are thought slight and worthless." He says the same in the first book of the De Officiis, where he treats of beneficence. Examples occur frequently in the speeches, so let us pass on to the use and treatment of great things.

units.la: Ex iis & cohortationes sumuntur, ad ea retinenda: & in eos, à quibus ea violata sunt, odia incitantur, & miseratio nascitur. Proprius locus augendi in iis rebus aut amissis, aut amittendi periculo. Nihil est enim tam miserabile, quàm ex beato miser. & hoc totum quidem moveat, si bona ex fortuna quis cadat, & à quorum charitate diuellatur, quæ amittat aut amiserit, in quibus malis sit, futurus ve sit, exprimatur breuiter. Cito enim exarescit lachryma, præsertim in alienis malis.
units.tr: From these also exhortations are drawn, to keep these things; and hatred is stirred up against those by whom they have been violated, and pity arises. The proper place for amplification lies in those things that have been lost, or in the danger of losing them. For nothing is so pitiable as a man who falls from happiness to misery. This whole theme will move if someone falls from good fortune and is torn away from those he loved, and if what he has lost or is losing, and in what evils he is or is going to be, is briefly set forth. For a tear dries quickly, especially at the misfortunes of others.

units.la: Ex his & cohortationes sumuntur. ) De tractatione agit, in qua hæc proponit consideranda: Finem, materiam, modum, & iudicium. Finis triplex est: cohortatio, odium, miseratio, ad hos fines omnes magnarum rerum sententiæ accommodandæ sunt. Hos tres fines indicat prima præceptione. ptione. Cohortationes (inquit) sumuntur, odia incitantur, miseratio nascitur. Materia sequitur, quæ in bonis & malis, lætis & tristibus cernitur. eam sequentibus sententijs indicat Cicero, usque ad eum locum: Citò enim arescit lachryma. Modus autem in breuitate orationis, qua lachrymas exprimere ab auditoribus conamur. nam commotis animis, diutius in conquestione morari nō oportebit. id voluit Cicero in illis verbis: Exprimatur breuiter, citò enim arescit lachryma, præsertim in alienis malis. De Inuent. autem lib. 1. extremo: Quemadmodum enim dixit rhetor Apollonius, lachryma nihil citius arescit. Hanc sententiā acceperat Cicero de ipsius Apollonij ore. Fuit enim is Ciceronis præceptor Apollonius, cognomento Molo, ut ipsemet Cicero alibi testatur. Sed in hac sententia, quam in Partit. ponit, duo dicit: tum lacrymam citò arescere in propriis malis, tum citius etiam in alienis. Cur autem lachrymæ citò inarescant, & fluere cessent, ea primum causa est, quòd in dolore & mærore constringitur & contrahitur animus unà cum cerebro, quæ contractio diuturna esse non posset; alioqui hominem extingueret. Dilatatur igitur citò, ut naturæ succurrat: in qua dilatatione statim lachrymæ cessant, quia non exprimuntur. Exemplum habes in spongia madefacta, quæ expressa pressa manu fundit aquas: manu uero explicata & remissa, non fundit. Deinde, nihil quod uehe‐mens & uiolentum fit, diutius in uno statu du‐ rare potest: præsertim in affectibus, qui sunt mo‐ mentanei & fugaces. Quod autem id lachrymis dicit accidere, ut citius inarescant, præsertim in alienis malis: id fit, quoniam aliena mala cum pro‐ cul à nobis sint, minus constringunt naturam: i‐ circo etiam citius desinunt lachrymæ.
units.tr: "From these also exhortations are drawn." He treats of arrangement, in which he proposes these things to be considered: the end, the matter, the manner, and the judgement. The end is threefold: exhortation, hatred, and pity; all the sentiments of great things are to be adapted to these ends. Cicero indicates these three ends in his first precept: exhortations are drawn, hatreds are stirred up, pity arises. The matter follows, which is seen in good and bad things, joyful and sad. Cicero indicates this matter in the following sentences, up to the point: "For a tear dries quickly." The manner lies in the brevity of the speech by which we try to draw tears from the hearers. For once the minds are moved, it will not be fitting to linger long in complaint. Cicero meant this in the words: "let it be set forth briefly, for a tear dries quickly, especially at the misfortunes of others." In the end of the first book of the De Inventione: "For as the rhetorician Apollonius said, nothing dries more quickly than a tear." Cicero had taken this sentiment from the lips of Apollonius himself. For this Apollonius was Cicero's teacher, surnamed Molo, as Cicero himself attests elsewhere. But in this sentiment, which he puts forward in the Partitiones, he says two things: that a tear dries quickly in one's own misfortunes, and even more quickly in those of others. Why tears dry quickly and cease to flow, the first cause is that in grief and sorrow the mind is constricted and drawn together along with the brain; such contraction could not last long, otherwise it would extinguish the man. So it is quickly relaxed, so that nature may come to its aid; and in this relaxation the tears stop at once, because they are no longer squeezed out. You have an example in a sponge soaked in water: when pressed by the hand it pours out water, but when opened and released by the hand, it does not pour out. Next, nothing that is vehement and violent can last long in one state, especially in the emotions, which are momentary and fleeting. That he says this happens to tears, so that they dry more quickly, especially at the misfortunes of others, happens because other people's misfortunes, being far from us, constrict our nature less; therefore the tears also cease more quickly.

units.la: Nec quicquam in amplificatio‐ ne nimis enucleandum est. minuta est enim omnis diligentia, hic au‐ tem locus grandia requirit.
units.tr: Nor should anything be elaborated too finely in amplification. For all careful attention to detail is trivial, whereas this place requires grand matters.

units.la: Nec quicquam in amplificatione nimis enu‐ cleandum est. ) Suprà, cum de verbis loquere‐ tur, laudauit quasi naturalem, & non explana‐ tam orationem. Idem hic facit in amplificatione rerum: præcipitąq; nõ esse nimis enucleatè & te‐nuiter omnia quæ mouere possunt, persequenda, sed maiora & grandiora. Et addit etiam ratio‐ nem: quòd minuta sit omnis diligentia illa, quæ omnia etiam minutissima persequi uolumus, quæ diligentia tenui dicendi generi atq; subtili adhi‐ benda est: hic autem locus grandia, exaggerata, amplificatáq; requirit.
units.tr: Nor should anything be elaborated too finely in amplification. Above, when he was speaking of words, he praised a style that is, as it were, natural and not elaborated. Here he does the same with the amplification of things, and he advises that everything that can move should not be pursued too minutely and delicately, but in larger and grander terms. He also gives the reason: all that careful attention is trivial, since we want to pursue even the very smallest details. Such care belongs to the plain and subtle kind of speaking, whereas this place requires grand, heightened and amplified matter.

units.la: Illud iam est iudicij, quo quaque in
units.tr: The next thing is a matter of judgement: in which kind of cause we should use each mode of amplifying.

units.la: {*} Suprà ... (commentary note in smaller type, partly illegible)
units.tr: Above ...

units.la: in caussa genere utamur agendi. In illis enim caussis, quæ ad delectationem exornantur, ij loci tractandi sunt, qui mouere possunt expectationem, admirationem, uoluptatem. In cohortationibus autem bonorum ac malorum enumerationes & exempla ualent plurimum. In iudiciis, accusatori feré, quæ ad iracundiam: reo plerunque, quæ ad misericordiam pertinent. Nonnunquam tamen accusator misericordiam mouere debet, & defensor iracundiam.
units.tr: For in those causes that are adorned for delight, the topics that can arouse expectation, admiration and pleasure should be handled. In exhortations to good and evil, enumerations and examples are of greatest force. In trials, the accuser should mostly stir up what pertains to anger, and the defendant mostly what pertains to pity. Sometimes, however, the accuser ought to arouse pity and the defender anger.

units.la: Illud iam est iudicij.) Iudicij est, intelligere & noffe, quæ sint in singulis caussarum generibus amplificandi genera & fines. Nam in genere demonstratiuo finis est delectatio, siue suauitas: eáq; comparatur & earum rerum natura quæ mouere possunt expectationem, admirationem, & uoluptatem: idq; tam honestis quàm turpibus. in genere deliberatiuo, cohortatio ad retinendas res suas, quemadmodum antea dixit: & in eos à quibus uiolatæ sunt, odia concitanda. id quod assequemur bonorũ enumeratione in suadendo,
units.tr: The next thing is a matter of judgement. It belongs to judgement to understand and to know what kinds and limits of amplification are proper to each kind of cause. For in the demonstrative kind the end is delight, or agreeableness, and this is brought about by the nature of those things which can arouse expectation, admiration and pleasure, whether they are honourable or shameful. In the deliberative kind, the end is exhortation to keep one's own possessions, as he said before, and the stirring up of hatred against those by whom they have been violated. We shall achieve this by enumerating good things in persuading, and bad things in dissuading, although we shall use examples suited to either.

units.la: {r} 4 dendo,& in dissuadendo malorum: etsi exemplis ad utrunque aptis utemur. Iam in genere iudiciali, accusatori propositum est, ut initio dixit, ut iratum faciat iudicem: non autem omnia ad misericordiam sunt assumenda. & hoc fit ordine naturali: verum hic ordo interdum pro commoditate causae mutatur, ita ut accusator misericordiam moueat, & defensor iracundiam. quod fecit Cicero in Rosciana, & Miloniana: in quibus duabus orationibus, omnia quae hic de amplificatione praecipiuntur, cum in aliis partibus & locis, tum maxime in peroratione efficit: nimirum ut irascatur iudex, mitigetur, inuideat, fauceat, contemnat, admiretur, oderit, diligat, cupiat, satietate afficiatur, speret, metuat, laetetur, doleat, qua in varietate, motuum ferentiorum Verrinae orationes suppeditabunt exempla: mitiorum, defensiones eiusdem, ut ipsemet dicit in Oratore ad Brutum.
units.tr: ... in persuading, and in dissuading from evils, although we shall use examples suited to each. Now in the judicial kind, the accuser's aim, as he said at the beginning, is to make the judge angry, and not all things are to be taken up for the sake of pity. This is done in natural order, but this order is sometimes changed according to the advantage of the case, so that the accuser moves pity and the defender moves anger. Cicero did this in the speeches for Roscius and for Milo. In these two speeches he achieves, in the peroration above all (though also in other parts and places), everything that is taught here about amplification: namely, that the judge be made angry, be softened, feel envy, be moved to tears, despise, admire, hate, love, desire, be filled with satiety, hope, fear, rejoice and grieve. In this variety of stronger emotions the Verrine speeches will supply examples, and in the milder ones his defences of the same kind, as he himself says in the Orator to Brutus.

units.la: DE ENVMERATIONE, altera Perorationis parte.
units.tr: ON ENUMERATION, the second part of the peroration.

units.la: Enumeratio reliqua est, nonnunquam laudatori, suasori non saepe, accusatori saepius quàm reo necessaria, Enumeratio reliqua est.) Enumeratio, autore Cicerone, est, per quam res dispersè & dissusè dictæ, unum in locum coguntur, & reminiscendi causša unum sub aspectum subiiciuntur. In enumeratione hæc consideranda hic proponuntur: primùm, quibus in causis ea utendum sit: deinde, quæ sint eius tempora, post, quibus personis conveniat enumeratio: & denique, qui sit in ea modus siue tractatio, hæc habet ordine Cicero. ac de primo ait: Enumeratio nonnunquam laudatori, suasori non sæpe, accusatori sæpius quàm reo necessaria. Ratio autem horum est, quod laudatori, siue qui orationem habet in genere demonstratiuo, nullus est propositus aduersarius: & oratio ipsa perpetua quadam narratione constat, nisi singatur aduersarius, quod raro fit & breuiter: idcirco vix enumerationem admittit. Suasori autè, idcirco non sæpe necessaria, tum quod huiusmomodi causæ minus sunt implicatæ controuersijs: quæ si essent, & multam haberent copiam, tum enumeratio esset adhibenda. Deinde, quoniam prudens est consilium, & de reb. futuris agitur, quæ non magnam requirunt recordationem. Itaq; eadem de causša, quæ admittitur pene proœmium, etiam enumeratio: sed non amplificatio ad impellendos animos, & in tuam sententiam pertrahendos. relinquitur ergo, ut fit propria enumeratio: atque adeo potius accusatoris, quàm rei rationem, Cicero infrà ponit: quòd reo ponenda sunt contraria, quorum dissolutio in breuitate latebit, aculei pungent. Atq; ita duo habemus ex quatuor, scilicet primum et tertium.
units.tr: Enumeration remains. Sometimes it is necessary for the panegyrist, not often for the one who persuades, and more often for the accuser than for the defendant. Enumeration remains. Enumeration, according to Cicero, is that by which things said scattered and dispersed are gathered into one place and placed under one view for the sake of remembering. In enumeration the following points are considered, and they are set out here: first, in what kinds of cause it should be used; then, what its times are; after that, to which persons enumeration is suited; and finally, what its manner or treatment is. Cicero treats these in this order. And about the first he says: "Enumeration is sometimes necessary for the panegyrist, not often for the one who persuades, and more often for the accuser than for the defendant." The reason for this is that for the panegyrist, or the one who speaks in the demonstrative kind, there is no opposing party set before him, and his speech consists of a continuous narrative, unless an adversary is invented, which seldom happens and then only briefly; therefore he hardly admits enumeration. The one who persuades does not need it often, because causes of this kind are less entangled in disputes; if they were, and had much matter, enumeration would then be applied. Further, since deliberation concerns the future and is prudent, it does not require much recollection of things. Hence in the same kind of cause in which the proem is almost admitted, enumeration is also admitted, but not amplification for moving minds and drawing them to your opinion. It remains, therefore, that enumeration becomes its own proper part, and so Cicero sets out its method more for the accuser than for the defendant, because for the defendant contrary points must be set forth, whose refutation will lie hidden in brevity while the points themselves will sting. And so we have two of the four, namely the first and third.

units.la: Huius ipsa tempora duo sunt: si aut memoriae diffidas eorum apud quos agas, uel interuallo temporis, uel longitudine orationis, aut frequentatis firmamentis orationis, & breuiter expositis, uim' est habitura caussa maiorem. Et reo rarius utendum est, quòd ponenda sunt contraria, quorum dissolutio in breuitate latebit, aculei pungent. Sed erit in enumeratione uitandum, ne ostentatio memoriae suscepta, uideatur esse puerilis. Id effugiet, qui non omnia minima repetet, sed breuia singula attingens, pondera rerum ipsa comprehendet.
units.tr: There are two circumstances of this: when you distrust the memory of those before whom you are pleading, either because of the lapse of time or the length of the speech, or when the supports of your speech have been frequently used, and only briefly set out; then your cause will have greater force. And the defendant should use it more rarely, because contrary points must be set forth, whose refutation will lie hidden in brevity, while the points themselves will sting. But in enumeration one must avoid that a display of memory undertaken should appear childish. This will be avoided by one who does not repeat every smallest point, but touches briefly on individual items, and grasps the weight of the matters themselves.

units.la: Huius ipsa tempora duo sunt.) Temporum nomine caussas intelligit, quibus ut enumeratione utamur, impellimur: quarum altera est memoria, altera uis. Memoria duo habet tempora, quae efficere ficere posint, ut auditorũ memoriæ diffidas, temporis interuallum, & orationis longitudo. inter uallum temporis intelligendum est, cum una causa à pluribus agitur: tunc inter primum & tertiũ siue quartum, aut etiam ultimum temporis spacium interuenit: ex quo effici potuit, ut disceptator firmamenta caussæ obliuioni tradiderit. idcirco tunc utendum est enumeratione, quod fecit Cicero in Quintiana. Idem quoq; intelligendum, si lõga sit oratio: ut pro Sestio, pro Milone, pro Plã cio. Sequitur quartũ, in quo modus & tractatio ui denda est: caq; est bipertita, ut primum uideamus quid sit in enumeratione uitandum, deinde quid sequendum. Vitanda est ostentatio memoriæ, quæ in puero tolerari possit, in uiro autẽ leuis & puerilis esse uideatur. Secundum igitur illud erit efficiendum, ut non omnia minima repetamus: sed ea, in quibus pondera rerum fuerunt, breuiter singula attingamus. nam illud datur commune præceptum ad enumerationem, ut ex unaquaque argumentatione, quoniam tota iterum dici non potest, nec debet, ea eligantur, quæ sunt grauissima, & unumquodque quàm breuissimè transfeatur: ut renouetur, non redintegretur oratio. Quapropter initium enumerationis, non ab exordio aut narratione, sed à diuisione sumendum est. Hic uidendum est, quomodo Ciceroni nostro cum Aristotele conueniat, in partiti-bus perorationis. nam Aristoteles ipse quatuor -ex partib.eam constare dicit:primum ex ea quæ efficit,ut auditor nobis bene velit,adversarijs ma-le:deinde ex amplificatione,&c diminutione:tum ex animorum comotione, ut afficiatur auditor : postremò ex enumeratione.sed facilis est recon-ciliatio.Tria illa priora,Ciceronis amplifica-ne continentur: nam illis tribus nihil aliud voluit Aristoteles,quàm varios mo-tus significare.
units.tr: These are its own two times. By "times" he means the reasons which move us to use enumeration: of these one is memory, the other is force. Memory has two circumstances which can make the hearers' memory unreliable: the interval of time and the length of the speech. An interval of time is to be understood when one cause is pursued over several sessions: then a space of time, from the first to the third or fourth, or even the last, intervenes, and as a result the advocate may have consigned the supports of his case to oblivion. Therefore in that case one should use enumeration, as Cicero did in the speech for Quinctius. The same must be understood if the speech is long, as in the speeches for Sestius, for Milo, and for Plancius.
