Next comes the fourth point, in which the manner and treatment of the matter must be considered; and this is twofold: first we should see what must be avoided in enumeration, then what must be followed. A display of memory is to be avoided, which may be tolerated in a boy but seems light and childish in a man. Therefore the next thing to ensure is that we do not repeat every small point, but touch briefly on each of those in which the weight of the matter lay. For this is the common precept for enumeration: from each argument, since the whole cannot and should not be said again, those should be chosen which are most weighty, and each should be passed over as briefly as possible, so that the speech is refreshed, not restored in full. Hence the beginning of the enumeration should be taken not from the exordium or the narration, but from the division. Here we must see how our Cicero agrees with Aristotle in the parts of the peroration. For Aristotle himself says that it consists of four parts: first, that which brings it about that the hearer wishes us well and our opponents ill; then amplification and diminution; next the arousing of the emotions, so that the hearer is moved; and last, enumeration. But the reconciliation is easy. Those first three are contained in Cicero's amplification; for by those three Aristotle meant nothing other than to signify various movements.

units.la: EXPLICATIONVM O- ratoriarum liber tertius.
units.tr: The Third Book of the Explanations of Cicero's Oratorical Partitions.

units.la: DE QVAESTIONE, Eius q; partibus.
units.tr: ON THE QUESTION AND ITS PARTS.

units.la: C. F. Quoniam & de ipso oratore, & de oratione dixisti, expone eum mihi nunc, quem ex tribus extremum propositi, quaestionis locum.
units.tr: Since you have spoken of both the orator himself and the oration, explain to me now the last of the three topics proposed, the place of the question.

units.la: C. F. Quoniam & de ipso Oratore & de oratione dixisti.) In tres partes diuisa initio fuit omnis doctrina dicendi: in unum oratoris, in orationem, & in quaestionem: de duobus superioribus diuinitus respondit Cicero, & nos duobus superioribus libris explicauimus. Quare nunc ex tribus, extremum quaestionis locum sibi exponi poscit filius. in cuius verbis illud obseruandum est, eum oratorem pro ut oratoris posuisse: idque non improprie, sed maxime proprie. ut si dicas statuam, sive sculptorem, metallum & statuam, vel artificem, materiam & opus. artifex est orator, materia quaestio, opus ipsum oratio. Sed in artifice uis & ars intelligitur, uti libro primo ostendimus. Sed quo facilius haec quaestionum distributio in sequentib. perspiciatur, praestat ea statim in ipso limine proponere.
units.tr: "Since you have spoken of both the orator himself and the oration." All teaching on speaking was at the beginning divided into three parts: the orator, the oration, and the question. Cicero has answered the first two divinely, and we explained those two in the earlier books. So now the son asks to have the last of the three topics, the question, explained to him. In these words one should note that Cicero has used "orator" in the sense of the orator's craft, and not improperly but very properly. Just as when you speak of a statue, you mean the sculptor, the metal and the statue, or the craftsman, the material and the work: the orator is the craftsman, the question is the material, and the oration itself is the work. But in the craftsman both power and skill are understood, as we showed in the first book. However, so that this division of questions may be more easily grasped in what follows, it is better to set it out right at the threshold.

units.la: QueQuæstionum genera Infinitum, quod propositum voco Cogitationis, cuius tria genera: Coniectura, Fuerit, Futurum fit. Definitio, Aliud, an idem sit. Descriptio generis alicuius, & quasi imago existit In quâ quæritur, Possit ne aliquid effici, quo modo fiat (primùm sit) Qualitatis, in quo quæritur: Simpliciter de Honestate, Utilitate, Æquabilitate. Comparatione, quid vel Honestius, Utilius, Æquius, Honestissimum, Utilissimum, Æquissimum. Finitum, quod causam appello, cuius sunt genera tria Actionis quod refertur ad Commodum, usumq;, quod cernitur in Persequendis, declinandis, officiis præstandis Affectibus regendis Exornationis, Deliberationis, Iudicij.
units.tr: Kinds of questions: the infinite, which I call the proposition of thought, of which there are three kinds: conjecture (whether a thing was), definition (whether it is one thing or another), and description (of some kind, a sort of image). In which is asked whether something can be brought about, and in what way it comes to be (the first kind, of possibility). Of quality, in which is asked simply about the honourable, the useful and the equitable; of comparison, what is more honourable, more useful, more equitable, most honourable, most useful, most equitable. The finite, which I call the cause, of which there are three kinds: of action, which relates to advantage and use; which is seen in pursuing, avoiding, performing duties, governing the emotions; of display, of deliberation, of judgement.

units.la: C.P. Duo sunt, ut initiò dixi, quæstionum genera: quorum alterum finitum temporib. & personis caussam appello: alterum infinitum, nullis neque personis, neque temporibus notatum, propositū uoco. Sed est consultatio quasi pars caussæ quædam, & controuersiæ. inest enim infinitū in definito, & ad illud tamen referuntur omnia.
units.tr: There are two kinds of questions, as I said at the beginning: one of them, limited by times and persons, I call the cause; the other, infinite, marked by neither persons nor times, I call the proposition. But consultation is, as it were, a certain part of a cause and of a controversy. For the infinite is contained within the finite, and yet all things are referred back to it.

units.la: C. P. Duo sunt, ut initiò dixi, quæstionum genera.) Et nos libro 1. bonam partem eorum quæ dicenda erant de quæstione, diximus. Superest igitur tantum, ut quæ hoc loco repetit Cicero, percurramus. In quo illud tenendum est, quæstionē esse omnis disputationis siue controuersiæ caput, ad quod omnis referatur oratio, siue disputatio. Continet enim hæc doctrina quæstionū tū genera caussarū, tum etiā statuū: ut interea omittam philosophiæ partes omneis, quæ hac quæstionū disciplina continetur. Illud quoq; obseruandū, definita quæstione eā esse, quæ personarū præcipuē notatione habet: infinita uero, quæ personarum præsertim complexu (etiāsi reliquorū attributorū aliquod adsit) libera est. Sed hoc loco emendemus scripturā, ubi dicit: Controuersia caussam appellô.illud uerbum Controuersiam expungendum est,tanquam adulterinum: aut si quis uelit retinere,contra tamen ueterum codicum fidem,addenda erit coniunctio, legendumq;: Controuersiam & causam appello.
units.tr: "There are two kinds of questions, as I said at the beginning." In book one we also treated a good part of what had to be said about the question. What remains, then, is only to go through what Cicero repeats at this point. In this matter one must keep in mind that the question is the head of every disputation or controversy, to which every speech or argument is referred. For this doctrine of questions contains both the kinds of causes and also the states of a case, not to mention all the parts of philosophy that are included in this discipline of questions. One should also note that a question is "definite" when it has its chief mark in the specifying of persons, but "infinite" when it is free of them, especially of a combination of persons (even though some of the other attributes may be present). But here we should correct the reading where he says "Controversy I call cause." The word "Controversy" must be deleted as a spurious addition. Or if anyone wishes to retain it, against the authority of the older manuscripts, a conjunction must be added and the text read: "Controversy and cause I call."

units.la: Sed est consultatio quasi pars causæ quedã.) Pars est,ut genus definitionis,siue sormæ, in qua definienda,pars esse dicitur: idq; ut in oratione, non ut in re ipsa.& est quidem in caussa propositum,sed finitum. neq; enim sine proposito probari quicquam potest in causa:ut nec in syllogismo quicquam effici sine propositione maiore. Cū autem loquimur de personis in aliqua questione, ea quoq; intelligendasunt quæ pro personis ponuntur. ponuntur autem pro personis,non certa semper & propria personarū nomina,sed incertaꞏ ut quidam,aliquis:itemq; Romanus, Atheniēsis,Gallus,Italus.ut,exempli caussa: Iure ne Galli bellum inferant Florentinis? & , An opem ferre Senensibus Galli debeant?
units.tr: "But consultation is, as it were, a certain part of a cause." A part is said to be, like the genus in a definition or the form, a part in the defining; and this is so in speech, not in the thing itself. The proposition is indeed in a cause, but as a finite one. For nothing can be proved in a cause without a proposition, just as nothing can be concluded in a syllogism without a major premise. When, however, we speak of persons in some question, those things must also be understood that are put in place of persons. They are put in place of persons not always as fixed and proper names of persons, but as indefinite ones: such as "someone" or "anyone", and likewise "a Roman", "an Athenian", "a Frenchman", "an Italian". For example: "Is it right for the French to make war on the Florentines?" and "Ought the French to bring aid to the Sienese?"

units.la: DE PROPOSITO, SIVE Consultatione, siue infinita quæstione.
units.tr: On the Proposition, or Consultation, or Infinite Question.

units.la: Quiramobrem prius de proposito dicamus,cuius genera sunt duo, Cognitionis alterum; eius scientia est sinis,ut ueri ne sint sensus. alterum actionis,quod refertur ad efficiendu quid: ut si quaeratur, quibus officijs amicitia colenda sit.Rursus superioris genera sunt tria: Sit nec ne, quid sit, quale sit. Sit nec ne:ut, ius in natura sit,an in more. Quid autem sit, sit ne ius id, quod maiori parti sit utile.Quale autem sit: iuste uiuere sit nec ne utile,
units.tr: Therefore let us first speak of the proposition, which has two kinds: one of knowing, whose end is knowledge, as when we ask whether the senses are true; and one of acting, which relates to bringing something about, as when we ask by what duties friendship should be cultivated. Again, the kinds of the former are three: whether a thing is or not, what it is, and what sort it is. Whether it is or not: as whether law exists in nature or in custom. What it is: whether that law is what is useful to the greater part. What sort it is: whether living justly is useful or not.

units.la: Quamobrem prius de propositio dicamus.) His uerbis constat, Ciceronem cognitionis & actionis quaestiones sub propositum subijcere, eiusq; facere parteis.
units.tr: Therefore let us first speak of the proposition. These words show that Cicero places the questions of knowing and of acting under the proposition, and makes them its parts.

units.la: Eius! scientia est finis.) Significat, nihil ultra scientiam in cognitionis quaestione quaerendum: ut intelligamus,ea inuenta quiescendum. nam actio nulla hic requiritur, sed mera consideratio, contemplatioq; naturae.
units.tr: Its end is knowledge. This means that in a question of knowing nothing beyond knowledge is to be sought, so that we understand that once it has been discovered we may rest. For no action is required here, but pure consideration and contemplation of nature.

units.la: Vt ueri ne sint sensus.) An sint ueri sensus, docet Aristoteles in libro de Sensibus primo, & libro de Somnijs, cap.2. Sed Cicero praeclare in Acad.lib.4. Meo autem iudicio,inquit, ita est maxima in sensibus veritas,si & sani sunt, & valentes, & omnia remouentur quae obstant & impediunt.itaq; & lumen mutari saepe uolumus,& situs earum rerum quas intuemur, & interualla, aut contrahimus, aut diducimus.
units.tr: Whether the senses are true. Aristotle teaches whether the senses are true in the first book On the Senses and in the book On Dreams, chapter 2. But Cicero says splendidly in the Academica, book 4: "In my judgment, truth in the senses is greatest if they are sound and strong, and all things that obstruct or impede them are removed. And so we often wish the light to be changed, and we either bring together or spread apart the position of the things we look at, and the intervals."

units.la: Alterum actionis.) Huius finis est actio. idirco ait, Quod refertur ad efficiendum quid: ut si quaeratur, quibus officijs amicitia colenda sit. Quemadmodum ea quae cognitionis sunt, physica tradit: sic quae sunt actionis, ea philosophiae pars quae moralis appellatur, cuius sunt multa partes. Quibus autem officijs colenda sit amicitia, praeclare docet in Laelio Cicero, ut alios omittā.
units.tr: Its end is action. The end of this kind is action. Therefore he says, "which relates to bringing something about, as when we ask by what duties friendship should be cultivated." Just as the things belonging to knowing are taught by physics, so those belonging to action belong to that part of philosophy called moral, which has many parts. By what duties friendship should be cultivated, Cicero teaches splendidly in the Laelius, to pass over others.

units.la: Rursus superioris genera sunt tria.) Superioris, id est cognitionis. quanquam sunt qui velint hanc esse propositi secundam diuisionem.
units.tr: Again, the kinds of the former are three. "The former" means the kind of knowing. Some, however, wish this to be the second division of the proposition.

units.la: Sit, nec ne.) Duas Aristotelis quaestiones in unam contraxit Cicero. nam non solum quaerendum est an sit, sed etiam quamobrem aliquid sit. Sed Cicero illam priorem quaestionem, quae de re est, tanquam confessam tacuit, & ad causam sive originem exemplum accommodauit, cum dixit, Ius in natura sit, an in more. non enim quaesiuit, an sit aliquod ius: sed natura ne an mos iuris efset causa. Si de virtute simpliciter ageretur, plura essent dicenda: sed quoniam de iure tantum quaerit, respondemus, partim a natura, partim a more ius ipsum oriri. Hinc ius aliud naturale, aliud legitimum sive ciuile: de quo Aristoteles in Ethicis lib. 5. & Iurisconsulti initio Digestorum.
units.tr: Whether a thing is or not. Cicero condensed two questions of Aristotle into one. For one must ask not only whether a thing is, but also why it is. But Cicero passed over in silence the former question, which concerns the fact itself, as if it were already admitted, and he fitted the example to the cause or origin when he said, whether law is in nature or in custom. For he did not ask whether there is some law, but whether nature or custom is the source of law. If virtue were treated simply, more would have to be said; but since he asks only about law, we answer that law itself arises partly from nature and partly from custom. Hence one law is natural, another legitimate or civil: on which Aristotle in Ethics book 5, and the jurists at the beginning of the Digest.

units.la: Quid autem sit.) Hoc definitione explicatur, ut alibi dictum est. ut si quis quaerat, an vera sit definitio quae dicat, Ius id esse quod maiori parti sit utile? alius verum quidem esse aiat, si utile ab honesto non separetur. quod si quis dicat illud esse ius quod maiori placitum sit parti, tunc negari potest: et afferri, illud ius esse, non quid maiori parti, sed meliori placeat.
units.tr: What it is. This is explained by definition, as has been said elsewhere. For example, if someone asks whether this definition is true which says: law is that which is useful to the greater part? Another will say it is true indeed, if the useful is not separated from the honourable. But if someone says that law is that which has pleased the greater part, then this can be denied, and it can be argued that that is law which pleases not the greater part but the better part.

units.la: Quale autem sit.) Quaestio est accidentis. quaeritur enim, Iuste viuere sit nec ne utile? quod idem est ac si quaereret: sit ne iustitia utilis? et est quidem, si veram utilitatem honestate metiamur. haec autem quaestio videri posit actionis, non cognitionis. Viuere enim est, aliquid agere. sed non proponitur, ut quidquam agatur: id est, quomodo iuste viuendum sit, aut quomodo sit exercenda iustitia: sed proponitur tanquam philosopho explicanda, ut sciatur, sit ne aliqua in vita iusta utilitas, sive beatitudo?
units.tr: What sort it is. This is a question of accident. For it is asked: is living justly useful or not? This is the same as asking: is justice useful? And indeed it is, if we measure true utility by honour. This question may seem to belong to action rather than to knowing. For to live is to do something. But it is not proposed that something be done, that is, how one must live justly or how justice is to be exercised; it is proposed to be explained by the philosopher, so that it may be known whether there is any just utility or happiness in life.

units.la: Actionis autem duo sunt genera. unum ad persequendum aliquid, aut declinandum: ut, quib. rebus adipisci gloriam possis, aut quomodo invidia vitetur. alterum, quod ad aliquod commodum usumque refertur: ut, quemadmodum sit respub. administranda,
units.tr: There are two kinds of action. One is for pursuing something or avoiding it: for example, by what means you may obtain glory, or how envy may be avoided. The other relates to some advantage or use: for example, how the commonwealth is to be administered,

units.la: aut quemadmodum in paupertate uiuendum.
units.tr: or how one is to live in poverty.

units.la: Actionis autem duo sunt genera.) Vt cognitionis quaestionem in sua quaedam genera distribuit: sic nunc quae sint actionis partes ostendit, facitque duas. priores quaestiones futuri temporis sunt, cernunturque in rebus bonis et malis: quorum illa sequenda, haec declinanda fugiendaque sunt. Idcirco quaerit, quibus rebus adipisci gloriam possis, quae bona est, et quā nondum sis adeptus: aut quomodo invidia vitetur, quā nondum laboresi. Quomodo autem gloriam adipisci possis, docet philosophi, cum de officijs tractant: et erat quondam Ciceronis liber de Gloria, qui iam non extat: et hoc tempore inter caeteros, opus non vulgare de ea edidit Hieronymus Osorius Lusitanus. De honore vero, qui est affinis gloriae, nos oratione aliquando habuimus, quam etiam edidimus: verum Sebastianus Foxius Morzillus librum unum sane doctum. Sed quemadmodum Socrates dicere solebat, quod etiam Cicero de Officijs refert, compendiosa via ad gloriam est, si talis sis, qualis videri cupis: et breviter quoque iter gloriae ostendit idem Cicero Philippica prima. De vitanda pariter invidia, post tot scriptores nullum praeceptum brevius dari potest, quam ut quo maior fueris, eo te submissius geras. Posterioris partis quaestio
units.tr: There are two kinds of action. Just as he divided the question of knowing into its kinds, so now he shows what the parts of action are, and makes two. The former questions concern the future and are discerned in good and bad things: of these the one is to be pursued, the other avoided and shunned. Hence he asks by what things you may obtain glory, which is a good you have not yet attained; or how envy may be avoided, which you do not yet suffer. How one may obtain glory the philosophers teach when they treat of duties; and there was once a book by Cicero On Glory, which no longer survives; and in our own time, among others, Jerome Osorius of Portugal has published a work on it that is far from common. On honour, which is akin to glory, we once gave an oration, which we also published; but Sebastian Foxius Morzillus has written one learned book on it. But as Socrates used to say, which Cicero also reports in On Duties, the short road to glory is to be such as you wish to seem; and Cicero himself briefly shows the road to glory in the First Philippic. Likewise, for avoiding envy, after so many writers no briefer precept can be given than this: the greater you are, the more humbly you should conduct yourself. The question of the latter part

units.la: stioe stiones præsentis sunt temporis, ad casq; mediæ quædam res referuntur, quæ in usu posite sunt. ut administratio Reipub. amici, genus, diuitiæ: quæ, ut ait Terētius in Heaut. perinde sunt, ut illius animus est, qui ea possidet. qui uti scit, ei bona sunt: illi qui non utitur recte, mala.
units.tr: ...concerns the questions of the present time, and to these certain intermediate things are referred, which are placed in use: such as the administration of the commonwealth, friends, birth, riches. These, as Terence says in the Heautontimorumenos, are just as the mind of the one who possesses them is: to one who knows how to use them they are good things; to one who does not use them rightly, they are bad.

units.la: {f} Vt quemadmodum fit Respub. administranda.) Nimirum ei, cui iam commissa est. Respondet Cicero de Officijs libro primo: Vt tutela, sic procuratio Reipublicæ, ad utilitatem eorum qui commissi sunt, non ad eorum quibus commissa est, gerenda est.
units.tr: How the commonwealth is to be administered: namely, by the one to whom it has already been entrusted. Cicero answers in On Duties, book 1: as guardianship, so the management of the commonwealth must be carried on for the advantage of those who have entrusted it, not of those to whom it has been entrusted.

units.la: Aut quemadmodum in paupertate uiuendum.) In paupertate uero ita uiuendum est, ut iis quæ adsunt contenti simus, quemadmodū Paulus apostolus monuit. Sed de administranda Repub. tum Plato, tum Aristoteles in Politicis, atq; his antiquior Moses, scripserunt.
units.tr: Or how one is to live in poverty. Indeed, in poverty one must live so that we are content with what is at hand, as the apostle Paul admonished. But on the administration of the commonwealth, both Plato and Aristotle in the Politics wrote, and before them Moses, who is older than these.

units.la: Rursus autē ex cognitionis consultatione, ubi sit, nec ne sit, aut fuerit, futurum ue sit quæritur, unū genus est quæstionis, posšitne aliquid effici: ut cum quæritur, ecquis nam perfecte sapiens esse possit. Alterum, quemadmodum quisque fiat: ut, quo nam pacto uirtus pariatur,
units.tr: Again, from the consultation of knowing, it is asked whether a thing is or is not, or has been, or will be. One kind of question is whether something can be brought about: as when it is asked whether anyone can be perfectly wise. The other is how each thing comes to be: by what means virtue is produced,

units.la: natura'ne, an ratione, an usu. Cuius generis sunt omnes, in quibus ut in obscuris, naturalibusq; quæstionibus caussæ, rationesque rerum explicantur.
units.tr: by nature, or by reason, or by practice. Of this kind are all those questions in which the causes and reasons of things are explained, as in obscure and natural matters.

units.la: Rursus autem ex cognitionis consultatione.) Tria in cognitionis quæstione quærenda esse dixit: An sit, Quid sit, Quale sit. Nunc primam illam partem, An sit, rursus divisit, primum in tria tempora. Nam nō solum quæritur, An sit aliqua perfecta Respublica, quod præsentis est temporis: sed etiam, an unquam fuerit, quod præteriti est: itemq;, an unquam futura sit? Deinde hæc tria tempora ad duos alios quærendi modos revocantur: quorum prior est, possit ne aliquid fieri hoc tempore, aut potuerit ne superioribus temporibus, aut possit etiam in posterum? ut cū quæritur, Num quis perfectè sapiens esse possit? Hæc quæstio tractatur à Cicerone in libris de Fin. et de Offic.lib.3. statim post præfationē. Vbi, quemadmodū duo genera sunt officiorum, perfectum alterum, alterum medium: sic et duo genera sapientum, quorū alij in perfectis Officijs versentur, alij in medijs istis et communibus, Perfectum autem sapientem, Stoicorum sententia, inueniri neminem, nec Socratem quidem ipsum, et ceteros qui sapiētes appellati sunt: sed quotquot sapientes appellantur, eos vulgi opinione appellari. Alter modus est, cum quaeritur, quemadmodum quidq; fiat? quo in genere quaestionis, de origine & causa cuiusque rei inquiritur: in quo Physici potißimum in explicandis obscuris naturae causis, rationibusq; versantur. ut, Quonam pacto virtus pariatur? natura ne, an ratione, an usu? Haec quaestio ex morali philosophia sumpta est. Fuerunt autem hac de re variae & dissidentes inter se sententiae philosophorum. Stoici enim à natura, Peripatetici usu & exercitatione: à natura tamen quandam facultatem esse, tanquam principium. Plato vero, nec natura nec usu omnino, sed divino quodam munere contingere virtutem existimauit. Ego autem (si licet honorarij arbitri munus subire) dicerem, hominem ad virtutem capessendam aptum factum esse natura: verum sine divino instinctu, veras virtutes nulla ratione posse quenquam adipisci.
units.tr: Again, from the consultation of knowing. He said three things are to be asked in the question of knowing: whether it is, what it is, and what sort it is. Now he divides that first part, whether it is, again, first into three times. For it is asked not only whether some perfect commonwealth exists, which concerns the present time, but also whether it ever was, which concerns the past, and likewise whether it ever will be. Then these three times are referred to two other modes of inquiry. The first is whether something can be done at this time, or could have been done in earlier times, or can be done in the future: as when it is asked, Can anyone be perfectly wise? This question is treated by Cicero in the books On Ends and in On Duties, book 3, immediately after the preface. There, just as there are two kinds of duties, the perfect and the intermediate, so too there are two kinds of wise men, some of whom are engaged in perfect duties, others in those intermediate and common ones. According to the opinion of the Stoics, the perfectly wise man is found to be no one, not even Socrates himself and the others who were called wise; however many are called wise, they are called so by the opinion of the crowd. The other mode is when it is asked how each thing comes to be. In this kind of question, inquiry is made into the origin and cause of each thing, and in this the natural philosophers are chiefly occupied in explaining the obscure causes and reasons of nature. As: by what means is virtue produced? By nature, or by reason, or by practice? This question is taken from moral philosophy. On this matter the opinions of the philosophers have been various and mutually disagreeing. For the Stoics held that virtue comes from nature, the Peripatetics from practice and exercise; yet from nature as a certain faculty, as a principle. Plato indeed thought that virtue comes neither from nature nor from practice at all, but by a certain divine gift. I, however (if I may take up the office of an honorary arbiter), would say that man has been made by nature apt to lay hold of virtue, but that without a divine impulse no one can by any means attain true virtues.

units.la: Illius autem generis, in quo quid sit id de quo agitur, quaeritur, duo sunt genera: quorum in altero disputandum est, aliud an idem sit, ut pertinacia & perseverantia.
units.tr: Of the kind in which the question is what the matter under discussion is, there are two sorts. In one of them we must debate whether one thing is the same as another or different, for example stubbornness and perseverance.

units.la: Illius autem generis. ) Haec quaestio ad definitionem tionem pertinet, cuius, ut antè dictum est, duo sunt genera: unum DialeCticum, alterum Oratorium. Illud proprium habet nomen generis, uo caturq; definitio, alterum descriptio. In priore genere disputari solet de eodem & alio. ut proposita quaestione, Sit ne pertinacia idem quod perseuerantia, an forsitan aliud? quod quidè elucere poterit ex utriusque definitione. Est enim perseuerantia (ut Cicero definit in fecundo de Inuentione) in ratione bene considerata stabilis & perpetua permanfio: eftq; fortitudinis pars. Pertinacia uerò, est quidem illa stabilis & perpetua permanfio, at non in ratione bene confiderata: non est igitur idem quod perseuerantia, etiamfi ei finitima est. Sed hic uidendum est, quot modis idem, aut aliud, quidpiam esse dicatur. Id autem, autore Ariftotele Top. libro primo, tribus dicitur modis: Numero, siue nomine, & specie, & genere. Numero quidè cadè sunt, quorum nomina plura, res uerò una est, quae συνώνυμα Graecè, & idem significantia Latinè uocantur: ut anima & uita, modestia & temperantia. Diuerfa, siue alia, cum ut nomina, sic quoq; res multae: ut tempus & locus, iustitia & modestia. Formae autem eiusdem dicuntur, quae etsi multa sunt, specie tamen nihil differunt, ut quae eidem formae subijciuntur: ut Socrates & Plato, uterq; enim homo. specie uero alia sunt, lupus & ouis. Genere item eadem sunt, quæ ad idem genus referuntur, ut homo & equus, quorum genus unum est, animal: Rhetorica & Dialectica, utraq; enim ars. Quæ autem sub diuersis generib. collocantur, ea genere differūt: quod de summis & mediis generibus intelligi potest. sed potissimum de summis, ut numerus & virtus; quorum ille quantitatis est, hæc uero qualitatis. Itē clementia & perseuerantia: illius nanq; genus est temperantia, huius autem fortitudo. In his autem trib. id quod unū & idem numero dicitur, idem uerissimè appellatur: cuius itē genera sunt tria. Quorum primū, & maximè proprium est, cū aliquid eodem nomine uel definitione explicatur: ut uis & officium oratoris, Rhetorica & benedicendi scientia. Secundo loco, ea quæ ciusdem sunt proprietatis: ut, animal sagax, plenum rationis, cōsilij, est homo: est enim ex proprietatib. descriptus. Vel cum dicimus, quod uim habet intelligendi. Postremò, cū ab aliqua re suffuita aliquid nominatur: ut, Christus, & qui Hierosolymæ cruci pro nobis suffixus est,
units.tr: "Of that kind": this question belongs to definition, which, as was said above, has two kinds: one dialectical, the other oratorical. The dialectical kind has the proper name "definition", and the oratorical is called "description". In the first kind it is customary to debate whether things are the same or different. For example, once the question is put, "Is stubbornness the same as perseverance, or perhaps something else?", this can be made clear from the definition of each. Perseverance, as Cicero defines it in the second book of the De Inventione, is a steady and lasting persistence in a well-considered purpose, and it is a part of fortitude. Stubbornness, however, is indeed a steady and lasting persistence, but not in a well-considered purpose. So it is not the same as perseverance, even though it is closely akin to it. But here we must consider in how many ways one thing is said to be the same as, or different from, another. According to Aristotle in the first book of the Topics, this is said in three ways: in number, or in name, in species, and in genus. In number, things are the same when their names are many but the thing is one; these are called [συνώνυμα] in Greek and in Latin "synonyms", things signifying the same: for example soul and life, modesty and temperance. Things are different or other when, as their names differ, so too do the things themselves: for example time and place, justice and modesty. Things are said to be of the same form when, though many, they differ in no species, as things subject to the same form: for example Socrates and Plato, for both are men. Things are different in species: for example wolf and sheep. Things are the same in genus when they are referred to the same genus: for example man and horse, whose genus is one, animal; or rhetoric and dialectic, for both are arts. Things placed under different genera differ in genus; this may be understood of the highest and of the middle genera, but chiefly of the highest, as number and virtue, of which the one belongs to quantity and the other to quality. Likewise clemency and perseverance: the genus of the former is temperance, of the latter fortitude. Of these three ways, what is said to be one and the same in number is most properly called the same, and this too has three kinds. The first, and most proper, is when something is explained by the same name or definition: for example the power and duty of the orator, rhetoric and the science of speaking well. In the second place are things that have the same property: for example, an animal that is keen, full of reason and judgement, is a man, for he is described by his properties; or when we say, "that which has the power of understanding". Lastly, when something is named from some thing fastened to it: for example, Christ, who was fixed to the cross at Jerusalem for us.

units.la: In altero autem descriptio generis alicuius, & quasi imago exprimenda est: ut, qualis sit auarus, aut quid sit superbia.
units.tr: In the second kind, a description of some genus, and as it were its image, must be set forth: for example, what sort of man a miser is, or what pride is.

units.la: In altero autem descriptio generis alicuius. ) Haec est illa oratoria definitio, de qua modo dicebam: quae aut personarum est, aut rerum descriptio. Personarum, ut qualis sit auarus, quem descripsit Horatius illa Ode, Nullus argento color est auaris, &c.
units.tr: "In the second kind, a description of some genus." This is that oratorical definition of which I was just speaking, which is a description either of persons or of things. A description of persons: for example what sort of man the miser is, whom Horace described in that ode, "No silver has any colour for the avaricious", and so on.

units.la: Cuius descriptio sumitur ex adiunctis, et verisimilibus. Rerum, ut quid sit superbia? ea autem est immoderata animi elatio, quemadmodum infra dicit Cicero: Et magnitudinem animi superbia in animis extollendis imitatur. Potest autem ea etiam ex adiunctis, quod saepe fecit Cicero in Orationibus, describi.
units.tr: Its description is drawn from adjuncts and probabilities. A description of things: for example, what is pride? It is an immoderate elation of spirit, as Cicero says below: "and pride imitates greatness of spirit in lifting up minds". It can also be described from adjuncts, as Cicero often did in his speeches.

units.la: Tertio autem in genere, in quo quale fit quaeritur, aut de honestate, aut de utilitate, aut de aequitate dicendum est. De honestate sic: ut, honestum ne sit pro amico periculum, aut inuidiam subire. De utilitate autem sic: ut, sit ne utile in repub. administranda uersari. De aequitate vero sic: ut, sit ne aequum amicos cognatis anteferre.
units.tr: In the third kind, in which the question concerns what quality a thing has, we must speak either of honourableness, or of usefulness, or of fairness. About honourableness, as: is it honourable to undergo danger or unpopularity for a friend? About usefulness, as: is it useful to take part in administering the commonwealth? About fairness, as: is it fair to prefer friends to kinsmen?

units.la: Tertio autem in genere, in quo quale.) Tertium quaestionum cognitionis genus partiendo eleganter explicat: cuius tria capita facit, honestatem, statem, utilitatem, & æquitatem: in quibus etiam contraria sunt intelligenda. hi enim sunt fines in tribus caussarum generibus, ut ante ostensum est. Nam honestas demonstratiui, deliberatiui utilitas, æquitas uero iudiciorum est propria. Quanquam hæc ipsa capita miscentur, & pro re nata uarientur: differunt autem inter se, quod honestas uirtutis atque animi est: utilitas corporis & rerum externarum, ab usu & utendo dicta: æquitas uero, iuris & legum. in his enim omnibus uersatur, qui nunc instituitur, orator.
units.tr: "In the third kind, in which the question concerns quality." Cicero explains the third kind of inquiry elegantly by division. He makes its heads honourableness, usefulness and fairness, and in these the contraries are also to be understood. For these are the ends in the three kinds of causes, as was shown before: honourableness is peculiar to the demonstrative, usefulness to the deliberative, and fairness to the judicial. Yet these heads are mixed together and vary according to circumstance. They differ from one another in that honourableness belongs to virtue and the mind, usefulness to the body and external things (so called from use and using), and fairness to right and laws. For it is in all these things that the orator who is now being instructed is occupied.

units.la: De honestate sic. ) Exemplū quæstionis pendet ex officiorum doctrina. Certè pro amico periculum, odium, & inuidia, in re honesta sunt subeunda: ut Cicero de Amicitia docet.
units.tr: "About honourableness, as..." The example of the question depends on the teaching about duties. Certainly, for a friend one must undergo danger, hatred and unpopularity, when the matter is honourable, as Cicero teaches in the De Amicitia.

units.la: De utilitate autem sic. ) Hoc exemplum ex Politicis sumptum, habet contrarias partes. Nam alij non esse Reipub. administrandam aiunt, cuiusmodi Pythagoras fuit. quod indicat Symbolum illud, A' fabis abstinere: quo intellexisse uoluunt, Rempub. nõ esse attingendam. Alij autem, ut Cicero de Offic. lib. 1. docet, etiam iniustum cum putant, qui accedere ad remp. nolit.
units.tr: "About usefulness, as..." This example, taken from politics, has opposing sides. For some say that the commonwealth should not be administered, as Pythagoras did, which the saying [ἀπὸ κυάμων ἀπέχεσθαι], "abstain from beans", is taken to indicate, by which they want it understood that the commonwealth should not be touched. Others, however, as Cicero teaches in the first book of De Officiis, think that one who is unwilling to approach the commonwealth is even acting unjustly.

units.la: De æquitate uerò sic. ) Et hoc ex morali philosophia, officijsq; manat: & sunt tempora, in quibus amicum propinquo anteferre debeas. alij autem contrà:ut Cicero de Offic.lib.1.copioſè & diuinitus docet.
units.tr: "About fairness, as..." This too comes from moral philosophy and the doctrine of duties, and there are times when you ought to prefer a friend to a kinsman. Others, on the contrary: as Cicero teaches fully and divinely in the first book of De Officiis.

units.la: Atqʒ in hoc eodem genere, in quo quale fit quæritur, exoritur aliud quoddam disputandi genus. Non enim simpliciter solum quæritur, quid honestum sit, quid utile, quid æquum: sed etiam ex comparatione, quid honestius, quid utilius, quid æquius:atqʒ etiam quid honestissimum, quid utilissimum, quid æquissimum. cuius generis illa sunt, quæ præstantissima sit dignitas uitæ, atque ea quidem, quæ dixi, cognitionis sunt omnia.
units.tr: And in this same kind, in which the question concerns quality, another kind of debate arises. For it is not only asked simply what is honourable, what useful, what fair, but also, by comparison, what is more honourable, more useful, more fair, and also what is most honourable, most useful, most fair. To this kind belong such questions as, which is the most excellent dignity of life? All the things I have mentioned belong to the inquiry into knowledge.

units.la: Atq; in hoc eodem genere.) Quæstio qualitatis est eius generis, ut in ea & simpliciter quæratur, & comparatè. De simplicibus quæstionibus hactenus: iam quomodo ex comparatione aliquid quæratur, docet. Aut enim duo proposita sunt, aut plura. si duo, tunc utrum honestius, utilius, aut æquius sit? sin plura, quid honestissimum, quid utilissimum, quid æquissimum: ut quæ præstantissima sit dignitas uitæ, id est, quod genus uitæ præstantissimum sit, ac potissimum eligendum. Quæ autem comparantur, ea uel differentia & diuersa inter se sunt, uel in aliquo contrariorum genere. Itemq; eadem res, uel in eodem fine, uel in diuersis finibus conferuntur. ut, honestius ne sit, mercatura opes parare, an militia: Vtrum sit beatius dare beneficium, an accipere. In diuersis uero finibus: ut, Sit ne plus utilitatis in bello suscipiendo, quam damni in pace facienda. Atq; haec omnia, ut diximus, ad cognitionis quaestionem spectant.
units.tr: "And in this same kind." A question of quality is of such a sort that it can be asked both simply and comparatively. Thus far on simple questions; now he teaches how something is asked by comparison. Either two things are proposed or several. If two, then the question is whether one is more honourable, more useful, or more fair; if several, which is most honourable, most useful, most fair: for example, which is the most excellent dignity of life, that is, which kind of life is most excellent and especially to be chosen. Things that are compared are either different and diverse from one another, or else they belong to some kind of contraries. Likewise the same thing is compared either with respect to the same end or with respect to different ends. For example: is it more honourable to acquire wealth by trade or by soldiering? Is it more blessed to give a benefit or to receive one? With different ends: for example, is there more advantage in undertaking a war than harm in making peace? All these, as we have said, pertain to the question of knowledge.

units.la: Restant actionis, cuius alterum est praecipiendi genus, quod ad ratione officij pertinet: ut, quemadmodum colendi sint parentes. alterum autem ad sedandos animos, & oratione sanandos: ut in consolandis moeroribus, ut in iracundia comprimenda, aut in timore tollendo, aut in cupiditate minuenda. cui quidem generi contrarium est disputandi genus, ad eosdem illos animi motus: quod in amplificanda oratione saepe faciendum est, uel gignendos, uel concitandos. Atque fere haec est partitio consultationum, Restant actionis.) Quemadmodum cognitionis quaestionem bis diuisit, sic etiam actionis quaestionem bis est partitus. Alteram igitur partem supra habuimus: hoc autem loco secundam. et differt ab illa haec. illa enim et comparatione habuit rerum persequendarum ac declinandarum, hoc est, honestarum et turpium, deinde quae ad commodum usumq; referuntur: haec autem reliquas officij actiones, affectuumq; doctrinam. Et ut moralis doctrinae duae sunt partes, quarum altera de uirtutibus cruitijs praecipit, altera de motibus animorum aut sedandis, aut sanandis: sic et quaestio actionis, quae finis est eius doctrinae, in totidem partes distribuenda est. Sedatur autem, minuendo: sanantur, prorsus tollendo et extirpando. Huc referuntur disputationes illae, subtilesq; orationes, quibus moerentes consolamur, et iracundiam eorum qui accensi sunt comprimimus, aut extinguimus, timorem tollimus, cupiditatem minuimus: quae sunt quatuor affectuum genera, quorum doctrina in Tusculanis & Cicerone traditur.
units.tr: There remain the questions of action, of which one kind is precept, which concerns the reasons of duty: for example, how parents ought to be honoured. The other kind concerns calming minds and healing them by speech: for example, in consoling grief, in restraining anger, in removing fear, or in lessening desire. The opposite of this kind is the kind of debate concerning the same emotions of the mind, which must often be used in amplifying a speech, either by arousing or by inflaming them. And this is roughly the division of deliberative questions. "There remain the questions of action." Just as he divided the question of knowledge in two, so too he divided the question of action in two. The first part we had above; this second part is what is treated here, and it differs from that one. For the former concerned the choice and avoidance of things to be pursued, that is, honourable and shameful, and then those referred to advantage and use; whereas this one concerns the remaining actions of duty and the teaching on the emotions. And just as the doctrine of morals has two parts, one of which teaches the virtues and the other the motions of the mind, either to be calmed or to be healed, so too the question of action, which is the end of that doctrine, must be divided into as many parts. Things are calmed by lessening, and healed by being wholly removed and rooted out. To this belong those disputations and subtle speeches by which we console mourners, and restrain or quench the anger of those who are inflamed, remove fear, and lessen desire: these are the four kinds of emotion, whose doctrine is handed down in the Tusculan Disputations and by Cicero.

units.la: Vt, quemadmodum colendi sunt parentes.) Aristoteles in Ethicis, et Cicero de Offic. sed omnium praestantissime leges Dei, oraculaq; divina tradunt.
units.tr: As for how parents ought to be honoured: Aristotle in the Ethics and Cicero in De Officiis teach this, but the laws of God and the divine oracles teach it most excellently of all.

units.la: Cui quidem generi contrarium.) Idcirco contrarium, quoniam duplex est doctrina de permotionibus, siue perturbationibus animorum: una philosophica, altera oratoria. Illa in sedandis & sanandis, ut dictum est: haec oratoria, ei contraria, in gignendis potissimum, & concitandis: quod in amplificanda oratione saepe faciendum esse, supra in praeceptis perorationis etiā docuit Orator. Hactenus de altera parte primae quaestionū partitionis, quae in propositis siue consultationibus versatur: deinceps de caussarum generibus dicendum esset, nisi pauca de ratione in-ueniendi & disponendi restarent.
units.tr: Which kind is opposite: it is opposite because the doctrine of emotions, or disturbances of the mind, is twofold: one is philosophical, the other oratorical. The former calms and heals them, as has been said; the latter, which is opposed to it, chiefly arouses and stirs them up. The orator has also taught in the precepts on the peroration that this must often be done in amplifying a speech. So far, on the second part of the first division of the question, which concerns proposals or deliberations. Next, the kinds of causes would have to be discussed, were it not that a few points about the method of invention and arrangement remain.

units.la: C. F. Cognoui: sed quae ratio est in his inueniendi, & disponendi, requiro. C. P. Quid tu aliám ne censes, & non eandem esse, quae est exposita, ut ex eisdem locis ad fidem & ad inueniendum ducantur omnia? Collocandi autem quae est exposita in alijs, ratio eadem huc trāsfertur.
units.tr: Son: I understand that, but I want to know what method there is for invention and arrangement in these matters. Father: Do you not think it is another method, and the same one that has been set out, so that everything is drawn from the same topics for proof and for invention? The method of arrangement, moreover, is transferred here in the same way as it was set out in the other cases.

units.la: C. F. Cognoui, sed quae ratio est.) Inuentio & dispositio, de qua hic loquitur filius, non est quaestionum, sed argumentorum ad ipsas quaestiones tradendas.
units.tr: "I understand, but what method is there?" Invention and arrangement, of which the son speaks here, belong not to the questions but to the arguments by which those questions are to be treated.

units.la: C, P. Quid tu.) Respondet pater, nullā aliam esse inueniendi aut collocandi rationem, quàm quæ sub initia Partitionum tradita est libro primo: ubi & nos quæ dicenda erant, diximus. Idcirco inde petenda sunt.
units.tr: "Father: Do you not think..." The father replies that there is no other method of invention or arrangement than the one handed down at the beginning of the Partitions in the first book, where we also stated what had to be said. Therefore they must be sought from there.

units.la: DE QVAESTIONE DE- FINITA, siue de generibus causarum.
units.tr: ON THE DEFINED QUESTION, OR ON THE KINDS OF CAUSES

units.la: Cognita igitur omni distributione propositarum consultationum, causarum genera restant omnino. Et earum quidē forma duplex est; quorum altera delectationem sectatur auriū: alterius ut obtineat, probet & efficiat, quod agit, omnis est suscepta contentio.
units.tr: Therefore, once the whole division of proposed deliberations is known, only the kinds of causes remain. Of these there are indeed two forms: one aims at delighting the ears, while the whole contest of the other is to win acceptance, to prove, and to bring about what it pursues.

units.la: Cognita igitur.) Duo genera quæstionum proponitarum facit: quorum alterum infinitum, sine ulla personarum, aliorumque temporum complexione, cuius partes in superioribus explicatæ sunt: alterum definitum certis personis & attributis, quod causam appellauit. De hoc igitur genere reliquæ partitiones docent, & in eo explicando assumuntur. Hoc autem loco repetit initio positam causarum partitionem, ut singularum partes diligentius explicet. Earum enim supra facta est mentio, propter collocationem, quæ una est Oratorij officij pars: hic uerò, ut quæ pertinent ad quæstionem definitam persequatur, quæ pars est materiæ Oratoris.
units.tr: Therefore, once... He makes two kinds of proposed questions: one unlimited, without any combination of persons or times, whose parts were explained above; the other defined by certain persons and circumstances, which he has called a cause. Therefore the remaining divisions teach about this kind, and are taken up in explaining it. In this place he repeats the division of causes set out at the beginning, so that he may explain the parts of each more carefully. Earlier, mention was made of them on account of arrangement, which is the one part of the orator's office; but here, so that he may pursue what pertains to the defined question, which is a part of the orator's material.

units.la: Et earum quidem forma duplex est.) Genera causarum, fine distinguit. nam cuius finis est delectatio, demonstratiuum genus appellatur: cuius autem fides ad probandum proposita est, id aut deliberatiuum, aut iudiciale nominatur. Deliberatiuum quidem, si futuri temporis habeatur ratio: Iudiciale, si præteriti: quæ partitio Aristotelis est in primo Rhetoricorum, de qua nos initio plura diximus.
units.tr: And indeed there are two forms of kinds of cause: he distinguishes them by their end. For the kind whose end is delight is called demonstrative; the kind whose trust is placed in proving is called either deliberative or judicial. It is deliberative if the consideration is of future time, judicial if of past time. This division is Aristotle's, in the first book of the Rhetoric, on which we spoke at some length at the beginning.

units.la: DE GENERE DEMON- stratiuo.
units.tr: ON THE DEMONSTRATIVE KIND

units.la: Itaque illud superius exornatio dicitur, quod cum latum genus esse potest, saneque uarium, unum ex eo delegimus, quod ad laudandos claros uiros suscepimus, & ad improbos uituperandos. Genus enim nullum est orationis, quod aut uberius ad dicendum, aut utilius ciuitatibus esse possit, aut in quo magis orator in cognitione uirtutum, uitiorumque ueruersetur. Reliquum autem genus caussarum, aut in prouisione poste‐ ri temporis, aut in præteriti discepta‐ tione uersatur: quorum alterum de‐ liberationis est, alterum iudicij. Ex qua partitione tria genera caussarũ extiterunt. Vnum, quod à meliori parte laudationis est appellatũ, deli‐ berationis alterũ, tertium iudicio‐ rum. quamobrẽ de primo primùm, si placet, disputemus. C. F. Mihi uero placet. C. P. Aclaudandi, uituperandi‐que rationes quæ non ad bene dicendum solum, sed etiam ad honeste uiuendum ualent, exponam breuiter, atque à principijs exordiar & laudandi, & uituperandi.
units.tr: Therefore that earlier kind is called ornamental; since it can be a broad kind, and indeed varied, we have chosen from it the one which we have undertaken for praising famous men and for censuring wicked ones. For there is no kind of speech that can be more fruitful for speaking, or more useful to states, or in which the orator is more engaged in knowing virtues and vices. The remaining kind of cause is concerned either with providing for future time or with debating past time: the one belongs to deliberation, the other to judgement. From this division three kinds of cause have arisen: one, which has been called from the better part of praise; the second of deliberation; the third of judgements. Wherefore let us discuss first, if you agree, the first. Son: Indeed I agree. Father: I will briefly set out the principles of praising and blaming, starting from the beginnings of both praise and blame, which are useful not only for speaking well but also for living honourably.

units.la: Quod ad laudandos claros uiros: ) His uerbis duas esse partes demonstratiui generis ostendit, laudem ac uituperationem, cum rerum, tum uel maxime personarum.
units.tr: "To praise famous men": by these words he shows that the demonstrative kind has two parts, praise and censure, of both things and, above all, of persons.

units.la: Genus enim nullum est.) Commendat hoc genus ab ornatu & dicendi copia, deinde ab utilitate & honestate. nihil est enim ad exaggerandum & amplificandam orationem accommodatius. tius, quàm aliquid augere & extenuare, laudare & uituperare cumulatissimè posse: Ac locis & laudandi & uituperandi, sæpe nobis est utendum in omni genere causarum, ex quo ubertas huius generis cognoscitur. Vtilitas autem in eo cernitur, quòd hoc genere ad uirtutem cohortari, à uitijs reuocare, uituperare improbos, laudare bonos possumus: quod ad homines meliores faciendos valet plurimum. quod quidem cum sine uirtutum & uitiorum cognitione, satis insigniter atque aptè fieri non possit, quàm sit non modò honestum ipsi Oratori, uerum etiam utile, perspicuum est. Nam huic generi omnis uirtutum & uitiorum est sylua subiecta. Verè igitur statim subijcit Cicero: Laudandi uituperandiq; rationes non ad benedicendum solum valere, sed etiam ad honestè uiuendum.
units.tr: For there is no kind...: He commends this kind for its ornament and abundance of speech, and then for its usefulness and honourableness. For nothing is more suited to exaggerating and amplifying a speech than being able to magnify and diminish, to praise and blame, to the fullest extent. Since we must often use the topics of praise and blame in every kind of cause, the richness of this kind is recognised from this. Its usefulness lies in this: by this kind we can urge people to virtue, call them back from vices, censure the wicked and praise the good, which is very effective in making men better. Since this cannot be done with sufficient distinction and aptness without knowledge of virtues and vices, it is clear how honourable, and indeed how useful, it is not only for the orator himself. For all the forest of virtues and vices is subject to this kind. Therefore Cicero rightly adds at once: the principles of praising and blaming are useful not only for speaking well but also for living honourably.

units.la: Omnia enim sunt profectò laudanda, quæ coniuncta cum uirtute sunt: & quæ cum uitijs, uituperanda. Quamobrem finis alterius est honestas, alterius turpitudo.
units.tr: For indeed all things that are joined with virtue are to be praised, and those joined with vices are to be blamed. Therefore the end of the one is honourableness, of the other shamefulness.

units.la: Omnia enim sunt profectò laudanda.) Demonstratiui generis utilitas, usus, & honestas, tum etiam partes, & fines quidam, indicata sunt: deinceps de eius materia, fine & tractatione docetur, ut tota eius generis cõfectio absoluatur. Materia igitur laudis est, non modò uirtus ipsa, uerumetiam quæ cum uirtute coniuncta sunt. uituperationis uero, uitia, & quæ uitiorum habet significationem. ex quo intelligitur, laudatori finem honestatem ipsam propositam esse: turpitudine uero, uituperatori. Nā illæ superior finis, sicut delectatio, in auditoribus ipsis cõsideratur.
units.tr: For indeed all things are to be praised...: The usefulness, use and honourableness of the demonstrative kind have been indicated, and also its parts and certain ends; next it is taught about its matter, end and treatment, so that the whole making of this kind may be completed. The matter of praise, therefore, is not only virtue itself but also what is joined with virtue; and of censure, vices and whatever has the meaning of vices. From this it is understood that the end proposed to the praiser is honourableness itself, but to the censurer, shamefulness. For the former end, like delight, is considered in the hearers themselves.

units.la: Conficitur autem ge.) Dictione appellat, oratione. nam pro uerbo aut uoce quasi quiddam, soli grammatici usurpauerunt. De tractatione iam agit, quæ bipartita est. nā in rebus primum, deinde in uerbis considerator. In rebus quidem, ut partibus orationis: in uerbis autem, ut sunt ornamenta. Ex partibus orationis solum ponit narratione, cum amplificatione, facta enim & res gestas commemorare oppus est, ex quibus exornatio constituitur: quæ narratio expositio, factorum, non perpetua in hoc genere, ut in aliis, sed in plures partes differta, locisq; distincta esse debet, ut ait Aristoteles Rhet.3.
units.tr: It is accomplished, however, by...: He calls it "dictio", speech; for only the grammarians have used the word for something like a single term or voice. He now treats the treatment, which is twofold: it is considered first in the matters, then in the words. In the matters, as the parts of speech; in the words, as ornaments. Of the parts of speech he mentions only narration, together with amplification; for it is necessary to recall deeds and things done, from which ornament is constituted. This narration, an exposition of deeds, is not continuous in this kind as in others, but must be divided into several parts and separated by places, as Aristotle says in Rhetoric 3.

units.la: Conficitur autem genus hoc dictionis, narrandis, exponendisq; factis, sine ullis argumentationibus, ad animi motus leniter tractandos magís, quàm ad fidem faciendam, aut confirmandam accômodatur. Non enim dubia firmantur, sed ea quæ certa, aut pro certis posita sunt, augentur. Quamobrem ex ijs quæ ante dicta sunt, & narrandi & augendi præcepta repetentur.
units.tr: This kind of speech is accomplished by narrating and setting out deeds, without any argumentation; it is suited to moving the feelings gently rather than to making or confirming trust. For doubtful things are not confirmed; rather, those that are certain, or put forward as certain, are enlarged. Therefore the precepts both of narrating and of amplifying will be repeated from what has been said before.

units.la: Sine ullis argumentationibus.) Rationem ipse statim subijcit, cur nulla argumentatio ad confir- mandum aut refellendum requiratur.
units.tr: Without any argumentation.) He immediately gives the reason why no argumentation is required either to confirm or to refute.

units.la: nam quæ fide egent, ea dubia & incerta sunt: laus autè ac uituperatio in certis & minimè dubijs uersatur. Frustra igitur in meridie lumen accenditur. De certis perspicuum quidem est, cuiusmodi est uirtus, aut insignis aliqua doctrina, aut illustre aliquod factum. ea enim aduersarium nullum habent. uerum si incerta sint quæ laudantur, aut uituperantur: etiamsi pro certis asseuerentur, ut uita Catonis, itemq; mors, tamen fidem interdum requirunt. quod non negat Aristoteles, & Cicero ipse usu confirmauit, ut in Orat. pro Pomp eio, & Philippica secunda. Sed quærat aliquis, cur nihil hoc loco de exordio & peroratione præcipiat? Respondeo: Quia non de Oratoris partibus proprie agitur, sed de quæstione ipsa, cuius parteis duæ proprie sunt, Narratio & motus, siue amplificatio: quae quidem amplificatio, non prorsus est expers fidei. Motus autem lenes & suaues debent esse. idcirco quae supra de suaui dicendi genere dicta sunt, itemque in narrandi [?] & augendi praeceptis repetenda erunt, & ad hunc locum comportanda.
units.tr: For matters that need proof are doubtful and uncertain, whereas praise and blame deal with what is certain and not at all doubtful. It is therefore pointless to light a lamp at midday. Among certain matters are plainly such things as a virtue, a notable piece of learning, or some famous deed, for these have no opponent. But if the things praised or blamed are uncertain, even when they are asserted as certain, such as the life of Cato, or his death, they nevertheless sometimes require proof. Aristotle does not deny this, and Cicero himself confirmed it by practice, as in the speech for Pompey and the Second Philippic. But someone may ask why he gives no instruction here on the exordium and the peroration. I answer: because he is not speaking strictly of the parts of the orator, but of the subject itself, whose two proper parts are the narration and the stirring of the emotions, or amplification; and this amplification is not entirely free of proof. The emotional appeals, however, must be gentle and soothing. Therefore what has been said above about the gentle style of speaking, and likewise the precepts on narration and amplification, must be repeated and brought together here.

units.la: Et quoniam in his caussis omnis ratio fere ad voluptatem auditoris, & ad delectationem refertur, utendū erit his in oratione singulorum verborum insignibus, quae habent plurimum suauitatis: id est, ut factis verbis, aut vetustis, aut translatis frequenter utamur, & in ipsa constructione verborum, ut paria paribus, & similia similibus saepe referantur: ut contraria, ut geminata, ut circumscripta numerose, non ad similitudinem versuum, sed ad explendum aurium sensum, apto quasi quodam verborum modo.
units.tr: And since in these kinds of cause almost all the method is directed to the pleasure and delight of the hearer, we shall have to use in our speech those distinctions of single words which contain the greatest charm: that is, we should frequently use words that are either archaic or transferred, and in the very construction of the words we should often set like against like, and similar against similar, as in contrasts, repetitions, and periods rounded with a measured rhythm, not in imitation of verses, but to satisfy the ear's sense, by a certain fitting arrangement of words.

units.la: Et quoniam in his caussis. ) Altera pars tractationis sequitur, in qua de ornamentis verborum simplicium & coniunctorum agitur. Sed primum finem huius generis epidictici proponit, tanquam huius tractationis caussam. Vt si quis quaerat, cur in hoc genere his uerborum et sententiarum insignibus utendum sit, quae plurimum habent suauitatis? respondendum est, quoniam hoc genus quasi ad inspiciendum uoluptatis et delectationis caussa comparatum est.
units.tr: And since in these kinds of cause.) The second part of the treatment follows, in which the ornaments of simple and combined words are discussed. But first he sets out the aim of this epideictic kind, as the purpose of this treatment. As if someone should ask why in this kind one must use these distinctions of words and sentences, which contain the greatest charm, the answer must be that this kind is designed, as it were, for the sake of display, for pleasure and delight.

units.la: Quod autem hic insignia uocat ornamenta ipsa, reddit ipse rationem in oratione, quia similia illis sunt quae in amplo ornatu scenae aut fori appellantur insignia: non quòd sola ornent, sed quòd excellant. Eadem ratio est horum, quae sunt orationis lumina, et quodammodo insignia, quas etiam conformationes, de Oratore libro tertio nominauit: quòd ex his quasi formam quandam capiat oratio. Haec autem in singulis uerbis enumerat, facta uerba, uetusta, translata. In constructione uero, seu coniunctione uerborum, paria paribus relata, et similia similibus, et contraria: deinde etiam geminata, et quae concinnè et numerose (modò absit nersus nimis insignis) cadunt, de quibus omnibus alibi satis dictum est. Nec tamen haec enumerauit, quòd non et alia suauitatem habeant, et ad hoc genus pertineant: sed quòd haec præcipua sint, utpote in quibus maior suauitas et delectatio sentiatur.
units.tr: As for why he here calls the ornaments themselves distinctions, he gives the reason in his own words: because they resemble what in the full decoration of the stage or the forum are called distinctions, not that they alone adorn, but that they stand out. The same reasoning applies to these, which are the lights of speech and in a way its distinctions, and which he also called figures of shape in the third book of On the Orator, because the speech takes on from them a certain form. He lists these in individual words: archaic words, transferred words. In the construction, or combination, of words, he lists: like set against like, similar against similar, and contraries; then also repetitions, and those that fall in a neat and measured way (provided the rhythm is not too conspicuous). All these have been discussed sufficiently elsewhere. He has not listed these as if other things did not also bring charm and belong to this kind, but because these are the principal ones, since in them a greater charm and delight is perceived.

units.la: Adhibendaq frequentius etiam illa ornamenta rerum sunt, siue quae mirabilia, nec opinata, siue significata monstris, prodigijs, oraculis: siue quae uidebuntur ei, de quo agimus, accidisse diuina, atque fatalia. Omnis enim expectatio eius qui audit, & admiratio, & improuisi exitus, habent aliquam in audiendo uoluptatem.
units.tr: Those ornaments of things also are to be used more often, whether they are wonderful and unexpected, or are signified by monsters, portents, and oracles, or are such that they seem to have happened to the person we are discussing by divine and fated means. For all the expectation of the hearer, and his admiration, and an unforeseen outcome, bring some pleasure in listening.

units.la: Adhibendaq; frequentius etiam illa ornamenta rerum.) Rerum ornamenta quae hic uocat, dupliciter intelligi possunt, aut enim illa intelligit, quae alioqui sententiarum dicuntur lumina: ut commoratio, illustris explanatio, et reliqua id genus: uel eas res quae magnae naturae sunt, & mirabiles, de quibus in amplificatione uidimus. Sic enim ut detur illa uerba adiecta tanquam explicandi causa, significare, cum ait: Siue quae mirabilia, nec opinata, item quae sequuntur. Nam ea omnia in rebus natura magnis cernuntur, habentq; delectationem, quemadmodum ipse in suaui genere docuit.
units.tr: Those ornaments of things also are to be used more often.) The ornaments of things which he calls here can be understood in two ways. Either he means those which are otherwise called the lights of sentences, such as the pause, the vivid explanation, and the rest of that kind; or he means those things which are of great and wonderful nature, which we have seen in the discussion of amplification. For thus the words added here, as an explanation, will mean: whether they are wonderful and unexpected, and what follows. For all these are seen in things of great nature, and they have delight, just as he himself taught in the section on the gentle style.

units.la: Delectat enim (inquit) quicquid est admirabile. Et paulo ante: Fit etiam suauis oratio (inquit) cum aliquid aut inuisum, aut inauditum, aut nouum dicas. & breuiter, omnia ex quibus attentio comcomparatur, de qua in præceptis exordiorum, suauitatem & uoluptatem habent. Hæc autem omnia cum alibi, tũ maximè in oratione de Pompeio imperatore deligendo, cumulatè & diuinitus præstitit hic Orator. Quæ autem appellauit similia similibus, trifariam intelligi possunt: primum ut à contrariis separentur (nam & paria paribus, & crebra crebris, & contraria contrariis referuntur) ut de Pompeio: Nõ auaritia ab instituto cursu ad prædam aleamq; reuocauit, non libido ad uoluptatem, non amœnitas ad delectationem. Deinde cum similes sunt exitus uerborum, postremò similia similibus quoq; agnominatione referuntur: ut, Non modò urbem, sed orbem etiam totum sua sapientia repleuit Christus. Præterea multa inopinata sunt, quæ non mirabilia: & mirabilia, quæ non monstrosa, ipsum etiam monstrum à prodigio differt: manus sex aut septem digitorum, & animal biceps, monstrosa sunt. prodigiosa uerò, cum quid cuenturũ prædicant. confunduntur tamen hæc interdum, unde Cic.de Diuin.1.Quia enim ostendunt, portendunt,monstrant, prædicunt: ostenta,portenta,monstra,prodigia dicuntur.
units.tr: For (he says) whatever is admirable delights. And a little earlier: a speech also becomes gentle (he says) when you say something hateful, or unheard of, or new; and in short, all the things by which attention is gained, of which we spoke in the precepts on exordiums, have charm and pleasure. Now the orator here has performed all these things abundantly and divinely, not only elsewhere, but above all in the speech on choosing Pompey as commander. As for what he called similar against similar, these can be understood in three ways. First, they are set against contraries (for like is set against like, and frequent against frequent, and contraries against contraries), as in the passage about Pompey: greed did not call him back from his chosen course to plunder and gain, nor lust to pleasure, nor charm to delight. Second, when the endings of the words are similar. Lastly, similar things are also related by a play on names, as: Christ filled not only the city but the whole world with his wisdom. Moreover, many things are unexpected without being wonderful, and wonderful things are not always monstrous; a monster also differs from a portent: a hand with six or seven fingers, and a two-headed animal, are monstrous, but portents are prodigious when they foretell something about to happen. Yet these are sometimes confused, whence Cicero, On Divination, book 1: because they show, portend, point out, or foretell, they are called omens, portents, monsters, and prodigies.

units.la: Sed quoniam in tribus generibus bona, mala'uc uersantur, externis, nis, corporis, & animi. prima sunt externa, quæ ducuntur à genere: quo breuiter, modicéq; laudato: aut si erit infame, prætermisso: si humile, vel prætereunto, vel ad augendam eius, quem laudas, gloriam tacto: deinceps, si res patiatur, de fortunis erit, & facultatibus dicendum: postea de corporis bonis, in quibus quidem, quæ uirtutem maxime significat, facillimè forma laudatur.
units.tr: But since goods and evils are found in three kinds, external, of the body, and of the mind, the external goods come first, and these are derived from birth. Of birth one should speak briefly and with moderate praise; or if it is disgraceful, pass it over; if humble, either pass it by or touch on it only to increase the glory of the person you are praising. Next, if the matter allows, one should speak of fortune and resources; afterwards of the goods of the body, among which beauty most clearly signifies virtue and is most easily praised.

units.la: Sed quoniam in tribus generibus bona malaque uersantur. )Reuertitur ad laudationum materiam, mox etiam de tractatione & collocatione agit. est autem materia, quemadmodum in uerisimilibus diximus (ex eodem enim loco hæc amenda sunt) triplex: Rerum externarum, corporis, & animi: quæ quidem bona, mala-que, profpe-ra aut aduersa dicuntur.
units.tr: But since goods and evils are found in three kinds.) He returns to the matter of praises, and soon also deals with its treatment and arrangement. The matter, as we said in the discussion of probabilities (for these points must be taken from the same place), is threefold: of external things, of the body, and of the mind. These goods and evils are called prosperous or adverse.

units.la: Prima sunt externa. ) Collocationem ordinem-que in ea triplici materia tractanda statuit, ac primum locum rebus externis assignat. & prima intelligi debent, non dignitate, sed cognitione. Sunt enim prima, quæ sese nobis offerunt cognoscenda. Sed quæret aliquis, si virtus una est, quæ quæ est per se ipsa laudabilis, & sine qua nil laudari potest: cur hic rerū externarū & corporis laudis materiā ponit? Respondeo, quēadmodū antea dictum est, non solū virtute ipsam per se, verūm quæ cōiūcta cū virtute sunt, esse lau dāda: ut quæ cum vitijs, vituperanda. In vsu enim rerū externarum, vel virtus, vel vicij elucescit maximè. In his igitur genus, & quæ à genere ducūtur, sumēda sunt: quod quidē triplicē habet cōsiderationem. Aut enim genus est clarū, virtute maiorū: aut infame vitijs, atq; aliqua turpitudine vitæ: aut humile & obscurū, non tamen aliqua macula cōtaminatū. Si clarū fuerit, breuiter & modicè laudandū est. nā nō industria & cōsilio cōparatur, sed fortuitò adnascitur. Deinde etiā, quia claritudo illa & nobilitas, nō nostra, sed aliorū virtute parta est. Sin infame & turpe fuerit, omnino prætermittendū: nisi vituperare quempiā voluerris. tūc etiā modicè ijsdem de caussis vituperandum est. In laude enim ea sunt vitāda, quæ aliquā turpitudinis nebulā possunt obtēdere. Si postremò fuerit humile atq; ignobile, duplex erit consultatio. Aut enim ad augendam eius, quem laudandum suscepueris, gloriam valet, tunc leuiter tangendum est. ut cum Cicero dicit: Sua virtute se maioribus præluxisse suis. Aut si ad laudem augendam nihil cōferre videatur, non secus quàm infàme prætercundum. A' genere ad ipsas facultates, opes, copias, est veniendum. At hæ sunt generis, de quo dictum est. deinde pecuniæ, propinquorum, amicorum, opum: sed hoc intelligitur esse faciendum, si res patitur: id est, si laudabiles adsint facultates. Postea de corporis bonis, cuiusmodi sunt valetudo, forma, vires, ingenium: in quibus quidè quæ virtutem maximè significat, rectissimè forma laudatur. Nam ut inquit ille,
units.tr: The external things come first.) He establishes the arrangement and order of treating this threefold matter, and assigns the first place to external things. The word "first" must be understood not in terms of worth but of knowledge: these are first because they present themselves to us to be known first. But someone will ask: if virtue alone is the one thing that is praiseworthy in itself, and without which nothing can be praised, why does he here put external things and bodily goods as matter for praise? I answer, as was said earlier, that not only virtue itself in itself but also things joined with virtue are to be praised, just as things joined with vices are to be blamed. For it is in the use of external things that either virtue or vice shines out most clearly. Therefore birth, and what derives from birth, must be taken up here, and this has a threefold consideration. For birth is either illustrious through the virtue of ancestors, or infamous through vices and some disgrace of life, or humble and obscure, yet not stained by any blemish. If it is illustrious, it should be praised briefly and moderately, for it is not acquired by effort and planning but comes to us by chance; and besides, that renown and nobility were gained not by us but by the virtue of others. But if it is infamous and shameful, it must be passed over altogether, unless you wish to blame someone; then even so it must be blamed moderately, for the same reasons: in praise one must avoid whatever could cast a cloud of disgrace. If finally it is humble and ignoble, there will be a twofold consideration. Either it serves to increase the glory of the person you have undertaken to praise, and then it should be touched on lightly, as when Cicero says that by his own virtue he shone out above his ancestors; or if it seems to contribute nothing to increasing the praise, it must be passed by no less than something infamous. From birth one must move on to the resources themselves: wealth, riches, and supplies. These belong to the kind of which we have spoken; then money, relatives, friends, and influence; but this is to be done only if the matter allows, that is, if there are praiseworthy resources. After that come the goods of the body, such as health, beauty, strength, and talent; among these, beauty, which most clearly signifies virtue, is most rightly praised. For, as that poet says,

units.la: Gratior est pulchro veniens in corpore virtus.
units.tr: "Virtue that comes in a beautiful body is more pleasing."

units.la: Quin & Physici ipsi mirantur, si in præstanti forma & specie, animus vitiosus inhabitet, aut in turpi & deformi bonus: quanquam de Galba dictum sit, Male Galbæ animam habitare, quod in turpi corpore bonus latêret animus. Contrà; de Therfite Homerico, qui intus & extra totus turpis erat. Nero autem scelestus, & formosus. sed hæc monstra sunt potius, quàm homines. Aristoteles certè formam non in postrema parte felicitatis ponit.
units.tr: Moreover, the natural philosophers themselves are amazed when a vicious mind dwells in a handsome, attractive body, or a good mind in an ugly, deformed one. Yet it has been said of Galba that his soul dwelt ill, because a good mind lay hidden in an ugly body. On the other hand, there is Homer's Thersites, who was ugly both inside and out. Nero, however, was wicked and handsome. But these are monsters rather than men. Aristotle, at any rate, does not place beauty among the last components of happiness.

units.la: Deinde est ad facta veniendum, quorum collocatio triplex est. aut enim temporum seruandus est ordo, aut in primis recentissimum quodque dicendum, aut multa & varia ria facta in propria uirtutum genera sunt dirigenda.
units.tr: Next we must come to deeds, and their arrangement is threefold. Either the order of the times must be kept, or the most recent deeds must be told first, or the many and varied deeds must be distributed under the particular kinds of virtue.

units.la: Deinde est ad facta veniendum.) In factis & rebus gestis maxime uirtus hominis enitet ac splendet: idcirco postrema collocantur. sic enim solent oratores: quae maxime nos retinere ac meminisse volunt, ea postrema dicunt. Nam recentissimum quodque maxime meminimus. Triplicem autem factorum collocationem tradit. Aut enim sequimur ordinem temporis, ut qua quicque aetate gestum factumue sit exponamus: quod facit Cicero in Antonij uituperatione, Philippica secunda. Aut contrario ordine, quasi retexentes a nouissimis incipiamus: & in antiquissima & prima desinamus, cuius rei exemplum nullum extat quod sciam: extitit tamen Ciceronis ipsius de Romanorum factis & gestis opus, teste Fusio Caleno, in oratione quam habuit pro Antonio, contra Ciceronem, quae ad nostras Philippicas ex Dione adiecta est: quod tamen exemplum Calenus ille artis ignarus, ad uituperationem adduxit. Sit igitur ille prior ordo componendi, & naturalis: alter uero resoluendi, artis magis quam naturae. Supererit tertius ille ordo praestantissimus, ut varia & diuersa facta in certa et propria uirtutum genera digeramus, & distribuamus. Quod fecit Cicero in Popeio laudando, ut exempli causa: Si quis bonus bonis fortunæ & corporis præditus fuerit, bene ijs usum: fi nõ habuerit, sapienter caruisse: fi ami ferit, moderatè tulisse. deinde, quid sapienter is quem laudet, quid liberaliter, quid fortiter, quid iuste, quid magnificè, quid pie, quid grate, quid humaniter, quid denique cum aliqua uirtute aut fecerit, aut tulerit: hæc & quæ sint eius generis, fa cilè uidebit, qui uolet laudare quempiam, & qui uituperare contraria. Quæ quidem à Cicerone lib.2. de Orat. extremo pene, liberaliter explicant ur: qui locus diligenter erit eloquentiæ studioso perdiscendus.
units.tr: Next we must come to deeds. It is in deeds and accomplishments that a person's virtue shines and stands out most, so these are placed last. Orators usually do this: what they most want us to retain and remember, they put at the end, since we remember most vividly whatever is most recent. He hands down a threefold arrangement of deeds. Either we follow the order of time, so that we set out what was done or happened at each age, as Cicero does in the invective against Antony, the Second Philippic. Or we reverse the order, beginning with the latest and ending with the oldest and first.
