As far as I know there is no example of this, though Cicero himself wrote a work on the deeds of the Romans, according to Fusius Calenus, in the speech he delivered for Antony against Cicero, which was added after Dio to our Philippics. Yet that ignorant Calenus used this example for invective. So the first order is the natural order of composition, while the second is one of unravelling, more a matter of art than of nature. The third order remains, the most excellent, in which we arrange and distribute various and diverse deeds under definite and particular kinds of virtue. Cicero did this in praising Pompey, for example: If a good man has been endowed with the goods of fortune and of the body, he used them well; if he has not had them, he went without them wisely; if he has lost them, he bore the loss with moderation. Then, whatever the man he is praising did wisely, what he did generously, bravely, justly, magnificently, piously, gratefully, humanely, and finally whatever he did or endured with some virtue, and whatever is of that kind: anyone who wishes to praise someone, or to censure the contrary, will easily see these things. Cicero explains these very fully near the end of the second book of De Oratore, and this passage should be learned thoroughly by anyone who studies eloquence.

units.la: VIRTVTVM ET VITIO- rum distributio.
units.tr: The distribution of virtues and vices

units.la: Sed hic locus uirtutum atq; uitiorum, latissime patens: ex multis & uarijs disputationibus, nunc in quandam angustam & breuem conkcludetur.
units.tr: But this topic of virtues and vices extends very widely; out of many and various discussions, it will now be brought together into a narrow and brief compass.

units.la: Sed hic locus uirtutum atq; uitiorum.) Ad laudis & uituperationis materiem redierat, & eius tractationem subijcerat: mentionemq; secerat uirtutis, quæ laudis maxima materia est, quemadmodum uitia uituperationis. Iam uirtutum partitionem aggreditur, quarũ genera tã quã in tabella descripta proponit. Et rectè qui- dem
units.tr: But this topic of virtues and vices. He had returned to the matter of praise and blame, and had added its treatment, and had mentioned virtue, which is the greatest material of praise, just as vices are of blame. Now he takes up the division of the virtues, whose kinds he sets out as if described in a table. And he rightly says that this topic extends very widely.

units.la: Sed hic locus uirtutum atq; uitiorum.) Ad laudis & uituperationis materiem redierat, & eius tractationem subijcerat. dem dicit, locū hunc latißime patēre. Nā tertiā philosophiæ partem, quæ à Græcis ἠθικὴ, à nobis Moralis appellari potest, cōplectitur: in quā præclara philosophorum ingenia, à Socrate primùm defudarunt, & eam uarijs copiosisq; disputationibus explicarunt. Sed noster Cicero, qui & ipse uarijs in libris, præsertim uerò de Ossicijs, oratorio more copiosè tractauit: nunc quasi honorarius arbiter, eam in hæc pauca, in quæ intuεatur orator, capita conclusit.
units.tr: But this topic of virtues and vices. He had returned to the matter of praise and blame, and had added its treatment. And he rightly says that this topic extends very widely. For it embraces the third part of philosophy, which the Greeks call ēthikē and which we may call moral: in this part the brilliant minds of the philosophers, beginning with Socrates, toiled, and explained it in various and copious discussions. But our Cicero, who himself treated it copiously in various books, especially in De Officiis, in the manner of an orator, now as it were acting as an honorary arbiter, has condensed it into these few headings, on which the orator should fix his attention.

units.la: Est igitur uis uirtutis duplex: aut enim scientia cernitur uirtus, aut actione. Nam quæ prudētia, quæ calliditas, quæq; grauissimo nomine sapientia appellatur, hæc scientia poslet una. quæ uerò moderandis cupiditatibus, regendisq; animi motib. laudatur, eius est munus in agendo, cui temperantiæ nomen est. Atq; illa prudentia in suis reb. domestica, in publicis ciuilis appellari solet. Tēperātia autē in suas itidē res, & in cōmunes distributa est, duobusq; modis in rebus cōmodis discernitur: & ea quæ absunt, non expetendo:
units.tr: There is therefore a twofold power of virtue: for virtue is discerned either by knowledge or by action. For prudence, cunning, and what is called by the weightiest name, wisdom, these belong to knowledge alone. But that which is praised for moderating desires and governing the movements of the mind has its office in acting, and it bears the name of temperance. Prudence, in its own affairs, is commonly called domestic, and in public affairs civil. Temperance too is distributed into its own affairs and common affairs, and in pleasant circumstances it is distinguished in two ways: by not desiring what is absent, and

units.la: ab iis quæ in potestate sunt abstinendo. In rebus autem incommodis est itidem duplex. nam quæ uenientibus malis obstat fortitudo, quæ quod iam adest, tolerat, & perfert, patientia nominatur. Quæ autem hæc uno genere complectitur, magnitudo animi dicitur: cuius est liberalitas in usu pecuniæ, simulque altitudo animi in capiendis incommodis, & maxime iniuriis, & omne quod est eius generis, graue, infesta tum, & turbulentum. In commune autem quæ posita pars est, iustitia dicitur: eaque erga deos religio, erga parentes pietas, uulgo autem bonitas, creditis in rebus fides, in moderatione animaduertendi lenitas, amicitia in benevolentia nominatur. Atque hæ quidem uirtutes cernuntur in agendo.
units.tr: by abstaining from what is within our power. In unpleasant circumstances too there is a twofold division. For fortitude, which withstands impending evils, and patience, which endures and bears what is already present, are so named. What embraces both under one genus is called greatness of mind: to it belong liberality in the use of money, and at the same time loftiness of mind in bearing misfortunes, and above all injuries, and everything of that kind that is grave, hostile, and troublesome. The part placed in common is called justice: toward the gods it is religion, toward parents piety, commonly goodness; in trusted matters it is fidelity, in the moderation of punishment gentleness, and in goodwill it is called friendship. And these virtues are discerned in action.

units.la: Est igitur uis uirtutis duplex. ) Discedit aliquo modo à consuetudine loquendi philosophorum, cum uim uirtutis duplicem esse dicit (nam illi, non uirtutis, sed animi dicerent) aliam intelligendi, ligendi, aliam uero appetendi. & in priore scientiam: in posteriore, in qua uoluntas inest, actionum domina ac regina, uim agendi collocarent. Sed Cicero quæstiones propositas respexit, & ad eas uirtutis partitionem proxime accommodauit. Est autem uirtus, animi habitus, naturæ modo rationi consentaneus: quæ tametsi à scientia differt (scientia enim cognitione contenta est, uir-tus uero actione cernitur) tamen scientiam Cicero uirtuti tanquam animi cuiusdam facultati siue affectioni subiectam, singulariter implicuit.
units.tr: There is therefore a twofold power of virtue. He departs in some way from the usual manner of speaking of the philosophers when he says that the power of virtue is twofold (for they would speak not of virtue but of the soul): one power is of understanding, the other of desire. In the former they would place knowledge; in the latter, in which the will resides, the mistress and queen of actions, the power of acting. But Cicero looked to the questions proposed, and closely adapted the division of virtue to them. Virtue is a habit of the mind, in accordance with reason, after the manner of nature. Although it differs from knowledge (for knowledge is content with cognition, while virtue is discerned in action), nevertheless Cicero singularly included knowledge within virtue, as subject to it, like a certain faculty or affection of the mind.

units.la: Nam quæ prudentia.) Prudentia est rerum bonarum & malarum scientia. Scientia autem, siue intelligentia est, per quam ea perspicimus, quæ sunt necessaria: uel est opinio, de eo quod scientia continetur. Calliditas est scientia, occulte subiens, cum aliqua honesta atque utili dis-simulatione. Est etiam alia calliditas uitiosa, de qua postea. Sapientia, est rerum diuinarum & humanarum scientia. Ad prudentiam pertinet domestica disciplina, & ciuilis, quæ Politica nominatur. Sub calliditate continentur uafrè dicta, & callidè facta, quæ Stratagemata in re militari dicuntur. Sapientiæ autem, Theologia, & humanæ artes: cuiusmodi sunt, Dialectica, Rhetorica, Geometria. Temperantia est, rationis in libidinem, atque in alios non rectos impetus
units.tr: Prudence is the knowledge of good and evil things. Knowledge, or understanding, is that through which we perceive those things which are necessary; or it is opinion concerning that which knowledge contains. Cunning is knowledge creeping in covertly, together with some honest and useful dissimulation. There is also another, vicious kind of cunning, about which we shall speak later. Wisdom is knowledge of divine and human things. To prudence belong domestic discipline and civil discipline, which is called politics. Under cunning are contained witty sayings and cleverly done deeds, which in military matters are called stratagems. To wisdom belong theology and the human arts, such as dialectic, rhetoric, and geometry. Temperance is reason's restraint of lust and of other improper impulses,

units.la: abijs quæ in potestate sunt absti-nendo. In rebus autem incommodis est itidem duplex. nam quæ uenientibus malis obstat fortitudo, quæ quod iam adest, tolerat, & perfert, patientia nominatur. Quæ autem hæc uno genere complectitur, magnitudo animi dicitur: cuius est liberalitas in usu pecuniæ, simulq; altitudo animi in capiendis incommodis, & maxime iniurijs, & omne quod est eius generis, graue, infedatum, & turbulentum. In commune autem quæ posita pars est, iusticia dicitur: eaq; erga deos religio, erga parentes pietas, uulgò autem bonitas, creditis in rebus fides, in moderatione animaduertendi lenitas, amicitia in beneuolētia nominatur. Atq; hæ quidem uirtutes cernuntur in agendo.
units.tr: by abstaining from what is within our power. In unpleasant circumstances too there is a twofold division. For fortitude, which withstands impending evils, and patience, which endures and bears what is already present, are so named. What embraces both under one genus is called greatness of mind: to it belong liberality in the use of money, and at the same time loftiness of mind in bearing misfortunes, and above all injuries, and everything of that kind that is grave, hostile, and troublesome. The part placed in common is called justice: toward the gods it is religion, toward parents piety, commonly goodness; in trusted matters it is fidelity, in the moderation of punishment gentleness, and in goodwill it is called friendship. And these virtues are discerned in action.

units.la: Est igitur uis uirtutis duplex. ) Discedit aliquo modo à consuetudine loquendi philosophorum, cum uim uirtutis duplicem esse dicit (nam illi, non uirtutis, sed animi dicerent) aliam intelligendi,aliam uerò appetendi. & in priore scientiam:in posteriore, in qua voluntas inest, actionum domina ac regina, uim agendi collocarent. Sed Cicero quæstiones propositas respexit,& ad eas uirtutis partitionem proxime accommodauit. Est autem uirtus,animi habitus, naturæ modo rationi consentaneus: quæ tametsi à scientia differt (scientia enim cognitione contēta est,uirtus uerò actione cernitur) tamen scientiam Cicero uirtuti tanquam animi cuiusdam facultati siue affectioni subiectam, singulariter implicuit.
units.tr: There is therefore a twofold power of virtue. He departs in some way from the usual manner of speaking of the philosophers when he says that the power of virtue is twofold (for they would speak not of virtue but of the soul): one power is of understanding, the other of desire. In the former they would place knowledge; in the latter, in which the will resides, the mistress and queen of actions, the power of acting. But Cicero looked to the questions proposed, and closely adapted the division of virtue to them. Virtue is a habit of the mind, in accordance with reason, after the manner of nature. Although it differs from knowledge (for knowledge is content with cognition, while virtue is discerned in action), nevertheless Cicero singularly included knowledge within virtue, as subject to it, like a certain faculty or affection of the mind.

units.la: Nam quæ prudentia.) Prudentia est rerũ bonarum & malarum scientia. Scientia autem, si- ue intelligentia est, per quam ea perspicimus, quæ sunt necessaria: uel est opinio, de eo quod scientia continctur. Calliditas est scientia, occulte subiens,cum aliqua honesta atque utili dissimulatione. Est etiam alia calliditas uitiosa, de qua postea. Sapientia, est rerum diuinarum & humanarum scientia. Ad prudentiam pertinet domestica disciplina, & ciuilis, quæ Politica nominatur. Sub calliditate continentur uastè di&ta, & callidè facta,quæ Stratagemata in re militari dicuntur. Sapientiæ autem,Theologia, & humanæ artes: cuiusmodi sunt,Dialectica,Rhetorica, Geometria. Temperantia est, rationis in libidinem, atque in alios non rectos impetus animi firma & moderata dominatio: ea actione & uoluntate continetur. Voluntas est boni cupiditas, siue appetitio. Temperantia, frugalitas quoque & moderatio nominatur. haec duas habet partes: animi magnitudinem, quae μεγαλοψυχία dicitur, & iusticiam. Illa in suis rebus, haec in communibus cernitur. Sub animi magnitudinem subijciuntur haec: Continentia, quae ἐγκράτεια: abstinentia, quae ἀπόχεσις: liberalitas & altitudo animi, quam εὐψυχίαν Graeci uocant. Animi magnitudo, est rerum magnarum & excelsarum, cum animi ampla quadam & splendida propositione, agitatio, atq; administratio. Continentia, est animi magnitudo, in ijs quae absunt non expetendis: uel, per quam cupiditas consilij gubernatione regitur. Abstinentia, est magnitudo animi, ab ijs quae in potestate sunt, abstinere suadens: quemadmodum dixit elegantèr Helena Ouidiana,
units.tr: Take prudence first. Prudence is the knowledge of good and evil things. Knowledge, or understanding, is that by which we perceive the things that are necessary; or it is opinion, concerning what is contained in knowledge. Cunning is a knowledge that creeps in covertly, joined with some honest and useful dissimulation. There is also another, vicious kind of cunning, which I will discuss later. Wisdom is the knowledge of divine and human things. Domestic and civil discipline, which is called Politics, belong to prudence. Under cunning are included deeds done with a show of boldness and acts done craftily, which in military affairs are called stratagems. Under wisdom are theology and the human arts, such as dialectic, rhetoric and geometry. Temperance is the firm and moderate mastery of reason over desire, and over the other unruly impulses of the mind; it is contained in action and will. Will is the desire, or appetite, for the good. Temperance is also called frugality and moderation. It has two parts: greatness of spirit, which is called megalopsychia [μεγαλοψυχία], and justice. The former is seen in one's own affairs, the latter in common affairs. Under greatness of spirit are these: self-control, which is enkrateia [ἐγκράτεια]; abstinence, which is apochesis [ἀπόχεσις]; liberality; and loftiness of spirit, which the Greeks call eupsychia [εὐψυχίαν]. Greatness of spirit is the active pursuit and management of great and lofty affairs, with a certain ample and splendid purpose of mind. Self-control is greatness of spirit in not seeking those things that are absent; or it is that by which desire is governed by the guidance of counsel. Abstinence is greatness of spirit, urging us to hold back from those things that are within our power; just as Ovid's Helen elegantly said:

units.la: Virtus est placitis abstinuisse bonis.
units.tr: Virtue is to have abstained from pleasing goods.

units.la: Continentia & abstinentia interdum idem sunt, quemadmodum apud Aristotelē in Ethicis, qui ait, continentiam impotentiae contrariam esse: neq; unam aliquam seperatam uirtutem, sed per omnes uirtutes fusam. Interdum uero continentia in pecunijs cernitur, abstinentia in uoluptatibus. Sed hic Cicero eas tempore inter se distinguens stinguit, siue loco: ut continentia sit absentium rerum, abstinentia præsentium. Sequitur libera litas, quæ, ut Plato ait, in quærendis erogandisq; pecunijs decorum seruat: uel, ut Aristoteles, in dandis accipiendisque pecunijs mediocritas, liberalitas dicitur. Altitudo animi, est afsectio in capiendis incommodis, & maximè iniurijs, siue imminentibus, siue præsentibus. Verum quæ ucnientibus aut imminentibus malis obstat, fortitudo dicitur: quæ uero præsentia tolerat, & perfert, patientia siue tolerantia. Definiunt autem fortitudinem, quam ἀνδρείαν vocant Græci, consideratam periculorum suscep-tionem, & laborum perpessionem, propter honestatem. Patientiam uero, honestatis aut utilitatis caussa rerum arduarum ac difficilium, uoluntariam ac diuturnam perpessionem. Alteram temperantiæ partem, iustitiā appellauimus. ea definitur, habitus animi, communi utilitate conseruata, suam cuique tribuens dignitatem. Hæc habet sex partes, Religionem, quæ θρησκείαν: pietatem, quæ ὁσιότητα: bonitatem, quæ χρηστότης Græce dicitur: & fidem, & lenitatem, & amicitiam. Religio est, quæ superioris cuiusdam naturæ, quam diuinam uocant, debitam & propriam curam, cærimoniamq; affert. Pietas, per quā sanguine coniunctis, patriæq; beneuolis officium cium & diligens tribuitur cultus. Bonitas, assectio quaedam animi est, quae sunt optima eligendi, & legibus omnibus libenter obtemperandi. Fides, est dictorum factorumq; constantia & veritas. Lenitas, in animaduertendo & puniendo moderatio: hanc Ariftoteles ἐπιείκειαν, καὶ πραότητα uocat: nos communi nomine æquitatem & lenitatem, & cum Cicerone etiam lenitudinem appellamus. Amicitia uoluntas erga aliquem, uel aliquos, rerum bonarum, illorum ipsorum caussa quos diligimus, cum pari uoluntate.
units.tr: Self-control and abstinence are sometimes the same, as in Aristotle's Ethics, where he says that self-control is the opposite of incontinence, and is not one separate virtue but spread through all the virtues. Sometimes, however, self-control is seen in money, and abstinence in pleasures. But here Cicero distinguishes them by time or place: self-control concerns absent things, abstinence present things. Next comes liberality, which, as Plato says, observes propriety in seeking and spending money; or, as Aristotle says, liberality is the mean in giving and receiving money. Loftiness of spirit is a disposition in bearing misfortunes, and especially injuries, whether impending or present. Indeed, that which opposes evils that are coming or impending is called fortitude; that which endures and bears those that are present is called patience or endurance. They define fortitude, which the Greeks call andreia [ἀνδρείαν], as the deliberate undertaking of dangers and the enduring of toils for the sake of honour; and patience as the voluntary and lasting endurance of difficult and arduous things for the sake of honour or usefulness. We have called the other part of temperance justice. It is defined as a disposition of mind that, preserving the common advantage, gives each person his due dignity. It has six parts: religion, which is threskeia [θρησκείαν]; piety, which is hosiotes [ὁσιότητα]; goodness, which in Greek is chrestotes [χρηστότης]; and faith, gentleness and friendship. Religion is the due and proper care and ceremonial service owed to a certain superior nature, which they call divine. Piety is the diligent service rendered to those joined by blood and to the well-disposed of one's country. Goodness is a certain disposition of mind, to choose what is best and to obey all laws willingly. Faith is the constancy and truthfulness of words and deeds. Gentleness is moderation in punishing and in exacting penalties; Aristotle calls this epieikeia and praotes [ἐπιείκειαν, καὶ πραότητα]; we call it by the common name equity and gentleness, and, with Cicero, also leniency. Friendship is the willingness toward someone, or some people, to bestow good things for the sake of those whom we love, with equal goodwill in return.

units.la: Sunt autem aliae quasi ministrae.) Sapientiae explicat partes: eas que facit, Grammaticam, Dialecticam, Rhetoricam, Arithmeticam, Musicam, Geometriam, Astronomiam: & quae paululum ab ijs deflectunt, ut sunt, ars equestris, venatio, & ars militaris. Cur autem eae ministrae, comitesq; sapientiae dicantur, docet Ariftoteles Top.1. qui cum duo genera quaestionum fecisset, actionis & cognitionis, tertium quaestionis genus addidit, adiumentum afferens reliquis duobus. Multa enim sunt (inquit) quae per fe ad cognoscendum nos non mouent, nisi aliorum causfa, ut per ea alia discamus. Ministrae igitur sunt, id est organa & instrumenta sapientiae & veritatis inuestigandae: Dialectica praesertim, ac RheRhetorica.comites vero,quoniam sapientia antecedit: & potior cura rerum esse debet, deinde orationis & sermonis. Et hic est ordo naturæ. Verùm in docendo, prior cura est orationis, deinde rerum. Rationem reddit Aristoteles in Ethicis,quoniam adolescentes per ætatem & cupiditates nondum idonei sunt discipuli sapientiæ. Interea tamen comitibus istis sese adiungunt, & bonis artibus quasi præcoluntur, ut idonei reddantur ad sapientiæ commercium. Virtus omnis cernitur, ante Cognitione, uel scientia, sub qua est Prudentia Domestica Civilis. Callidi tas Sapientia rerum Vafre dicta Stratagemata. Divinarum Humanarum Grammatica Dialectica Rhetorica Geometria Arithmetica Musica Astronomia Venatio Equestris res Ars militaris. Actione, cuius est temperantia seu frugalitas, seu moderatio, sub qua Animi magnitudo in suis rebus, cuius est Continentia Abstinentia Liberalitas Altitudo animi. Fortitudo Patientia. Iustitia, in rebus communibus: aut Religione Pietate Bonitate Fide Lenitate Amicitia.
units.tr: Other arts, as it were handmaids, etc. This sets out the parts of wisdom: these are grammar, dialectic, rhetoric, arithmetic, music, geometry and astronomy; and those which turn somewhat aside from them, such as horsemanship, hunting and the military art. Aristotle, in the Topics book 1, explains why these are called handmaids and companions of wisdom. Having made two kinds of questions, of action and of knowledge, he added a third kind, of inquiry, which supplies help to the other two. For many things (he says) do not move us to know them in themselves, but only for the sake of others, so that through them we may learn other things. They are therefore handmaids, that is, the instruments and tools for investigating wisdom and truth, dialectic and rhetoric especially. They are companions, however, since wisdom comes first, and the greater care should be for things, and then for speech and discourse. This is the order of nature. But in teaching, the care for speech comes first, then for things. Aristotle gives the reason in the Ethics: young people, because of their age and desires, are not yet fit pupils of wisdom. Meanwhile, however, they attach themselves to these companions and are, as it were, prepared in the good arts, so that they may be made fit for dealings with wisdom. All virtue is seen before knowledge or science, under which lie domestic and civil prudence; cunning, the wisdom of things spoken craftily, the stratagems; of divine and human things, grammar, dialectic, rhetoric, geometry, arithmetic, music, astronomy, hunting, horsemanship and the military art. In action, of which temperance is the business, whether frugality or moderation, under which greatness of spirit in one's own affairs, of which self-control, abstinence, liberality and loftiness of spirit are the parts; fortitude and patience. Justice, in common affairs, or by religion, piety, goodness, faith, gentleness and friendship.

units.la: DE ARTIBVS LIBERALIBVS.
units.tr: ON THE LIBERAL ARTS.

units.la: Sunt autem aliæ quasi ministræ, comitesq; sapientiæ: quarum altera, quæ sint in disputando vera atq; falsa, quibusq; positis, quid sequatur, distinguit, & iudicat, quæ virtus omnis in ratione, scientiaq; disputandi sita est. altera autem oratoria. nihil enim est aliud eloquentia. tia, nisi copiose loquens sapientia, quæ ex eodem hausta genere, quo illa, quæ in disputando, uberior est, atq; latior, & ad motus animorum, uulgiq; sensus accommodatior.
units.tr: There are also other arts, as it were handmaids and companions of wisdom. One of them distinguishes what is true and false in disputation, and what follows from given premises, and passes judgment on these matters. All this skill lies in the reason and science of disputing. The other is oratory, for eloquence is nothing but wisdom speaking copiously. Drawn from the same kind of source as the art of disputing, it is richer and broader, and better suited to moving the minds of men and the feelings of the crowd.

units.la: Sunt & aliæ.) Quæ sint in disputando vera atq; falsa.) Dialectica à Rhetorica distinguit: & dialectica appellat disputandi scientiā, Rhetoricam verò, copiosè loquendi sapientiā. Posset autē aliquis mirari, quòd prius comites sapientiæ appellarit, nunc verò sapientiā Oratoriam rationem appellet. Sed sciat, idcirco id fieri, quoniam species nomen generis retinet. Deinde respicit Stoicorum sententiā, qui hasce artes atq; adeò ipsam eloquentiā & virtutē et sapientiā esse voluerūt, nimirū ex rebus ipsis, nō ex oratione sola eloquētiā æstimates: quā de re copiosè disputat Cic. de Orat. lib. 3. Nā ut idē in Oratore dicit: Eloquētiæ, sicut reliquarū rerū, fundamētū sapiētia est.
units.tr: "And there are others." "What is true and false in disputing." Dialectic is distinguished from rhetoric: dialectic is the science of disputing, while rhetoric is the wisdom of speaking copiously. Someone might wonder why Cicero earlier called these the companions of wisdom, and now calls the art of oratory wisdom. But let him know that this happens because the species keeps the name of the genus. Next, he has regard to the opinion of the Stoics, who wanted these arts, and indeed eloquence itself, to be virtue and wisdom. They judged eloquence not from speech alone but from the things themselves. Cicero discusses this at length in De Oratore, book 3, for as he says in the Orator: wisdom is the foundation of eloquence, as it is of all other things.

units.la: Quæ ex eodē hausta genere.) Dicit eloquentiam sub eodē genere cōtineri, quo disputādi ratiōnem. id quod in Oratore præclarè ostēdit his uerbis: Esse igitur perfectè eloquentis puto, non eam solū facultatē habere, quæ sit eius propria, fuse latéq; dicendi: sed etiā uicinā eius atq; finitimam Dialecticorū scientiā assumere. quanquam aliud uidetur oratio esse, aliud disputatio: neq; idem loqui esse, quod dicere: attamen utrunq; in differendo est, ut disputandi ratio & loquendi Dialecticorum fit, Oratorum autem dicedi & ornandi. quibus uerbis differere genus facit, ad disputandum & dicendum, loquendum & ornandum. Ergo Dialectica genus est rationis disputandi & dicendi.
units.tr: "Drawn from the same kind of source." He says that eloquence is contained under the same genus as the method of disputing. He shows this clearly in the Orator in these words: "I think, then, that a man who is perfectly eloquent should not only possess that faculty which is peculiar to him, of speaking fully and broadly, but should also take up the science of the Dialecticians, which is close and neighbouring to it. Although speech seems one thing and disputation another, and to speak is not the same as to discourse, yet both consist in arguing: the method of disputing and speaking belongs to the Dialecticians, but that of discoursing and embellishing to the Orators." By these words he makes the genus cover both disputing and discoursing, speaking and embellishing. Therefore dialectic is a kind of reasoning in disputing and discoursing.

units.la: Vberior est, atq; latior.) Aliud discrimen inter Dialectica & Rhetoricam: hæc uberior & latior est, illa angustior & breuior: illa uera atque falsa distinguit, quid ex quaque re posita sequatur indicat: hæc ad motus animorum uulgiq; sensus, id est, ad persuadendum, omnia trahit & accommodat. Atq; etiā Aristoteles principio artis Rhetoricæ dicit, illam artem quasi ex altera parte respondere Dialecticæ. ut hoc uidelicet differant inter se, quod hæc ratio dicendi latior fit, illa loquendi contractior. Ac post Aristotelē Zenone, à quo disciplina Stoicorum est, manu demonstrare solebat, quid inter has artes interesset. Nam cum comprehissiset digitos, pugnumq; fecerat, Dialecticam aiebat eiusmodi esse: cum autem diduxerat, & manum dilatauerat, palmæ illius similem eloquentiam esse dicebat.
units.tr: "Richer and broader." This is another difference between dialectic and rhetoric: the latter is richer and broader, the former narrower and briefer. The one distinguishes true from false and shows what follows from any given premise; the other draws and adapts everything to the emotions of minds and the feelings of the crowd, that is, to persuasion. Aristotle also says at the beginning of his Rhetoric that this art corresponds, as it were, to dialectic from the other side, so that they differ in this: the method of discoursing becomes broader, that of speaking more compressed. After Aristotle, Zeno, from whom the Stoic school takes its origin, used to demonstrate by hand what separated these arts. When he had closed his fingers and made a fist, he said that dialectic was of this kind; when he had opened them out and spread his hand, he said that eloquence was like the palm of that hand.

units.la: Custos uero uirtutum omnium, dedecus fugiēs, laudemq; maximè, consequens uerecundia est,
units.tr: The guardian of all the virtues, which shuns disgrace and most of all pursues praise, is modesty.

units.la: Custos uero uirtutum.) Verecundiam custodem omnium uirtutum appellat. Puto tamen illum, decorū uerecundiæ nomine intelligere. Nā & de Offic. lib.1. Iusticiæ (inquit) partes sunt, non violare homines: Verecundiæ, non offendere.in quo maximè perspicitur uis decori, quod quidem in hunc modum eodem loco uidetur definire,ut decorum illud esse dicamus, quod elucet in uita,mouetq; approbationem eorum quibus cum uiuitur, ordine & constantia & moderatione dictorum omnium atq; factorum. & ut uenustas & pulchritudo corporis seceraini non potest à ualetudine: sic hoc de quo loquimur decorum, totum quidem illud est cum uirtute consusum, sed mente & cogitatione distinguitur. Ex his uerbis apparet,non esse unam aliquam separatam uirtutem uerecundiam, sed cum reliquis omnibus uirtutibus coniunctam, quæ etiam pudoris & modestiæ nomine appellatur,sicq; definitur de Inuentione lib.2.Modestia est,per quam pudor honestus claram & stabilem comparat autoritatem. Pudor autē, est metus quidam dedecoris & infamiæ. Aristoteles Ethicorum 4. Quæ definitiones singulæ bene cū hoc Ciceronis loco quadrāt. Græcè autem ναοµότης hæc uirtus appellari potest, itemq; πρέπον, quod proprie nobis decorum dicitur.
units.tr: "The guardian of the virtues." He calls modesty the guardian of all the virtues. I think, however, that he means by the name of modesty what is becoming. For in & De Officiis book 1 he says: "The duties of justice are not to harm men; those of modesty, not to give offence." In this the force of what is becoming is most clearly seen. In the same place he seems to define it in this way: we may call that becoming which shines forth in life and wins the approval of those among whom we live, through the order, consistency and moderation of all that we say and do. And just as grace and beauty of body cannot be separated from good health, so this decorum of which we speak is wholly blended with virtue, yet is distinguished by the mind and thought. From these words it is clear that modesty is not one separate virtue, but is joined with all the other virtues. It is also called by the name of shamefastness and moderation, and is defined thus in the De Inventione, book 2: "Modesty is that through which honourable shame gains a clear and stable authority. Shame is a certain fear of disgrace and infamy." Aristotle, Ethics book 4, agrees. Each of these definitions fits well with this passage of Cicero. In Greek this virtue can be called modesty [αἰδημοσύνη], and likewise [πρέπον], which we properly call decorum.

units.la: Atque hi sunt quidem fere quasi quidam habitus animi sic affecti & constituti, ut sint singuli inter se proprio uirtutis genere distincti, à quibus, ut quaeq; res gesta est, ita fit honesta necesse est, summe{que} laudabilis.
units.tr: These, then, are almost like certain habits of mind, so disposed and constituted that each is distinct from the others by its own kind of virtue. From each of them, as each deed is done, it necessarily becomes honourable and most praiseworthy.

units.la: Atq; hi sunt quidem. ) Concludit, uirtutes omnes, quas enumerauit, habitus esse animi. Est autem habitus animi aut corporis, constans & absoluta aliqua in re perfectio: ut uirtutis aut artis perceptio alicuius, aut cuiusuis scientiae, itemq; corporis aliqua commoditas, non natura data, sed studio & industria comparata. Sic enim de habitu Aristoteles & Cicero sentiunt. Quod autem dicit, Fere, significat se non subtiliter, sed pingui Minerua, uirtutes descripsisse. & quod dicit, Quasi quidam habitus, non negat habitus esse: sed illud uult, eas uirtutes laudandas esse, etiamsi non perfectae in aliquo sint, sed uirtutum imagines tantum.
units.tr: "And these are indeed..." He concludes that all the virtues he has listed are habits of the mind. A habit of mind or body is a settled and complete perfection in some matter, such as the grasp of a virtue or an art, or of any science, and likewise a bodily fitness not given by nature but acquired by zeal and effort. This is how Aristotle and Cicero understand a habit. When he says "almost," he signals that he has described the virtues not with fine subtlety but with a rough hand. And when he says "as it were certain habits," he does not deny that they are habits, but means that these virtues are to be praised even if they are not perfect in anyone, and are only images of virtues.

units.la: Sic affecti & constituti.) Quod inepti dicunt, dispositi. Intelligit autem hos habitus sic esse comparatos, ut proprietate quadam inter se distinguantur, & communitate coniungantur. Nam alia est prudentiae, alia iustitiae, itemq; aliarum rum proprietas & quasi subiecta materies, ut ex singularum definitionibus cognosci potest. Illud tamen commune omnes habent tanquam uinculum, quod honestate continentur: ex quo sequitur, etiam laudabiles esse. Nam honestum, quod Graeci καλὸν dicũt, id est, quod cum per se sit expetendum, est etiam laudabile, ut Aristoteles & Cicero definiuerunt. Sunt igitur quatuor, quae in singulis uirtutib. inueniũtur, quod sunt habitus: quod proprietate distinguũtur, quod honestae sint, quod laudabiles, & expetendae.
units.tr: "So disposed and constituted." Where foolish people write "dispositi," he means that these habits are so composed that they are distinguished from one another by a certain particular property, and joined by a common bond. For prudence has one property, justice another, and so on for the rest; their properties and, as it were, their underlying matter can be known from the definitions of each. Yet all have this in common, like a chain: they are held together by honour. From this it follows that they are also praiseworthy. For the honourable, which the Greeks call [καλὸν], that is, what is to be sought for its own sake, is also praiseworthy, as Aristotle and Cicero defined it. So there are four things found in each of the virtues: they are habits; they are distinguished by their property; they are honourable; and they are praiseworthy and to be sought.

units.la: Sunt autem alij quidam perfecti animi habitus ad uirtutē, quasi preculti & praeparati rectis studijs, & artibus: ut in suis rebus, studia literarum, ut numerorum ac sonorum, ut mensurae, ut siderum, ut equorum, ut uenandi, ut armorum: in communibus, propensiora studia in aliquo genere uirtutis colendo, aut diuinis rebus deseruiendo, aut parentibus, amicis, hospitibus praecipue atq; insigniter diligendis. Atq; haec quidem uirtutum, uitiorum autem sunt genera contraria,
units.tr: "There are also certain other habits of a perfected mind, toward virtue, as it were pre-cultivated and prepared by upright pursuits and arts: in their own matters, the study of letters, of numbers and sounds, of measurement, of the stars, of horses, of hunting, of arms; in common matters, the leaning of one's zeal toward cultivating some kind of virtue, or serving divine things, or especially and remarkably loving parents, friends and guests. These are the habits of virtue; the kinds of vice are contrary to them."

units.la: Sunt autem alij. ) Alios dicit habitus esse artium, alios uirtutum: & hi habitus quos hic enumerat, ad sapientiam & prudentiam referendi sunt. Enumerat autem breuiter hic Cicero reliquas liberales artes, quoniam dialecticae tantum & Rhetoricae mentionem fecerat, in ministris comitibusq; sapientiae: utiturq; ratione ea diuidedi, quae usus est supra: ut hi habitus partim sint in suis rebus, alij in communibus. In suis rebus, sunt studia literarum, id est Grammaticae: nam fere Cicero literarum nomine Grammaticam intelligit. item numerorum, hoc est Arithmeticae: sonorum, id est Musicae: mensurae, id est Geometriae: siderum, id est Astronomiae, siue astrologiae: equorum, id est equitandi: venandi, quae complectitur omnia venationum & aucupiorum genera: armorum, id est rei militaris, & tractandorum armorum scientia. Ex subiectis enim rebus singularum, artes ipsas significauit.
units.tr: "There are also others." He says that some habits belong to the arts and others to the virtues, and that the habits he lists here are to be referred to wisdom and prudence. Here Cicero briefly lists the other liberal arts, since he had mentioned only dialectic and rhetoric, the ministers and companions of wisdom. He uses the same method of division as above, so that these habits are partly in their own matters and partly in common ones. In their own matters are the studies of letters, that is, grammar, for Cicero generally understands grammar by the name of letters; likewise of numbers, that is, arithmetic; of sounds, that is, music; of measurement, that is, geometry; of the stars, that is, astronomy or astrology; of horses, that is, horsemanship; of hunting, which embraces all the kinds of hunting and fowling; of arms, that is, the science of warfare and of handling weapons. For he has named the arts themselves from the subject matter of each.

units.la: Perfecti animi habitus. ) Intelligit non tam perfectos habitus, quam animorum perfectorum. Nam in quib. hae sunt artes, perfecti animi sunt, & doctrinis absoluti.
units.tr: "Of a perfected mind." He means not so much perfect habits as the habits of perfected minds. For in those in whom these arts are present, the minds are perfected and complete in learning.

units.la: Ad uirtutem. ) Quibus uirtus ipsa ornatur. Exornatur enim & splendescit artium cognitione uirtus. atq; etiā illis artib. praeculti & praeparati animi, faciliorem ad uirtutē inueniūt uiā. In communibus propensiora studia.) Haec sunt, quae diximus in commune conferri: utpote iustitiae officia & munera, quae omnia ad alios referuntur: ut religio ad Deum, & ad res divinas publice tractandas: Pietas ad parentes, & amicos amandos & colendos: hospitalitas, ad hospites accipiendos, humaniterq; tractandos. Ergo prout quisq; erit aliquo genere virtutis aut artis ornatus, ita ex eo laudandus erit: & contrà, ex propriis vitijs vituperādus. Nam enumeratis virtutibus, vitiorum genera contraria intelligenda sunt. Quomodo autem haec singula sint tractanda, praeclarè docet Cicero, secundo de Oratore libro, in demonstratiui generis doctrina.
units.tr: "To virtue": these are the things by which virtue itself is adorned. For virtue is embellished and made to shine by knowledge of the arts, and minds already cultivated and prepared in those arts find an easier path to virtue. "In common, more inclined studies": these are the things we said are conferred on the common good, namely the duties and offices of justice, all of which are directed toward others: such as religion toward God and the public handling of divine matters; piety toward parents, and toward loving and cherishing friends; hospitality, toward receiving guests and treating them kindly. Therefore, in proportion as each person is adorned with some kind of virtue or skill, so he is to be praised for it, and conversely, blamed for his own vices. For once the virtues are listed, the contrary kinds of vice are to be understood. How each of these is to be treated, Cicero teaches admirably in the second book of De Oratore, in the doctrine of the demonstrative genus.

units.la: DE VITIIS, VIRTVTIBUS OPPOSITIS.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE VICES OPPOSED TO THE VIRTUES

units.la: Cernenda autem sunt diligenter, ne fallant ea nos vitia, quae virtutem videntur imitari.
units.tr: These must be carefully discerned, lest those vices deceive us which seem to imitate virtue.

units.la: Cernenda autem sunt diligenter, ne fallant.)
units.tr: These must be carefully discerned, lest they deceive us.

units.la: Virtus inter duo extrema mediocritas est, extrema omnia viciosa. Verum alterum apertè vicium est, facileq; cernitur: ut cum imprudentia prudentiae, stultitia sapientiae, temperantiae intemperantia, fortitudini ignavia, liberalitati avaritia, iustitiae iniustitia, pietati impietas, malitia bonitati, fidei perfidia, crudelitas lenitati, inimicitiæ amicitia, itemq; arti inscitia, & uirtuti uitiofitas contrario nomine opponitur. Verum quædam uitia sunt, quæ propinqua & finitima uirtutibus esse uidentur: absunt autem quàm longiffime, quemadmodum recte Horatius de uitijs ait, quæ nos fallát specie uirtutis & umbra. Nam ut inquit Ouidius,
units.tr: Virtue is the mean between two extremes, and both extremes are vicious. Of these, one is plainly a vice and is easily recognised: as imprudence is opposed to prudence, folly to wisdom, intemperance to temperance, cowardice to fortitude, avarice to liberality, injustice to justice, impiety to piety, malice to goodness, perfidy to faith, cruelty to gentleness, enmity to friendship; likewise ignorance is opposed to skill, and vicious conduct to virtue, under contrary names. But there are some vices which seem close and neighbouring to the virtues, though they are in fact as far removed as possible; just as Horace rightly says of vices that they deceive us with the appearance and shadow of virtue. For, as Ovid says:

units.la: Et mala sunt uicina bonis, errore sub illo
units.tr: And evils lie near to goods, and under that error

units.la: Pro uitio uirtus crimina sæpe tulit.
units.tr: Virtue has often borne the crimes of vice.

units.la: De his etiam Cato apud Sallustium in coniuratione Catilinæ. Iampridem equidem (inquit) nos uera rerum uocabula amisimus: quia bona aliena largiri, liberalitas: malarum rerum audacia, fortitudo uocatur. Sic unicuiq; uirtuti finitimum uitium reperitur, aut certo iam nomine appellatum, ut audacia, quæ fidentiæ: pertinacia, quæ perseucrantiæ finitima est: aut fine ullo certo nomine, quæ omnia, item uti contraria rerum bonarum, in rebus uitandis reponemus.
units.tr: Cato also says this of them, in Sallust's Conspiracy of Catiline: "For a long time now," he says, "we have lost the true names of things: for lavishing other people's goods is called liberality, and daring in wicked deeds is called courage. Thus each virtue has a neighbouring vice, either already known by a definite name, such as rashness, which is akin to confidence, or obstinacy, which is akin to perseverance; or else without any definite name. All of these, like the contraries of good things, we shall set out among the things to be avoided."

units.la: Nam & prudentiam malitia, & temperantiā immanitas in voluptatibus aspernandis, & magnitudinē animi superbia in animis extollendis, & despicientia in contemnēdis honoribus, & liberalitatem effusio,
units.tr: For malice imitates prudence, and severity in rejecting pleasures imitates temperance, and pride in exalting oneself imitates greatness of spirit, and contempt in despising honours imitates indifference, and extravagance imitates liberality,

units.la: & fortitudine audacia imitatur, & patientia durítia immanís, & iustitiam acerbitas, & religionem superstitio, & lenitatem mollítia animí, & uerecundiam timiditas, & illam disputandi prudentiã concertatio, captatioȩ uerborum, & hanc oratoríam uim ínanís quædam profluentía loquendi.
units.tr: and recklessness imitates fortitude, and harshness imitates endurance, and bitterness imitates justice, and superstition imitates religion, and softness of mind imitates gentleness, and timidity imitates modesty, and the contentiousness of argument imitates the prudence of disputing, and verbal trickery and empty fluency imitate that power of oratory.

units.la: Nam & prudentiã malitia.) Præclarè hic Cicero, quæ quamque uirtutem uidentur imitari, uitia enumerat: in quibus enumerandis ordinem suprapositum, & descriptionem uirtutum sequitur. Quod autem hic opponit prudentiæ maliciam, nimiam intelligit calliditatem: quoniam calliditatem ipsam supra in bonis numerauit. Hoc autem præclarum est, quòd fere nobis singula uitia ita breuiter describit, & tanquã definit. uelut cũ dicit, esse in uoluptatibus aspernãdis nimium studium: & superbiam, in animis extollendis affectionem: & despicientiam, in contemnendis honoribus, abiectionem quandam animi: & effusionem, opum pecuniarumq; immoderatum sumptum: & audaciã, fortitudinis exuperantiam: & duriciam, inanem & efferatam patientiam; & acerbitatem, ius quoddã summum, &
units.tr: "For malice imitates prudence": Cicero here admirably lists the vices which seem to imitate each virtue, and in listing them he follows the order laid down above and the description of the virtues. As for what he sets against prudence, namely malice, he means excessive cunning, since he has already counted cunning itself among the goods. It is also admirable that he briefly describes each vice almost as if defining it. Thus when he says that there is excessive zeal in rejecting pleasures; pride is an excessive exaltation of the mind; contempt, in despising honours, is a kind of abjection of spirit; extravagance is an immoderate expenditure of wealth and money; recklessness is an excess of courage; harshness is an empty and savage endurance; bitterness is a certain extreme right and

units.la: & et nimiam seueritatem: et superstitionem, religionis peruersum usum: et mollitiem animi, nimiam lenitatem: et timiditatem, nimiam verecundiam: et sophisticam concertationem, captationemque verborum, et falsam eloquentiam, inanem profluentiam loquendi.
units.tr: and excessive severity; superstition is a perverse use of religion; softness of mind is excessive gentleness; timidity is excessive modesty; and sophistical contentiousness and verbal trickery, together with false eloquence, are empty fluency in speaking.

units.la: Studijs autem bonis similia uidentur ea, quae sunt in eodem genere nimia. Quamobrem omnis uis laudandi, uituperandiq;, ex his sumetur uirtutum uitiorum'que partibus.
units.tr: Those excesses within the same class seem similar to good pursuits. Therefore all the power of praising and blaming will be drawn from these parts of the virtues and vices.

units.la: Studijs autem bonis.) Studia bona, bonarum artium sunt: sed in his etiam uitium est quoddam, quod speciem uirtutis potest fallere. Id autem est (ut Cicero de Offic. lib. 1.) cum quis nimis magnum studium, multamque operam in res obscuras atque difficiles confert, easdemque non necessarias. Sed hic dicat aliquis, ad quid conducit hæc uitiorum, quæ uirtutis speciem sibi uendicat, cognitio? Respondeo: Ad duo: primum, ne illorum ignoratione in errorem inducamur: deinde contra aduersarium, sua uitia uirtutum colore sucantem, aut nostras uirtutes uitiorum nominibus obruentem.
units.tr: Studious pursuits, however, are good. Good pursuits belong to the good arts, but even within them there is a certain vice which can deceive by the appearance of virtue. This is (as Cicero says in De Officiis, book 1) when someone devotes excessive zeal and much labour to obscure and difficult matters, and to things that are not necessary. But someone may say here: what is the use of knowing these vices, which claim the appearance of virtue? I answer: for two reasons. First, so that we are not led into error through ignorance of them; second, against an opponent who disguises his own vices with the colour of virtue, or overwhelms our virtues with the names of vices.

units.la: Quamobrem omnis uis laudandi.) Loci laudationum dationum & uituperationum duplices sunt: alij communes, cuiusmodi sunt Dialectici ac Rhetorici illi ampliores, tanquam genera reliquorum: alij sunt proprij Ethices, aut singularum artium. primum igitur & praecipuum locum ijs dat, qui proprij sunt: ut uirtutes & uitia, artes & inertiae.
units.tr: Therefore all the power of praising. The topics of praise and blame are twofold: some are common, such as those broader topics of the dialecticians and rhetoricians which serve as the genera of the rest; others are proper to ethics, or to individual arts. He therefore gives the first and chief place to those which are proper, such as virtues and vices, skills and failings.

units.la: Sed in toto quasi contextu orationis haec erunt illustrāda maximē, quemadmodum quisque generatus, quemadmodum educatus, quēadmodum institutus, moratusque fuerit. & si quid cui magnū, aut incredibile acciderit, maximeque si id diuinitus accidisse potuerit uideri, tum quod quisque senserit, dixerit, gesserit, ad ea quae propositā sunt uirtutum genera accommodabuntur, ex illisque ipsdem inueniendi locis causae rerū, & cuentus, & consequentia requirentur. neque uero mors eorū, quorū uita laudabitur, silentio praeteriri debebit: si modo quid erit animaduertendum, aut in ipso genere mortis, aut in ijs rebus quae post mortem erunt consecutae,
units.tr: But in the whole, as it were, texture of the speech, these things will be illustrated most of all: how each person was born, how he was brought up, how he was trained and what his character was. And if anything great or incredible has befallen someone, especially if it could seem to have happened by divine agency, then what he has felt, said, or done will be fitted to the kinds of virtue proposed, and from those same places of invention the causes of events, the outcomes, and the consequences will be sought. Nor should the death of those whose life is praised be passed over in silence, provided there is anything worth noting either in the very manner of death or in the things that followed it.

units.la: x Sed in toto quasi contextu orationis.) Hactenus generalia tradidit, & quae in infinita quaestione continentur: nunc autem, quomodo ex illis generibus & rebus universis ad personas traducendi & tractandi sint, docet: quod causae est, & definitae quaestionis. Ex quo perspicuum est, duo genera sententiarum ab Oratoribus in hoc genere esse tractanda: unum generale, de virtutibus & vitiis ipsis, sine ullo personarum complexu: alterum, temporibus & personis definitum. Ut cum de virtutibus Pompeij, & vitiis Catilinae dicunt, quae duo duabus ratiocinationis propositionibus respondent, maiori & minori. Exempli causa; si quis dicat, Laudabile semper fuit pro patria mori: laudandus igitur Sulpitius, qui pro patria in legatione mortuus est. Prior ad thesin, posterior ad hypothesin pertinet. Sed videamus duo illa verba. Contextum orationis vocat, quod alibi filum appellavit, sumpta translatione a telis, quae filis cotexuntur. Quod autem illustrāda esse praecipit, illustri genere dicendi tractanda & exornanda esse intelligimus, quo de genere dictum est supra.
units.tr: In the whole, as it were, texture of the speech. Up to this point he has set out general matters, which are contained in an infinite question. Now, however, he teaches how these general kinds and universal matters are to be brought down to and treated in individual persons, which is the matter of a case and a defined question. From this it is clear that orators in this genre must handle two kinds of statements: one general, concerning the virtues and vices themselves, without any linking to persons; the other defined by times and persons. For example, when they speak of the virtues of Pompey and the vices of Catiline, these two correspond to the two premises of an argument, the major and the minor. For example, if someone says: "It has always been praiseworthy to die for one's country; therefore Sulpicius, who died on an embassy for his country, is to be praised." The former pertains to the thesis, the latter to the hypothesis. But let us consider those two words. He calls it the "texture of the speech," which elsewhere he called the thread, a metaphor taken from the threads woven together in cloth. And since he instructs that these things are to be illustrated, we understand that they are to be treated and adorned in the illustrious style of speaking, which was discussed above.

units.la: Quemadmodum quisque generatus.) Iam locos personarum enumerat, quae attributa vocantur. facit autem locos octo: ortum, educationem seu victum, institutionem seu mores, casus, opinionem, orationem, facta & dicta, mortem. quibus adduntur loci dialectici tres: caussæ, euentus siue effecta, & consequentia, in quibus antecedentia quoq; intelliguntur: non quòd non & alijs uti possimus, sed quòd hi sint præcipui, & tales qui omitti non debeant. In ortu consideranda sunt, patria, parentes, tempus, & nascendi modus: in educatione, pueritiæ & adolescentiæ mores: in institutione, quos magistros artium, quos uiuendi præceptores habuerit, quibus amicis usus fit. In casibus illud uidendum erit, si quid diuinitus ei accideris, aut accidere potuerit. nam leues casus, & minutarum rerum, omittendi sunt. In opinione, quæ fuerint eius studia, quæ ue consilia, siue de rebus diuinis, siue naturalibus & humanis. Ex oratione autem, quæ mentis & opinionum interpres est, maximè homines aut laudantur, aut uituperantur. idcirco dicebat Socrates: Loquere, ut te uideam. ex oratione enim arbitrabatur se, qualis quisq; esset, posse cognoscere. In factis autem, & rebus gestis, maxima materia laudis, aut uituperationis elucescit. In morte postremò duo uidenda sunt. genus nimirum mortis ipsum, tum quæ post mortem alicui euenerunt. Cuius rei exempla suppeditabit Philippica 14: itemq; Antonij in Cæsaris funere laudatio, quam ex Dione ad Philippicas nostras adiecimus.
units.tr: As each person was born. Now he lists the topics of persons, which are called attributes. He makes eight topics: origin, upbringing or way of life, education or character, circumstances, opinion, speech, deeds and words, and death. To these are added three dialectical topics: causes, outcomes or effects, and consequences, in which antecedents are also understood. This is not because we cannot use others, but because these are the principal ones, and such that they should not be omitted. In origin, one must consider country, parents, time, and the manner of birth; in upbringing, the morals of boyhood and youth; in education, which teachers of the arts and which masters of living he had, and what friends he used. Under circumstances, one must see whether anything has befallen him by divine agency, or could have befallen him; for slight accidents and trivial matters are to be omitted. Under opinion, one considers what his pursuits were, and what his plans, whether concerning divine, natural, or human matters. Men are most of all praised or blamed by their speech, which is the interpreter of the mind and opinions; for this reason Socrates used to say: "Speak, that I may see you." For he thought that he could come to know what sort of person each man was from his speech. In deeds and things done, the greatest material for praise or blame shines forth. Finally, in death two things must be considered: the kind of death itself, and what happened to someone after death. Examples of this will be supplied by the Fourteenth Philippic, and likewise by Antony's funeral oration for Caesar, which we have added to our Philippics from Dio.

units.la: IN M. T. CICERONIS DE GENERE DELI- BERATIVO.
units.tr: On Cicero's Deliberative Genus

units.la: C.F. Accepi ista, didicique breuiter, non solum quemadmodum laudare alterum, sed etiam quemadmodum eniterer, ut possem ipse iure laudari. Videamus igitur deinceps in sententia dicenda, quam uiam, & quae praecepta teneamus.
units.tr: C.F. I have received those instructions and learned them briefly: not only how to praise another, but also how I might strive so that I myself could rightly be praised. Let us therefore next see, in delivering an opinion, what method and what precepts we should follow.

units.la: C. F. Accepi ista, didicique breuiter.) Docilis adolescens, fructum que ex hac laudis praeceptione percepit, fatetur: nimirum se didicisse non modo qua ratione alterum laudare, sed etiam, quid faciens ipse merito laudari posset. Qui cum haec diceret, respexit ad illa quae a patre initio huius generis audiuit, laudandi ac uituperandi rationes non ad benedicendum solum, sed etiam ad honeste uiuendum ualere. Petit igitur, ut de secundo genere causarum uiam & praecepta tradat.
units.tr: C. F. I have received those instructions and learned them briefly. The docile young man, who has gained profit from this teaching on praise, confesses it: clearly he has learned not only the method of praising another, but also what he himself might do so as to deserve praise. In saying this, he recalls what he heard from his father at the start of this kind of discourse: that the methods of praising and blaming serve not only for speaking well but also for living honourably. He therefore asks that the father now teach the method and precepts for the second kind of cause.

units.la: C. P. Est igitur in deliberando finis utilitas, ad quem omnia referuntur in consilio dando, sententiaque dicenda, ut illa prima sint suasori, aut dissuasori uidenda: quid aut possit fieri, aut non possit: & quid aut necesse cesse sit, aut nō necesse. Nam si quid effici nō potest, deliberatio tollitur, quamuis utile sit.
units.tr: C. P. In deliberation, then, the end is utility, and everything is referred to it when giving counsel and delivering an opinion. So the first things the one who urges or dissuades must consider are these: what can or cannot be done, and what is or is not necessary. For if something cannot be brought about, the deliberation is removed, however useful it may be.

units.la: C. P. Est igitur in deliberando finis utilitas.) Est hæc deliberationis partitio & doctrina tota Aristotelis. Nam primum de huius generis fine sic ait Rhet.1. In deliberando finis est, utilitas & detrimentum. Qui enim suadet aliquid, illud tanquam melius suadet: & qui dissuadet, tanquā deterius dissuadet. Alia uero omnia huc referuntur: ut si quid iustum aut iniustum, honestum aut turpe dicatur. Idem tamen Aristoteles Eth.2.cap.3. deliberantibus tria proponit: Honestum, utile, iucundū. Tria itē contraria, quæ homines declinare solent: turpe, non utile, molestum. Sed paulo post hæc tria ad duo reuocat. Etenim (inquit) quicquid honestum, quicquid utile, id omne iucundum. Cicero uero, etsi unam utilitatem hic nominat, non tamen reijcere honestatem putandus est. nam eam intelligit, quæ in discernendis bonis malisq; uersatur, ut post dicet, Sed utilitatem unam proponit, quoniam ad eam (ut paulo ante ex Aristotele ostendi) alia omnia referuntur. Nam & iustum & honestum, ita vulgo expeti solent, si utilia & bona uideantur: alioqui uetantur & respuuntur. Per hanc litem generibus auditorū distinctis, flindis, infrà componit hic noster Orator.
units.tr: C. P. In deliberation, then, the end is utility. This division of deliberation and the whole teaching on it belong to Aristotle. For first, Aristotle speaks of the end of this kind of speech in the Rhetoric, book 1: "In deliberation the end is utility and harm. For he who urges something urges it as better, and he who dissuades urges against it as worse. All other things are referred to these, such as whether something is said to be just or unjust, honourable or shameful." Yet Aristotle in the Ethics, book 2, chapter 3, sets three things before deliberators: the honourable, the useful, and the pleasant; and three contrary things which people usually avoid: the shameful, the unprofitable, and the unpleasant. But a little later he reduces these three to two: "For," he says, "whatever is honourable, whatever is useful, that is all pleasant." Cicero, though he names only one utility here, is not to be thought to reject honour; for he understands it as that which is involved in distinguishing good from evil, as he will say later. But he sets forth one utility because all other things are referred to it, as I showed a little earlier from Aristotle. For both the just and the honourable are commonly sought in this way, if they seem useful and good; otherwise they are forbidden and rejected. Our orator here arranges the matter in this way, with the hearers' divisions kept distinct, as our Orator sets out below.

units.la: Quid aut possit fieri, aut non possit.) Locos deliberationis enumerat. Sunt autem summatim hi: Fieri posse, fieri non posse, facile, difficile, necesse, non necesse, magnum, parvum. Sed facile, respondet ei quod fieri potest: & difficile, ei quod fieri non potest: Magnum, ei quod necessarium est. Parvum, ei quod non est necessarium. Nam ea utilitas, quae nimis magna cum difficultate haberi potest, omitti: & quae parva est, contemni solet. Facile autem & magna omnes adipisci cupiunt. Sunt igitur deliberationis loci veri & aperti tres, ut finem pro loco ponamus: utile, necessarium, facile: atque hi in suadendo. In dissuasione vero, non utile, non necessarium, non facile.
units.tr: What can or cannot be done. He lists the topics of deliberation. These, in summary, are: possible, impossible, easy, difficult, necessary, not necessary, great, small. "Easy" corresponds to what can be done; "difficult" to what cannot be done; "great" to what is necessary; "small" to what is not necessary. For a utility that can be had only with very great difficulty is usually set aside, and one that is small is usually despised. But everyone desires what is easy and great to obtain. So there are three true and open topics of deliberation, if we take the end as the topic: the useful, the necessary, the easy; and these are used in urging. In dissuading, however, the topics are: not useful, not necessary, not easy.

units.la: Et si quid necesse est (necesse autem id est, sine quo salvi, liberi esse non possumus) id est reliquis & honestatibus in civili ratione, & commodis anteponendum. Cum autem quaeritur, quid fieri possit, videndum etiam est, quam facile possit. Nam quae perdifficilia sunt, perinde habenda sunt, ac si effici non possint. Et cum de necessitate attendemus, & si aliquid non necessarium videbitur, uidendum tamen erit, quàm sit magnum. Quod enim permagni interest, pro necessario saepe habetur.
units.tr: And if something is necessary (and necessary is that without which we cannot be safe or free), it must be placed before all other honourable and advantageous things in the civic reckoning. When we ask what can be done, we must also see how easily it can be done. For things that are extremely difficult are to be regarded just as if they could not be done. And when we consider necessity, if something seems not necessary, we must nevertheless see how great it is. For what matters very greatly is often regarded as necessary.

units.la: Et, si quid necesse est.) Necessitatem definit, id est, necessariam utilitatem: ea enim utilitas necessaria intelligitur, sine qua salui liberi ue esse non possumus. de qua autem necessitate hic loquatur, ex Rhetorum doctrina indicandum erit. De Inuentione libro 2, duplicem ipse facit necessitudinem, siue necessitatem: unam cum adiunctione, siue exceptione: alteram simplicem, & absolutam. Prioris exemplum est: Necesse est Saguntinos se dedere Annibali, nisi malint fame perire. Posterioris: Necesse est Saguntinos uenire in Annibalis potestatem. Illic in superiore adiunctio est, Nisi malint fame perire. Si enim id maluerint, non est necesse. Inferius non item: propterea quòd, siue uelint Saguntini se dedere, siue famem perpeti, atque ita perire, necesse est eos uenire in Annibalis potestatem. Ex qua diuisione iam liquet, Cicero nem hoc loco de ea que cum adiunctione necessitudo dicitur, loqui: quasi diceret, De ea hic necessitate loquor, que ea conditione necessaria est, si modò salui aut liberi esse uolumus. Nam illa altera absoluta, omnem deliberationem tollit, ut de Oratore libro 2. ait Antonius: Inciditur omnis
units.tr: And if something is necessary. He defines necessity, that is, necessary utility: for that is understood as necessary utility without which we cannot be safe or free. What kind of necessity he means here must be shown from the teaching of the rhetoricians. In the book On Invention, book 2, he himself makes two kinds of necessity: one with a qualification or exception, and another simple and absolute. An example of the first: "It is necessary for the Saguntines to surrender to Hannibal, unless they prefer to perish by famine." Of the second: "It is necessary for the Saguntines to come into Hannibal's power." In the first there is a qualification above, "unless they prefer to perish by famine"; for if they preferred that, it would not be necessary. In the second there is no such qualification, because whether the Saguntines are willing to surrender or to endure famine and so perish, it is necessary that they come into Hannibal's power. From this division it is now clear that Cicero here speaks of that necessity which is called necessity with a qualification, as if he were saying: "I am speaking here of that necessity which is necessary on this condition, if only we wish to be safe or free." For the other, absolute necessity removes all deliberation, as Antonius says in the book On the Orator, book 2: "All deliberation is cut off,

units.la: iam deliberatio,si intelligitur non posse fieri,aut si necessitas affertur. Et qui id docuit non uidentibus alijs,is plurimum uidit.
units.tr: once it is understood that a thing cannot be done, or once necessity is alleged. And he who taught this, when others did not see it, saw very much."

units.la: In ciuili ratione.) Necessitas haec, in qua aut salus,aut libertas sita est,anteponitur,si fiat comparatio, reliquis omnibus honestis & utilibus. Paria autem sunt, salus & libertas, sine quibus nec honestate nec utilitate ulla frui licet, in ciuili dūtaxat ratione, id est in Repub. & libera ciuitate.In priuata uero re, non item. Nam uir fortis malit uitam amittere, quàm infamiā subire. At in Repub. summa honestas est, summumq; bonum, libertas ipsa: nihilq; infame esse potest, quod ad patriæ salutem necessarium sit.
units.tr: In the civic reckoning. This necessity, in which safety or liberty lies, is placed before all other honourable and useful things, if a comparison is made. Safety and liberty are equal, since without them one can enjoy neither honour nor any utility; but this holds only in the civic reckoning, that is, in the commonwealth and a free state. In a private affair it is not so. For a brave man would prefer to lose his life than to submit to infamy. But in the commonwealth the highest honour, and the supreme good, is liberty itself; and nothing can be infamous that is necessary for the safety of the fatherland.

units.la: Itaq; cum cōstet hoc genus causfarū ex suasione & dissuasione, suasori proponitur simplex ratio, si & utile est,& fieri potest, fiat. Dissuasori duplex:una,si non utile est, ne fiat: altera,si fieri non potest, ne suscipiatur. Sic suasori utrumque docendum est,dissuasori alterū infirmare satis est.
units.tr: Therefore, since this kind of cause consists of urging and dissuading, the one who urges is given a single line of argument: if a thing is both useful and possible, let it be done. The one who dissuades has a twofold line: first, if a thing is not useful, let it not be done; second, if it cannot be done, let it not be undertaken. Thus the one who urges must teach both points, while for the one who dissuades it is enough to weaken one of them.

units.la: Itaq; cum constet hoc genus causarum ) Tractationis nunc duo præcepta ponit: alterum suasoris,dissuasoris alterū. suasori ad tractandū simplicem orationem propositam esse dicit, quod eodem
units.tr: Therefore, since this kind of cause consists of... He now lays down two precepts of treatment: one for the one who urges, the other for the one who dissuades. He says the one who urges has a simple line of argument to treat, because in the same way

units.la: Itaq; cum constet hoc genus causarum ) Tractationis nunc duo præcepta ponit: alterum suasoris,dissuasoris alterū. dem modo utilitas & facultas semper docenda est:dissuasori duplicem. Nam aut non utile esse quod assertur, probare debet: aut fieri non posse. non quidem utrunque. Ergo bipertita est uia, ita ut aut hoc, aut illud ostendat. Nam utrouis ostenso, contrariam sententiam dissolueret, aut infirmaret. Idcirco alterū coniunctione proponit, alterum disiunctione. At in coniunctione simplex est ratio, in disiūctione duplex. Hosce locos præclarè tractauit Cicero 7. Philippica, cum bellum suadet in Antonium suscipiendum, & pacem non esse admittendam.
units.tr: Therefore, since this kind of cause consists of... He now lays down two precepts of treatment: one for the one who urges, the other for the one who dissuades. utility and possibility must always be taught; the one who dissuades has a double line. For he must prove either that what is alleged is not useful, or that it cannot be done; not, indeed, both. So the way is twofold, so that he shows either this or that. For if he shows either, he would overturn or weaken the contrary opinion. Hence he sets forth the one by conjunction and the other by disjunction. But in the conjunction the argument is simple, in the disjunction it is double. Cicero handled these topics admirably in the seventh Philippic, when he urges that war be undertaken against Antony and that peace not be admitted.

units.la: RERVM VTILIVM, BO- narumq; diuisio.
units.tr: The division of useful things and of goods.

units.la: Quare quoniam in his uersatur omne consilium duobus, de utilitate ante dicamus, quæ in discernēdis bonis, malisq; uersatur. Bonorum autem partim necessaria sunt, ut uita, pudicitia, libertas: ut liberi, coniuges, germani, parentes. partim non necessaria: quorum alia sunt per se expetenda, ut ea quæ sita sunt in officiis, atque uirtutibus: alia, quod aliquid commodi efficiunt, ut opes, & copiæ. Eorum autem, quæ propter se expetuntur, partim honestate ipsa, partim commoditate aliqua expetuntur. Honestate, ea quæ proficiscuntur ab iis virtutibus, de quibus paulo ante est dictum, quæ sunt laudabilia ipsa per se. Commoditate autem aliqua, quæ sunt in corporis aut fortunæ bonis expetenda: quorum alia sunt quasi quodammodo cum honestate coniuncta, ut honos, ut gloria: alia diuersa, ut uires, forma, ualetudo, nobilitas, diuitiæ, clientelæ. Est etiam quasi quædam materies, subiecta honestati; quæ maximè spectatur in amicitiis: amicitiæ autem charitate, & amore cernuntur. Nam cum deorum, tum parentum, patriæque cultus, eorumque hominum, qui aut sapientia, aut opibus excellunt, ad charitatem referri solet. Coniuges autem, & liberi, & fratres, & alij quos usus, familiaritasque coniunxit, quanquam etiam charitate ipsa, tamen amore maximè continentur.
units.tr: Since all deliberation turns on two things, let us first speak of usefulness, which lies in distinguishing good from bad. Some goods are necessary, such as life, chastity and liberty, and also children, spouses, brothers and parents. Others are not necessary. Of these, some are to be sought for their own sake, such as those things that consist in duties and virtues. Others are sought because they bring some advantage, such as wealth and resources. Of the things sought for their own sake, some are sought for honour itself and some for some advantage. Things are sought for honour when they proceed from those virtues mentioned a little earlier, which are praiseworthy in themselves. Things are sought for some advantage when they are to be desired among the goods of body or fortune. Of these, some are in a way joined with honour, such as esteem and glory, while others are different, such as strength, beauty, health, nobility, riches and clienteles. There is also a kind of matter that underlies honour, which is especially seen in friendships. Friendships, however, are recognised by affection and love. For the worship of God, of parents and of country, and of those men who excel in wisdom or in wealth, is usually referred to affection. Spouses, children, brothers and others whom use and familiarity have joined to us are held together chiefly by love, although also by affection itself.

units.la: Quaere quoniam in his versatur omne consilium duobus.) Dupliciter haec verba intelligi possunt: nimirum omne consilium in suadendo dissuadendoq; versari: atque in suadendo bonum, in dissuadendo vero malum: aut in his duobus, si utile sit, et si fieri possit. Sed utraque ratio conuenit, magis autem posterior.
units.tr: "Since all deliberation turns on two things": these words can be understood in two ways. Clearly all deliberation consists in persuading and dissuading: in persuading, of the good; in dissuading, of the bad. Or it consists in these two things, namely whether a thing is useful and whether it can be done. Both interpretations agree, but the latter more so.

units.la: De utilitate ante dicamus.) Vtilitatis uidetur quandam definitionem ex rebus subiectis, et materia eius, afferre: ut intelligamus, utilitatem pro facultate et ratione, bona a malis discernendi. Sint igitur duo capita et genera summa, bonum et malum: tum quoniam contraria bonis facile intelliguntur, et a parte meliore debet fieri partitio, bonorum partitionem instituit.
units.tr: "Let us first speak of usefulness": he seems to give a certain definition of usefulness from its subject and matter, so that we understand usefulness as the capacity and reason for distinguishing good from bad. There are therefore two heads and highest kinds, good and bad. Since contraries to goods are easily understood, and division should proceed from the better part, he sets up a division of goods.

units.la: Bonorum autem partim necessaria sunt.) Diuisionem bonorum hic mirabile et artificiosam nabis describit, sed tamen ex Peripateticorum et Academicorum fontibus deriuatam: ut perspicuum esse poterit ex Ethic. 1. libro Aristotelis, et Rhe-toricorum: deinde Ciceronis de Inuent. libro 2. ubi genera rerum expetendarum persequitur. Cum illa enim, haec bonorum partitio, exceptis duobus primis capitibus, rerum necessariarum et non necessariarum, consentit. Neque enim hic aliud uult, quam bonorum alia honestate sola expetenda esse, alia commoditate sola: alia et commoditate simul, et & honestate. In his prima & postrema per se sunt expetenda, quia in utroq; membro honestus cernitur: a quibus tanquam a meliori genus ipsum bonorum appellatur, & utrunq; per se expetendum dicitur: quoniam ad honestatem bonos & gloria, & id genus alia referuntur. Honestum in animi bonis est, eluceteq; in virtutibus & officijs: reliqua partim in bonis corporis, partim fortunae numerantur. Sed hanc pulcherrimam Ciceronis bonorum descriptionem, quam quidam confusam, & minime sibi constantem esse existimant, praestat in tabulas digerere, ut ex consusione in ordinem vindicetur. Bonorum alis Necessaria Vita Pudicitia Libertas Coniuges Liberi Germani Parentes. Non necessaria, alia Commoditate sola, quae diversa dicuntur a superioribus Corporis Vires Forma Valetudo. Fortune Nobilitas Divitiae Clientela. Per se expetenda Commoditate & honestate, ut Gloria. Honor. Honestate, quae animi sunt Virtutes, ut Prudentia Iustitia Fortitudo Temperantia. Officia, quae amicitias praesertim continenter, Charitate ut Dei Parentum Patriae Sapientium Potentium. Amore Coniugum Liberorum Fratrum Familiarum. Igitur
units.tr: "Some goods are necessary": here he describes a remarkable and skilful division of goods, yet one derived from the sources of the Peripatetics and the Academics. This will be clear from Aristotle's first book of the Ethics and the Rhetoric, and then from Cicero's De inventione, book 2, where he pursues the kinds of things to be sought. For this division of goods agrees with that one, apart from the first two heads, namely necessary and unnecessary things. For here he means nothing else than that some goods are to be sought for honour alone, some for advantage alone, and some for advantage and honour together. In these, the first and last are sought for their own sake, because honour is seen in each member. From these, as from the better, the very genus of goods is named, and both are said to be sought for their own sake, since glory and other such things are referred to honour. Honour lies in the goods of the mind and shines forth in virtues and duties; the rest are counted partly among goods of the body and partly among goods of fortune. But this very beautiful description of goods by Cicero, which some think confused and not consistent with itself, is better set out in tables, so that it may be vindicated from confusion into order. Of goods, some are necessary: life, chastity, liberty, spouses, children, brothers, parents. Some are not necessary: those sought for advantage alone, which are called different from the above: bodily goods, strength, beauty, health; goods of fortune, nobility, riches, clienteles. Those to be sought for their own sake are sought for advantage and honour together, such as glory and esteem. Those for honour: the virtues of the mind, such as prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance; duties, which especially hold friendships together: by affection, as toward God, parents, country, the wise and the powerful; by love, as toward spouses, children, brothers and households. Therefore

units.la: Iam igitur, propositā descriptione, eiusq; partes & membra explicemus. Vtilia definit Aristoteles Rhet. lib. 1. ex quorū usu fructum capimus. uel Vtile est, quod ciuitatis statum conseruat. Bonum codē libro, & de Moribus, id esse dicit, quod omnes expetāt. Honestum, siue pul-brum alio loco ex eodem definimus, quod cum propter se fit expetēdū, est etiā laudabile: uel honestū est, quod cum uirtute & officio fit: uel quod cum bonū sit, est etiam iucundū, quatenus bonū. Laudabile uero, ut ad Herennium lib. 3. definitur, quod cōficit honestā & præsentē & consequentē commemoratione. Necessaria ipse paulo ante esse dixit, sine quibus salui liberi ue esse non possumus. Itaq; cōtrario modo, non necessaria erunt ea, sine quibus illa superiora possumus retinere: uel quibus si careamus, infœlices tamen non erimus, modo non omnibus, sed quibusdam destituamur.
units.tr: Now, having set out the description, let us explain its parts and members. Aristotle defines useful things in the first book of the Rhetoric as those from whose use we derive fruit, or: the useful is that which preserves the state of a community. In the same book, and in the Ethics, he says that the good is that which all desire.
