Elsewhere we define the honourable, or fine, from the same source: that which, being done for its own sake, is also praiseworthy; or the honourable is that which is done with virtue and duty; or that which, being good, is also pleasant, insofar as it is good. Praiseworthy, indeed, is defined, as in the Ad Herennium, book 3, as that which produces an honourable remembrance both present and subsequent. He himself said a little earlier what necessary things are: those without which we cannot be safe or have children. Therefore, in the contrary way, the unnecessary things will be those without which we can keep the former, or which, if we lack them, will not make us unhappy, provided we are not deprived of everything but only of some things.

units.la: Vita.) ut hic accipitur, est motus cum sensu & ratione.
units.tr: Life, as it is understood here, is motion together with sensation and reason.

units.la: Pudicitia.) siue castitas, integritas est animi quædam, contra uenereas uoluptates.
units.tr: Chastity, or purity, is a certain integrity of mind against venereal pleasures.

units.la: Libertas.) naturalis est facultas, eius quod cuique facere libet, nisi si quid ui aut iure prohibeatur. Inst. 1. de iure person.
units.tr: Liberty is the natural power of doing what one pleases, unless something is forbidden by force or by law. Institutes, book 1, on the law of persons.

units.la: Liberi.) sunt filij filiæue legitimo ex cōiugio procreati. nam hic de spuriis non agitur.
units.tr: Children are the sons and daughters born in lawful marriage; for illegitimate children are not treated here.

units.la: Coniuges.)id est,coniugiū,siue matrimoniū,est uiri & mulieris cōiunctio,indiuiduā uitæ cōsuetudinem continens.Inst.lib.1.de Patr.potestate.
units.tr: Spouses: that is, marriage, or matrimony, is the union of man and woman, containing an indivisible way of life together. Institutes, book 1, on paternal power.

units.la: Germani.) sunt eodē ex genere & stirpe eādem orti,præsertim fratres & sorores.
units.tr: Brothers are those born of the same kind and the same stock, especially brothers and sisters.

units.la: Parētes.)pater materúe,à quibus ,pcreati sumus.
units.tr: Parents are the father or mother from whom we have been born.

units.la: Opes.) cuiuscunque generis facultates, quibus iuuari possumus.
units.tr: Resources are facilities of any kind by which we can be helped.

units.la: Copia.)rerū siue opum affluentia, ad beatam cōferens vitā:Plat. apud Speusippum: Honos est præmium uirtutis, iudicio studioq; ciuiū delatus ad aliquē: Cic. uel ut Arist. Rhet.1. signū gloriæ, ex plurimis in alios meritis comparatæ.
units.tr: Abundance is an affluence of things or of resources, contributing to a happy life. Plato, in Speusippus: honour is the reward of virtue, conferred on someone by the judgement and zeal of citizens. Cicero, or as Aristotle says in the Rhetoric, book 1: a sign of glory, acquired from many merits toward others.

units.la: Gloria.) est frequens de aliquo fama,cū laude: De Inuent.2.Vel est consentiens laus bonorū,incorrupta uox bene iudicantium de excellenti uir-tute:Tusc.3.Aristoteles Rhet.1.
units.tr: Glory is frequent report about someone together with praise. De inventione, book 2. Or it is the agreeing praise of good men, the uncorrupted voice of those who judge rightly about excellent virtue. Tusculan Disputations, book 3. Aristotle, Rhetoric, book 1.

units.la: Vires.) facultatem alterum monendi,quomodocunq; libeat,esse definit.
units.tr: Strength he defines as the capacity of one to move another in whatever way he pleases.

units.la: Forma.) Quáquam alia viri est,alia mulieris, alia adolescētis,alia senioris, generatim tamē ita à Cicer. Tusc. 4.definitur,ut sit pulchritudo corporis,quedam apta figura membrorum, cum co-loris quadam suauitate.
units.tr: Beauty is different in a man, in a woman, in a youth and in an old man; yet in general it is defined by Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book 4, as bodily beauty, a certain fitting figure of the limbs, together with a certain sweetness of colour.

units.la: Valetudo.) ut idem de Amicitia ait, opportuna est,ut dolore careas, & muneribus singare corporis, uel, ut Tuscul. 4. Sanitas est corporis temperatio, cùm ea congruunt inter se, è quibus constamus. Aristoteles autem Rhet. 1. ualetudinē ita accipiēdam scribit, ut morbo uacuum sit corpus, & ad usus bene constitutum.
units.tr: Health, as the same man says in On Friendship, is opportune, so that you are free from pain and have the bodily functions in good order. Or, as in the Tusculan Disputations, book 4: health is a temperament of the body, when those things from which we are composed agree with one another. Aristotle, in the Rhetoric, book 1, writes that health should be understood as a body free from disease and well constituted for its functions.

units.la: Nobilitas.) est generis antiquitas & claritas, uirtute aut opibus, aut alia re quæ in precio sit, parta. Rhet. 1.
units.tr: Nobility is the antiquity and distinction of a family, acquired by virtue, or by wealth, or by some other thing that is held in esteem. Rhetoric, book 1.

units.la: Diuitiæ.) parum differunt à copijs. Rerū est possessio, quæ multitudine & copia, & magnitudine & pulchritudine excellant, cum securitate.
units.tr: Riches differ little from resources. They are the possession of things which excel in number, abundance, size and beauty, together with security.

units.la: Clientelæ.) Clientum multitudo, quæ teob- seruent & colant.
units.tr: Clienteles: a multitude of clients who respect and cultivate one.

units.la: Amicitia.) est omnium diuinarum humanarumq; rerum cum beneuolentia & charitate coniunctio: uel, ut de Inuent. lib. 2. ait, Amicitia uoluntas erga aliquem rerum bonarum, illius ipsius causa quem diligit, cum eius pari uoluntate.
units.tr: Friendship is a union of all divine and human things with goodwill and affection; or, as he says in De inventione, book 2, friendship is the will toward someone for the sake of good things, for the sake of the one whom we love, with that person's equal will in return.

units.la: Charitas.) est beneuolentia quædam sanctior erga honoratiores, cum quadam obseruantia.
units.tr: Affection is a certain holier goodwill toward those of higher rank, with a certain deference.

units.la: Amor.) beneuolentia & studium erga pares, uel inferiores.
units.tr: Love is goodwill and zeal toward equals or inferiors.

units.la: Materies subiecta honestati.) dicitur, in quâ honestas elucet, occasionēq; habet laudis: ut in colēdo Deo, parētibus, patria, propinquis, amicis.
units.tr: The matter underlying honour is that in which honour shines forth and has an occasion for praise, as in worshipping God, in honouring parents, country, kinsfolk and friends.

units.la: In his igitur rebus cū bona sint, facile est intellectu, quæ sint contraria.
units.tr: Since these things are good, it is easy to understand which things are their contraries.

units.la: In his igitur rebus.) Cum bona sint, facile est intellectu quae sint contraria: Mala haud dubie bonis contraria sunt, & expetendis fugienda, & utilibus inutilia, vitae mors, pudicitiae impudicitia, libertati servitus, orbitas liberis, caelibatus coniugio, germanis fratrum destitutio & propinquorum solitudo, parentib. pupilli, officijs maleficia, virtutib. vitia, honestati turpitudo & uitiositas, commoditati incommoditas, imbecillitas uiribus, deformitas formae, valetudini inualetudo & morbus, ignobilitas nobilitati, paupertas diuitijs, clientelis contemptio, amicitiae inimicitia, honori ignominia, gloriae infamia. Quae omnia contrario modo, atque superiora, describenda erunt.
units.tr: Since these things are good, it is easy to understand which are their contraries. Bad things are undoubtedly contrary to goods, and to things to be sought are the things to be avoided, and to useful things the useless: death to life, immodesty to chastity, servitude to liberty, childlessness to children, celibacy to marriage, the abandonment by brothers and the solitude of kinsfolk to brothers and kin, orphanhood to parents, wrongdoing to duties, vices to virtues, turpitude and depravity to honour, disadvantage to advantage, weakness to strength, deformity to beauty, sickness and disease to health, ignobility to nobility, poverty to riches, contempt to clienteles, enmity to friendship, dishonour to honour, infamy to glory. All of these are to be described in the opposite way to the things above.

units.la: Quod si semper optima tenere possemus, haud sane, quoniam quidem ea perspicua sunt, consilio multum egeremus. Sed quia temporibus, quae uim habet maximam, perspe cuenit, ut utilitas cum honestate certet, earumque rerum contentio plerunque deliberationes efficit, ne aut opportuna propter dignitatem, aut honesta propter utilitatem relinquatur, ad haec difficultate explicandu praecepta referamus. Quòd si semper optima tenere possemus.) Deliberatio non in perspicuis et minimè dubijs, sed in ancipitibus bonis malisq; versatur. Nā de perspicuis nemo disputat, aut deliberat: sed de ijs, de quibus inter homines controversia est, opinioq; varia, non certa scientia, ut Aristoteles multis in locis docet.
units.tr: If we could always hold to what is best, we would certainly need little counsel, since those things are plain. But because it very often happens in times, which have the greatest force, that usefulness contends with honour, and the conflict between these things usually produces deliberations, we will refer the precepts for explaining this difficulty so that neither the expedient is abandoned for the sake of honour nor the honourable for the sake of usefulness. "If we could always hold to what is best." Deliberation does not concern things that are plain and not at all doubtful, but moves among goods and evils that are uncertain. For nobody debates or deliberates about plain matters, but only about those on which there is controversy among men and varied opinion, not certain knowledge, as Aristotle teaches in many places.

units.la: Sed quia temporibus. ) Tempora pro occasionibus & circumstantijs, quae vocât, ponuntur. sed incidunt (inquit de Offic. lib. 1. Cicero) saepe tempora, cum ea quae maximè videtur digna esse iusto homine, coq; quem virum bonum dicimus, commutantur, fiuntq; contraria, ita ut ne depositum quidem semper reddendum sit: ut si qui deposuit, postea furiosus factus sit, & id genus alia.
units.tr: "But because of times." Times are used for occasions and circumstances, which they call circumstances. Cicero says in De Officiis book 1: "Times often change so that those things which seem most worthy of the just man, and of the man we call good, are altered and become their opposites, so that not even a deposit must always be returned: as if someone who deposited something afterwards became insane," and other things of that kind.

units.la: Perspepe evenit, ut utilitas cum honestate certet.) Omnis deliberandi ratio in quinq; partes à Cicerone distributa est: primùm enim quaeritur, honestum ne factu sit, an turpe: & duobus propositis honestis, utrum honestius. Deinde, utile, an contrà inutile: & duobus propositis utilibus, utrum utilius. Quintum dubitandi genus est, cum pugnare videtur cum honesto, id quod videtur esse utile. Cū enim utilitas ad se rapere, honestas contrà revocare ad se videtur, fit ut distrahatur deliberando animus, afferatq; ancipitè curà cogitandi. Hæc autem pugna non in rebus ipsis inest,sed in hominũ opinione, qui aliquid putát utile esse,quod nõ sit honestũ:aut honestũ,quod non sit utile.idcirco utilia relinquũt, putantes se illis retentis,dignitatem amissuros: aut honesta te retenta,utilitate carituros.Id quod recte per uidens Cicero,præcepta hoc loco ad hanc difficultatem explicandam accommodauit. Dictum est enim supra, in deliberando finem utilitatem esse. Hic cõtrà ueniet alius, & dicet:non utilitatem,sed dignitatem & honestatem utilitati anteferendam esse:eam ob caussam,finem eum deliberanti propositum esse. Ergo hanc quæstionem dirimit,& conciliat, generibus auditorum diligenter propositis.
units.tr: "It very often happens that usefulness contends with honour." Cicero divided the whole method of deliberation into five parts. First, one asks whether a thing to be done is honourable or shameful, and, with two honourable courses proposed, which is more honourable. Then, whether it is useful or on the contrary useless, and, with two useful courses proposed, which is more useful. The fifth kind of doubt arises when what seems to be useful appears to conflict with the honourable. For when usefulness seems to draw one to itself and honour on the contrary to call one back, the mind is torn apart in deliberation and is held in an uncertain state of thought. This conflict, however, does not lie in the things themselves, but in the opinion of men, who think something is useful which is not honourable, or honourable which is not useful. Hence they abandon useful things, thinking that by keeping them they will lose their dignity, or they will lack usefulness if they keep honourable things. Cicero, seeing this rightly, has adapted the precepts here to explain this difficulty. For it was said above that in deliberation the end is usefulness. Here, on the contrary, another will come and say that not usefulness but dignity and honour are to be placed before usefulness; for this reason that end is set before the one deliberating. So he resolves and reconciles this question, carefully setting out the kinds of hearers.

units.la: Et quoniam nõ ad veritate solũ, sed etiam ad opiniones eorum qui audiunt, accõmodanda est oratio, hoc primum intelligamus,hominũ duo esse genera:alterum indoctum & agreste, quod anteferat semper utilitatem honestati: alterum expolitum,quod rebus omnibus dignitatem anteponat. Itaq; huic generi laus,honor,gloria, fides, iusticia, omnisq; virtus:illi aũt alteri quæstus, emolumẽtu,fructusq; proponitur,
units.tr: And since speech must be adapted not only to the truth but also to the opinions of those who hear, let us first understand that there are two kinds of men: one untaught and rustic, which always places usefulness before honour; the other refined, which places dignity before all things. Therefore to the latter kind praise, honour, glory, good faith, justice and all virtue are offered, but to the other gain, profit and advantage are proposed,

units.la: atque etiam uoluptas, quæ maximè est inímica uirtuti, boniq; naturam fallaciter imitando adulterat, quam immanissimus quisque acerrimè sequitur: neque solum honestis rebus, sed etiam necessariis anteponit, in suadendo, cum ei generi hominum consilium des, sæpe sanè laudanda est.
units.tr: and also pleasure, which is most hostile to virtue and deceitfully imitates and corrupts the nature of the good, and which the most savage men pursue most keenly; to such men, indeed, a speaker who gives counsel will often rightly give pleasure, placing it not only before honourable things but even before necessary ones, when he is advising that kind of men.

units.la: Et quoniâ non ad veritatë solum.) Hoc dicit, oratorem bonum ad tractandas hominum mentes sese accommodare, quæ sæpenumero opinione potius quàm veritate ducantur.
units.tr: "And since not only to the truth." He says that a good orator adapts himself to handling the minds of men, which are often led more by opinion than by truth.

units.la: Hoc primum intelligamus, hominum duo efse genera.) Hæc partitio Aristotelis est ex primo libro ad Nicomachum de Moribus, neq; repugnat, quòd Aristoteles videtur tria hominum genera facere. Nam genus hoc doctũ & expolitum, siue politicum, duo genera continet: alterum literatũ, eorũ qui in sapiētiæ contemplatione versantur: alterũ, quod in actione potius, & in administrāda Repub. uoluptatē capit: tertiũ uero, genus indoctum & agreste, minimeq; politicũ, partim utilitate emolumētisq; capitur, partim uoluptate, quæ uirtuti aduersatur maximè, boniq; naturam (ut ait Cicero) fallaciter imitando adulterat. dulterat & corrumpit. Quid igitur cum his generib.hominum faciat Orator? Expolito illi generi,laudem,honore, gloriam,fidem, iusticiam, reliquasq; uirtutes:huic autem alteri,quæstus, emolumenta,fructusq; proponet, atq; etiam uoluptates & iucunditates, si eis senserit acerrimè permoueri. At quem in finem? nimirum,non ut impellat, aut ad turpes utilitates, aut ad dulces voluptates:sed, ut eis quasi commodissimis uehiculis ad veras utilitates commoditatesq; traducat. Nam etiamsi finis proponatur utilitas, is est potius in suasore,id quod præclarè, imò diuinitus docuit Cicero de Orat.lib.2.his verbis: Ergo in suadendo nihil est optabilius,inquit,quàm dignitas.nam qui utilitatem putat, nô quid maximè uelit suasor, sed quid interdum magis sequatur,uidet. Nemo est enim,præsertim in tam clara ciuitate, quin putet expectandam maximè dignitatem:sed vincit utilitas plerunq;,cum subest ille timor:ea neglecta, ne dignitatè quidem posse retineri. Adhuc sententia Ciceronis explicatiuimus: superesset modò, ut quædam vocabula breuiter definiamus. Incipiamus igitur à primo, deinde reliqua persequamur. Opportuna,nunc utilia intelligit.alias opportuna dicuntur, quæ in ipsa occasione posita sunt, quæ Græci εὐκαιρα uocant. Dignitas idem est quod honestas. & obseruanda unaáest pulchra commutatio in his uerbis: Ne aut opportuna propter dignitatem, aut honesta propter utilitatẽ relinquátur. Laus, est oratio, quæ uirtutis magnitudinẽ explicat. Arist. Rhet.
units.tr: "Let us first understand that there are two kinds of men." This division is Aristotle's, from the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics, and it does not conflict with the fact that Aristotle seems to make three kinds of men. For this refined and polished kind, or civic kind, contains two kinds: one literary, of those who are occupied in the contemplation of wisdom; the other, which takes its pleasure rather in action and in administering the commonwealth. The third kind, however, is the untaught and rustic kind, least civic, which is captured partly by utility and profit, partly by pleasure, which is most opposed to virtue and, as Cicero says, deceitfully imitates and corrupts the nature of the good. What then should the orator do with these kinds of men? To the refined kind he will propose praise, honour, glory, good faith, justice and the other virtues; to the other kind gain, profit and advantages, and even pleasures and delights, if he has perceived that they are very strongly moved by these. And to what end? Surely not to drive them towards base advantages or sweet pleasures, but so that, as by the most convenient vehicles, he may lead them to true utilities and advantages. For even if usefulness is proposed as the end, it is rather in the case of the one persuading, as Cicero excellently and indeed divinely taught in De Oratore book 2, in these words: "Therefore in persuading," he says, "nothing is more to be desired than dignity. For he who thinks of usefulness does not see what the persuader most wants, but what he sometimes pursues more. For there is no one, especially in so renowned a state, who does not think dignity is above all to be expected; but usefulness conquers for the most part when that fear lies beneath, and if usefulness is neglected, dignity cannot even be retained." So far we have explained Cicero's meaning; it remains only that we briefly define certain terms. Let us begin then with the first and go on through the rest. "Opportune" here means useful; elsewhere things are called opportune which lie in the occasion itself, which the Greeks call [εὐκαιρα]. "Dignity" is the same as honour. And the beautiful antithesis in these words is to be observed: "lest either the opportune be left for the sake of dignity, or the honourable for the sake of usefulness." "Praise" is a speech which explains the greatness of a virtue; Aristotle, Rhetoric 1.

units.la: 1. Quæstus, utilitas ex pecunia: cui cõtraria est iactura. Emolumentũ, accessio cuiuscũq; rei, quæ prosit quoquo modo: cõtrariũ, decessio & detri mentũ. Fructus, utilitas quæ ex re fructuosa capitur, ut reditus & ucctigalia: Arist. Rhet. 1. Videtur aũt Cicero hæc uocabula explicare uoluisse de Fin. li. 3, cũ ait: Et emolumẽta & detrimẽta, quæ ὠφελήματα & βλάμματα appellant, communia esse uoluerunt. Quorum altera prosunt, nocent altera. Nec solum ea communia, uerũ etiã paria esse dixerũt. Incommoda aũt aut commoda (ita enim ἀνσηγήματα & ἀνοχρηγή ματα appello) communia esse uoluerũt, paria noluerũt. illa enim quæ prosunt, aut quæ nocẽt, aut bona sunt, aut mala: quæ sint paria necesse est. Cõmoda autem, aut incõmoda, in eo genere sunt, quæ præposita & reiecta dicimus: ea possunt paria nõ esse. sed emolumenta cõmunia esse dicũtur: rectè aũt facta & peccata, non habẽtur cõmunia. Ex his Ciceronis uerbis, illud colligimus: Cõmoda esse emolumẽtis potiora, idcircõ præponenda: & reiecta, quæ uocat, id est incommoda, detrimẽtis magis esse reijciẽda. Volupta-tem. tem, ait Arist. Rhet. 1. motum animi esse subitū, sub sensum cadentem, ad explendam naturā. De Morib. uero lib. 7. motū qui cum suauitate quodam naturā mouet, & ad eā affluit, & illabitur. neq; aliter Cicero de Fin. secundo, nisi quod breuius, Voluptatem iucundū motum in sensu, desinit. Intelligit autem hoc loco de uoluptate cōmuni, qua pleriq; tanquā à blandiß. dominis, à uirtute detorquētur. alioqui sunt etiā honestæ uoluptates, ut quæ ex reb. honestis & cōcessis capiuntur. Sunt item turpes & obscœnæ, ut quæ contra honestū & leges percipiuntur. Sed suboritur hic quæstio, cur dixerit hoc loco de uoluptate, quam immanissimus quisque acerrimè sequitur, cū contrà dixerit supra: Temperantiā immanitas in uoluptatib. aspernādis imitatur. Ita est: uidetur enim cōtraria, quæ nō sunt, si rectè intelligatur. Immanissimus quisq; pro intemperātissimo, quiq; ad uoluptates (ut inquit Aristot.) tanq�争 belluæ ad pastum, accurrit: illic uero immanitas pro duritie quadā, & nimia seueritate, ac potius stupore capitur. non enim propria est hominis, huiusmodi iucūdi sensus uacuitas. Sed si quis huiusmodi sit, qui uoluptate nulla afficiatur, quiq; nihil putet interesse inter aliā rē & aliā, is prosectò procul absit à natura hominis, hominicq; exuerit necesse est. Eth. lib. 3. Voluptati aduersatur dolor ac molestia. y Et illud uidendum, quanto magis homines mala fugiāt, quàm sequantur bona. Nam neq; honesta tam expetunt, quàm deuitant turpia. Quis enim honorem? quis gloriam? quis laudem? quis ullum decus tam unquam expetat, quàm ut ignominiam, infamiam, contumeliam, dedecus fugiat? quarum rerum dolor grauis est. Est genus hominum ad honestatem natum, malo cultu, prauisq; opinionibus corruptum. Quare in cohortando atque straedēdo propositum quidem nobis erit illud, ut doceamus, qua re bona cōsequi, malaq; uitare possimus. Sed apud homines bene institutos plurimum de laude, & de honestate dicemus, maximeq; ea uirtutum genera tractabimus, quae in communi hominū utilitate tuenda, augendaq; uersantur. Sin apud indoctos, imperitosq; dicemus, fructus, emolumenta, uoluptates, uitationesq; dolorum proferantur, ad-dandantur etiam contumeliæ, atque ignominiæ. Nemo enim est tā agrestis, quem non si ipsa minus honestas, contumelia tamen & dedecus magnopere moueat. Quare quod ad utilitatem spectat, ex iis quæ dicta sunt, reperietur.
units.tr: "Gain" is usefulness from money, to which loss is the opposite. "Emolument" is an addition to any thing which benefits in whatever way; its opposite is decrease and detriment. "Produce" is the usefulness which is taken from a fruitful thing, such as revenues and taxes; Aristotle, Rhetoric 1. Cicero seems to have wished to explain these terms in De Finibus book 3, when he says: "Emoluments and detriments, which they call [ὠφελήματα] and [βλάμματα], they wanted to be common; of which the one benefits and the other harms. Nor did they say these were only common, but also equal. Discommodities and commodities (for so I call [ἀνσηγήματα] and [ἀνοχρηγήματα]) they wanted to be common but not equal. For those things which benefit, or which harm, are either good or bad, and necessarily equal. But commodities or discommodities are in that class which we call preferred and rejected; these may not be equal. But emoluments are said to be common; rightly done and sinned things are not regarded as common." From these words of Cicero we gather this: commodities are to be preferred to emoluments and therefore placed before them; and rejected things, which he calls discommodities, that is, are to be rejected more than detriments. "Pleasure," Aristotle says in Rhetoric 1, is a sudden movement of the soul, falling under the senses, to fill up nature; in the Ethics book 7, a movement which moves nature with a certain sweetness and flows into it and glides into it; Cicero in De Finibus book 2 says no differently, except more briefly: "pleasure is a pleasing movement in the sense." He understands here common pleasure, by which most men are turned away from virtue as if by flattering masters. Otherwise there are also honourable pleasures, such as those taken from honourable and permitted things; likewise there are shameful and obscene ones, such as those perceived against what is honourable and against the laws. But here a question arises: why did he speak here of pleasure, which the most savage man most keenly pursues, when on the contrary he said above: "Savagery imitates temperance in rejecting pleasures"? It is so: these seem contrary only if they are not rightly understood. "Most savage man" stands for the most intemperate, and the man who runs to pleasures, as Aristotle says, like beasts to pasture; there "savagery" is taken for a certain hardness and excessive severity, or rather stupor. For the emptiness of such pleasant sensation is not proper to man. But if anyone is of such a kind that he is affected by no pleasure and thinks there is no difference between one thing and another, he is surely far removed from human nature and must have cast off humanity; Ethics book 3. Pain and distress are opposed to pleasure. And one must also consider how much more men flee evils than pursue goods. For they do not seek honourable things as much as they avoid base ones. For who ever desires honour, who glory, who praise, who any decoration as much as they flee disgrace, infamy, insult and dishonour? The pain of these things is grievous. There is a kind of men born for honour but corrupted by bad training and perverse opinions. Therefore in exhorting and persuading, our purpose will indeed be this: to teach by what means we can obtain good things and avoid evils. But among men well educated we will speak much of praise and honour, and we will treat especially those kinds of virtue which are concerned with protecting and increasing the common usefulness of men. But if we speak among the untaught and inexperienced, let profits, emoluments, pleasures and the avoidance of pains be put forward, and insults and ignominies added too. For there is no one so rustic that insult and dishonour do not move him greatly, even if the thing itself is less honourable. Therefore what concerns usefulness will be found from what has been said.

units.la: Et illud uidendum, quanto magis homines mala fugiant, quàm sequantur bona. ) Quæ ratio esset in suadendo, dissuadendoq;, politis & impolitis hominibus adhibenda, separatim docuit: nunc quæ utrisque communia sint, docet. Quia igitur nullus est tam agrestis (inquit Cicero) id est, ferus & impolitus, quem non si minus dignitas ipsa & laus, at ignominia & dolor moucat, utriusq; generis mala sunt proponenda. Sunt enim, ut idem Cicero de Officijs lib.1. ait, qui in rebus contrarijs parum sibi constent: voluptatem sequerissime contemnant, in dolore sint molliores: gloriam negligant, frangantur infamia. Cur autem magis homines mala fugiant, quàm sequantur bona: aut non tam honesta expetant, quàm uitent turpia, cum præsertim genus hominum sit ad honestatem natum, ut ipse inquit, rationem unam reddit, quod malo cultu prauisq; opinionibus corruptum sit. de qua re etiam etiā in Tusculanæ tertiæ proœmio quæritur:ubi esse quidē nobis igniculos et semina innata uirtu tũ scribit,sed ea celeriter malis morib.opinionibusq; depravatis, sic extingui,ut nusquā naturæ lumen appareat. cuius mali caussas, ait esse peruersam educatione parentū & magistrorū,tum lectione poetarū, postremò consuetudine vulgi atq; imperitæ multitudinis. Accedit etiā (quod ipse ignorauit) uitiositas illa ab ipso cŏceptu & ortu cŏtracta, propter primi parentis flagitiū: ita ut cum lacte ipso,immò cū spiritu & uita, errorē suxisse atq; hausisse uideamur.Est præterea in ipsa mali natura hæc uis,ut plus possit ad corrumpendū, quàm bonum ad sanandū & conferuandū:quemadmodū exiguū ueneni,totū uini ca dū potest inficere: & atramẽti uncia,lactis pon do atrū saccere. Cõsideratis igitur generib.hominum atq; naturis,in cohortādo & suadendo eas sentētias eligemus,quæ naturis eorū sint consentanceæ maximè.Doctis & politis laudē & decus, maximeq; ea uirtutū genera quæ in cōmuni hominū utilitate tuenda augēdaq; uersantur, proponemus: cuiusmodi sunt, lusticia primùm ipsa, deinde fides, liberalitas,religio,pietas,bonitas, fortitudo,atq; id genus alia, ad hominum societatem tuendã accommodata.Indoctis uerò & im- peritis,emolumēta,uoluptates, cæteraq; huiusmodi. Vtrisq; aut in communi, dedecus & ignominiam, tanquam stimulos & aculeos admonebimus, quib. eos ad id quod uolumus impellamus. Quod si horum exempla requiris, legendae tibi erunt potissimum perorationes Philippicarum, primae, secundae, tertiae, quartae, sextae. Sed quaedam uocabula expendamus. Ignominia, est honoris ex aliqua uel turpitudine uel iniuria diminutio. Infamia, famae gloriaeq; obscuratio. hinc dicimus, ignominia seu infamia notare. Cotumelia (ut 2. Rhet.lib.Arist. definit) dicitur, cum quis laedit ac dolore afficit aliquem in ea re, unde illi qui patitur, ignominia nascitur. uel breuius: Contumelia est, cum conceptione iniuria: à contemnendo enim contumelia dicitur, ut Vlp.ait de Iniur. & famos. libellis.l.1. Cicero uero in Oratione pro Coelio, maledicti speciem facit. nam tria subiicit maledicto, contumeliam, conuicium, & urbanitatem. Atque haec de utilitate: deinceps de eo quod fieri possit, aut non possit, praecipietur.
units.tr: And one must also consider how much more eagerly men avoid evils than they pursue goods. He has taught separately what method of persuading and dissuading should be used with polished and unpolished men; now he teaches what is common to both. Because there is no one so rustic (says Cicero), that is, so wild and unpolished, whom honour and praise do not move, if not more, at least disgrace and pain do, the evils of both kinds must be set before them. For, as the same Cicero says in De Officiis book 1, there are those who are inconsistent in their opposing attitudes: they utterly despise pleasure yet are softer in pain; they neglect glory yet are crushed by infamy. But why men avoid evils more than they pursue goods, or seek less what is honourable than they shun what is shameful, since the human race is born for honour, as he says, he explains by one cause: it has been corrupted by bad culture and depraved opinions. He also inquires into this matter in the preface to the third book of the Tusculan Disputations, where he writes that in us there are indeed little sparks and seeds of innate virtue, but these are quickly extinguished by bad morals and depraved opinions, so that the light of nature appears nowhere. He says the causes of this evil are a perverse upbringing by parents and teachers, then the reading of poets, and finally the habit of the common and unskilled crowd. Added to these is (which he himself did not know) that vice contracted from the very conception and origin, on account of the crime of our first parent; so that we seem to have sucked in error with the very milk, indeed with the breath and life itself. Moreover, there is in the very nature of evil this power, that it can do more to corrupt than good can do to heal and preserve: just as a little poison can infect a whole cask of wine, and an ounce of ink can blacken a pound of milk. Therefore, having considered the kinds and natures of men, in exhorting and persuading we shall choose those sentiments which best agree with their natures. To the learned and polished we shall propose praise and honour, and especially those kinds of virtue which are concerned with preserving and increasing the common good of men: such as justice first of all, then faith, liberality, religion, piety, kindness, fortitude, and others of that sort, suited to preserving human society. But to the unlearned and unskilled, profits, pleasures, and other things of this kind. To both, in common, we shall point out disgrace and dishonour as goads and spurs, by which we drive them to what we want. If you seek examples of these, you should read chiefly the perorations of the Philippics: the first, second, third, fourth and sixth. But let us weigh some words. Ignominy is a diminishing of honour through some baseness or injury. Infamy is an obscuring of fame and glory. Hence we say to brand with ignominy or infamy. Contumely (as Aristotle defines it in the second book of the Rhetoric) is said to occur when someone harms and afflicts another in a matter from which disgrace arises for the one who suffers it.

units.tr: ON CAUSES

units.tr: What can be brought about, and whether it can, and how easily it can be done and how far it is expedient, is commonly asked, and this must be seen chiefly from those causes which bring about any matter. Causes are of several kinds, for some are of such a nature that they themselves are discussed in the preface to the third book of the Tusculan Disputations, where he writes that in us there are indeed little sparks and seeds of innate virtue, but these are quickly extinguished by bad morals and depraved opinions, so that the light of nature appears nowhere. Cicero, however, in the speech for Caelius, makes a kind of slander: for he places three things under slander, contumely, reproach and urbanity. And these things concerning utility; next it will be taught what can or cannot be done.

units.la: DE CAVSSIS.
units.tr: ON THE CAUSES.

units.la: Quid autem possit effici, nec ne possit, in quo etiā quam facile possit, quāqʒ expediat, quæri solet, maxime ex caussis ijs, que quamqʒ rem efficiat, est uidendū. Caussarū autē genera sunt plura, nā sunt aliæ quæ ipsæ conficiunt, aliæ quæ uim aliquam ad conficiendũ afferunt. Itaque illę superiores, conficientes uocentur: hæ reliquæ ponantur in eo genere, ut sine his confici non possit. Conficiens autem causa alia est absoluta & perfecta per se, alia aliquid adiuuans, & efficiendi socia quædā: cuius generis uis uaria est, & sæpe aut maior, aut minor, ut & illa quæ maximam uim habet, sola sæpe causa dicatur.
units.tr: Whether something can be brought about, and whether it can be done easily and is expedient, is usually asked; and above all one must look at the causes by which each thing is effected. There are several kinds of causes. Some bring a thing about themselves; others contribute some force towards bringing it about. The former may accordingly be called effecting causes, and the rest belong to the class of those without which the thing cannot be effected. An effecting cause is either complete and sufficient in itself, or helps in some way as a kind of partner in producing the effect. The force of this second kind varies and is often greater or less, so that the cause with the greatest force is often alone called the cause.

units.la: Quid autem possit effici, nec ne possit.) Primus locus, atq; adeò deliberationis finis, utilitas est. Secundus, de ui efficiedi quærit. De utilitate dictum est, iam de facultate dicetur. At ex causis potissimum uis efficiendi spectatur. quæ causa fuit Ciceroni, ut hoc loco partitione causarum proponeret cognoscendam: quæ cognitio ad conielturas quoque pertinet. subtilius tamen causarum genera docuit in Topicis, utpote proprio & idoneo subtilioris artis loco: nunc autem crassiore Minerua, accommodatè tamen ad præsens institutum. Nos quoq; , quoniam satis apertus est locus, genera ipsa in tabula describemus: post, pauca annotabimus.
units.tr: "Whether something can be brought about, or not." The first topic, and indeed the end of deliberation, is usefulness. The second asks about the power of bringing about. Usefulness has been discussed; feasibility will now be discussed. But the power of bringing about is chiefly judged from the causes. This was Cicero's reason for proposing here, by a division of causes, something to be known, and this knowledge also pertains to conjectures. He taught the kinds of causes more subtly in the Topics, as being the proper and fitting place for the finer art. Now, with a coarser Minerva, yet suitably for the present purpose, we too, since the topic is clear enough, will set out the kinds themselves in a table, and afterwards add a few remarks.

units.la: Causa
units.tr: Cause

units.la: PARTITIONES.
units.tr: DIVISIONS.

units.la: Causarum alie Sine quibus non efficiuntur Locus Planum, montosus Salubris, pestilens Cultus, incultus Facultates Arma, sive instrumenta Pecunia Socij Materia Personæ - Tempora Contra quas Cum quibus Nox, Dies, Hyems, Æstas Confecientes; alie Impellentes propter Finem Laus & gloria Voluptas Principium Consilium Colloquium Natura Emolumentum Adiuvantes & socii, quarum alie Maxime Natura Magister Imperator Maiores Vsus Præcepta Centurio Minores Studium Miles Equus Absolute, ut Sol lucis Ignis calor Prætor iudiciorum.
units.tr: Of causes, some are those without which things are not effected: place, flat or mountainous; healthy or pestilential; cultivated or uncultivated; resources, arms or instruments; money; allies; material; persons; times, with whom and against whom; night, day, winter, summer. Effecting causes are others, which impel: on account of the end, praise and glory, pleasure; the beginning, counsel, conversation, nature, advantage. Helpers and allies, of which some are chief: nature, master, commander, greater experience, precepts; centurion; lesser ones: zeal, soldier, horse. Absolute ones, as the sun is to light, fire to heat, the praetor to judgments.

units.la: Posse fieri dicuntur, quae quoquo modo, siue facile siue difficile, fieri possunt. Facilia uero, ut ait Aristoteles lib. Rhet. 1. sunt, quae uel sine molestia, uel breui tempore confici possunt. Difficilia, quae cum molestia, uel temporis longitudine fiunt. Expedire est, non modo utile esse, uerum etiam ex dignitate & honestate esse. sunt enim quatuor haec uerba distinguenda, ut etiam Cicero ipse distinguit: Oportere, licere, decere, expedire. Oportere, est officij: Licere, legu & iuris: Decere, temporum & personarum: Expedire, utilitatis & honestatis.
units.tr: Those things are said to be possible which can be done in some way, whether easily or with difficulty. Easy things, as Aristotle says in the first book of the Rhetoric, are those that can be accomplished either without trouble or in a short time; difficult things are those done with trouble or over a long time. To be expedient is not merely to be useful, but also to accord with dignity and honour. For these four words must be distinguished, as Cicero himself distinguishes them: oportere, licere, decere, expedire. Oportere (what ought to be done) belongs to duty; licere (what is permitted) to law and right; decere (what is fitting) to times and persons; expedire (what is advantageous) to usefulness and honour.

units.la: Sunt autem aliae causae, quae aut propter principium, aut propter exitum Conficientes uocantur. Cum autem quaeritur, quid sit optimum facto, aut utilitas, aut spes efficiendi ad assentiendum impellit animos.
units.tr: Some causes, however, are called effecting because of their beginning or their end. When it is asked what is best to do, either usefulness or the hope of accomplishing it drives minds to assent.

units.la: Sunt autem aliae causae. ) Has causas in conficientium causarum genere reponit: quoniam etsi non necessario, tamen impulsione quadam conficiunt. Quamobrem & nos impellentes appellabimus. Sunt autem duae, Principium & finis. Principium est, ut Arist. Physic. 2. ait, unde primum mutationis aut quietis origo ducitur: ut is qui consilium dedit, aut coepit, causa est: & pater filij. ueluti etiam si dicas, Helenā caussam fuisse excidij Troiani: aut Catonē Carthaginis euertēdæ, qui cōfiliū dedit. Cicero alibi uocat primordia rerū, & quasi præcurrētia. Finis est, cuius caussa aliquid fit: ut ambulatio propter ualetudinē: bellū propter commoditatē, aut gloriā, aut pacē: doctrina propter utilitatē et dignitatē.
units.tr: "Some causes, however." He places these causes in the class of effecting causes, since, although they do not bring about by necessity, they do so by a certain impulsion. Wherefore we shall also call them impelling causes. There are two: the beginning and the end. The beginning, as Aristotle says in the second book of the Physics, is that from which the first origin of change or rest is derived: thus the one who gave counsel or started a thing is a cause; the father of the son; just as if you were to say, Helen was the cause of the fall of Troy, or Cato of the destruction of Carthage, since he gave the counsel. Cicero elsewhere calls these the first beginnings of things, as it were running ahead. The end is that for the sake of which something is done: walking for the sake of health; war for the sake of convenience, or glory, or peace; learning for the sake of usefulness and dignity.

units.la: Et quoniam de utilitate iam diximus, de efficiēdi ratione dicamus. Quo toto genere quibuscum, & cō tra quos, quo tempore, aut quo lo‑ co', aut quibus facultatibus armo‑rū, pecuniæ, fociorū, earūue rerum quæ ad quāqʒ rem efficiendā pertinent, possimus uti, requirendū est.
units.tr: And since we have already spoken of usefulness, let us speak of the manner of bringing about. In this whole kind we must inquire with whom, and against whom, at what time, in what place, and with what resources of arms, money, allies, or other things pertaining to the effecting of each matter, we may act.

units.la: Et quoniam de utilitate iam diximus.) Attributiones numerat, quas Græci ωήρισμένοις uocant, propterea quod negotia ipsa circunstent, & sine quibus efficitur nihil: cuiusmodi sunt, personæ, tempus, locus, facultates, instrumenta, & cætera id genus.
units.tr: "And since we have already spoken of usefulness." He enumerates the attributes, which the Greeks call [περιεστηκότα], because the matters themselves are surrounded by them, and without them nothing is effected. Such are persons, time, place, resources, instruments, and the like.

units.la: Neque solum ea sunt quæ nobis suppetunt, sed etiam illa quæ aduersantur, uidenda. Et si ex contentione procliuiora erunt nostra, non solum effici posse, quæ suademus, erit pere persuadendum: sed curandũ etiam, ut illa facilia, procliuia, iucunda uideantur.
units.tr: We must consider not only those things which lie at our disposal but also those which oppose us. And if, on comparing the two sides, our own prospects prove more favourable, we must not only persuade that what we advise can be done, but also take care that those things appear easy, favourable and pleasant.

units.la: Neq; solum ea sunt.)
units.tr: Not only those things are.

units.la: Dissuadentibus autem aut utilitas labefactanda est, aut efficiendi difficultates efferendae: neque aliis ex praeceptis, sed ijsdem ex suasionis locis.
units.tr: Those dissuading must either weaken the usefulness or magnify the difficulties of accomplishing the thing; and this is done not from other precepts but from the same topics of persuasion.

units.la: Dissuadentibus autem.)
units.tr: Those dissuading.

units.la: Vterque uero ad augendum habeat exemplorum, aut recentium, quo notiora sint, aut ueterum, quo plus autoritatis habeant, copiam. Maximeq; sit in hoc genere meditatus, ut possit uel utilia, ac necessaria saepe honestis, uel hæc illis anteferre. Ad commouendos autem animos maxime proficient, si incitandi erunt huiusmodi sententiæ, quæ ad explendas cupiditates, aut ad odiū satiandum, aut ad ulciscendas iniurias pertinebunt. Sin autem reprimendi, de incerto statu fortunæ, dubiisq; euentis rerum futurarum, & retinendis suis fortunis, si erunt secundæ: sin autem aduersæ, de periculo commonendi. Atq; hi quidem sunt perorationis loci. Principia autem in sententiis dicendis breuia esse debebunt. Non enim supplex, ut ad iudicem, uenit orator: sed hortator, atq; autor. Quare proponere, qua mente dicat, quid uelit, quibus de rebus dicturus sit, debet, hortari que ad se breuiter dicentem audiendum.
units.tr: Each side should have a plentiful supply of examples to amplify its case, either recent, so that they are better known, or ancient, so that they carry more authority. And the speaker should especially practise in this kind, so that he can often prefer things useful and necessary to things honourable, or the reverse. To move minds, the most effective sentiments will be those that are to incite men towards satisfying their desires, sating their hatred, or avenging their injuries. But if men are to be restrained, then one should speak of the uncertain state of fortune, the doubtful outcome of future events, and of keeping one's fortunes if they are favourable; or, if they are adverse, of warning against danger. These are the topics of the peroration. The beginnings of speeches in giving opinions should be brief. For the orator does not come as a suppliant, as he would before a judge, but as an exhorter and adviser. Therefore he ought to set out in what spirit he speaks, what he wants, and on what matters he is about to speak, and to exhort his hearers briefly to listen to him.

units.la: Vtrq; uero ad augendum.) De tractatione z delideliberationis hic agitur, cuius ordine tabella ob oculos ponemus, ut clarius perspiciatur, si prius quaedam annotauerimus. Et primum de amplificatione: de qua, quod antea suo loco satis dictum sit, nihil dicemus. Exemplum est, alicuius facti aut dicti praeteriti, cum certi autoris nomine propositio. ad Herecn. lib. 4. Exempla quoniam testimoniorum similia sunt, conuenit, quemadmodum illa, a probatissimis sumi: quae et recentia, et uetera sunt, et nostrae ciuitatis, et externa. noua et nostratia notiora sunt: uetera et aliena plus habet autoritatis, si modo sint grauia aut personarum dignitate, aut cuentuum magnitudine, aut rerum uarietate. Tenenda igitur, praeter alia, est Oratori omnis antiquitas, exemplorumque uis, ut Cicero de Oratore affirmat. In comparatione utilium et honestorum debet Orator esse meditatus, id est, e. ... citatus ac paratus, ut possit nunc utilia sive necessaria honestis, nunc honesta utilibus anteferre: quod quidem saepenumero faciendum est. Et facere expeditius poterit, si locos communes de his rebus habuerit paratos ex omni de moribus doctrina. Motus diximus esse animi incitationem, sive appetitus uehementiorem: cuius genera prima sint, aegritudo, metus, voluptas, et cupiditas. Sed Cicero hic cupiditatis nomine, non tam cupiditatem ipsam, quam intellexit, quae opponitur metui. Est autem spes, expectatio boni: Odiū uero, ira inueterata: Vltio ab iracūdia proficiscitur, quæ est ulciscēdi libido. nā quod in beneficio gratia, id in iniuria ultio nominatur, ut postea dicet Cicero. Solicitudo, ægritudo cū cogitatione definitur. Metus, opinio impendētis mali. Idcirco autē solicitudo & metus in animis reprimēdis & sedādis adhibētur, quoniā nihil est quod iratū, odioq; inflammatū, & sibi præsidentem, magis restinguat & frenet, quàm si solicitudinē metumq; injicias, ut Arist.li.2.Rhet.docet. Nō enim sup.)Ratio, cur principia in hoc genere breuia esse debeat: Quo niā, inquit, ut hortator atq; autor, id est suasor, aut dissuasor, rei suscipiēdæ, aut nō suscipiendæ, atq; ad dandū cōsiliū venit, quod maximè cupit auditor. Initio enim Partitionū dixit, Principia uel nō longa, uel sæpe nulla in dando cōsilio esse: quod ad audiendum, qui deliberant, satis sint sua causa parati. Secus in iudicijs, ubi ad iudicem supplex uenit Orator, idcirco maiore molitione est præparādus, et cōciliandus. Hic aut satis est, si intelligāt, qua mēte dicat, & quid uelit suasor: nimirū, cum uenire propter ipsorū utilitatē, aut dignitatem, ex quo beneuolentia: & quibus de rebus dicturus fit. ut Cicero in Manliana, de genere belli primùm, deinde de magnitudine, tum de Imperatore deligendo: ex quo docilitas. Postremò se breuiter esse dicturum polliceri debet, ex quo attentio comparatur. Nam breuitas non modò Senatoris, sed etiam oratoris magna laus est, in sententia dicenda, ut Cicero ait de Legibus lib.3.
units.tr: Each side, to amplify. Here the handling of deliberation is treated; we shall set its order before the eyes in a table, so that it may be seen more clearly, once we have first noted certain things. And first, about amplification: since this has been said sufficiently in its own place, we shall say nothing more about it. An example is a proposition of some past deed or saying, with the name of a certain author (Ad Herennium, book 4). Since examples are similar to testimonies, they should, as with those, be taken from the most approved sources: both recent and ancient, both from our own state and from abroad. New and domestic examples are better known; old and foreign ones carry more authority, provided they are weighty either by the dignity of the persons, the magnitude of the events, or the variety of the matters. Therefore, among other things, the orator must have command of all antiquity and the force of examples, as Cicero affirms in De Oratore. In comparing the useful and the honourable, the orator ought to be practised, that is, trained and ready, so that he can now prefer useful or necessary things to honourable ones, and now honourable things to useful ones; and this must indeed very often be done. He will be able to do it more readily if he has commonplaces on these matters ready from all moral teaching. We said that emotions are the stirring of the mind, or a more vehement appetite; the first kinds of these are grief, fear, pleasure and desire. But Cicero here, under the name of desire, meant not so much desire itself as what is opposed to fear. Hope is the expectation of good; hatred is long-standing anger; vengeance arises from wrath and is the lust for revenge. For what is called gratitude in a benefit, that is called vengeance in an injury, as Cicero will say later. Anxiety, grief, is defined together with a thought. Fear is the opinion of impending evil. Anxiety and fear are applied to restrain and calm minds, because nothing more quenches and curbs a man who is angry, inflamed with hatred, and in control of himself than if you instil anxiety and fear, as Aristotle teaches in the second book of the Rhetoric. For not... The reason why the beginnings in this kind ought to be brief is this: the exhorter and adviser, that is, the one who persuades or dissuades from undertaking or not undertaking a matter, comes to give counsel, which is what the hearer most desires. For at the beginning of the Partitions he said that beginnings, either not long or often none at all, are enough when giving counsel, since those who deliberate are already sufficiently prepared to listen by their own cause. It is otherwise in judicial cases, where the orator comes as a suppliant to the judge and must therefore be prepared and win him over with greater effort. Here it is enough if they understand in what spirit the speaker speaks and what the adviser wants: namely, that he has come for the sake of their usefulness or dignity, whence benevolence arises; and on what matters he is about to speak, as Cicero does in the Manilian law speech: first on the kind of war, then on its magnitude, then on the choice of commander, whence docility arises. Lastly he ought to promise that he will speak briefly, whence attention is won. For brevity is great praise not only of a senator but also of an orator in giving an opinion, as Cicero says in the third book of De Legibus.

units.la: Tota autem oratio simplex & grauis, & sententijs debet ornatior esse, quàm uerbis.
units.tr: The whole speech should be plain and dignified, and it should be more ornate in its thoughts than in its words.

units.la: Tota autem oratio. ) De elocutionis tractatione intelligenda sunt haec, in qua tria requiruntur: simplicitas in uerbis, ut uidelicet quàm minimus sit uerborum ornatus, nec ex uerbo dilatetur oratio: Grauitas in rebus, nam in seueritate consilij uix est locus iocis: Ornatus in sententijs, quod sic intelligendum est, non ut sententiarum ornamenta adhibenda sint, sed ut loco eorum sententias adhibeamus de uita & moribus hominum sumptas, quae ex locis communibus de quaque re sumendae sunt. Vniuersa autem haec tractationis ratio, hac tabella dilucidè continetur. Tractatio deliberationis considerātur Amplificatione, quæ est potissimum perorationis, habetœ Exemplorum copia Recentiorum quæ sunt vel Nostra Externa. Veterum Copiratio nem Utilium, sive necessariorum Honestorum. Commotiones animorum Cupiditatem, sive spem Odium Ultionem, sive iram. Sedationes, quæ fit aut Sollicitudine in secundis retinendis, Metu in adversis amittendis. Principiis, quæ constat Brevitate Benevolentia Docilitate Attentione. Elocutione Simplici, verbis Graui, rebus Ornata, sententiis.
units.tr: "The whole speech": these remarks are to be understood as concerning the treatment of style, in which three things are required: simplicity in words, that is, that the ornament of words be as minimal as possible, and the speech not be stretched out by means of wordiness; dignity in subject matter, for in serious counsel there is hardly room for jokes; and ornament in thoughts. This last is to be understood not as meaning that the ornaments of thoughts are to be applied, but that in their place we should apply thoughts drawn from the life and manners of men, which are to be taken from the commonplaces about each subject. The whole method of this treatment is set out clearly in the following table. The treatment of deliberative oratory is considered under Amplification, which belongs chiefly to the peroration, and has: an abundance of examples, of recent ones, which are either our own or foreign, and of ancient ones; a comparison of the useful, or necessary, and the honourable; stirrings of the emotions: desire, or hope; hatred, or the wish for revenge, or anger; calmings, which come about either by anxiety in keeping prosperity, or by fear in losing adversity. The beginning consists of brevity, goodwill, docility and attention. Style is plain in words, dignified in subject matter, ornate in thoughts.

units.la: DE GENERE IVDICIALI.
units.tr: On the Judicial Genus.

units.la: C. F. Cognoui iam laudationis & suasionis locos: nūc quæ iudicijs accōmodata sunt expecto, idq; nobis genus restare unum puto. C. P. Recte intelligis, atq; eius quidē generis finis est æquitas; quæ non sim pliciter spectatur, sed ex comparatione nonnunq;: ut cū de uerissimo accusatore disputatur: aut cum hæreditatis sine lege, aut sine testamento petitur possessio: in quibus causis, quid æquius, æquissimum ue sit, quærit: quas ad causas facultas petitur argumentationū ex iis, de quibus mox dicetur, æquitatis locis.
units.tr: C. F. I already know the topics of praise and of persuasion; now I look for those suited to judgments, and I think one kind remains. C. P. You understand correctly. The end of this kind is equity, which is judged not simply but sometimes by comparison, as when it is disputed who is the most genuine accuser, or when possession of an inheritance is sought without law or without a will. In such cases the question is what is fairer or most fair, and the power of argument is sought from those topics of equity that will be discussed shortly.

units.la: C. F. Cognoui iam laudationis, & suasionis locos.) Transitione utitur filius, ut intelligat pater, cum & quæ tractata sunt meminisse, & quæ desiderantur intelligere. Superest enim causa iudicialis: quæ tractata, & in suas partes distributa, perfectæ erunt Oratoriæ partitiones. idcirco dicit, unum tantum restare genus.
units.tr: "I already know the topics of praise and of persuasion." The son uses a transition so that the father may understand both that the matters already treated have been remembered and that the remaining ones are grasped. For a judicial cause is what remains, and once it has been treated and divided into its parts, the Oratorical Partitions will be complete. Hence he says that only one kind remains.

units.la: C. P. Recte intelligis, atq; eius quidē generis finis est æquitas.) Quemadmodū reliquis causarum rum generib. suos fines proposuit, sic et nunc iudicijs fine esse dicit æquitatè: quæ quidè nō modo iudicialis causæ, uerùetiā omnis iuris & fons et finis esse dicitur. Est autem ea, quā Aristoteles, ut antè diximus, uocat ἐπιείκειαν: cstq; ius nō scrip ptum, naturæ hominis consentaneū, quo iura le gesq; scriptæ explicātur, & emendantur, ut Ari stot. Eth. 5. sentit. Ius enim omnia recta et inflexibilia exigit: æquitas uerò, de iure multū remittit.
units.tr: "You understand correctly, and the end of this kind is equity." Just as he set out ends for the other kinds of causes, so now he says that equity is the end of judicial causes. This equity is said to be the source and end not only of judicial causes but of all law. It is what Aristotle, as we said before, calls [ἐπιείκειαν] epieikeia: it is a law not written, agreeing with human nature, by which written laws and statutes are explained and corrected, as Aristotle thinks in the Ethics, book 5. For law demands that everything be right and unbending, whereas equity greatly relaxes the strictness of law.

units.la: Quæ nō simpliciter spectatur.) Aequitatis duplex est tractatio. Simplex: ut, æquum ne fit amico aduersus propinquū in iudicio adesse. & quæ comparationem habet: ut, Cicero ne an Cecilius Verrem accusare debeat. quod Cicero in prima Verrina, quæ Diuinatio dicitur, quærit.
units.tr: "Which is not viewed simply." Equity is treated in two ways. The simple way is whether it is fair for someone to appear in court against a relative of a friend. The comparative way is, for example, whether Cicero or Caecilius ought to prosecute Verres, which Cicero asks in the first Verrine, called the Divinatio.

units.la: Aut cū hæreditatis sine lege.) Vt excepli caussa: si duo uel plures nulla lege nulloq; testamento hæreditatem petant, tunc æquitate coparanda, cui danda sit hæreditas, cognoscitur. Qui autem hæreditatem petūt, aut alter nulla æquitate fretus, alter cum æquitate petit: uel uterq; ius habet. illic æquū cum iniquo cōparatur: hic cū æquo æquius, aut æquissimū. Et hoc est quod ait Cicero, in quibus causis quid æquius, æquissimum ue fit, quæritur. Quòd si quis dicat, Vnde petendi argumentationum loci? respondet Cicero, ex æquitatis partibus, de quibus paulo post dicetur.
units.tr: "Or when possession of an inheritance is sought without law." For instance, if two or more persons seek an inheritance with neither law nor will, then by comparing equity it is determined to whom the inheritance should be given. If one claimant relies on no equity while the other claims with equity, or if both have a right, then what is fair is compared with what is unfair in the first case, and with what is fair, fairer or most fair in the second. This is what Cicero means when he says that in such cases the question is what is fairer or most fair. If someone asks, "Whence are the topics of argument to be sought?", Cicero answers: from the parts of equity, which will be discussed shortly.

units.la: Atqș
units.tr: And

units.la: Atque etiam ante iudicium de constituendo ipso iudicio solet esse contentio, cum aut sit ne actio illi qui agit, aut iam ne sit, aut num iam esse desierit, aut illa ne lege, his ne verbis sit actio quæritur: quæ etiam si antequam res in iudicium venit, aut concertata, aut dijudicata, aut confecta non sunt, tamen in ipsis iudiciis permagnum sæpe habet pondus, cum ita dicitur: Plus petisti, sero petisti, non fuit tua petitio, non a me, non hac lege, non his verbis, non hoc iudicio: quarum causarum genus est positum in iure ciuili, quod est in priuatarum ac publicarum rerum lege: aut more positum: cuius scientia neglecta ab oratoribus plerisque, nobis ad dicendum necessaria videtur.
units.tr: Indeed, before the trial there is often a dispute about establishing the very court: whether there is an action for the one who sues, or whether there is now none, or whether it has ceased to exist, or whether the action is under this law or those words. Even if these matters have not yet been contested, decided or concluded before the case comes to trial, they often carry great weight in the trial itself, when one says: "You sued for too much; you sued too late; your claim was not valid; not against me; not under this law; not in these words; not in this court." Such kinds of cause are laid down in civil law, which rests on the statutes or customs governing private and public affairs. Orators for the most part neglect knowledge of these matters, but it seems necessary for us in speaking.

units.la: Atq; etiam ante iudicium.) Hæc quæ iam explicare aggreditur Cicero, pertinent ad eum statum, quem translationis in Rhetoricis consuerunt appellare, quem & ipse Cicero adolescens statum fecit: sed postea eruditior factus, repudiauit, etiamsi Hermagoram eius inuentorem fuisse existimaret.Hoc autem loco aperte subijcit qualitati, quemadmodum etiam de Oratore fecit: & recte quidè. nam quæcunq; in hac parte requiruntur, ea iuris & iniuriæ partibus contincentur, qui loci qualitatis omnino sunt. Definiamus tamen translationem, ut ex ea quid hoc caput contineat, intelligatur. Translatio est, cum aut quem, aut qui cum, aut quomodo, aut apud quos, aut quo iure, aut quo tempore, agere oporteat, quæritur: aut omnino aliquid de commutatione aut infirmatione actionis agitur. quæ definitio consentanea est ijs, quæ hoc loco tradit Cicero. Nam cum de æquitate quæritur, id fit duobus modis: aut ante iudicium, uel in ipso iudicio. ante quidem, aut persona cõtrouersiam ficit: ut, sit ne actio illi qui agit. uel tempus: ut, iam ne sit, aut nũ iam esse desierit actionis tempus? uel lex: ut, Illa ne lege sit agendum, ut ipse pro Cluëtio & pro Cecinna disputat. Vel verba pacti, aut scripti: ut, ijs ne uerbis, aut scripto sit actio legitima. uel quantitas: ut, Plus petisti. uel forma: ut, non hoc iudicio, id est iudicij forma agendum fuit. quæ omnia ante ipsum iudicium quæ ri solent. Antequam res in iudicium uenit.) Id est, antequam constituta sit actio. Aut certata.) id est, à partibus disputata. Aut dijudicata.) hoc est, disceptatoris & iudicis sentètia z pronunciata. Aut cōstītā.) Hoc est, absoluta ac perēpta, ita ut nulla iam actio aut appellatio sit. Sūt enim ij gradus iudiciorum. Cōstituuntur enim prius iudicia & actiones: deinde cōcertantur & disputantur caussæ: post dijudicantur: postremò consiciuntur & perimūtur. Quæ, etiāsi pleraq; horum ante iudicium tractantur, tamen in ipsis iudicijs permagnum sæpe habet pondus, & uictoriam sæpe alteri afferūt parti. ut si quis petitori dicere possit, Plus petisti. nam, quemadmodum inquit Cicero, caussa cadit is qui plus petit quàm par est: & qui non quemadmodum oportet egerit. Refertur autem hoc ad quantitatem, ut diximus: Sero petisti, ad tempus. non fuit tua petitio: id est, iure tu petere nō debuisti: non àme, quæ ad personam referuntur. De reliquis diximus.
units.tr: "And indeed before the trial." What Cicero now sets out to explain pertains to the state which the rhetoricians usually call the translation (transference), a state which Cicero himself as a young man made into a category, though later, becoming more learned, he rejected it, even though he thought Hermagoras was its inventor. In this passage he openly appends it to the quality, as he also did in the De Oratore, and rightly so. For whatever is required in this part is contained within the parts of right and wrong, which are altogether topics of quality. Nevertheless, let us define the translation so that it is clear what this head contains. The translation is the question of whom, or with whom, or in what manner, or before whom, or under what law, or at what time, one ought to bring an action; or generally, some matter concerning the alteration or invalidation of an action is treated. This definition agrees with what Cicero teaches in this place. For when the question of equity arises, it does so in two ways: either before the trial or in the trial itself. Before the trial, it makes a controversy either about the person, as whether there is an action against the one who sues, or about the time, as whether the time for the action is now past or has ceased to be; or about the law, as whether one should proceed under this law, as Cicero himself argues for Cluentius and for Caecina; or about the words of the agreement or document, as whether the action is valid under these words or in writing; or about the amount, as "You sued for too much"; or about the form, as "not in this court", that is, the action should have been brought in a different form of court. All these are usually inquired into before the trial itself. "Before the matter comes into court": that is, before the action has been established. "Or contested": that is, debated by the parties. "Or decided": that is, pronounced upon by the sentence of the arbiter or judge. "Or concluded": that is, finished and brought to an end, so that there is no longer any action or appeal. For there are these stages of judgments: first the courts and actions are established, then the causes are contested and disputed, then they are decided, and finally they are concluded and ended. Although most of these are treated before the trial, they often carry great weight in the trials themselves, and often give victory to the other party. For example, one may say to the plaintiff, "You sued for too much." For, as Cicero says, a cause falls for one who asks more than is right and who has not proceeded as he ought. This refers to quantity, as we said; "You sued too late" refers to time; "your claim was not valid" means that by right you ought not to have sued; "not against me" refers to the person. We have spoken of the rest.

units.la: Quarum caussarum genus est positū in iure ciuili.) Hoc dicit, ne quis putet ex locis æquitatis solis, se omnia probare posse. Nā et ius ciuile necessariū est, quēadmodū ipse quoq; de Oratore multis argumētis ostēdit. Perdiscēdū, inquit, ius ciuile, cognoscēdæ leges, percipienda omnis antiquitas, Senatoria consuetudo, disciplina Reip. iura sociorum, fœdera, pactiones, caussa imperij cognoscenda est.
units.tr: "Of which kind of cause the genus is laid down in civil law." He says this so that no one thinks he can prove everything from the topics of equity alone. For civil law is also necessary, as he himself shows by many arguments in the De Oratore. "Civil law must be thoroughly learned," he says, "the laws must be known, all antiquity must be grasped, the custom of the Senate, the discipline of the commonwealth, the rights of allies, treaties and agreements, and the cause of empire must be understood."

units.la: Quare de cōstituendis actionib.
units.tr: On the setting up of actions

units.la: accipiendis subeundisq; iudiciis, de excipiēda iniquitate actionis, de cōparanda æquitate, quod ea fere generis eius sunt, ut quandoq; in ipsum iudicium sæpe dilabantur, tamē ante iudicia tractanda uideantur, paululū ea seporo à iudiciis, tempore magis agendi q; disimilitudine generis.
units.tr: on admitting and undertaking trials, on excluding unfairness in an action, and on securing equity. Since these matters generally belong to the kind that often slip into the trial itself, they nonetheless seem to be treated before trials, and I separate them a little from trials, more by the time of pleading than by any difference in kind.

units.la: Quare de constituendis actionibus.) Constituere actiones, est actorem admittere: qui cū admissus est, agere iure potest.
units.tr: Quare de constituendis actionibus.) To set up actions is to admit the plaintiff; once he has been admitted, he can lawfully bring suit.

units.la: Accipiendis subeundisq; iudiciis.) Accipere iudicia, est formam iudicij probare, nulla exceptione oppositā: itemq; actoris intentionem non caussari. Ex quo sequitur, iam subeundum et ferendum illud iudicium, cum sit admissum.
units.tr: Accipiendis subeundisq; iudiciis.) To accept a trial is to approve the form of the trial, with no exception raised against it, and likewise not to challenge the plaintiff's claim. From this it follows that the trial, once admitted, must now be undergone and endured.

units.la: De excipienda iniquitate actionis.) Excipere iniquitatem, est actoris dolum malum cauere, ne tibi in iudicio fiat iniuria.
units.tr: De excipienda iniquitate actionis.) To exclude unfairness is to guard against the plaintiff's malicious deceit, so that no wrong is done to you in the trial.

units.la: De cōparanda æquitate.) Vt qui sit accusator, aut petitor admittendus, intelligas, æquitatis ipsius comparatione: quid æquum, quid æquius, quid æquissimum, ut ante diximus. Hæc omnia, etsi interdum in ipsum iudicium ueniunt, id tamen fieri nō deberet. nam ante iudicium potius tractanda sunt, et discutienda: ut nihil postea sit, quod pronunciata. Aut cõfecta.) Hoc est, absoluta ac perépta, ita ut nulla iam actio aut appellatio sit. Sūt enim ij gradus iudiciorum. Costituuntur enim priùs iudicia & actiones: deinde cõcertantur & disputantur caussæ: post dijudicantur: postremò consiciuntur & perimūtur. Quæ, etiasi pleraq; horum ante iudicium tractantur, tamen in ipsis iudicijs permagnum sæpe habet pondus, & uictoriam sæpe alteri afferūt parti. ut si quis petitori dicere possit, Plus petisti. nam, quemadmodum inquit Cicero, caussa cadit is qui plus petit quàm par est: & qui non quemadmodum oportet egerit. Refertur autem hoc ad quantitatem, ut diximus: Sero petisti, ad tempus. non fuit tua petitio: id est, iure tu petere nõ debuisti: non à me, quæ ad personam referuntur. De reliquis diximus.
units.tr: De cōparanda æquitate.) So that you may understand who ought to be admitted as accuser or claimant, by comparing equity itself: what is fair, what is fairer, and what is fairest, as we said before. Although all these matters sometimes come up in the trial itself, that should not happen. For they ought to be handled and examined before the trial, so that nothing remains afterwards that is pronounced. Or completed.) That is, finished and brought to an end, so that there is no longer any action or appeal. For there are these stages of trials: first the trials and actions are set up; then the cases are contested and disputed; afterwards they are decided; finally they are concluded and ended. And although most of these are dealt with before the trial, they often carry great weight in the trials themselves and often give victory to the other party. For example, one may say to the claimant, "You have claimed too much." For, as Cicero says, the case falls to the one who claims more than is right, and who has not pleaded as he ought. This refers to quantity, as we said: "You claimed too late, at the wrong time": your claim was not valid, that is, you ought not to have claimed it by law. The other points, which relate to the person, we have discussed.

units.la: Quarum caussarum genus est positū in iure ciuili.) Hoc dicit, ne quis putet ex locis æquitatis solis, se omnia probare posse. Nã et ius ciuile necessariũ est, quëadmodū ipse quoq; de Oratore multis argumētis ostēdit. Perdiscēdū, inquit, ius ciuile, cognoscēdæ leges, percipienda omnis antiquitas, Senatoria consuetudo, disciplina Reip. iura sociorum, fœdera, pastiones, caussa imperij cognoscenda est.
units.tr: "The kind of these cases rests in civil law." He says this so that no one thinks he can prove everything from considerations of equity alone. For civil law is also necessary, as Cicero himself shows by many arguments in De Oratore. "The civil law must be thoroughly learned," he says, "the laws must be known, all antiquity must be grasped, senatorial custom, the discipline of the republic, the rights of allies, treaties, agreements, and the basis of imperial power must be understood."

units.la: Quare de costituendis actionib.
units.tr: Why on the setting up of actions

units.tr: De excipienda iniquitate actionis.) To exclude unfairness is to guard against the plaintiff's malicious deceit, so that no wrong is done to you in the trial.

units.la: De cõparanda æquitate.) Vt qui sit accusator, aut petitor admittendus, intelligas, æquitatis ipsius comparatione: quid æquum, quid æquius, quid æquissimum, ut ante diximus. Hæc omnia, etsi interdum in ipsum iudicium veniunt, id tamen fieri nõ deberet. nam ante iudicium potius tractanda sunt, & discutienda: ut nihil postea sit, quod quòd iudicij cursum impedire posse videatur.
units.tr: De cõparanda æquitate.) So that you may understand who ought to be admitted as accuser or claimant, by comparing equity itself: what is fair, what is fairer, and what is fairest, as we said before. Although all these matters sometimes come up in the trial itself, that should not happen. For they ought to be handled and examined before the trial, so that nothing remains afterwards that seems able to impede the course of the trial.

units.la: Paululū ea separo à iudicijs. ) Hic aperte dicit Cicero, non esse nouum statū, sed genere qualitatis aut æquitatis contineri. differunt tantum tempore, non natura.
units.tr: "I separate them a little from trials." Here Cicero plainly says that this is not a new status, but is contained within the kind of quality or equity. They differ only in time, not in nature.

units.la: Nam omnia, quæ de iure ciuili, aut de æquo & bono disceptantur, cadunt in eam formā, in qua quale quid sit ambigitur, de qua dicturi sumus: quæ in æquitate, & iure maxime consistit.
units.tr: For all the matters disputed under civil law, or concerning what is equitable and good, fall into that form in which it is in doubt what sort of thing something is, which we are about to discuss, and which chiefly consists in equity and law.

units.la: Nam omnia.) Probat, qualitate contineri sta-tum translationis, hoc pacto: Omnia quæ de iure ciuili, aut de æquo & bono disceptātur, sub qualitatem cadunt: huiusmodi autem est iste status translationis: igitur sub quantitatem cadit, & genere qualitatis atque æquitatis continetur. Iam quædam supra posita, ne intelligentiam impediant, definienda nobis sunt. Hereditas, est successio in uniuersum ius, quod defunctus habuit mortis suæ tempore. ff. de Reg. iur. tit. 62. aliter definit Cicero in Topicis. Lex est, quod Populus Romanus, Senatorio magistratu interrogante (ueluti Consule) constituebat. Inst. lib. 1. tit. 2. §. constat. Siue (ut Atteius Capito) lex est generale iussu populi, aut plebis, rogante magistratu. Testamentum,est uoluntatis nostræ iusta sententia,de eo quod post mortem nostrâ fieri uelimus. Vlp.ff. 28.tit. de Testament.& ult. uol. Possessio, ut Aelius Gallus ait, est usus fundi uel ædificij.ff.50.tit.16. Iudicium, est legitimus actus trium personarum, iudicis, Actoris, & Rei.De uer.signif. Actio, siue caussa, ius est persequêdi in iudicio,quod sibi debeat.Quas Ἀίνας uocarunt Athenienses,eas Romani actiones dixere, ab eo q, ad iudicia aguntur rei. Inst. lib.4.de Act. quanquam etiam pro iudicio ponatur. Petitio,est legitima suæ rei postulatio. Ius Ciuile est,quod quisq; populus ipse sibi constituit: uel ut Cic.de Oratore libro primo,est legitima atq; usitata in rebus caussisq; ciuium, æqualitatis conseruatio. Ius priuatum est, quod ad singulorum utilitatem spectat : Publicum, quod ad statum rei Romanæ. sic enim diuiditur & definitur ius, Inst. de Iust.& iur. §. Iuris præcepta. Mos,siue consuetudo,ius est quoddam, quod sine lege,æquè ac si legitimum sit,usi tatû est.ad Herꝯ.2. Estq; iuris nō scripti pars: nam altera est æquitas. Qualitas, ex qua quidq; quale nominatur: ut iustum, iniustum: iure feci, non iure fecisti.
units.tr: "For all the matters." He proves that the status of transfer is contained in quality, in this way: all the matters disputed under civil law, or concerning what is equitable and good, fall under quality; but the status of transfer is of this kind; therefore it falls under quality and is contained in the kind of quality and equity. Now some of the terms set out above, so that they do not hinder understanding, must be defined by us. An inheritance is the succession to the whole law that the deceased had at the time of his death (ff. de Reg. iur., tit. 62). Cicero defines it differently in the Topics: a law is what the Roman people established when asked by a senior magistrate (such as a consul). (Inst. lib. 1, tit. 2, §. constat.) Or (as Atteius Capito says) a law is a general decree of the people or the plebs, at the request of a magistrate. A will is the lawful declaration of our intention concerning what we wish to be done after our death (Ulp. ff. 28, tit. de Testament. & ult. vol.). Possession, as Aelius Gallus says, is the use of a piece of land or a building (ff. 50, tit. 16). A trial is the lawful act of three persons: judge, plaintiff, and defendant (De verb. signif.). An action, or case, is the right of pursuing in court what is owed to one. Those which the Athenians called [ἀγωγάς], the Romans called actions, from the fact that by them cases are brought to trial (Inst. lib. 4, de Act.), although it is also used for the trial itself. A petition is the lawful demand of one's own property. Civil law is what each people has established for itself; or, as Cicero says in the first book of De Oratore, it is the lawful and customary preservation of equality in the affairs and cases of citizens. Private law is what concerns the advantage of individuals; public law is what concerns the state of the Roman commonwealth. For law is divided and defined in this way (Inst. de Iust. & iur., §. Iuris praecepta). Custom, or usage, is a kind of law which, without statute, has been practised as if it were enacted. (Ad Herenn. 2.) And it is a part of unwritten law, for the other part is equity. Quality is that from which something is named as being of a certain kind: as just, unjust; I acted lawfully, you did not act lawfully.

units.la: DE STATIBVS.
units.tr: ON THE STATUSES

units.la: In omnib.igitur caussis tres sunt gra-
units.tr: In all causes, therefore, there are three degrees,

units.la: gradus, ex quibus unus aliquis capiedus est, fi plures nō queas ad refiftedum. Nam aut ita cōfiftendum est, ut quod obijcitur factū neges: aut illud quod factū fateare, neges eā uim habere, atq; id esse quod adueríarius criminetur. Aut fi neq; de facto, neque de facti appellatione ambigi potest, id quod arguere, neges tale esse, quale ille dicat: & rectum esse, quod feceris, concedendū ue defendas. Ita primus illeftatus, & quasi conflictio cum aduersario, coiectura quadam: secūdus aut definitione, aut descriptione, atque informatione uerbi: tertius ęqui & ueri, & recti & humani ad ignoscendū disputatione tractādus est.
units.tr: from which one must be chosen, if you cannot resist with several. For either you must stand firm in such a way that you deny the fact that is objected to you; or, while admitting the fact, you deny that it has that force and is what your opponent charges. Or, if there can be no doubt either about the fact or about the name given to the fact, you deny that the thing you are charged with is such as he says, and you defend that what you did was right, or ought to be conceded.
