Thus the first is handled by conjecture, as a kind of clash with the adversary; the second by definition, description and the explanation of the word; the third by a disputation about equity, truth, rightness and humanity, in order to win pardon.

units.la: In omnib.igitur causis tres sunt gradus.) De statibus & constitutionib. caussarum, eorumq; proprijs locis, deinceps doctrina tradetur: in quib.primum illa uideda sunt, quid sit status, & unde ducatur, quaeuc statum faciat: tū, quot sint constitutionū genera: & postremò, sint ne in omnib.causis status, statū definit Cicero de Inuē. lib.1. prima conflictione caussarũ, ex depulsione intentionis perfectā: in Topicis vero, statũ dicit cum esse, in quo primum insistit, quasi ad repugnandũ, cõgressa defensio. Statum à consistendo, siue insistendo dictum esse, vt in Topicis: Refutatio aut accusationis, inquit, in qua est depulsio criminis, Græcè ςάσις dicitur, Latinè appelletur status, in quo primum insistit, quasi ad repugnandũ congressa defensio. Alij à verbo ςασιάζειν, quod dissidere significat: quoniam in eo actor & patronus potissimum dissentiunt & dissident. possit etiā ab ιςάνai, id est à statuendo quòd in eo quid in cõtroversiā veniat, & de quo disceptãdũ fit, statuatur. Sed re intellecta, in verborũ usu faciles esse debemus, ut Cic. de Finib. 3. monet. Ego tamẽ in eo Ciceroni assentior. Quæ aut statũ faciat, nostrũ Ciceronẽ sequẽtibus, & ipsam veritatem, facilè erit aidere. Oritur enim ex intentione & defensione. Verum quoniam, nisi esset aliqua criminis depulsio, ex sola criminis intentione nulla esset controversia: idcirco à depulsione potius statum oriri dicemus. ut recte dixerit Cicero, in refutatione accusationis, in qua est depulsio criminis, statum esse: atque ita composita est omnis controversia, quæ existere ex hoc loco solet. Nam cum quis dicit, Fecisti: nisi alius dicat, Non feci, aut iure feci? nullus est status. sed depulsione posita, statim illud quaerendum sequitur, an fecerit? aut, an iure fecerit? Quot vero sint status genera prima, magna est quaestio: sed auctoritas et ratio tria tantum esse concludit. Auctoritas, quoniam Cicero in postremis suis de Oratoria facultate libris, omnibus tres tantum esse statuit: quemadmodum hoc loco etiam, cum ait, in omnibus causis tres esse gradus. Ratio autem partiendi et dividendi hoc idem docet, ne partes aut species cum generibus miscceamus, et paucitate in dividendo retineamus. Quicunque igitur status, praeter hos tres, illi alicuius horum species sint necesse est: id quod et in his Partitionibus, et in secundo de Oratore copiose idem docet Cicero, ad quos locos diligentem lectorem reiicimus. Sed praeclarum est referre, quod de statibus in Oratore ad Brutum scriptum reliquit. Erit enim (inquit) Oratori perspectum, nihil ambigi posse, in quo non aut res controversiam faciat, aut verba. Res, aut de vero, aut de recto, aut de nomine. Verba, aut de ambiguo, aut de contrario. Nam si quando aliud in sententia videtur esse, aliud in verbis, genus est quoddam ambigui: quod ex praeterito verbo fieri solet, in quo, quod est ambiguorum proprium, res duas significari videmus. Vult enim dicere, omnem controversiam aut ex materia, aut ex forma oriri: nā in reb. materia est orationis, in uerbis forma. Sed iam illud quartum uideamus: esse statum in iudiciali genere nemo ambigit: in sententia quoq; dicenda, propè omnes concedūt. In laudatione negant pleriq; : propterea q; laus sit præteritorū atq; horum quæ certissima sunt. at in certis nulla est cōtrouersia,nemoq; de perspicuis ambigit:ergo in laudatione nullus est status. Sed fallit eos uocis ambiguitate perspicuum est. Status enim non modò pro eo in quo est controuersia, capitur: sed etiam pro summo cuiusuis caussæ capite accipitur, atq; in hunc modum definitur: Status est, summa caussæ propositio, ad quam omnia referuntur. Huc adiungenda sunt,quæ in Topicis hac de re scripsimus. Iam superest,ut uerba quædam explicemus.
units.tr: "In all causes, therefore, there are three degrees." Afterwards the doctrine will be given about the statuses and the constitutions of causes, and their proper places. In these matters the following must be seen first: what a status is, whence it is derived, and what makes a status; then how many kinds of constitution there are; and finally whether there are statuses in all causes. Cicero, in the first book of On Invention, defines the status as the complete first clash of causes arising from the rebuttal of the charge; but in the Topics he says the status is that in which the defence first takes its stand, as if to resist, once the contest has begun. The status is said to be named from standing firm (consistere) or taking one's stand (insistere), as in the Topics: "The refutation of the accusation, in which lies the rebuttal of the charge, is called in Greek stasis [στάσις], in Latin it is called status, the point in which the defence first takes its stand, as if to resist once the contest has begun." Others derive it from the verb stasiazein [στασιάζειν], which means to be at odds, because in this the prosecutor and the advocate chiefly disagree and are at odds. It could also come from histanai [ἱστάναι], that is, from establishing, because in it what comes into controversy, and what is to be disputed, is established. But once the matter is understood, we ought to be easy about words, as Cicero warns in the third book of On Ends. Yet in this I agree with Cicero. As for what makes a status, following our Cicero and the truth itself, it will be easy to see. It arises from the charge and the defence. But since, unless there were some rebuttal of the charge, there would be no controversy from the charge alone, we shall say rather that the status arises from the rebuttal. So Cicero rightly said that the status lies in the refutation of the accusation, in which is the rebuttal of the charge; and in this way every controversy that usually arises from this topic is composed. For when someone says, "You did it," unless another says, "I did not do it," or "I did it rightfully," there is no status. But once the rebuttal is put, there immediately follows the question, whether he did it, or whether he did it rightfully. As for how many kinds of status there are at first, that is a great question; but authority and reason conclude that there are only three. Authority, because Cicero, in the last books of his On the Orator's Craft, established that there are only three for all; as he also does here, when he says that there are three degrees in all causes. Reason of division and partition teaches the same, so that we do not mix parts or species with genera, and in dividing we keep to a small number. Therefore, whatever statuses there are besides these three, they must be species of one of these; which Cicero teaches copiously in these Partitions and in the second book of On the Orator, to which places we send the diligent reader. But it is worth noting what he left written about statuses in the Orator to Brutus. "The orator," he says, "will have it clearly understood that nothing can be in dispute in which the matter does not make the controversy, or the words do. The matter is either about the true, or the right, or the name. The words are either about the ambiguous, or the contrary. For if at some time something seems different in the sense and in the words, it is a kind of ambiguity, which usually arises from a word in the past tense, in which, as is proper to ambiguous things, we see two things signified." For he means that every controversy arises either from the matter or from the form; for in things the matter is of the speech, in words the form. But now let us look at the fourth point: that there is a status in the judicial genus, no one doubts; that there is one in the speech of advice, almost all concede. In praise, many deny it, on the ground that praise concerns past things and those things which are most certain; but in what is certain there is no controversy, and no one doubts what is plain; therefore in praise there is no status. But they are deceived by the ambiguity of the word: for "status" is taken not only for that in which the controversy lies, but is also understood as the summit of any cause, and it is defined in this way: the status is the proposition of the cause as a whole, to which everything is referred. To this should be added what we have written on this matter in the Topics. It remains now to explain certain words.

units.la: In omnibus tres sunt gradus. ) A' pugnantib. sumpta locutio est,qui locum pugnæ capiūt, qui in gradu insistunt,ad refistēdum parati. itaq; dixit,Capere gradū, ut capere locū dicitur. Nam qui decertāt,locū tutissimum, si quo modo possint, primum capiunt: sin minus,tutissimo proximū,aut saltem tertium, ne prorsus hostiū iniurijs pateant. Sic in caussis tres sunt gradus, quorum tutissimus est.facti negare si possis, in quo est cōiectura:secundus,si factum negare nō possis,id te iure fecisse defendas,in quo est qualitas: tertius,nō tantū esse crime,quantū aduersarius criminetur,quod est definitiōis.ergo ex his unus aliquis capiendus est,si plures nō possis.Quòd si plures,unus tamen erit præcipuus: reliqui eū iu uabūt: sicq; unus semper erit in singulis caussis status.
units.tr: "In all there are three degrees." The expression is taken from fighters, who take up the place of battle; those who stand on a degree are ready to resist. Hence he said "to take a degree," as one says "to take a place." For those who contend first take the safest place, if they can in any way; but if not, the next safest, or at least the third, so as not to be left wholly open to the assaults of the enemies. So in causes there are three degrees, of which the safest is: if you can deny the fact, which is conjecture; the second: if you cannot deny the fact, you defend that you did it rightly, which is quality; the third: that it is not as great a crime as the adversary charges, which belongs to definition. Therefore one of these must be taken, if you cannot take several. But if several, still one will be the principal, and the others will support it; and thus in each cause there will always be one status.

units.la: Secundus aūt definitione. Tria ponit definitionū genera: Definitione ipsam perfeƈtā, quæ ex genere & proprietate cōstat:Descriptione, quæ oratoria est definitio, atque ob id liberior: Informatione uerbi,quæ notatio dicitur, & uocabuli explicatio. Sed modū definitionis oratoriæ pōst docebit,ut supra quoq; docuit.Nisi hūc locū ita intelligere uelimus, ut duo tantū definitionum genera secerit,descriptione,& uerbi informatione: aut definitioni descriptionem subiccerit,quasi explicās quid nomine definitionis intellexerit,nimirū descriptionem,quòd eá siēe sola in caussis utantur oratores. nam particulam Aut,semel tantum posuit: id quod solet facere, cum duo tantum sunt membra.
units.tr: "But the second by definition." He gives three kinds of definition: definition proper, which consists of genus and property; description, which is the rhetorical definition and therefore freer; and explanation of a word, which is called notation, and the explanation of a term. But he will teach the mode of rhetorical definition later, as he also taught above. Unless we wish to understand this place so that he distinguished only two kinds of definition, description and explanation of a word; or so that he made description a subordinate of definition, as if explaining what he meant by the name of definition, namely description, because orators use only this in causes. For he put the particle "or" only once, which he is accustomed to do when there are only two members.

units.la: Tertius æqui & ueri,& recti,& humani.)Nō plures hic nominat status,sed unū. nā æquū, uerum & reƈtū,idē sunt:quæ admodū ipse lib. 2.de Legib.atq; alibi ostēdit.Statū enim qualitatis & iuris his nominib. intelligit: secus q in Oratore, ubi ueri nomine,saƈti et cōiecturæ quæstione ap pellat: recti aut, qualitatis. ait enim, Nihil ambi gi posse, in quo nō aut res cōtrouersiā faciat, aut ucrba: res aut de ucro, aut de recto, aut de nomine. Quod autē addidit, Et humani ad ignoscēdū, deprecatione respexit, quæ hoc genere qualitatis continetur. humanū enim dicitur factū, quod hu mana fragilitate uenià mereri nōnūquā uidetur.
units.tr: "The third of equity, truth, rightness and humanity." He names here not several statuses but one. For the equitable, the true, and the right are the same, as he himself shows in book 2 of De Legibus and elsewhere. He understands by these names the status of quality and of law; otherwise in De Oratore, where he calls it by the name of truth, the question of fact and conjecture, and the right, the quality. For he says: "Nothing can be in doubt in which the controversy does not lie either in the matter or in the words: the matter concerns either the true, or the right, or the name." What he added, "and human, for forgiveness," refers to deprecation, which is contained in this genus of quality. For an act is called human when it seems sometimes to deserve pardon on account of human frailty.

units.la: Et quoniam semper is qui defendit, non solum resistat oportet aliquo statu, aut insiciādo, aut definiē do, aut æquitate opponenda, sed etiam ratione subijciat recusationis suæ: primus ille status rationem habet, inquit, criminis, ipsam negationem, infitiationemq; facti. Secundus, quod non fit in re, quod ab aduersario ponitur in uerbo. Tertius, quod id recte factum esse defendet, quod sine ulla nominis cōtrouersia factū fateat. Deinde unicuique rationi opponendū est ab accusatore, id quod si nō esset in accusatione, caussa omnino esse nō posset. Itaq; ea quę sic referunt, cōtinentia causarū uocēt: quanq; nō ea magis, formatio quædã:ut antequâ caussa suscipiatur, hæc diligenter præparètur: Quæ sit caussa,intentio,depulsio,status,ratio,continês,siue firmamentū: ꝳ postremò,quæ sit quæstio iudicij propria,quæ tum disceptatio, tũ iudicatio nominatur.De caussa satis multa dicta sunt:de statu quo que nõnihil: sed tamẽ illud nõ prætæribimus,statum Rhetores appellare,quod quæstione appellât Dialectici,quæ s̓ιγμα dicitur:qua posita, ut dialecticis inuenieda ratio est ad propositū coprobandū,sic oratori ad id quod statuit tuendū. eam ratione illi μέσον,hoc est medиū uocāt:quasi ad extrema coniungenda aptū quiddam. Rhetores αἴτιον, id est caussam, propterea quòd actionū caussas inquirūt. appellât etiam cōmuni nomine συνέχοντα,id est continētia caussarum: quia sine his caussa nõ staret,ut Cicero ipse docet.ἀντιμένον aut, quâ iudicationem in Topicis uertit,respondet dialecticorū ἀναλύσεα, quæ conclufionū formas,ꝳ argumentorū uim seorsim expendunt. Sed uocabula ipsa artis definiamus. Intentio, est accusatoris infimulatio, qua in aduersarii crimē impingit. Depulsio, est defensoris recusatio, qua aut inficiando, aut definiendo, aut æquitate apponenda crimen quasi telum àse depellit. Ratio est,quæ cõtinet defensionem,sine qua ne parua quidem dubitatio remorari damnatione potest. Firmamentum est, quod contra rationem defensionis affertur, sine quo accusatio stare non potest. Iudicatio, est propria iudicij quæstio, ex rationis & ex firmamenti conflictione orta. Nam ut ex duorum inter se corporum collisione sonus, sic ex rationis & firmamenti conflictione quæstio et iudicatio exoritur quædam: in qua quid dicuntur in iudicium, & de quo disceptetur, quæri solet. Vt, exempli caussa, si dicas, Fecisti, hæc erit intentio: Non feci, aut, Non hoc feci, aut, Iure feci, depulsio erit. Prima coniectura, in qua quæritur, an fecerit? Secunda nominis, an hoc fecerit? Tertia iuris, an iure fecerit? qui status appellatur. In primo, pro ratione ponitur negatio, sive inficiatio: in secundo, definitio definitioni opponitur: in tertio caussa, nimirum aut oportuisse, aut licuisse: aut si aliter non possis, imprudentia, aut necessitate, aut casu factum esse. Sequitur ratio defensoris: Quia prius res, non publica fuit, quam de ærario surripuit: non igitur fuit peculatus. & hæc ratio ad definitionem spectat. Vel quia uim attulit, iure occidi: quod ad qualitatem. Continens, sive firmamentum accusatoris: Nō tamen ciuem indemnatum occidere licuit. Ex quibus illud in disceptationem veniet: An sine iudicio, uim inferentem ulcisci fas sit, nec ne?
units.tr: And since the one who defends must always not only resist with some status, whether by denying, or defining, or by setting against the charge the plea of equity, but also must add the ground of his rebuttal, that first status, he says, has the ground of the charge, namely the very denial and disavowal of the act. The second is that which is not in the thing, but which the opponent places in the word. The third is that he will defend that what he admits to have been done was done rightly, without any controversy about the name. Then against each ground the prosecutor must set something in reply; and if this were not in the accusation, the case could not exist at all. Therefore those things which they report in this way they call the continents of causes, though these are not so much parts as a kind of preparation: so that before a case is taken up, these are carefully prepared: what the case is, the charge, the rebuttal, the status, the ground, the continent or firmament; and finally what is the proper question of a trial, which is called both the dispute and the judgment. Enough has been said about the cause; something also about the status. Yet we shall not pass over this, that the rhetoricians call the status what the dialecticians call the question, which is called zētēma [ζήτημα]. Once it is set, just as the dialectician must find the method for proving his proposition, so the orator must find it for defending what he has taken a stand on. The dialecticians call this meson [μέσον], that is, the middle, as something fitted to join the extremes. The rhetoricians call it aition [αἴτιον], that is, the cause, because they inquire into the causes of actions. They also call it by the common name synechonta [συνέχοντα], that is, the continents of causes, because without these a cause would not stand, as Cicero himself teaches. The term antimenon [ἀντιμένον], by which in the Topics he renders judgment, corresponds to the dialecticians' analyseis [ἀναλύσεις], which weigh separately the forms of conclusions and the force of arguments. But let us define the technical terms themselves. The charge is the prosecutor's accusation, by which he assails the opponent's crime. The rebuttal is the defender's refutation, by which, either by denying, or by defining, or by setting equity against it, he drives the charge away from himself as if it were a missile. The ground is that which contains the defence, without which not even a slight doubt can delay condemnation. The firmament is what is brought against the ground of the defence, without which the accusation cannot stand. The judgment is the proper question of a trial, arising from the clash of ground and firmament. For as sound arises from the collision of two bodies, so from the clash of ground and firmament arises a certain question and judgment, in which it is usually asked what is brought into judgment and what is to be disputed. For example, if you say, "You did it," this will be the charge; "I did not do it," or "I did not do this," or "I did it rightly," will be the rebuttal. The first is conjecture, in which it is asked whether he did it; the second is of name, whether he did this; the third is of law, whether he did it rightly; this is called the status. In the first, denial or disavowal is set as the ground; in the second, definition is set against definition; in the third, the cause, namely that it was right, or permitted, or, if you cannot otherwise, that it was done through imprudence, necessity or chance. Then comes the defender's ground: since the thing was not public before he stole it from the treasury, it was therefore not peculation; and this ground concerns definition. Or, because he used force, he was rightly killed; this concerns quality. The continent, or firmament, of the prosecutor: yet it was not permitted to kill an uncondemned citizen. From these the question will come into dispute: whether it is lawful or not to take vengeance without a trial on one who uses force.

units.la: Nam prima aduersariorū contetio diffusam habet quæstionē: ut in cōiectura, cæperit ne pecunias Decíus. In definitione, minuerit ne maiestatem Norbanus. In æquitate, iure ne occiderit Opimíus Gracchū. Hæc, quę primam contētionem habent ex arguendo & resistēdo lata, ut dixi, & confusa sunt. Rationum & firmamentorum cōtentio adducit in angustā disceptationem. ea in coniectura nulla est. Nemo enim eius, quod negat factū, rationem aut potest, aut debet, aut solet reddere. Itaque in his causis eadem & prima quæstio, & disceptatio est extrema.
units.tr: For the first contention of the opponents has a broad question. In conjecture: did Decius take the money? In definition: did Norbanus diminish majesty? In equity: did Opimius rightly kill Gracchus? These cases, which have the first contention drawn out by argument and rebuttal, are, as I said, broad and confused. The contention of reasons and proofs narrows the dispute. In conjecture there is none of this, for no one can, ought to, or usually does give a reason for a fact he denies. So in these cases the first question and the final dispute are the same.

units.la: In illis autem, ubi ita dicitur, Non minuit maiestatē, quòd egit de Cepione turbulentius. Populi enim Rom. doloriustus, uim illam excitauit, nō tribuni actio. Maiestas autem, quoniam est magnitudo quædam populi Rom. in eius potestate ac iure retinendo, aucta est potius quàm diminuta: & ubi ita refertur,
units.tr: In those cases where it is said, "He did not diminish majesty, because he acted too violently against Scipio," the people of Rome, being rightly distressed, provoked that violence, not the tribune's action. Majesty, since it is a certain greatness of the Roman people, lying in its power and in its right to keep that power, has been increased rather than diminished. And where it is put this way:

units.la: Maiestas est in imperij, atq; in omni pop.Rom.dignitate: quā minuit is, qui per uim multitudinis rem ad seditionē uocauit. existit illa discepatio, Minuerit ne maiestatē, qui uoluntate pop.Ro. rem grata & æquā per uim egerit? In his autē caussis, ubi aliquid recte factum, aut concedendū, esse factū defendatur, cum est facti subiecta ratio. sicut ab Opimio, Iure feci, salutis omnium & conseruādæ Reipub. caussa: relatumq; est ab Decio, Ne sceleratissimum quidem ciuem sine iudicio iure ullo necare potuisti. oritur illa disceptatio, potuerit ne recte salutis Reipub. caussa ciuem euersorem ciuitatis indemnatum necare.
units.tr: "Majesty resides in the authority of empire and in the whole dignity of the Roman people; whoever calls the matter to sedition by the force of a crowd diminishes it." From this arises the dispute: did he diminish majesty who, acting by the will of the Roman people, carried out a pleasing and just measure by force? In those cases where something rightly done is defended, or must be conceded to have been done, the reason for the deed is set beneath it, as when Opimius says, "I acted rightly, for the sake of the safety of all and the preservation of the Republic," and Decius replies, "You could not by any right kill even the most criminal citizen without trial." That dispute arises: could he rightly kill, without trial, a citizen who was overturning the state, for the sake of the safety of the Republic?

units.la: Nam prima aduersariorum cōtentio.) Et hæc ad illum quem proxime dixi caussæ apparatu, & quasi designatione pertinet. docet enim, quid status à reliquis cōtinentib. differat. Statuū, rationū, & firmamentorū & iudicationū exēpla proponit: deniq; quomodo ex hypothesi fiat thesis, docet. Status generis uim habet, et cuiusdā rei uniuersæ,utpote in quo summa rei implicita continetur.Reliqua,ut ratio, & firmamentū,& iudicatio,tanquam forma sunt,quæ iam perfectius aliquid ac certius indicat.ut,exēpli caussa: Qui insidiatorem dicit,iam explicatius aliquid dixit, quàm cum improbum nominauit. Eodem modo si quis quærat,Liceat ne hominē occidere? consusum & latè patens: at licuerit ne pro salute Reipub. ciuem seditiosum indemnatum necare, angustius & certius. Ad hanc autem angustam disceptationem,rem adduxerunt,tum defensoris tũ accusatoris rationes. Sed quaerat aliquis, an in tribus generibus caussarũ sint eædē rationes, eademq; extrema ex rationibus quæstio? Respondet Cicero: In coniectura nullam esse à statu separatam atq; si in stam: in reliquis duobus generibus esse.Cur autem in coniectura non fit,rationem triplicem affert: Quòd non possit,quòd non debeat,quòd non soleat,eius quòd factū negatur,ratio reddi.Nō potest,quia nulla est.Non debet, quia nullo iure astringitur aliquis reddere quod nō accepit: est enim ratio affirmationis propria,nō negationis.Non solet,quia moris nō est. Quid ergo faciendum in huiusmodi caussis? Prima quæstio,quæ status dicitur,pro ratione et disceptatione habenda. ut, Cæpisti contra leges pecunias Deci. Nō cæpi. Status & iudicatio se-
units.tr: "For the first contention of the opponents": this too belongs to the preparation and, as it were, the outline of the case I mentioned just before. For he teaches how the status differs from the other constituents. He sets out examples of status, reasons, proofs and judgments, and finally teaches how a thesis arises from a hypothesis. The status has the force of a genus, of a whole matter, since the sum of the matter is contained in it implicitly. The others, reason, proof and judgment, are like forms, which now indicate something more perfect and certain. For example, one who calls someone an ambusher has said something more explicit than one who calls him wicked. In the same way, if someone asks, "Is it permitted to kill a man?" the question is confused and widely extended; but "Was it permitted to kill without trial a seditious citizen for the safety of the Republic?" is narrower and more certain. Both the defender's and the accuser's reasons bring the matter into this narrow dispute. But someone may ask whether in the three kinds of cause the reasons are the same, and whether the final question arising from the reasons is the same? Cicero answers that in conjecture there is no status separate from the constituent, as if it were the same thing; in the other two kinds it is separate. He gives a threefold reason why in conjecture this does not happen: that the reason for the denied fact cannot be given, that it ought not be, and that it is not customary. It cannot, because there is none. It ought not, because no law binds anyone to give a reason for what he did not receive; for a reason belongs to affirmation, not to denial. It is not customary, because it is not the usage. What then should be done in such causes? The first question, which is called the status, is to be held as both reason and dispute; for example, "You began to take Decius's money contrary to the laws." "I did not begin."

units.la: Sed in grauissimis firmamentis & illa ponenda sunt, si qua ex scrípto legis, aut testamēti, aut uerborum ipsius iudicij, aut alicuius stípulatiónis, aut cautionis opponuntur defensioni contraria.
units.tr: But in the weightiest proofs those too must be put forward, if any are opposed to the defence, drawn from the text of a law, or of a will, or from the words of the judgment itself, or from some stipulation or security.

units.la: Sed in grauissimis firmamentis.) Qualitatis duplex est consideratio: una, in æquitatis & iuris ratione posita est: altera, in scripto. illa ratio naiis, hæc legitima appellatur. Quomodo autē rationes & iudicationes in priore genere inueniendæ essent, ostendit: idē nunc in altera docet.
units.tr: "But in the weightiest proofs": the consideration of quality is twofold. One lies in the reasoning of equity and right; the other lies in the written text. The first is called natural, the second legal. He has shown how reasons and judgments are to be found in the former kind; now he teaches the same in the latter.

units.la: Est uero legitima constitutio, cū in scripto, aut ex scriptis controuersia nascitur. quæ etiamsi legitima à lege, hoc est à re firmissima nomen habet, non magis tamen in legibus quàm in testamentis, in iudicatis, in stipulationibus, in cautionibus, reliquisq; rebus quæ in scripto aguntur, possunt controuersiæ eædem existere. Lex quid sit, item testamentum, ante dictum est. Iudicatum, id est, de quo sententia lata est, aut decretum interpositū. Heren. lib. 2. Stipulatio, uerborum est conceptio, quibus is qui interrogatur, daturum factúrum ue se quod interrogatus est, respondet. De Verb. oblig. ff. lib. 45. Cautio, est stipulatio omnis, quæ nobis caucmus, cautosq; facimus. cimus de re quæ nobis debeatur: cuiusmodi sunt chirographa, et syngraphæ, et satisdationes, siue fideiussiones.
units.tr: Indeed the legal constitution arises when the controversy arises from writing, or from writings. Although it is called legal from the law, that is, from the most firm matter, the same controversies can arise no less in wills, in judgments, in stipulations, in securities, and in other things transacted in writing than in laws. What a law is, and likewise a will, has been said before. A judgment is that concerning which a sentence has been pronounced or a decree issued (Herennius, book 2). A stipulation is the formulation of words by which the one questioned replies that he will give or do what he was asked (On Verbal Obligations, Digest, book 45). A security is every stipulation by which we secure ourselves and make ourselves safe. It concerns a thing owed to us, such as chirographs and syngraphs, and sureties or guarantees.

units.la: Ac ne hoc quidem genus in eas caussas incurrit, quæ cōiectura continentur. Quod enim factum negatur, id argui non potest scripto: ne in definitionem quidem uenit, generè scripti ipsius. Nam etiamsi uerbum aliquod de scripto definiendum est, quam uim habeat, ut cum ex testamentis quid sit penus, aut cū ex lege prædiŋ quæritur, quæ sint ruta casa, nō scripti genus, sed uerbi interpretatio controuersia parit.
units.tr: Nor does this kind fall into those cases which are contained under conjecture. For the fact that is denied cannot be argued from writing; nor does it come into definition, which belongs to the kind of writing itself. For even if some word from a text must be defined, and its force is in question, as when what a "penus" is is asked from wills, or what "ruta casa" means is asked from a law on land, the controversy arises from the interpretation of the word, not from the kind of writing.

units.la: Quod enim factum negatur.) Duo hic facit: primum, neq; in coniecturam, neq; in definitionem incidere firmamentum, si caussa ex scripto oriatur: alterum, hoc genus statuum, qui legitimi uocantur, ad solam qualitatem pertinere: esseq; eius partes, quæcunq; ex scripto nascantur controuersiæ. Vtrunq; ratione probat, et de coniectura quidem prius hoc modo: Quod enim factum negatur, ut ratione, sic nec scripto, id est, scripti iure argui, defendi ue potest. Non cadere etiam
units.tr: "For the fact that is denied": here he does two things. First, the constituent does not fall into conjecture or definition if the cause arises from writing. Second, this kind of status, called legal, pertains only to quality, and its parts are all the controversies that arise from writing. He proves both by reason. And concerning conjecture, he proves the first point in this way: what fact is denied cannot be argued or defended by reason, and so neither by writing, that is, by the force of a text.

units.la: Quod enim factum negatur.) Duo hic facit: primum, neque in coniecturam, neque in definitionem incidere firmamentum, si causa ex scripto oriatur. quid maximè significetur. in scripti, sententiæqʒ cōtentione, utrū potius sequatur iudex: in cōtrarijs scriptis, utrū magis sit cōptobandum.
units.tr: "For the fact that is denied": here he does two things. First, neither the proof nor the definition falls into the conjecture, if the cause arises from writing, what is chiefly signified, in the contention of the writing and of the sentence, which the judge should follow more; in opposed writings, which should be more approved.

units.la: Cum autē plura significantur scripto.) Legitimi status tria genera facit, ut etiā in Topicis, Ambigui, scripti & sententiæ, & contrariarū legum siue scriptorum: quæ tria de Oratore lib.2. ad unum ambiguorum genus reuocat. Nam aut ambiguū est, scriptū ne an sententia scriptoris sequi debeamus: aut ex cōtrarijs legibus, utra sit alteri præferenda: ex ambigua oratione aut verbo, in qua significatione accipere velimus. Ita fit, ut unū genus in ijs causis quæ propter scriptū ambiguntur relinquatur, si est scriptum aliquid ambiguè. Ex ambiguo controuersia nascitur, cum scriptum duas aut plures res significat. ut si lex talis sit lata, Meretrix coronam auream ne habeto: si habuerit, publica esto. Cōtrouersia nascitur in hunc modum. alter dicit meretricem publicari debere, quòd lex dicat, Meretrix publica esto: alter cōtrà, Corona publicari debere, quòd in auro & in corona facile est, in meretrice non itē. Ex quo iudicatio oritur, utra significatio & sententia sit accipienda. Ex scripto uerò & sententia nascitur cōtrouersia, cū videtur scriptoris uoluntas cum scripto ipso dissentire: ut si lex sit quae vetet, peregrinum in murum ascendere. Peregrinus autem, quum sensisset adesse hostes, in murum ascendit, et civitatem liberavit. accusatur, quasi contra legem fecerit. Respondet se quidem murum concendisse, sed etiam una patriam liberasse: quod haud dubie voluit legislator. Existit disceptatio, an, quid murū ascenderit, et civitate liberaverit, contra legem fecisse dicaturid est, sit ne ex scripto an sententia legis iudicandū. Ex contrariis legibus disceptatio existit, cum alia lex iubet aut permittit, id quod alia lex fieri vetat, hoc modo, ne ab exemplis Rhetorum discedamus. Lex vetat, cum qui de pecuniis repetundis damnatus sit, in concione orationem habere: altera lex iubet, augurem in demortui locum, qui petat, in cocione nominari. Augur quidam damnatus de pecuniis repetundis, in demortui locū qui petat, nominavit: contra legem fecisse dicitur; ille dicit, se ex lege fecisse. Quaestio est, utri legi sit adhaerendum, aut quomodo contrariae leges conciliandae sint.
units.tr: "But when several things are signified by the writing": the legal statuses make three kinds, as also in the Topics: ambiguity of writing and of sentence, and of contrary laws or writings. In On the Orator, book 2, Cicero reduces these three to one kind of ambiguity. For either the writing is ambiguous, so that we must ask whether to follow the text or the author's intention; or the contrary laws must be weighed, to see which should be preferred to the other; or an ambiguous phrase or word must be taken in which sense we wish. Thus it happens that one kind is left in those causes which are in doubt because of the writing, if something in the writing is ambiguous. The controversy arises from ambiguity when the writing signifies two or more things. For example, if a law was passed in this way: "Let a prostitute not have a golden crown; if she has one, let it be public property." The controversy arises in this way: one says the prostitute ought to be confiscated, because the law says, "Let the prostitute be public property"; the other says, on the contrary, that the crown ought to be confiscated, because gold and a crown are easily made public property, but a prostitute is not. From this arises the judgment as to which meaning and sense is to be accepted. But from the writing and the sense together arises a controversy when the author's will seems to disagree with the writing itself: for example, if there is a law forbidding a foreigner to climb the wall. A foreigner, when he perceived that enemies were near, climbed the wall and freed the city. He is accused as if he had acted against the law. He replies that he indeed climbed the wall, but also freed his country, which the lawgiver undoubtedly wished. The dispute arises whether, since he climbed the wall and freed the city, he is said to have acted against the law, that is, whether it must be judged from the writing or from the sense of the law. A dispute arises from contrary laws when one law commands or permits what another law forbids. For example, to avoid departing from the examples of the rhetoricians: one law forbids a man condemned for extortion to make a speech before the assembly; another law orders that an augur be named in the assembly to fill the place of a dead man who is sought. An augur who had been condemned for extortion named a candidate to fill the place of a dead man. He is said to have acted against the law; he says he acted according to the law. The question is which law is to be adhered to, or how the contrary laws are to be reconciled.

units.la: Disceptatio autem, cum est constituta, propositā esse debet oratori, quo omnes argumentationes repetitae, ex inveniendi locis coniciantur.
units.tr: Once the dispute has been established, it should be laid before the orator, so that all the arguments drawn from the places of invention can be gathered together.

units.la: B quod quanquam satis ei est, qui ui⁕ det, quid in quoq; loco lateat, quíq; íllos locos tanquâ thesauros aliquos àrgumētorum notatos habet: tamē ea quæ sunt certarum cauffarū propria, tangemus.
units.tr: Although anyone who sees what lies hidden in each place, and who has those places marked out like treasuries of arguments, has enough for this, I will nonetheless touch on those points that belong to particular causes.

units.la: Disceptatio autē cum est constituta.) Quid utilitatis habeat, disceptationis inuētio: tum quot sint locorū genera, ex quib. argumenta ad propositam quæstionē depromātur. Prima utilitas est, quòd nouit orator, quò argumēta sint referenda, ut ne quid alienum à caussa dicat, & quomodo iudex tractandus sit. Deinde, iudex ipse ex proposita disceptatione intelligit, quid expectare, quid'que sequi debeat. Locorum autem duo sunt genera. Alij generales & communes, de quibus libro primo dictum est, quum fontes inuentionis aperirentur: alij sunt statuum singulorum proprij, quas hic Cicero causas appellat: de quib. deinceps ordine explicabit. Maiores & latiores illi sunt, hi uerò angustiores & certiores. Ac [...] certo homini illi satis essent: hi uerò [...] biles, & minus acutis necessarij [...] sic de Orat. 2. Quod autem genus (inquit) cuiq; se maxime conueniat, non est art scribere: sed est mediocris ingenij iudicare. Est igitur haec quasi transitio à definitione causarum, & praeparatione, ad minores & angustiores causarum partes, & locos.
units.tr: When the dispute has been established. There are two things to note here: what advantage the invention of the dispute has, and how many kinds of places there are from which arguments for the proposed question are drawn. The first advantage is that the orator knows where his arguments are to be referred, so that he says nothing foreign to the cause, and how the judge is to be handled. Next, the judge himself understands from the proposed dispute what he should expect and what he ought to follow. There are two kinds of places. Some are general and common, of which we spoke in the first book, when the sources of invention were opened up; others are proper to the individual states, which Cicero here calls causes, and which he will explain in order below. The former are greater and broader, the latter narrower and more certain. [...] for a certain kind of man those would be enough; these, however, [...] and are necessary for minds that are less sharp. Thus in De Oratore, book 2: "As for what kind suits each man most, it is not a matter of art to write, but a matter of moderate ability to judge." This, then, is in a way a transition from the definition of causes and their preparation to the smaller and narrower parts and places of causes.

units.la: DE CONIECTVRA.
units.tr: ON CONJECTURE

units.la: In coniectura igitur, cum est in inficiando reus, accusatori haec duo prima sunt: sed accusatorem pro omni actore & petitore appello. possunt enim etiam sine accusatore in causis haec eandem controversiarum genera versari.
units.tr: In conjecture, then, when the defendant denies the charge, these two points come first for the accuser. I call the accuser any plaintiff or claimant. These same kinds of controversy can also arise in cases without an accuser.

units.la: In coniectura igitur.) Absoluta praeparatione causarum, iam singulorum statuum locos describit proprios: ac primum coniecturae, quam copiosius tractat, quoniam est (ut alibi diximus) Oratoris propria, & in ea Cicero excellit maximè. Coiectura ... de locos accusatoris, pos[?] ... [illegible, ~10 letters] ... nem ... tertius, nō tantū esse crime, quantū aduersarius criminetur, quod est definitiōis. ergo ex his unus aliquis capiendus est, si plures nō possis. Quod si plures, unus tamen erit præcipuus: reliqui eū in uabūt: sicq; unus semper erit in singulis causis status.
units.tr: In conjecture, then.) Having completed the preparation of cases, he now describes the proper topics of each status, and first those of conjecture, which he treats more fully, since (as we have said elsewhere) it is the orator's own province, and in it Cicero especially excels. Conjecture ... topics of the accuser ... [illegible] ... third, that the crime is not as great as the adversary alleges, which belongs to definition. Therefore one of these is to be taken, if you cannot take several. But if there are several, one will nonetheless be the principal, and the rest will be subordinate to it. Thus there will always be one status in each case.

units.la: Secundus aūt definitione. Tria ponit definitionū genera: Definitione ipsam perfectā, quæ ex genere & proprietate cōstat: Descriptione, quæ oratoria est definitio, atque ob id liberior: Informatione uerbi, quæ notatio dicitur, & uocabuli explicatio. Sed modū definitionis oratoriæ post docebit, ut supra quoq; docuit. Nisi hūc locū ita intelligere uelimus, ut duo tantū definitionum genera fecerit, descriptione, & uerbi informatione: aut definitioni descriptionem subiecerit, quasi explicās quid nomine definitionis intellexerit, nimirū descriptionem, quod ea fere sola in causis utantur oratores. nam particulam Aut, semel tantum posuit: id quod solet facere, cum duo tantum sunt membra.
units.tr: The second is from definition. He sets out three kinds of definition: definition proper, which consists of genus and property; description, which is the orator's definition and therefore freer; and explanation of a word, which is called notation and the explaining of a term. He will teach the manner of oratorical definition later, as he taught above too. Unless we wish to understand this passage as meaning that he made only two kinds of definition, description and explanation of the word, or that he added description to definition, as though explaining what he meant by the name of definition, namely description, since orators mostly use that alone in cases. For he used the particle "or" only once, which he is accustomed to do when there are only two members.

units.la: Tertius æqui & ueri, & recti, & humani.)Nō plures hic nominat status, sed unū. nā æquū, uerum & rectū, idē sunt: quēadmodū ipse lib. 2. de Legib. atq; alibi ostēdit. Statū enim qualitatis & iuris his nomin. intelligit: secus q; in Oratore, ubi ueri nomine, facti et coiectura quæstione appellat: pellat: recti aut, qualitatis. ait enim, Nihil ambigi posse, in quo nō aut res cōtroversia faciat, aut verba: res aut de vero, aut de recto, aut de nomine. Quod autē addidit, Et humani ad ignoscēdū, deprecatione respexit, quæ hoc genere qualitatis continetur. humanū enim dicitur factū, quod humana fragilitate veniā mereri nōnūquā videtur.
units.tr: The third: of the fair, the true, the right and the humane.) He names here not several statuses but one. For the fair, the true and the right are the same, as he himself shows in book 2 of De Legibus and elsewhere. By these names he understands the status of quality and of law. Otherwise, in the Orator, where he calls it the question of the true, of fact and conjecture, or of the right, of quality. For he says that nothing can be in dispute where there is not either a matter in controversy or words: the matter concerning the true, or the right, or the name. What he added, "and the humane," for pardon, looks to the plea for mercy, which is contained under this kind of quality. For a deed is called humane when it seems sometimes to deserve pardon on account of human frailty.

units.la: Et quoniam semper is qui defendit, non solum resistat oportet alicuo statu, aut infitiādo, aut definiēdo, aut æquitate opponenda, sed etiam ratione subiiciat recusationis suæ: primus ille status rationem habet, inquit, criminis, ipsam negationem, infitiationemq; facti. Secundus, quod non fit in re, quod ab adversario ponitur in verbo. Tertius, quod id recte factum esse defendet, quod sine ulla nominis cōtroversia factū fateat. Deinde unicuique rationi opponendū est ab accusatore, id quod si nō esset in accusatione, causa omnino esse nō posset. Itaq; ea quę sic referunt, cōtinentia causarū uocēt: quanq; nō ea magis, formatio quædā: ut antequā caussa suscipiatur, hæc diligenter præparetur: Quæ sit caussa, intentio, depulsio, status, ratio, continēs, siue firma mentiū: & postremò, quæ sit quæstio iudicij propria, quæ tum disceptatio, tū iudicatio nominatur. De caussa satis multa dicta sunt: de statu quoque nonnihil: sed tamē illud nō prætereibimus, statum Rhetores appellare, quod quæstionē appellat Dialectici, quæ sτάσις dicitur: qua posita, ut dialecticis inueniēda ratio est ad propositū coprobandū, sic oratori ad id quod statuit tuendū. eam rationē illi μέσον, hoc est medium uocāt: quasi ad extrema coniungenda aptū quiddam. Rhetores αἴτιον, id est caussam, propterea quòd actionū caussas inquirūt. appellat etiam cōmuni nomine συνέχοντα, id est continētia caussarum: quia sine his caussa nō staret, ut Cicero ipse docet. ηγέμενον aūt, quā iudicationem in Topicis uertit, respondet dialecticorū ἀναλύσει, quā conclusionū formas, & argumentorū uim seorsim expendunt. Sed uocabula ipsa artis definiamus. Intentio, est accusatoris infimulatio, quā in aduersarium crime impingit. Depulsio, est defensoris recusatio, quā aut inficiando, aut definiendo, aut æquitate apponenda crimen quasi telum à se depellit. Ratio est, quæ cōtinet defensionem, sine qua ne parua quidem dubitatio remorari rári damnatione potest. Firmamétum est, quod contra rationem defensionis affertur, sine quo accusatio stare non potest. Iudicatio, est propria iudicij quæstio, ex rationis & ex firmaméti cõflictione orta. nam ut ex duorũ inter se corporum collisione sonus, sic ex rationis & firmaméti cõslictione quæstio et iudicatio exoritur quædam: in qua quid deueniat in iudicium, & de quo disceptetur, quæri solet. Vt, exempli caussa, si dicas, Fecisti, hæc erit intentio: Non feci, aut, Non hoc feci, aut, Iure feci, depulsio erit. prima cõiectura, in qua quæritur, an fecerit? secunda nominis, an hoc fecerit? tertia iuris, an iure fecerit? qui status appellatur. In primo, pro ratione ponitur negatio, siue insiciatio: in secundo, definitio definitioni opponitur: in tertio caussa, nimirum aut oportuisse, aut licuisse: aut si aliter non possis, imprudentia, aut necessitate, aut casu factum esse. Sequitur ratio defensoris: Quia priuata res, nõ publica fuit, quam de ærario surripui: non igitur fuit peculatus. & hæc ratio ad definitionem spectat. Vel quia uim attulit, iure occidi: quod ad qualitatem. Continens, siue firmamentum accusatoris: Nõ tamen ciuem indemnatum occidere licuit. ex quibus illud in disceptationem ueniet: An sine iudicio, uim inferentem ulcisci sas sit, nec ne?
units.tr: Since the defender must always not only resist by some status, whether by denial, by definition, or by setting equity against the charge, but also add a reason for his refusal, that first status, he says, has the reason of the charge, namely the denial itself and the disavowal of the deed. The second is that what the adversary asserts is not done in the thing but in the word. The third is that the deed was done rightly, which he defends, and which he admits was done without any dispute over the name. Then the accuser must set something against each reason, and if he did not, the case could not exist at all. Therefore those things that are referred in this way they call the continents of causes, although these are rather a kind of formation, so that before a case is taken up they are carefully prepared: what the case is, the charge, the rebuttal, the status, the reason, the continent or firm support of the matter; and finally, what is the proper question of the trial, which is called both the dispute and the judgment. Enough has been said about the case, and something about the status. Yet we will not pass over this: the rhetoricians call the status what the dialecticians call the question, which is called stasis [στάσις]. Once this is posed, just as the dialectician must find a method for proving his proposition, so the orator must find one for defending what he has established. The rhetoricians call that method middle [μέσον], as it were something apt for joining the extremes. They call it cause [αἴτιον], because they inquire into the causes of actions. He also calls it by the common name continents of causes [συνέχοντα], because without these the case would not stand, as Cicero himself teaches. The guiding principle [ἡγεμονικόν], which he rendered as judgment in the Topics, corresponds to the dialecticians' analysis [ἀναλύσει], by which they weigh separately the forms of conclusions and the force of arguments. But let us define the terms of the art themselves. The charge (intentio) is the accuser's imputation, by which he fixes the crime upon his adversary. The rebuttal (depulsio) is the defender's refusal, by which he wards off the charge from himself, as it were a missile, either by denial, by definition, or by setting equity against it. The reason is what contains the defence, without which not even a slight doubt can delay a condemnation. The firm support (firmamentum) is what is brought against the defender's reason, without which the accusation cannot stand. The judgment is the proper question of the trial, arising from the clash of reason and firm support. For as a sound arises from the collision of two bodies, so from the clash of reason and firm support a certain question and judgment arises, in which it is usually asked what comes into the trial and what is to be disputed. For example, if you say, "You did it," this will be the charge; "I did not do it," or "I did not do this," or "I did it rightly," will be the rebuttal. The first is conjecture, in which it is asked whether he did it; the second is of the name, whether he did this; the third is of law, whether he did it rightly, which is called the status of quality. In the first, a denial or disavowal is put forward as the reason; in the second, definition is set against definition; in the third, the cause, namely that it was necessary or allowed, or, if you cannot argue otherwise, that it was done through inadvertence, necessity or chance. Then comes the defender's reason: because the thing was private, not public, which I took from the treasury; therefore it was not peculation. This reason relates to definition. Or: because he used force, he was rightly killed, which relates to quality. The continent, or firm support of the accuser, is: yet it was not lawful to kill an uncondemned citizen. From these there will arise the question: whether or not it is right to avenge, without a trial, one who uses force?

units.la: Nam prima aduerfariorũ contetio diffusam habet quæstionẽ: ut in cõiectura, caperit ne pecunias Decius. In definitione, minuerit ne maiestatem Norbanus. In æquitate, iure ne occiderit Opimius Gracchũ. Hæc, quę primam contētionem habent ex arguendo & refistēdo lata, ut dixi, & confusa sunt. Rationum & firmamentorum cõtentio adducit in angustã disceptationem. ea in coniectura nulla est. Nemo enim eius, quod negat factũ, rationem aut potest, aut debet, aut solet reddere. Itaque in his causis eadem & prima quæstio, & disceptatio est extrema. In illis autem, ubi ita dicitur, Non minuit maiestatẽ, quòd egit de Cepione turbulentius. Populi enim Rom. dolor iustus, uim illam excitauit, nõ tribuni actio. Maiestas autem, quoniam est magnitudo quædam populi Rom. in eius potestate ac iure retinendo, aucta est potius quam diminuta: & ubi ita refertur,
units.tr: For the first contention of the adversaries has a diffuse question: as in conjecture, whether Decius took the money; in definition, whether Norbanus diminished majesty; in equity, whether Opimius rightly killed Gracchus. These, which have their first contention arising from arguing and resisting, are, as I said, broad and confused. The contention of reasons and firm supports leads to a narrow dispute. In conjecture there is none of this. For no one can, must or usually gives a reason for what he denies having done. Therefore in these cases the first question and the final dispute are the same. But in the others, where it is said, "He did not diminish majesty, because he acted rather turbulently against Cepio": the just grief of the Roman people aroused that violence, not the tribune's action. And majesty, since it is a certain greatness of the Roman people, residing in its power and in the right of retaining it, was increased rather than diminished; and where it is referred thus,

units.la: Maiestas est in imperij, atq; in omni pop.Rom.dignitate: quā minuit is, qui per uim multitudinis rem ad seditionē uocauit. existit illa disceptatio, Minuerit ne maiestatē, qui uoluntate pop.Ro. rem grata & æquā per uim egerit? In his autē caussis, ubi aliquid recte factum, aut conce dendū, esse factū defendatur, cum est facti subiecta ratio. sicut ab Opi mio, Iure feci, salutis omniū & con seruādæ Reipub. caussa: relatumq; est ab Decio, Ne sceleratissimum quidem ciuem sine iudicio iure ullo necare potuisti. oritur illa disceptatio, potuerit ne recte salutis Rei pub.caussa ciuem euersorem ciuitatis indemnatum necare.
units.tr: Majesty resides in the empire and in all the dignity of the Roman people, and is diminished by him who through the violence of a crowd has called the matter to sedition. That dispute arises: did he diminish majesty who by violence carried out a matter pleasing and just to the will of the Roman people? But in those cases where something rightly done is defended, or must be conceded to have been done, the reason of the deed is set forth. Thus Opimius says, "I did it rightly, for the sake of the safety of all and the preservation of the commonwealth," and Decius has replied: "You could not by any right have killed even the most wicked citizen without a trial." That dispute arises: could he rightly kill, for the sake of the safety of the commonwealth, an uncondemned citizen who was overthrowing the state?

units.la: Nam prima aduersariorum cōtentio.)Et hæc ad illum quem proxime dixi caussæ apparatū, & quasi designatione pertinet.docet enim, quid status à reliquis cōtinentib. differat. Statuū, ratio-nū, & firmamentorū & iudicationū exēpla proponit: denique quomodo ex hypothesi fiat thēsis, docct. Status generis unius habet, et cuiusdā rei uniuersæ,
units.tr: For the first contention of the opponents belongs to the preparation of the case I have just mentioned, and as it were to its outline. It shows how a status differs from the other containing elements. It sets out examples of statuses, reasons, firmaments and judgments, and finally teaches how a thesis arises from a hypothesis.

units.la: Ex ratione uniuersi status, ut supra dictum. uniuersæ, utpote in quo summa rei implicita contineatur. Reliqua, ut ratio, et firmamentū, et iudicatio, tanquam forma sunt, quæ iam perfectius aliquid ac certius indicat. ut, exēpli caussa: Qui insidiatorem dicit, iam explicatius aliquid dixit, quàm cum improbum nominauit. Eodem modo si quis quærat, Liceat ne homine occidere? confusum et latè patens: at licuerit ne pro salute Reipub. ciuem seditiosum indemnatum necare, angustius et certius. Ad hanc autem angustam disceptationem, rem adduxerunt, tum defensoris tũ accusatoris rationes. Sed quærat aliquis, an in tribus generibus caussarū sint eædē rationes, eadémq; extrema ex rationibus quæstio? Respondet Cicero: In coniectura nullam esse à statu separatam atq; sci in stam: in reliquis duobus generibus esse. Cur autem in coniectura non sit, rationem triplicem affert: Quòd non possit, quòd non debeat, quòd non soleat, eius quòd factū negatur, ratio reddi. Nō potest, quia nulla est. Non debet, quia nullo iure astringitur aliquis reddere quod nō accepit: est enim ratio affirmationis propria, nō negationis. Non solet, quia moris nō est. Quid ergo faciendum in huiusmodi caussis? Prima quæstio, quæ status dicitur, pro ratione et disceptatione habenda. ut, Cepisti contra leges pecunias Deci. Nō cepi. Status et iudicatio sequitur: coeperit ne contra leges pecunias P.Decius? Hic nihil aliud fuisset,nisi ut coiectura lo cis capisse probetur. In definitione vero, et qualitate, perspicua est disceptatio: quemadmodum hic apertis exemplis, ijsque è Romano foro sumptis, Cicero demonstrat, sed apertius et copiosius in secundo de Oratore. quae exempla, tum quia perspicua sunt, tum quia copiosius ibidem explicantur, omittimus.
units.tr: A status is of one kind and concerns one whole matter, as stated above, since in it the sum of the matter is implicitly contained. The remaining elements, such as the reason, the firmament and the judgment, are like a form, which indicates something more fully and certainly. For example, someone who calls a man an ambusher has said something more explicit than one who calls him wicked. Likewise, if someone asks, "May a man be killed?", the question is confused and broad. But "May a seditious citizen be killed without trial for the safety of the Republic?" is narrower and more precise. Both the defender's and the prosecutor's reasons have brought the matter to this narrow dispute. But someone may ask whether the reasons are the same in all three kinds of causes, and whether the final question arising from the reasons is the same. Cicero answers that in conjecture there is no status separate from and distinct from the reason, whereas in the other two kinds it is so. He gives a threefold reason why in conjecture there is no reason to be given for the thing that is denied: it cannot be done, it ought not to be done, and it is not customary. It cannot, because there is none. It ought not, because no one is bound by any law to give what he has not received, for the reason belongs to affirmation, not to denial. It is not customary, because it is not the custom. What, then, should be done in such causes? The first question, which is called the status, must be held as the reason and the dispute. For example: "You took money from Decius contrary to the laws." "I did not take it." The status and the judgment follow: "Did P. Decius begin to take money contrary to the laws?" Here nothing else would be at issue than to prove by conjecture that the place was taken. In definition and quality, however, the dispute is plain. Cicero demonstrates this here with open examples taken from the Roman forum, but more openly and fully in the second book On the Orator. We omit these examples, both because they are plain and because they are explained more fully in that place.

units.la: Relatiuĕ est ab Decio.) Relatiu, id est oppositi: ut referendi verbo saepius paulo antè usus est.
units.tr: Relatum est from Decius.) "Relatum," that is, "opposed": as he used the verb "refer" a little earlier.

units.la: Ne sceleratissimum quidem ciuem.) Hac ratione usus est contra Clodium ad Pontifices, ubi ait: At quid tulit legis scriptor peritus, callidus: Velitis, iubeatis, ut M. Tullio aqua et ignis interdicatur? crudele, nefarium, ne in scelaratissimo quidem ciue ferendum, sine iudicio.
units.tr: "Not even the most wicked citizen." He used this argument against Clodius before the Pontiffs, where he says: "But what did the skilled and crafty author of the law propose, that you should will and order that water and fire be denied to Marcus Tullius? Cruel, abominable, and not to be borne even against the most wicked citizen, without trial."

units.la: Ita disceptationes eae, quae in his controuersiis oriuntur, quae sunt certis personis & temporibus notatae, fiunt rursus infinitae: detractisque tem poribus & personis, rursum ad consultationis formam, rationemque re-uocantur.
units.tr: Thus the disputes that arise in these controversies, which are marked by certain persons and times, become again unlimited. When the times and persons are removed, they are again brought back to the form and reasoning of a general inquiry.

units.la: Ita disceptationes eae.) Hoc ulti, iudicationes omnes definitae esse, cum tamen ex hypotheticis oriantur. nam q; quæstio finita, detractis attributis, ad infinitum transfertur: & hæc, adiunctis ijsdem, ad definitum reuocatur. Sed tamen quoniam latius de genere quàm de parte disceptare licet, ut ipse ad Brutum scribit, debet Orator à proprijs personis & temporibus semper, si potest, auocare controuersiā: ut quod in uniuerso atq; in infinita quæstione probatum fit, id in parte definitaq; probari fit necesse. Omnes enim controuersiæ ad uniuersi generis uim naturāq; referuntur. Nam in ea ipsa causa, de qua ante dixit, nihil pertinet ad Oratoris locos Opimij persona, nihil Decij, de ipso enim uniuerso genere infinita quæstio est: Num pœna uideatur esse assiciendus, qui ciuē ex Senatusconsulto patriæ conseruandæ caussa interfecerit, cū id per leges non liceret. Quin etiam in ipsis, ubi de facto ambigitur, caeperit ne cōtra leges pecunias P. Decius, argumenta & criminum & defensionis, reuocentur oportet ad genus, & ad naturam uniuersam: quod sumptuosus, de luxuria: quod alieni appetens, de auaritia: quod seditiosus, de turbulentis & malis ciuibus: quod à multis arguitur, de genere testium: contraq; quæ pro reo dicentur, omnia necessariò à tempore, atq; homine, ad communes rerum & generū summas revoluentur. De Oratore lib.2.
units.tr: "Thus the disputes that arise." He says this because all judgments are defined, although they nevertheless arise from hypothetical questions. For a question that is finite, once its attributes are removed, is transferred to the infinite; and this, when the same attributes are added, is brought back to the definite. But since it is permitted to argue more broadly about the genus than about the part, as he himself writes to Brutus, the orator should always, if he can, withdraw the controversy from its particular persons and times. What is proved in the universal and infinite question must necessarily be proved in the particular and defined one. For all controversies are referred to the force and nature of the universal genus. Indeed, in that very case of which he spoke before, nothing pertains to the orator's topics concerning the person of Opimius, nothing concerning that of Decius. For the question is infinite concerning the universal genus itself: whether one who has killed a citizen by decree of the Senate, for the sake of preserving the fatherland, when this was not permitted by law, seems to deserve punishment. Indeed, even in those cases where the fact is in doubt, whether P. Decius began to take money contrary to the laws, the arguments both of the charges and of the defence ought to be referred to the genus and to the universal nature. Thus, that he is extravagant is referred to luxury; that he is greedy for others' goods, to avarice; that he is seditious, to turbulent and bad citizens; that he is accused by many, to the kind of witnesses. And conversely, whatever is said on behalf of the defendant must necessarily be turned from the time and the man to the common sums of things and kinds. On the Orator, book 2.

units.la: Sed in grauissimis firmamentis & illa ponenda sunt, si qua ex scrí‐ pto legis, aut testamēti, aut uerbo‐rum ipsius iudicij, aut alicuius stipu‐ latiónis, aut cautionis opponun‐tur defensioni contraria.
units.tr: But among the most serious firmaments those must also be set forth, if any are advanced against the defence, from the wording of a law or a will, or from the wording of a judgment itself, or of some stipulation or bond.

units.la: Sed in grauisimis firmamentis.) Qualitatis duplex est consideratio: una, in æquitatis & iu‐ ris ratione posita est: altera, in scripto. illa ratio naális, hæc legitima appellatur. Quomodo autē rationes & iudicationes in priore genere inue‐ niendæ essent, ostendit: idē nunc in altera docet. Est uero legitima constitutio, cū in scripto, aut ex scriptis controuersia nascitur, quæ etiamsi le‐gitima à lege, hoc est à re firmissima nomen ha‐ bet, non magis tamen in legibus quàm in testa‐ mentis, in iudicatis, in stipulationibus, in cautio‐nibus, reliquisq; rebus quæ in scripto aguntur, possunt controuersiæ eædem existere. Lex quid sit, item testamentum, ante dictum est. Iudica‐ tum, id est, de quo sententia lata est, aut decre‐ tum interpositū. Heren.lib.2. Stipulatio, uerbo‐ rum est conceptio, quibus is qui interrogatur, daturum factūrum ue se quod interrogatus est, respondet. De Verb.oblig.ff.lib.45. Cautio, est stipulatio omnis, quæ nobis cauemus, cautosq; fa‐cimus. cimus de re quæ nobis debeatur: cuiusmodi sunt chirographha, & syngraphæ, & satisdationes, siue fideiussiones.
units.tr: "But among the most serious firmaments." There is a twofold consideration of quality: one is founded on the reasoning of equity and right, the other on the written text. The former is called natural, the latter legitimate. He has shown how the reasons and judgments are to be found in the former kind; now he teaches the same for the latter. A legitimate status arises when the controversy arises from a writing or from writings. Although it takes its name "legitimate" from lex, that is, from a thing most firm, controversies of the same kind may arise not only in laws but also in wills, in judgments, in stipulations, in bonds, and in other matters that are transacted in writing. What a law is, and likewise a will, has been said before. A judgment is that concerning which a sentence has been pronounced, or a decree has been interposed (Rhetorica ad Herennium, book 2). A stipulation is the formulation of words by which the one who is questioned answers that he will give or do what he was asked (Digest, On Verbal Obligations, book 45). A bond is any stipulation by which we secure ourselves and make ourselves safe concerning something owed to us; such are the chirographs, the syngraphs, and the sureties, or guarantees.

units.la: Acne hoc quidem genus in eas causas incurrit, quæ coiectura continentur. Quod enim factum negatur, id argui non potest scripto: ne in definitionem quidem uenit, genere scripti ipsius. Nam etiamsi uerbum aliquod de scripto definiendum est, quam uim habeat, ut cum ex testamentis quid sit penus, aut cū ex lege prædiĭ quæritur, quæ sint ruta cæsa, nō scripti genus, sed uerbi interpretatio controuersiā parit.
units.tr: Does this kind not also fall among those cases that are contained in conjecture? For what is denied to have been done cannot be argued from writing; it does not even enter into definition by the kind of writing itself. Even if some word in a writing needs defining, and we ask what force it has, as when we ask from wills what penus is, or from a law of landed property what ruta caesa are, the kind of writing does not create the controversy. The interpretation of the word does.

units.la: Quod enim factum negatur.) Duo hic facit: primum, neq; in coniecturam, neq; in definitionem incidere firmamentum, si causa ex scripto oriatur: alterum, hoc genus statuum, qui legitimi uocantur, ad solam qualitatem pertinere: effecq; eius partes, quaecunq; ex scripto nascantur controuersiæ. Vtrunq; ratione probat, & de coniectura quidem prius hoc modo: Quod enim factum negatur, ut ratione, sic nec scripto, id est, scripti iure argui, defendi ue potest. Non cadere etiam
units.tr: "What is denied to have been done." This passage makes two points: first, that neither conjecture nor definition supplies a firm ground of argument if the case arises from writing; second, that this kind of status, which is called legal, pertains only to quality, and that all disputes arising from writing are its parts. He proves both by reason. He treats conjecture first, as follows: what is denied to have been done cannot be argued or defended by reason, and so not by writing either, that is, by the law of writing. That it does not fall also

units.la: Quod enim factum negatur.) Duo hic facit: (note continues as printed above) etiam in definitione, distinctione ostedit. Aliud est, de genere scripti controuersiam esse: aliud, de uerbi alicuius, quod in scripto fit, interpreta-tio est. Cötrouersia autē nulla est in scripto, de scripti genere, ut de testamēto, aut de lege prędij: sed, exempli caussa, quid sit pœnus, quæ res testamento legata est, itemq; quæ sint ruta cæsa in prædij uenditione & lege: quæ quidem uerbi interpretatio natura status mutare non potest, qui iure testamentorū & prædiorū, hoc est qualitate continetur. Pœnus est, quicquid esu potuq; continetur.l.qui pœnū.de pœnu legata.Lex prędij est, quæ de prædiorū possessione, seruitutib. & mancipio agit: de quibus multa Iurisconsulti. hoc ius prædiatoriū appellatur: cuius qui periti sunt, prædiatores nominantur. Prædia uerò sunt, domus & ager: eáq; tam rustica, quàm urbana & suburbana, ut de uerb. significatione docent Iurisconsulti. Ruta cæsa quæ sint, uidendū est l fundi.de Empt.& uendit. ff. 19. Item de uerb. signif.ubi in rutis cæsis ea uult esse Scæuola, quæ terra non tenentur: quæq; opere structili tectorio uue non continentur. Sed quod hic Cicero negat,definitionis statū legitima cōstitutione contineri, in eo à seipso dissentit, qui de Inuen.lib.2. definitione eidem subijcit statui. Et hoc nihil mirum est.solent enim magni uiri errores suos corrigere: secus ac pleriq; faciunt, qui errore semel suscepti mordicus tuentur: id sibi laudi fore arbitrantes, quod maximo uitio dandu est, cu laus sit potius, in errore mutare sententiam: alioqui frustra studeremus, nisi in melius proficere daretur. Quāobrē Cicero doctior ætate & usu factus, illis iuuenilib. scriptis ueriora certioráq; subiecit. Nā & ipse eos libros sibi adolescéti excidisse, in proœmio librorū de Oratore testatur. Sed rursum obijciat fortasse aliquis, quod in Topicis nouos status appellet eos, qui ex scripto existunt. Verum aducrtendū est, cum non simpliciter status nouos dicere, sed, Quasi status nouos: illud intelligens, noua qualitatis capita & partes, id quod multis probat de Oratore libro secundo.
units.tr: "What is denied to have been done." This passage makes two points: (1) that the dispute cannot fall under definition either, and this is shown by a distinction. One thing is to have a controversy about the kind of writing; another is to have an interpretation of some word that occurs in a writing. There is no controversy in a writing about the kind of writing, as with a will or a law of landed property. Rather, for example, the question is what penus is, which thing is bequeathed by will, and likewise what ruta caesa are, in the sale of land and in the law. Such an interpretation of a word cannot change the nature of the status, which is contained in the law of wills and of landed estates, that is, in quality. Penus is whatever is contained in food and drink (see the law qui penum, on legacies of penus). The lex praedii is the law that deals with the possession of landed estates, servitudes and mancipation, on which the jurists have much to say. This law is called ius praediatorium, and those skilled in it are called praediatores. Praedia are houses and fields, both rural and urban and suburban, as the jurists teach in their discussion of the meaning of words. On which things are ruta caesa, see the law fundi (on purchase and sale, Digest 19), and also on the meaning of words, where Scaevola holds that those things are ruta caesa which are not held by the ground and are not contained in a structure of brick, plaster or the like. But where Cicero here denies that the status of definition is contained in legal constitution, he dissents from himself, since in De Inventione book 2 he subjoins the same status to definition. This is no cause for wonder. Great men are accustomed to correct their errors, unlike most people, who, once they have taken up an error, defend it tooth and nail, thinking it a credit to themselves, when it ought rather to be counted the greatest fault, since the praise lies in changing one's opinion when one is in error; otherwise we would study in vain, unless it were granted to advance to better things. Therefore Cicero, made wiser by age and experience, appended truer and more certain things to those youthful writings. For he himself testifies in the proem to the books De Oratore that those books had slipped out in his youth. But someone may perhaps object again that in the Topics he calls new statuses those that arise from writing. It must be noted, however, that he did not say simply "new statuses" but "as it were new statuses," meaning by this new heads and parts of quality, which he proves by many arguments in book 2 of De Oratore.

units.la: Cum autem plura significantur scripto propter uerbi, aut uerborū ambiguitatē, ut liceat ei qui contradicat, eo trahere significationē scripti, quo expediat, aut uelit: aut etiā si ambigue scriptū non sit, uel à uerbis uoluntatem & sententiam scriptoris abducere, uel alio se eadē de re contrarie scripto defendere: tum disceptatio ex scripti contentione existit, ut in ambiguis disceptetur, quid maximè significetur. in scripti, sententiæq; cötentione,utrū potius sequatur iudex: in cötrarijs scriptis, utrū magis sit cöprobandum.
units.tr: When a text can carry several meanings because of an ambiguous word or phrase, so that the one who contradicts it may twist its meaning in whatever direction suits him or he wishes; or even when the text is not ambiguous, he may draw the will and intention of the author away from the words, or defend his own position on the same matter by a contrary writing: then a dispute arises from a conflict over the writing. In ambiguous matters the question is what is most fully meant; in a conflict between the writing and the intention, whether the judge should follow the one or the other; in contrary writings, which should be preferred.

units.la: Cum autè plura significantur scripto.)Legitimi status tria genera facit, ut etiā in Topicis, Ambigui,scripti & sententiæ,& contrariarū legum siue scriptorum: quæ tria de Oratore lib.2. ad unum ambiguorum genus reuocat. Nam aut ambiguū est, scriptū ne an sententia scriptoris sequi debeamus: aut ex cōtrarijs legibus,utra sit alteri præferrenda:ex ambigua oratione aut uerbo,in qua significatione accipere uelimus.Ita fit, ut unū genus in ijs causis quæ propter scriptū ambiguntur relinquatur, si est scriptum aliquid ambiguè. Ex ambiguo controuersia nascitur, cum scriptum duas aut plures res significat. ut si lex talis sit lata, Meretrix coronam auream ne habeto:si habuerit,publica esto.Cōtrouersia nā-scitur in hunc modum.alter dicit meretricem publicari debere,quod lex dicat, Meretrix publica esto: alter cōtrā,Coronā publicari debere,quod in auro & in corona facile est, in meretrice non ite.Ex quo iudicatio oritur,utra significatio & sententia sit accipienda. Ex scripto uerò & sen-tētia nascitur cōtrouersia, cū uidetur scriptoris volun
units.tr: When several things are signified by a writing. Legal status makes three kinds, as also in the Topics: ambiguity of the writing and of the intention, and contrary laws or writings. Cicero, in De Oratore book 2, reduces these three to one kind of ambiguity. For either the writing is ambiguous, so that we must ask whether we should follow the writing or the author's intention; or, from contrary laws, which of them is to be preferred to the other; or, from an ambiguous phrase or word, in which meaning we wish to take it. So it comes about that one kind is left among those cases which are in doubt because of a writing, if something is written ambiguously. The controversy arises from ambiguity when a writing signifies two or more things, as if a law were passed to this effect: "A prostitute shall not have a golden crown; if she has one, let it be public property." The controversy arises in this way: one party says the prostitute must be confiscated, because the law says "let the prostitute be public property"; the other, on the contrary, says the crown must be confiscated, because this is easily done with gold and a crown, but not with a prostitute. From this the judgment arises as to which meaning and sense is to be accepted. But the controversy arises from the writing and the intention when the will of the author seems

units.la: No notes. uoluntas cum scripto ipso dissentire: ut si lex sit quæ uetet, peregrinum in murum ascendere. Peregrinus autem, quum sensisset adesse hostes, in murum ascendit, & ciuitatem liberauit. accusatur, quasi contra legem fecerit. Respondet se quidem murum conscendisse, sed etiam una patriam liberasse: quod haud dubie voluit legislator. Exiftit disceptatio, an, quid murum ascenderit, & ciuitate liberauerit, contra legem fecisse dicaturid est, sit ne ex scripto an sententia legis iudicandum. Ex contrariis legibus disceptatio existit, cum alia lex iubet aut permittit, id quod alia lex fieri uetat, hoc modo, ne ab exemplis Rhetorum discedamus. Lex uetat, eum qui de pecuniis repetundis damnatus sit, in concione orationem habere: altera lex iubet, augurem in demortui locum, qui petat, in cœcione nominari. Augur quidam damnatus de pecuniis repetundis, in demortui locum qui petat, nominauit: contra legem fecisse dicitur; ille dicit, se ex lege fecisse. Quæstio est, utri legi sit adhærendum, aut quomodo contrariae leges conciliandæ sint.
units.tr: to disagree with the writing itself: as if there were a law forbidding a foreigner to climb onto the wall. A foreigner, however, when he perceived that enemies were near, climbed the wall and freed the city. He is accused as if he had acted against the law. He replies that he did indeed climb the wall, but that he also freed the fatherland at the same time, which the lawgiver undoubtedly intended. A dispute arises whether, because he climbed the wall and freed the city, he is said to have acted against the law; that is, whether the matter is to be judged by the writing or by the intention of the law. Dispute arises from contrary laws when one law orders or permits what another law forbids, as in this example, so as not to depart from the examples of the rhetoricians: one law forbids a man condemned for extortion to make a speech in the assembly; another law orders that an augur be nominated in the assembly to fill the place of a deceased augur, for whoever seeks it. A certain augur, condemned for extortion, nominated in the assembly someone to fill the place of the dead augur who sought it. He is said to have acted against the law; he says he acted in accordance with the law. The question is which law is to be adhered to, or how the contrary laws are to be reconciled.
