units.la: Disceptatio autem, cum est constituta, propositia esse debet oratori, quo omnes argumentationes repetitæ, ex inueniendi locis conjiciantur. quod quanquam satis ei est, qui ui˨ det, quid in quoq; loco lateat, quíq; illos locos tanquã thesauros aliquos argumetorum notatos habet: tamẽ ea quæ sunt certarum caussarũ propria, tangemus.
units.tr: Once the dispute has been set up, it ought to be laid before the orator, so that all arguments may be drawn from the places of invention. Although this is enough for one who sees what lies hidden in each place, and who has those places marked as it were as treasuries of arguments, nevertheless we shall touch on those things which are proper to particular cases.

units.la: Disceptatio autẽ cum est constituta.) Quid utilitatis habeat, disceptationis inuetio: tum quot sint locorũ genera, ex quib. argumenta ad propo˨ sitam quæstionẽ depromãtur. Prima utilitas est, quòd nouit orator, quò argumẽta sint referenda, ut ne quid alienum à caussa dicat, & quomodo iudex tractandus sit. Deinde, iudex ipse ex propo˨sita disceptatione intelligit, quid expecta˨ re, quid'que sequi debeat. Locorum autem duo sunt genera. Alij generales & communes, de quibus libro primo dictum est, quum fontes inuentionis aperirentur: alij sunt statuum singulorum proprij, quas hic Cicero causas appellat: de quib. deinceps ordine explicabit. Maiores & latiores illi sunt, hi uerò angustiores & certiores. Acuto & experto homini illi satis essent: hi uerò nec acutis inutiles, & minus acutis necessarij sunt. qua de re sic de Orat. 2. Quod autem argumen˨ torum genus (inquit) cuiq; caussarum generi maxime conueniat, non est artis exquisitæ pręscribere: sed est mediocris ingenij iudicare. Est igitur hæc quasi transitio à definatione causarum, & præparatione, ad minores & angustiores causarum partes, & locos.
units.tr: Once the dispute has been set up.) This sets out the usefulness of the invention of the dispute, and then how many kinds of places there are from which arguments for the proposed question are drawn. The first usefulness is that the orator knows where his arguments are to be referred, so that he says nothing foreign to the case, and how the judge is to be handled. Then the judge himself understands from the proposed dispute what he should expect and what he ought to follow. There are two kinds of places. Some are general and common, about which was said in the first book, when the sources of invention were laid open; others are the particular places of the individual statuses, which Cicero here calls causes, and which he will explain in order afterwards. The former are greater and broader, the latter narrower and more certain. For a sharp and experienced man the former would suffice; the latter are not useless even to the sharp, and are necessary for the less sharp. On this matter he says thus in De Oratore 2: "As to which kind of argument best suits each kind of case, it is not the part of exact art to prescribe, but of a middling talent to judge." This is therefore a kind of transition from the definition of causes and their preparation to the smaller and narrower parts and places of the causes.

units.la: DE CONIECTVRA.
units.tr: ON CONJECTURE.

units.la: In coniectura igitur, cum est in inficiando reus, accusatori hæc duo prima sunt: sed accusatorem pro omni actore & petitore appello. post sunt enim etiam sine accusatore in causis hæc eandem controuersiarū genera uersari.
units.tr: In conjecture, then, when the defendant denies the charge, the accuser has these two first things. I call the accuser every plaintiff and petitioner, since these same kinds of dispute also arise in cases without an accuser.

units.la: In coniectura igitur.) Absoluta præparatione causarum, iam singulorum statuum locos describit proprios: ac primum coniecturæ, quam copiosius tractat, quoniam est (ut alibi diximus) Oratoris propria, & in ea Cicero excellit maximè. Coiecturam definit, deinde locos accusatoris, post defensoris: postremò collocationem partium tam accusatoris quàm defensoris docet. Coniectura est (inquit) quum est in inficiando reus: id est, quum factum negatur.
units.tr: In conjecture, then.) Having finished the preliminaries of cases, he now describes the topics proper to each issue, and first those of conjecture, which he treats more fully, since it is (as we have said elsewhere) the orator's own domain, and Cicero excels in it above all. He defines conjecture, then gives the topics for the accuser, and afterwards for the defender, and finally teaches the arrangement of the parts for both accuser and defender. Conjecture is (he says) when the defendant denies the charge, that is, when the deed itself is denied.

units.la: Sed accusatorem pro omni actore.) Hæc inserit, ut quid nomine accusatoris intelligi velit, declaret. Nam accusatorem proprie dixere, qui crimen intenderet, idq; in rebus capitalib. aut infamiæ, latius tamen capitur pro omni actore & petitore. titore. Quare in omnibus actionibus accusationem quodammodo intelligi necesse est, siue criminum sint, siue ciuiles.
units.tr: But I call the accuser every plaintiff.) He adds this to explain what he wants to be understood by the name accuser. For strictly speaking, those were called accusers who brought a charge, and that in capital cases or cases of infamy; yet the term is taken more broadly for every plaintiff and petitioner. Hence in all actions one must in some sense understand accusation, whether they concern crimes or civil matters.

units.la: Possunt enim etiam, ) Vt in petitione bonorum & possessionum, & deliberatione, & aliis, si accusator proprie capiatur. nam in ea etiam coniectura, uel definitio, uel ius cadunt: quæ tria sunt generalia controuersiarum genera.
units.tr: For they can also, ) As in the petition for goods and possessions, and in deliberation, and in other cases, if "accuser" is taken strictly. For in these too, conjecture, or definition, or law, may arise; and these three are the general kinds of dispute.

units.la: Sed hęc duo sunt ei prima caussa, & euentus. Caussam appello rationem efficiendi: euentum, id quod est effectum. atq; ipsa quidem partitio caussarum paulo ante in suasionis locis distributa est. Quæ enim in consilio capiendo futuri temporis præcipiebantur, quamobrem aut utilitatem uidentur habitura, aut efficiendi facultatem, eadem, qui de facto arguimetabitur, colligere debebit. Quare obrem & utilia illi, quem arguet, suisse, & ab eo effici potuisse demonstret. Vtilitatis coniectura mouetur, si illud quod arguitur, aut spe bonorum, aut malorum metu, fecisse dicitur: quod fit acrius, quo illa in utroq; genere maiora ponuntur. Spectatur etiam ad caussam facti, motus animorum, si ira recens, si odiū uetus, si ulciscendi studium, si iniuriæ dolor, si honoris, si gloriæ, si imperij, si pecuniæ cupiditas, si periculi timor, si æs alienū, si angustiæ rei familiaris, si audax, si leuis, si crudelis, si impotens, si incautus, si insipiens, si amans, si commota mēte, si uinolentus, si cum spe effi ciendi, si cum opinione celandi: aut si patefactum esset, depellendi criminis, uel perrumpendi periculi, uel in longinquum tempus differendi: aut si iudicij pœna leuior, quàm facti præmium: aut si facinoris uoluptas maior, quàm dānationis dolor. His ferē rebus facti suspicio confirmatur, cum & uoluntatis in reo caussæ reperiuntur, & facultas. In uoluntate autē utilitas ex adeptione alicuius commodi, uitationeq; alicuius incommodi quæritur: ut aut spes, aut metus impulísse uideatur, aut alius repentinus animí motus, qui e‑tiam citius in fraudé, quàm ratio uti litatis impellít. quãobrem sint hæc dicta de causis.
units.tr: But these two are the first things for him, the cause and the outcome. I call the cause the reason for doing something, and the outcome that which is the effect. And indeed the division of causes was set out a little earlier, in the places on persuasion. For the things that were taught for taking counsel about the future, namely why people seem likely to have some advantage or the ability to act, these the one who argues about a deed must also gather. So he must show both that the advantage was useful to the man he accuses and that he could have brought it about. Conjecture from advantage is moved if the thing charged is said to have been done either from hope of gains or from fear of losses; and it is the more forceful the greater these are set out in either sort. The motives of the mind are also examined as causes of the deed: if there was recent anger, old hatred, a desire for revenge, the pain of an injury, a lust for honour, for glory, for power, for money, fear of danger, debt, straitened family finances; if the man is bold, frivolous, cruel, uncontrolled, incautious, foolish, in love, disturbed in mind, drunk; if he acted in hope of success, or in the belief that he could conceal it; or, if it were discovered, that he could ward off the charge, break through the danger, or put off judgment to a far distant time; or if the penalty of the court is lighter than the reward of the deed; or if the pleasure of the crime is greater than the pain of condemnation. By such things a suspicion of the deed is mostly confirmed, when causes of will in the defendant are found, and also ability. As to will, advantage is sought in gaining some benefit or avoiding some harm, so that either hope or fear seems to have driven him, or some other sudden motion of the mind, which drives even more quickly to fraud than reason does to advantage. These, then, are the things said about causes.

units.la: Sed hæc duo sunt ei prima. )Cœperat cõiectu‑ræ locos diuidere: sed ambigui nominis distin‑ guendi caussa, coáctus est quædam interponere. quare nunc revocat suprà cœptam orationem ἐπαναλήψιν, ut vocant Græci: ,Cicero verbi re‑vocationem appellat,de Orat.lib.3.
units.tr: But these two are the first things. ) He had begun to divide the topics of conjecture, but to distinguish an ambiguous term he was forced to interpose some matters. Therefore he now returns to the discourse begun above, a recapitulation [ἐπανάληψιν], as the Greeks call it. Cicero calls it the repetition of a word, De Oratore book 3.

units.la: Caussam appello.) Hac definitione comprehendit duo Rhetorum capita, ratiocinationem & impulsionem. Ratiocinationem definiunt;diligentem & cõsideratam faciendi aliquid, aut non faciendi excogitationem: quo in genere commodorum spes, & metus incommodorum ponitur. Impulsionem uero, quæ sine cogitatione, per quandam affectionem animi facere aliquid hortatur: ut amor, iracundia, &c.
units.tr: I call the cause.) By this definition he includes two heads of the rhetoricians, reasoning and impulse. They define reasoning as a careful and considered thought of doing or not doing something; under this kind belong the hope of advantages and the fear of harms. Impulse, however, is that which urges one to do something without thought, through some passion of the mind, such as love, anger, and so on.

units.la: Euentum, id quod est effectum. ) Factum etiam appellant Rhetores, ut ipse de Inuentione libro secundo. Sed quid euentus nomine intelligatur, paulo post clarius docebit.
units.tr: The outcome, that which is the effect. ) The rhetoricians also call it the deed, as he does himself in the second book of the De Inventione. But what is meant by the name outcome he will teach a little later, more clearly.

units.la: Quæ in consilio capiendo) Præceptio caussarum & effectuum, deliberationis & coniectura communis est. Idcirco quæ in suasione su‑ prà de eis dicta sunt, ad hunc locu sunt aßumeda. Est tamen illud discriminis inter illam & hanc tractationem, quòd deliberatio futuri temporis est, iudicium præteriti: illa rerum agendarum, hoc actarum. In deliberatione Orator conatur efficere, ut & uelit auditor, & fieri posse putet, id quod optet: in coniectura, ut iudex persuadeatur, & uoluisse reum, & potuisse facere, quod fecisse arguitur. Est igitur coniectura, & præteriti temporis, ut in iudicio: & futuri, ut in consilio capiendo: & præsentis, ut in demonstratione, quum factum negatur. ut illud, Sit ne Anglia ea infula, in quam maximè cupiat Cæsar exercitum ducere.
units.tr: Which in taking counsel) The teaching on causes and effects is common to deliberation and to conjecture. Therefore what was said above about them in persuasion must be taken up for this place. There is, however, this difference between that treatment and this one: deliberation concerns the future, judgment the past; the former concerns things to be done, this one things done. In deliberation the orator tries to bring it about that the hearer both wishes and thinks possible what he desires; in conjecture, that the judge is persuaded both that the defendant was willing and that he was able to do what he is charged with having done. Conjecture therefore concerns the past, as in a court; the future, as in taking counsel; and the present, as in a demonstration, when the deed is denied, as in that line, "Is that Britain, that island into which Caesar most wishes to lead his army?"

units.la: Vtilitatis coniectura mouetur.) Hæc pertinent ad propositum finem, ex ipso genere caussarum.
units.tr: Conjecture from advantage is moved.) These pertain to the proposed end, from the very kind of causes.

units.la: Quod fit acrius.) Significat bona & mala, siue spem & metum, exaggerada esse, quo acrius moveant.
units.tr: Which is more forcefully.) He signifies that goods and evils, or hope and fear, are to be magnified, so that they move more forcefully.

units.la: Spectantur etiam ad caussam.) Hæc ad impulsionem referuntur: quæ sunt quædam caussæ, finem præcurrentes.
units.tr: The causes are also examined.) These are referred to impulse: they are certain causes that run ahead of the end.

units.la: Si cum spe efficiendi.) Facultatum sunt hæc, & ad caussas efficientes pertinere uidentur, Addunt Rhetores & locum, & tempus, & occasionem, & alia nonnulla. Sed de his dictum est in utriuerisimilium locis.
units.tr: If with hope of accomplishing.) These belong to abilities, and seem to pertain to efficient causes. The rhetoricians add also place, time, opportunity, and some others. But these were discussed in the places on what is likely.

units.la: C. F. Teneo, & quæro qui sint illi euentus, quos ex caussis effici dixisti. C. P. Consequentia quædã signa præteriti, & quasi impressa facti uestigia, quæ quidem uel maximè suspicionem mouent, & quasi tacita sunt criminum testimonia. Atque hæc quidem grauiora, quòd caussæ communiter uidetur insimulare, & arguere omnes posse, quorum non interfuerit aliquid. Hæc proprie attingunt eos ipsos qui arguuntur, ut telum, ut uestigium, ut cruor, ut deprehensum aliquid, quod ablatum, ereptum ue uideatur, ut responsum inconstanter, ut hæsitatum, ut titubatum, ut cum aliquo uisus, ex quo suspicio oriatur: ut eo ipso in loco uisus, in quo facinus: ut pallor, ut tremor: ut scriptum, aut obsignatum, aut depositum quippiam. Hæc enim & talia sunt, quæ aut in re ipsa, aut etiam antequam factum est, aut postea suspiciosum crimen efficiant.
units.tr: C.F. I hold, and I ask what those outcomes are which you said arise from causes. C.P. Certain consequent signs of the past, and as it were impressed traces of the deed, which indeed most of all move suspicion, and are as it were silent testimonies of crimes. And these are the weightier, because causes are commonly thought to implicate and accuse all who had some interest in the matter. These touch most directly the very persons who are accused: such as a weapon, a footprint, blood, something caught in the act, something that seems taken away or snatched, a reply given inconsistently, hesitation, faltering, being seen with someone from whom suspicion arises, being seen in the very place of the crime, pallor, trembling, something written, sealed, or deposited. For these and such things either in the deed itself, or even before the deed, or afterwards, make the crime suspicious.

units.la: C.F.Teneo,& quæro. ) Teneo,de causis quæ proposuisti: & quæro,de euentis, altero coniectura capite.
units.tr: C.F. I hold, and I ask. ) I hold, concerning the causes you have set out; and I ask, concerning the outcomes, the second head of conjecture.

units.la: C.P.Confequetia quædam signa præteriti. ) Explicato priore cõiectura capite, in quo causæ fuerůt,uenit ad alterum, euectorum scilicet, quæ sunt effecta de caussis. Ostendit autem certius & clarius,qui sint euentus, & quid ab effectis ipsis caufarũ differåt: tum etiam ab ipsis quoq; caufsis. Nam effectus odij aut sphci,cædes fuit: euentus autem, quæ ex cæde consecuta sunt, quædam signa præteriti, & quasi impressa factí uestigia,ta citaq; criminum testimonia. hæc argumenta & signa uocant Rhetores.
units.tr: C.P. Certain consequent signs of the past. ) Having explained the first head of conjecture, in which the causes lay, he comes to the second, namely of outcomes, which are effects arising from causes. He shows more exactly and clearly what the outcomes are, and how they differ from the effects themselves, and also from the causes themselves. For the effect of hatred or envy was a killing; but the outcomes, which followed from the killing, are certain signs of the past and as it were impressed traces of the deed, and so silent testimonies of crimes. The rhetoricians call these arguments and signs.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem grauiora. ) Iam quid à caufis differant euenta, ostēdit:causse enim illæ quas paulo ante explicauit, communiores sunt, & in certius rem indicant: euenta uero , propius rem attingunt. suntq; rerū propriæ notæ. Nam caufsæ etiam in eum conferri possunt, ad quem crimen nihil pertinet. potest enim commoditas ad eum peruenisse,qui non occiderit:at signa & euenta,uix possunt: ut, pallet, titubat, ergo conscius est: cum telo cruento, in loco facinoris ipsius est Vlysses,ergo Aiacem necauit.
units.tr: And these are the weightier. ) Now he shows how outcomes differ from causes: for those causes which he has just explained are more general, and point to the matter less certainly; but outcomes touch the matter more closely, and are the proper marks of things. For causes can also be attributed to someone to whom the crime has no connection: advantage may have reached a man who did not kill; but signs and outcomes can hardly do so: as, he is pale, he falters, therefore he is guilty; he is found with a bloody weapon in the place of the deed, therefore Ulysses killed Ajax.

units.la: Hæc enim & talia sunt, quæ aut in re ipsa. ) Tripartito distribuit hæc signa:in ea quæ cum re, ante rem, & post rem, suspicionem criminis faciunt: & recte quidem. Sed cur ea ante consequentia signa praeteriti appellauit? Respondeo, Quoniam & si ante quam factum est, & in ipsa re quoque reperiuntur, tamen maxima ex parte factum ipsum consequuntur: idcirco ab eo quod saepius & certius est, consequentia appellauit.
units.tr: These and similar things are signs that arise either in the matter itself, or before the act, and after it, and they create suspicion of the crime; and rightly so. But why did he call those signs that come before the act "consequent" signs of the past? I answer: although they are found before the deed and also in the deed itself, they mostly follow the deed, and so he called them "consequent" from the fact that they are more frequent and more certain.

units.la: Quae si non erunt, tamen causis ipsis, & efficiendi facultatibus niti oportebit: adiuncta illa disputatione communi, non fuisse illum tam a-mentem, ut indicia facti aut effugere, aut occultare non posset, ut ita apertus esset, ut locum criminis relinqueret. Communis ille contra locus, audaciam temeritati, non prudentiae esse coniunctam.
units.tr: If these signs are lacking, we must still rest on the causes themselves and on the abilities to carry out the deed, adding that common argument: that he was not so mad as to be unable to hide or escape the evidence of the deed, so that he would be so open as to leave the scene of the crime. That common argument, on the other hand, holds that audacity is joined to rashness, not to prudence.

units.la: Quae si non erunt.) Quid agendum sit, si i-stiusmodi euentis & signis deflituamur, monet. Ac duo esse docet: unum, ut in ipsis causis, id est, in voluntate & facultatibus commoremur, easque uersemus diligenter: alterum ut locis communibus utamur. Locos communes nominamus, qui transferri in multas causas possunt, aut quibus in utranque partem uti licet. Tres autem ponit: primum & posteremum accusatoris, medium uerò defensoris:quem ideo proponit, ut accusator, quid contrà à defensore dici possit,uideat,eiq; alia sententia resistat. Locorum præterea communium alij sunt finiti, & personarum: ut, Non fuisse illum tam amentem,ut indicia facti aut effugere, aut occultare non posset. Alij infiniti & generales: ut, Audaciam temeritati solere, non prudentiæ esse coniunctam.Hoc loco usus est Cicero pro Cluentio, quum Sassiam audacem quidem esse dicit ad scelus, sed non satis callidam ad occultandum crimen.
units.tr: If these signs are lacking.) He advises what should be done if we are deprived of such events and signs. He teaches that there are two things to do: first, to dwell on the causes themselves, that is, on the will and the abilities, and to examine them carefully; second, to use common topics. We call common topics those that can be transferred to many cases, or that may be used on either side. He gives three: the first and last belong to the accuser, the middle one to the defender, whom he puts forward so that the accuser may see what can be said against him by the defender, and may oppose another view to it. Moreover, some common topics are limited and concern particular persons, as: that he was not so mad as to be unable to hide or escape the evidence of the deed. Others are unlimited and general, as: that audacity is usually joined to rashness, not to prudence. Cicero used this topic in the speech for Cluentius, when he says that Sassia was bold indeed in crime, but not clever enough to conceal it.

units.la: Sequitur autem ille locus ad augendū,non esse expectandum,dum fateatur, argumentis peccata convincì. Et hic etiam exempla ponentur. Atqþ hæc quidē de argumentis.
units.tr: Next comes that topic for amplifying: that we must not wait until the accused confesses before we conclude that his sins are proved by arguments. Examples will also be given here. And so much for arguments.

units.la: Sequitur autē ille locus. ) Hic locus ualet ad impellendos animos iudicū, ad reum condenandū,etsi de crimine non fateatur, modò argumetis res constet: id quod exemplis confirmandum dicit,id est,similib.iudicijs,& rebus iudicatis, quorum authoritas plurimū ualet in caussis, id quod in Verrem ostedit Cicero. Coniecturæ autē locos pertractatos penè omnes inueniet, qui pro Rosc. Amer.pro Milone, pro Cœlio, & in Catilinam, diligenter orationes perlegerit. longum nimis ef-set,
units.tr: Next comes that topic.) This topic is useful for moving the minds of judges, for condemning the accused even if he does not confess the crime, provided the matter is established by arguments. He says this must be confirmed by examples, that is, by similar judgments and decided cases, whose authority carries great weight in causes, as Cicero shows in the case of Verres. Whoever carefully reads through the orations for Roscius of Ameria, for Milo, for Caelius, and against Catiline will find almost all the topics of conjecture treated. It would be too long and tedious to heap up examples of each conjectural topic one by one.

units.la: set, & molestum, singulos cõiectura locos exemplis cumulare. Quoniam uero implicatiora hæc rudibus, etiam in ipso Cicerone uideri possint, totum hunc locum caussarum & euentorum, in tabula descriptum proponimus. Cöëctu-ris loci Quæstiones Euentus, sunt que- dam facti quasi vestigia, vel ante, vel in ipsa re, vel post Telum Vestigium Crux Ablatum sive captum aliquid, ut pallium, annulus. Responsio inconstans Haesitatio Titubatio Vultus, vel [?] Cum aliquis, ex quo suspicio in ipso facinoris loco. Item Pallor, Tremor, Obstipatum, Scriptum, Depositum. Causa, sive efficiens ratio Voluntas Fines Spes bonorum Metus malorum. Motus, seu impulsio Tra recens Odium vetus Vrficeti studium Iniuria, dolor Honoris Gloria Imperij Pecunie. Facultas Spes efficiendi Opinione celandi Perrumpendi Differendi Comparatio Volantis & doloris. Periculi Criminis Timor periculi Aes alienum. Angustia rei familiaris. Audacia Luxus Crudelitas Premij & poenae Item Impotentia Timeritas Infirmitas Amor Amicitia Vinolentia.
units.tr: Since these matters may seem too intricate for beginners, even in Cicero himself, we present this whole topic of causes and events, set out in a table. Topics of conjecture: questions; events, which are certain traces of the deed, either before, in, or after the act itself: weapon, trace, cross; something taken away or seized, such as a cloak or a ring; inconsistent answer; hesitation; stammering; the face, or the look of someone, from which suspicion arises at the scene of the crime; likewise pallor, trembling, a stiffened or obstinate state, something written, something deposited. Cause, or efficient reason: will; ends; hope of goods; fear of evils. Motive, or impulse: recent anger; old hatred; zeal for a party; injury, grief; honour; glory; power; money. Ability: hope of doing it; belief that it can be hidden; breaking through; delaying; comparison of flight and pain. Danger: fear of the charge; fear of danger; debt; straitened household finances. Audacity; luxury; cruelty; reward and punishment. Likewise: lack of self-control; rashness; weakness; love; friendship; drunkenness.

units.la: Sin autem erit etiam testium facultas, primùm, genus erit ipsum laudandum: dicendumque, ne argumentis tenerctur reus, ipsum sua cautione fecisse: testes effugere non potuisse. Deinde singuli laudentur. Quæ autem essent laudabilia, dictum est.
units.tr: But if there is also an opportunity for witnesses, first the class of witnesses itself must be praised, and it must be said that the accused, by his own caution, has made it so that he could not be held by arguments, and could not escape the witnesses. Then individual witnesses are to be praised. What was praiseworthy has been said.

units.la: Sin autem erit etiam testium facultas.) Duplex est coniectura probatio, uelut etiam in locis inuentionis dictum est: artis particeps una, altera artis expers. de illa, ut ex causis & effectis eruatur, dictum est: iam de ea quæ ab arte remota est, præcipit. Ea uero in tractatione testium & quæstionum posita est. Primùm igitur testium consideratio bipartita est. Nam & de toto genere testium, & de singulis testibus, dicendum erit. Primùm ergo, genus erit ipsum laudandum: deinde etiam singuli testes. Genus bifariam intelligi potest. uno modo, ut totàs ciuitates gentem que intelligamus. ut pro Cluentio: Adsunt Ferrētani, homines nobilissimi. Itē in Verrem, ubi laudat sæpe totas ciuitates, earũq; decreta. Deinde genus, totâ ipsam testimonij dicēdi ratio-nem: ut si quis dicat, testimoniorum fidem maximam esse: idcirco eius authoritatem, sine uitio / iudicum, reijci non posse. nam multa huiusmodi & pro testimonijs,& contra testimonia dici cō‑ modè possunt.
units.tr: If there is also an opportunity for witnesses.) Conjecture has a twofold proof, as was also said in the topics of invention: one part belongs to art, the other lies outside art. How the first is drawn out from causes and effects has been said; now he gives precepts about the kind that is remote from art. This is laid down in the treatment of witnesses and questions. First, then, the consideration of witnesses is twofold, for we must speak both of the whole class of witnesses and of individual witnesses. So first the class itself is to be praised, and then also individual witnesses. The class can be understood in two ways: in one way, as whole communities and peoples, as in the speech for Cluentius: "Here are the people of Ferentinum, most noble men." Likewise in the speech against Verres, where he often praises whole communities and their decrees. Then the class can mean the whole manner of giving testimony itself: as if someone should say that the credibility of testimonies is greatest, and therefore their authority cannot be rejected without fault on the judges' part. For many such things can fittingly be said both in favour of testimonies and against them.

units.la: Dicendumq;, ne argumentis teneretur reus.) Duo sunt tempora, quibus testimonijs uti possu‑ mus. Vnum,quum argumenta,factiq; uestigia nō desunt (quod quidem ad maiorem firmitatem fa‑cit:nam & ipsa signa,etiamsi alioqui grauia sint, tamen indigent testimonij & grauioris confirma‑ tionis, ut ipse Cicero de Inuentione libro primo testatur. Alterum tempus est, quum notæ factorum desunt,testes uerò non desunt.hoc igitur tem‑ pore quid agendum sit,præcipit:dicendum nimi‑ rum, quo minus signa facti extent.reum sua cau‑ tione & prouisione fecisse,hominum tamen ocu‑ los atque aures uitare nequinisse.
units.tr: "And it must be said that the accused was not held by arguments." There are two occasions on which we may use testimonies. One is when arguments and traces of the deed are not lacking (which indeed adds to greater firmness, for the signs themselves, even if otherwise weighty, still need testimony and a weightier confirmation, as Cicero himself attests in the first book of On Invention). The other occasion is when the marks of the deed are lacking but witnesses are not lacking. In this case he instructs what must be done: it must be said, namely, that the signs of the deed are fewer, that the accused by his own caution and foresight has made it so, yet he could not avoid the eyes and ears of men.

units.la: Deinde singulí laudentur.) Laudandos e‑tiam singulos testes, ante dictum est. ut pro Ar‑ chia:Ipse adest, uir summa authoritate, & reli‑ gione ac fide,M.Lucullus.
units.tr: "Then individual witnesses are to be praised." It was said earlier that individual witnesses are also to be praised, as in the speech for Archias: "He himself is present, Marcus Lucullus, a man of the highest authority, religion and good faith."

units.la: Quæ autem essent laudabilia, dictum est.) In locis uerisimiliũ,ubi de personis agit:itéq; ubi generis demonstratiui materiam & locos descri‑ bit,inde sumêda materia: pronti in quoque testiũ aliquid laudabile inuenietur.
units.tr: "What was praiseworthy has been said." In the topics of probabilities, where he treats of persons, and again where he describes the matter and topics of the demonstrative kind, material is to be drawn from there; for in any witness something praiseworthy will readily be found.

units.la: Deinde etiam argumento fir‑ mo:quia tamen sæpe falsum est,pos‑ sereʒte non credi uiro bono, & firmo:sine uicio iudicis non posse non credi. Atque etiam,si obscuri testes erunt, aut tenues,dicendum erit,non esse ex fortuna fidem ponderandam: aut eos esse cuiusq; locupletissimos testes, qui id, de quo agatur,facillime scire possint.
units.tr: "Then also by a firm argument": yet because it is often false, it can be said that a good and steady man is not to be disbelieved, and that without fault in the judge one cannot fail to believe him. And again, if the witnesses are obscure or of humble means, it must be said that credibility is not to be weighed by fortune, or that they are the most wealthy witnesses of all, who could most easily know what is in question.

units.la: Deinde etiam argumento firmo. Vt loci communis sententiam unam posuit, quum laudandum est genus testium,si argumenta definiunt: sic unam singulis testibus laudandis subijcit. Argumentum firmum accipit,non pro eo quod necessario factū demonstret: ut si cicatrix est, fuit igitur vulnus: sed pro eo quod reuera apparet ipsum, & cernitur:ut cruor,ut pallor:quae quidem certo cernuntur, tamen non semper factum arguunt. potuit is cruor e naribus fluxisse, potuit in necatum aliquis casu incidisse, telum de corpore extraxisse, hominis casum miseratus attrectasse:potest pallor ex subito metu,non ex conscientia esse, ut multi natura timidi sunt. Itaque tunc firmum erit signum, sed falsum tamen: multa enim probabilia falsa.
units.tr: "Then also by a firm argument." As in the common topic he set down one view, when the class of witnesses is to be praised, if the arguments settle it, so he now adds one view for praising individual witnesses. He takes "firm argument" not in the sense of what demonstrates that a thing was necessarily done, as: if there is a scar, then there was a wound; but in the sense of what truly appears and is seen, such as blood, or pallor; these are certainly seen, yet they do not always prove the deed. That blood may have flowed from the nostrils; someone may have come upon a man who had been killed by chance, drawn out the weapon from the body, and handled him out of pity for the man's fall; pallor may come from sudden fear and not from a guilty conscience, as many are naturally timid. Thus a sign will be firm, but still false, for many probable things are false.

units.la: Atque etiam si obscuri testes erunt. Ex hoc loco colligere licet, duo esse genera testium: alios claros, & locupletes: alios obscuros, & tenues. Quae hactenus praecepta sunt, ea prius genus attingunt: quae nunc dicit, alterum (ponit autem duas sententias, quibus utendum fit, & quae sint amplificandae) est, in testibus probitatem, non fortunam esse spectandam: alterum, cum esse testem satis locupletem & grauem, qui optime id nouit & scit, de quo interrogatur. Ita altera sententia sumitur a probitate, altera a scientia eius rei qua de agitur. Testis enim officium est, dicere quae scierit, aut audierit: ut Cornificius infra lib. 4. scribit.
units.tr: "And also if the witnesses are obscure." From this place it may be gathered that there are two kinds of witnesses: some illustrious and wealthy, others obscure and humble. The precepts given so far touch first on the class; what he now says, the other (he gives two views which must be used and which are to be amplified), is that in witnesses we must look to their integrity, not their fortune; and the other, that a witness should be sufficiently wealthy and weighty, who best knows and understands what he is asked about. Thus one view is taken from integrity, the other from knowledge of the matter in question. For it is the duty of a witness to say what he has known or heard, as Cornificius writes below in book 4.

units.la: Sin quaestiones habitae, aut postulatio ut habeantur, causam adiuuabunt, confirmandum genus primum quaestionum erit, dicendum de ui doloris, de opinione maiorum, qui eam rem totam nisi probassent, certe repudiassent. De institutis Atheniensium, Rhodiorum, doctissimorum hominum, apud quos etiam (si quod acerbissimum est) liberi, ciuesque torquentur. De nostrorum etiam prudentissimorum hominum institutis, qui, cum de seruis in dominos quaeri noluissent, de inceftu tamen, & coniuratione, quæ facta me consule est, quærendum putauerunt.
units.tr: But if trials have already been held, or a demand that they be held, and these help the case, the first kind of trial must be defended: we must speak of the force of torture, and of the opinion of our ancestors, who, unless they had approved the whole practice, would surely have rejected it. We must speak of the institutions of the Athenians and the Rhodians, most learned peoples, among whom (a most bitter thing) even free men and citizens are tortured. We must also speak of the institutions of our own most prudent men, who, although they would not have slaves questioned against their masters, nevertheless thought that inquiry should be made into incest and into the conspiracy that was formed in my consulship.

units.la: Sin quæstiones habitæ.) Siue habitæ sint quæstiones, siue postulentur, eadem tractatio est: continetq; capita quinque. nam aut de re ipsa, deq; genere quæstionum uniuerso dicendum est: aut de opinione maiorum: aut exempla sunt repetenda: aut quæ ab aduersarijs afferri solent, refellêda: & postremò fides est quæstioni habitæ facienda. De genere quæstionum dicetur, si utiliter & necessariò inuentas esse ostendemus: si solas ex omni genere testimoniorum esse ueras, quòd uis doloris extorquere soleat ueritatè. De opinione maiorum, qui cū singulari sapientia fuerint, inuentas repudiassent, nisi earum utilitatem in iudicijs magnam esse comperissent. Exempla aut externa erunt, aut nostratia: atque eadem uel uetusta, uel nostræ memoriæ, & noua, quorum uis eo maior erit, quo illustriores & sapientiores fuerint ij à quibus sumentur: ut Israelitarum, Atheniensium, Rhodiorum, Romanorum, Venetorum: quæ exempla historiæ suppeditabunt.
units.tr: But if trials have been held. Whether trials have been held or are being demanded, the treatment is the same, and it contains five heads. For we must speak either about the thing itself and the whole kind of trial, or about the opinion of our ancestors, or examples must be cited, or the objections usually brought by opponents must be refuted, and finally, credence must be given to the trial that has been held. The kind of trial will be discussed if we show that it was devised usefully and necessarily, and that it alone, of every kind of evidence, is sure to draw out the truth, since the force of pain usually extracts the truth. On the opinion of our ancestors: men of singular wisdom would have rejected trials they had devised unless they had found their usefulness in judgments to be great. The examples will be either foreign or domestic, and either ancient or within our own memory, or recent; their force will be the greater the more illustrious and wiser those are from whom they are taken: such as the Israelites, the Athenians, the Rhodians, the Romans, the Venetians. Histories will supply these examples.

units.la: Apud quos etiam.) Liberos homines & ciues Romæ non cōfuetos fuisse torqueri, præter historiam, & Ciceronis orationes, etiam libri Pandectarum iuris, & Codex Iustiniani, titulo de quæstionibus lib. 4 testatur. Sed ne seruos quidem in dominorum caput torquere licuit, nisi in paucis, ijsq; atrocioribus maleficijs: uelut de incestu, de coniuratione, siue de Maiestate, quemadmodum eodem titulo habetur. De incestu est quaesitum Ciceronis tempore in Clodium: et de Maiestate, in coniuratione Catilinae. Incestus, siue incestum, dicitur flagitium, quod cum ea committitur, cum qua nuptias contrahere non licet, ut eodem ff. tit. lib. 5. Martianus ait:
units.tr: Among whom even. That free men and citizens at Rome were not accustomed to be tortured is attested, besides by history and Cicero's speeches, also by the books of the Pandects of law and the Code of Justinian, under the title On Questions, book 4. But not even slaves were permitted to be tortured against the lives of their masters, except in a few, and those the most atrocious, crimes: for instance incest, conspiracy, or treason, as is set out under the same title. Incest was investigated in Cicero's time against Clodius, and treason in the conspiracy of Catiline. Incest, or incestum, is the name for a shameful act committed with a person with whom marriage is not permitted, as Marcianus says in the same title of the Digest, book 5:

units.la: Irridenda etiā disputatio est, qua solent uti ad infirmādas quaestiones: & meditata, puerilisq; dicenda: tum facienda fides, diligenter esse, & sine cupiditate quaesitum: dictaq; quaestionis argumentis, & coiectura pōderanda. Atq; haec accusationis fere membra sunt.
units.tr: The argument which people use to weaken trials must also be ridiculed, and it must be called contrived and childish. Then credence must be given to the trial: that it was conducted carefully and without partisanship; and the arguments and conjectures of the trial must be weighed. These are almost the parts of the accusation.

units.la: Irridenda etiam disputatio est.) Quartum est tractationis caput, de diluendis aduersariorū rationibus contra quaestiones: quas rationes supra, ubi de argumentatione ageret, multas memorauit. Diluentur autē et infirmabuntur, si eas tanquam meditatas et pueriles, hoc est, ficlas et nugatorias irridebimus.
units.tr: The argument must also be ridiculed. This is the fourth head of the treatment, on refuting the opponents' arguments against trials, which arguments he mentioned above, where he dealt with argumentation. They will be refuted and weakened if we ridicule them as contrived and childish, that is, fictitious and frivolous.

units.la: Tum facienda fides.) Quinta et postrema quaestionis tractandae pars, qua fidem habitae quaestioni sacimus. Huius duo sunt loci, alter à diligentia & moderatione quærendi: alter, à verisimilitudine dictorum in ipsa quæstione. Dicta cum argumentis & signis comparabimus: ostendemusq; omnia inter se cõsentire. hæc sunt quæ accusatori in coniectura seruanda esse præcipit.
units.tr: Then credence must be given. This is the fifth and last part of treating a trial, by which we give credence to the trial that has been held. It has two topics: one from the diligence and moderation of the inquiry, the other from the likelihood of the statements made within the trial itself. We shall compare the statements with the arguments and signs, and show that all agree with one another. These are the things the prosecutor is instructed to observe in conjecture.

units.la: Defensionis autem primùm infirmatio caussarum, aut non fuisse, aut non tantas, aut non sibi soli, aut commodius potuisse idem consequi: aut non his esse moribus, nõ ea uita: aut nullos animi motus, aut non tam impotentes fuisse.
units.tr: The defence, first, weakens the causes: by showing either that they did not exist, or were not so great, or did not concern the accused alone, or that the same result could have been achieved more conveniently; or that he did not have such habits or such a way of life; or that there were no emotions of mind, or that they were not so overpowering.

units.la: Defensionis autè primũ infirmatio causarũ.) Ratio defensionis in coniecturis refellendis pendet ex contrarijs locis, quibus usus est accusator. Nam ut accusator ex causis, & consequetibus signis, ex testibus & quæstionibus, horumq; partibus crimen ostendere conatus est: sic ex eadem infirmatione crimen refellet, qui defendit. Et primùm ad diluendas causas hæc afferenda sunt.
units.tr: The defence, first, weakens the causes. The method of defence in refuting conjectures depends on the opposite topics which the prosecutor used. For just as the prosecutor tried to show the crime from causes and consequent signs, from witnesses and trials, and from their parts, so the defender refutes the charge by the same kind of weakening. And first, these are the things to be brought forward for dissolving the causes.

units.la: Aut non fuisse.) Id est, nullas fuisse causas cur id faceret, cum nullũ maleficium sine causa suscipiatur. Si causa nulla erit, nec maleficiũ, ut, Quid odisset Clodiũ Milo, segetē ac materiem suæ gloriæ? Non modo nihil prodest, sed obest etiam, Publi <bl>blij</bl> Clodij mors Miloni. Nullas quoq; caussas su-isse, sæpe ostendit pro S.R.Amerino.
units.tr: That they did not exist. That is, that there were no causes why he would have done it, since no wrongdoing is undertaken without a cause. If there is no cause, there is no wrongdoing either, as when Milo, what reason did he have to hate Clodius, the seed and substance of his own glory? Not only does the death of Publius Clodius do Milo no good, it actually harms him. He often shows, in the defence of Sextus Roscius of Ameria, that there were no causes either.

units.la: Aut non tătas.) id est, leues esse causas. Clodio magna caussa, magna spes in Milonis morte proposita erat: in Milone non modò non tanta, sed etiam nulla, in morte Clodij fuit. Item pro S. Roscio: Patri non placebat? Quam ob caussam? necesse est enim, eam quoq; iustam, & magnam, & perspicuam fuisse. Item: Ille quo crimen commenticium confirmaret, nō inueniebat: ego res tam leues, qua ratione infirmem, reperire non possum.
units.tr: Or not so great. That is, that the causes were slight. For Clodius there was a great cause and a great hope in Milo's death; in Milo's case there was not only not so great a cause, but no cause at all for Clodius's death. Likewise in the defence of Sextus Roscius: "Did it not please the father?" For what reason? For it must be that this reason too was just, great, and clear. Likewise: "He did not find anything with which to confirm the fabricated charge; I cannot find any reason, so slight a matter, by which to weaken it."

units.la: Aut non sibi soli.) Hoc præcepto significat uitium in caussis, cum communes appelluntur. Inuidebat Clodio Milo, at maior in Clodio inuidia caussa.
units.tr: Or not to himself alone. By this precept he signifies the fault in causes when they are common to many. Milo was hated by Clodius, but the hatred in Clodius was a greater cause.

units.la: Aut commodius potuisse.) Duo hic intelliguntur: aut ueras non fuisse caussas, aut alias commodiores fuisse. De priore sic: Patri non placebat fi-lius: nam cum in prædia rustica relegarat. At id alij multi patres, qui filios diligunt suos, sactitare solet. Potest hoc exemplum etiā ad communes referri. De altero sic pro Milone, cum occasionem occidēdi Clodij tractat: Quē igitur cum omnium gratia noluit, hunc voluit cum aliquorū querela? quem iure, quē loco, quem tempore, quem impunè non est ausus: hunc iniuria, iniquo loco, alieno tēpore, periculo capitis, non dubitauit occidere?
units.tr: Or that the same could have been done more conveniently. Two things are understood here: either the causes were not true, or other, more convenient causes existed. About the former, thus: "The father did not like the son; for he had sent him away to his country estates." But this, many other fathers who love their sons are wont to do. This example can also be referred to common causes. About the latter, thus in the defence of Milo, when he treats the opportunity for killing Clodius: "Why then did he wish to kill, with the displeasure of some, the man whom he did not wish to kill with the favour of all? Whom he did not dare to kill lawfully, in a suitable place, at a suitable time, with impunity: this man, by injustice, in an unsuitable place, at an improper time, at the risk of his life, he did not hesitate to kill?"

units.la: C 3 Aut Pro Milone: Reliquum est, ut iam illum natura ipsius consuetudoq; defendat: hunc autem haec eadem coarguant. Pro S. Roscio, in prima parte multa huiusmodi, quae ad personam pertinent, tractantur: ut, Qua in re, praetereo illud, quod mihi m. mo argumento ad huius innocentiam poterat ej, in rusticis moribus, in uictu arido, in hac horrida multaq; uita, istiusmodi maleficia gigni non solet.
units.tr: Or in the defence of Milo: "It remains that now his very nature and custom should defend him, but these same things should convict this man." In the defence of Sextus Roscius, in the first part, many things of this kind are treated that pertain to the person: as, "In this matter I pass over that, which could have been a very strong argument for his innocence, that in rustic customs, in a meagre diet, and in this rough and laborious life, crimes of this kind are not usually born."

units.la: Haec ad impulsionem pertinent. ut in cade: Quid simile Milonis? cuius semper fuit, nec P. Clodius, cū in iudicium detrahi non posset, ui oppressam civitatem teneret. Item paulo post: Tamen se Milo continuit, & P. Clodium ad iudicium bis, ad uim nunquam uocauit.
units.tr: These things pertain to impulse, as in the case of the killing: "What is like Milo? For whom there was always..." and "nor did Publius Clodius, when he could not be dragged into court, hold the state oppressed by force." Likewise a little later: "Yet Milo restrained himself, and called Publius Clodius to court twice, and never to violence."

units.la: Facultatum autem infirmatione utetur, si aut uires, aut animū, aut copias, aut opes abfuisse demonstrabit: aut alienum tempus, aut locum non idoneum, aut multos arbitros, quorum crederet nemini: aut non se tam ineptum, ut id suscipéret, quod occultare non posset: neque tam amentē ut poenas ac iudicia contemneret.
units.tr: The defence will weaken the means if it shows that the strength, the spirit, the resources, or the wealth were lacking; or that the time was unsuitable, or the place unfit, or that there were many witnesses, in whom he would trust no one; or that he was not so foolish as to undertake what he could not conceal, nor so mad as to scorn punishments and trials.

units.la: Facultatum aute infirmatione.) Earū quas hic enumerat facultatum, uires, animus, copia, opes, tempus, locus, ad spem perficiendi: arbitri occultatio, ad spem celandi: pœnæ, ad opinionem periculi, aut depellendi, aut differendi: & ad comparationem, de qua supra diximus, pertinent. Ad facultatis refutationem pertinet illud pro S. Roscio: Ego contrà ostendo, non modò nihil eorum fecisse S. Roscium, sed ne potuisse quidem facere. Item alia multa ibidem illustria exempla facultatum: ut etiā pro Milone, & pro Cluentio. & non mo-dò facultatum, sed etiam omnium quæ ad coniecturam faciunt, ampla seges est & in prima, & in secunda in Catilinâ oratione.
units.tr: By weakening the means. Of the means he lists here, strength, spirit, resources, wealth, time and place pertain to the hope of carrying the act through; the presence of witnesses to the hope of concealment; punishments to the notion of danger, either to be avoided or deferred; and these pertain to the comparison we spoke of above. To the refutation of means belongs that passage in the defence of Sextus Roscius: "I, on the contrary, show that Sextus Roscius not only did none of these things, but could not even have done them." There are also many other illustrious examples of means in the same speech, as also in the defences of Milo and of Cluentius. And not only of means, but of all that bears on conjecture, there is a broad harvest, both in the first and in the second Catilinarian oration.

units.la: Confequētia autem diluet, exponendo, non esse illa certa indicia facti, quæ etiam nullo admisso consequi possent. consistetq; in singulis, & ea aut eorum quæ ipse facta esse dicet, propria esse defendet potius quàm criminis. aut si cum accusatore communia essent, pro periculo potius, quàm contra salutem valere debere.
units.tr: The consequences, on the other hand, he will dissolve by explaining that those were not certain indications of the deed, which could follow even without its being committed. This consists in individual points, and he will defend either that they are peculiar to the things he himself says were done, rather than to the crime; or, if they were common to the prosecutor as well, that they should count in favour of the danger rather than against the safety of the accused.

units.la: Confequētia autem diluet exponēdo.) Quomodo diluantur quæ obijciuntur facti uestigia, tria præcepta tradit: quorū illud commune est, ut quæ conglobata & condensata contorsit accusator, ea defensor singula diluat, ut debiliora disiuncta quàm coniuncta esse uideantur. Huius præceptionis sententiā nemo melius assecutus est, quàm Latomus, cuius uerba, ne quis forte requirat, subiicia: Certa signa sunt, propria ac necessaria, quæ infirmantur, si ostendantur non semper consequi, hoc est, non esse propria ac necessaria: ut, Non solum ueneno, sed etiam morbo corpus tumescere: non semper metum esse ex delicti conscientia. Aut alio uertenda erant, docendumq;, cuiusuis potius esse quàm criminis propria: ut, sepelisse ex misericordia, non ut crimen celaret: & timuisse, titubasse, fugisse propter falsam suspicionem, & quod calumniatores sciret paratos sibi esse. Aut si communia sint cū aduersario, hoc est, tam pro illo, quàm pro nobis ualentia, dicendum erit, pro periculo potius quàm contra salutem ualere oportere: ut, Quod sepelierit, in bonam, non in malam partem interpretandum esse: occurrendum hominum periculis, & subleuandos potius laborantes, quàm affligendos esse.
units.tr: Confequētia autem diluet exponēdo.) Next he gives three rules on how the traces of the deed that are brought against us may be refuted. The first is general: the defender should take each point that the accuser has piled up and knotted together and refute it separately, so that the weaker points appear weaker when separated than when joined. No one has grasped the sense of this rule better than Latomus, whose words I add in case anyone asks: "Certain signs are those that are proper and necessary; they are weakened if it can be shown that they do not always follow, that is, that they are not proper and necessary. For example: the body swells not only from poison but also from disease; fear does not always arise from a consciousness of guilt." Or they must be turned to another purpose, and it must be shown that they are the proper marks of something other than the crime: for example, that he buried the body out of pity and not to hide the crime; that he was afraid, faltered, or fled because of a false suspicion, and because he knew that his accusers were ready to attack him. Or if the points are common to both sides, that is, if they count as much for the other side as for us, it must be said that they ought to weigh in favour of the danger (of the accused) rather than against his safety: for example, that his burying the man is to be interpreted in a good sense and not a bad one; that one should come to the aid of men in danger and help those who are in trouble rather than afflict them.

units.la: Testiumq;, & quæstionum genus uniuersum, & quod poterit in singulis, ex reprehensionis locis, de quibus ante dictum est, refellet. Testium̃q; quæstionum genus.) De caussarum & argumentorum refutatione dixit,nunc breuiter de testibus & quæstionibus: quoniam supra, cum generatim loci reprehensionis traderentur, de eis quæ erant necessaria,dicta sunt. Horum diluendorum duplicem esse uiam ostendit: unam, quæ genus uniuersum complectatur: altera, quæ singula attingat. Vt illa, de toto genere testium, quàm sit infirmum: & argumenta rerū esse propria,testimonia uoluntatum. Et de singulis testibus,si natura uani,si leues,si cum ignominia: itē̃q; cætera quæ in iisdem locis enumerantur. Idem quoque de quæstionibus dicendum erit, quemadmodū Cicero pro Sylla: Tormenta illa gubernat dolor, moderatur natura cuiusq; tum animi tum corporis: regit quæsitor, fleƈtit libido, corrumpit spes,infirmat metus, ut in tot rerum angustijs nihil ueritati loci relinquatur. Cōtra singulorum quæstiones, ut pro Cluetio: Contra iterum habita de seruis Opianici à Sassia quæstionem.
units.tr: He will refute the whole class of witnesses and questions, and whatever can be refuted in each case, from the places of reproof discussed above. The class of witnesses and questions.) He has spoken of the refutation of causes and arguments; now he speaks briefly of witnesses and questions, since above, when the places of reproof were set out in general, the necessary points were already discussed. He shows that there are two ways of dealing with these: one that takes in the whole class, the other that touches each particular case. The first is to show how weak the whole class of witnesses is, and that arguments are the proper evidence of facts while testimonies are evidence of wills. The second is to show, for each individual witness, whether he is of no account, whether he is frivolous, whether he is disgraced, and likewise the other points listed in the same places. The same should be said about questions, as Cicero does in the Pro Sylla: "Pain governs those torments, the nature of each person, both of mind and body, moderates them; the examiner rules, lust bends, hope corrupts, fear weakens, so that amid so many distresses no room is left for the truth." Against individual questions, as in the Pro Cluentio: "Again, on the contrary, the question put to the slaves of Opianicus, taken by Sassia."

units.la: Harum caussarum principia suspiciosa ad acerbitatem ab accusatore ponentur. Denunciabiturq; insidiarum commune periculum, excitabunturq; animi ut attendant.
units.tr: The opening of these causes is to be made suspicious, so as to rouse hostility, by the accuser. The common danger of plots is to be announced, and the minds of the hearers are to be stirred so that they pay attention. The opening of these causes.) He has taught up to this point about the whole treatment of conjecture; now about…

units.la: Harum caussarum principia.) De uniuersa coiectura tractatione haẞtenus præcepit: nunc de
units.tr: Harum caussarum principia.) He has so far taught about the whole handling of conjecture; now

units.la: singulis cöiecturalis orationis partibus, dcq; sententiarum in eis collocatione agit. Accusatoris principia, cum propositum eius sit, ut iratum faciat iudice, & ad acerbitatem impellat, suspiciosa esse debent: hoc est, certis notis praeteritarum & futurarum rerum respersa. Ergo tria genera sententiarum adhibebit: unum ad indignationem, alterum ex communi periculo ad terrorem, tertium ad attentionem, ut non solum diligenter audiat, sed etiam audeat fortiter iudicare. Tale principium est accusationis secundae in Verrem.
units.tr: he deals with each part of a speech on conjecture, and with the arrangement of the sentences within them. The accuser's opening, since his aim is to make the judge angry and drive him toward harshness, must be full of suspicion: that is, it must be sprinkled with clear marks of past and future events. So he will use three kinds of sentences: one to stir indignation, another to produce fear from the shared danger, and a third to gain attention, so that the judges not only listen carefully but also dare to judge boldly. Such is the opening of the second speech against Verres.

units.la: A reo autem querela cõflati criminis, collectarumq; suspicionum, & accusatoris insidiae, & item commune periculum proferetur, animiq; ad misericordiam allicientur, & modice benevolentia iudicum colligetur. Narratio autem accusatoris erit, quasi membratim gesti negotij suspiciosa explicatio, sparsis omnibus argumentis, obscuratis defensionibus. Defensoris, aut praeteritis, aut obscuratis suspicionum argumentis, rerum ipsarum eventus erit, casusq; narrandi.
units.tr: From the accused, however, will be brought a complaint about the trumped-up charge and the collected suspicions, and also about the accuser's plots and the common danger; the minds of the judges will be drawn toward pity, and a moderate goodwill of the judges will be gathered. The accuser's narration will be a suspicious explanation, as it were, of the business done, set out part by part, with all the arguments scattered through it and the defences obscured. The defender's narration will consist of the outcome of the events themselves and the circumstances of the case, with the arguments of suspicion either passed over or obscured.

units.la: A reo autè querela.) Quid faciendum sit contra reo: totidem sunt adhibenda remedia, quot sunt illata vulnera. Commemorabit igitur incommoda
units.tr: A reo autè querela.) What must be done against the accused: there are as many remedies to apply as there are wounds inflicted. So the accused will recount his own disadvantages

units.la: sua reus, & de aduersariorum calunijs & insidijs querela proferet, quibus innocente & destitutu opprimere conatur. Deinde comune periculu denunciandu & fignificandu, nisi ista licentia cohibuerint iudices. Postremo animi iudicu erunt cociliadi, atq; ad misericordia & beneuolentia mode rate leniterq; flectedi: hac quomodo fiat, Quintiana & Rosciana defensiones facile docebunt.
units.tr: and will make a complaint about the calumnies and plots of his opponents, by which they try to crush him when he is innocent and abandoned. Then the common danger is to be announced and pointed out, unless the judges check such licence. Finally, the minds of the judges are to be won over, and gently and moderately bent toward pity and goodwill. How this is done the defences of Quinctius and Roscius will easily show.

units.la: Narratio accusatoris duo habere debet: primum, ut nihil actu, nihil dictu, nusquâ uentu, aut habitum, nihil deniq; tentatum sine caussa putetur: id fiet, si suspiciones interiectas habuerit, ex comunibus rerum & personarum locis: si dispersa argumenta. Secundum, ut que contra à defensore dici possunt, cogitet: eaq; nō tā refutare, quàm obscurare, aut extenuando, aut irridendo, conabitur: cuiusmodi sunt in Verrem prope infinita. Defensor simplicem & dilucidâ euentorum, id est factorum & casuum expositione debet habere, cum attenuatione suspicionum, ne se arte defendere uelle uideatur. id asequetur, aut praeteritis, id est dissimulatis suspicionum argumentis & caussis, quae quidem refutari non possunt: aut obscuratis, si nō possunt praeteriri. Hoc ipsum facit Cicero in narratione Cluentiana, cum Cluentij in Sassiam matrem odium dissimulare non posset.
units.tr: The accuser's narration should have two features. First, nothing done, nothing said, nowhere gone, nothing held, nothing finally attempted, should seem to be without cause: this will happen if he has inserted suspicions drawn from the common places of things and persons, and scattered arguments. Second, he should think about what can be said against him by the defender; and he will try to obscure these points rather than refute them, either by belittling them or by ridiculing them: of this kind there are almost endless examples in the speech against Verres. The defender should have a simple and clear account of the outcome, that is, of the facts and circumstances, with the suspicions played down, so that he does not seem to wish to defend himself by art. He will achieve this either by passing over the arguments and causes of suspicion, that is, by leaving them unmentioned, which indeed cannot be refuted; or, if they cannot be passed over, by obscuring them. Cicero does exactly this in the Cluentius narration, when he could not hide Cluentius's hatred of his mother Sassia.

units.la: In confirmādis autem nostris argumentationibus, infirmandisque contrariis, sæpe erunt accusatori motus animorum incitandi, reo mitigandi. atque hæc quidem utriq; maxime in peroratione facienda: alteri frequentatione argumentorum, & coaceruatione uniuersa: alteri, si plane caussam redarguendo explicarit, enumeratione, ut quicq; diluerit, & miseratione ad extremum.
units.tr: In confirming our own arguments, and in weakening the opposing ones, there will often be emotions to be stirred in the mind of the accuser and calmed in the accused. These are to be used chiefly in the peroration: by the accuser, through the repetition of arguments and the heaping up of everything together; by the defender, if he has explained the case plainly while refuting it, through enumeration, so that he goes over each point he has answered, and finally through appeals to pity.

units.la: In confirmandis autem nostris.) De confirmatione & refutatione coniectura, quoniam locos antea tradidit, hic de solis motibus præcipit: ut nihil mirum accusator argumentis uehementiam & acrimoniam adiungat, incitandis ad iracundiam animis: defensor uero in iisdem motibus mitigadis & sedandis intendat.
units.tr: In confirmandis autem nostris.) On the confirmation and refutation of conjecture, since he has already given the places, he here teaches only about the emotions: so that the accuser, not surprisingly, adds vehemence and bitterness to his arguments, stirring the minds to anger; the defender, on the other hand, should aim to soften and calm those same emotions.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem utriq; maximè.) De peroratione actoris & rei, duo ponit præcepta: commune utriusq; alterum, alterum proprium singulorum. Commune illud est, ut quæ de motibus præcepit in confirmatione & refutatione, ea maximè ab utroque in peroratione seruentur. Sunt enim omnia uehementiora in peroratione & conclusione. Propria uero illa: accusatoris esse, frequentare
units.tr: And these are used chiefly by each side.) On the peroration of the accuser and the accused he gives two rules: one common to both, and the other proper to each side. The common one is that what he has taught about the emotions in confirmation and refutation should be especially observed by both in the peroration, since everything is more vehement in the peroration and conclusion. The proper ones are these: it belongs to the accuser to repeat

units.la: illegible, ~2 letters tare & coacceruare sua in unum locum argumenta,ut coniuncta & conglobata uim habeant maiorem:ut ipse in septima Verrina facit. Rei autem contrà,singula seorsim ordine (siquidem ea in refutatione explicauit) quasi enumerando tractare: breues rationes intertexere: & ad extremum,ad misericordiam orationem couertere. Nam ut motuum genere inter se differunt accusator ac defensor, ita etiam argumentorum collocatione: ut in peroratione Cluentiana.
units.tr: and heap his arguments into one place, so that, joined and gathered together, they have greater force, as he does in the seventh speech against Verres. The accused, on the other hand, should treat each point separately, in order (since he explained them separately in the refutation), as if counting them off, to weave in brief reasons, and at the end to turn his speech toward pity. For as accuser and defender differ in the kind of emotions they stir, so too they differ in the arrangement of their arguments, as in the peroration of the speech for Cluentius.

units.la: DE STATV DEFINITIVO.
units.tr: ON THE DEFINITIVE STATUS

units.la: C.F. Scire mihi iam uideor, quemadmodum coniectura tractanda sit: nunc de definitione audiamus. C. P. Communia dātur in isto genere accusatori defensoriq; praecepta. Vter enim definiendo, describēdoq; uerbo magis ad sensum iudicis, opinionemq; penetrarit, & uter ad cōmunem uerbi uim, & ad eā praeceptionem, quam inchoatam habebunt in animis, ij qui audient, magis & propius accesserit, is uincat necesse est. Non enim argumētando hoc genus tractatur, sed tanquam explicando, excutiendoq; uerbo: ut si in reo pecunia
units.tr: C.F. I now think I understand how conjecture is to be handled; let us hear about definition. C.P. In this kind of issue there are rules common to prosecutor and defendant. For whichever of them, by defining and describing the term, has more successfully reached the judge's understanding and opinion, and has come closer to the common meaning of the word and to the preconception that the hearers have already formed in their minds, that one must win. This kind of issue is not handled by argument, but by explaining and unfolding the term, as when, if the defendant has been acquitted of money-taking and then brought to trial again, the prosecutor defines prevarication as every corruption of the court by the defendant, while the defence defines it as only the prosecutor's corruption by the defendant.

units.la: In confirmādís autem nostrís ar‑ gumentationibus , infirmandísqúe contrarijs,sepe erunt accusatori mo‑ tus animorum incitandi, reo miti‑ gandi.atque hæc quidem utriq; ma‑ xime in peroratione facienda: alteri frequentatione argumentorum, & coaceruatione uniuersa: alteri,si pla‑ nè caussam redarguendo explicarit, enumeratione, ut quicq; diluerit, & miseratione ad extremum.
units.tr: In confirming our arguments, and refuting the opposing ones, the prosecutor will often need to stir up the emotions of his hearers, and the defendant to soothe them. This is to be done mainly in the peroration: the prosecutor by the repetition of his arguments and by gathering them all together, the defendant by going through each point in order, if he has explained his case by refuting it, and at the end by appealing to pity.

units.la: In confirmandis autem nostris.) De confirma‑ tione & refutatione coniecturæ, quoniam locos antea tradidit, hic de solis motibus præcipit: ut ni‑ mirum accusator argumentis uehementiam & a‑crimoniam adiungat, incitandis ad iracundiam animis: defensor uero in iisdem motibus mitigâdis & sedandis intendat.
units.tr: "In confirming our arguments": Since he has already taught the places for confirming and refuting conjecture, here he gives precepts only about the emotions. Namely, the prosecutor should add vehemence and bitterness to his arguments, to arouse the minds to anger; the defendant, on the other hand, should aim at calming and soothing those same emotions.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem utriq; maxime.) De pero‑ ratione actoris & rei, duo ponit præcepta: com‑ mune utriusq; alterum, alterum proprium singu‑lorum. Commune illud est, ut quæ de motibus præ‑ cepit in confirmatione & refutatione, ea maxime ab utroque in peroratione feruentur. Sunt enim omnia uehementiora in peroratione & conclu‑sione. Propria uero illa: accusatoris esse, frequen‑tare tare & coaceruare sua in unum locum argumenta,ut coniuncta & conglobata uim habeant maiorem: ut ipse in septima Verrina facit. Rei autem contrà, singula seorsim ordine (siquidem ea in refutatione explicauit) quasi enumerando tractare: breues rationes intertexere: & ad extremum, ad misericordiam orationem cõuertere. Nam ut moatuum genere inter se differunt accusator ac defensor, ita etiam argumentorum collocatione: ut in peroratione Cluentiana.
units.tr: "And this is to be done mainly in each": Concerning the peroration of prosecutor and defendant he gives two rules: one common to both, and one peculiar to each. The common rule is that what he has taught about the emotions in confirmation and refutation should be especially pressed by each in the peroration. For everything is more vehement in the peroration and conclusion. The peculiar rules are these: it is the prosecutor's part to repeat and gather his arguments into one place, so that, joined and massed together, they have greater force, as he himself does in the seventh Verrine. The defendant, on the contrary, should take each point separately in order (since he has explained them in his refutation), as if counting them up, weave in brief reasons, and at the end turn his speech to pity. For just as prosecutor and defendant differ in the kind of emotion, so also in the arrangement of their arguments, as in the peroration of the Cluentian speech.

units.la: DE STATV DEFINITIVO.
units.tr: ON THE DEFINITIVE STATUS

units.la: C.F. Scire mihi iam uideor, quemadmodum coniectura tractanda sit: nunc de definitione audiamus. C. P. Communia dátur in isto genere accusatori defensoriq; præcepta. Vter enim definiendo, describēdoq; uerbo magis ad sensum iudicis, opinionemq; penetrarit, & uter ad cõmunem uerbi uim, & ad eã præceptionem, quam inchoatam habebunt in animis, ij qui audient, magis & propius accesserit, is uincat necesse est. Non enim argumētando hoc genus tractatur, sed tanquam explicando, excutiendoq; uerbo: ut si in reo pecunia absoluto, rursusque reuocato, praeuaricatione accusator esse definiat, omne iudicij corruptela, ab reo: defensor autem non omnem, sed tantummodo accusatoris corruptelam ab reo. Sit ergo haec contentio prima uerborum, in qua etiam si propius accedat ad consuetudinem mentemque sermonis defensoris definitio, tamen accusator sententia legis nititur. Negat enim probari oportere, eos qui leges scripserunt, ratum habere iudicium, si totum corruptum sit, si unus accusator corruptus sit, rescindere nititur aequitate, ut illa quasi scribenda lex sic esset: quaeque tamen compleceretur in iudiciis corruptis, ea uerbo uno praeuaricationis comprehendi dicitur.
units.tr: C.F. I now think I understand how conjecture is to be handled; let us hear about definition. C.P. In this kind of issue there are rules common to prosecutor and defendant. For whichever of them, by defining and describing the term, has more successfully reached the judge's understanding and opinion, and has come closer to the common meaning of the word and to the preconception that the hearers have already formed in their minds, that one must win. This kind of issue is not handled by argument, but by explaining and unfolding the term, as when, if the defendant has been acquitted of money-taking and then brought to trial again, the prosecutor defines prevarication as every corruption of the court by the defendant, while the defence defines it as only the prosecutor's corruption by the defendant. This first contest over words is therefore one in which, even if the defence's definition comes closer to the usage and meaning of the speech, the prosecutor still relies on the sense of the law. For he denies that those who wrote the laws meant a verdict to stand if the whole court was corrupted; if only the accuser was corrupted, he tries to annul it by appeal to equity, as though the law had been written in such a way that what is in fact embraced in corrupt courts were comprehended in the single word "prevarication."

units.la: C. F. Scire iam mihi uideor.) Interloquitur filius, tu ut intelligat pater, an ea quae tradidit perceperit, et meminerit sequentium: tum ut decenter a coiectura ad definitionis tractationem trafeatur.
units.tr: C.F. "I now think I understand": The son interjects, so that the father may see whether you have grasped what was taught and remember what follows, and so that the transition from conjecture to the handling of definition is made fittingly.

units.la: C. P. Communia dantur in isto genere.) Diximus ante, conflare hoc genus ex prima definitione, ne, & altera quam refert aduersarius. quid autem esset definitio, quae ue eius genera & modus, in confirmatione indicatum est. iam quae fit eius tractatio, docetur. Sunt autē huius generis praecepta fere omnia utriusq; partis communia: nisi quòd, ut in omnibus caussis fieri solet, ut alterius partis argumenta sint probabiliora, sic etiā in hac euenit, ut defensoris meliores sint partes: tum etiā dicēdi copia, fi modo caussa fit aliqua grauis, ex inuentionis & amplificationis locis maior, quàm accusatoris. Et quāquā ita fit, tamē quomodo ab utra- que parte, quae cōmunia fūt, tractāda sint, docet.
units.tr: C.P. "Common rules apply to this kind": We said before that this kind is formed from the first definition, and the other which the opponent brings forward; what definition is, and its kinds and method, was indicated in the confirmation. Now its handling is taught. Almost all the rules of this kind are common to both parties, except that, as is usual in all cases, one side's arguments are more probable; so in this case too it happens that the defendant's position is the stronger. Then too, the abundance of speech, if the case is at all weighty, is greater from the places of invention and amplification than the prosecutor's. And although it is so, he still teaches how the common matters are to be handled by each side.

units.la: Vter definiēdo describendoq; uerbo.) Oratori ad sensum cōmunem, atq; ad hominum opinionē dicēdum est, non ad ueri necessitatē & scientiam. Quare in definiēdo, fi nomē criminis cōtrouersiā pariat, descriptionibus utitur, & uerbi explicatione copiosa sæpius, quàm subtili & limata illa Dialecticorum ac philofophorū definitione. Cur autēid faciat, ratione ipse reddidit de Orat.lib.2. ut & nos supra in confirmatione annotauimus.
units.tr: "The one who defines and describes the term": The orator must speak according to common sense and popular opinion, not according to the necessity of truth and science. Hence, in defining, if the name of the charge gives rise to controversy, he uses descriptions and a copious explanation of the word more often than that subtle and polished definition of the dialecticians and philosophers. Why he does this he himself explained by reason in the second book of On the Orator, as we also noted above in the confirmation.

units.la: Vt fi in co reo pecunia absoluto.) Ponit exemplū huius status, ut ad id rationem tractationē& accommodet: atq; ex hoc uno similes aliæ causæ, quo tractādæ sint modo, intelligatur. Finge Ver- rē accusari de prævaricatione, quòd pecunia absolutus sit corrupto iudicio: negare autem Verrē, eam esse praevaricationem, qua ab reo corrupta tur iudices: accusator praevaricationem esse definiat, omnem iudicij corruptelā ab reo, id est, quae ab reo profecta sit. Verres autem contrā referat: non omnē corruptelam praevaricatione esse, sed tantū accusatoris ab reo, id est, cum ab reo pecunia corrumpitur accusator, ut se vincì patiatur. Hinc status existit, quid praevaricatio: hoc est, utra sit definitio verior. ea autem erit verior et melior, quae magis ad sensum iudicis, opinionēq; penetrarit, quaeq; ad commune verbi usum, et ad eam praeceptionem notionem ue quam inchoatā habebūt in animis ij qui audient, propius accesset. Ergo rationes utrēq; affert, quibus suā definitione probet. Et quoniā ex contrariis definitionibus quaestio exoritur nova, scripti et sententiae, accusator suam legis sententia et aequitate defendit: defensor contrā, verba legis multis modis tuetur. Accusator igitur duo haec habet argumenta: primum ex minore, iniquum esse, si accusator solus corruptus sit, praevaricatione dici: si omnes iudices, nō dici. Secundū ex vi verbi, quod uno praevaricationis verbo legislator etiā corruptelā iudicum comprehenderit: atq; idcirco idem esse, ac si lex de corruptis etiam iudicibus loqueretur. id quod poterit etiam similibus loquendi formulis ostendere, si eas in promptu habuerit.
units.tr: "As when, if the defendant has been acquitted of money-taking": He gives an example of this issue, so that the reasoning and treatment may be adapted to it, and so that from this one example it may be understood how similar cases are to be handled. Suppose Verres is accused of prevarication, because he was acquitted of money-taking through a corrupted court; Verres denies that this is the prevarication by which the judges are corrupted by the defendant. The prosecutor defines prevarication as every corruption of the court by the defendant, that is, one that has proceeded from the defendant. Verres, on the other hand, argues that not every corruption is prevarication, but only the prosecutor's corruption by the defendant, that is, when the prosecutor is bribed by the defendant to allow himself to be overcome. Hence the issue arises: what is prevarication, that is, which definition is the truer. That definition will be the truer and better which more closely reaches the judge's understanding and opinion, and which comes closer to the common use of the word and to the preconception or notion which the hearers have already formed in their minds. So each side brings reasons by which to prove its own definition. And since a new question arises from the opposed definitions, concerning the wording and the meaning of the statute, the prosecutor defends his view by the sense and equity of the law, while the defence, on the contrary, protects the words of the law in many ways. The prosecutor therefore has two arguments: first, from the lesser, that it would be unjust to call it prevarication if only the accuser were corrupted, but not if all the judges were. Second, from the force of the word: the lawgiver, by the single word "prevarication", also included the corruption of the judges, and so it is the same as if the law spoke of judges who were corrupted as well. This he will be able to show also by similar forms of speech, if he has them ready to hand.

units.la: Defensor autem testatur consuetudinem sermonis, uerbíq; uím ex cõtrario reperiet, quasi ex uero accusatore. cui cõtrarium est nomen præuaricationis, ex consequentibus: quòd ea litera de accusatore soleat dari iudici, ex nomine ipso, quod significat eum, qui in contrarijs caussis, quasi uarie esse positus uideatur.
units.tr: The defence, on the other hand, appeals to the usage of speech and will find the force of the word from its opposite, as if from a true accuser.
