The opposite of "prevarication" is the name of the accuser, taken from its consequences: that letter is usually given to the judge about the accuser, from the name itself, which signifies one who appears to be placed variously in opposed causes.

units.la: {·} Defensor autem testatur.) Iam suppeditat lo cos defensori, qui tamen etiam infra ad accusato rem pertinere dicentur. Loci sunt, ex consuetudine sermonis, ex contrarijs, ex consequentibus, & ex nomine ipso: id est, ex notatione, & nominis interpretatione. Ex consuetudine loquentiu sic: Omnes intelligere, uocabulum præuaricationis uniús accusatoris esse, non totius iudicij. Sic Catonem, exempli causa, sic Terentium esse locutum. Ex contrario, si accusator qui corruptus non est, uerus accusator dicitur: ergo qui corruptus est, is solus præuaricator appellabitur. Vero enim accusatori opponitur præuaricator. Ex consequentibus hoc modo: Si præuaricatio est omnis iudicij corruptela ab reo, de condemnando, aut de absoluendo, aut amplificando, de omni corruptore litera datur iudici: nō de omnibus, sed de solo accusatore dari solet. Igitur unius tantū accusatoris est prævaricatio. alterū enim alterius est cōsequens. Sunt qui putēt, diligentius inquirendū esse, quæ sit ea litera, de qua hic agit: quod adhuc inuentum non sit, aut explicatū. Equidē existimo, literam esse exillis trib. unā, quarum mentionem facit Asconius Pædianus in tertiam Verrinam: quarum quæ fuit condemnādi, C: absoluendi, A: ampliādi, N.L. dabant: ac extrema nota significabant, non liquere, unde ampliatio nascebatur: quo uerbo significabatur, amplius esse de causa cognoscendū. Ex nomine ipso, quod significat eum qui in contrarijs causfis, quasi uariè positus esse uideatur. At id accusatoris unius esse potest. nam cum secundum alteram tantum partē pronunciet iudex, solus accusator relinquitur, qui duabus sedeat sellis, atqʒ colludat. Nam prævaricandi interpretationem tenuit Labeo, autore Vlpiano de Prævaricatoribus l. prima, ff. 47. Prævaricator, inquit Vlpianus, est quasi uaricator, qui diuersam partē adiuuat, prodita causa sua: quod nomē à uaria certatione tractum, ait Labeo. Nam qui prævaricatur, ex utraq; parte cōsistit, quinimò ex altera. Is autem prævaricator proprie dicitur, qui publico iudicio accusauerit. Accusatorum temeritas tribus modis detegitur, & tribus poenis subij citur. Aut enim calumniantur, aut praevaricantur, aut tergiuersantur. Calumniari est, falsa crimina intendere: Praevaricari, utra crimina abscondere: tergiuersari, in universum ab accusatione desistere. Haec Martianus ad S.C. Turpilianum l.prima. ff. 48. Quod si quis dicat, Quae igitur actio crit in eos qui ob iudicandum pecuniam acceperint? Respondeo, actio est repetundarum, ut ad L. Iul. Repetun. l. 3. ff. 48.
units.tr: "The defence, on the other hand, appeals": Now he supplies places for the defence, which will nevertheless be said below to pertain also to the prosecutor. The places are: from the usage of speech, from opposites, from consequences, and from the name itself, that is, from etymology and the interpretation of the name. From usage of speech, thus: everyone understands that the term "prevarication" belongs to the accuser alone, not to the whole court. So Cato, for example, so Terence spoke. From the opposite: if an accuser who is not corrupted is called a true accuser, then the one who is corrupted will alone be called a prevaricator, for the prevaricator is opposed to the true accuser. From consequences, in this way: if prevarication is every corruption of the court by the defendant, whether about condemning, or acquitting, or deferring judgment, then the letter is given to the judge about every corrupter, yet it is not customarily given about all, but only about the accuser. Therefore prevarication belongs to the accuser alone, for the one is the consequence of the other. Some think that the letter of which he speaks here should be investigated more carefully, since it has not yet been found or explained. I myself think it is one of those three letters which Asconius Pedianus mentions in the third Verrine: of these, C was given for condemning, A for acquitting, N.L. for amplifying, and the final mark signified that it was not clear, whence the amplification arose; by this word it was signified that the case needed further examination. From the name itself, which signifies one who appears to be placed variously in opposed causes. But that can belong to the accuser alone; for when the judge pronounces in favour of only one side, only the accuser remains, who sits on two stools and colludes. For Labeo held the interpretation of prevarication, on the authority of Ulpian, On Prevaricators, first book, Digest 47: "A prevaricator," says Ulpian, "is as it were a varicator, one who helps the opposing side after betraying his own cause"; Labeo says this name was derived from varied contention. For the one who prevaricates stands on both sides, or rather on the other. Such a prevaricator is properly called one who has brought an accusation in a public trial. The rashness of accusers is revealed in three ways, and they are subject to three penalties. For they either calumniate, or prevaricate, or tergiversate. To calumniate is to bring false charges; to prevaricate is to conceal charges; to tergiversate is to desist from the accusation altogether. So Martianus, on the Senatus consultum Turpillianum, first book, Digest 48. But if someone should say: what action then will lie against those who have accepted money to judge? I reply: the action is for extortion, as in the Lex Julia on extortion, third book, Digest 48.

units.la: Sed huic tamen ipsi confugiendum est ad aequitatis locos, ad rerum iudicatarum autoritatem, ad finem aliquem periculi. communeq; sit hoc praeceptum, ut cum uterque definierit, quamaxime potuerit ad communem sensum, uimq; uerbi: tum similibus exemplisq; eorum, qui ita locuti sunt, suam definitionem, sententiamq; confirmet. atq; accusatori in hoc genere causarum locus ille communis: Minimis esse concedendum, ut is qui de re confiteatur, uerbi se interpretatione defendat.
units.tr: But even so, the accuser must have recourse to the topics of equity, to the authority of decided cases, and to some end of the danger. This should be a common rule: whichever side has defined the term, he should, as far as he can, appeal to common usage and the force of the word; and he should then confirm his definition and opinion by similar examples and by those of writers who have used the word in this way. And the accuser has this common topic in this kind of case: that the least things must be conceded, so that the one who admits the fact defends himself by interpreting the word.

units.la: Sed huic tamen ipsi confugiendum est. ) Superioribus quatuor locis defensoris addit tres alios, æquitatem, rerum iudicatarum autorita‐tem: tertium à periculo, siue ab incōmodis. Ab æquitatis locis hoc modo: iniquum esse, eos uelle lege teneri, qui ca lege comprehensi non sunt. hoc nullo iure fieri, nulla æquitate posse. A rebus iudicatis, sic iudicia præuaricationis esse semper de accusatoribus habita, de iudicib. nul‐ la. A periculo, ut Cicero pro Cluē. Video quàta, & quàm periculosa, & quàm infinita quæstio tenetur ab accusatoribus, cum eam lege quæ in ipsos scripta sit, in totum iudicium transferre conantur. Item accusatorem sui periculi caussa nō res solum conuertere, uerumetiam uerba cōmu‐tare conari: quem locum Cicero ponit de Inuen. lib. 2. Sic quæ incōmoda consecutura sint, eo cō‐ cesso quod uoluit, ostendit.
units.tr: But even so, he must have recourse to these very topics. The defender adds three other topics to the earlier four: equity, the authority of decided cases, and the third, from danger, or from inconveniences. From the topics of equity, thus: it is unjust that those should wish to be bound by a law who have not been caught by that law. This cannot be done by any right, nor can it be done by any equity. From decided cases: thus, prosecutions for collusion have always been held to lie against accusers, and against judges never. From danger, as Cicero says in the pro Cluentio: "I see how great, how dangerous and how endless a question the accusers are pursuing, when they try to carry over into the whole trial the law written against themselves." Likewise, the accuser tries to alter not only the facts for his own danger's sake, but also the words; Cicero sets out this topic in De inventione, book 2. Thus he shows what inconveniences would follow, once the concession he wanted is granted.

units.la: Communeq; sit hoc præceptum.) Significat, hoc præceptum, quemadmodum & reliqua, esse commune, in hoc genere caussæ. nam & de hoc suprà dictum est. uel est, ac si concludês diceret: Communeigitur sit hoc præceptum. Nam epilo‐go transit ad locos communes accusatoris & de‐senforis: mox ad locos insitos reuertitur, ut & hos ostendat esse utriusq; communes. Nam supe‐ riores illi similium & exemplorum assumpti sunt, & autoritate constat. similium namq; nomine, hic res iudicatæ intelliguntur. Exépla uerò sunt testimonia locutionū tum ex sermone, tum scriptis bene loquentium desumpta.
units.tr: "And this should be a common rule." He means that this rule, like the others, is common in this kind of case; for this too was said above. Or it is as if he were concluding and saying: "Therefore let this rule be common." For in the epilogue he passes to the common topics of accuser and defender, and soon returns to the topics inherent in the matter, to show that these too are common to both sides. For those earlier topics, of likeness and examples, were taken up, and rest on authority. Under the name of likeness, decided cases are here understood. But examples are testimonies of expressions drawn both from the speech and from the writings of good speakers.

units.la: Atq; accusatori in hoc genere.) Locus communis accusatoris & defensoris, ab æquitate sumitur, sed contrario modo. Nam accusator, quoniā sententia legis nititur, locis communibus utetur, qui contra scriptum pro sententia dari solet. ut, Indignū esse, ubi de re constat, de verbis velle contendere. Defensor autē contrā, queritur, se non re, sed iniqua verbi interpretatione urgeri, cum apertam habeat in ipsis verbis, legeq; sententiam. Et id genus alia opponet, quæ pro scripto dici solent.
units.tr: And the accuser in this kind of case. The common topic of accuser and defender is taken from equity, but in opposite ways. For the accuser, since his argument rests on the sense of the law, will use common topics which are usually brought forward in favour of the sense against the written text, as: it is unworthy, when the fact is established, to wish to dispute about words. The defender, on the other hand, complains that he is pressed not by the matter but by an unfair interpretation of the word, when he has the plain sense of the law in the words themselves. And he will set against this other arguments of the same kind, which are usually urged in favour of the written text.

units.la: · Defensor autem de ea, quā propositui, æquitate nitatur: & ea cum secum faciat, nō re, sed deprauatione uerbi se urgeri queratur. Quo in genere percensere poterit plerosq; inueniēdi locos. Nam & similibus utitur, & contrariis, & consequentibus quanquam uterq;: tamē reus, nisi plane erit absurda causa, frequentius. Amplificandi autē causa, quæ aut cum digrediētur à causa, dici solent, aut cum perorabunt, hæc vel ad odium, vel ad misericordiam, díam, uel omnino ad animos iudi– cum mouendos, ex iis quæ sunt an– te posita, sumentur: si modo rerum magnitudo, hominum ue aut inui– dia, aut dignitas postulabit.
units.tr: The defender, however, relies on the equity which he has proposed; and since that equity is on his side, he complains that he is pressed not by the matter but by a distortion of the word. In this kind of case he can go through most of the topics of invention. For he uses likes, opposites and consequences, although both sides do so; yet the defendant does so more often, unless the case is plainly absurd. For the purpose of amplification, which are usually made either when they digress from the case or when they sum up, the topics will be drawn from those set out above, either to arouse hatred, or pity, or in general to move the minds of the judges, provided that the greatness of the matter, or the envy or the dignity of the men, requires it.

units.la: Defensor autem.) Ia redit ad locos artis, quibus quanq; frequentius utatur reus (nisi causa plane sit absurda, hoc est, iniqua et aliena) tamen ab utroq; sunt percensendi. Loci sunt cum alij, tum maxime similia, contraria, de quibus satis dictum est lib. 1.
units.tr: "The defender, however." He returns to the topics of the art, which the defendant uses rather more often (unless the case is plainly absurd, that is, unjust and foreign to the matter), yet they must be gone through by both sides. The topics are of several kinds, but chiefly likes and opposites, of which enough was said in book 1.

units.la: Amplificandi autem causa.) De amplificationis tractatione tria docet: eius locu, modum, et tempus. Locus est uel in confirmando, cum digredimur a causa: uel in peroratione. Modus circa affectus uersatur: quorum precipui sunt in hac causa, odiu et miserieordia: illud accusatoris, hanc defensoris, quæ ex amplificationis locis, qui sunt pra positi sunt, sumetur. Tempora duo sunt, quibus amplificatione uti possumus: si res sint magnæ, et periculosæ: aut si hominu uel inuidia, uel dignitas postulabit. Nam ut ipse de Inuen. lib. 2. ait: Illi quidem communes loci, qui aut calumniæ accusatorum demonstrandæ, aut miserieordiæ captandæ, aut facti indignandi, aut a miserieordia deterrendi causa sumuntur, ex periculi magnitudine, non ex causæ genere ducuntur. Quemad–momodum Antonij fecisse docet, in Norbani cauſſa maiestatis,lib.3.de Oratore.
units.tr: "For the purpose of amplification." He teaches three things about the handling of amplification: its place, its measure and its time. The place is either in confirmation, when we digress from the case, or in the peroration. The measure concerns the emotions; of these the chief in this kind of case are hatred and pity: the first belongs to the accuser, the second to the defender, and they are drawn from the amplifying topics that have been set out. There are two times when we can use amplification: if the matters are great and dangerous, or if the envy or the dignity of the men requires it. For as Cicero himself says in De inventione, book 2: "Those common topics which are used either to expose the calumny of accusers, or to catch pity, or to stir indignation at the deed, or to turn the audience away from pity, are drawn from the greatness of the danger, not from the kind of the case." He shows that Antonius did this in the defence of Norbanus on a charge of treason, in book 3 of De oratore.

units.la: DE STATV QVALITATIS.
units.tr: On the Status of Quality

units.la: Habeo ista:nunc ea, quae cum quale sit quippia disceptatur, queri ex utraque parte deceat, uelim audire. C. F. Confiteantur in isto genere, qui arguuntur, se id fecisse ipsum, in quo reprehenduntur.
units.tr: "I have these points; now I should like to hear the arguments on both sides about those matters which are in dispute as to what kind of thing something is." Gaius: "Those who are accused in this kind of case should admit that they did the very thing for which they are reproached."

units.la: C.F. Habeo ista:nunc ea.) Ex definitione ad qua litatis statum transit: quaeritq; utriusq; partis, id est, accusatoris & defensoris locos.
units.tr: "I have these points; now I should like..." This passes from the definition to the status of quality, and asks for the arguments of each side, that is, the places used by the prosecutor and by the defence.

units.la: C. P. Confiteatur in isto genere.) Cum reus non solum se fecisse, verum etiam id ipsum fecisse, quod arguitur, confitetur, hoc est, cum non solum de facto, sed etiam de facti nomine constat: tum superest, ut iure se fecisse dicat. ex quo iuris, uel, ut Rhetores loquuntur, iuridicialis status nominatur. Ergo tunc ex iuris partibus sunt argumenta depromenda. Hoc est igitur, quod hic Cicero se omne iuris ratione explicaturu esse proponit. id quod non ita intelligendum est, quasi uniuersam iuris scholam ac doctrinam uelit explicare: (quod exiguo uolumine fieri non posset) sed quod summam iuris diuisione, ut eteri illa partiendi facultate uelit proponere: & ut postea dicet, breuiter quasi fontes
units.tr: "Those who are accused in this kind of case should admit..." When the defendant not only admits that he did something but also admits that he did the very thing he is accused of, that is, when there is agreement not only about the deed but also about the name of the deed, then what remains is for him to say that he did it by right. From this the status is called juridical, or, as the rhetoricians say, the juridicial status. Therefore the arguments must then be drawn from the parts of law. This is why Cicero here proposes that he will explain the whole of law by its principles. This should not be understood as if he wished to expound the entire school and doctrine of law, which could not be done in a small volume, but rather that he wishes to set out a summary division of law, by that faculty of division which is his own, and, as he will say later, briefly to open up, as it were, the springs of equity. This division of law is most excellent, and anyone who followed it could bring all law into order, which has been sought so eagerly for so many years. Cicero himself, in the first book of De oratore, gave no hint of this. But here let us briefly demonstrate the individual parts. Law, according to Celsus, is the art of the good and the fair; that is, according to Ulpian's interpretation, by which the fair is separated from the unfair and the lawful is distinguished from the unlawful. (De iustitia et iure, l. 1, Digest, bk. 1.)

units.la: D 4 equi æquitatis aperire. Est autem hæc iuris partitio pulcherrima, quam aliquis secutus,posset, quod tantopere iam tot annos expetitur, ius omne in ordine redigere: qua de re & ipse lib.1.de Orat. nihil admonuit. Sed nos hoc loco breuiter sin gulas partes demostremus. Ius primum, autore Celso, est ars boni & æqui: id est, interprete Vlpiano, quo æquum ab iniquo separatur, & licitum ab illicito discernitur. De iust. & iur.l.1.ff.lib.1.
units.tr: But since they say that they acted by right, the whole reasoning of law must be explained to us. It is divided into two primary parts, nature and law, and the force of each kind is distributed into divine and human law. Of these, one belongs to equity and the other to religion. The force of equity is twofold: one kind is defended on the ground of what is straight, true, just, and (as it is said) fair and good; the other pertains to a reciprocal return of favour, for in a benefit it is called grace, and in an injury it is called vengeance. These things are common to nature and to law. But the proper things of law are those which are written, and those which are kept without writing, either by the law of nations or by the custom of ancestors.

units.la: Sed quoniam iure se fecisse dicunt, iuris est omnis ratio nobis explicanda: quod diuiditur in duas partes primas, naturā atq; legem: & utriusque generis uis, in diuinū & humanum ius est distributa. quorū æquitatis est unum, alterum religionis. Æquitatis autem uis est duplex: cuius altera directi, & ueri, & iusti, & (ut dicitur) æqui & boni ratione defenditur. altera ad uicissitudinem reference gratiæ pertinet, quod in beneficio gratia, in iniuria ultio nomi natur. Atq; hæc communia sunt natu- ræ atq; legis: sed propria legis & ea quæ scripta sunt, & ea quæ sine literis, aut gentium iure, aut maiorum more retinentur.
units.tr: "Which is divided into two primary parts, nature and law." Jurists begin their division of law from public and private; how rightly, they themselves must judge. Certainly all law, whether divine, human, public, private, or of any other kind, must flow from nature and from institution or will, for these are the sources of all law. Aristotle, in the fifth book of the Ethics, divides what he himself calls civil law, namely that which belongs to man alone, who alone is a civil animal, into natural and legal law; this division differs in no way from this division of our teacher Cicero. By nature, however, he understands natural law, and Aristotle defines it thus: that law whose force is the same among all. Ulpian, however, puts it this way: natural law is that which nature has taught all animals. For this law, he says, is not peculiar to the human race, but belongs to all animals which are born in the sky, on the land, or in the sea. Hence comes the union of male and female, which we call marriage; hence the procreation of children, hence their upbringing. Yet let no one think that the jurists were so stupid as to want law, which proceeds from reason and mind, to be present in beasts, which lack reason and deliberation and are not to be counted as speaking creatures.

units.la: Quod diuiditur in duas partes primas, naturam atque legem.) Iurisconsulti à publico & priuato suam iuris diuisionem auspicatur: quàm rectè, uiderint ipsi. certè à natura et instituto, siue uoluntate, omne ius tum diuinum, tum humanum, tum publicum, tum priuatum, & si qua alia genera sunt, manare necesse est. Illi enim sunt omnis iuris fontes. Aristoteles quidem in quinto de Morib. ius, quod ipse ciuile uocat, nimirum ab homine, qui solus ciuile animal est, in naturale & legitimum partitur: quae diuisio nihil ab hac doctoris nostri Ciceronis discrepat. Naturam uero, ius naturae, siue naturale intelligit. id ab Aristotele ita definitur: cuius ius idem apud omnes ualet. Vlpianus autem sic: Ius naturale est, quod omnia animalia docuit. nam ius istud, inquit, non humani generis proprium est, sed omnium animalium, quae in coelo, quae in terra, quae in mari nascuntur. Hinc maris atq; foeminae coniunctio, quam nos matrimonium appellamus: hinc liberorum procreatio, hinc educatio. Nemo tamen exi\u00adstimet tam stupidos fuisse iurisconsultos, ut ius quod à ratione & mente proficiscitur, in bestiis inesse voluerint, quae rationis & consilij expertes, numerandiq; & loquedi sunt.
units.tr: Which is divided into two primary parts, nature and law. Jurists begin their division of law with public and private, and let them see for themselves how rightly they do so. Certainly all law, whether divine or human, public or private, and any other kinds there may be, must flow from nature and from institution, or will. For these are the sources of all law. Aristotle, in the fifth book of the Ethics, divides the law which he himself calls civil, that is, the law made by man, who alone is a civic animal, into natural and legal law. This division does not differ at all from the division of our teacher Cicero here. By natural law, however, he means the law of nature, or natural law. Aristotle defines it thus: the law whose force is the same among all men. Ulpian defines it thus: natural law is that which all animals have been taught. For that law, he says, is not peculiar to the human race, but belongs to all animals born in the heavens, on the earth, and in the sea. Hence comes the union of male and female, which we call marriage; hence the procreation of children, and hence their upbringing. Yet no one should think that the jurists were so stupid as to want the law that proceeds from reason and mind to be present in beasts, which lack reason and counsel and are counted and called speechless.

units.la: Sed quoniā quaedā naturæ impulsu faciunt, quæ homines quoque, sed ratione adhibita: idcirco quadam similitudine ius appellarunt naturale, illas affectiones, quas πεφυκὰς Græci uocant. Nam uel ipsis quæ Vlpianus ponit exemplis, uidere licet, eum non de illo iure quod homines solos attingit, intellexisse, sed de quadam naturali facultate: quam, ut dixi, per quandam similitudinē, ius appellauit. Lex autē, quam alterā iuris partē facit hic Cicero, ius legitimum ab Aristot. uocatur, atq; ita definitur: Esse ius, quod initio nihil interfuit, sic an secus fieret: cum autē latū positūq; est, iam interest. ueluti, captū mina redimi: aut, capra immolari, non duas oues. præterea, quæ lege cauta sunt de reb. singulis, ut quæ publicis decretis sancita sunt. Ex hoc Aristotelis loco constat, unde: suam hanc partitionē sumpserit Cicero. nam in his uerbis, et lex diuina et humana, et publica et priuata continetur. Huius legis definitio, quoniam diuinas et humanas leges cōplectitur, non rectè ex iure ciuili mihi assumi uidetur. Quin potius adhibenda fuit illa ex libro 1. de Legibus: Lex est recta ratio imperandi atq; prohibendi: quam qui ignorat, is est iniustus, siue illa scripta est uspiam, siue nusquam.
units.tr: But since some things are done by an impulse of nature, which men also do, though with reason applied, for this reason they called by a certain likeness natural law those inclinations which the Greeks call natural impulses [πεφυκὰς]. For from the very examples Ulpian gives one can see that he did not mean that law which touches men alone, but a certain natural faculty, which, as I said, he called law by a certain likeness. The law, however, which Cicero here makes the other part of law, is called legitimate law by Aristotle, and is defined thus: it is law that at the beginning made no difference whether a thing was done this way or otherwise, but once it has been enacted and laid down, it now makes a difference. For example, that a captive may be ransomed for a mina, or that a goat rather than two sheep be sacrificed. Besides these, there are the things that are provided by law concerning individual matters, such as the things sanctioned by public decrees. From this passage of Aristotle it is clear where Cicero took this division of his. For in these words both divine and human law, and public and private law, are contained. The definition of this law, since it embraces both divine and human laws, does not seem to me to have been rightly taken from civil law. Rather, that definition from the first book of On the Laws ought to have been used: law is right reason in commanding and forbidding; whoever is ignorant of it is unjust, whether it has been written down anywhere or nowhere.

units.la: Et utriusq; generis uis.) Tam naturalis quàm legitimi iuris partes sunt duæ: diuinum, quo ad
units.tr: And the force of each kind. Both parts of natural law and of legal law are two: the divine, by which we are driven to religion, and the human, by which we are driven to equity.

units.la: religionem impellimur: & humanū, quo ad æ- quitatem. Ex hoc naturali diuino iure sunt omnes illæ notiones ac sententiæ: Esse aliquam cœle stem uim,numen'ue diuinum, quo cuncta regantur & gubernentur: idcirco ei aliquem esse cultum & religionem exhibendū. Nulla enim gens tā fera,nemo omniū tā est immanis,cuius mente non imbucrit decorū opinio. Multi de dijs praua sentiūt (id enim uiciofo more effici solet) oēs tamē esse uim et natura diuina arbitrantur. Tusc.1.
units.tr: From this natural divine law come all those notions and opinions: that there is some heavenly power or divine will by which all things are ruled and governed, and that therefore some worship and religion is to be shown to it. For no nation is so savage, and no man so monstrous, that the opinion of what is fitting has not been steeped into his mind. Many think wrongly about the gods (for this is commonly done through a corrupt habit), yet all believe that there is a divine power and nature. Tusculan Disputations 1.

units.la: Quorum æquitatis est unum. ) Hic æquitatem ad humanum tātum ius uult pertinere, idq; distinguēdi tantum gratia,ut singulæ partes sua habeāt et propria uocabula. Alioqui in Topicis, ubi non tam subtiliter hæc descripsit,æquitatem etiam religionis genus statuit. Acquitas est naturæ sententia,de rebus licitis & illicitis, nusquam scripta,sed animis nostris insita. de qua est illa Ciceronis descriptio pro Milone: Est enim hæc, iudices,nō scripta,sed nata lex: quam nō didicimus, accepimus, legimus, uerum ex natura ipsa arripuimus, hausimus, expressimus: ad quā non docti,sed facti: non instituti,sed imbuti sumus.
units.tr: Of which one is equity. Here he wishes equity to pertain only to human law, and this only for the sake of distinction, so that each part has its own proper name. Otherwise, in the Topics, where he has not described these things so precisely, he counts equity also as a kind of religion. Equity is the sentiment of nature concerning things lawful and unlawful, written nowhere but implanted in our minds. Of it is that description of Cicero in the speech for Milo: for this, judges, is not a written but a born law, which we have not learned, received, or read, but have snatched, drawn, and drawn out from nature itself; to which we have been made, not taught; formed, not instructed; steeped, not schooled.

units.la: Acquitatis autem ius est duplex. ) Duo genera facit æquitatis: unum,quod per se directum, uerum,iustū,bonū & æquū est(hæc enim omnia unū idēq; significāt) quod inquā per se,non alterius respectu æquum & boni est: quod est aliud nihil, quàm ucra illa & germana iustitia: ut, boneste uiuere, alterum non lædere, per se rectum æquumq; est. Alterum, quod non per se, sed ad aliud refertur: cuius duæ sunt partes, gratia, & ultio. Nam quanquam gratia in bonam & malam partem capiatur, unde est bona & mala gratia: tamen proprie in beneficio referendo, gratia dicitur: in ulciscenda iniuria, ultio siue uindicatio. Gratia definitur de Inuent. 2. in qua amicitiarum & officiorum alterius memoria, et alterius remunerandi uoluntas continetur. Vindicatio, per quā ius & iniuria, & omnino omne quod obfuturū est, defendendo aut ulciscēdo propulsatur. ad ius gentium hanc partem referunt iurisconsulti, ff. li. 1. de iust. & iur. Sed intelligendum est, ius naturæ esse duplex: alterum, omnium animantium commune: alterum, gentiū tantum, id est humani generis proprium, quod idcirco ius humanum à Liuio appellatur. De duplici hoc iure aperte & distincte disserit Cicero de Offic. lib. 1. Idem facit Aristoteles in Ethicis. Falsum igitur est, quod quidam censent, philosophos ius naturæ cum gentium iure confundere.
units.tr: The right of equity is twofold. He makes two kinds of equity: one which is directed in itself, true, just, good, and equitable (for all these words mean one and the same thing), which, I say, is equitable and good in itself and not in relation to another; this is nothing other than that true and genuine justice, as, to live honourably and not to harm another is right and equitable in itself. The other is that which is not in itself but is referred to another, and it has two parts: grace and vengeance. For although grace is taken in a good and a bad sense, whence there is good grace and bad grace, yet properly grace is said of repaying a benefit, and vengeance or vindication of avenging a wrong. Grace is defined in the De Inventione book 2, where the memory of friendships and duties of another, and the will to repay another, are contained. Vindication is that by which right and wrong, and in general everything that is likely to harm, is repelled by defending or avenging. The jurists refer this part to the law of nations, Digest, book 1, title on justice and right. But it must be understood that the law of nature is twofold: one common to all living things, the other belonging only to the nations, that is, peculiar to the human race, which is why Livy calls it human law. Cicero discusses this twofold law openly and distinctly in On Duties, book 1. Aristotle does the same in the Ethics. It is therefore false, as some think, that the philosophers confuse the law of nature with the law of nations.

units.la: Atq; hæc communia sunt.) Commune est naturæ & legis, ut utraque diuina & humana sit: & utraque per se sit, & ad aliud referatur. Nam lex per se quidem consideratur, ut sit recta ratio in animo sapientis, ut ante dixi: & ad alterum, cum de pramio poena que statuit. Aut scripto, aut sine literis, sed more & consensu.
units.tr: And these things are common. Nature and law share this: each is both divine and human, and each is considered in itself and also in relation to something else. Law is considered in itself as right reason in the mind of the wise, as I said before, and in relation to something else when it fixes reward and punishment. It is either written or unwritten, the latter maintained by custom and consent.

units.la: Sed propria legis.) Communia naturæ & legis capita descripsit: nunc quæ legis sint propria, docet. Lex igitur primum aut divina est, aut humana: & utraque aut scripta, aut non scripta. divina lex scripta, ut tabulæ Mosæ, in quibus Deus leges inciderat. Non scripta, ut quæ Dei voce Abrahamo de circumcisione data est, diuque more retenta. Item que Christi filij Dei, qui literam ipse non scripsit. Hanc etiam divisionem habet Aristoteles Scripti & non scripti iuris, libro octauo Ethicorum: habent etiam Iurisconsulti, appellant que ius ciuile, quod sic definiunt: Ius ciuile est, quod neque in totum à naturali vel gentium iure recedit, neque per omnia ei seruit: itaque cum aliquid addimus, vel detrahimus iuri communi, ius proprium, id est ciuile efficimus. ff. libro primo, l. sexta. Cicero autem in Topicis sic eleganter à causis definit: Ius ciuile est, æquitas constituta ijs qui eiusdem ciuitatis sunt, ad res suas obtinendas.
units.tr: Now he teaches what belongs properly to law. Law is therefore either divine or human, and each is either written or unwritten. Divine law is written, like the tables of Moses on which God had inscribed the laws. It is unwritten, like what God gave to Abraham by voice concerning circumcision, which was long kept by custom; likewise that of Christ the Son of God, who himself wrote no letter. Aristotle also makes this division into written and unwritten law, in book 8 of the Ethics. The jurists have it too, and they call it civil law, which they define thus: civil law is that which neither wholly departs from natural law or the law of nations nor serves it in every respect. So when we add to or take away from the common law, we make it proper, that is, civil. Digest, book 1, law 6. Cicero, in the Topics, defines it elegantly by its causes: civil law is equity established for those who belong to the same state, for securing their own affairs.

units.la: Et ea qua sine literis, ) Ius non scriptum intelligit, telligit, cui duas nunc subijcit partes: ius gen‑tium, & morem maiorum. Sed hæc est tantum inchoata partitio, quam paulo post absoluet.
units.tr: "And that which is without letters": he means unwritten law, which he now divides into two parts, the law of nations and the custom of the ancestors. But this is only a begun division, which he will complete shortly afterwards.

units.la: Ius gentium definit Vlpianus, quo gentes huma‑ næ utuntur: latiusq; patere, libri iurisconsul‑torum docent, quàm hic uelit Cicero. nam ut pa‑ rentibus & patriæ pareamus, ut gratiam bene‑ meritis referamus, ut uim atq; iniuriam propul‑ semus, id ante in naturæ partibus positum est. relinquitur ergò, ut reliqua quæ ab ijsdem iurif‑ peritis numerantur, intelligamus. Cuiusmodi sunt, à gentibus de religione accepta cæremoniæ & ritus, bella item et seruitutes, & manumissiones, & omnes pene contractus, quæ omnia iure gen‑ tium esse uolunt. ff. lib. 1. Inst. lib. 1. de iure nat. §. ius gétium. Et hoc est ius illud naturale, humani ge‑ neris proprium, ut ante ostendimus. Omni autem in re consensus omnium gentium, lex naturæ pu‑ tanda est. Inst. 1.
units.tr: Ulpian defines the law of nations as that which the peoples of mankind use. The books of the jurists show that it extends more widely than Cicero here wishes. For that we obey parents and country, that we repay kindnesses to those who deserve them, that we repel force and injury, has already been placed among the parts of nature. It remains, therefore, that we understand the rest, which the same jurists enumerate. Of this kind are the ceremonies and rites of religion received from the nations, likewise wars, slaveries and manumissions, and almost all contracts, all of which they want to belong to the law of nations. Digest, book 1; Institutes, book 1, on natural law, §the law of nations. And this is that natural law, proper to the human race, as we showed before. Moreover, in every matter the agreement of all nations is to be regarded as the law of nature. Institutes 1.

units.la: Scriptorum autem priuatum a‑ liud est, publicum aliud. Publicum, lex, senatusconsul. fœdus: priuatum, tabulæ, pactum, conuentum, stipu‑latio. Quæ autem scripta non sunt, ea aut consuetudine, aut conuentis hominum, & quasi consensu obti‑ nentur. Atque etiam hoc in primis, ut nostros mores, legesq; tucamur, quodammodo naturali iure prascriptum est.
units.tr: Of written law, one kind is private and another is public. Public: laws, senatus consulta, treaties. Private: tablets, pacts, agreements, stipulations. Those things that are not written are upheld by custom, or by agreements of men and, as it were, by consent. And indeed this above all, that we should protect our customs and laws, has in a way been prescribed by natural law.

units.la: Scriptorum autem.) Diuidit scriptū ius in priuatum & publicum. publicū definiunt, quod ad statum rei Romanæ spectat. Romanæ dixerunt illi, propter eius Reip summā maiestatē. nos aūt pro re Romana, Rep. dicemus, hoc modo: ius publicū est, quod ad statū Reip. spectat. Priuatū, quod ad singulorum utilitatē. Publici iuris partes illi faciunt, sacra, sacerdotes, & magistratus: quæ quidem non excludit Cicero (nam & sub lege subijcit diuinū quoq; ius) sed quas ipse partes ponit, hæ sunt magis propriæ: nimirum leges, senatusconsulta, fœdera. Plura tamen illi scripto iuri suo tribuunt, legem, plebiscitum, se- natusconsultum, principum placita, magistratuum edicta, responsa prudentum. omittunt tamen fœdera, quæ haud dubie & publici iuris sunt, & scripti. Sed legum nomine, tum plebiscita, tum magistratuum edicta, tum principum placita comprehendit: responsa uero prudentum, cum de iure ciuili loquatur, nequaquam excludit. Nam & hæc omnia in definitione iuris, quæ enumeratione constat, in Topicis recensuit.
units.tr: Scriptorum autem.) He divides written law into private and public. They define public law as what concerns the condition of the Roman commonwealth. They said "Roman" on account of the supreme majesty of that commonwealth. We, however, for a Roman matter, will say "of the commonwealth", in this way: public law is what concerns the condition of the commonwealth. Private law is what concerns the advantage of individuals. Those others make the parts of public law sacred rites, priests, and magistrates. Cicero does not exclude these (for he also subordinates divine law under law), but the parts he himself sets down are more proper to it, namely laws, senatus consulta, and treaties. They nonetheless assign more to their written law: law, plebiscite, senatus consultum, decrees of princes, edicts of magistrates, and opinions of the learned. They omit treaties, however, which are undoubtedly both of public law and written. But under the name of laws he includes plebiscites, edicts of magistrates, and decrees of princes. The opinions of the learned, since he is speaking of civil law, he by no means excludes. For in the Topics he listed all of these in the definition of law, which consists in enumeration.

units.la: Harum partium definitionem ex iure ciuili sumendæ sunt: Institlib.1. de Iure nat. §. Constat autem. Priuatum ius tripertitò diuidunt, in naturale, gentium & ciuile. Cicero aliter has partes disponit, ut uidimus: ac priuati iuris partes facit, tabulas, pacta, conuenta, stipulationes. Tabulæ, literæ quæcunque sunt, in quibus testimonia iuris nostri continentur: ut testamenta, codicilli, & priuatæ de rebus nostris tabulæ, quarū sunt multa & uaria genera. Pactum, siue pactio quid essetitemq; stipulatio, alibi docuimus, ex ff. lib. 2. de pactis. Conuentum, conueniens in Topicis appellauit. Iurisperiti etiam conuentionem, ut Vlpianus eodem loco: Conuentionis uerbum generale est, inquit, ad omnia pertinens, de quibus negotij contrahendi transfigendiq; caussa consentiunt, qui inter se agunt.
units.tr: The definitions of these parts are to be taken from civil law: Institutes, book 1, on natural law, §"it is established". They divide private law threefold into natural, of nations, and civil. Cicero arranges these parts differently, as we have seen, and makes the parts of private law tablets, pacts, agreements, and stipulations. Tablets are whatever writings contain the evidence of our law, such as wills, codicils, and private tablets concerning our property, of which there are many and various kinds. What a pact or agreement is, and what a stipulation is, we have taught elsewhere from the Digest, book 2, on pacts. Agreement (conventum) he called "conveniens" in the Topics. The jurists also call it convention, as Ulpian does in the same place: "The word convention is general," he says, "and pertains to all things on which those who deal with each other agree for the sake of contracting or concluding business."

units.la: Quæ autem scripta non sunt.) Inchoatam supra iuris non scripti partitionem ordine absoluit. tres enim partes facit, ut omnia coniungamus: quarum una gentiu iure, altera more & consuetudine maiorum, tertia couentis hominū, & recenti consensu cötinetur. Quid ius gentiu esset, quid couentū, dictum est: de consuetudine uero unū aut alterū locū afferā. Primo definitione ipsius Ciceronis de Inuet. li. 2. Consuetudinis autem ius esse putatur, id quod uoluntate omnium, sine lege uetustas comprobauit.huic consentanece Vl pianus,Diuturna cõsuetudo,inquit,pro iure & lege,in ijs quæ non ex scripto descendunt, obser uari solet.ff.de leg.l.33.
units.tr: "But those things which are not written": he completes in order the division of unwritten law begun above. For he makes three parts, so that we may join everything together: one of these is contained in the law of nations, another in the custom and practice of the ancestors, and a third in the agreements of men and recent consent. What the law of nations is, and what agreement is, has been said. I will bring forward one or two passages about custom. First, Cicero's own definition in De Inventione, book 2: "The law of custom is thought to be that which antiquity has approved by the will of all, without a law." Ulpian agrees: "A long-standing custom is usually observed as law in those matters which do not derive from writing," Digest, on law, law 33.

units.la: Atq; etiã hoc in primis.) Additur hoc tanquã vinculũ reliquorũ, de legibus & morib. tuendis & cõseruandis.Nam si leges & mores uolũtate introducta sunt,nõ omnino natura,illud tamẽ penè in ipsa natura insitũ est,ut nostros mores, legesq; tueri uelimus:qui locus cõmunis sæpe à Cicerone usurpatur.uelut pro Cluëtio,cum ait:Indignum esse, in ea ciuitate,quæ legibus contineatur,discedi à legibus. deinde subijcit illam præclara similitudinẽ:Vt corpora nostra sine mẽte, sic ciuitas sine lege suis partib. & neruis ac sanguine et mẽbris uti nõ potest.legũ ministri magi stratus, legũ interpretes,iudices, legũ deniq; idcirco omnes serui sumus,ut liberi esse possimus.
units.tr: "And indeed this above all." This is added as the bond of the rest, concerning the protection and preservation of laws and customs. For if laws and customs were introduced by will, not altogether by nature, yet it is almost implanted in nature itself that we wish to protect our customs and laws. This is a commonplace often used by Cicero, for example in the Pro Cluentio, where he says that it is unworthy, in a state that is governed by laws, to depart from the laws. Then he adds that splendid comparison: just as the body cannot use its parts, sinews, blood and limbs without the mind, so a state without law cannot function. The ministers of the laws are the magistrates, the interpreters of the laws are the judges; finally, we are all therefore slaves of the laws, so that we may be able to be free.

units.la: Et quoniam breuiter aperti sontes sunt quasi quidã æquitatis, medítatá nobis ad hoc caussarum genus esse debebũt ea, quæ dicêda erũt ín orationíb.de natura, de legibus,de more maiorum, de propulsanda iniuria,de ulciscenda,de omni parte iuris.
units.tr: And since the sources of equity have been briefly laid open, the things that must be said in speeches should be prepared by us for this kind of cause: concerning nature, concerning laws, concerning the custom of the ancestors, concerning the repelling of injury, concerning avenging, and concerning every part of law.

units.la: E
units.tr: E

units.la: Et quoniam.) Epilogus huius partitionis iu‐ ris:quo admonet, locos nudos, quos notauit, ef‐ fe iuris & naturalis & ciuilis doctrina, atq; antiquitatis exemplis & moribus replendos & ordinandos.Cuius scientia non ex Rhetorum libellis, sed ex iurisperitorum commentarijs petenda est: sine cuius,etsi non summa ac perfecta, at aliqua tamen cognitione iuris & iniuriae,caussae tractatio non possunt.Fontes tamen omnis iuris in philosophorum commentarijs & disputationibus de Moribus & legibus continentur. Quamobrem non modo oratori, verum etiam iurisconsulto suturo proderit,in illa philosophiae parte versatum esse,Platonis & Aristotelis de Moribus & Republ.nec non Ciceronis de Officijs & Legibus libros euoluisse,qui ad omnem iuris partem viam patefaciant. Sed exercitatio meditatioq; doctrinae accedat oportet, sine qua proferre nihil aut parum poterimus.
units.tr: "And since." This is the epilogue of this division of law, by which he advises that the bare topics he has noted are to be filled out and arranged with the teaching of both natural and civil law, and with examples and customs of antiquity. Knowledge of these is not to be sought from the little books of the rhetoricians, but from the commentaries of the jurists. Without some knowledge of law and injury, if not a complete and perfect one, the handling of a cause cannot proceed. Nevertheless, the sources of all law are contained in the commentaries and disputations of the philosophers on morals and laws. Therefore it will benefit not only the orator but also the future jurist to be versed in that part of philosophy and to have unrolled the books of Plato and Aristotle on morals and the republic, as well as Cicero's books on Duties and on Laws, which open the way to every part of law. But practice and meditation on learning must be added, without which we can produce little or nothing.

units.la: Si imprudéter aut necessitate,aut casu quippiā fecerit,quod nō concederetur iis,qui sua spote & uoluntate fecissent,ad eius facti de precatio nē ignoscēdi petēda uenia est, quae sumetur ex plerisq; locis æquitatis.
units.tr: If someone has done something through imprudence, or necessity, or chance, which would not be permitted to those who had done it of their own accord and will, then pardon must be sought for that deed by a plea for forgiveness, which will be drawn from many places of equity.

units.la: Si imprudenter. ) Qualitas ea quae iure nititur,quae & iuridicialis appellatur,rursum bipertita est. nam & absoluta qualitas est, & affumpta, ut Rhetores uocant. Absoluta est, quae ipsa in fe,ut nihilforis affumatur,cõtinet iuris & iniuriae quaestione. Assumptiua, quae ipsa ex fe nihil firmi dat ad recusationem, facti ue defensionem:foris autem aliquid defensionis affumit. Ad absolutam pertinet, quae adhuc de iure tradidit. nunc paucis de assumptiua admonet.de qua plura supra in qualitatis partitione, cum de confirmatione ageretur,tradidit.Faciunt autem assumptiuae partes quatuor, comparationem, relationem, fiue translationem criminis,remotionē criminis,& concessionem.hanc postremam hic ponit Cicero,non uerbo & nomine, sed re & partibus. Concessio dicitur,cum reus non id quod factum est defendit,sed ut ignoscatur postulat.hac in duas diuidunt partes:in purgationem fiue excufationem,& deprecationem. Purgatio est, cū factum conceditur, culpa uero aliqua de caussa remouetur.Haec partes habet tres, quas etiā hic Cicero numerat: Imprudentiam, fiue inscitiam, casum fiue fortunam,& necessitatem: haec enim omnia excusationem habet facti aliquâhonestā. Quod nō concederetur.) De altera cōceffionis parte loquitur,quae deprecatio dicitur.Est enim deprecatio,cū et peccaffe,& cōfulto peccaffe fe reus cōfitetur,& tamen ut ignoscatur postulat.
units.tr: If he did something imprudently or by necessity or chance, which would not be granted to those who acted of their own will and choice, pardon must be sought for that deed by way of deprecation; this is drawn from the many places of equity. Qualities that rest on law, which are also called juridical, are again of two kinds: there is the absolute quality and the assumptive, as the Rhetoricians call them. The absolute is that which contains within itself the question of right and wrong, without taking anything from outside. The assumptive gives nothing firm of itself for refutation or defence of the fact, but takes something of defence from outside. The absolute belongs to what he has taught so far about law; now he briefly warns about the assumptive, of which he taught more above, in the division of quality, when dealing with confirmation. The parts of the assumptive are four: comparison, transference of the charge, removal of the charge, and concession. Cicero sets out this last here, not by word and name but in substance and parts. Concession is said to occur when the defendant does not defend what was done, but asks to be pardoned. This is divided into two parts: purgation, or excuse, and deprecation. Purgation is when the deed is conceded but the fault is removed for some cause. It has three parts, which Cicero also enumerates here: imprudence or ignorance, chance or fortune, and necessity; for all of these carry some honourable excuse for the deed. "Which would not be granted": he speaks of the other part of concession, which is called deprecation. For deprecation is when the defendant confesses both that he has sinned and that he sinned deliberately, and yet asks to be pardoned.

units.la: E Sunt uerò hæc uerba à superioribus omnino distinguenda & separanda.neq; enim prorsus spō-te fit,quod aut imprudentia,aut necessitate, aut casu fortuna ue peccatur.
units.tr: Indeed these words must be entirely distinguished and separated from those above. For what is done through imprudence, necessity, or chance or fortune is not done altogether of one's own will.

units.la: Quæ sumetur ex plerisque locis æquitatis.) Locos & partes purgationis posuit:iam deprecationis partes unde sint sumendæ, indicat. Ex plerisq; æquitatis locis,inquit, non ab omnibus, sed ex certis. Qui loci diligenter in Rhetoricis de Inuent.recensentur,atq; omnes fere ex æquitate pendent, hoc est, ex gratia referenda: quidam etiam ex more & consuetudine. Quin etiá exempla harum omnium partiū,ex isdem Rhetoricis abundè suppeditantur. Oportet enim etiam ipsam ueniam aliquo æquitatis saltem colore niti, alioqui repudiabitur.
units.tr: "Which will be taken from the many places of equity." He has set out the places and parts of purgation; now he indicates whence the parts of deprecation are to be taken. "From the places of equity," he says, not from all of them but from certain ones. These places are carefully listed in the Rhetoric of the De Inventione, and nearly all of them depend on equity, that is, on the returning of grace; some also depend on custom and usage. Indeed, examples of all these parts are abundantly supplied from the same Rhetorics. For it is necessary that pardon itself rest on some colour of equity at least; otherwise it will be rejected.

units.la: • Ius Natura Diuinum, quod religione continetur. Humanum, æquitate Per se, quod dicitur Directum Verum Iustum Æquum Bonum. Ad aliud Gratia, in beneficio. Vltio, in iniuria. Lex Diuina Scripta Publica Priuata. Non scripta. Humana Scripta Publica Lex Senatus consultū Fœdus. Priuata Tabulæ Pactū Cōuētū Stipulatio. Non scripta Ius gentium Mos maiorum.
units.tr: Law: Natural: Divine, which is contained in religion; Human, through equity itself, which is called Direct, True, Just, Equal, Good. Towards another: Grace, in benefit; Vengeance, in injury. Law: Divine: Written, Public, Private; Unwritten. Human: Written: Public: Decree of the Senate, Covenant; Private: Tablets, Pact, Agreement, Stipulation. Unwritten: Law of nations, Custom of the ancestors.

units.la: Sed quoniâ quædâ naturæ impulsu faciunt, quæ homines quoque, sed ratione adhibita: idcirco quadam similitudine ius appellarunt naturale, illas affectiones, quas πρηχὰς Græci uocant. Nam uel ipsis quæ Vlpianus ponit exemplis, uidere licet, cum non de illo iure quod homines solos attingit, intellexisse, sed de quadam naturali facultate: quam, ut dixi, per quandâ similitudinê, ius appellauit. Lex aut, quam alterâ iuris partê facit hic Cicero, ius legitimû ab Aristot. uocatur, atq; ita definitur: Esse ius, quod initio nihil interfuit, sic an secus fieret: cum aut latû positiúq; est, iam interest. ueluti, captû mina redimi: aut, caprâ immolari, non duas oues. præterea, quæ lege cauta sunt de reb. singulis, ut quæ publicis decretis sancita sunt. Ex hoc Aristotelis loco constat, unde suam hanc partitionê sumpserit Cicero. nam in his uerbis, & lex diuina & humana, & publica & priuata continetur. Huius legis definitio, quoniam diuinas & humanas leges copleEtitur, non rectè ex iure ciuili mihi assumi uidetur. Quin potius adhibenda fuit illa ex libro 1. de Legibus: Lex est recta ratio imperandi atq; prohibendi: quam qui ignorat, is est iniustus, siue illa scripta est uspiam, siue nusquam.
units.tr: But since certain things are done by the impulse of nature, which men also do, though with reason applied, therefore by a certain similarity they called those affections which the Greeks call prochas [πρηχὰς] natural law. For from the very examples Ulpian gives, one can see that he understood not that law which touches men alone, but a certain natural faculty, which, as I said, he called law by a certain similarity. But the law which Cicero makes the other part of law here is called legitimate law by Aristotle, and is defined thus: it is law which at first made no difference whether it was done this way or that, but once it has been laid down and enacted, it matters; for example, that a captive be redeemed for a mina, or that a goat be sacrificed rather than two sheep. Moreover, those things secured by law concerning individual matters, as those sanctioned by public decrees. From this passage of Aristotle it is clear whence Cicero took this division; for in these words both divine and human, and public and private law, are contained. The definition of this law, since it embraces divine and human laws, does not seem to me to be rightly taken from civil law. Rather, that from the first book of On Laws ought to have been applied: Law is right reason in commanding and forbidding; whoever is ignorant of it is unjust, whether it is written anywhere or nowhere.

units.la: Et utriusq; generis uis.) Tam naturalis quàm legitimi iuris partes sunt duæ: diuinum, quo ad relireligionem impellimur: & humanū, quo ad æ- quitatem. Ex hoc naturali diuino iure sunt omnes illæ notiones ac sententiæ: Esse aliquam cœlestem uim, numen'que diuinum, quo cuncta regantur & gubernentur: idcirco ei aliquem esse cultum & religionem exhibendū. Nulla enim gens tā fera, nemo omniū tā est immanis, cuius mente non imbucrit deorū opinio. Multi de dijs praua sentiūt (id enim uiciofo more effici solet) oēs tā- mē esse uim et natura diuinā arbitrātur. Tusc. 1.
units.tr: And of both kinds the force... Both parts of natural and of legitimate law are two: divine, by which we are impelled to religion, and human, by which we are moved to equity. From this natural divine law come all those notions and opinions: that there is some heavenly power and divine will by which all things are ruled and governed, and that therefore some worship and religion is to be shown to it. For no nation is so savage, no man so monstrous, whose mind has not been imbued with the opinion of the gods. Many think wrongly about the gods (for this is usually done through vicious custom), yet all think that there is a divine power and nature. Tusc. 1.

units.la: Quorum æquitatis est unum.) Hic æquitatem ad humanum tātum ius uult pertinere, idq; distinguēdi tantum gratia, ut singulæ partes sua habeāt et propria uocabula. Alioqui in Topicis, ubi non tam subtiliter hæc describit, æquitatem etiam religionis genus statuit. Æquitas est naturæ sententia, de rebus licitis & illicitis, nusquam scripta, sed animis nostris insita. de qua est illa Ciceronis descriptio pro Milone: Est enim hæc, iudices, nō scripta, sed nata lex: quam nō didicimus, accepimus, legimus, uerum ex natura ipsa arripuimus, hausimus, expressimus: ad quā non docti, sed facti: non instituti, sed imbuti sumus.
units.tr: "Of which equity is one." Here he wants equity to pertain only to human law, and this merely for the sake of distinction, so that each part has its own proper name. Elsewhere, in the Topics, where he does not describe these things so subtly, he sets equity down as a kind of religion too. Equity is the sentiment of nature concerning lawful and unlawful things, nowhere written but implanted in our minds. Of it is that description of Cicero's in Pro Milone: "For this law, judges, is not written but born; which we have not learned, received, or read, but have snatched, drawn and expressed from nature itself; to which we were not taught but made, not instructed but imbued."

units.la: Æquitatis autem ius est duplex.) Duo genera facit æquitatis: unum, quod per se directum, uerum, iustū, bonū & æquū est (hæc enim omnia unū idēq; significāt) quod inquā per se, non alterius respectu æquum & bonu est: quod est aliud nihil, quàm uera illa & germana iusticia: ut, boneste uiuere, alterum non lædere, per se rectum æquumq; est. Alterum, quod non per se, sed ad aliud refertur: cuius duæ sunt partes, gratia, & ultio. Nam quanquam gratia in bonam & malam partem capiatur, unde est bona & mala gratia: tamen proprie in beneficio referendo, gratia dicitur: in ulciscenda iniuria, ultio siue uindicatio. Gratia definitur de Inuent. 2. in qua amicitiarum & officiorum alterius memoria, et alterius remunerandi uoluntas cõtinetur. Vindicatio, per quã ius & iniuria, & omnino omne quod obfuturũ est, defendendo aut ulciscedo propulsatur. ad ius gentium hanc partem referunt iurisconsulti, ff. li. 1. de iust. & iur. sed intelligendum est, ius naturæ esse duplex: alterum, omnium animantium commune: alterum, gentiũ tantum, id est humani generis proprium, quod idcirco ius humanum à Liuio appellatur. De duplici hoc iure aperte & distincte disserit Cicero de Offic. lib. 1. Idem facit Aristoteles in Ethicis. Falsum igitur est, quod quidam censent, philosophos ius naturæ cum gentium iure confundere.
units.tr: Moreover, the law of equity is twofold. He makes two kinds of equity. One is what is in itself direct, true, just, good and equal (for all these words signify one and the same), which, I say, is equal and good in itself and not in respect of another; this is nothing other than true and genuine justice, as living honestly and not harming another is in itself right and equal. The other is what is referred not to itself but to another, and it has two parts: grace and vengeance. For although grace is taken in a good and in a bad sense, whence there is good and bad grace, yet properly grace is said of returning a benefit, and vengeance or vindication of avenging an injury. Grace is defined in De Inventione 2 as containing the memory of friendships and services received from another, and the will to repay him. Vindication is that by which right and wrong, and in general whatever is about to harm, is repelled by defending or avenging. The jurists refer this part to the law of nations (Digest 1, De iustitia et iure); but it must be understood that natural law is twofold: one common to all living things, the other only of nations, that is, proper to the human race, which is therefore called human law by Livy. Cicero discusses this twofold law openly and distinctly in De Officiis book 1, and Aristotle does the same in the Ethics. It is therefore false, what some think, that the philosophers confuse natural law with the law of nations.

units.la: Atq; hæc communia sunt.) Commune est natu- ræ & legis, ut utraque diuina & humana fit: & utraque per se fit, & ad aliud referatur. Nam lex per se quidem consideratur, ut sit recta ratio in animo sapientis, ut ante dixi: & ad alterum, cum de præmio pœnaque statuit. Aut scripto, aut sine literis, sed more & consensu.
units.tr: And these things are common. What is common to nature and to law is that each is both divine and human, and each is both considered in itself and referred to another. For law is considered in itself, as it is right reason in the mind of the wise, as I said before; and with respect to another, when it lays down reward and punishment. It is either written or unwritten, but by custom and consent.

units.la: Sed propria legis.) Communia naturæ & legis capita descripsit: nunc quæ legis sint propria, docet. Lex igitur primum aut divina est, aut humana: & utraque aut scripta, aut non scripta. divina lex scripta, ut tabulæ Mosæ, in quibus Deus leges inciderat. Non scripta, ut quæ. Dei voce Abrahamo de circuncisione data est, diuque more retenta. Item quæ Christi filij Dei, qui literam ipse non scripsit. Hanc etiam diuisionem habet Aristoteles Scripti & non scripti iuris, libro octauo Ethicorum: habent etiam Iurisconsulti, appellant quem ius ciuile, quod sic definiunt: Ius ciuile est, quod neque in totum à naturali vel gentium iure recedit, neque per omnia ei seruit: itaque cum aliquid addimus, vel detrahimus iuri communi, ius proprium, id est ciuile efficimus. ff. libro primo, l. sexta. Cicero autem in Topicis sic eleganter à causis definit: Ius ciuile est, æquitas constituta ijs qui eiusdem ciuitatis sunt, ad res suas obtinendas.
units.tr: But the proper things of law. He has described the common heads of natural and legal law; now he teaches what belongs properly to law. Law, therefore, is first either divine or human, and each is either written or unwritten. Divine law is written, like the tablets of Moses, on which God had engraved laws; unwritten, like that which was given to Abraham by God's voice concerning circumcision and long retained by custom; likewise that of Christ the Son of God, who himself wrote no letter. Aristotle also has this division of written and unwritten law, in Book 8 of the Ethics. The jurists too have it, calling it civil law, which they define thus: "Civil law is that which neither wholly departs from natural law or the law of nations, nor serves it in all things; so when we add or subtract something from the common law, we make a proper law, that is, civil." Digest, book 1, law 6. Cicero, however, in the Topics, defines it elegantly from its causes: "Civil law is equity established for those who belong to the same state, for keeping their own things."

units.la: Et ea qua sine literis, ) Ius non scriptum intelligit, telligit, cui duas nunc subijcit partes: ius gen‐tium, & morem maiorum. Sed hæc est tantum inchoata partitio, quam paulo post absoluit. Ius gentium definit Vlpianus, quo gentes huma‐ næ utuntur: latiusq; patêre, libri iurisconsulto‐ rum docent, quàm hic uelit Cicero. nam ut pa‐ rentibus & patriæ pareamus, ut gratiam bene‐ meritis referamus, ut uim atq; iniuriam propul‐ semus, id ante in naturæ partibus positum est. relinquitur ergò, ut reliqua quæ ab ijsdem iurif‐ peritis numerantur, intelligamus. Cuiusmodi sunt, à gentibus de religione acceptæ cæremoniæ & ritus, bella item et seruitutes, & manumissiones, & omnes pene contractus, quæ omnia iure gen‐ tium esse uolûnt. ff. lib. 1. Inst. lib. 1. de iure nat. §. ius gétium. Et hoc est ius illud naturale, humani ge‐neris proprium, ut ante ostendimus. Omni autem in re consensus omnium gentium, lex naturæ pu‐ tanda est. Inst. 1.
units.tr: "And those things which are without letters": he means unwritten law, and now divides it into two parts: the law of nations and the custom of the ancestors. But this is only a provisional division, which he completes a little later. Ulpian defines the law of nations as the law which the peoples of mankind use. The books of the jurists teach that its scope is wider than Cicero here intends. For that we should obey parents and country, repay kindness to those who have deserved well, and repel force and injury, was placed earlier among the parts of nature. It remains, then, that we understand the remaining things which the same jurists enumerate. Such are the ceremonies and rites of religion received from the nations, likewise wars, slavery, manumissions, and almost all contracts, all of which they wish to be under the law of nations (Dig. 1; Inst. 1, On natural law, §. the law of nations). This is that natural law, proper to the human race, as we showed earlier. Moreover, in every matter the consensus of all nations is to be regarded as the law of nature (Inst. 1).

units.la: Scriptorum autem priuatum a‐ liud est, publicum aliud. Publicum, lex, senatuscôsul. fœdus: priuatum, tabulæ, pactum, conuentum, stipu‐ latio. Quæ autem scripta non sunt, ea aut consuetudine, aut conuentis hominum, & quasi consensu obti‐ ncntur, nentur. Atque etiam hoc in primis, ut nostros mores, legesq; tueamur, quodammodo naturali iure praescriptum est.
units.tr: Written law is one thing when private, another when public. Public: law, senatus consultum, treaty; private: tablets, pact, agreement, stipulation. Those things which are not written are upheld either by custom or by agreements of men and, as it were, by consent. Indeed, it is prescribed in the first place by natural law that we should defend our customs and laws.

units.la: Scriptorum autem.) Diuidit scriptu ius in priuatum et publicum. publicu definiunt, quod ad statum rei Romanæ spectat. Romanæ dixerunt illi, propter eius Reip summa maiestate. nos aut pro re Romana, Rep. dicemus, hoc modo: ius publicu est, quod ad statu Reip. spectat. Priuatu, quod ad singulorum utilitate. Publici iuris partes illi faciunt, sacra, sacerdotes, et magistratus: quae quidem non excludit Cicero (nam et sub lege subiicit diuinu quoq; ius) sed quas ipse partes ponit, hæ sunt magis propriæ: nimirum leges, senatusconsulta, fœdera. Plura tamen illi scripto iuri suo tribuunt, legem, plebiscitum, senatusconsultum, principum placita, magistratuum edicta, responsa prudentum. omittunt tamen fœdera, quæ haud dubie et publici iuris sunt, et scripti. Sed legum nomine, tum plebiscita, tum magistratuum edicta, tum principum placita comprehendit: responsa vero prudentum, cum de iure ciuili loquatur, nequaquam excludit. Nam et hæc omnia in definitione iuris, quæ enumeratione constat, in Topicis recensuit.
units.tr: Scriptorum autem: Here he divides written law into private and public. Public law they define as that which concerns the state of the Roman commonwealth. Those men said "Roman" because of the supreme majesty of that republic; we, for our part, shall say "of the commonwealth" instead of "Roman", in this way: public law is that which concerns the state of the commonwealth; private law is that which concerns the advantage of individuals. Those men make the parts of public law to be sacred things, priests, and magistrates. Cicero does not exclude these, for he also subjoins divine law below; but the parts which he himself sets down are more properly so: namely laws, senatus consulta, and treaties. Yet those men attribute more to their written law: statute, plebiscite, senatus consultum, decrees of the emperors, edicts of magistrates, and opinions of the learned. They nevertheless omit treaties, which are undoubtedly both of public law and written. But under the name of laws he includes plebiscites, magistrates' edicts, and imperial decrees; the opinions of the learned, since he speaks of civil law, he by no means excludes. For he also reckoned all these in his Topics, in the definition of law, which consists in enumeration.

units.la: Harum partium definitionem ex iure ciuili sumenda sunt: Instit.lib.1. de iure nat. §. Constat autem. Priuatum ius tripertito diuiduntur, in na-turale, gentium & ciuile. Cicero aliter has partes disponit, ut uidimus: ac priuati iuris partes facit, tabulas, pacta, conuenta, stipulationes. Tabulæ, literæ quæuis sunt, in quibus testimonia iuris nostri continentur: ut testamenta, codicilli, & priuatæ de rebus nostris tabulæ, quarum sunt multa & uaria genera. Pactum, siue pactio quid esset, itemq; stipulatio, alibi docuimus, ex ff. lib. 2. de pactis. Conuentum, conueniens in Topicis appellauit. Iurisperiti etiam conuentionem, ut Vlpianus eodem loco: Conuentionis uerbum generale est, inquit, ad omnia pertinens, de quibus negotij contrahendi tranfigendiq; caussa consentiunt, qui inter se agunt.
units.tr: The definitions of these parts are to be taken from civil law (Inst. 1, On natural law, §. Moreover). Private law is divided into three kinds: natural, of nations, and civil. Cicero arranges these parts differently, as we have seen: and he makes the parts of private law to be tablets, pacts, agreements, and stipulations. Tablets are any writings in which the testimonies of our law are contained, such as wills, codicils, and private records concerning our affairs, of which there are many and various kinds. What a pact or pacting is, and likewise a stipulation, we have taught elsewhere, from Dig. 2, On pacts. Agreement: Cicero called it "conveniens" in the Topics. The jurists also call it "conventio", as Ulpian says in the same place: "The word conventio is general, pertaining to all matters on which those who deal with one another agree, for the sake of contracting or settling a transaction."

units.la: Quæ autem scripta non sunt.) Inchoatam supra iuris non scripti partitionem ordine absoluit. tres enim partes facit, ut omnia coniungamus: quarum una gentiu iure, altera more & consuetudine maiorum, tertia couentis hominum, & re-centi consensu continetur. Quid ius gentium esset, quid couentum, dictum est: de consuetudine uero unu aut alterum locum afferà. Primo definitione ipsius Ciceronis de Inuent. li. 2. Consuetudinis autem ius esse putatur, id quod uoluntate omnium, sine lege uetustas comprobauit. huic consentanee Vl pianus, Diuturna consuetudo, inquit, pro iure & lege, in ijs quæ non ex scripto descendunt, obser uari solet. ff. de leg. l. 33.
units.tr: "But those things which are not written": he completes in order the division of unwritten law begun above. For he makes three parts, so that we may join them all together: one of these is contained in the law of nations, another in the manner and custom of the ancestors, and the third in agreements of men and recent consent. What the law of nations is, and what agreement is, has been said; of custom I shall cite one or another passage. First, the definition of custom by Cicero himself, in On Invention, book 2: "Custom is thought to be law, that which long antiquity has approved by the will of all, without a statute." Consistent with this, Ulpian: "Long-standing custom is usually observed as law and statute in matters which do not derive from writing" (Dig., On laws, l. 33).

units.la: Atq; etiā hoc in primis.) Additur hoc tanquā vinculū reliquorū, de legibus & morib. tuendis & conseruandis. Nam si leges & mores volutate introducta sunt, nō omnino natura, illud tamē penè in ipsa natura insitū est, ut nostros mores, legesq; tueri uelimus: qui locus cōmunis sæpe à Cicerone usurpatur. uelut pro Cluētio, cum ait: Indignum esse, in ea ciuitate, quæ legibus contineatur, discedi à legibus. deinde subijcit illam praclara similitudine: Vt corpora nostra sine mēte, sic ciuitas sine lege suis partib. & neruis ac sanguine et mēbris uti nō potest. legū ministri māgi stratus, legū interpretes, iudices, legū deniq; idcirco omnes serui sumus, ut liberi esse possimus.
units.tr: "And indeed this above all": This is added as the bond of the others, concerning the defence and preservation of laws and customs. For if laws and customs have been introduced by will, they are not altogether from nature; yet it is almost implanted in nature itself that we wish to defend our customs and laws. This commonplace is often used by Cicero, as in the speech for Cluentius, where he says: "It is unworthy, in a state which is held together by laws, to depart from the laws." Then he adds that striking comparison: "As our bodies cannot use their parts and sinews, blood and limbs without mind, so a state cannot without law." Magistrates are ministers of the laws, interpreters of the laws, judges; and so we are all, finally, slaves of the laws, that we may be free.

units.la: Et quoniam breuiter aperti sontes sunt quasi quidā æquitatis, meditatā nobis ad hoc caussarum genus esse debebūt ea, quæ dicēda erūt in orationib. de natura, de legibus, de more maiorum, de propulsanda iniuria, de ulciscenda, de omni parte iuris.
units.tr: And since the sources of equity have been briefly disclosed, the kinds of cases should be prepared for us, which must be spoken in orations: concerning nature, concerning laws, concerning the custom of the ancestors, concerning repelling injury, concerning avenging it, concerning every part of law.

units.la: Et quoniam.) Epilogus huius partitionis iuris: quo admonet, locos nudos, quos notauit, esse iuris & naturalis & ciuilis doctrina, atq; antiquitatis exemplis & moribus replendos & ornandos. Cuius scientia non ex Rhetorum libellis, sed ex iurisperitorum commentariis petenda est: cuius, etsi non summa ac perfecta, at aliqua tamen cognitione iuris & iniuriae, causse tractari non possunt. Fontes tamen omnis iuris in philosophorum commentariis & disputationibus de Moribus & legibus continentur. Quamobrem non modo oratori, verum etiam iurisconsulto suturo proderit, in illa philosophiae parte versatum esse, Platonis & Aristotelis de Moribus & Republ. nec non Ciceronis de Officijs & Legibus libros euoluisse, qui ad omnem iuris partem viam patefaciant. Sed exercitatio meditatioq; doctrinae accedat oportet, sine qua proferre nihil aut parum poterimus.
units.tr: "And since": This is the epilogue of this division of law, by which he warns that the bare topics he has noted are the teaching of natural and civil law, and are to be filled and adorned with examples of antiquity and with customs. Knowledge of these is not to be sought from the little books of the rhetoricians, but from the commentaries of the jurists; without some knowledge of law and of wrong, though not complete and perfect, causes cannot be handled. Yet all the sources of law are contained in the commentaries and disputations of the philosophers on morals and laws. Wherefore it will benefit not only the orator but also the future jurist to be versed in that part of philosophy, and to have read through the books of Plato and Aristotle on morals and the commonwealth, and also Cicero's books On Duties and On Laws, which open the way to every part of law. But practice and meditation on learning must be added, without which we shall be able to produce nothing, or little.

units.la: Si imprudéter aut necessitate, aut casu quippiā fecerit, quod nō cōcederetur ijs, qui sua spōte & uoluntate fecissent, ad eius facti de precatio nē ignoscēdi petēda uenia est, quæ sumetur ex plerisq; locis æquitatis.
units.tr: If through imprudence, or necessity, or chance, someone has done something which would not be granted to those who had done it of their own accord and will, pardon must be sought, to be asked for in the plea for forgiveness of that deed, which will be drawn from the commonplaces of equity.

units.la: Si imprudenter. ) Qualitas ea quæ iure nititur, quæ & iuridicialis appellatur, rursum bipertita tita est. nam & absoluta qualitas est, & assumppta, ut Rhetores uocant. Absoluta est, quæ ipsa in se, ut nihil foris assumatur, cōtinet iuris & iniuriæ quæstionē. Assumptiua, quæ ipsa ex se nihil firmi dat ad recusationem, facti ue defensionem: foris autem aliquid defensionis assumit. Ad absolutam pertinēt, quæ adhuc de iure tradidit. nunc paucis de assumptiua admonet. de qua plura supra in qualitatis partitione, cum de confirmatione ageretur, tradidit. Faciunt autem assumptiuæ partes quatuor, comparationem, relationem, siue translationem criminis, remotionē criminis, & concessionem. hanc postremam hic ponit Cicero, non verbo & nomine, sed re & partibus. Concessio dicitur, cum reus non id quod factum est defendit, sed ut ignoscatur postulat. hæc in duas diuidunt partes: in purgationem siue excusationem, & deprecationem. Purgatio est, cū factum conceditur, culpa uero aliqua de causa remouetur. Hæc partes habet tres, quas etiā hic Cicero numerat: Imprudentiam, siue infscitiam, casum siue fortunam, & necessitatem: hæc enim omnia excusationem habet facti aliquā honestā. Quod nō concederetur.) De altera cōcessionis parte loquitur, quæ deprecatio dicitur. Est enim deprecatio, cū et peccasse, & cōsultò peccasse se reus cōfitetur, & tamen ut ignoscatur postulat.
units.tr: "If through imprudence": This quality, which rests on law and which is also called juridical, is again twofold. For there is an absolute quality and an assumptive one, as the rhetoricians call it. The absolute is that which contains within itself, without anything being taken from outside, the question of right and wrong. The assumptive is that which of itself gives nothing firm for refutation or defence of the deed, but takes something of defence from outside. To the absolute belong those things which he has so far taught about law; now he briefly reminds us of the assumptive, of which he has taught more above, in the division of quality, when confirmation was treated. The assumptive parts are four: comparison, relation or transference of the charge, removal of the charge, and concession. Cicero sets down this last here, not by word and name, but in substance and parts. Concession is said to occur when the accused does not defend what was done, but asks to be pardoned. This is divided into two parts: purgation or excuse, and deprecation. Purgation is when the deed is conceded, but the fault is removed for some reason. It has three parts, which Cicero also enumerates here: imprudence or ignorance, chance or fortune, and necessity; for all these have some honourable excuse for the deed. "Which would not be granted": he speaks of the other part of concession, which is called deprecation. For deprecation is when the accused confesses both that he has sinned and that he sinned deliberately, and yet asks to be pardoned.

units.la: Sunt Ius Natura Diuinum, quod religione continetur. Humanū, æquitate Per se, quod dicitur Directum Verum Iustum Æquum Bonum. Ad aliud Gratia, in beneficio. Vltio, in iniuria. Lex Diuina Scripta Publica Priuata. Non scripta Humana Scripta Publica Lex Senatus cōsultū Fœdus. Priuata Tabulæ Pactū Cōuētū Stipula-tio. Non scripta Ius gentium Mos maiorum.
units.tr: Law is of several kinds: natural, divine (which is contained in religion), and human. Law may be proper to itself through equity, and this is called the right, the true, the just, the fair, and the good. Law may also be directed toward another: grace, in a benefit; vengeance, in an injury. Divine law is written or unwritten, and the written kind is public or private. Human law is written or unwritten. Written public law includes statute, decree of the Senate, and covenant (foedus). Written private law includes tablets, pact, agreement, and stipulation. Unwritten law includes the law of nations and the custom of our ancestors.
