units.la: Expositum est, ut potui breuissimè, de omni controuersiarum genere, nisi præterea tu quid requiris.
units.tr: I have set out, as briefly as I could, every kind of controversy, unless you require anything further.

units.la: Expositum est, ut potui. ) Dicit se, quàta breuitate potuerit, omnia summa capita statuum exposituisse: & est uerum. nam uix breuius tot res, tã dissipatæ, tot partes implicatæ, explicari potuerūt. Callidè aūt cæteros qualitatis status cõtrouersiasq; dissimulat, ut filij exploret ingenium.
units.tr: I have set out, as far as I was able. He says that he has set out, with as much brevity as he could manage, all the main headings of the issues. And this is true, for such a number of matters, so scattered and so intricately linked, could scarcely have been explained more briefly. But he cleverly passes over the other categories of status and controversies, so that his son may test his ability.

units.la: DE SCRIPTO ET SEN- tentia.
units.tr: On Writing and Meaning

units.la: C.F. Illud equidem, quod iam unum restare uideo, quale sit: cum disceptatio uersatur in scriptis. C. P. Recte intelligis. eo enim expositio, munus promisi omne confecero. Sunt igitur ambigui duobus aduersarijs præcepta communia. Vterq; enim hanc significationem, qua utetur ipse, dignam scriptoris prudentia esse defendet. Vterque id, quod aduersarius ex ambigue scripto intelligendum esse dicet, aut absurdū, aut inutile, aut iniquum, aut turpe esse defendet, aut etiam discrepare cum cæteris scriptis, uel aliorum, uel maximè si poterit, eiusdē, quamcp defendet ipse, eam rem & sententiam quemuis prudentem & iustum hominem, si integrum daretur, scripturum fuisse, sed planius: eamcp sententiam, quam significari posse dicet, nihil habere aut captionis, aut uitij. Contrariam autem si probarit, fore ut multa uitia, stulta, iniqua, contraria consequantur.
units.tr: C.F. Indeed, I see that one thing still remains: what kind it is, namely when the dispute turns on writings. C.P. You understand rightly. For with that explanation I have fulfilled the whole task I promised. There are therefore precepts common to both opponents in the case of ambiguity. Each will defend that meaning which he himself uses as worthy of the writer's prudence. Each will defend that the meaning which his opponent says should be drawn from the ambiguous writing is absurd, useless, unjust, or shameful, or else that it conflicts with the other writings, whether of others or, most of all if he can, of the same author. And he will defend that any prudent and just man, if he had been left free, would have written the very thing he himself defends, but more plainly. And he will argue that the meaning he says can be signified has no capacity for deception or fault. If, on the other hand, he proves the contrary, many foolish, unjust, and contrary consequences will follow.

units.la: Illud quidem.) Memorem adolescentem uides: qui unum controuersiarum genus reflare probe sciat: quale sit, cum in scripto versatur disceptatio. Huius igitur tractationem & locos requirit.
units.tr: Indeed, that one. You see a mindful young man, who knows well that one kind of controversy remains: what it is, when the dispute turns on a writing. He therefore asks for its treatment and its topics.

units.la: Recte intelligis.) Laudat filij diligentiam, qui uideat, eo posito, munus Partitionum esse confectum.
units.tr: You understand rightly. He praises the diligence of his son, who sees that, with this point settled, the task of the Partitions is complete.

units.la: Munus promisi.) Initio enim, id filio poscenti uidimus promissum: uidelicet, se de omni doctrina dicendi præcepta ordine traditurum.
units.tr: The task I promised. For at the beginning we saw this promised to the son when he asked for it: namely, that he would hand down the precepts of all the teaching of speaking in order.

units.la: Sunt igitur ambigui.)Tria, ut ante uidimus, in scripto controuersiarum genera facit: unum ambigui, secundum scripti & uoluntatis, tertium contrariarum legum. His trib. ordine explicatis, perorabit.
units.tr: There are therefore ambiguities. As we saw before, he makes three kinds of controversy in writing: one of ambiguity, the second of writing and intention, and the third of contrary laws. When these three have been explained in order, he will conclude.

units.la: E
units.tr: E

units.la: In hoc genere ambigui communia sunt duo aduſ[?]arijs, petitori ſcilicet, ac recuſatori, præcepta, communesq; loci. Vterq; enim suam scripti significationem laudat: utrq; alterius ex isdem locis uituperat. Quinàm uero uel commendationis, uel uituperatiõis sint loci, tum ex hac Ciceronis notatione, tum ex aliis Rhetoricis libris clarius est, quàm ut cuiusquàm egeat explicatione. Sed magno tamè usu ac doctrina opus est, ad ambigua intelligenda, quæ doctrina ferè à Dialecticis traditur. Ambiguū hic capitur, cum quod scriptum est, in varias significationes trahi potest. Huius cõtroversiæ hoc exemplū dat Cicero. Paterfamilias, cum filiũ hæredē faceret uasorum argentearum centū pondo, uxori suæ sic legauit: Hæres meus, uxori mæ uasorum argentearum pondo centū, quæ uolet, dato. Post mortē eius uasa magnifica & preciosè scelata, petit à filio mater: ille se, quæ ipse uolet, debere dicit. quæritur, de quo testator intellexerit uerba illa, Quæ uolet. Nam tā ad matrē, quàm ad filiũ, referri posse uidentur. Iuris tamē cõsulti matri adiudicant. huiusmodi sunt multa in Pãdectis, de Auro & argẽto legato: uelut l.8. & 9. lib.34. De ambiguis hac lege ponit Celsus, tit. de leg. l.19. In ambigua uoce legis, ea potius accipiēda est significatio, quæ uitio caret: præsertim cũ etiā uoluntas legis ex hoc colligi possit.
units.tr: In this kind of ambiguity there are two sets of precepts and common topics for the two opponents, that is, for the claimant and the objector. For each praises the meaning of the writing, and each criticises the other's meaning from the same topics. What the topics of commendation or criticism are, is clearer from this note of Cicero and from other rhetorical books than that anyone needs explanation. But much practice and learning are needed to understand ambiguities, and this learning is largely handed down by the dialecticians. Here 'ambiguous' is taken to mean that what is written can be drawn into various meanings. Cicero gives this example of such a controversy. A father of a family, making his son heir, left his wife, by this wording, a hundred pounds' weight of silver vessels: "Let my heir give to my wife a hundred pounds' weight of silver vessels, whichever she wishes." After his death the mother asks her son for the vessels, magnificent and finely chased. He says that he must give whichever he himself wishes. The question is what the testator meant by those words, "whichever she wishes." For they seem able to be referred both to the mother and to the son. However, the jurists adjudge them to the mother. There are many such cases in the Pandects, on silver and gold bequeathed, as in laws 8 and 9 of book 34. Celsus lays down this rule about ambiguities in the title on legacies, law 19: in an ambiguous word of a law, that meaning is rather to be accepted which is free of fault, especially since the intention of the law can also be gathered from this.

units.la: Cum autē aliud scriptor sensisse uidetur, & aliud scripsisse, qui scrí‐pto nitetur, eum re exposita, recita‐ tione uti oportebit: deinde instare aduersario, iterare, renouare, inter‐ rogare, num aut scriptū neget, aut contra factum inficietur. Post iudi‐ cem ad uím scripti uocet: hac cōfir‐ matione usus, amplificet rem lege laudanda, audaciāq; confutet eius: qui cum palàm contra fecerit, idq; fateatur, adsit tamen, factumq; de‐ fendat. Deinde infirmet defensio‐ nem, cum aduersarius aliud uoluis‐ se, aliud sensisse scriptorē, aliud scrí‐ psisse dicat, nō esse ferendū, à quo‐ quam potius latoris sensum, quàm à lege explicari. cur ita scripserit, si ita non senserit? Cur cum ea, quæ plane scripta sint, neglexerit, quæ nunquã scripta sint proferat? Cur prudentissimos in scribendo uiros summæ stultitię putet esse damnan‐ dos? Quid impedierit scriptorem, quo minus excíperet illud, quod
units.tr: When the writer seems to have meant one thing and to have written another, the one who relies on the writing will need to set out the matter and use recitation. Then he should press his opponent, repeating, renewing, and questioning whether he either denies what was written or, on the contrary, denies the deed. After that he should call the judge to the force of the writing. Using this confirmation, he should amplify the matter with the law to be praised, and refute the audacity of the one who, having openly acted against it and admitted it, nevertheless appears and defends the deed. Then he should weaken the defence, when the opponent says that the writer wished one thing, meant another, and wrote something else. It must not be tolerated that the meaning of the author should be explained by anyone rather than by the law itself. Why would he have written so, if he had not meant so? Why would he have neglected what was plainly written and bring forward what was never written? Why would one think that the most prudent men in writing should be condemned for the greatest folly? What would have prevented the writer from including that which

units.la: aduersarius, tanq́ si exceptum es- set, ita dicit se secutū. Vtetur exemplis iis, quibus idem scriptor: aut si id non poterit, quibus alij, quod excipiendum putarint, exceperint. Quæreda etiam ratio est, si qua poterit inueniri, quare nō sit exceptū: aut iniqua lex, aut inutilis futura dicetur, aut alia caussa obtemperādi, alia abrogandi: dissentire aduersarij uocem, atq̈ legis. Deinde amplíficandi caussa, de conseruandis legi bus, de periculo rerumpublicarum atq̈ priuatarū, cùm aliis locis, tum in perorādo maxime, grauiter erit, uehementerq̈ dicendum.
units.tr: The opponent, as if the point had been excepted, says that he followed it. He will use the examples that the same writer used, or, if he cannot, those by which others who thought it should be excepted have excepted it. We should also seek, if any reason can be found, why it was not excepted: either the law will be called unjust or useless, or there is one reason for obeying it and another for abrogating it, and the opponent's voice differs from that of the law. Then, for amplification, about preserving the laws and about the danger to commonwealths and private interests, we must speak weightily and forcefully, both in other places and especially in the peroration.

units.la: Cum autem aliud scriptor sensisse uidetur.) Scripti et sententiæ cōtroucrsia pluribus explicatur, propterea quod difficiliorem habeat doctrinam, usumq; maiorem. incidit enim sæpissimè in legibus explicandis, in testamentis, in in- terdictis, in religionis controuersijs, ac deniq; in omnium autorum explicatione. Primum igitur Cicero cum instituit, qui scriptū defendat: post etiam, qui sententiā. Hæc autè scriptū tuentis in- stitu-
units.tr: When, however, the writer seems to have meant something else.) The controversy between the writing and the intention is explained by many, because it has a more difficult doctrine and greater practical use. It arises very often in explaining laws, wills, interdicts, disputes about religion, and finally in the explanation of all authors. Cicero therefore first sets out the instruction for one who defends the written text, and afterwards for one who defends the intention. The instruction for one defending the written text is

units.la: ritu. stitutio bipartita est. prior pars octo cõtinet capita, siue locos, quibus scriptū confirmatur: altera, septem ad infirmandā aduersarij defensionē. cū pugnandū est, nõ modo nos idoneis armis instructos esse oportet, sed etiā aduersariorū nofse & artes et arma debemus: ut quomodo illis resistendū sit, intelligamus. Loci pro scripto sint, expositio, scripti recitatio, percunctatio, iteratio, renouatio, interrogatio, demõstratio, amplificatio. Expositio est, totius cõtroversiæ propositio, et designatio, hoc modo: M. Coponius testamentum fecit, atq; ita scriptū reliquit: Si mihi filius gignitur, isq; priusquā in tutelā suā uenerit moritur, tū mihi M. Curius sit hæres. Coponius moritur sine liberis: posthumus ei nullus nascitur: Curius hæreditatē adit: agnati Coponij iure experiuntur. Scæuola pro agnatis caussam agit, atq; ex scripto negat, nisi posthumus & natus, & antequā in suā tutelā ueniesset, mortuus esset, hæredem Curiū esse non posse, qui esset secundū posthumū & natū & mortuū hæres institutus. Crassus aut defendit: hac Coponiū mente fuisse, ut si filius nõ esset, qui in tutelā uenïsset, M. Curius esset hæres. Nõ desistit uterq; in ea caussa in autoritatibus, in exēplis, in testamentorū formulis, hoc est in medio iure ciuili uersari. Scæuola i- gitur in hūc modū agere cœpit, ac primùm testamenti měti uerba recitare: Verba tibi recitari uis Craffe, recitata sunt: audiuisti haud dubiè: Si mihi filius gignitur, is que prius moritur, &c. tum ut mihi M. Curius sit hæres. Deinde instare pergit, & percütari: an' nō hæc sunt testamenti uerba? non' ne hæc Coponij uoluntas? an non perspicua sunt? quid quæris, quid melius? Clarius nihil esse potest. Tu iterare recitationem: Si mihi filius gignitur, audis'ne? oportere filiu gigni? Isq; anteq; in tutelā uenerit. ergo natu fuisse oportuit. quid deinde? Mortuus sit. uixerit igitur oportet. Hæc te intelligere puto. Tum renouare percunctationem, & rursus instare aduersario: Recitata tibi uerba sunt Coponij, & sic scriptum esse non ne- gas: quid igitur petis? num tibi uidetur latina, clara, & sine ulla ambiguitate perscripta? quid horum negare potes? Tum interrogare quaedam cum diuisione, sine complexione: Nū ea esse forte uerba negas? at recitata tibi sunt, & hic coram omnibus pronunciata. num te M. Curi contra testamentū fecisse, qui hæreditatē adieris? at constat, idq; ipse fateris? Tum uim scripti argumentis demonstrare, & iudicem ad id sequendū uocare: Quid per Deum immortalem aliud est, C. Aquili, Si mihi filius gignitur, isq; ante pubertatem moritur, quid si mihi nullus sit filius qui in tutelā ueniat, Curius ne sit hæres? Hæc est te- statotestatoris cōditio, et exceptio, ut nisi posthumus & natus, & ante tutelæ tempus mortuus sit, ne sit hæres Curius. Hanc tibi legem præscripsit, C. Aquili, qui testamentum fecit, quam in iudicando sequi debeas: hanc verborum vim atq; sententiā, à qua te recedere tua fides, integritas, sapientiā prohibet. Tum amplificare à scripti, vel scriptoris collaudatione, & ab aduersariorum audaciæ reprehensione: De Testamento agitur, C. Aquili, quo in priuatis ciuiū actis nihil firmius esse maiores nostri voluerunt: agitur de postrema Coponij voluntate, quam ipse claris, nō obscuris: latinis, non barbaris: proprijs, non alienis verbis consignavit: ita ut nil præterea sit requirendū. Quod cum ita sit, licet audaciā mirari aduersariorum, qui cum contra id quod testamento secerint, & faciant, tamē ausint etiamnū coram te, C. Aquili, publici & priuati iuris seuerissimo tutore stare, factiq; defensionem quærere: quæ res non facto solum nocet, sed etiam exemplo. Hæc à Scævola pro scripto dicta sint. Sequuntur loci illi septem, qui ad rationes aduersarij diluendas ualent: quorum primus est, aduersarij sententiæ contemptio, & interpretationis irrisio. Aliud, inquit, voluit testator, aliud scripsit. hoc tu attendis & audis silentio, C. Aquili, sicut debes pro tua patientia. Sed tamen quid ineptius hoc
units.tr: two-part. The first part contains eight heads, or topics, by which the written text is confirmed; the second, seven, for weakening the defence of the opponent. When we must fight, we ought to be equipped not only with suitable arms but also to know the arts and weapons of our adversaries, so that we understand how to resist them. The topics for the written text are: exposition, recitation of the text, questioning, repetition, renewal, interrogation, demonstration, and amplification. Exposition is the statement and outline of the whole controversy, in this way: Marcus Coponius made a will and left it written thus: "If a son is born to me, and he dies before he comes into his guardianship, then let Marcus Curius be my heir." Coponius dies without children; no posthumous child is born to him; Curius takes up the inheritance; the agnates of Coponius bring the action under the law. Scaevola pleads for the agnates and, from the text, denies that Curius can be heir unless the posthumous child was both born and died before entering his own guardianship, since Curius was instituted heir as second to the posthumous child who was born and died. Crassus, on the other hand, defends that Coponius's intention was that, if no son came into guardianship, Marcus Curius should be heir. Neither of them stops in this case from dwelling on authorities, examples, and forms of wills, that is, from working within the middle of civil law. Scaevola therefore began to proceed in this way, and first to recite the words of the will: "Do you want the words recited to you, Crassus? They have been recited; you have heard them, beyond doubt: 'If a son is born to me, and he dies before...' then 'let Marcus Curius be my heir.'" Then he goes on to press and to question: "Are these not the words of the will? Is this not Coponius's wish? Are they not plain? What more do you seek, what better? Nothing can be clearer. You repeat the recitation: 'If a son is born to me'—do you hear? That a son must be born. And he, before he comes into guardianship—therefore he had to be born. What next? 'Dies.' So he must have lived. I think you understand this." Then he renews the questioning and presses his opponent again: "The words of Coponius have been recited to you, and you do not deny that they are written thus; what then do you ask? Does it not seem to you that they are written in Latin, clearly, and without any ambiguity? Can you deny any of this?" Then he questions certain points, one by one, without linking them: "Do you perhaps deny that these are the words? But they have been recited to you, and pronounced here before everyone. Did you, Marcus Curius, not act against the will, when you took up the inheritance? But that is agreed, and you yourself admit it?" Then he sets out the force of the text by arguments and calls the judge to follow it: "What, by immortal God, is this other than: 'If a son is born to me, and he dies before puberty'—what if I have no son who comes into guardianship: is Curius to be heir? This is the condition and exception of the testator, that unless the posthumous child is both born and dies before the time of guardianship, Curius is not to be heir. Gaius Aquilius, this is the law that he who made the will has prescribed to you, which you ought to follow in judging: this is the force and meaning of the words, from which your good faith, integrity, and wisdom forbid you to depart." Then he amplifies, from the praise of the text or of its writer, and from the rebuke of the boldness of the opponents: "This is a matter of a will, Gaius Aquilius, in which our ancestors wished nothing to be firmer among the acts of private citizens. It concerns the last wish of Coponius, which he himself set down in clear, not obscure words, in Latin, not barbarous, in his own words, not borrowed ones, so that nothing further need be sought. Since this is so, we may wonder at the boldness of the opponents, who, although they have acted and still act against what the will has set down, nevertheless dare to stand before you, Gaius Aquilius, the most severe guardian of public and private law, and to seek a defence for their deed; a thing that harms not only by the deed but also by the example. These are the things said by Scaevola for the written text. Next come those seven topics which serve to refute the opponent's arguments, the first of which is contempt for the opponent's opinion and ridicule of his interpretation. 'The testator wished one thing,' he says, 'and wrote another.' You hear this, Gaius Aquilius, in silence, as you ought, in keeping with your patience. But yet, what could be more absurd than this

units.la: {*} à Scævola: marginal mark at left. hoc dici, aut fingi potest, quàm homines de his rebus, quas maximè intelligi uelint, aliud sentire, & aliud loqui uel scribere? nemo iam testamenta, nemo stipulationes, nemo leges ullas intelliget ut scriptæ sunt: sed ex eorū ingenio qui cōtrà secerint, iudicet, possessiones sq; det. Secundus à sententia & loco communi: Voluntatē & sententiā scriptoris queris? eam tibi ille patefacit: à nullo enim melius, quàm ab ipsius scripti uerbis explicari potest. Ea est mens, ea sententia & uoluntas, quæ literis ipsius & scripto continetur, quam suæ uoluntatis quasi imaginem esse voluit. Tertius locus, rationis altera percunctatio, siue ut Rhetores uocant, quæstio. Hanc quadripartitò diuidit Cicero: quarum duo priora exempla ad finem pertinēt, reliqua duo ad caussam efficientem. Age quæso, cur ita scripsit, si ita non sensit? cur si ita sensit, aliter scripsit? cur prudentissimos in scribendo uiros summæ stultitiæ putas esse dānandos? Quid obsecrò scriptorem impedierit, quo minus exciperet illud, quod uos, tanquam si exceptum esset, ita dicitis uos esse secutos? Quartus locus, ab exemplis, uel eiusdem scriptoris, uel aliorum, qui quod excipiendum putarent, disertè exceperint: ut nihil sit opus aliquid hominum scriptis, quòd ipsi non exceperint, affingere. Consucesse eos qui aut leges, ges, aut testamenta scribant, exceptionibus uti. cui addi potest ille similis locus: Ab exemplis earum rerum, quæ cum aduersarijs sententia redderetur, & uoluntas afferretur, à scripto potius iudicatæ sunt. Quintus locus, à caussa, quamobrem non sit exceptum. Queris, quare Coponius non exceperit: Sin mihi nullus sit posthumus, tum ut mihi ille, uel illi hæredes sint? Quia uidebat homo politus, ineptum esse, si pluribus perscripsisset, quod paucis breuiter & absolutè poterat. Deinde uir prudens intelligebat, nullo posthumo nato, iure ad agnatos hæreditatem uenire. Quòd si natus esset, & ante tutelæ tempus decessisset, grati hominis & memoris esse existimauit, ad eum hæreditatē uenire, qui pro patre filij tutor & curator extitisset. Sextus locus, à collatione scripti & sententiæ, quæ aduersarij uoce, & testamenti, dissentire ostendimus. Attende quæso C. Aquili, dum scriptum cum horum sententia contendo. Testamentū dicit: Si mihi filius gignitur, & moritur. isti, Si mihi nullus filius sit. Scripti nostri uox est, ut tum sit Curius secundus hæres: isti, primum esse uolunt. Tuæ igitur sapientiæ est Aquili, uidere, utrum tibi sequendum sit: id ne quod diligenter perscriptū sit: an id quod contrà scriptum acute sit, ne dicam audaciter & ineptè, excogitatum. Septimus locus, amplificationem continet, quæ constat duobus communibus locis: quorum alter est, de conseruandis legibus & scriptorum auctoritate, de periculo rerumpublicarum atque prouatarum, si semel à scripto recedatur. cuius exempla sunt in oratione pro Cluentio illustria. Locus uero amplificationis est, cum in tota confirmatione, tum in peroratione, maxime quod in ea fit proprius amplificationis locus, ut alibi quoque dictum est. & hæc à scripto dicta sint.
units.tr: *From Scaevola (marginal mark at left). What can be said or invented more absurd than that men, about the very things they most want understood, think one thing and say or write another? No one will now understand wills, stipulations, or any laws as they are written. Instead, let the judge decide the possessions and so on from the character of those who acted against them. Second, from the meaning and a commonplace: Do you seek the will and meaning of the writer? He reveals it to you, for it can be explained by nothing better than the very words of the writing. That is the mind, the meaning, and the will that is contained in his letters and writing, which he wished to be, as it were, an image of his will. Third is the place of the other question of reason, which the rhetoricians call the question. Cicero divides this into four parts: the first two examples concern the end, the other two the efficient cause. Come now, I ask: why did he write thus if he did not think thus? Why, if he thought thus, did he write otherwise? Why do you think the most prudent men in writing should be condemned for the greatest folly? What, I ask, would have prevented the writer from making that exception which you, as if it had been made, say you have followed? Fourth is the place from examples, either of the same writer or of others, who explicitly made whatever exception they thought should be made. So there is no need to attach to men's writings something they did not themselves except. It is customary for those who draw up laws or wills to use exceptions. To this can be added that similar place: from examples of those things which, when the opposing opinion was set forth and the will brought forward, were judged rather from the writing. Fifth is the place from the cause why it was not excepted. You ask why Coponius did not make an exception: "But if I have no posthumous child, then let it be either him or his heirs who are mine?" Because the refined man saw it would be foolish to write at length what he could say briefly and absolutely. Next, the prudent man understood that, if no posthumous child was born, the inheritance passes by law to the agnates. But if the child was born and died before the time of guardianship, he judged it the mark of a grateful and mindful man that the inheritance should come to him who had stood as tutor and curator for the son in place of the father. Sixth is the place from the comparison of the writing and the meaning, which we have shown to differ by the words of the opponent and of the will. Please attend, Aquilius, while I set the writing against their meaning. The will says: "If a son is born to me and dies"; they say: "If I have no son." The voice of our writing is that then Curius the second is heir; they want the first to be. It is therefore for your wisdom, Aquilius, to see which you ought to follow: that which was written out carefully, or that which was cleverly, I will not say boldly and foolishly, devised against what is written. The seventh place contains amplification, which rests on two commonplaces: one concerns the preservation of laws and the authority of writings, and the danger to commonwealths and private fortunes if one ever departs from the writing; its examples are famous in the speech for Cluentius. The place of amplification, however, lies both in the whole confirmation and especially in the peroration, where the proper place of amplification is found, as was said elsewhere. And let this be said about the writing.

units.la: Ille autem qui se sententia legis, uoluntatemque defendet, in consilio, atque in mente scriptoris, non in uerbis ac litteris uim legis positam esse defendet: quodque nihil exceperit in lege, laudabit, ne diuerticula peccatis darentur, atque ut ex facto cuiusque iudex legis mentem interpretaretur.
units.tr: But he who defends the force of the law in its meaning and will, and who holds that the power of the law lies in the intention and mind of the writer, not in the words and letters, will praise the fact that nothing was excepted in the law, so that no loopholes are given to wrongdoers, and so that the judge may interpret the mind of the law from the deed of each person.

units.la: Deinde erit utendum exemplis, in quibus omnis æquitas perturbetur, si uerbis legum ac non sententiis pareatur. Deinde genus eiusmodi calliditatis & calumniæ retrahatur in odium iudicis, cum quadam inuidiosa querela, & si incidet impudentiæ caufla, quæ non ad delictū, sed ad casum, necessitatémue pertinéat, quod genus paulo ante attígímus, erit ĩsdem ęquitatis sententijs contra acerbitatem uerborum deprecandum.
units.tr: Then examples must be used in which all equity would be overturned if one obeyed the words of the laws rather than their meanings. Next, this kind of cunning and calumny should be brought into hatred of the judge with a certain invidious complaint. And if the charge of impudence arises, which pertains not to a fault but to chance or necessity, the kind we touched on a little earlier, it must be deprecated with the same sentiments of equity against the harshness of the words.

units.la: Ille autem qui se sententia legis, uoluntatęq; defendit.) Iam partes eius qui contra scriptum à sententia stabit, sequuntur. Huius quæstionis tractatio quinq; locis nititur, sententia communi, caussis, exemplis, querela, & deprecatione. His locis cū uteretur Crassus aduersus Q. Mutium Scæuolã, eam obtinuit, ut pro Cecinna testatur Cicero. Primum enim, omni dicendi copia illum communem locum exornauit: in cõsilio atq; in mente scriptoris, & utilitate cõmuni, non in uerbis ac literis uim legis aut alterius monumēti positū esse. Tu me ad uerbū uocas? Nego oportere, nego obtineri posse: nego ullā rē esse, quæ aut cõprehendi satis, aut caueri, aut excipi possit, si aut præteriṫo aliquo uerbo, aut ambigue posito, sententia & re cognita non id intelligatur, sed id quod dicitur ualebit. Quæ lex, quod Senatuscõsultum, quod magistratus edictum, quod fœdus aut pastio, quod (ut ad priuatas res redeam) testamentū, quæ iudicia, aut stipulationes, aut paSti & conuenti formula non infirmari, aut conuelli potest, si ad uerba rem deflectere uelimus? consilium autè eorum qui scripserunt, & ratione & autoritatem relinquamus. Sermo hercule & familiaris & quotidianus non cohærebit, si uerba inter nos aucupabimur. Deniq; imperiū domesticū nullū erit, si seruulis hoc nostris cōcesserimus, ut ad uerba nobis obediāt: nō ad id quod ex uerbis intelligi possit obtemperent. Quæ res igitur valet? uoluntas & sententia regnare debet in iudicijs, atque in omni imperio ac sermone: quæ si tacitis nobis intelligi posset, uerbis omnino nō uteremur. Quia nō potest, uerba reperta sunt, non quæ impedirent, sed quæ indicaret uoluntate. Deinde quod nihil excepisset Coponius in testamento, quo Curium hæredem esse voluit, caussas attulit Crassus, scriptoreq; laudauit. Sed quid opus fuit pluribus rem apertissimā, & uel pueris notam, inuoluere? Quid enim apertius, quàm à Coponio eū hærede esse institutū, nullo nato filio: qui filio nato, atque intra pubertatis annos, uel eodē die quo editus esset, mortuo, succedere debuit. Quid enim refert, quo paćto nullus supersit filius, siue quòd natus non fit, siue quod mortuus: neq; enim vir prudentissimus, ut nostris, existimauit se, qui testamētum recitaret, quòd quiuis facere posset, habiturū, sed qui metem assequi, & uoluntatē interpretari poßent. Nam cum intelligeret, quales uiri de huiusmodi controuersijs iudicarent: idcirco quæ perspicua uidentur esse, non adscripsit, quod uos nō scripti sui recitatores, sed consilij & uoluntatis interpretes sore putaret. Quanquā C. Aquili, neminē unquā sore tam stultum cogitauit, qui in re tam perspicua hæreret, atq; in luce tenebras, & nodum in scirpo (ut dicitur) quæreret. Post exemplis, autoritatibus & testamentorū formulis sententiā suam confirmauit. Exemplis nunc uti, uidelicet, nihi necesse est harū rerum omnū: Nō occurrit unicuiq; uestrum aliud alij in omni genere exemplū, quod testimonio fit, non ex uerbis totū pendere ius, sed uerba seruire hominū consilijs, & autoritatibus? Lex usum & autoritatē fundi iubet esse biennū. At utimur eodem iure in ædibus, quæ in lege nō appellātur. Actio est in actore præsentē his uerbis: Quādoquidem te in iure conspicio, hac actione Appius ille cæcus uti non posset: si tam uerē homines uerba consectarētur, quàm rem, cuius caussa uerba sunt, nō considerarēt. Testamēto, si excitatus hæres esset pupillus Cornelius, isq; iam annos uiginti haberet: uobis interpretibus amitteret hæreditatem? Veniunt in mentem mihi permulta, uobis plura recuperatores certò scio. Verū ne nimiū multa cōpleƈtar,uestra diligētia prohibeor. Deinde genus eiusmodi calliditatis & calūniæ retraxit in odiū iudicis, cum quadā inuidiosa querela. Illud autē in tota oratione tua, Q. Muti, mihi maximē mirū uidebatur, te tantū & talem iurisperitum, qui nobis iura descripseris, dicere, nullius hominis autoritate à scripto recedi oportere. Quod ego tamen si nō nunc primum, neq; in hac causa solū audeo, tamē admodū mirabar abste quēadmodū diceretur. Nam cæteri tum ad istam hortationē decurrunt, cū se in causa putant habere æquum & boni, quod defendant: si contrà uerbis & literis, &c, ut dici solet, summo iure, quod sæpe summa iniuria est, cōtenditur, solent eiusmodi iniquitati & boni & æqui nomen dignitatemq; opponere. Tū illud, quod dicitur, sic uenire irridet: tū aucupia uerborū & literarū tendiculas, in inuidiā uocant: tū uociferātur, ex æquo & bono, nō ex callido uersutoq; iure rem iudicare oportere: scriptū sequi, calumniatoris esse: boniq; iudicis, uoluntatē scriptoris autoritatēq; defendere. In ista uerò caussa cum tu fis, qui tā diligenter & tā callidè uerbis cōtrouersias, nō æquitate defendas, & iura non utilitate cōmuni, sed literis exprimas, qui potes dicere, autoritati obtemperare non oportere? Et simul C. Aquili indignitatē iniquitatēq; hominū ui-de, de, qui tenuibus litteris, & obscuris notis, leges, foedera, pacta, edicta, testamenta, iura omnia divina & humana, imperia, communesq; omnium sententias & sermone obtemperare uellent, atq; ex ijs de uita & necce, de fortunis omnium mortalium, iudicia fieri. Deprecatio non in ciuili causa, sed in ijs quae contra leges facta uidetur, locum habet. Quod si acciderit assumptiuae qualitatis locis, ac praesertim concessionis partibus, de quibus supra dictum est, utetur qui uolet. Possumus tamen contra scripta niti, si dixerimus, quod ex scripto ex uerbis aliquis uelit, non posse fieri, non lege, non more, non natura, non bono & aequo: quae omnia uoluisse scriptorem, nemo dubitet. Ad sententiae defensionem sunt iurisconsultorum aliquot dicta praeclara, tit. de leg. uelut illud Celsi l. 17. Scire leges non est uerba earum tenere, sed uim & potestatem. Item eiusdem l. 18. Benignius leges interpretandae sunt, quo uoluntas earum conferatur. Item Pauli l. 23. Minime sunt mutanda, quae semper interpretatione certam habuerant. Item Modestini l. 25. Nulla iuris ratio aut aequitatis benignitas patitur, ut quae salubriter, pro utilitate hominum introducuntur, ea nos duriore interpretatione contra eorum commodum producamus ad seueritatem. Item Paulus l. 29. Contra legem facit, qui id facit quod lex prohibet: in fraudem uero legis,qui sententiâ eius circumuenit. Item Vlpianus l. 30. Fraus enim legi fit, ubi id fit quod fieri noluit,fieri autem non uetuit:& quod dicitur ῥητὸν ἀπὸ διανοίας, hoc dicitur fraus ab eo quod contra legem fit.Atque hæc de scripto & sententia.
units.tr: He who defends himself by the meaning and will of the law. Now follows the part of the speaker who stands on the intention against the written text. The treatment of this question rests on five topics: common agreement, causes, examples, complaint, and deprecation. When Crassus used these topics against Q. Mucius Scaevola, he won the case, as Cicero testifies in the speech for Caecina. First, he adorned the common topic with every resource of eloquence: that the force of a law or of any other document lies not in the words and letters but in the purpose of the writer and the common good. "Do you call me back to the word?" I deny that it ought to be done, and I deny that it can be upheld. I deny that there is anything that can be sufficiently comprehended, guarded against, or excepted if, through some omitted word or an ambiguously placed one, the meaning and the matter known are not understood, and what is said prevails instead. What law, what decree of the Senate, what edict of a magistrate, what covenant or pact, or (to return to private affairs) what will, what judgments, what stipulations, or what formula of a bargain and agreement could not be weakened or overturned if we chose to bend the matter to the words? Let us rather leave the purpose of those who wrote, both its reason and its authority. Truly, ordinary and everyday conversation would not hold together if we hunted for words in each other's speech. Finally, there would be no authority in the household if we allowed our servants this, that they obey us in words, not that they comply with what can be understood from the words. What then is valid? Will and intention ought to reign in courts and in every command and conversation; if these could be understood without our speaking, we would not use words at all. Because they cannot, words were discovered, not to hinder but to indicate the will. Next, because Coponius had excepted nothing in his will, by which he wished Curius to be heir, Crassus brought forward reasons and praised the writer. But why was there any need to wrap a very plain matter, known even to boys, in more words? For what is plainer than that Coponius named him heir with no son born, and that if a son were born and died within the years of puberty, even on the day he was brought forth, the heir should succeed? For what does it matter by what means no son survives, whether because he was not born or because he died? That most prudent man, unlike ours, did not think that he who recited the will would have what anyone could do, but that those who could grasp the mind and interpret the will would. Since he understood what sort of men judge such controversies, he therefore did not add what seem plain, because he thought you would be not mere reciters of his writing but interpreters of its counsel and will. Yet Gaius Aquilius never thought anyone would be so foolish as to stick at a matter so clear, and seek darkness in the light and a knot in a bulrush, as the saying goes. Afterwards he confirmed his opinion with examples, authorities and forms of wills. Is there now any need, of course, to use examples of all these things? Does not each of you find, from testimony in every kind of case, that the law depends wholly not on words, but that words serve the counsels and authority of men? The law orders that the use and possession of land be for two years. Yet we apply the same right to buildings, which the law does not name. An action is brought against a plaintiff present, with these words: "Since I see you in court," by which action that blind Appius could not proceed. If men pursued words as closely as they considered the matter for whose sake the words exist, would you, as interpreters, lose the inheritance if the pupil Cornelius, named heir in a will, were now twenty years old? Many things come to my mind, and you recuperators surely know many more; but lest I embrace too much, I am restrained by your diligence. Next, he drew this kind of cunning and calumny back into hatred of the judge, with a certain invidious complaint. But in your whole speech, Q. Mucius, what seemed most astonishing to me was that you, so great and so learned a jurist, who have set out the laws for us, say that one should not depart from the written text on anyone's authority. Yet although I do not now dare this for the first time, nor only in this case, I was greatly puzzled how you could say it. For others run to that exhortation when they think they have something fair and good to defend in their cause; if, on the contrary, the strict letter of the law is pressed with words and letters, as is commonly said, which is often the greatest injustice, they are accustomed to set the name and dignity of goodness and fairness against such iniquity. Then they mock the saying "thus it comes"; then they cry out against the snares of words and letters as odious; then they clamour that the matter should be judged by what is fair and good, not by a cunning and crafty law; that to follow the written text is the mark of a calumniator, and that it is the mark of a good judge to defend the will and authority of the writer. But in this case, since you are the one who so diligently and so cunningly contends over disputes with words, defending not by fairness but by the letter, and who expresses laws not by common utility but by their letters, how can you say that one should not obey authority? And at the same time, Gaius Aquilius, see the indignity and iniquity of men who, with petty letters and obscure marks, want to obey laws, pacts, edicts, wills, all divine and human rights, commands, and the common opinions and speech of all, and from these to make judgments about the life and death and fortunes of all mortals. Deprecation has its place not in a civil case, but in those which are seen to be made against the laws. If it happens to fall under the places of the assumptive quality, and especially the parts of concession, of which we spoke above, whoever wishes may use them. We may nevertheless strive against writings if we say that what someone wants from the writing or the words cannot be done: not by law, not by custom, not by nature, not by good and fairness; and no one doubts that the writer wished all these things. For defending the intention there are several famous sayings of the jurists, tit. de leg., such as that of Celsus, l. 17: "To know the laws is not to hold their words but their force and power." Likewise of the same, l. 18: "Laws are to be interpreted more kindly, so that their will may be brought together." Likewise Paul, l. 23: "Those things which have always had a settled interpretation are by no means to be changed." Likewise Modestinus, l. 25: "No reason of law or kindness of fairness permits us, by a harsher interpretation, to carry those things which are introduced wholesomely for the advantage of men over to severity against their interest." Likewise Paul, l. 29: "He acts against the law who does what the law forbids; but he who gets around its intention acts in fraud of the law. Likewise Ulpian, l. 30: For a fraud is done against the law when that is done which it wished not to be done, though it did not forbid it to be done; and what is said [ῥητὸν ἀπὸ διανοίας], that is, by the letter as opposed to the intention, is called fraud by one who acts contrary to the law. And these points concern the written text and the intention.

units.la: DE CONTRARIIS LEGIBVS.
units.tr: ON CONTRARY LAWS.

units.la: Sin scripta inter se dissentient tanta series artis est, & sic inter se sunt pleraque conexa & apta,ut que paulo ante præcepta dedimus ambigui,quæque proxime sententiæ & scripti, eadem ad hoc genus causæ tertium transferatur. Nam quibus locis in ambiguo defendimus eam significationem quæ nos adiuuat, eisdem in contrariis legibus nostra lex defendenda est.Deinde est efficiendum,ut alterius scripti sententiam, alterius uerba defendamus. Ita quæ modo de scripto sententiaque præcepta sunt, eadem huc omnia transferamus.
units.tr: If the writings disagree with one another, there is such a close sequence of method, and so many points are linked and fit together, that the rules we gave a little earlier for ambiguity, and those closest to the meaning and wording of a writing, are to be carried over to this third kind of case. For in the places where, under ambiguity, we defended the interpretation that helps us, in the case of contrary laws our law must be defended in the same places. Next, we must work to defend the meaning of one writing and the words of the other. So all the rules just given about wording and meaning we transfer here in full.

units.la: Sin scripta inter se dissentiunt.) Appellant hunc postremum statum contrariarum legum, melius hic Cicero, qui genus posuit, non parte. Possunt enim non modo leges, (legum autem nomine, et leges et plebiscita, et Senatusconsulta intelligi debent) uerum etiam pactiones, conuenta, stipulationes, tabulae, atq; alia scriptorum genera inter se differentire. Sed in legibus attendendum maxime. Fere aut his modis differunt, cum eadem de re altera iubet, altera uetat: aut cum altera cogit, altera permittit: aut cum altera statim aliquid fieri vult, altera cum mora: aut cum una de genere omni, altera de parte quadam loquitur. Monet Cicero, ex proximis superioribus duabus controuersijs, ambigui et scripti et sententiae locos esse sumendos, et ad contrarias leges in utraque parte transferendos: id quod etiam Hermogenes scribit in libro de Statibus. In rhetoricis tamen de Inuentione, Cicero locos huic generi proprios assignat: etsi ibidem etiam monet, ex aliis statibus plerosque posse sumi. Quare qui uolet, eos ibidem uidere poterit. Exempla uero contrarium legum, praeter Rhetores, suppeditabut etiam libri Pandectarum: quanquam pleriq; negent. Sed Budaeus satis aperte illos redarguit in Annotationibus, quas in Pandectas scripsit. Esse autem interdum contrarias leges, testatur etiam Paulus iurisc. l. 28. tit. de leg. Sed et posteriores leges ad priores pertinent, nisi sint contrariae: idq; fraudem uero legis, qui sententia eius circumuenit. Item Vlpianus l. 30. Fraus enim legi fit, ubi id fit quod fieri noluit, fieri autem non uetuit: et quod distat ῥητὸν ἀπὸ διανοίας, hoc distat fraus ab eo quod contra legem fit. Atque haec de scripto et sententia.
units.tr: If the writings disagree with one another.) They call this last state of contrary laws, Cicero puts it better here, since he named the genus, not a part. For not only laws can differ among themselves (under the name of laws we must understand statutes, plebiscites and decrees of the Senate), but also agreements, contracts, stipulations, tables of laws, and other kinds of writings. But in the case of laws, attention must be paid above all. Laws usually differ in these ways: when one orders something concerning the same matter and the other forbids it; or when one compels and the other permits; or when one wants something done at once and the other with a delay; or when one speaks of a whole genus and the other of a certain part. Cicero advises, from the two preceding controversies, that the places of ambiguity, of the writing and of the meaning, are to be taken and carried over to contrary laws on either side; Hermogenes also writes this in his book on the States. In the rhetorical works, however, in On Invention, Cicero assigns places peculiar to this kind; though he also advises there that many can be taken from the other states. Whoever wishes may see them there. Examples of contrary laws, apart from the rhetoricians, will also be supplied by the books of the Pandects, although many deny it. But Budé refutes them quite clearly in the Annotations which he wrote on the Pandects. That contrary laws sometimes exist is also attested by the jurist Paul, law 28, title on laws. But later laws also pertain to earlier ones, unless they are contrary; and this is proved by many arguments. He who circumvents the intent of the law by its meaning commits a fraud on the law. Likewise Ulpian, law 30: A fraud is done to the law when that is done which one did not wish to be done, yet it is not forbidden to be done; and as the saying [ῥητὸν ἀπὸ διανοίας] differs from the intention, so fraud differs from what is done against the law. And these things concerning the writing and the meaning.

units.la: DE CONTRARIIS LEGIBVS.
units.tr: ON CONTRARY LAWS.

units.la: Sin scripta inter se dissentient tanta series artis est, & sic inter se sunt pleraque connexa & apta, ut que paulo ante praecepta dedimus ambigui, quaeque proxime sententiae & scripti, eadem ad hoc genus causse tertium transferatur. Nam quibus locis in ambiguo defendimus eam significationem quae nos adiuuat, eisdem in contrariis legibus nostra lex desenda est. Deinde est efficiendum, ut alterius scripti sententiam, alterius verba defendamus. Ita quae modo de scripto sententiaque praecepta sunt, eadem huc omnia transferamus.
units.tr: But if the writings disagree with one another, there is such a fine sequence of method, and so many of its parts are so closely linked and fitted together, that the precepts we gave a little earlier for ambiguous matters, both for the sense and for the wording, must be carried over to this third kind of case. For wherever in an ambiguous matter we defended the meaning that helps us, in the same places our law must be defended in the case of contrary laws. Then we must set about defending the sense of one writing and the words of the other. Thus let us transfer to this place all the precepts just given about the writing and its sense.

units.la: Sin scripta inter se dissentiunt.) Appellant hunc postremum statum contrariarum legum, melius hic
