units.la: hic Cicero, qui genus posuit, non partè. Possunt enim non modò leges, (legum autem nomine, & leges & plebiscita, & Senatusconsulta intelligi debent) uerùm etiam pactiones, conuenta, stipulationes, tabulæ, atq; alia scriptorum genera inter se differentire. Sed in legibus attendendum maximè. Ferè aut his modis differentiùt, cum eadē de re altera iubet, altera uetat: aut cū altera cogit, altera permittit: aut cū altera statim aliquid fieri uult, altera cū mora: aut cū una de genere omni, altera de parte quadā loquitur. Monet Cicero, ex proximis superioribus duabus controuersijs, ambigui & scripti & sententiæ locos esse sumēdos, & ad contrarias leges in utrāq; partē trahendus transferendos: id quod etiam Hermogenes scribit in libro de Statibus. In rhetoricis tamen de Inuētione, Cicero locos huic generi proprios assignat: etsi ibidem etiam moneat, ex aliis statibus plerosque posse sumi. Quare qui uolet, eos ibidem uidere poterit. Exēpla uerò contrarium legum, præter Rhetores, suppeditabūt etiā libri Pandectarū: quanquā pleriq; negent. Sed Budæus satis aperte illos redarguit in Annotationibus, quas in Pandectas scripsit. Esse autem interdū contrarias leges, testatur etiam Paulus [urisc.l.28.tit.de leg. Sed & posteriores leges ad priores pertinent, nisi sint contrarie: idq; F 4 idq; multis argumētis probetur. Nos hoc unum exemplum ex ijsdem Pandectis proferemus, in l. per seruū, de usu & habitatione. quæ sic habet: Deniq; si fructus deducto usu legatus sit, inutile esse legatum, Pomponius lib. 5. scribit. Contraria uero huic legi est illa, in l. huic stipulationi. tit. sequenti. Ergo etsi fructus sine usu obtigerit, stipulatio locū habebit. Hæc enim omnino inter se differentiunt. Altera enim inutilem dicit stipulationem, in eadem materia, altera utilem.
units.tr: here, Cicero, who gave the kind, not a part. For not only laws (under the name of laws both laws, plebiscites and decrees of the Senate should be understood) but also agreements, covenants, stipulations, tablets and other kinds of writings can differ from one another. Yet in the case of laws attention must be paid above all. They usually differ in these ways: when in the same matter one orders and the other forbids; or when one compels and the other permits; or when one wants something done at once and the other allows delay; or when one speaks of the whole genus and the other of some part. Cicero advises that, from the two preceding controversies just discussed, the places of ambiguity in the writing and in the sense are to be taken and carried over to contrary laws on either side; this Hermogenes also writes in his book On States. In his Rhetoric, however, in the De Inventione, Cicero assigns places peculiar to this kind; although in the same place he also advises that many can be drawn from the other states. Whoever wishes may therefore look there. Examples of contrary laws, besides those from the rhetoricians, will also be supplied by the books of the Pandects, although many deny it. But Budé clearly enough refutes them in the Annotations which he wrote on the Pandects. That contrary laws do sometimes exist is also attested by Paulus the jurist (l. 28, tit. de leg.): "But later laws also pertain to earlier ones, unless they are contrary"; and this is proved by many arguments. We shall bring forward only this one example from the same Pandects, in the law per servum, de usu et habitatione, which reads thus: "Finally, if the fruits were bequeathed with the use deducted, the legacy is useless, as Pomponius writes in book 5." Contrary to this law is that in the law huic stipulationi, in the following title: "Therefore, even if the fruits come without the use, the stipulation will have effect." For these differ entirely from one another: the one calls the stipulation useless, the other useful, in the same matter.

units.la: PARTITIONVM ORA- TORIARVM conclusio.
units.tr: The Conclusion of the Oratorical Partitions

units.la: EXPOSITAE sunt tibi omnes oratoriæ partitiones, quæ quidem e media illa nostra Academia floruerunt: nec sine ea aut inueniri, aut intelligi, aut tractari possunt. Nam & partiri ipsum, & definire, & ambiguí partitiones diuidere, & argumentorum locos nosse, & argumētationem ipsam concludere, & uidere quæ sumenda in argumentando sint, quidq; ex ijs quæ sumpta sunt efficiatur, & uera à falsis, uerisimilia ab incredibilibus dijudicare, & distinguere, & aut male sumpta, aut male malè cōclusa reprehendere, & ea- dē uel angustè differere, ut dialecti- ci qui appellatur: uel ut oratorē decet, latè exprimere, illius exercitationis, & subtiliter disputandi, & copiosè dicēdi artis est. De bonis uerò reb. & malis, æquis, iniquis, utilibus, inutilib. honestis, turpib. quam potest habere orator, sine illis maxi marū rerū artib. facultatè aut copiā. Quare hæc tib ifint, mi Cicero, quæ exposui, quasi iudicia fontiū illorū: ad quos fi nobis ĭsdē ducib. alijs'ue peruenefis, tū & hæc ipsa melius, & multa maiora alia cognosces. C. F. Ego uero, ac magno quidē studio, mí pater, multisq̧ ex tuis præclarifmis munerib. nullū maius expecto.
units.tr: All the oratorical partitions, those which flourished in that middle Academy of ours, have now been set out for you. Without the Academy they can be neither discovered, nor understood, nor handled. For to divide a thing and define it, to separate ambiguous terms into their divisions, to know the topics of arguments, to conclude an argument, to see what must be assumed in arguing and what follows from what has been assumed, to distinguish true from false and probable from incredible, to find fault with premises that were badly taken or conclusions that were badly drawn, and either to argue narrowly, as the dialectician is said to do, or, as befits the orator, to express oneself broadly: all this belongs to that exercise and that art of subtle disputing and copious speaking. As for good and bad things, equitable and iniquitous, useful and useless, honourable and shameful, the orator can have no resources or abundance in these matters of the greatest importance without those arts. Therefore, my Cicero, let these things be yours, which I have set out, as it were the streams flowing from those sources. If with the same guides, or with others, you reach those sources, then you will know these things better, and many far greater things besides. C. F. Indeed I shall, my father, and with great eagerness; and from your most splendid gifts I expect nothing greater.

units.la: Expositæ sunt tibi.) Hæc totius huius dialogi conclusio est, in qua sunt hi loci præcipui. Primo loco indicat, unde hæce partitiones sumpferit, & quibus ex fontibus hauserit. Deinde, sine dialecticæ & moralis philosophiæ cognitione, Oratorem esse non posse. Tum, quæ sint Dialecticæ partes & officia. Quarto loco, quid dialectica à rhetorica differat. Quintò, quæ sit doctrinæ moralis subiecta materies. Vltimò, hortatione ad eas artes discendas extimulat.
units.tr: "Expositae sunt tibi." This is the conclusion of the whole dialogue, and it contains these principal points. First, it indicates where these partitions were taken from and from which sources he drew them. Second, that without knowledge of dialectic and moral philosophy the orator cannot exist. Third, what the parts and duties of dialectic are. Fourth, in what way dialectic differs from rhetoric. Fifth, what is the subject matter of moral doctrine. Last, it urges the reader by exhortation to learn these arts.

units.la: Omnes oratoriæ partitiones.) Ergo frustra quærūtur meliores & perfectiores libri, cū hic unus omnia Oratoria præcepta, eaq; ad reminiscendum aptissima ratione cōpleCtatur, ut initiò diximus. Nam cum in tres partes distributa sit omnis doctrina dicendi, & eas omnes partiendo & diuidendo singulas ad extremā usq; particulā deduxerit & explicauerit, pspicuū est, omnes ab eo oratorias partitiones expōsitas esse.
units.tr: "Omnes oratoriae partitiones." Therefore the search for better and more perfect books is in vain, since this one work embraces all the oratorical precepts, and in the most suitable arrangement for remembering them, as was said at the beginning. For since the whole doctrine of speaking has been distributed into three parts, and he has divided and subdivided each of them down to its smallest particle and explained it, it is clear that he has set out all the oratorical partitions.

units.la: Quæ quidē è media nostra Academia floruerunt.) Vnde & hanc partiendi doctrinam, & quæ partitionibus his continētur præcepta hauserit, ingenuè fatetur: nimirum ab ea Academia, hoc est, ex Platonis, ac potissimū Aristotelis doctrina & libris. Nā Academicos ueteres & Peripateticos eosdē fuisse, multis locis testatur Cicero, ut de Finib. lib. 4. & 5. & in proœmio lib. de Officijs. re enim cōsentientes, uocabulis disserebant. Academiam nostram appellat, indicans se Academicum esse. Nam cum multæ essent à Socrate philosophorū ṫiquam profeminatæ famislie, Academicā Cicero adamauit, propter differendi libertatē, atq; ubertatē. Fuit enim cōsuetudo Academiæ, probabilia sequi, & de omnib. rebus reb.in contrarias partes copiosè differere:suâq; illà ἐπoχὴ, id est,assensionis retentionē seruare. Quà de re in Acad.quaest.& in 3.de Orat.multa.Quòd autē dicit floruerūt,pro efflonuerūt,id est,extiterūt & manarūt,positū est:ut in proœmio de Orat. Ex rerum cognitione efflorescat & redundet oportet oratio. Est enim translatum uerbum à stirpibus,è quibus cum existunt flores, & prodeunt, florere siue efflorescere dicuntur.
units.tr: "Quae quidem e media nostra Academia floruerunt." Here he openly admits from where he drew this doctrine of division and the precepts contained in these partitions: namely from that Academy, that is, from the teaching and books of Plato, and above all of Aristotle. For Cicero testifies in many places that the old Academics and the Peripatetics were the same, as in the De finibus books 4 and 5, and in the preface to the book De officiis: they agreed in substance and differed only in terminology. He calls it "our Academy," indicating that he is an Academic. For although many schools of philosophy had sprung from Socrates, Cicero embraced the Academic school because of the freedom and richness of its debate. For it was the custom of the Academy to follow what is probable and to argue copiously on all subjects on opposite sides, while keeping its suspension of judgment, that is, its withholding of assent (epochē). On this subject there is much in the Academica and in book 3 of De oratore. That he says "flourished" (floruerunt) instead of "sprang forth" (effloruerunt), that is, "came into being and flowed out," is used as in the preface to De oratore: "Speech ought to blossom and overflow from knowledge of things." The word is transferred from plants, from whose stems flowers come forth and appear, and so they are said to flower or bloom.

units.la: Neq; sine ea) Sine Academia, hoc est,sine philosophia. Sed Academiā nominauit tāq; principe atq; eruditissimā philosophādi rationem. Omnis nāq; rerū optimarū cognitio,atq; in his exercitatio,philosophia nominatur. Ex Academicorū autē scriptis & institutis, ut ipse de Fin.lib.5.scribit,cū omnis doctrina liberalis,omnis historia,omnis sermo elegans fumi potest:iū uarietas est tā tā artiū , ut nemo sine eo instrumēto ad ullā rē illustriorē satis ornatus possit accedere. Ab his oratores, ab his imperatores, & rerū publicarū principes extiterūt:ut ad minora ucniā. Mathematici, poetæ,musici,medici deniq; ex hac, tanq; ex omniū artiū officina ꝑfecti sūt.Nō mirū igitur si dicit, Partitionū oratoriarū doctrinā sine Academia nec inueniri,quod ad priorē partē dialectica pertinet,quæ τομικὴ diciturinec intelligi,quod est iudicij,quæ pars ὑφιτικὴ & ἀναλυτικὴ nominatur: nec tractari, quod est exercitationis, posse.
units.tr: "Neque sine ea." "Without the Academy," that is, without philosophy. But he named the Academy as the chief and most learned method of philosophizing. For the knowledge of the best things, and the exercise in them, is called philosophy. From the writings and institutions of the Academics, as he himself writes in De finibus book 5, since every liberal learning, all history, and all elegant discourse can be drawn, and the variety of the arts is so great, no one can approach any more distinguished subject adequately equipped without that instrument. From these came orators, from these generals and leaders of states, to mention lesser things: mathematicians, poets, musicians, and physicians were finally perfected from this, as from the workshop of all the arts. It is no wonder, then, that he says the doctrine of oratorical partitions cannot be discovered without the Academy, since the first part, which pertains to dialectic and is called tomikē [τομικὴ], belongs to it; nor understood, which concerns judgment, the part called hypitikē [ὑφιτικὴ] and analytikē [ἀναλυτικὴ]; nor practised, which belongs to exercise.

units.la: Nam & partiri ipsam.) Probat a dialectica officijs primum, sine Academicorum doctrina Oratorem esse non posse, tradit enim dialectica viam & rationem partiendi, definiendi, ambigua distinguendi, argumenta ex locis inueniendi, quae omnia sunt inventionis. Deinde argumenta explicandi: ac tum maioris proposititionis, tum minoris, cum medio collocatione: quidque ex eis efficiatur, veras enunciationes a falsis, verisimiles ab incredibilibus discernere, quae iudicij & acuminis sunt. Postremo, aut male sumpta, aut male conclusa reprehendere: id est, fallaces conclusiunculas indicare & refellere, quod eius artis est, quam in ἐλέγχος tradit Aristoteles.
units.tr: "Nam et partiri ipsam." He first proves from the functions of dialectic that the orator cannot exist without the teaching of the Academics. For dialectic hands down the way and method of dividing, defining, distinguishing ambiguous terms, and finding arguments from topics, all of which belong to invention. Then it explains arguments, both the major and the minor premise, and their placing together with the middle term; and it shows what follows from them, and distinguishes true statements from false, and probable from incredible, which belong to judgment and sharpness of wit. Finally, it finds fault with what was badly assumed or badly concluded; that is, it points out and refutes fallacious little conclusions, which belongs to that art which Aristotle handed down in the Elenchus [ἐλέγχος].

units.la: Et eadem vel angustè disserere.)Discrimen indicat dialecticae ac Rhetoricae: quarum quum sit una eademque materia, de omni re proposita ex ijsdem locis disserere: hoc tamen differt inter se, quod haec ratio dicendi latior, illa loquendi & disputandi cōtractior est, ut ipse in Orat.ait. Hinc licet veram utriusque definitione elicere, ut dialectica angustè & subtiliter disputandi arte esse dicamus, rhetorica vero latè & copiosè dicendi.
units.tr: "Et eadem vel anguste disserere." He indicates the difference between dialectic and rhetoric. Since both have one and the same subject matter, namely to argue about any proposed question from the same topics, they nevertheless differ in this: this mode of speaking is broader, while that of reasoning and disputing is more compressed, as he himself says in the Orator. From this one may draw a true definition of each: we say dialectic is the art of disputing narrowly and subtly, but rhetoric the art of speaking broadly and copiously.

units.la: De bonis vero reb.) Locos praecipuos, quib. doctrina de moribus continetur, memorat, ut perspicuum fiat, Oratorem ea carere non posse, si nomen suum tueri, dignitatemq; uelit. Id cum in alijs oratorijs libris magnificè osten-dit, tum de Orat. lib. 1. sic disputatione concludit: Quare hic locus de uita & moribus, totus est Oratori perdiscendus. Et in Oratore fatetur, se oratorè, quicunque fit, non ex rhetorū officinis, sed ex Academiæ sp̃acijs extitisse. Bona & mala sunt, ut ostendimus, triplicia: animi, corporis, & fortunæ. Sed hic quæ bona sunt, per se & generaliter intelligit. Æqua & iniqua, iuri & iustitiæ, & eorum cōtrarijs attribuūtur. Vtilia & inutilia ad bona quidè & mala referūtur, sed quæ ita propter aliud sunt, ut ostensum est in deliberatione. Honesta & turpia, in bonis & malis animi cernūtur, interdū etiā corporis & fortunarū, cum ex decoro considerantur. Rursus mala & bona, itemq; utilia & inutilia, suasionis & dissuasionis fines supra positi sunt: æqua & iniqua, ad iudicia pertinent: honesta & turpia, ad laudationes & uituperationes: quæ tria sunt genera, in quibus præcipuè uersatur Orator. Ex quo efficitur, necessariam esse moralem & ciuilem Philosophiam Oratori.
units.tr: "De bonis vero rebus." He recalls the principal topics that contain the doctrine of morals, so that it becomes clear that the orator cannot do without them, if he wishes to maintain his name and his dignity. He shows this magnificently in other oratorical books, and in De oratore book 1 he concludes the discussion thus: "Therefore this topic of life and morals is wholly to be learned thoroughly by the orator." And in the Orator he confesses that he himself became an orator, whatever he is, not from the workshops of the rhetoricians but from the grounds of the Academy. Goods and evils are, as we have shown, threefold: of the mind, of the body, and of fortune. But here he understands by good things those in general. Equitable and iniquitous are attributed to law and justice and their opposites. Useful and useless are referred to good and evil, but such things as are useful for something else, as was shown in the discussion of deliberation. Honourable and shameful are discerned among the goods and evils of the mind, and sometimes also of the body and fortune, when they are considered in terms of propriety. Again, good and evil, and likewise useful and useless, have been set forth as the ends of persuasion and dissuasion; equitable and iniquitous pertain to judgments; honourable and shameful to praise and blame. These three are the kinds in which the orator is chiefly occupied. From this it follows that moral and civil philosophy is necessary for the orator.

units.la: Quare hæc tibi sint, mi Cicero.) Clausula huius perorationis, ab utilibus hortatur enim filium, ut ad fontes ipsos accedat: id est, ad libros Platonis & Aristotelis, si & quæ ipse tradidit in his Partitionib. uelit intelligere, quæ ab ijsdēsontib. quasi riuuli quidā deducta sunt, & multa alia lōgè præstātiora cognoscere. Hac eadem translatione usus est de Orat. lib.1. Equidē uobis ( inquit ) quoniā ita uoluistis, fontes, unde bauriretis, atq; itinera ipsa ita putaui demonstrāda esse, & ut fieri solet, digitū ad fontes intendere.
units.tr: "Quare haec tibi sint, mi Cicero." This is the closing sentence of this peroration, in which he urges his son to go to the very sources: that is, to the books of Plato and Aristotle, if he wishes to understand the things he himself has handed down in these Partitions, which were drawn from those same sources like little streams, and to know many other things far superior. He uses the same metaphor in De oratore book 1: "Indeed, since you wished it so," he says, "I thought the sources from which you might draw, and the very routes, ought to be shown to you, and, as is usual, to point the finger at the sources."

units.la: Fontium illorum. ) Illorū, ad ipsos fontes demonstrādos refertur, non ad personam aliquam illorū fontium, quos modò indicaui. Sunt tamen qui legant illarum, ut ad artes, aut ad res bonas & malas, quas memorauit, referatur.
units.tr: "Fontium illorum." "Those" refers to the sources themselves to be pointed out, not to any person of those sources whom I have just mentioned. There are, however, some who read "illarum" (of those), so that it refers to the arts, or to the goods and evils he mentioned.

units.la: Ad quos si nobis eisdem ducibus. ) Si me autore & magistro usus fueris, si tibi locos philosophiæ Romano sermone explicauero: quod quidē fecit. Nam & ad ipsum filiū tres de Ossicijs libros scripsit, in quibus locos de morib. & ciuili ratione illustrauit: eūq; ibi hortatur, ut nō solum orationes suas, sed etiam de philosophia libros studiosè legat. Cicero enim omnes fere philosophiæ locos, quos Oratori necessarios esse putauit, in suis dialogis copiosa oratione explicauit: ut ab uno eodemq; autore, quæ hic dicit Oratori necessaria esse, haberemus.
units.tr: If I have used you, with these same leaders, as my guide and teacher, if I have explained to you in the Roman tongue the topics of philosophy, which indeed he did. For he also wrote three books On Duties to his own son, in which he illuminated the topics of morals and civil conduct, and there he urges him to read not only his speeches but also his books on philosophy diligently. For Cicero explained in copious discourse almost all the topics of philosophy which he thought necessary for the orator in his dialogues, so that we might have from one and the same author the things which he here says are necessary for the orator.

units.la: C.F. Ego uero, ac magno quidem studio, mi pater. ) His uerbis mirificum studium suum, & magnum quendam ardorem animi ostendit filius: quod mirificè ualet ad patrem, ut philosophiæ locos ei tradere, & se ducem ad eos quos dixit fontes præbere uelit, accendendum.
units.tr: C.F. Indeed I do, my father, and with great zeal. By these words the son shows his remarkable eagerness and a certain great ardour of mind, which is wonderfully effective in kindling the father to wish to hand over to him the topics of philosophy and to provide himself as a guide to the sources he has named.

units.la: Nos uero etiam ex ijsdem fontib. unde hæc ipsa sunt hausta, Partitiones doctoris nostri Ciceronis irrigare, & luce aliqua doctrinæ illuminare conati sumus: non equidè ut ab illis fontib. adolescentes abstrerrēe, sed potius ut magis incitarem. Sic enim solent, qui denuum referta habent preciosis mercibus, quædam per transennā spectanda prætereuntibus proponere, ut eos ad spectandum, deinde etiam ad alia maiora petenda alliciant. Quisi accesserint, & proferri sibi alia poposcerint, tum dies ille mercator eos introducit, eis què alia longè maiora & preciosiora, quorum illa tantum specimen fuerat, ostendit, summendiq; copiam facit. Nam ut Socratem illum solitum aiût dicere, perfectum sibi opus esse, si quis satis esset concitatus exhortatione sua ad studium cognoscendæ percipiendæq; uirtutis: sic ego intelligo, si his nostris commentariolis adolescentes ad illa maiora & pleniora quærenda accesi fuerint, me operam & oleum, quod dicitur, nequaquam perdidisse.
units.tr: We too have tried to water Doctor Cicero's Partitiones from the very same springs from which these things themselves were drawn, and to illuminate them with some light of learning; not indeed to frighten young men away from those sources, but rather to spur them on the more. For those who have a storehouse full of precious wares are accustomed to set out some things to be looked at through a window for passers-by, so that they may attract them to look, and then to seek other, greater things. If they come near and ask to be shown other things, then that merchant admits them and shows them other, far greater and more precious things, of which the former were only a sample, and gives them the chance to buy. For as Socrates, as they say, used to say, his work was complete if someone had been roused enough by his exhortation to the study of knowing and grasping virtue; so I judge that if young men have been moved by these little commentaries of ours to seek those greater and fuller things, I have by no means wasted my labour and, as the saying goes, my oil.

units.la: EXPLICATIONVM C. S. C. in Oratorias Partitiones
units.tr: Explanations of C. S. C. on the Oratorical Partitions

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: SVMMA PRAECE- PTORVM DE ARTE dicendi, ex tribus Ciceronis libris de Oratore, distincte ac dilucide collecta, & exemplis ex eiusdem Orationibus breuiter il- lustrata.
units.tr: A Summary of the Precepts on the Art of Speaking, Collected Distinctly and Clearly from Cicero's Three Books On the Orator, and Briefly Illustrated with Examples from His Orations.

units.la: VM is igitur fit orator, hoc tam graui dignus nomine, qui, quacunq; res inciderit, quae fit dictione explicanda, prudenter & compositè, et ornatè, et memoriter dicat, cum quadam etiam actionis dignitate, ab illo penitus pernoscendi sunt omnes animorum motus, quos hominum generi rerum natura tribuit, ad mentes auditorum uel ad irā, aut odium, aut dolorem incitandas, uel ab ijsce ijsdē permotionibus ad lenitatem misericordiaq; reuocandas. hoc enim est proprium oratoris, oratio grauis, & ornata, & hominum sensibus ac mentibus accommodata. Tenenda praeterea est omnis antiquitas, exemplorumq; uis, cum in rerum & temporum ordine, in consiliorum ratione, in uarijs rerum euentis posita, non parum afferat ad persuadendum utilitatis. Neq; legum aut iurisciuilis scientia negligenda est: ut si de testamentis, de hæreditatibus, de obligationibus, de actionibus, de emptione & venditione, de locatione, de pecuniis repetundis, de pœnis, de sicariis, de iniuriis dicendum contigerit (quod fere sæpissime fit) possit prudenter, copiosè, copioséq; dicere. Accedat eodem oportet scientia rei militaris, si quando occurrerit aut contra Imperatorem, aut pro Imperatore differere: de Repub. de bello, de pace, de inducijs, de præsidio militum, de custodia ciuitatis. Adsit etiam necesse est lepos quidam, facetiæq;, & eruditio libero digna homine, celeritasq;, & breuitas, & respondendi et lacessēdi subtili uenustate atq; urbanitate cōiuncta. Quid dicā de philosophia? quæ cum in tres partes distributa sit, in naturæ obscuritatem, in differendi subtilitatē, in uitam atq; mores, duo illa relinquēda, idq; inertiæ nostræ largiendū: tertium verò, quod semper oratoris fuit, nisi tenue erit, magnus esse omnino minimè poterit. Quare hic locus de uita & moribus totus oratori perdiscēdus: ut quid oportuerit de rebus bonis aut malis, expetēdis aut fugiēdis, honestis aut turpibus, utilibus aut inutilibus, de uirtute, de iustitia, de continentia, de prudentia, de magnitudine animi, de liberalitate, de pietate, de amicitia, de fide, de officio, cæterisq; uirtutibus, contrariisq; uitijs, facilime eloquatur. Et certè nemo poterit esse omni laude cumulatus orator, nisi erit omnium rerum magnarum, atq; artium scientiam consequutus. Etenim ex rerum cognitione efflorescat et redundet oportet oratio: quæ nisi subiecta ab oratore percepta & cognita, inanem quandam habet elocutionem, ac pene puerilem. Vnde non sine ratione illius artem nullis terminis circumscribunt, quo minus ei liceat uagari quà uelit. Etenim quum cæteræ fere artes seipsas per singulas tueantur: oratoris autem, quæ est scientiter, & perite, & ornatè dicere, non habet definitam aliquam regionem, cuius finibus septa teneatur: cum plena perfectaq; esse nequeat, nisi de omnibus rebus possit uariè, copiosèq; dicere. Quare maximo in errore uersantur, qui artem mimicè putât esse hanc dicendi: quòd ita nati simus, ut & blandiri, & supplicitèr insinuare ijs, à quibus esset petendum, & aduersarios minaciter terrere, & rem gestam exponere, & id quod intenderemus, confirmare: & id quod contradiceretur, refellere: ac ad extremum deprecari aliquid, & conqueri, non aduertentes artem esse imitationem, atq; animaduersionem naturæ, cum nonnullos temerè hæc facere, ac sine ulla ratione uideamus: nonnullos autem institutione atq; obseruatione rem dissolutâ, diuulsamq; conglutinare, & ratione quadam constringere: quod totum proculdubio artis est, non fortunæ, aut casus existimandum. Quamobrem quum ignota quondam omnibus, ac diffusa late uiderentur, excogitare, ornare, disponere, meminisse, agere, bis adhibita est extrinsecus animaduersio quædam, qua in ordinem artemq; redigerentur. De quibus omnibus, ut, quemadmodum proposuimus, aliquid pertractemus, ab ipsa inuenien diratione sumamus exordium. Non ignorandum est, omnem orationē esse aut de infinita rei quæstione, sine designatione personarum & temporum: aut de re certa in personis ac temporib. lo cata. Infinita mihi uidetur, in qua aliquid gene ratim quæreretur, hoc modo: an intueri lucem cē fas esse uideatur, qui à se homine occisum esse fateatur. Certa autem, in qua quid in personis, & in constituta re, et definita quæreretur: cuiusmodi sunt, quæ in foro, atq; in ciuiū causis, disceptā tionibusq; uersantur. Eæ mihi uidentur aut in li te ordinanda, aut in cōsilio dādo, aut in laudatio ne (ut adiunxit Aristoteles) esse positæ. Sed iste omnes ctrouerfiæ ad uniuersi generis uim & naturam referuntur. nam si quæratur, Interæ fecit Clodium Milo defendēdæ salutis causa, nihil pertinet ad oratoris locos Milonis personæ. de ipso enim uniuerso genere infinita quæstio est, num poena uideatur esse afficiendus, qui alterum uitæ tuendæ causa intercmit. Nulla deniq; est causa, in qua id quod in iudicium uenit ex rei persona, ac non generum ipsorum uniuersa dis-putatione quæratur. Itaque omnia necessario à tempore atque homine ad communes rerum & generum summas reuoluuntur. In utraq; autem re quicquid in controuersiam uenit, in eo quæriur, factum ne sit: aut si est factum, quale sit, aut etiam quo nomine uocetur. Nam illud quod quidam adiungunt, Recte ne factum sit: totum in eo est, quod quale sit quærimus. Exist-unt etiam controuersiæ ex scripti interpretatione, cum aut scriptum sit ambiguum, aut contrarium, aut dissidens à scribentis sententia. Istæ autem controuersiæ non debent à facti qualitate seiungi. nunquam enim tam quæritur, quale sit genus ipsius rei, quàm in scripto. Ita tria omnino remanent, quæ in disceptationem aut controuersiam cadere possunt, an aliquid sit, quale sit, & quid sit. Quamobrem danda opera est, ut orator primum reum examinet, ut causa cognita, statim quæ sit causa ambigui cogitet, an facti, an qualitatis, an definitionis. Ac omnes fere causæ, quæ quidem sunt criminum, plerunq; inficiatione defenduntur. nam & de pecunijs repetundis, de sicarijs, de beneficijs, de peculatu, inficiari necesse est. Sape autem, non fit nec ne, sed qualis sit quaeritur: ut in causa Milonis, in qua nihil de Clodij nece negabat, sed id iure, ut uim ui illatam propulsaret facti esse dicebat. Iure autem omnia defenduntur, quae sunt eius generis, ut aut oportuerit, aut licuerit, aut necesse fuerit, aut imprudentia, aut casu facta esse videatur. Postremo quid nocetur, quaeritur: in qua parte illud animaduertendum est, nō esse affectandas minutas illas definitiones verbi, de quo disceptatur, sed omni copia dicendi dilatandum & explicandum, ne definitio reprehenso uerbo uno, aut addito, aut adempto, e manibus extorqueatur, neue redoleat doctrinam exercitationemq; pene puerilem: ne ue prius àmēte iudicis praeterlabatur, quàm percepta sit. In his autem controuersijs pertractandis probatione opus est. Ad probandum autem, duplex est oratori subiecta materies. una rerum earum, quae non excogitantur ab oratore, sed in re positae, ratione tractantur: ut leges, tabulae, testimonia, quaestiones. ut: Quod si duodecim tabulae nocturnum furem quoquo modo, diurnum uero, si se telo defenderit, interfici impune uoluerunt: quis est, qui, quoquo modo quis interfectus sit, puniendum putet? Archias non est professus, imo uero his tabulis professus est, quae sola ex illa professione collegioq; praetorū obtinent publicarum tabularum authoritatem. Mimitatus est Miloni Clodius. uos ex Marco Fauonio audistis, Clodium sibi dixisse, periturum Milonem triduo. Clodius impudicus est, cum sorore germana nefarium stuprum fecisse. L. Lucullus iuratus, se quaestionibus habitis dixit coperiisse. Altera est, quae tota in disputatione et argumentatione oratoris collocata est, ita in super-iori genere de tractandis argumentis, in hoc autem etiam de inueniendis cogitandum est. Et primum genus illud earum rerum quae ad oratorem referuntur, meditatum nobis in perpetuum ad omnem usum similium causarum esse debebit. Nam et pro legibus, et contra leges: et pro tabulis, et contra tabulas: et pro testibus, et contra testes: et pro quaestionibus, et contra quaestiones dicere solemus. In posteriori vero genere tres dicendi rationes requiruntur: una conciliandorum hominum, altera docendorum, tertia cogitandorum. Harum trium partium, prima lenitatem orationis, secunda acumen, tertia vim deflectit. Nam hoc necesse est, ut is qui nobis causam adiudicaturus est, aut inclinatione voluntatis in nos propendeat, aut defensionis argumentis adducatur, aut animi permotione cogatur. Sed quoniam illa pars, in qua rerum ipsarum explicatio ac defensio posita est, uidetur omne huius generis quasi doctrinam continere, de ea primum loquemur. Ad hanc autem consequendam, primum orator natura causae uideat, quid faciat causam: id est, quo sublato controversia stare non possit: deinde quid veniat in iudicium, quod hoc modo quaeritur: Interfecit Clodium Milo. quid facit causam? quod tuendae salutis causa. hoc tolle, causa non erit. At insidiatum Miloni Clodium negabant accusatores. veniet igitur in iudicium, uter utri insidias fecerit. Postea videat locos probationum, qui ex sua vi atque natura assumuntur. assumuntur autem ex sua vi, cum aut res quae fit tota quaeritur, aut pars eius, aut uocabulum quod habeat, aut quippiam, rem illam quod attingat. Si res tota quaeritur, definitione universa uis explicanda est. ut pro Ligario: Atq; ille non mediocri cupiditate arripuit imperium, si illud imperium esse potuit, quod ad priuatum clamore multitudinis imperitae, nullo publico consilio de re rebatur. Sin pars, partitione: ut pro C. Rabirio perduellionis reo. Atq; uidemus haec in rerum natura tria fuisse, ut aut cum Saturnino esset, aut cum bonis, aut lateret. Latere, mortis erat instar turpissimae: cum Saturnino esse, furoris et scelevis: uirtus, et honestas, et pudor, cum consulib. esse cogebat. Sin ex uocabulo, ut in Paradoxis: Laudetur uero hic Imperator, aut etiam appelletur,aut hoc nomine dignus putetur. Quo˒ modo?aut cui tandē hic libero imperabit,qui nō potest cupiditatib.suis imperare?Sin ab eo quod rem attingat,plures sunt argumentorum sedes ac loci.nam & coniuncta quærimus & genera, & partes generibus subiectas,& similitudines, & dissimilitudines,& contraria, et consequen˒ tia, & consentanea, & quasi præcurrentia, & repugnantia,& causas rerum uestigabimus,& ea quæ ex causis orta sunt,& maiora,paria,mi˒ nora quæremus. Ex coniunctis sic argumen˒ ta ducuntur,ut pro lege Manilia: Etenim si ues˒tigalia neruos esse Reipub. semper duximus: eum certe ordinem, qui illa exercet,firmamen˒ tum cæterorum ordinum recte esse dicemus. Ex genere autem, ut pro Milone: Sin hoc & ratio doctis, & necessitas barbaris, & mos genti˒bus,& feris natura ipsa præscripsit, ut omnem semper uim quacunque ope possent à corpore, à capite,à uita sua propulsarent: non potestis hoc facinus improbum iudicare,quin simul iudicetis, omnib. qui in latrones inciderint,aut illorum telis, aut uestris sententijs esse pereundum. Ex parte autem ea quæ subiecta est generi, in M.Antonium prima: Quæ lex melior?utilior? optima etiā in Repub. sæpius flagitata? quàm ne prætoriæ prouinciæ plufquā annū, ne plus˒quam quam biennium consulares obtinerentur? Hac le ge sublata, uidentur ne acta Cæsaris seruari? Ex similitudine, ut in ostaua: In corpore si quid e‐ iusmodi est, quod reliquo corpori noceat, uri ac secari patimur, ut membrorum aliquod potius, quàm totum corpus intereat: sic in Reipublicæ corpore, ut totum saluum sit, quicquid est pesti‐ ferum, amputetur. At ex dissimilitudine in ter‐ tia: Certus autem dies non ut sacrificij, sic consi‐ lij expectari debet. Iam ex contrario, pro Milo‐ ne: Obuiam fit ei Clodius, expeditus in equo, nulla rheda, nullis impedimentis, nullis Græcis co‐ mitibus, ut solebat, sine uxore, quod nunquam se‐ re: cum hic insidiator, qui iter illud ad cædem sa‐ ciendâ apparasset, cum uxore ueheretur, in rhe da penulatus, uulgi magno impedimento, ac muliebri & delicato ancillarum puerorumq; comitatu. Ex consequentibus, pro Roscio: Si lege oc‐ cifus est Roscius, bona quoq; lege uenisse fateor: sin autem constat, contra omnes non modo ue‐ teres leges, uerum etiam nonas occisum esse, bo‐ na quo iure, aut quo modo, aut qua lege uenie‐ rint quæro? Ex cõsentaneis, ut pro Milone: Ob‐ uiam fit ei Clodius, expeditus in equo, nulla rhe da, nullis impedimētis, nullis Græcis comitibus, ut solebat: sine uxore, quod nunquam siere. units.tr: Whoever is to become an orator, worthy of so weighty a name, must thoroughly learn all the emotions of the mind that nature has given to the human race, so that he may speak of whatever matter arises in a way that is prudent, well arranged, ornate and easy to remember, and with a certain dignity of delivery. He must be able either to stir the minds of his hearers to anger, hatred or grief, or, by the same emotions, to soothe them and call them back to mercy. For this is the proper task of the orator: a speech that is weighty, ornate and fitted to the feelings and minds of men. Moreover, all antiquity must be kept in view, and the force of examples, since in the order of events and times, in the reasoning of counsels, and in the various outcomes of affairs, these contribute no little to persuasion. Nor may he neglect knowledge of the laws and of the civil law, so that if he has to speak about wills, inheritances, obligations, actions, buying and selling, leasing, extortion, penalties, assassins or injuries (which happens very often), he may be able to speak prudently and fully. Knowledge of military affairs must also be added, for whenever he has to argue either against or on behalf of a commander, or about the state, war, peace, truces, the garrisoning of troops, or the defence of the city. There must also be a certain wit and pleasantry, and learning worthy of a free man, and quickness and brevity, joined with a subtle charm and urbanity in answering and in attacking. What shall I say of philosophy? Since it is divided into three parts, the obscurity of nature, the subtlety of disputation, and life and morals, the first two may be left aside and granted to our idleness; but the third, which has always belonged to the orator, unless it is thin, can never make him truly great. Therefore the whole of this part concerning life and morals must be learned by the orator, so that he may speak with the greatest ease about what must be sought or avoided among good and bad things, about the honourable and the base, the useful and the useless, about virtue, justice, self-control, prudence, greatness of spirit, liberality, piety, friendship, faith, duty, and the other virtues and their contrary vices. Indeed, no one can be an orator crowned with every praise unless he has attained knowledge of all great matters and arts. For speech ought to flourish and overflow from knowledge of things; and speech that is not founded on subjects grasped and understood by the orator has an empty and almost childish eloquence. Hence it is not without reason that men have not confined his art within any limits, so that he may range wherever he wishes. For while the other arts for the most part protect themselves each within its own boundaries, the art of the orator, which is to speak wisely, skilfully and elegantly, has no fixed region enclosed by definite limits; it cannot be full and perfect unless he can speak variously and copiously on all subjects. Therefore they are in very great error who think that this art of speaking is merely a matter of imitation, because we are born so as to flatter, to insinuate ourselves humbly with those from whom we must seek something, to terrify adversaries with threats, to set out an action, to confirm what we intend, to refute what is contradicted, and finally to plead for something and complain; they do not notice that art is the imitation and observation of nature. We see some men do these things rashly and without any reason, while others, by training and observation, gather a loose and scattered matter and bind it together with a certain method. All of this must undoubtedly be reckoned the work of art, not of fortune or chance. Therefore, since the things to be done were once unknown to all and seemed widely scattered, the task of inventing, ornamenting, arranging, remembering and delivering was given to an external observation, by which they might be reduced to order and to an art. To treat of all these things, as we proposed, let us take our beginning from invention. We must not be ignorant that every speech concerns either an unlimited question of a matter, without specification of persons and times, or a definite matter placed in particular persons and times. I consider a question unlimited when something is asked in general, as: whether it is right for someone to look upon the light who confesses that he has killed a man. A definite question is one in which something is asked about particular persons and an established and defined matter; such are those that arise in the forum and in the disputes of citizens' cases. These, I think, are placed either in the ordering of a lawsuit, in giving counsel, or in praise (as Aristotle added). But all these controversies are referred to the force and nature of the whole kind. For if it is asked whether Milo killed Clodius in defence of his safety, the persons of Milo have nothing to do with the topics of the orator; the question concerns the whole kind itself, namely whether a man who has killed another in order to protect his own life ought to be punished. Finally, there is no case in which what comes into judgment is asked from the person of the accused, and not from the universal discussion of the kinds themselves. Thus everything of necessity is reduced from the time and the man to the common headings of things and kinds. In either sort of matter, whatever comes into controversy is asked about in this way: whether a thing has been done; or, if it has been done, of what kind it is; or also by what name it is to be called. For what some add, whether it was rightly done, is entirely contained in our inquiry into what kind it is. There are also controversies arising from the interpretation of a writing, when the writing is either ambiguous, or contrary, or at odds with the intention of its author. But these controversies ought not to be separated from the quality of the deed; for it is never asked so much what kind of thing the matter itself is, as what the writing means. Thus three things altogether remain that can fall into dispute or controversy: whether something is, what kind it is, and what it is. Therefore care must be taken that the orator first examines the defendant, so that, once the case is known, he may at once consider what the question of the matter is: whether it concerns the fact, the quality, or the definition. And almost all causes concerning crimes are generally defended by denial; for in cases of extortion, assassination, benefits, or embezzlement, one must necessarily deny. Often, however, the question is not whether something was done or not, but what kind of thing it was; as in the case of Milo, in which he did not deny the killing of Clodius, but said that it was done by right, to repel force with force. Now everything is defended by right that is of such a kind that it seemed either to have been required, or to have been permitted, or to have been necessary, or to have been done through imprudence or chance. Finally, one asks what harm has been done; and here it must be noted that one should not pursue those petty definitions of the word under dispute, but should expand and explain it with the full abundance of speech, lest the definition be snatched from our hands by the criticism of one word, added or removed, and lest it smell of a training and practice that is almost puerile, or lest it slip from the mind of the judge before it has been grasped. But in handling these controversies there is need of proof. For proof, the orator has a twofold matter laid before him. One is of those things which are not invented by the orator but lie in the case and are treated by reason: such as laws, documents, testimonies, and interrogations. For example: "If the Twelve Tables wished that a thief at night might be killed in any way, and a thief by day, if he defended himself with a weapon, might be killed with impunity: who is there who thinks that a man killed in any way should be punished?" "Archias did not make a declaration; but indeed he made it in these records, which alone, from that declaration and the college of the praetors, hold the authority of public records." "Clodius imitated Milo. You have heard from Marcus Favonius that Clodius said to him that Milo would perish within three days." "Clodius is shameless, for he committed an abominable debauchery with his own sister." "Lucullus, under oath, said that he had discovered it when the examinations were held." The other kind lies wholly in the disputation and argumentation of the orator; and in the earlier kind, concerning the handling of arguments, in this one we must also think about invention. And that first kind of things that pertain to the orator ought to be prepared by us for perpetual use in every similar case. For we are accustomed to speak both for laws and against laws, both for documents and against documents, both for witnesses and against witnesses, both for interrogations and against interrogations. In the second kind, three methods of speaking are required: one for winning over men, another for teaching them, and a third for moving them. Of these three parts, the first bends the mind by gentleness of speech, the second by sharpness, and the third by force. For it is necessary that he who is about to judge our cause should either lean toward us by an inclination of will, or be brought over by the arguments of the defence, or be compelled by an emotion of the mind. But since that part, in which the explanation and defence of the things themselves is placed, seems to contain as it were the whole doctrine of this kind, we shall speak of it first. To attain this, first the orator must see the nature of the cause: what makes up the cause, that is, what, if removed, the controversy cannot stand. Then what comes into judgment, which is asked in this way: "Milo killed Clodius." What makes up the cause? That it was done for the sake of defending his safety. Take this away, and there will be no cause. But the accusers denied that Clodius had lain in ambush for Milo; therefore it will come into judgment which of the two laid the ambush for the other. Afterwards let him look at the places of proof, which are taken from their own force and nature. They are taken from their own force when either the whole matter that is done is in question, or a part of it, or the word that it bears, or something that touches that matter. If the whole matter is in question, its force must be explained by a full definition, as in the speech for Ligarius: "And he seized power with no small desire, if that could be called power which he disputed about in private, by the clamour of an ignorant crowd, without any public counsel." If it is a part, by division; as in the speech for Gaius Rabirius, a defendant on a charge of treason: "And we see that in the nature of things there were three options: that he should be with Saturninus, or with the good men, or hide. To hide was like the most shameful death; to be with Saturninus was a mark of madness and wickedness; virtue, honour and shame compelled him to be with the consuls." If it is from the word, as in the Paradoxes: "Let this commander indeed be praised, or even called by that name, or thought worthy of it. In what way? Or over whom free men will this man rule, who cannot rule his own desires?" If it is from what touches the matter, there are several seats and places of arguments. For we seek conjoined things and kinds, and parts subordinate to kinds, and likenesses and unlikenesses, and contraries, and consequences, and things consonant, and things that go before as it were, and things opposed; we will track down the causes of things, and what has arisen from causes, and we will seek greater, equal and lesser things. From conjoined things arguments are drawn in this way, as in the speech for the Manilian law: "For if we have always thought that the tax-farmers are the sinews of the republic, we shall certainly say rightly that the order which carries these out is the support of the other orders." From the kind, as in the speech for Milo: "But if reason has prescribed this to the learned, necessity to the barbarians, custom to peoples, and nature itself to the wild beasts, that they should always repel every force, by whatever means they can, from their body, their head, and their life, you cannot judge this wicked deed without at once judging that everyone who falls into the hands of robbers must perish either by their weapons or by your sentences." From a part subordinate to the kind, in the first speech against Mark Antony: "What law is better? More useful? Even the best, and often demanded in the state? Is it not that praetorian provinces should not be held for more than a year, and consular provinces for not more than two years? If this law is abolished, do the acts of Caesar seem to be preserved?" From likeness, as in the eighth speech: "If in the body there is something of such a kind that it harms the rest of the body, we allow it to be burned and cut, so that some part of the limbs may perish rather than the whole body; so in the body of the republic, whatever is pestilent must be cut away, so that the whole may be safe." And from unlikeness, in the third speech: "A fixed day, however, ought to be awaited not as for a sacrifice, but as for counsel." Now from the contrary, in the speech for Milo: "Clodius met him, riding on horseback without any carriage, without any baggage, without any Greek attendants, as he usually did, without his wife, which he never did; whereas this ambusher, who had prepared that road for the slaughter, was being carried with his wife in a closed carriage, with a great hindrance to the crowd, and with the womanly and pampered retinue of maids and boys." From consequences, in the speech for Roscius: "If Roscius was killed under a law, I admit that his goods were also sold under a law; but if it is established that he was killed against all laws, not only the old ones but even the new, I ask by what right, or in what way, or under what law his goods were sold." From things consonant, as in the speech for Milo: "Clodius met him, riding on horseback, without any carriage, without any baggage, without Greek attendants, as he usually did, without his wife, which he never had." From things opposed, in the speech for Ligarius: "Would he, if he had been able to escape in the manner of Lucullus, have preferred Utica to Rome, to be with Publius Actius rather than with his most harmonious brothers, to be with strangers rather than with his own people?"

units.la: G lincullo modo euadere, Vticæ potius quàm Romæ? cum P. Actio, quàm cum concordissimis fratribus? cum alienis esse, quàm cum suis maluisset? Ex præcurrentibus, ut pro Milone: Interim cum sciret Clodius (neq; enim erat difficile scire,) iter solenne, legitimum, necessarium, ante diem tertium decimum calendarum februarij Miloni esse Lanuuium ad flaminem prodendum, quod erat dictator Lanuuij Milo, Roma subitò ipse profectus pridie est, ut ante suum fundum, quod re intellectum est, Miloni insidias collocaret. Ex causis autem rerum sic, pro lege Manilia: Itaq; hæc uobis prouincia Quirites, si et bel-li utilitatem, et pacis dignitatem sustinere uul-tis, nō modò à calamitate, sed etiam à metu calamitatis est defendenda. Ex ijs autem quæ sunt orta de causis, pro Ligario: Causa tum dubia, quod erat aliquid in utraq; parte, quod probari posset: nunc melior certè ea iudicanda est, quam et-iam dij adiuuerunt. Ex maiore, pro Cecinna: Qui exercitus armatos mouet, is aduocationem togatorum non uidebitur mouisse? Ex minore, pro lege Manilia: Maiores uestri sæpe mercatoribus ac nauiculatoribus iniuriosius tractatis, bella gesserunt: uos tot ciuium Romanorum millibus uno nuncio atq; uno tempore necatis, quo tandem animo esse debetis? Ex pari, pro Q. Roscio Comœdo: Nihil interest inter periurum, et mendacem. nam qui mentitur peierare etiâ consuevit. Sed iam ad eam partē accedamus, quae in ratione conciliationis posita est. Valet enim plurimum ad vincendum, probari mores, instituta et facta, et vitam eorum qui agent causas: et eorum, pro quibus: et item, improbari aduersariorum: valetque in primis ad victoriam in causis cōsequendam, animos eorum, apud quos agitur, conciliari quàm maximè ad benevolentiam, cum erga oratorem, tum erga illum, pro quo dicet orator. Conciliantur autem animi dignitate hominis, rebus gestis, existimatione vitae: in oratore; maximè lenitate vocis, vultus, pudoris significatione, verborum comitate, facilitate, liberalitate, pietate, grati animi opinione, mansuetudine: ut si quid persequatur adversus, inuitum ac coactum se id facere praefeferat. Reorum etiam exprimere mores oratione, iustos, integros, religiosos, timidos, perterrentes iniuriarum, vel in principijs, vel in re narrada, vel in peroratione, tantam habet uim, si est suauiter et cum sensu tractatum, ut saepe plus quàm causa valeat. Huic autem est illa differ adiuncta ratio orationis, quae alio quodam genere mentes iudicū permouet, impellitq;, ut aut oderint, aut diligant, aut inuideat, aut saluum uelint, aut metuant.
units.tr: Or could he have escaped in some way, at Utica rather than at Rome? Would he have preferred to be with Publius Actius rather than with his most harmonious brothers, with strangers rather than with his own? From preceding circumstances, as in pro Milone: Meanwhile Clodius, who knew (for it was not hard to know) that Milo had the customary, lawful and necessary journey to Lanuvium on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, to appoint the flamen, since Milo was dictator of Lanuvium, set out suddenly from Rome the day before, so that he might lay an ambush for Milo before his own estate, as was in fact understood. From the causes of things, thus in pro lege Manilia: Therefore this province, Quirites, if you wish to uphold both the advantage of war and the dignity of peace, must be defended not only from disaster but also from the fear of disaster. From those things which have arisen from causes, in pro Ligario: The case was then doubtful, since there was something on each side that could be proved; now it must certainly be judged the better one, which even the gods have favoured. From the greater, in pro Caecina: Will he who moves armed armies be thought not to have moved the summoning of men in togas? From the lesser, in pro lege Manilia: Your ancestors often waged wars when merchants and shipmasters were treated with injury; you, with so many thousands of Roman citizens killed by a single message at one time, in what frame of mind ought you finally to be? From the equal, in pro Q. Roscio Comoedo: There is no difference between a perjurer and a liar, for he who lies is also accustomed to perjure himself. But now let us come to that part which rests on the method of winning goodwill. For it contributes most to winning a case to have the morals, institutions, deeds and lives of the advocates, and likewise of those for whom they speak, approved, and those of the opponents disapproved; and it is especially effective for victory in court that the minds of those before whom the case is argued be won over as far as possible to goodwill, both towards the orator and towards the one for whom the orator speaks. Minds are won by the dignity of the man, by his achievements, and by the esteem in which his life is held, in the case of the orator; above all by the gentleness of voice and countenance, by the expression of modesty, by courtesy of words, affability, generosity, piety, the reputation of a grateful spirit and mildness, so that if he pursues anyone with harshness, he shows that he does so unwillingly and under compulsion. To express in one's speech the morals of the defendants, that they are just, upright, scrupulous, timid, and frightened of wrongs, whether at the beginning, in the narration of facts, or in the peroration, has such power, if it is handled pleasantly and with feeling, that it often counts for more than the case itself. To this is joined that other kind of speech which, by another sort of appeal, moves and impels the minds of the judges, so that they either hate or love, either envy or wish well, or fear.

units.la: {marks in text are underlined words: autem animi digni, metuant, aut spernant, aut cupiant, aut abhorreant, aut lætentur, aut mereant, aut misereanttur, aut punire uelint, aut ad eos motus adducantur, si qui finitimi sunt, & propinqui ijs ac talibus animi perturbationibus. Atque illud in primis sagacissimè est ab oratore inuestigandum, quo magis declinet animus iudicis, quid sentiat, quid existimet, quid expectet, quid uelit, quò deduci oratione facillimè posse uideatur, ut facilius eum ut currentem incitare possit. Oportet autem eos motus, quos orator adhibere uolet, iudici, ut in seipso impressos atque inustos efse præseferat uerbis, sententijs, uoce, uultu, collachrymatione denique ipsa: neque enim facile est perficere, ut irascatur iudex, si orator ipse id lente ferre uideatur: neq; ut oderit, nisi ipsum flagrantem odio ante uiderit: neque ut ad misericordiam adducatur, nisi ille ipse dicendo, agendoq; signa doloris ostenderit. Hæc autem sere sunt in iudicum animis molieнda: amor, odium, iracundia, inuidia, misericordia, spes, læ-titia, timor, molestia. Sentimus autem amorem conciliari, si id uelle uideamur, quod sit utile ipsis, apud quos agamus defendere; si aut pro bonis uiris, aut certe pro ijs qui illis boni atque utiles sint, laborare. Enitendum præterea est, ut ostendat orator, in ea re quam defendat, aut dignitatem inesse, aut utilitatem: eumq;, cui conci-lit hunc amorem, significet nihil ad utilitatem suam retulisse, ac nihil omnino fecisse causa sua. hæc autem omnia moderate ab eo sunt facienda, ne quos ob benefacta diligi voluerit, eorum laudem atque gloriam, cui maximè inuideri solet, nimis uideatur efferre. Ex ijs ijsdē locis, & odium in alios struet, uel à se dimouebit. Eademq; hæc genera tractanda sunt in iracundia uel excitanda, uel sedanda. nam si quod ipsis qui audiunt, perniciosum aut inutile sit, id factum augeat, odium creatur: sin quod aut in bonos uiros, aut in eos quos quisque minimè debuerit, aut in Rempublicam: tum excitatur, si non tam acerbum odium, tamen aut inuidiæ aut odij non dissimilis offensio. Item timor incutitur aut ex ipsorum periculis, aut ex communibus: interior est ille proprius, sed hic quoque communis ad eandem similitudinem est perducendus. par, atque una ratio est spei, lætitiæ, molestiæ. Horum longè autē est acerrimus inuidiæ motus, tam in ea comprimenda, quàm in excitanda. Inuident autem homines maximè paribus, aut inferioribus: cum se relictos sentiunt, illos autem dolent euolasse. Sed etiam superioribus inuidetur sæpe uehementer, et eo magis, si intolerantius se iactant, & æquabilitatem communis iuris praestantia dignitatis aut fortunae suae transeunt: quae si inflammanda sunt, maxime dicendum est non esse uirtute parta, deinde uitijs, atque peccatis: tum si erunt honestiora, aut graviora, tamen non esse tanti ullamerita, quanta insolentia hominis, quantumque fastidium. ad sedandā autem, magno illa labore, magnis periculis esse parta: nec ad suum commodum, sed ad aliorum esse collata: sesque, si quam gloriam peperisse uideatur, tametsi ea non sit iniqua merces periculi, tamen ea non delectari, totamque abijcere atque deponere: omninoque perficiundum est, ut haec opinio minuatur, et illa excellens opinione fortuna cum laboribus et miserijs permixta esse uideatur. Iam misericordia mouetur, si is qui audit, adduci potest, aut illa quae de altero deplorentur, ad suas res reuocet; quas aut tulerit acerbas, aut timeat, aut intuens alium crebro ad seipsum reuertatur. ita cum singuli casus humanarum miseriarum graviter accipiuntur, si dicuntur dolenter: tum adflicta et prostrata uirtus maxime luctuosa est. et ut illa altera pars orationis, quae probitatis commendatione boni uiri debet speciem tueri, lenis atque summissa: sic haec, quae suscipitur ab oratore, ad commutandos animos, atque omni ratione flectendos, intenta ac uehemens esse debet.
units.tr: {Marks in the text are underlined words: the judges' minds are moved in these ways: that they fear, or despise, or desire, or shrink from, or rejoice, or deserve, or pity, or wish to punish, or are led to those emotions which are neighbouring and akin to these and similar disturbances of the mind. And above all the orator must investigate most shrewdly, to what the judge's mind inclines, what he feels, what he thinks, what he expects, what he wishes, and by what speech he can most easily be brought, so that he may more easily be roused by him as he runs. But the emotions which the orator wishes to employ ought to be shown to the judge as though impressed and branded upon the speaker himself, by words, sentences, voice, countenance, and finally by tears; for it is not easy to bring it about that the judge be angry if the orator himself seems to bear it calmly, nor that he hate unless he has first seen the orator himself burning with hatred, nor that he be moved to pity unless the orator himself has shown signs of grief in his speaking and gesturing. These are the feelings which are to be brought about in the minds of judges: love, hatred, anger, envy, pity, hope, joy, fear, distress. Now we perceive that love is won if we seem to wish what is useful to those whom we are defending; if we labour for good men, or at least for those who are good and useful to them. Furthermore, the orator must strive to show that there is either dignity or usefulness in the matter he defends, and he must make it clear to the one whose love he is winning that he has referred nothing to his own advantage and has done nothing at all for his own cause. All this must be done with moderation, lest, when he wishes to be loved for good deeds, he seem to extol too much the praise and glory of the one to whom envy is most usually directed. From the same topics he will both build up hatred against others, or remove it from himself. And these same kinds are to be handled in arousing or calming anger. For if something harmful or useless to the hearers themselves is increased by the act, hatred is created; but if it is directed against good men, or against those whom no one ought to have harmed, or against the commonwealth, then anger is roused, even if it is not so bitter a hatred, yet an offence not unlike envy or hatred. Likewise fear is instilled either from their own dangers or from common ones; the former is more personal, but the latter too must be brought to the same likeness. The method of hope, joy and distress is equal and one. Of these, the movement of envy is by far the most vehement, both in checking it and in arousing it. Men envy most those who are their equals or inferiors, since they feel they have been left behind, and grieve that the others have flown past. But even superiors are often envied vehemently, and the more so if they boast too intolerably and pass beyond the equality of common right by the excellence of their rank or fortune; and if these are to be inflamed, it must be said above all that they were not won by virtue but by vices and sins; then, if they are more honourable or weighty, yet that they are not worth so much merit as the man's insolence and disdain amount to. But to calm it, one must say that those things were won by great labour and great dangers, and were gathered not for one's own advantage but for others; and that if the man seems to have won some glory, even though that is not an unfair reward for danger, yet he takes no delight in it, and casts it off and lays it down entirely; and above all it must be brought about that this opinion be diminished and that that outstanding fortune be seen to be mixed with labours and miseries. Now pity is stirred if the hearer can be led to refer to his own affairs those things which are lamented about another, which he has either suffered bitterly or fears, or, looking upon another, keeps returning often to himself. Thus when single cases of human misery are received with weight, if they are told with feeling, then virtue afflicted and prostrate is most mournful. And just as that other part of the speech, which by commending uprightness ought to maintain the appearance of a good man, is gentle and subdued, so this part, which the orator undertakes to change minds and bend them by every means, ought to be intense and vehement.

units.la: { } — no footnote on this page. debet. Sed est quaedam in his duobus generibus, quorum alterum lene, alterum uehemens esse uo‑ lumus, difficilis ad distinguendum similitudo. Nam ex illa lenitate, ad hanc uim acerrimam, influat oportet aliquid: & ex hac ui nonnun‑quam animi aliquid influendum est illi lenita‑ ti. In utroque autem genere dicendi, & princi‑pia tarda sunt, & exitus tamen ipsi & producti esse debent. Nam neque assiliendum statim est ad illud genus orationis uehemens: nec cum in eam orationem ingressus sis, celeriter dis‑ scedendum est. Sed in perturbationibus excitan‑ dis in primis consideretur, postulet ne causa. nam neque paruis in rebus adhibendae sunt hae di‑ cendi faces: neque ita animatis hominibus, ut nihil ad eorum mentes oratione flectendas pro‑ ficere possimus, ne aut irrisione, aut odio di‑ gni putemur, si aut tragedias agamus in nu‑ gis, aut conuellere adoriamur ea quae non pos‑ sint commoueri. Sed quoniam tribus rebus om‑ nes ad nostram sententiam perducimus, aut do‑ cendo, ut diximus, aut conciliando, aut permo‑ uendo: una ex tribus his rebus res praenobis est ferenda, ut nihil aliud nisi docere uelle uideâ‑ mur: reliquae duae, sicuti sanguis in corpori‑ bus, sic illae in perpetuis orationibus fusae es‑se debebunt. Quoniam uero ad hoc idem uide‑ tur pertinere uel ad sedandas, uel ad molliedas, uel ad recreandas iudicum mentes, risus, & facetiarum tractatio, de his quoq; aliquid breuiter afferemus. De risu autem quinq; sunt quae quaerantur: unum, quid sit: alterum, unde sit: tertium, sit ne oratoris uelle risum mouere: quartum, quatenus: quintum, quae sint genera ridiculi. Atque illud primum, quid sit ipse risus, quo pacto concitetur, ubi sit, quomodo existat, atque ita repente erumpat, ut eum cupientes tenere nequeamus, & quomodo simul latera, os, uenas, multa, oculos occupet, uiderint Physici. neq; enim ad nos hoc pertinet. Locus autem ridiculorum, unde proueniunt, turpitudine et deformitate quadam continetur. haec enim ridentur uel sola, uel maxime. Est autem, ut ad illud tertium uenia, oratoris, mouere risum, uel quod ipsa bilaritas beneuolentiam conciliat ei, per quem excitata est: uel quod admiramur omnes dicme, uno saepe in uerbo positum, maximeque respondetis, nonnunquam etiam lacessentis: uel quod frangit aduersarium, quod impedit, quod eleuat; quod deterret, quod refutat, uel quod ipsum oratorem politum esse hominem significat, quod eruditum, quod urbanum, maximeque; quod tristitiam ac seueritatem mitigat & relaxat: odiosaque res saepe, quas argumentis dilui non facile est, ioco risuq; dissoluit.
units.tr: {} — no footnote on this page. debet. But there is in these two kinds, of which we wish one to be gentle and the other vehement, a similarity that is difficult to distinguish. For from that gentleness something must flow into that most vehement force, and from that force something of feeling must sometimes flow into that gentleness. In each kind of speaking, both the beginnings are slow, and yet the endings themselves ought to be extended. For one must neither leap at once into that vehement kind of speech, nor, once one has entered upon such speech, depart from it quickly. But in arousing the emotions one must above all consider what the case requires; for these torches of speech are not to be applied to trivial matters, nor to men so disposed that we can accomplish nothing by speech to bend their minds, lest we be thought worthy of ridicule or scorn, if we perform tragedies over trifles, or set about shaking those things which cannot be moved. But since we bring all men to our opinion by three things, either by teaching, as we have said, or by winning favour, or by moving, one of these three must be carried before us, so that we seem to wish nothing but to teach; the other two, like the blood in bodies, ought to be poured through the whole of the speech. Since indeed the handling of laughter and witticisms seems to pertain to this same end, whether to calm, or to soften, or to refresh the minds of judges, we shall also briefly say something about these. There are five questions to be asked about laughter: one, what it is; second, whence it comes; third, whether it is the orator's business to wish to move laughter; fourth, how far; fifth, what kinds of the ridiculous there are. And as to the first, what laughter itself is, how it is excited, where it is, how it arises, and how it bursts out so suddenly that we cannot hold it back when we want to, and how at once it occupies the sides, the mouth, the veins, the cheeks and the eyes, let the natural philosophers see to that; for this does not pertain to us. Now the place of the ridiculous, whence it arises, is contained in a certain baseness and deformity; for these things alone, or above all, are laughed at. And as for the third question, whether it is the orator's part to move laughter, the answer is yes: either because cheerfulness itself wins goodwill for the one through whom it is aroused; or because we all admire, in speech, what is placed in a single word, and especially in replies, and sometimes also in provocations; or because it breaks down the adversary, hinders him, lifts up the speaker, deters, and refutes; or because it shows that the orator himself is a polished man, learned, and urbane; and above all because it softens and relaxes sadness and severity; and often it dissolves, by jest and laughter, matters that are hateful and cannot easily be dissolved by arguments.

units.la: Quatenus autem sint ridicula tractanda oratoris, perquàm diligenter uidendum est, id quod in quærendi quarto loco posueramus. nam nec insignis improbitas, & scelere iuncta, nec rursus miseria insignis agitata ridetur. facinorosi maiori quadam ui, quàm ridiculi, uulnerari uolunt: miseri illudi nolunt, nisi si se forte iactant. parcendum est autem maximè charitati hominum, ne temere in eos dicamus qui diliguntur. In hac autem re non modò illud præcipitur, ne quid insulse: sed etiâ, si quid perridiculè possis. Tria uerò sunt genera facetiarum, ut ad illud perueniamus, quod ultimo loco posueramus: quorum unum re tractatur, alterum dicto: simul re & dicto, tertium re, si quando quid, tanquam aliqua fabella, narratur, in qua ita facta demonstranda sunt, ut mores eius de quo narres, ut sermo, ut uultus omnes exprimantur: ut ijs qui audiunt, tum geri illa, fieriq; uideantur. In dicto autem ridiculum est id, quod uerbi aut sententiæ quodam acumine mouetur: sed uerborum tollitur, si uerba mutaueris: sententiarum permanet, quibuscunq; uerbis uti uelis. Sed quoniâ infinitus est facetiarum numerus, ideo his breuiter explicatis, non progrediamur ulterius. Sed quum iam satis à nobis de generis iudicialis inuentione dictum sit quàm breuissimè, quamuis ad deliberatiuum etiam,
units.tr: How far jokes may be used by the orator must be considered very carefully, as we set out to do in the fourth place of invention. For a conspicuous wickedness joined with crime is not laughed at, nor is conspicuous misery laughed at when it is mocked. Criminals want to be wounded with a certain greater force than by ridicule; the wretched do not want to be mocked, unless perhaps they make a show of their misery. We must above all spare people's affection, so that we do not speak rashly against those who are loved. In this matter the rule is not only to avoid anything foolish, but also, if you can, to say something most amusing. There are three kinds of witty remarks, and to reach the one we placed last: one consists in the matter, another in the words, and a third, which combines matter and words, when something is related like a little story, in which the deeds must be so displayed, and the character, speech and expression of the person you describe so fully portrayed, that those who hear it seem to see those things being done and happening. A witty remark in words is one that is moved by some sharpness of expression or of thought: a verbal joke is destroyed if you change the words, but a joke of thought remains, whatever words you choose to use. But since the number of witty remarks is unlimited, having explained these briefly, let us not proceed further. Yet since we have said enough, as briefly as possible, about the invention of the judicial kind, although what we have said could also be applied to the deliberative and demonstrative kinds, we shall now turn to treating the particular invention of the two remaining kinds.

units.la: H etiam, et demonstratiuum, quae diximus, possint accommodari, ad propriam reliquorum duorum generum inuentionem tractandam accedemus. Et ut ab eo quod in laude et uituperatione positum est, exordiamur: dico, perspicuum esse alia in homine optanda, alia laudanda. Optantur pecuniae, genus, propinqui, amici, opes, ualetudo, forma, uires, caeteraque quae sunt aut corporis, aut externa. Verum quoniam ipsa uirtus in harum rerum usu ac moderatione maxime cernitur, tractata etiam in laudationibus haec sunt, naturae et fortunae bona: ut si habuerit ille, quem laudamus, bene his usum: si non habuerit, sapienter caruisse: si amiserit, moderate tulisse dicamus. In his etenim summa laus est, non extulisse se in potestate, non fuisse insolentem in pecunia, non se praetulisse aliis propter abundantiam fortunae: ut opes et copiae non superbiae uideantur, ac libidini, sed bonitati ac moderationi facultatem et materiam dedisse. Virtus autem, quae est per seipsa laudabilis, ac sine qua nihil laudari potest, plures habet partes. Sunt enim aliae uirtutes, quae uidentur in moribus hominum, et quaedam comitate ac beneficentia positae: aliae, quae in ingenii aliqua facultate. In his tamen illae potissimum commendantur, quae non ipsis, qui eas in se habent, sed generi hominum num fructuosæ putantur. Sed tamen in laudando iungenda sunt etiam hæc genera virtutum. Ferunt enim aures hominum, cum illa quæ iucunda & grata, tum etiam illa quæ mirabilia sunt, in virtute laudari. Et quoniam singularum virtutum sunt certa quædam officia & munera, & sua cuique virtuti laus propria debetur, erit explicandum in laude iustitiæ, quid cum fide, quid cum æquabilitate, quid cum eiusmodi aliquo officio is qui laudabitur fecerit. Item eadem in cæteris, res gestæ ad cuiusque virtutis genus, & uim & nomen accommodabuntur.
units.tr: And to begin with what concerns praise and blame: I say that it is evident that some things in a man are to be wished for, others to be praised. Money, birth, relatives, friends, wealth, health, beauty, strength, and the other things that belong either to the body or are external, are wished for. But since virtue itself is seen most clearly in the use and moderation of these things, those goods of nature and fortune are also treated in panegyrics: so that if the man we praise has used them well, we may say so; if he has lacked them, that he went without them wisely; if he has lost them, that he bore their loss with moderation. For the highest praise lies in this: not to have become proud through power, not to have been arrogant in money, not to have put oneself above others on account of abundance of fortune; so that wealth and resources seem to have offered the means and material not for pride and lust, but for goodness and moderation. Virtue, which is praiseworthy in itself and without which nothing can be praised, has many parts. For some virtues appear in people's conduct and consist in courtesy and beneficence; others lie in some faculty of the mind. Among these, however, those are chiefly commended which are thought to be useful to the human race rather than to those who possess them. Yet in praising, these kinds of virtue must also be joined together. For people's ears welcome the praise of virtue in those qualities that are both pleasing and agreeable, and also in those that are wonderful. And since each of the individual virtues has certain fixed duties and functions, and its own proper praise is due to each, in praising justice we must explain what the person being praised did in regard to good faith, what in regard to fairness, and what in regard to some duty of this kind. Likewise in the other virtues, the deeds performed will be fitted to the kind and force and name of each virtue.

units.la: Gratissima autem laus eorum factorum habetur, quæ suscepta uidentur à uiris fortibus, sine emolumento ac præmio: quæ vero etiam, cum labore ipsorum, hæc habent uberrimam copiam ad laudandum: quod & dici ornatissime possunt, & audiri facillime. Ea denique virtus esse uidetur præstantis uiri, quæ est fructuosa aliis, ipsi autem laboriosa, aut periculosa, aut certe gratuita. Magna etiam illa laus, & admirabilis uideri solet, tulisse casus sapienter aduersos: non fractum esse fortuna: retinuisse in rebus asperis dignitatem. Neque tamen illa non ornant, habiti honores, decreta virtutis præmia, res gestæ iudicijs hominum comprobatæ: in quibus etiam felicifœlicitatem ipsam deorum immortalium iudicio tributam, laudationis est. Sumendæ autem res es=runt, aut magnitudine præstabiles, aut nouitate primæ, aut genere ipso singulares. neq; enim paruæ, neq; usitatæ, neq; uulgares admiratione, aut omnino laude dignæ uideri solent. Vituperandi autem præcepta contrarijs ex uitijs sumenda es=se, perspicuum est. Sed ut aliquando ad tertium genus causæ peruenianus, suadere aliquid, aut dis= suadere grauissimæ mihi uidetur esse personæ. nam & sapientis est, consilium explicare suum de rebus maximis: & honesti & diserti, ut mente prouidere, authoritate probare, orationæ persua= dere possit. Ergo in suadendo nihil est optabilius, quàm dignitas. nam qui utilitatem putat, non quid maximè uelit suasor, sed quid interdum magis sequatur, uidet. nemo est enim, præsertim in clara ciuitate, quin putet expetendam maximè dignitatem: sed uincit utilitas plerunq;, quum subest ille timor, ea neglecta, ne dignitatem quidem posse retineri. Controuersia autem inter homines sententias, aut in illo est, utrum sit utilius: aut etiam, cum id conuenit, certatur, utrum honestati potius, an utilitati consulendum sit? Quæ quia pugnare inter se uidentur, qui utilitatem defendit, enumerabit commoda pacis, opum, potentiæ, pecuniæ, uectigalium, præsidij militum, utilitates cæterarum rerum, quarũ fructum utilitate metimur. itemq; incommoda contrariorũ.
units.tr: The most welcome praise is given to those deeds that brave men are seen to undertake without profit or reward; and those that also involve their own toil offer the richest material for praise, because they can be spoken of most elegantly and heard most readily. Indeed, that virtue seems to belong to an excellent man which is useful to others but laborious, dangerous, or at least unrewarded for himself. That great and admirable praise is also usually thought to lie in having borne adverse chances wisely: not to have been broken by fortune, to have kept one's dignity in harsh circumstances. Nor do the honours one has received, the rewards of virtue decreed, and deeds approved by the judgment of men fail to adorn a man; and in these, even the good fortune itself, attributed to the judgment of the immortal gods, belongs to praise.
