The matters to be chosen are either remarkable for their greatness, or first in their novelty, or singular in their very kind; for things that are small, ordinary, or commonplace are usually not thought worthy of admiration or of praise at all. That the precepts of blame are to be drawn from the contrary vices is clear. But now, to come at last to the third kind of cause: to advise something or to dissuade from it seems to me the business of a most serious person. For it belongs to the wise man to set out his own counsel on the greatest matters, and to the honest and eloquent man to be able to foresee with his mind, prove with his authority, and persuade with his speech. Therefore in advising nothing is more to be wished for than honour. For the man who thinks only of advantage sees not what the advisor most wishes, but what might sometimes follow more closely. For there is no one, especially in a famous state, who does not think that honour is above all to be desired; but advantage usually prevails, when that fear lurks that, if it is neglected, honour itself cannot be kept. But the dispute among men's opinions lies either in this: which is more advantageous; or else, when both are agreed, the question is which should be consulted, honour or advantage. Since these seem to conflict with each other, the one who defends advantage will enumerate the benefits of peace, of resources, of power, of money, of revenues, of the protection of soldiers, and the advantages of other things, whose fruit we measure by advantage; and likewise the disadvantages of their opposites.

units.la: Qui ad dignitatē impellet, maiorum exempla, quæ erunt vel cũ periculo gloriosa, colliget: positeritatis immortalem memoriam augebit, utilitatem ex laude nasci defendet, semperq; cum dignitate esse coniunctam. Sed quid fieri possit, aut non possit, quidq; etiam fit necesse, aut non fit, in utraq; re, maximè est quærendũ. Ad cõsilium autem de Repub. dandũ, caput est, nosse Rempublicam: ad dicendum vero probabiliter, nosse mores ciuitatis: qui quia crebrò mutantur, genus quoque orationis est sæpe mutandum. Et quanquam una fere uis est eloquentiæ, tamen quia summa dignitas est populi, grauissima causa Reipublicæ, maximi motus multitudinis, genus quoque dicendi grandius quoddam & illustrius esse adhibendum videtur: maximaq; pars orationis admonenda est ad animorum motus: nonnunquam aut cohortatione, aut commemoratione aliqua, aut in spem, aut in metum, aut ad cupiditatem, aut ad gloriam concitandos: sæpe etiam à temeritate, iracundia, spe, iniuria, invidia, crudelitate, revocandos. Exposui fere, ut potui, in omni genere causarum, quæ sequi possimus, quæ sugere, quæ spectare, qua omnino in causis ratione versari. Proximum est, ut de dispositione orationis, ut proposuimus, aliquid breuiter pertrãctemus. Cuius ratio duplex est: altera, quam afferit natura causarum: altera, quae oratorum iudicio & prudentia comparatur. Nam ut aliquid ante rem dicamus, deinde ut rem exponamus, post ut eam probemus nostris praesidijs confirmandis, contrariisq; refutandis: deinde ut concludamus, atq; ita peroremus. hoc dicendi genus natura ipsa praescribit. Vt uero statuamus ea quae probandi, docendi, persuadendi causa dicenda sunt, quemadmodum componamus, id est uel maxime proprium oratoris prudentiae. Nam & digredi ab eo quod proposuerit, atq; agas, permouendorum animorum causa, saepe utile est. Itaq; uel narratione exposita, saepe datur ad commouendos animos digrediendi locus: uel argumentis nostris confirmatis, uel contrarijs refutatis: uel utroq; loco, uel omnibus, fi habet eam causa dignitatem, atq; copiam, recte id fieri potest. Sed quemadmodum in oratore optimus quisque, sic in oratione firmiffimum quidque primum esse debebit: dum illud tamen in utroque teneatur, ut ea quae excellant, feruentur etiam ad perorandum: fiq; erunt mediocria, in medium agmen conijciantur. His omnibus rebus confideratis, tum deniq; id quod est primum, dicendum: postremo debemus cogitare, quo utamur exordio. nam fi quando id primum muni inuenire uoluerimus, nullum nobis occurret, nisi aut exile, aut nugatorium, aut vulgare, aut commune. Principia aut dicendi causarum propria esse, ab earumq; uisceribus deduci oportet.
units.tr: The one who urges toward honour will gather examples from the ancestors, which, even when they involved danger, were glorious; he will enlarge the immortal memory of posterity, he will argue that advantage arises from praise, and that it is always joined with honour. But what can or cannot be done, and what is necessary or not necessary to be done, must be sought above all in each matter. For giving counsel about the state, the essential thing is to know the commonwealth; but for speaking persuasively, to know the character of the citizens; and since these change often, the style of speech too must often be changed. And although the power of eloquence is almost one and the same, yet because the dignity of the people is supreme, the cause of the commonwealth most serious, and the movements of the multitude very great, the style of speaking also seems to require something grander and more illustrious; and the greater part of the speech must be directed to stirring the emotions of minds: sometimes by exhortation, or by some recollection, to rouse them either to hope, or to fear, or to desire, or to glory; often too they must be called back from rashness, anger, hope, injustice, envy, and cruelty. I have set out, as well as I could, for every kind of cause, what we may follow, what avoid, what aim at, and in general how one should proceed in causes. Next it is in order that we briefly treat of the arrangement of the speech, as we proposed. Its method is twofold: one is that which the nature of the causes prescribes, the other is that which is acquired by the judgment and prudence of orators. For to speak first about the matter, then to set the matter out, afterwards to prove it by strengthening our own supports and refuting the opposing ones, and then to conclude, and so bring it to an end: this order of speaking nature itself prescribes. But to decide what things are to be said for the sake of proving, teaching, and persuading, and how we should arrange them, this is especially the proper business of the orator's prudence. For to digress from what one has proposed and is handling, for the sake of stirring the minds, is often useful. Therefore, either after the narration has been set out, there is often an opportunity given for a digression to move the minds; or after our arguments have been confirmed, or the contrary ones refuted; or at either point, or at all of them, if the cause has the dignity and abundance for it, this can rightly be done. But just as in an orator the best man comes first, so in a speech the strongest point should come first; provided that it is observed in both cases that those things which excel are to be reserved also for the peroration, and those which are middling are to be placed in the middle of the line. When all these things have been considered, then at last what comes first is to be spoken; finally we ought to consider which exordium we should use. For if we want to find that first part at once, nothing will present itself to us except what is slight, trifling, vulgar, or commonplace. The beginnings of speeches ought to be peculiar to the causes and drawn from their very inner parts.

units.la: Idcirco tota causa pertētata atq; perspecta, locis omnibus mucetis atq; instructis, cōsiderandū est, quo principio fit utendum. Sumetur enim ex his reb. quæ erunt uberrimæ uel in argumētis, uel in ijs partibus, ad quas diximus digredi sæpe oportere. Ita et moneti aliquid afferret, cum erunt pene ex intima defensione depromptā: et appare bit ea nō modo nō esse cōmunia, nec in alias causas posse transferri: sed penitus ex ea causa, quæ tunc agitur, defluxisse. Omne autem principiū, aut rei totius quæ agetur significationē habere debebit: aut aditū ad causam, et munitionē: aut quoddā ornamentū, et dignitatē. Sed oportet, ut ædibus ac templis uestibula et aditus, sic causis principia pro portiōe rerū præponere. Itaq; in paruis atq; frequentib. causis ab ipsa re sæpe est exordiri cōmodius: cum uero crit utendū principio, aut ex reo, aut ex aduersario, aut ex re, aut ex ijs apud quos agitur, ducemus sententias. Ex reo, quæ significet uirū bonū, quæ liberalē, quæ calamitosum, quæ misericordia dignū, quæ uaieat contra falsam cirminationē. Ex aduersario, ijsdē ex locis fere cōtraria. Ex re, si crudelis, si in fanda, si praeter opinionem, si immerito, si misera, si ingrata, si indigna, si noua, si quae restitui fanariq; no possit. Ex ijs aut apud quos agetur, ut benevolos beneq; exciistimantes efficiamus. Maxima vero copia principiorum ad iudicem aut alliciendum aut incitandum ex ijs locis trahitur, qui ad motus animorum concitandos inerunt in causa: quos tamen totos in principio explicari non oportebit, sed tantum impelli primo iudice leniter, ut iam inclinato, reliqua incumbat oratio.
units.tr: Therefore, once the whole case has been tested and examined and all the topics have been gathered and equipped, we must consider which beginning to use. It will be taken from those matters that are most fruitful either in the arguments or in those parts to which we said it is often right to digress. Thus it may also bring some persuasion, since it will be drawn almost from the innermost part of the defence, and it will be evident that these matters are not only not commonplace, nor can they be transferred to other cases, but have flowed entirely from the case now being argued. Every beginning, moreover, ought to have either an indication of the whole matter to be treated, or an approach to the case and a fortifying of it, or some ornament and dignity. But just as buildings and temples have vestibules and approaches, so cases should have beginnings placed in front in proportion to the matter. Therefore in small and frequent cases it is often more convenient to begin from the matter itself. When a beginning must be used, we shall draw our sentiments from the defendant, from the opponent, from the matter, or from those before whom the case is argued. From the defendant: what shows him to be a good man, a generous man, one who is in misfortune, one worthy of pity, one who is strong against false accusation. From the opponent: roughly the opposite, drawn from the same places. From the matter: if it is cruel, impious, beyond expectation, undeserved, wretched, ungrateful, unworthy, new, or such that it cannot be restored or repaired. From those before whom the case is argued: so that we make them well-disposed and judging us fairly. The greatest supply of beginnings for winning over or stirring up the judge is drawn from those topics which will be present in the case for arousing the emotions of the mind. These need not all be unfolded at the beginning, however, but only the first judge gently pushed, so that, now inclined, the rest of the speech may lean upon him.

units.la: Connexa autem ita esse cohaerenti orationi debebunt, ut tanquam cohaerentia cum omni corpore membra esse videantur, non ut sibi audientiam velle facere videantur. Sed quando utendum, aut non sit narratione, consilij est. neq; enim, si nota res est, nec si dubium sit quid gestum sit, narrari oportet: nec si aduersarius narrauit, nisi si refellemus, ne illa quae suspicionem & crimen efficient, contraq; nos erunt, acriter persequamur, et quicquid poterit, detrahamus. Fiet autem narratio brevis, si verbum nullum redundet: & cum tantum verborum est, quantum necesse est.
units.tr: The parts that are joined to the speech must be connected to the coherent whole in such a way that they appear to be members cohering with the whole body, not as if they wanted to win the hearers' attention for themselves. But whether narration should be used or not is a matter of judgement. For if the matter is well known, or if it is doubtful what was done, it need not be narrated; nor, if the opponent has narrated, need we narrate unless we are going to refute him, and then we should pursue vigorously, and strip away as far as we can, whatever will create suspicion and accusation and turn against us. The narration will be brief if no word is superfluous, and there are only as many words as are necessary.

units.la: Erit autem perspicua, si verbis usitatis, si ordine temporum conseruato, si non interrupte narrabimus. Sequitur, ut causa ponatur: in quo uidendum est, quid in controversiam veniat: tunc fugigerenda sunt firmamenta causae coniunctē, & infirmandis contrarijs, et tuis cõfirmandis. nam que una in causis ratio quædam est eius orationis, quæ ad probandam argumentationem valet: ea autem & confirmationem & reprehensionem quærit. Sed quia neq; reprehendi, quæ contrà dicuntur, possunt, nisi tua cõfirmes: neq; hæc confirmari, nisi illa refellas: idcirco hæc, & natura, & utilitate, & tractatione coniuncta sunt. Omnia uero concludenda plerunque rebus augendis, uel inflammando iudice, uel mitigando: omniaq; cùm superioribus orationis locis, tum maximè extremo, ad mentes iudicum permouendas, et ad utilitatem nostrā uocandas conferenda sunt. Cum uero omnis ex re atq; uerbis constet oratio: neq; uerba sedem habere possint, si rem subtraxeris: neq; res lumen, si uerba semoueris: cũ de rebus hactenus, earumq; series dictum sit, ad uerborum elocutionem iam nostra conuertetur oratio: quæ in hoc posita est, ut latinè, ut plane, ut ornatè, ut ad id quodcunq; agetur, aptè dicamus. Sed illa duo superiora linquamus, quæ cognitionem habent facilem. neq; enim conandi est, docere eum dicere, qui loqui nesciat: nec speran dum, qui latinè non possit, hunc ornatè esse dicturum: neq; uero qui non dicat quod intelligamus, hunc posse quod miremur dicere, & ad ornatum uerborum deueniamus. Cum igitur omnis rii oratio conficiatur ex uerbis, eorum primum nobis ratio simpliciter uidenda est, deinde coniuncte. nam est quidā ornatus orationis, qui ex singulis uerbis est: alius, qui ex continuatis, coniunctisq; cōstat. Ergo utemur uerbis aut ijs quae propria sunt, et certa quasi uocabula rerum, pene unà nata cum rebus ipsis: aut ijs quae transferuntur, et quasi alieno in loco collocantur: aut ijs quae nouamus, et facimus ipsi. In propriis est igitur uerbis ea laus oratoris, ut abiecta atque obsoleta fugiat: lectis atq; illustribus utatur, in quibus plenum quiddam ac sonans inesse uideatur. Sed in hoc uerborum genere proprioru̇m delectus est quidam habendus: atq; is aurium quodam iudicio ponderandus: in quo consuetudo etiam bene loquendi ualet plurimum. Quoniam uero in propriis uitium tantummodo uitamus, in quo nō magna est laus oratoris, quid ipse ædificet, et in quo adiungat artem, id esse à nobis quaerendum atq; explicādum uidetur. Tria sunt igitur, quae in uerbo simplici orator affert ad illustrandā atq; exornandā orationē: aut inusitatum uerbum, aut nouatum, aut translatum. quia uero inusitata, prisca fere, ac uetusta, et ab usu quotidiani sermonis iam diu intermissa, poetarumq; licentiae liberiora, quam oratorum, sed quae tamen propter antiquitatem habent aliquando in oratione dignitatem, ut proles, foboles,effari,nuncupari,opinabar,rebar,in proprijs sunt,de ijs nihil dico. Ita duo omnino remanent simplicium uerborum genera, quae afferrat splendore orationi, nouatorū scilicet,& transla-torum. Nouantur autem uerba, quae ab eo qui dicit, ipso gignuntur,ac fiunt uel coniungendis uerbis, ut uersutiloquus: uel sine coniunctione, ut incuruescere. Proximus ille modus trāsfe-rendi uerbi latè patet, quē necessitas genuit,inopia coacta & angustijs: post aūt delectatio,iucunditasq; celebrauit. Nam ut uestis frigoris depellendi causa primò reperta, post adhiberi coepta est ad ornamentum etiam corporis, et dignitatem: sic uerbi translatio instituta est inopiae causa,frequentata delectationis. Nam gemmare uites,luxuriem esse in herbis,laetas segetes etiam rustici dicunt. quod enim declarari uix uerbo proprio potest,id translato quum est dictum illustrat,id quod intelligi uolumus,eius rei,quam alieno uerbo posfuimus, similitudo. Ergo hae trāslationes,quasi mutuationes sunt,cum quod non habeas,aliunde fumas: illae autem,quae non inopiam indicant,sed orationi fplēdoris aliquid accersunt,delectant maximè, cum uerbum similitudine quadam in alieno loco tanquam in suo positum agnoscitur. quod fi nullam habet similitudinem tudinem cum eo, repudiatur. Quamobrem ea transferri oportet, quæ aut clariorem faciunt rem: ut concionum procellas, eloquetiæ flumen. aut quæ rem totam siue facti alicuius, siue consilij magis significent: ut illa, incensum ira, inflammatum cupiditate, lapsum errore. aut breuitas causa, ut illud pro Milone: Magnum fuit Milonis conficere illam pestem. non potuerunt breuiis proprijs uerbis tot scelera exponi, quàm sunt uno significata translato. Qua in re fugienda est dissimilitudo, ne cœli ingentes fornices dicamus: quũ nulla sit in sphæra fornicis similitudo. Deinde uidendum est, ne longè simile sit dustum. nam libentius copulum, quàm syrtim matrimonij dixerim: uoraginem bonorum potius, quàm Charybdim. facilius enim ad ea quæ uisa, quàm ad illa quæ audita sunt, mentis oculi feruntur. Summa uero laus est uerbi transferendi, ut sensum feriat id quod translatum fit. Qua re fugienda est omnis turpitudo carum rerum, ad quas eorum animos qui audiunt, trahat similitudo. Nolo morte dici Africani castratã Rempublicam: nolo sterceus curiæ dici Glauciam, quamuis sit simile. est enim in utroque deformis cogitatio similitudinis. Nolo præterea translatum esse maius, quàm res postulet, ut tempestas ceommeffationis: aut minus, ut commeffatio tempestatis. aut angustius, quàm illud proprium, ac suum: ut, me adiri abnuto: melius esset ueto, prohibeo, absterreo. Atque etiam, si uereamur ne paulò durior translatio esse uideatur, mollie da est præposito sæpe uerbo. ut in M. Antonii: Manendum mihi statucbã in uigilia quasi quasidam consulari, ac senatoria. Etenim uerecunda esse debet translatio, ut deducta esse in alienum locum, non irruisse uideatur. Fit & aliud genus translationis non uno uerbo, ut superiora, sed pluribus continuatis, ut aliud dicatur, & aliud intelligatur. ut pro Rabirio perduellionis reo: Nec tuas unquam rationes ad eos scopulos appulisses, ad quos S. Titij afflictam nauem, & in quibus C. Deciani naufragium fortunarũ uideres. in quo obscuritas fugienda est, ne ex allegoria fiat ænigma. Est & aliud genus, cum ornandi causa uerbum propriũ proprio commutatur: ut, Cuncta Asia atque Græcia uestrum auxilium expectare propter periculi magnitudinem coguntur, pro Asiaticis & Græcis. ex quo genere Martem commune, pro bello, in oratione pro Milone dixit Cicero: curiam pro senatu, campum pro comitijs, togam pro pace, arma ac tela pro bello: & uirtutes & uitia pro ipsis, in quibus illa sunt. ut, Insidiator superatus, ui uicta uis, uel potius oppressa uirtute audacia est. Huic sunt finitima illa minus ornata, sed tamen non ignoranda, cum intelligi uolumus aliquid aut ex parte totum, ut mucronem pro gladio: ut pro Ligario, Cuius latus mucro ille petebat: aut ex toto partem, ut ferrum pro gladio: ut Post reditum in senatu, Cum ferro & facibus tota urbe uolitantes. aut ex uno plures: ut, Romanus prælio uictor, pro Romanis. aut cum ex pluribus unum, ut pro Milone: Sed stulti sumus, qui Drufum, qui Africanū, Pompeium, nosmetipsos cum Clodio comparamus: cum de seipso tantum modo loqueretur. Diximus de singulorum uerborum uirtute: sequitur uerborum continuatio, quæ duas res maximè, collocatione primū, deinde modum quendam, formamq; desiderat. Collocationis est componere & struere uerba sic, ut neue asper eorum concursus, neue hiulcus sit: sed quodammodo coagmentatus & leuis, ut iam stam orationem efficiat, ut cohærente, ut lenem, ut æquabiliter fluentem. Hoc assequemur, si uerba extrema cum consequentibus primis ita iungemus, ut neue asperè occurrant, neue uastius diducantur. Collationem subsequitur modus & forma uerborum: in quo illud est uel maximum uitium, quod uersus in oratione si efficitur coniunctione uerborum, uitium est: & tamen eam coniunctionem sicuti uersum numerose cadere,
units.tr: The narration will be clear if we use familiar words, keep the order of the times, and do not break it off. Next comes the statement of the case: here we must see what is in dispute. Then the supports of our case are to be joined together, the opposing arguments weakened, and our own strengthened. For there is one and the same method of speaking that serves to prove an argument, and that seeks both confirmation and refutation. Yet what is said against us cannot be refuted unless we confirm our own points, and our points cannot be confirmed unless we refute theirs; therefore these are joined together in nature, in usefulness and in treatment. Indeed, all of them should generally be concluded with the amplification of the matters, either by inflaming the judge or by softening him, and all of them, both in the earlier places of the speech and most of all in the conclusion, are to be applied to move the minds of the judges and to call them to our advantage. Since every speech consists of both matter and words, and words cannot have a place if you take away the matter, nor the matter its light if you remove the words, and since we have now spoken so far about the matters and their sequence, our discourse will turn to the expression of words, which consists in this: that we speak in good Latin, clearly, elegantly, and fittingly to whatever subject we are treating. But let us set aside those two earlier points, which are easy to grasp. For one should not try to teach someone to speak who does not know how to talk, nor should we expect that one who cannot speak Latin will speak elegantly; nor, indeed, can one who does not say what we can understand be able to say what we might admire, and so arrive at ornament of words. Since, then, all speech is made up of words, we must first consider the nature of individual words on their own, and then in combination. For there is one kind of ornament of speech that belongs to single words, and another that consists of words strung together and joined. So we shall use words either those that are proper, and as it were the fixed names of things, born almost together with the things themselves; or those that are transferred, and placed as it were in a foreign place; or those that we coin and make ourselves. The praise of the orator in proper words lies in avoiding what is cast off and obsolete, and in using chosen and illustrious words, in which something full and resonant seems to be present. But within this kind of proper word a certain selection must be made, and it must be weighed by a sort of judgement of the ears, in which the custom of speaking well has the greatest force. Since, however, in proper words we only avoid faults, which is not a great praise for an orator, we must seek and explain what he himself builds, and where he brings in his art. There are therefore three things that the orator brings to a simple word in order to illuminate and adorn his speech: an unusual word, a coined word, or a transferred word. As for unusual words, which are for the most part archaic and ancient, and long since dropped from the usage of everyday speech, and which are freer in the licence of poets than of orators, but which nonetheless sometimes have dignity in speech because of their antiquity, such as proles, foboles, effari, nuncupari, opinabar, rebar, these belong to proper words, and I say nothing of them. Thus only two kinds of simple words remain that bring splendour to speech: coined words and transferred words. Words are coined when they are born from the speaker himself and are made either by joining words together, as versutiloquus, or without joining, as incuruescere. The next mode, the transference of a word, extends widely; necessity gave birth to it, constrained by poverty and straits, and afterwards delight and pleasantness made it famous. For just as clothing was first invented to ward off cold, and afterwards began to be used for the adornment and dignity of the body too, so the transference of a word was instituted for the sake of poverty and frequented for the sake of delight. For country folk too say that vines are "budding with gems," that there is "luxuriance" in herbs, and that the crops are "joyful." For what can scarcely be declared by a proper word is illuminated, when it is spoken as a transfer, by the likeness of that thing which we wish to be understood and which we could not name with a word of its own. Therefore these transfers are like borrowings: when you lack something, you take it from elsewhere. But those that do not indicate poverty and add some splendour to the speech delight most of all, when a word is recognised by a certain likeness as placed in a foreign place as if it were in its own. But if it has no likeness to that thing, it is rejected. Therefore those things should be transferred which either make the matter clearer, as the storms of sermons, the flood of eloquence; or which signify the whole matter of some deed or plan more fully, as those: inflamed with anger, set on fire by desire, fallen into error. Or for the sake of brevity, as in that passage in the speech for Milo: "It was a great thing for Milo to have destroyed that pest." So many crimes could not have been set out in such brief proper words as they are signified by one transferred word. In this matter one must avoid dissimilarity, so that we do not speak of the "vaulted arches" of the heavens, since there is no likeness of a vault in the sphere. Next one must see that the comparison is not too remote. For I would rather call marriage a "harbour" than a "quicksand," and the wealth of good men a "whirlpool" rather than a "Charybdis." For the eyes of the mind are carried more readily to those things that have been seen than to those that have been heard. The highest praise of a transferred word is when what is transferred strikes the sense. Hence all foulness must be avoided in those things to which the likeness draws the minds of the hearers. I do not want the republic to be called "castrated" by the death of Africanus, nor the Curia's "dung" to be called Glaucia, although it may be similar; for in both there is an ugly notion of likeness. I also do not want a transfer to be larger than the matter requires, as the "tempest of a drinking-party," or smaller, as the "drinking-party of a tempest," or narrower than that proper and own word: as "to tell me to approach is to refuse," where it would be better to say "forbid," "prohibit," "scare off." And even if we fear that a transfer may seem a little harsh, it should be softened by the addition of a preposition, as often with a word. As in Marcus Antonius: "I resolved to remain, as it were, on the watch of a consular and senatorial..." For a transfer ought to be modest, so that it seems to have been led into a foreign place, not to have burst into it. There is also another kind of transfer, not by one word, as above, but by several strung together, so that one thing is said and another understood. As in the speech for Rabirius, accused of treason: "Nor would you ever have driven your reasons onto those rocks on which you might see the wrecked ship of S. Titius, and in which the shipwreck of C. Decianus' fortunes lies." In this, obscurity must be avoided, lest the allegory become a riddle. There is also another kind, when for the sake of ornament a proper word is exchanged for another proper word: as, "All Asia and Greece are compelled, because of the magnitude of the danger, to expect your help," for "the Asians and the Greeks." To this kind belongs "Mars common" for war, which Cicero used in the speech for Milo; "curia" for the senate, "campus" for the assemblies, "toga" for peace, "arms and weapons" for war; and virtues and vices for the very persons in whom they are: as, "The ambusher was overcome; violence, conquered by force, or rather, boldness, was crushed by virtue." Close to these are those less ornate but still not to be ignored, when we wish something to be understood either as a part for the whole, as "point" for sword: as in the speech for Ligarius, "that point was seeking his side"; or the whole for a part, as "iron" for sword: as in the speech after his return to the senate, "flying about the whole city with iron and torches"; or one for several, as "a Roman, victor in battle," for Romans; or several for one, as in the speech for Milo: "But we are fools who compare Drusus, Africanus, Pompey, ourselves with Clodius," when he was speaking only of himself. We have spoken of the power of individual words; next comes the continuity of words, which requires two things above all: first arrangement, and then a certain measure and form. The arrangement consists in composing and building words so that their concurrence is neither harsh nor gaping, but somehow fitted together and smooth, so that the speech is made firm, cohesive, gentle, and flowing evenly. We shall achieve this if we join the final words to the following initial words in such a way that they do not meet harshly, nor are separated too widely. The measure and form of words follows the arrangement; in this, the greatest fault is that if verses are produced by the combination of words in speech, that is a fault; and yet we want that combination to fall rhythmically, as a verse does, and to fit and be completed.

units.la: & & quadrare et perfici volumus. Neq; quicquam est, quod magis oratorem ab imperito dicendi, ignaroq; distinguat, quàm quòd ille rudis incondite fundit quantum potest: & id quod dicit spiritu, non arte determinat. Orator autem sic alligat sententiam verbis, ut eam numero quodam complectatur, et astricto, ut soluto: ut verba neque alligata sint, quasi certa aliqua lege versuum: neq; ita soluta, ut vagentur. Quamobrem illud est in primis efficiendum, ne fluat oratio, ne vagetur, ne insistat interius, ne excurrat longius, ut membris distinguatur, ut cõuersiones habeat absolutas.
units.tr: We want it to be fitted together and finished with a certain rhythm. Nothing distinguishes the orator more from the unskilled and ignorant speaker than this: the latter pours out as much as he can, carelessly, and governs what he says by breath rather than by art. The orator, however, binds his thought to words so that he embraces it with a certain rhythm, bound yet loose. The words are not bound as if by some fixed law of verse, nor so loose that they wander. Therefore the first thing to be achieved is that the speech does not flow aimlessly, does not wander, does not dwell too long within itself, does not run out too far, but is divided into clauses and has complete periods.

units.la: Quare primi & postremi pedes sunt ratione quadam numerorum seruādi: quia medij latere possunt: modò ne circuitus ipse verborum sit aut breuior, quàm aures expectant: aut longior, quàm vires atq; anima patiatur: sed in extremitate variandi sunt pedes, ne aut animorum iudicijs repudientur, aut aurium satietate. Atq; ideo horum pedum vicissitudines efficient, ut neque ij satientur, qui audient, fastidio similitudinis: nec nos id quod faciemus, dedita opera facere videamur.
units.tr: Hence the first and last feet must be observed according to a certain rule of numbers, since the middle ones may be less strict; provided only that the circuit of words is neither shorter than the ears expect nor longer than the breath and lungs can bear. The ends must be varied, lest they be rejected by the judgment of minds or by the surfeit of ears. Thus the alternation of these feet will ensure that neither those who listen grow weary through the tedium of sameness, nor do we seem to be doing on purpose what we do.

units.la: Postquam vero haec omnia adhibuerimus, quae a nobis dicta sunt de singulorum laude verborum, de coniunctione, de numero, atque forma: tum est quasi luminibus distinguenda, & frequentanda omnis
units.tr: Once we have applied all these things that we have said about the merit of individual words, about their combination, about rhythm and form, then the whole speech must be, as it were, set off and studded with the lights of figures, both of thought and of words.

units.la: oratio sententiarum atque uerborum. Nam & commoratio una in re permultum mouet, & il lustris explanatio: rerumq;, quasi gerantur, sub aspectum penè subiectio, quæ & in exponenda re plurimum ualet, & ad illustrandum id quod exponitur, & ad amplificandum, ut ijs qui audient, illud quod augebimus, quantum efficere oratio poterit, tantum esse uideatur. & huic contraria sæpe præcisio est, & plus ad intelligendum, quàm dixeris, significatio, & distincte concisa breuitas, & extenuatio, & huic adiuncta illusio, & ab re non longa digressio: in qua cum fuerit delectatio, tum reditus ad rem aptus & concinnus esse debebit: propositio, quid sis dicturus, & ab eo quod est dictum, sciunctio, & reditus ad propositum, & iteratio, & rationis apta conclusio: tum augendi, minuendi ue causa ueritatis superlatio atque traiectio, & rogatio: atq; huic finitima, quasi percunctatio, expositio sententiæ suæ: tum illa, quæ maxime quasi irrepit in hominum mentes, alia dicentis ac significantis dissimulatio, quæ est periucunda, cum in oratione, non cõtentione, sed sermone tractatur: deinde dubitatio, tum distributio, tum correctio, uel ante uel post quàm dixeris, uel cũ aliquid à te ipso reijcias. præmunitio est etiá, ad id quod aggrediare, et reiectio in alium: communicatio, quæ
units.tr: Every speech is made of sentences and words. For a prolonged dwelling on one matter moves greatly, and so does clear explanation; and so does the placing of things almost before the eyes, as if they were being done, which is most effective both in setting out a matter, in illustrating what is set out, and in amplifying it, so that to the hearers what we magnify seems as great as speech can make it. Often opposed to this is abridgement, and a meaning conveyed more than what you have said, and brevity cut short distinctly, and understatement, and with it irony, and a digression not far from the subject; in which, when there has been some delight, the return to the matter must be apt and neat: a statement of what you are going to say, a separation from what has been said, a return to the proposition, repetition, and a conclusion fitted to the argument. Then there is the superlative and transposition of the truth, for the sake of increasing or diminishing, and questioning; and akin to this, as it were, the putting of questions, and the setting out of one's own opinion; then that figure which most of all creeps, as it were, into people's minds, the dissimulation of what one says and means, which is very pleasing when the matter is handled in conversation rather than in contention; then doubt, then distribution, then correction, either before or after you have spoken, or when you reject something from yourself. There is also anticipation, for what you are about to attack, and transfer of the objection to another; communication, which

units.la: .... que est quasi cũ ijs ipsis, apud quos dicas, deliberatio, morum ac uitæ imitatio, uel in personis, uel sine illis, magnum quoddam ornamentũ orationis, & aptum ad animos cõciliandos uel maxime, sæpe autem etiam ad commouēdos. Personarum ficta inductio, uel grauissimum lumen augendi, descriptio, erroris inductio, & in hi laritatem impulsio, anteoccupatio: tum duo illa quæ maximè mouent, similitudo & exemplum, digestio, interpellatio, contentio, reticentia, commendatio: uox quædam libera, atq; etiam effre natior augēdi causa, iracundia, obiurgatio, pro missio, deprecatio, obsecratio, declinatio breuis à proposito, non ut superior illa digressio, purgatio, conciliatio, lesio, optatio, atq; execratio. His fere luminibus illustrant orationem sententiæ. Orationis autem ipsius tanquam armorum est, uel ad usum comminatio, & quasi petitio: uel ad uenustatem ipsam tractatio. nam & gemi natio uerborum habet interdum uim, leporem alias, & paulum immutatum uerbum atq; deflexum: & eiusdē uerbi crebra tum à primo repetitio, tum in extremum conuersio, & in eadem uerba impetus & concursio, & adiunctio, & progressio, & eiusdē uerbi crebrius positi quædam distinctio, & reuocatio uerbi: & illa quæ similiter desinunt, aut quæ cadunt similiter: aut
units.tr: .... is, as it were, a deliberation with those very people before whom you speak, and an imitation of manners and of life, either in persons or without them: a great ornament of speech, and especially apt for winning minds, and often also for moving them. Then the feigned introduction of persons, which is a most weighty light for amplifying; description; the induction of error; the impulse toward laughter; anticipation. Then those two which move most of all, likeness and example; distinction; interruption; contention; reticence; commendation; a certain free voice, and something more elevated for the sake of amplifying; indignation; rebuke; promise; supplication; entreaty; a brief departure from the proposition, not like that digression mentioned above; purgation; reconciliation; injury; wishing; and cursing. These figures, more or less, illuminate speech as regards its thoughts. But speech itself, as it were its arms, is either the threat and, as it were, the attack for use, or the handling of it for elegance. For the doubling of words sometimes has force, sometimes charm; and a word slightly altered and turned aside; and the frequent repetition of the same word, both at the beginning and by turning it to the end; and attack and concourse upon the same words; and addition, and progression; and a certain distinction of the same word placed more often; and recall of a word; and those that end alike, or fall alike; or

units.la: I quæ paribus paria referuntur, aut quæ sunt inter se similia. Est etiam gradatio quædam, & conuersio, & uerborum concinna transgressio, & contrarium & dissolutū, & declinatio & repetitio, & exclamatio & imminutio, & quod in multis casibus ponitur: & quod de singulis rebus propositis ductum, refertur ad singula: & ad propositum subiecta ratio, & item in distributis suppositā ratio, & permissio: & rursum alia dubitatio, & improuisum quiddam: et dinumeratio, et alia correctio: et disputatio, et quod continuatum, & interruptū: & imago, & sibi ipsi responsio: & immutatio, & disiunctio, et ordo, et relatio, et digressio, et circumscriptio. Hæc sunt, uel horum similia, quæ sententiis orationē, uerborumq; conformationibus illuminent. Sed quoniam duæ sunt partes orationis illustrandæ, ac totius eloquentiæ cumulandæ, quarum altera dici postulat ornatē, de qua diximus: altera aptē, hoc est, quod maximè decet in oratione, de qua breuiter agendum uidetur, quanquā id quidem perspicuum est: non igitur omni causæ, nec auditori, neq; personæ, neque tempori congruit unum genus orationis. Nam & causæ capitis alium quendam uerborum sonum requirunt: aliū rerum priuatarum, atq; paruarum: & aliud dicendi genus deliberationes, aliud laudationes: aliud iudicia, aliud sermones: aliud consolatio, aliud obiurgatio: aliud disputatio, aliud historia desiderat. Refert etiam, qui audiant, senatus, an po-pulus, an iudices: frequentes, an pauci, an singuli, & quales ipsi quoq; oratores, qua sint aetate, honore, autoritate debet uideri. tempus pacis an belli, festinationis an ocij. Itaq; hoc loco nil aliud sane est, quod praecipi posse uideatur, nisi ut figuram orationis plenioris, & tenuioris, & item illius mediocris, ad id quod agimus accommodatam deligamus, ut humilia subtiliter, magna grauiter, mediocria temperate dicantur. Ornamentis ijsdem uti fere licebit alias contentius, alias summissius: omniq; in re posse quod deceat facere, artis & naturae est: scire quid, quandoq; deceat, prudentiae. Sed iam his breuiter explicatis, memoria nobis opus est, quam ijs qui exercere uoluerint, arte quadam loci sunt capiendi, & ea quae memoria tenere uellet, effingenda animo, atque in his locis collocanda: sic fore, ut ordine rerum, locorum ordo conseruaret: res autem ipsas, rerum effigies notaret. Ea etenim maxime animis nostris effinguntur, quae sunt a sensu tradita, atq; impressa: acerrimus autem ex omnibus nostris sensibus, est sensus uidendi. Quare facillime animo teneri possunt ea, quae percipe-rentur auribus, & cogitatione, si etiam oculorum comendatione animis traderentur,ut res cæcas, et ab aspectus iudicio remotas, conformatio quæ‑dam, & imago & figura ita notaret, ut ea quæ cogitando cõplecti uix possemus, intuêdo qua‑ si teneremus. Quare hac exercitatione non e‑ ruenda memoria est, si est ulla naturalis: sed cer‑ te, si latet, euocanda est. Memoriam sequitur d‑ctio, ut tandè ad ultimâ nostri sermonis partem peruenjamus, quæ una Demosthenis testimo‑ nio in dicendo maximè dominatur: in qua pri‑mùm uocem moderari debemus, et apte oratio‑num formæ accommodare. Aliud enim uocis ge‑ nus iracundia sibi assumit, acutum, incitatū, cre‑ brò incidens: aliud miseratio ac mœror, flexibi‑ le, plenum, interruptum, flebili uoce: aliud me‑ tus, dimissum et hæsitans, et abiectum: aliud uis, contentum, uchemens, imminens, quadam incita‑tione grauitatis: aliud uoluptas, effusum, lene, te‑ nerum, hilaratū ac remissum: aliud molestia, si‑ ne cõmiseratione, graue quiddam, & uno pres‑ su ac sono obductu. Omnes autem hos uocis mo‑tus, subsequi debet gestus uniuersam rem et sen‑ tentiam significatione declarans, laterum inflec‑ xione: manus autem minus arguta, digitis subse‑ quens uerba, nõ exprimens: brachiū procerius proiectū, quasi quoddam telū orationis: supplo‑ sto pedis in contentionib. aut incipiēdis, aut fi‑niendis. niendis. Sed in ore sunt omnia: in eo aut ipso dominatus est omnis oculorum. Quare, ipsorum est magna moderatio. nam oris non est nimium mutanda species. Oculi sunt, quorum tum intentione, tum remissione, tum coniectu, tum bilaritate motus animorum significemus apte cum genere ipso orationis. est enim actio, quasi sermo corporis, quo magis menti cogruens esse debet. Oculos enim natura nobis ad motus animorum declarandos dedit. Exposui breuiter, quas partes oratore habere oporteat: eas uero facile cofe quemur diligentia, imitatione et exercitatione, sine quibus inanes erunt omnes a nobis suscepti labores.
units.tr: those that refer like things to like, or that are similar to one another. There is also a certain gradation, and conversion, and a neat transgression of words, and the contrary and the loosened, and declination and repetition, and exclamation and diminution, and that which is placed in many cases; and that which, drawn from particular matters proposed, is referred to each; and the reason added to the proposition, and likewise the reason supplied in the distributed parts; and concession; and again another doubt, and something unforeseen; and enumeration, and another correction; and disputation, and what is continuous and interrupted; and image, and answer to oneself; and change, and disjunction, and order, and relation, and digression, and circumlocution. These, or things like them, are what adorn speech with thoughts and with the shaping of words. But since there are two parts of speech to be illustrated and of all eloquence to be enriched, one of which requires to be ornate, as we have said, and the other apt, that is, what is most fitting in speech, which seems to need to be treated briefly (though this is indeed plain), one kind of speech does not suit every cause, every hearer, every person, or every occasion. For causes involving life and death require one tone of words, those concerning private and trivial matters another; deliberative speeches require one kind, panegyrics another; trials one, conversations another; consolation one, rebuke another; disputation one, history another. It also matters who the hearers are, whether senate, or people, or judges; whether many, or few, or single; and what sort of speakers they themselves are, what age, rank and authority they ought to appear to have; whether the time is one of peace or war, of haste or leisure. Therefore on this point there is really nothing else that seems to be taught, except that we choose the fuller, the plainer, and likewise the middle style of speech, as suits what we are doing: that humble matters be treated plainly, great matters weightily, and middling matters temperately. It will generally be permitted to use the same ornaments now more intensely, now more gently; and to be able in every matter to do what is fitting belongs to art and nature; to know what is fitting, and when, belongs to prudence. But now that these things have been briefly set out, we have need of memory, which those who wish to practise should grasp by a certain art of places, and should form in the mind the things they wish to retain, and place them in those places: so that the order of the places would preserve the order of the matters, and the images of the things would mark the things themselves. For those things are most firmly fixed in our minds that have been handed down and impressed by the senses; and the keenest of all our senses is the sense of sight. Therefore those things which are perceived by the ears and by thought can be held most easily in the mind if they were also handed down to the mind through the recommendation of the eyes; so that some shaping, image and figure would mark things that are blind and remote from the judgment of sight, in such a way that we would hold by looking what we could scarcely grasp by thinking. Therefore by this exercise the memory is not to be drawn out, if it is natural at all; but certainly, if it lies hidden, it is to be called forth. Memory is followed by delivery, so that at last we may come to the final part of our discourse, which alone, by the testimony of Demosthenes, rules most in speaking. In it we must first govern the voice and adapt it to the forms of the speeches. For one kind of voice is assumed by anger: sharp, urged on, often breaking in; another by pity and sorrow: flexible, full, broken, with a plaintive voice; another by fear: slackened, hesitant and abject; another by force: strained, vehement, threatening, with a certain urgency of gravity; another by pleasure: outpoured, gentle, tender, cheerful and relaxed; another by distress without compassion: something heavy, with one pressure and sound, closed in. But all these movements of the voice ought to be followed by gesture, expressing the whole matter and thought by its meaning: a bending of the sides; the hand less lively, following the words with the fingers without expressing them; the arm thrust out rather tall, as a kind of weapon of speech; the foot stamped in contentions, either when they begin or when they end. But all things are in the face, and in the face itself all the power lies in the eyes. Therefore their moderation is of great importance; for the appearance of the mouth must not be changed too much. The eyes are the means by which we signify the movements of our minds, by their intensity, by their relaxing, by their glance, by their brightness, fitted aptly to the very kind of speech. For delivery is, as it were, the speech of the body, and it ought to agree the more closely with the mind. For nature gave us eyes to declare the movements of the mind. I have briefly set out what parts the orator ought to have; these we shall easily attain by diligence, imitation and practice, without which all the labours we have undertaken will be in vain.

units.la: PRAECEPTA ARTIS RHETORICAE SVMMATIM de multis, ac Syntomata, à Iulio Seuerìano collecta.
units.tr: The Precepts of the Art of Rhetoric in Summary, on Many Matters, and Syntomata, Collected by Julius Severianus.

units.la: Orsitan nec usurpatorem ardui operis, atque irriti laboris, Desideri, fateare, quòd hunc libellum ad te de arte dicendi scriptum miserim: quum possis aduertere, nihil me Rhetorum praeceptis adiunxisse, sed quae in ipsis sparsim legeram, in quasdam sermonis angustias coartasse. Denique si haec quisquam digna astimet, quae in manus sumat, reperiet ea me de ueteribus perstrinxisse, quibus quotidie ad forensem campum adolescentia imbuta proludit: quorum si nota uis est, sylucscentium uidelicet praeceptorum, uideri certè possum plura his ademisse, quàm addidisse. Namq; ueteres res ita nobis praecepta reliquerunt, ut etiam sui nominis sempiternam memoriam propagarent. Ego non ullius famae cupidus, sed immensi laboris molestiā considerans, certos tibi ad compendium gymnasij forensis tramites constitui, quos ad memoriam reparadā facili lectione percurrerees. Animaduerti praeterea (uideris quid caeteri teri sentiant) obesse dicentibus rhetoricæ artis nimiam disciplinam. Memento tamen, non ante tibi hæc esse compendia relegenda, quàm ingenium tuum Tulliana arte subegeris. Oratorijs artibus nemo instrui potest, nisi cui ingenium, & frequens studium est. Primùm animi sit oportet quædam naturalis ad uidendas edifcendasq; res potentia, tum uox, latus, decor, ualetudo, frugalitas, laboris patientia. Necessaria deinde oratiionum frequens lectio est, quæ nos exemplo conformet: neque earum modo, sed & historiarum & carminum, ex quibus compositio dicendi non in totum trahenda est. Nam per lectiones sapientum præcepta noscuntur, sine quibus nihil subtile, neque magnificum cogitari potest. Iuris uerò ciuilis nec omittendum studium est, nec penitus appetendum. nam nec rudis esse debet orator: & si se multum iuris scientiæ dederit, plurimum de cultu orationis atque impetu amittet. Huic & ueteres oratores legendi sunt, & præsentes audiendi. Super hæc frequenter scribendum, agendum, & declamandum est. His enim rebus oratorum fiducia simul cum facundia comparatur. In cæteris ferè studijs uerum quæritur: finis autem oratoriæ artis est, uerisimilia dixisse, uel tantum contendisse, quantum res passa fit ad uictoriam. Proxime quærendum est, quo genere orationis uti debeat orator: Atticorum ne nobis sequenda sit actio, qui breues astrictiq; & acres sunt, pure inter ipsas res aculeosq; uersantes, qui que affectum ex occulto petunt: an imitanda nobis sit Asianorum licentia, qui uagi ac fusi, rapere potius affectibus, quam disputationibus persuadere didicerunt. Sit tamen Romanus orator Asiatico presior, Attico copiosior. Ego uero ipsum oratorem eligere arbitror, & probare genus orationis, quo magis capi suum iudicem senserit: aliter apud eum, quem latior delectabit oratio: aliter apud eum, quem astrictior: aliter apud superiorem, aliter apud uacuum, aliter apud distractum: nec sic in priuatis causis, ubi semper iudices festinant, quemadmodum in publicis: nec sic in accusationibus, ut in patrociniis. Maxima itaque ars erit, semper circumspicere, quid persone, quid loco, quid tempori conueniat.
units.tr: Perhaps, Desiderius, you will consider me a presumptuous meddler in a difficult task and a pointless labour, since I have sent you this little book on the art of speaking. You may notice that I have added nothing to the precepts of the rhetoricians. I have only gathered into a small compass what I had read scattered through them. If anyone thinks these things worth taking up, he will find that I have touched on the ancients, from whom young men are daily trained for the forum before they enter it. If their substance is known, namely that of scattered precepts, I may certainly appear to have taken away more than I have added. The ancients left us their precepts in such a way that they also secured the lasting memory of their own names. I, desiring no fame of my own but considering the trouble of such a great labour, have laid out for you short paths to the forum's schoolroom, which you may run through by easy reading to refresh your memory. I have also noticed (you will see what others think) that an excessive study of the rules of rhetoric is a hindrance to speakers. Remember, however, that these summaries are not to be reread by you until you have trained your mind in the Tullian art. No one can be instructed in the arts of oratory unless he has a natural aptitude and frequent study. First, the mind must have a certain natural power for seeing and learning things; then a voice, strength, grace, good health, temperance, and patience in labour. Next, frequent reading of orations is necessary, which shapes us by example; and not only of orations, but also of histories and poems, from which the composition of speech is not to be drawn entirely. For through reading the precepts of the wise are learned, without which nothing subtle or elevated can be conceived. Yet the study of civil law must be neither neglected nor pursued to excess. For an orator should not be untrained in it, but if he devotes himself too much to legal learning, he will lose much of the polish and vigour of his speech. For this purpose the ancient orators must be read, and living ones heard. Beyond these things, one must write, practise speaking, and declaim often. For by these means the confidence of orators is acquired together with their eloquence. In most other studies one seeks truth; but the end of the oratorical art is to say what is plausible, or to contend only as far as the matter allows for victory. Next, one must ask what style of speaking the orator ought to use: whether we should follow the action of the Attics, who are brief, compressed, and sharp, moving purely among the facts and their points, and who seek emotion covertly; or whether we should imitate the license of the Asians, who are diffuse and expansive, and who have learned to sweep the emotions along rather than persuade by argument. Yet the Roman orator should be more restrained than the Asian and fuller than the Attic. I think, however, that the orator should choose and approve the style of speaking by which he has perceived his judge to be more readily captured: one manner before a man who is delighted by a broader speech, another before one who prefers a tighter one; one before a superior, another before an idle judge, another before a distracted one. Nor is the same to be done in private cases, where judges are always in a hurry, as in public ones; nor in prosecutions as in defences. The greatest art, therefore, will be to look constantly around and consider what suits the person, the place, and the time.

units.la: De disponendis criminibus.
units.tr: On Arranging the Charges.

units.la: Quidam a maximis criminibus ad leuissima gradum fecerunt, aut a leuissimis ad maxima. Nos primum aestimamus, actore quasi membra quaedam facere debere: ut separet quae ad lubidinem, quae ad auaritiam, quae ad crudelitatem, aliud ue quod ad noxae genus pertinet: aut si non genera criminum, tempora tamen discernat. Primo (utputa) quæ ante militiam facta sunt, quæ in militia, quæ post militiam. aut seiungat ea quæ ad priuatas causas, deinde ea quæ ad publicas pertinent, aliud ue simile: ut Cicero, qui crimina Veris et in tempora et in genera diuisit. Nam primus liber continet, quæ ante Siciliensem praturam commisit: quatuor insequentes, ea quæ in praetura Siciliensi. tum in his ipsis, secundus ad priuatorum furta pertinet, tertius frumentariam rationem, quartus sacrilegia, quintus maiestatis crimina comprehendit. Deinde inter ipsa unius generis crimina, in primis magna ponito: quæ minima sunt, in medium congerantur: quæ maxima, ultimis partibus reseruabis. ut de graui crimine, quod à Cicerone in ultimam partem dilatum est. Ita iudicis animus et occupabitur, et ualidissima maxime memoriæ mandabit. Hinc est quòd Cicero pro Scauro, reprehendit aduersarij confusam criminationem. ait enim: Et quoniam congesta fuit accusatio, magis aceruo quodam criminum, non distinctione aliqua generum, et uarietate.
units.tr: Some have made a step from the greatest charges to the slightest, or from the slightest to the greatest. We judge that the speaker should first make, as it were, certain limbs of the case: he should separate those charges that concern lust, those concerning greed, those concerning cruelty, or any other that pertains to a kind of wrongdoing; or, if not the kinds of charges, at least he should distinguish them by time. For example: first, those acts done before military service, those during service, and those after it. Or he should separate those that concern private causes from those that pertain to public ones, or some other similar division, as Cicero did when he divided Verres' charges both by time and by kind. For the first book contains what he committed before his Sicilian praetorship; the four following books, what he did during his Sicilian praetorship. Then, within these, the second book deals with the private thefts, the third with the grain accounts, the fourth with sacrileges, and the fifth comprises the charges of treason. Next, among the charges of a single kind, place the great ones first; let the smallest be gathered into the middle; and reserve the greatest for the final parts, as with the grave charge which Cicero deferred to the last part. In this way the judge's mind will be occupied, and the most forceful points will be entrusted most firmly to memory. Hence it is that Cicero, in the speech for Scaurus, rebukes his opponent's confused accusation. For he says: "And since the accusation was heaped up, more like a heap of charges than any arrangement by kinds and variety."

units.la: De Principijs.
units.tr: On the Principles.

units.la: De principijs nihil putaui dicendum: quandoquidem ad ea quæ arte seruanda sunt, natura duce sæpius perducitur.
units.tr: I have thought that nothing should be said about the principles, since, when it comes to those things which must be observed by art, nature more often leads the way.

units.la: De Narrationibus.
units.tr: On Narrations.

units.la: Narrationis certũ est tres esse uirtutes,ut dilucida sit,ut breuis, ut uerisimilis. Dilucida fit, si apud nescientem narres,in qua intueberis initium,medium,& finem,ita ut ipsa narratio ordinem suum habeat. facile enim percipitur, ubi quod sequitur ex priore pendet. Interdū aliqua suo loco memoriæ nostræ non occurrisse fingemus. Breuis fit, si circuncifis quibusdam superfluis,sola que necessaria sunt posueris. Quæcunque enim tibi mediocriter prosunt argumentis, uel disputationibus, perseuerabunt. Verisimilis ideo,ut credatur,& corporis robustissimi fuisse cum, à quo duos tresve occisos uideri uoluerit. adijcere etiam occasionem,quæ perficiundæ rei fuerit:ut dicas, dormientes oppressos. Personas verò nominibus,quibus notissimæ sunt,nuncupabis: si hoc parum est, etiam aliquas notas adijcies, ut Scipio Africanus, ut Annibal Pœnus, & similia. Nunquam narrationem,nisi perfectam, reliqueris: sed ubi iudicè minus intellexisse perspexeris,nunquam ei tarditatem ingenij obiecteris:sed in te culpam retorque, quòd parum dixeris. Vbi longior narratio est,quo sit dilucida magis, admonere iudicè debes quid exposueris, uel quid expositurus sis:ut,Dixi de me,dicam de aduersario. Neq; alienum est,ubi lõgior fuerit ex-positio positio uel narratio, extremam ita finire, ut admoncas quaecunq; dixeris. Verba autem narrationis ex media consuetudine esse debent. Simplex sermo, etsi uicina compositio in expositionibus plus mora nocet, nec loquentis personas narrationibus inseras.
units.tr: It is certain that a narration has three virtues: that it be clear, that it be brief, and that it be plausible. It is made clear if, when speaking before someone who does not know the matter, you keep in view its beginning, middle and end, so that the narration itself has its own order. For what follows from what precedes is easily grasped. Sometimes we shall pretend that some point did not occur to our memory at its proper place. It is made brief if, after cutting away certain superfluous details, you set down only what is necessary. For whatever contributes moderately to your arguments or disputations will remain. It is made plausible so that it will be believed: for example, that the man was of very robust body, from whom he wished it to appear that two or three had been killed. You may also add the occasion that made the deed possible, as when you say that the men were overwhelmed while asleep. You will name the persons by the names by which they are best known; if that is not enough, you will add some distinguishing mark, as "Scipio Africanus," "Hannibal the Carthaginian," and the like. Never leave a narration incomplete. But when you see that the judge has understood less than he should, never blame him for slowness of mind; rather turn the fault back upon yourself, because you have said too little. Where the narration is longer, so that it may be clearer, you ought to remind the judge what you have set forth, or what you are about to set forth, as in: "I have spoken about myself; I shall speak about my opponent." Nor is it out of place, when an exposition or narration has been rather long, to end the final part in such a way that you recall to the judge all that you have said. The words of a narration, moreover, ought to be taken from ordinary conversation. Use plain speech, and a close arrangement of words as well, and do not insert the speakers' own persons into narrations, since in expositions delay does more harm.

units.la: Minuitur praeterea offensa longioris orationis, si te praetermittere aliqua simulaueris. In aliquibus post quaestiones ponenda narratio est, in aliquibus in ultimo. Nam pro natura causarum narratio uariatur: nec semper debet orator ueterum se praeceptis addicere, sed scire debet incidere nouam materiam, quae noui aliquid postulet. Narrari pro eo non expedit, qui omnia quae ab accusatore dicuntur, tantummodo negat: nec ibi se fuisse. Talis causa Syllae fuit, negantis sibi quicquam cum Catilina conuenisse contra Rep. Tales fere sunt ambitus causae, et Repetundarum: in quibus unum rei patrocinium est, se nullas dedisse uel accepisse pecunias. Superuacua narratio est, ubi nota res est, de qua ambigitur: ut nihil stultius sit, quam si apud scientes narres. Alterum genus est, in quo utriq; aeque superuacua narratio est: ubi quod facit quaestionem, abunde propositione indagari potest, etiamsi ignotum est. Nec aliquam narrationem a Cicerone admissam putemus, nisi pro natura causarum.
units.tr: Furthermore, the offence caused by a lengthy speech is lessened if you pretend to pass over some things. In some cases the narration is to be placed after the questions, in others at the end. For the narration varies according to the nature of the causes, and the orator should not always bind himself to the precepts of the ancients, but should know that a new matter may arise which calls for something new. A narration is not advantageous for one who merely denies everything the accuser says and says that he was not even there. Such was the cause of Sulla, who denied that he had had any dealings with Catiline against the state. Such, for the most part, are the cases of electoral corruption and of extortion, in which the one defence of the accused is that he has given or received no money. A narration is superfluous when the matter is well known and yet is in doubt; so it would be most foolish to narrate before those who know it. There is another kind in which the narration is equally superfluous for both sides: when that which raises the question can be sufficiently investigated by the proposition, even if it is unknown. Nor should we think that Cicero admitted any narration except according to the nature of the causes.

units.la: Edebat enim non solum patrocinia causarum, sed & exempla dicendi. Euenit ut ante sit respondendum, quam sit ponenda ratio. ut pro Milone. Incidunt causae, in quibus quod summa habet quaestionis, magna ex parte tractandum sit: & sic sit ponenda narratio, ut provocare no vel * ut pro Habito. In narrationibus res exponimus, probamus argumentatione. Narratio, insinuatio est totius causae, quemadmodum facta est. expositio vero, quae non de causa nascitur: ut, Est honesto genere natus, splendide magistratum gesserit. non potest videri narratio, sed expositio alicuius rei, quae causam adiuuat: nec dat quaestioni materiam, sed pro argumento ponitur, vel inter argumenta.
units.tr: For he set forth not only the defences of causes but also examples of speaking. It happens that a reply must be made before the account is given, as in the speech for Milo. Causes arise in which what holds the chief place of the question must be handled for the most part, and so the narration is to be placed in such a way that it does not provoke [the opponent]... as in the defence of Habitus. In narrations we set forth the facts and prove them by argument. A narration is an insinuation of the whole cause, as it was done. An exposition, however, which does not arise from the cause, as "He was born of an honourable family and held office with distinction," cannot be seen as a narration but as the exposition of some matter which helps the cause. It does not supply material for the question but is put forward as an argument, or among the arguments.

units.la: De disponendis Argumentis.
units.tr: On Arranging the Arguments.

units.la: Litigatores quidem instruunt argumentis advocatos. Artis patronorum est, ut haec disponat, figurent, ordinent, augeat, ut his affectus intermisceant. In primis uideto, quae ex ijs sint valentia, vel quae infirmiora sint argumenta. nam quae erunt valentia, longiori oratione non prosequimur, ne aut dubitare de his uideamur: aut plura dicendo, ponamus aliquid, adversum quod disputari possit. Namque in argumentis infirmioribus versatur Oratorius labor, qualia sunt, Occidisti hominem: cruentam enim uestem habuisti. haec uerisimilia sunt, non utiq; uera: quae uarijs sunt attollenda rationibus, quæ tractatu fiunt potètia. Præterea in potestate sua habere debet Orator, ut & causam maximè breuiter peroret: & paruulam diu extendat. Sed quùm breuiter dicendum erit, argumenta tantùm ponet, sine ullis ornamentis. Cum autem dicere diu uoluerit, omne argumentum ornatius exequetur. Cum plura erunt argumenta, à ualidis incipies: inualidiora desines: medium imbecillioribus replebis. Vtputa, ualidum argumentum est, Inimicus: mediocre, ebrius: ualidissimum est, In rixa hominem occidit. Si unum ualidum argumentum est, & unum friuolum, à ualido incipies, friuolum prosequêris: rursum ualidum repetes. Argumentatio illa melior & fidelior uideri potest, quæ obscuratur, cum aliquibus partibus causa laborat. utilius ordinem quæstionum confundimus, quas ex toto tractare non expedit. Scias, nunquam confitenda esse quæ nocent: interdum non neganda. quòd Cicero pro Milone sequutus uideri potest. nam interfectum ab eo Clodium neq; negauit, neque fassus est. Non negauit, quia sic confessus est, tanquam occidisset: fassus non est, quia inscio eo dixit à seruis occisum, cum hi dominum interemptum arbitrarentur.
units.tr: Litigants, to be sure, supply their advocates with arguments. It is the art of the advocates to arrange these, shape them, order them, amplify them, and to mix the emotions into them. First of all, look to which of them are strong and which are weaker. For we do not pursue the strong ones at great length, lest we seem to doubt them, or, by saying more, put forward something against which a reply can be made. The oratorical labour is spent on the weaker arguments, such as "You killed the man: for you had a bloodstained garment." These are plausible, not certainly true; they must be lifted up by various considerations, which by handling make them powerful. Moreover, the orator ought to have it in his power both to conclude the cause very briefly and to extend a trivial one at length. But when he must speak briefly, he will put forward only the arguments, without any ornament; when he wishes to speak at length, he will develop every argument more richly. When there are several arguments, you will begin with the strong ones, end with the strongest, and fill the middle with the weaker. For instance, a strong argument is "He was an enemy"; a moderate one, "He was drunk"; the strongest is "In a brawl he killed a man." If there is one strong argument and one trifling one, you will begin with the strong, pursue the trifling one, and then return to the strong. That argumentation may seem the better and more trustworthy which is obscured when the cause is weak in some parts. It is more useful to blur the order of the questions, which it is not advantageous to treat in full. You should know that what harms us should never be confessed, though sometimes it should not be denied. Cicero, in the speech for Milo, may seem to have followed this rule. For he neither denied that Clodius had been killed by Milo nor admitted it outright. He did not deny it, because he confessed it as though he had killed him; he did not admit it, because he said, without his knowledge, that Clodius had been killed by slaves, who thought their master had been slain.

units.la: Præterea utilius existimo, disputationem ad speciem paucarum rerum & formarum conuertere, casq; astruere & exaggerare. Potius est ea nim plures res in unam cogere, q unam in plures diuidere. In omni materia quærendū puto, quid sit quod maxime nos foucat, aut urgeat. huc enim uires suas conferre debet Orator, ut q, maxime nos premit, frangat. Sicut tamē genus caussæ quiddā cōtra nos recipit ualentissimū, sic pro nobis omnis caussa aliquid ualetius habere debet.
units.tr: Furthermore, I think it more useful to turn the dispute toward the appearance of a few things and forms, and to establish and magnify these. It is better to gather many things into one than to divide one into many. In every matter, I think, we should ask what is the thing that most troubles or presses upon us. For the orator ought to direct his strength there, so that he may break what presses us most. But just as the kind of cause admits something very strong against us, so every cause ought to have something stronger on our side.

units.la: De propositione aduersarij.
units.tr: On the opponent's proposition.

units.la: Responsurus autem aduersario, primū id quod ille posuerit, uerbis infirmioribus pronunciato: quæ uero incredibilia uisa fuerint, aut imbecilla, ita uniuersa ponentur, sicuti ab aduersario dicta sunt. ut est illud, Bostarē igitur quendā dixit Norensem, fugiētem é Sardinia Scauri aduentum. & infrà addit, etiam augendi criminis causa, prius illum sepultum, quàm huic cœnam esse sublatam. Eucnit ut propositionem aduersarij uerbis nostris ultra fidem extollentes, incredibilem faciamus. item, propositioni aduersarij si natura sui incredibilis fuerit, cum quodam impetu animi, ac ridicula admiratione respondebimus. ut est illud: Septingenta millia passuum biduo cursa sunt. & respondet: O rem incredibilem, ò cupiditatem inconsideratam, ò nuncium uolucrem. & infrà: Roma trans alpes biduò ueniunt, ò hominē fortunatum, qui eiusmodi nuncios, seu potius pegasos habeat. Propositio co quod aduersarius dixerit, respondebimus duobus modis: aut non esse id, aut non ideo nos vinci debere. Propositis quib. respondituri sumus, quaerendum nobis erit, an inter se comparata repugnantia sint, ut suis armis corruant. ut Cicero de Antonio: Auunculum suum sceleratum esse fatebatur: poena affectu quaerebatur. Item pro Caelio: Cur aut tam familiaris fuisti, ut aurum commodares: aut tam inimicus, ut venenum timeres? Similiter pro Gallo, ubi accusator pecunias obiecit. ibi enim dum singula inter se comparat, alterum altero Tullius diluit. Item, ultimum erit docere, quod aduersarius dixerit, etiam pro nobis esse, ut, pro Milone Cicero: quod lex promulgata de quaestione fuisset, quam pro se esse ostendit. Argumentis vero omnib. aduersarij respondere non est necessarium. finem enim non habebit oratio: et satis erit propositionibus repugnasse. His sane argumentis respondendum erit, quib. credit iudices commoueri: sin vero aduersarius suis argumentis confutare nequiveris, alijs raticinib. quod posuerit conuellito. De vitijs argumentorum, quae aduersarij male posuerint, plene a Tullio insinuatum est. De Statibus.
units.tr: When we are about to answer the opponent, we should first state what he has put forward in weaker words. Whatever seemed incredible or feeble should be presented exactly as the opponent stated it. For example: "Bostar, then, said that a certain Norensian, fleeing from Sardinia at the approach of Scaurus..." And further on he adds, to increase the charge, that the man was buried before dinner had been cleared away for him. It happens that if we raise the opponent's proposition beyond belief in our words, we make it seem incredible. Likewise, if the opponent's proposition is incredible in its own nature, we shall reply with a certain vehemence of spirit and mocking wonder. For example: "Seven hundred thousand paces were covered in two days." And the reply: "O incredible thing! O reckless greed! O winged messenger!" And further on: "They come from across the Alps to Rome in two days! O fortunate man, who has such messengers, or rather Pegasi!" We shall answer a proposition in one of two ways, either by denying that it is so, or by denying that we ought therefore to be defeated. Once we have the propositions we are going to answer, we must inquire whether, when compared with one another, they are contradictory, so that they fall by their own weapons. For example, Cicero on Antonius: he admitted that his uncle was a criminal, yet the penalty was sought out of affection. Likewise in the speech for Caelius: "Why were you either so intimate with him that you lent him gold, or so hostile that you feared poison?" Similarly in the speech for Gallus, where the accuser objected to money. For there, while Tullius compares the individual points with one another, he refutes one by means of the other. Also, last, it will be useful to show that what the opponent said is even in our favour, as Cicero does in the speech for Milo, where he shows that a law concerning the court had been promulgated, and that this law is on his side. It is not necessary to answer all of the opponent's arguments: the speech would have no end, and it will be enough to have opposed his propositions. To these arguments, certainly, we must reply, those by which the judges are thought to be moved. But if you cannot refute the opponent's arguments by your own, overturn what he has put forward by other reasons. Concerning the faults of arguments which opponents have badly put forward, Tullius has set out fully. On the Statuses.

units.la: Status tres sunt, ubi quod a te factum obiicitur, negas. Coniectura est, ubi quod a te factum fatebere. fateris, & negas eam uim nominis habere quam aduersarius criminatur. Finis est, sineq; de facto, neq; de nomine ambigitur. sed si iure factū contendis, qualitas nominatur.
units.tr: There are three statuses, in which you deny what is charged against you as having been done by you. Conjecture is where you admit what was done by you: you admit it, but deny that it has the force of the name the opponent charges it with. Definition is where there is no dispute either about the deed or about the name. But if you contend that the deed was done lawfully, it is called quality.

units.la: De Coniectura.
units.tr: On Conjecture.

units.la: In coniecturalibus causis hinc argumenta sumuntur: à personis, causis, facultatibus, uerisimilibus, signis. Signum causam aut antecedit, aut in eadem est, aut sequitur. Item proferuntur auditiones, suspiciones, spolia, quaestiones, indices, fama uel opiniones, & multa similia, quae rerū uarietas sumministrat. A persona, ut Cicero pro Cluentio: Cum esset, inquit, egens, sumptuosus, audax, callidus, perfidiosus, ad omnem maliciam & fraudem uersare mentem suam coepit. A causa: Satis ne igitur cernitis, quibus ille mercedibus, quibus emolumentis, quibus praemijs incitatus, &c. A facultatibus, ut Tullius: Seruos agresteis & barbaros, quibus syluas publicas depopulatus erat, ex Apenino deduxerat: & reliqua. A uerisimili: Quid, quod caput est audaciae, iudices, quis ignorat maximā illecebram esse peccandi, impunitatis spem? & reliqua. A signis, quae causam antecedunt, instrumentum, iter, & similia. Simul sunt, pugna, clamor, & similia. Sequuntur, ut in ueneficio, liuor & tumor: in cede, uulnus & sanguis. Auditiones, ut Tullius: Vos ex M. Fauonio audistis, Clodiū sibi dixisse: & auditis, uiuo Clodio, periturum Milonē. Post diem tertium gesta res est, quam dixerat: cum ille non dubitarit aperire quid cogitarit, uos potestis dubitare quid fecerit? Suspiciones, ut pro Scauro: Quae quidem suspicio ualuit, etiam ob hanc causam, quòd cum agerent parentalia No renses, & reliqua. Spolia, ut est illud; Ille deos, decorū spoliis ornare noluit: Hic ornamenta Mi nerue Virginis in meretriciam domum transtulit, & similia. Quæstiones, ut est: Cum igitur de furto quæreretur, & de eo furto quod ille sine controuersia fecerat: cum ille de eo quod non quærebatur, uerbum nullum fecit: de ueneno sta tim dixit, & reliqua. Indices, cum iudici offeruntur, uel certè ut est: Venit index ad Pineam matrem, neq; obscurus, neq; incertus. Fama, uel opinio, ut Cicero: Opinio fuit duplex: una non ab horrens à statu, naturaq; rerum, & rei. Argu mentorum omnium enumeratione aducertite studiosam uideri: quandoquidem in his plus ingenij uis dominetur, arsq; ipsa magis à natura prosecta dicatur. Sed nec quisquam æstimet argumentum his numeris præfinitum, siquidem tanta esse possunt, quanta orator intento acriter ingenio reperire ualuerit: non tamen omne genus causa rū omnia argumenta habet. Nā quid opus est illic de causa disputare, ubi non apparet: aut de persona aduersarij aliquid dicere, quum integra sit.
units.tr: In conjectural causes, arguments are drawn from these sources: from persons, causes, means, probabilities, signs. A sign either precedes the cause, or is within it, or follows it. Also brought forward are reports, suspicions, spoils, interrogations, informers' evidence, rumour or opinion, and many similar things which the variety of affairs supplies. From the person, as Cicero says in the speech for Cluentius: "When he was needy, extravagant, bold, cunning, treacherous," his mind began to turn to every wickedness and fraud. From the cause: "Do you not see clearly enough by what rewards, what profits, what prizes he was incited," and so on. From means, as Tullius: he had brought down from the Apennines the rough and barbarous slaves with whom he had laid waste the public forests, and the rest. From probability: "What, that which is the very head of audacity, judges, who does not know that the greatest enticement to wrongdoing is the hope of impunity?" and so on. From signs which precede the cause: the instrument, the route, and similar things. Signs which accompany it: fighting, shouting, and the like. Signs which follow it: as in poisoning, a livid bruise and swelling; in murder, a wound and blood. Reports, as Tullius: "You heard from Marcus Favonius that Clodius had said to him, and you hear, while Clodius lives, that Milo will perish. Three days later the thing was done that he had said; since he did not hesitate to reveal what he intended, can you doubt what he did?" Suspicions, as in the speech for Scaurus: "This suspicion had weight, also for this reason, that when the people of Nora were holding their ancestral rites," and the rest. Spoils, as in that line: "He would not adorn the gods with the spoils of the gods' honour; this man transferred the ornaments of the Virgin Minerva to a brothel," and similar things. Interrogations, as in: "When therefore there was a question of theft, and of that theft which he had undoubtedly committed, while he said no word about what was not asked, at once he spoke of poison," and the rest. Informers' evidence, when they are offered to the judge, or certainly as in: "An informer came to Pinea's mother, neither obscure nor uncertain." Rumour or opinion, as Cicero: "There was a double opinion: one not at odds with the status and the nature of things and of the matter."
