It seems worthwhile to be careful in enumerating all the arguments, since in these the power of wit prevails the most, and the art itself is said to proceed more from nature. But let no one suppose that the number of arguments is fixed by these categories, since they can be as many as the orator, sharpening his wit with attention, has been able to discover. Yet not every kind of cause has all the arguments. For what need is there to dispute about a cause where it does not appear, or to say anything about the opponent's person when it is untouched?

units.la: De Fine.
units.tr: On the Definitive Issue

units.la: In finitiuo statu quaeritur, ut, an sit imminuta maiestas? nam primus locus accusatoris est, quā deui nominis quaeritur, ut generalis eius sit definitio, breuis, aperta, et ex opinione hominū ducta, hoc modo: Maiestatem minuere, est de dignitate aut potestate populi Romani aliquid derogare. quae definitio ut vera probetur, multis argumentis, aut rebus, vel exemplis similibus confirmabitur. Post speciatim sa ctum eius qui accusatur describendo subiungere, ut id quod reū fecisse arguis, simile sit ei quod supra definieris. Ergo generalis definitio erit: Maiestatem minuere, est de dignitate aut potestate populi Ro. aliquid derogare. Species criminis erit, ostendere quid aduersarius specialiter fecerit, vel dixerit, ut probetur maiestas imminuta. Post loco communi confirmare, per quem facti atrocitas cum indignatione augetur. Definsoris autem locus est, aduersarij definitionem prius infirmare, si falsa ex opinione hominum, aut moribus monstrabitur. Post suam definitionem, ac si veram, ponere: quae multa argumentatione, et exemplis, similibus, confirmabitur. deinde, suscepti facti ab ipsa definitione dissimile esse ostendere: post, locum communem subijcere, per quę indigna putantur: accusatorem, non res solum, sed et verba, in periculum innocentis conuertere. Sic Cicero pro Quintio, aduersarij definitionem ex opinione hominum reprehendit: si qui unū aliquem fundū quauis ratione possideat, ipsum autem dominum patiatur cætera prædia tenere, is, inquit, ut opinor, prædium, nō bona uideatur alterius possidere. et ponit definitionē suā: Quid est, inquit, possidere? nimirum in possessione esse earum rerum, quæ possunt eo tempore possideri. Probat Nævium non bona, sed prædium possedesse: Cum domus erat, inquit, Romæ, seruiū in ipsa Gallia, priuata Publij Quinti prædia, quæ nunquā ausus es posidere. et colligit: Quòd si bona Quintij possideres, possidere omni eo in re deberes. At, si factū aduersarij tutò definire nequiueris, et verborum tuorum laqueos infirmare posse conspexeris, rem ipsam tanquam indignam, iudici demonstrabis.
units.tr: In the definitive state the question is whether the majesty of the people has been diminished. The first task of the prosecutor is to ask what the name of the charge means, and to give a general definition that is brief, clear, and drawn from common opinion, in this form: "To diminish majesty is to take something away from the dignity or power of the Roman people." To prove that this definition is true, it will be confirmed by many arguments, facts, or similar examples. Afterwards, the prosecutor describes the particular deed of the accused, and adds it, so that the act he charges the defendant with is like what he defined above. The general definition will therefore be: "To diminish majesty is to take something away from the dignity or power of the Roman people." The specific charge will be to show what the opponent did or said in particular, so that the diminution of majesty is proved. After this comes a commonplace, through which the atrocity of the deed is increased with indignation. The task of the defence is first to weaken the opponent's definition, by showing that it is false according to common opinion or custom. Afterwards, the defence sets out its own definition, as if it were true; this is confirmed by many arguments and similar examples. Then it shows that the deed in question is unlike the definition itself. Last, it adds a commonplace through which such things are judged unworthy: that the prosecutor turns into a danger to the innocent not only the facts but also the words. So Cicero, in the speech for Quinctius, criticises his opponent's definition on the basis of common opinion: "If someone," he says, "possesses some single farm by whatever title, while the owner himself allows him to hold the other estates, he seems, I think, to possess a farm, not the goods of another." And he gives his own definition: "What is it," he says, "to possess? Surely it is to be in possession of those things which can be possessed at that time." He proves that Naevius possessed not the goods but a farm: "When there was a house at Rome," he says, "a slave in Gaul itself, private estates of Publius Quinctius, which you never dared to possess." And he concludes: "But if you had possessed the goods of Quinctius, you ought to have possessed them in every respect." But if you find that you cannot safely define your opponent's deed, and see that the snares of your own words can be weakened, you will show the matter itself to the judge as unworthy.

units.la: De Qualitate.
units.tr: On Quality

units.la: In qualitate per coniecturam quaeritur, quale sit: hoc est, utrum iure factum sit, an iniuriâ?
units.tr: In the quality stage, which is decided by conjecture, the question is what sort of act it was: that is, whether it was done rightly or wrongly.

units.la: De Affectibus.
units.tr: On the Emotions

units.la: Raro affectus narrationibus interponuntur, quia non nisi grauium causarum sunt: sed ubi inferi possunt, magnum pondus rebus accommodant, dant. Cum uero aliquem affectu, hoc est, aut inuidiam, aut misericordiam, uel quid simile commouemus, formam uel speciem narrationis excedere non debemus: sed affectus qui in narratione latebit, eadem explicita reddendus erit, atque exequendus. Euenit ut sit narratio, quae inter se locos communes partiatur, quos etiam affectus uocamus: qui non erunt in ultimum, hoc est, post narrationē differendi. Sed haec narratio grauissimi criminis erit, in qua cum se primum assectus obtulerint, statim interponendi sunt. Neque enim possunt simul omnes post narrationem reddi ut est: Praedonum dux Heracleo repente praeter spem classem pulcherrimam populi Romani, quum primum inuesperasceret, inflammari incedió, iussit. ac mox interponit affectum: O tempus miserum atq; acerbum prouinciae Siciliae, O casum illum multis innocentibus calamitosum. Ad narrationem redit: Affertur, inquit, nocte intempesta grauis huiusce mali nuncius Syracusas. Rursum, dum narrat excedit. Quo neq; Atheniensium, inquit, gloriosissimae classes cum mari plurimum poterant, & reliqua. Rursum, ad narrationem redit: Eo ne, inquit, pirata penetrabit, quo simul atq; adisset, non modo à latere, sed & a tergo, magnam partem urbis relinquebat. Rursum excedit: Siculos ne milites, ara-torum.
units.tr: Emotions are rarely inserted into narrations, because they belong only to weighty cases; but where they can be introduced, they give great weight to the matter. When we stir up some emotion, that is, indignation, pity, or something similar, we ought not to go beyond the form or appearance of the narration; rather, the emotion that lies hidden in the narration must be rendered and carried out as if it were openly stated. It happens that a narration divides its commonplaces among its parts, which we also call emotions; these are not to be deferred to the end, that is, until after the narration. But such a narration will concern a most grave crime, in which, as soon as the emotions present themselves, they must be inserted at once. For they cannot all be rendered together after the narration, as it stands. The leader of the pirates, Heracleo, suddenly, beyond all expectation, when it was just growing dark, ordered the most splendid fleet of the Roman people to be set on fire. Then he inserts the emotion: "O wretched and bitter time for the province of Sicily! O that disaster, calamitous for so many innocent people!" He returns to the narration: "A report of this grievous calamity," he says, "is brought to Syracuse in the dead of night." Again, while narrating, he digresses: "Where neither the most glorious fleets of the Athenians, when they had the greatest power at sea," and so on. Again he returns to the narration: "Where the pirate," he says, "would make his way, and as soon as he had arrived there, he left a large part of the city not only exposed at its side but also at its back." Again he digresses: "Will he not take the Sicilian soldiers, the ploughmen, the children, whose fathers had ploughed up so much grain by their labour that it sufficed for the Roman people and for all Italy?" And again he digresses in another way: "and a wretched and most bitter spectacle, that the glory of the city has become a mockery." He returns to the narration: "After the pirates had come out of the harbour," he says...

units.la: {y} (page ends) torum ne liberos, quorum patres tantum labore suo frumenti exararant, ut populo Romano rotiq; Italiae sufficeret? Et item aliter excedit: & spectaculum miserum atq; acerrimum, ludibrio esse urbis gloriam. Ad narrationem redit: Postquam e portu, inquit, piratae non metu aliquo adfecti, sed satietate exierunt, & reliqua. Pleriq; nuda argumenta posuerunt, affectus ve-rò perorationibus, hoc est epilogis reseruarūt. Scire autem nos debemus, affectus qui ex quaestionibus nascuntur, statim ut propositioni responsuri sumus, esse reddendos. Alibi enim quàm ubi nati sunt, interponi, uel augeri non possunt, ut est: Ad uadimonium non uenit Quintius. Et statim interponit affectum, antequam quaestioni respondeat: Si res ista, inquit, ꝟ. auisima sua sponte uideretur, tamen necessitudinis nomine leuaret, & reliqua talia sunt. Affectus autem qui de omni causa nascuntur, perorationibus reseruābuntur. Omnis pene argumentatio, moralem disputationem recipit: sed non omnis affectu. Moralis argumentatio, de natura hominum, uel morum consuetudine ducitur. ut Cicero: Hic ego dubitem in eam disputationem ingredi, quae ducātur ex natura hominum, atq; omnium sensibus, & omnia quae sequuntur. Ergo, sicut argumentatio illa melior crit, quae moralis fuerit: sic per-oraorationes affectus fiunt meliores. Cicero sane per omnem orationem, affectum inserit. Nam odio Clodij iudices turbat, euerfurü fuisse remp. sed prius Milone, qui obstabat, occiso. Affectus nanq; hi sunt, ira, odium, misericordia, liuor, metus, spes. odium, siue ira, exante actæ uitæ facinoribus colligitur: quorum commemoratio ad hoc fit in iudicio, non ut exinde nasci causa uideatur, sed ut odiosa uita hominis comprobetur. ut Cicero, qui flagitia Clodij superioris uitæ retexuit: Cuius nefandum, inquit, adulterium in publicis uinaribus, sanctissimæ fœminæ comprehenderunt, cum: cuius supplicio senatus solemnes religiones expiandas sæpe censuit: eum, quem cum sorore germana nefandum stuprum fecisse, eque sequuntur. Iram cum odio, quum multa crimina congerimus, ut Cicero: Non furem, sed erepto-rem: non adulterum, sed expugnatorem pudicitiæ, et reliqua, quod in principijs sæpius irritatur. Miserocordiâ mouemus, si ab ijs nos impugnari dicimus, quorum auxilio tuti esse deberemus: ut Cicero pro Oppio. Vel quum alicuius calamitates commemoramus: quùm magnitudinem periculi ostendimus, sicuti pro Cornelio Cicero. Liuorem autem simul cum odio, ut Caluus in Vatinium, quum dicit: Hominem nostræ ciuitatis audacissimū, de factione diuitem, sordidū, malcmaledicum accuso. nam & diuitiæ de factione quæsitæ, interpositæ sunt, ut his iudices inuiderent. Metum facere Cicero tentat in Verrem, quum ait: Quis hoc non perspicit, præclarè nobiscum actum iri, si populus Romanus istius unius supplicio contemptus fuerit? & quæ sequuntur. Non est, inquit, in hoc peccandi locus iudices. Confirmat enim aliis iudicibus dānari Verrem, & senatum iudicandi potestatem amissurū. Ad spem redit in eodem loco: Adduxi enim hominem, in quo reconciliarem existimationem iudiciorum amissam: redire in gratiam cum populo Romano, satisfacere exteris nationibus possetis. de quo si uerè ac religiose iudicaueritis, auctoritas ea quæ in uobis remanere debet, hærebit. Contrà dicenda erūt, ne specie miserationis, ne ira deducantur à fide, aut de odio. Vt Cicero pro Cœlio, quum dicit, in quondam odiū fit iniustum uocatus: Vel de liuore, agere tanquā apud maleuolos: de timore, loqui tanquam apud timidos: de spe, quum uana spe solicitare iudices uelint. Affectus sibi aliquotiens uicini sunt: ut, cum misericordia mouetur, statim & odiū concitatur. aut ubi utrunq; non est, alterum tamen commouetur: aut liuore excitatur, si tamen appareat: aut spe animus iudicis solicitabitur: qui tamen affectus certam sedem non habent. nam per totam orationem spargendi sunt. Cicero miſericordiam mouet, quum ait: Patres ij quos uidetis, iacebant in limine, matresq; miserae perno ſtabant ad hostium carceris. Ad iram redit, cum ſubijcit: Aderat ianitor carceris, carnifex praetoris, mors terrorq; sociorum. Item, ad misericordiam redit: Non uita liberum, sed mortis celeritatem precio redimere cogebantur parětes. Rursum odium mouet: Lætaris tu in omniu gemitu, & triumphas. Metum quoq; miscet: Quo confugient socij? Affectus tunc maiore gratiam habent, si ex ijs moueant, quae iam probata sunt. Affectus ex his trahitur: à re, à persona, à loco, à causa, à tempore, à signis, à facultatibus, à toto ad partes, à partibus ad totum, à contrario, à minori ad maius, à maiori ad minus, à simili, et à barbaris gentibus, & à bestijs & in animalib. ducitur, & de caeteris locis unde & argumenta sumuntur. Nec te moueat, quòd hinc & argumenta duci supra retulerim: siquidē illa omnino circūstantia, unde ad conuincendum reum argumenta sumuntur: inde etiam posquā crimen prouocaueris, affectus cōmouentur. Ante omnia illud cōsiderandum est, ut quum aliqua res natura sui grauis fuerit, ipsa tantū sola, inuidiā moueamus ne aliquas rationes alias adferendo, res, quae per se gravis est, dubia uideatur: quae nonnunquā so-larc. la repetitione augetur. ut illud est: Matrē tuam cæcidisti, repeto affectum, quum irascendum dico ei qui hominem occidit. A persona, dum queror magis, esse iugulatum. A causa, dum officio in Romano populo uincitur. A loco, quū dico, in foro. A tempore, quum dico, luce, palam. A signis, ut Cicero: Te prætore Siculi milites palmarum stirpibus, piratæ Siculo frumento alebantur. A toto ad partes: Inuidia facta est, Rempp. uniuersam petis, et ad partes descendit: Templa deorum immortalium, tecta urbis, uita omnium ciuium, Italiam totam, ad exitium et uastitatem uocas. A parte ad totum: Vbi unus, puta, ciuis laesus, tota respublica laesa dicatur, ut est: Non tu hoc loco Gauiū, non unum hominē nescio quem, sed communem libertatem in crucem egisti. A facultatibus: Cleomenes huius libidini nec aduersari poterat, nec audebat: erat enim prætor, qui maximam habebat potestatem. Inde Tullius transit inuidiam. à contrario misericordiam mouet Cicero, quum dicit: Forteis et animosos, et se acriter ipsos morti offerentes seruari cupimus: eorumq; nos miseret, qui nostrā misericordiam requirunt. Item à contrario: Si qui deos colant, laudantur, sacrilegi puniendi sunt. A pari: Qui parentes contemnit, et deos negligit. A consequenti: Qui semel deliquit, semper maiora conatur. A repugnanti, ut Cicero de Antonio: Animam suum sceleratum esse fatebatur, poena adsectum querebatur. A minori ad maius: Servi mehercule mei, si me isto pacto metuerent, quo te metuunt omnes cives tui, domum meam relinquendam putarem: tu tibi urbem non arbitraris? A maiore ad minus: Quo neq; Atheniensium gloriosissimæ classes, cum mari plurimum potuerunt, bellis sæpe conatæ, nunquam aspirare potuerunt, eo ne te prætore, pirata penetrauit? A simili: Eryphilam accepimus in fabulis ea cupiditate, ut quum uidisset monile, ut opinor, ex auro et gemmis, pulchritudine eius incensa, salutem uiri proderet: similis est, inquit, istius cupiditas. A barbaris gentibus: Si tu apud Persas, aut extrema India deprehensus Verres ad supplicium duceretur, quid aliud clamares, nisi te civem esse Romanum? et tibi ignoto apud ignotos, apud barbaros in extremis atq; ultimis gentibus positos, et reliqua. Item a bestiis et inanimalibus. Vt Cicero: Denique, si non ad homines, verum ad bestias, aut etiam (ut longius progrediar) si in aliqua desertissima solitudine, ad saxa et ad scopulos hæc conqueri ac deplorare vellem, tamen omnia muta, atque inanimalia tanta tam indigna rerum acerbitate moverentur. Affectus hactenus crescunt, ut quum eum qui sit cacæsus, occisum: qui sit improbus, latronem nominemus. Si extollendum aliquid fuerit, ampliora uerba ponenda sunt cum ipsis nominibus. ut Cicero: Non furem, sed creptorem: non adulterum, sed expugnatorem pudicitiæ: nō sacrilegum, sed hostem sacrorum religionumq;: nō sicarium, sed crudelissimum carnificem ciuium sociorumq;, in uestrum iudicium adduximus. Item crescit affectus, ut quum unum crimen sit sententiæ, hic uerba unum significantia, acervo quodam congeruntur. ut est: Quid enim tuus ille Tubero districtus in acie Pharsalica gladius agebat? cuius latus mucro ille petebat? qui sensus erat armorum tuorum? quæ tua mens, oculi, manus, ardor animi? quid cupiebas? quid optabas? Ergo alibi congeries multorum criminum enumeratio est, hic unius, uerbis facta multiplicatio. Similiter, aderat ianitor carceris, carnifex prætoris, mors terror que sociorum et ciuium Romanorum, lictor Sestius. Affectus tanto plus valet, quanto uerbis firmioribus extollitur. In argumentis enim enucleata diligentia, in affectibus grandiloquium quæritur. Sunt etiam alij loci communes, qui magis ad causam ex periculi magnitudine, non ex causæ genere ducuntur: quæ tamen non re per totam causam, sed in omne genus causæ incidunt. Citò tamen principijs aptantur, ut mifericordiam captent: quum aut aduersariorum calumnias, factiones, solitudinem suscepti, uel cetera eius infortunia memoramus. ut pro Varenno: Amici deficiunt, cognati deserunt. Et rei aut accusatorum calumniam prodimus, ut in eodem loco: In inimicissima ciuitate urgent, instant, insequuntur: studio, multitudine, pecunia, periurio pugnant. Contrà species minuendi haec est: ut eū qui pulsauit, tetigisse: qui uulnerauit, laesisse dicamus. ut Cicero: Vulnus quod acu punctum uideretur: Item, uxores suas à coena redeuntes attrectatas esse. nanq; affectus nisi uim animi habeat, nullus est: nec proderit inuentus. ut Cicero de eodē: Vt dolere, ut flere, ut ardere uideamur.
units.tr: ...the sons of the ploughmen, whose fathers had by their own labour tilled so much grain that it sufficed for the Roman people and all of Italy? Then he digresses again: "and a sight most wretched and most bitter, that the glory of the city should be made a mockery." He returns to the narrative: "After the pirates left the harbour, not moved by any fear but by satiety," and so on. Most writers have set out the bare arguments and reserved the emotions for the peroration, that is, the epilogue. We should know, however, that emotions arising from the questions should be given as soon as we are about to answer the proposition. For they cannot be inserted or intensified anywhere other than where they arise, as in: "Quintius did not come to the bail-hearing." And at once he inserts the emotion before he answers the question: "If that matter, most unwelcome as it is, were to appear in its own right, yet it would be lightened by the name of kinship," and the rest are of this kind. Emotions, however, that arise from the whole cause will be reserved for the perorations. Almost every argument admits of moral discussion, but not every one admits of emotion. Moral argument is drawn from the nature of men or from the customs of their conduct, as in Cicero: "Shall I hesitate to enter upon that discussion which is drawn from the nature of men and the feelings of all, and all the things that follow from them?" Therefore, just as that argument will be better which is moral, so the emotions in perorations become better. Cicero, to be sure, inserts emotion throughout the whole speech. For by Clodius' hatred he disturbs the judges, and that the state had been overturned, but first, after Milo, who was in the way, had been killed. The emotions are these: anger, hatred, pity, envy, fear, hope. Hatred or anger is gathered from the crimes of a man's earlier life; the recollection of these is made in court not so that the cause may seem to arise from them, but so that the hateful life of the man may be proved. As Cicero, who unravelled the disgraceful acts of Clodius' earlier life: "whose unspeakable adultery, they say, in public baths, the most holy women caught; for whose punishment the senate often decreed solemn rites of expiation; the man who, they say, committed an unspeakable rape with his own sister," and so on. We stir anger together with hatred when we pile up many charges, as Cicero: "not a thief but a plunderer, not an adulterer but a violator of chastity," and the rest, which is repeatedly inflamed at the beginnings. We move pity if we say we are attacked by those by whose help we ought to be safe, as Cicero in the case of Oppius; or when we recall someone's misfortunes, as when we show the magnitude of danger, as Cicero does for Cornelius. Envy, together with hatred, as Calvus against Vatinius, when he says: "I accuse a man of our state most reckless, rich from faction, filthy, a wicked slanderer; for both riches gained by faction are added, so that the judges might envy him." Cicero attempts to cause fear against Verres when he says: "Who does not see that we shall have done splendidly if the Roman people has been despised in the punishment of this one man?" and what follows. "There is no room for sin here, judges," he says. For he confirms that Verres is to be condemned by the other judges, and that the senate will lose the power of judging. He returns to hope in the same place: "For I have brought a man through whom you could restore the lost esteem of the courts, be reconciled with the Roman people, and satisfy foreign nations. If you judge him truly and conscientiously, that authority which ought to remain in you will cling to you." Things must be said against these, so that the judges are not led from their trust by a show of compassion or by anger or hatred. As Cicero for Caelius, when he says: "he is called unjustly into a hatred of the past." Or speak about envy as though before malicious men; about fear, speak as though before the timid; about hope, when they wish to disturb the judges with empty hope. The emotions are sometimes close to one another: so that when pity is stirred, hatred is at once aroused as well; or where neither is present, another is nevertheless stirred; or the mind is excited by envy, if it is evident; or the mind of the judge will be disturbed by hope. Yet these emotions have no fixed seat; they must be scattered through the whole speech. Cicero stirs pity when he says: "The fathers whom you see were lying on the threshold, and the wretched mothers stood at the gate of the prison." He returns to anger when he adds: "The gaoler was present, the praetor's executioner, the death and terror of our allies." Again, he returns to pity: "The parents were forced to buy not the life of their children but the speed of their death." Again he stirs hatred: "You rejoice in all this groaning and triumph." He also mixes in fear: "Where will the allies flee?" Emotions have greater grace when they move from things already proved. Emotions are drawn from these: from the thing, from the person, from the place, from the cause, from the time, from signs, from means, from the whole to the parts, from the parts to the whole, from the contrary, from the less to the greater, from the greater to the less, from the like, and from barbarian peoples, and from beasts, and they are drawn from inanimate things, and from the other topics from which arguments are also taken. Do not be troubled that I have above stated that arguments are drawn from these same sources; for those very circumstances from which arguments are taken to convict the defendant are also the source from which, once you have called up the charge, the emotions are moved. Above all this must be considered: when some matter is by its nature weighty, we should stir up odium by that thing alone, and not by adducing other reasons, lest the matter which is weighty in itself seem doubtful; this is sometimes increased by repetition, as in: "You killed your mother," I repeat the emotion, when I say that one must be angry with the man who kills a human being. From the person, while I complain more that he was butchered. From the cause, when he is convicted in his duty to the Roman people. From the place, when I say: in the forum. From the time, when I say: in daylight, openly. From signs, as Cicero: "When you were praetor, the Sicilian soldiers were fed on palm stems, the pirates on Sicilian grain." From the whole to the parts: "It was an outrage; you attack the whole commonwealth," and he descends to the parts: "the temples of the immortal gods, the houses of the city, the lives of all the citizens, all Italy, you summon to ruin and devastation." From a part to the whole: where one citizen, say, is wronged, the whole commonwealth is said to be wronged, as in: "Here you have crucified not Gavius, not some single man, but common liberty." From means: "Cleomenes could neither oppose this lust nor dared to; for he was praetor, who had the greatest power." Then Tullius passes on from envy. From the contrary Cicero stirs pity when he says: "We wish the brave and spirited, who offer themselves fiercely to death, to be saved; and we pity those who demand our pity." Likewise from the contrary: "If some worship the gods, they are praised; sacrilegious persons must be punished." From the like: "He who despises parents and neglects the gods." From the consequent: "He who has once offended always attempts greater things." From the contradictory, as Cicero of Antonius: "He confessed that his soul was wicked, yet complained that he was subjected to punishment." From the less to the greater: "My slaves, by Hercules, if they feared me in the way that all your citizens fear you, I would think I must leave my house; and you do not think you should leave the city?" From the greater to the less: "Where neither the most glorious fleets of the Athenians, when they were most powerful at sea, though often attempted in wars, could ever breathe, there under your praetorship did the pirate penetrate?" From the like: "We have heard in the fables of Eriphyle, with that greed, that when she had seen a necklace, I suppose of gold and gems, her passion kindled by its beauty, she betrayed her husband's safety: such, he says, is the greed of that man." From barbarian peoples: "If Verres had been caught among the Persians or in farthest India and were being led to punishment, what else would you cry out than that you are a Roman citizen? And you, unknown among the unknown, placed among barbarians in the furthest and remotest nations," and so on. Likewise from beasts and from inanimate things. As Cicero: "Finally, if I wished to complain and lament these things not to men but to beasts, or even (to go further) in some most deserted wilderness, to rocks and crags, yet all dumb and inanimate things would be moved by so great and so undeserved a bitterness of events." Emotions grow in this way: when we call one who has been beaten 'killed', and one who is wicked 'a robber'. If something is to be magnified, larger words must be placed alongside the names themselves, as Cicero: "We have brought before your judgment not a thief but a plunderer, not an adulterer but a violator of chastity, not a sacrilegious man but an enemy of sacred rites and religion, not an assassin but the most cruel executioner of citizens and allies." Likewise the emotion grows when, although there is one charge for the sentence, words signifying one thing are heaped up in a sort of pile, as in: "For what was that sword of your Tubero doing, drawn in the battle of Pharsalus? At whose side was that point aimed? What was the purpose of your arms? What was your mind, your eyes, your hand, the heat of your spirit? What were you desiring? What were you wishing for?" Thus elsewhere the enumeration of many crimes is a heaping up; here it is a multiplication of one by words. Similarly: the gaoler of the prison was present, the praetor's executioner, the death and terror of the allies and Roman citizens, the lictor Sestius. An emotion is worth so much the more as it is raised with firmer words. For in arguments a carefully polished precision is sought; in emotions, a grand and lofty eloquence. There are also other common topics which are drawn less from the kind of cause than from the magnitude of the danger to the cause; these do not belong to the whole cause but fall into every kind of cause. They are, however, quickly fitted to the beginnings, to win pity; when we recall either the calumnies, factions, or solitude of the accused, or his other misfortunes. As in the speech for Varenus: "Friends fail, kinsmen desert." And we expose the calumny of the accused or of the accusers, as in the same place: "They press, insist, pursue in the most hostile state: they fight with zeal, numbers, money, and perjury." On the contrary, this is the way of diminishing: we say that the one who struck has merely touched, and the one who wounded has merely injured; as Cicero: "A wound which seemed to have been pricked with a needle." Likewise, that their wives, returning from dinner, were handled. For an emotion, unless it has force of mind, is nothing, and an invented one will not profit. As Cicero of the same man: "that we seem to grieve, to weep, to burn."

units.tr: On Epilogues.

units.la: Epilogos de omni causa reperies, & maxime quae misericordiam mouere posse conspexeris: qui tamen erunt breues, nec diu profequedi. nam lachrymis comparati sunt, quibus nihil citius arefcit. Scire autem debes, in omnib. fere officijs caput esse artis, decere quod facias. Horum praeterea natura praeceptorum est, ut etiam obesse uideantur, si mediocriter nota sint: quae tunc infinitum prodeerunt, si animo frequenti usu sculpta permanserint.
units.tr: You will find epilogues for every kind of case, especially for those you see can stir pity. They should be brief, however, and not drawn out at length, for they are designed for tears, and nothing dries up more quickly than tears. You should also know that in nearly all duties the essence of the art is to do what is fitting. Moreover, the nature of these precepts is such that they may even seem harmful if they are only moderately known, but they will be of infinite benefit if they remain engraved in the mind through frequent practice.
